about: YOUR WRITING - every text slot in the game has a key (the panel shows [write: key] where there's none yet). Add an entry for a key to give it your text; options and outcomes take keys too. The game never writes story text itself.

entries.text: The king's toll
The toll man comes down to the boat with his tally stick. The king's tenth is taken on what you sell here, and he asks what you carry.
A new hull. The king's tenth is taken on what you sell here, when you sell it. What I look for now is what may not leave the realm at all. Name what is in her.
The same hull. Name what is in her, as you did before.
You hid nothing last time. I looked.
That was a kind thought, last time. I have forgotten it, as a man in my place must.
Last time you showed me a skin with a seal on it. It was good. I had it read to me twice, in case it was not.
Last time there was more under your ballast than ballast. I tap everything of yours now. Stand back from the boards.
You know the law. No mail coat leaves the realm, and no Christian is sold out of it. I say it to every hull, so that none can say he was not told.

The emperor's law since Thionville: no swords and no mail to the east or the north, but through the king's posts. What is found is forfeit, half to the palace and half to the man who finds it. I am the man who finds it.
She sits deep. Name what is in her, from the stern forward.
Empty. Then there is nothing to toll until you sell, and nothing to talk about either.
Declare the cargo
Hide the swords under the ballast
Give him something (12 d)
Show the charter
Sea-stone
A bead-maker sits in a litter of yellow chips, sorting a sack of raw amber into what he can use and what he was cheated with. The second heap is the larger.
This came through three hands before mine. Each hand kept a little and called it weight.
It comes from the Ests. Seven days east of Sliesthorp if the wind holds, the Wends' land on your right hand the whole way, then a river mouth, then a lake. So I am told. I make beads.
They pick it up off the beach after the autumn gales. The old story is that they were surprised anyone paid for it. Somebody has been telling them since.
Is that sea-stone in your boat? Bring it here. I want to see how badly you were cheated, and by whom, because it may have been my cousin.
They have a tongue of their own that nobody learns. But there are Danes on that beach with scales, and Norse will serve you as far as the scales go.
Sit by his bench for the afternoon and watch how he tells good from bad
Buy a sack of his raw amber and have him sort it in front of you
Ask what he would pay for amber brought straight from the lake

He rubs a lump on his sleeve and holds it over the sweepings: chaff jumps to it. He drops a handful in a bowl of brine: the amber floats, the stone and the glass go down. He puts a piece to your lip. Amber is warm. Glass is cold. That is the whole of it, he says, and it took him six years.

He tips your sack out and sorts it as he talks: sleeve, brine, lip. A fifth of it goes on the floor. He does not give the silver back for the fifth. He says you have just bought the cheapest thing he sells, and he does not mean the amber.
Six sacks, he says, clean, inside eight moons. Half as much again as the market gives. He does not offer to tell you how to know clean from dirty, and you did not ask.
A wake on the lake

The beach at Truso is full of boats and nobody is selling. Up in the fort they are drinking, and by the sound they have been at it some time. A Dane with a pair of folding scales in his belt comes down to see who you are.
You have come to a wake. The king of this fort is dead and he is still in his house. He will be there a good while yet. A small man lies a month before they burn him. A king, half a year sometimes.
Until he burns, the king's store is shut, and the king's store is where the amber is. His kin drink and play away what he owned. What you see sold on the beach is gleanings.
And do not go looking for a greater king to complain to. Every fort in this land has its own, and no two of them are friends.
A bead-maker sent you. Seven days, he said? He has never made the passage. He is right, mind. It annoys me.
A stranger at a wake drinks. Then we see what he is.
He will hold out two bowls. Mind which. Here the king and the rich men drink mares' milk. Mead is for the poor and the slaves. And nobody on this shore brews ale. They have never tasted it.
Take the mares' milk, and keep your face still
Take the mead: it is what you know
Send to the boat for the last of your own ale and pour it for them
It is thin and sour and it bites the tongue. You drink all of it. The steward watches your face the whole way down, finds nothing there, and seats you at the upper end, among men who own horses.

The mead is good. They seat you at the lower end, by the door, among men with sand in the seams of their clothes. By the third bowl you understand, without a word in common, that these are the ones who pick the amber up.

Your crew watch their ale go up the hill. The dead king's brother drinks, waits, and drinks again. He asks, through the Dane, what it is made of. Barley. He says they feed that to horses. Then he holds the bowl out to be filled.
The cold house
They take you in to see the dead king. He lies on a bench in his own house, dressed, his weapons beside him, and the room is as cold as the bottom of a well. Your breath shows. His does not.
Ten weeks dead. Smell. Nothing. There is one kin among them that can make cold, and they are sent for when a great man dies.
I have seen her set down two bowls, one of water and one of mead, and both were skinned with ice by morning. Summer or winter. She does not care which.
Go and stand outside a moment. Feel the sun on your neck. Then come back in and tell me how it is done, because I have been here twelve winters and I cannot.
The Dane wants to know how. The Dane always wants to know how.
You drank the milk, so you may stand at his head. That is a place. Do not waste it by touching anything.
Those along the wall are his goods. There is less each day: it goes in drink and on the gaming board. Lay something by him if you like. It will be drunk or ridden for with the rest.
Lay silver at the dead man's feet, as his own people do
Ask the woman, through the Dane, how the cold is made
Stand where you are told and keep your hands to yourself
You weigh out fifteen pennies' worth and lay it by his feet. Nobody thanks you. The old woman looks at the silver, then at you, for about as long as it takes to count a stranger.

She lifts a board under the bench. Below is a pit lined with moss and straw and packed with lake ice, cut at midwinter, grey and hard as stone. That is half, the Dane says for her. She puts the board back. The other half is in a pot she does not open.
She says something short. The Dane does not put it into Norse. After that you are given a place by the door, where it is warmer, and where you can see nothing.
You stand and count. A heap of raw amber. Marten skins tied in forties. A sword. Silver cut small. A bridle with silver on it. A kettle. The Dane says there were two more heaps at the last moon.
Three heaps
A woman has spread a cloth on the shingle: yellow lumps in three heaps, wetted so they shine. She names one price for all of it. The Dane holds his scales and looks at the lake.
Sea-stone. West shore, after the storm. All good. Weigh it, Dane.
I weigh. I do not say what is on the pan. That is how a Dane keeps a house on this beach, and she knows I keep to it.
They say the Ests do not know what the stuff is worth. That was true in somebody's grandfather's time. Now they know to the grain what a stranger does not know.
You pick it up like a man who has sat at a bead-maker's bench. Good. Then this is a fair fight, and I shall enjoy it.
One word for nothing, because I liked how you tied up your boat. Half the trade here is knowing what is in the heap.
The men you drank mead with are down the shore, picking over last night's weed. They sell too. Not so prettily laid out. I did not tell you that.
Test it piece by piece: sleeve, brine and lip
Buy by the look of it
Buy nothing. Ask her to show you what she would not buy herself
Go round her: the men from the low bench sell on the shore itself

A third of her middle heap is pine resin boiled hard, and two fine pieces are yellow glass, cold on the lip. She watches you find each one. Then she laughs, sweeps them into her apron, and fills four sacks with true stone at the price she named for the false.
You point at the dullest heap because the shiny ones look too willing. She stops smiling. Four sacks, and all of it draws chaff when the Dane, who cannot help himself, rubs a piece on his sleeve.

On the boat you try a piece on your tongue and it tastes of a pine wood. Resin, most of it, and some glass. One sack in four is true. When you go back she shows you, kindly, how you could have known: sleeve, brine, lip. She does not give back the silver.

She is delighted. She rubs, she floats, she holds pieces to your lip like a mother feeding a child, and names each thing in her own tongue until you can say it. You leave with empty hands and a morning's worth of her words.

Down the shore three men are raking weed with forked sticks. They sell as it comes, sand and all: nobody has had time to cheat with it. Five sacks. The woman on the cloth watches you carry them past and says one word, which you do not yet know.
Every tongue burns
A Frisian from the Weser mouth has died of a fever in the Dane's guest house, a very long way from a priest. His son comes to you because you are the only other baptised skipper on the lake.
They say he must be burned. Every man who dies here is burned, whatever tongue he spoke. And if one bone of him is found unburnt, there is a great atonement to pay.
He was baptised. He wanted to lie in earth and get up out of it on the last day. I promised him earth. I did not know then what I was promising.
It is their law, and it is my house he died in. If a bone of him turns up whole, I am the one who pays, and it would buy that boat of yours twice. I like the boy. I like my house more.
The fire is no shame. We give it to kings.
If you mean to row a dead man down the lake tonight, do not tell me. And know that the fishermen here do not sleep, and they count boats.
Take the body out by night and bury him in the sand of the spit, by the sea
Stand by the son at their fire, and say the prayers you know
Pay the atonement beforehand, so that nobody rakes the ash too closely

Down the lake with muffled oars, out by the river, and onto the long spit before light. You dig above the weed line and tie two pieces of driftwood for a cross. The son gives you what his father had on him, and a riddle the old man was fond of, about a thing that was water and will be water again.

A fishing boat lies across the river mouth, and then three. Nobody is struck. The dead man goes back up the lake and burns next day with everyone watching. Your share of what the Dane must pay is sixty pennies' weight. The son says you tried, and means it.

The Ests burn him well, with his knife and his cloak, as they would one of their own. You say the Our Father and the Creed, the son says them after you, and your crew stand a long way back. Afterwards the women rake the ash for bone and find none. The steward nods to you as to a man who can be taken places.

The steward weighs your silver, and the women who rake the ash rake it quickly. One small bone goes home to the Weser inside the son's shirt, to lie in earth. He gives you his father's riddle for thanks: a thing that was water and will be water again.
The day is named
The king will be burned at the second new moon from now. The steward has begun to divide what is left of his goods into five heaps, and the fort has begun to talk about horses.

On the day, they lay his goods along the road in heaps. The biggest a mile from the fort, the next nearer, the smallest by the gate. The riders start five or six miles out. First horse to the far heap takes it, and so on inward.
Anyone may ride. Strangers too. That is why a fast horse costs more on this shore than anything else with legs, and why the Wends keep their good ones at home.
The far heap is sea-stone, marten, and his silver. Tell your friend. He looks like a man who counts.
The barley drink. Bring more for my brother's burning. Bring someone who knows how it is made.
He means it. Nobody brews here. Honey is cheap and barley is horse feed. A woman from the west who can brew would be a wonder, and wonders are well paid at a burning.
Two moons. Time enough to see Sliesthorp and be back, if you do not stop to argue with anyone on the way.
Say you will be back with a horse
Say you will be back with ale and a woman who can brew it
Say only that you will be there

The steward holds up one finger, then two: one horse, twice the price. The Dane says that is his opening, and that a horse which has stood seven days in a boat should be walked a week before anyone sits on it.
The king's brother has the Dane say it twice so there is no mistake: malt, six sacks, at double, and the woman. He has no word for malt. He says the barley before it is the drink.
The steward shrugs, then thinks better of it and asks for cloth: four bolts of the Frisian stuff, for cloaks at the burning. He will pay over the market for it. A wake uses up cloaks.
The grey and the brew-wife

Behind the landing a Jute is walking a string of horses, one of them a lean grey that the others give room to. Next door is an alehouse where the ale is good and the woman who makes it is not pleased with her life.
The grey. Do not look at the others, they pull carts. He was bred on the heath and nothing has passed him yet. I have stopped racing him. Nobody will bet.
For the Ests? Then you know why I am not ashamed of the price. Sell him there on the morning of a burning and you could buy my whole string and me with it.
He has never been in a boat. Lay him down on straw, tie a cloth over his eyes, and put a man at his head who is not afraid of him. If the man is afraid, the horse will know before the man does.
A whole people that has never tasted ale. And a king who pays. I have brewed in my husband's brother's house since my husband died, and he drinks the profit. I can be in your boat tonight.
I want malt of my own choosing and a cauldron that has never had fish in it. And a share. Not a wage. A share.
East? There is nothing east but Wends and honey. Drink up. If you ever find a place that wants a brew-wife and has no brother-in-law in it, come and tell me.
Buy the grey at his price
Take the brew-wife east, for a share
Take both: the horse in the bottom of the boat and the woman on top of the malt
Not now

Two hundred and forty pennies, which is two horses. He goes into the boat sideways, on straw, blindfold, with your steadiest man at his head. The Jute watches from the bank and says he will miss the horse and not the argument.

She comes down at dusk with a cauldron, two sacks of malt she has smelt every handful of, a bundle of bog myrtle, and nothing else. She does not look back at the house. She sits on the malt and asks which way is east.

The horse lies in the bottom on straw with a cloth over his eyes. The brew-wife sits on her malt above him and tells him he is a fool to be afraid of water. By the second day he will take barley from her hand and from nobody else's.
You look at the grey a while. The Jute lets you look. The moon is getting on, he says, and so is the horse.
The gate on the water

The Wends' land has lain to one side of you for three days. Now a long low boat puts out from it with more oars than you have men, and a man in her bow holds up an open hand, which may mean peace and may mean five.
This water has a lord. The lord has a gate. I am the gate.
Swear on the water that you carry nothing for the king of the Danes. Then give what a guest gives, or do not. I remember both kinds.
A horse. In a boat. Going east. I know where that horse is going, Frisian, and I know what he is worth there. Be glad I am an honest gate.
Sea-stone from the Ests. They kept you waiting, I can see it in your beard. They keep everyone waiting. It is the only thing they have plenty of besides honey.
Heave to and swear on the water, as he asks
Heave to, swear, and give a guest's gift for his peace this season
Keep the sail full and do not stop

You put your hand in the sea over the side and say you carry nothing for any king. He watches the hand, not your face. Then he drinks a cup of whatever you have, makes no remark on it, and lets go your gunwale. It has cost the afternoon.

You swear, and weigh him fifteen pennies' worth. He weighs it again on scales of his own. Then a crock of honey comes back over the gunwale, because a guest's gift is answered. Until the leaves fall, he says, his boats will know yours.

The wind is on your side of the argument. Their oars keep pace for as long as a man can hold his breath, and then they do not. The man in the bow lowers his hand. He does not look angry. He looks like someone making a note.

The wind drops behind the point, and oars do not need wind. He comes over your side, takes his gift himself, and counts generously. Forty pennies' weight. Next time, he says, swear first. It is cheaper, and the water likes it.
The mile

The heaps are out along the road: the smallest by the gate, the largest a mile off where the road tops the rise. Five miles beyond that, every fast horse in the land is being walked in circles. The dead king is still in his house. He goes to the fire when the last heap is taken.
First to the far heap takes it, the next takes the next. The man who comes last to the gate heap gets a cloak and a kettle and is laughed at until spring.
By tonight he will own his weapons and the clothes he lies in, and those burn with him. They think it a clean way to finish. Twelve winters here, and I have come round to it.
A stranger may ride. A stranger may win. A stranger may not complain.
Your horse has been looked at by everyone who matters. Two of them asked me his price. I said you had not come seven days in an open boat to sell.
Her ale has been working three days in my storehouse and it smells right. She says if one more of the king's kin opens that door to look, she is going home.
You brought yourself. Well. Somebody has to stand at the gate and say afterwards who was first.
While they ride, nobody watches the near heaps but the dead man's women. Do not let me see you think it. A thief at a burning pays more than silver, and so does the man whose guest he is.
Ride for the far heap
Have the ale carried up to the fire
Stand at the gate with the Dane and watch
While every eye is on the road, lift what you can from the near heaps and be on the lake by dark

You remember very little of five miles. A ditch. Somebody's elbow. The horse deciding, somewhere past the second heap, that he did not care to see another horse's tail. Then the rise, and a heap of amber and marten and cut silver with a bridle on top, and nobody there before you.

He runs like a horse that has spent seven days lying in a boat: well, and a little late. Three are past the rise before you. You pull up at the heap by the second ditch, which is a sack of sea-stone and some good cloth, ahead of two kings' sons. Nobody laughs.

The cask goes up to the fire on a pole between two of the king's kin. The brew-wife walks behind it with her ladle like a priest with a cross. By the time the last rider is in, there is a crowd about her three deep, and the mead is standing unpoured.

From the gate you see dust, then horses, then one horse. A boy on a dun mare takes the far heap and stands on it, howling. The Dane names each rider as he comes in. At dusk they carry the king out and burn him, and the fort is quiet for the first time since you came.

The women are watching the road like everyone else. A sack of sea-stone and a bundle of marten go under your cloak, and you are on the lake before the first horse tops the rise. Behind you somebody begins to shout, in the Dane's voice, and not at you. At him.

An old woman you took for part of the wall has you by the wrist, and she is one of the cold-making kin, and her hand is like the room. They take back what you lifted and eighty pennies' weight besides. They do not kill a thief at a burning. They walk you to your boat. The Dane does not come down.
The Frisian on the horse
The king burned at dusk with his weapons and his clothes. This morning the women rake the ash for bone, and your horse stands at the Dane's door with half the fort looking at him.
The far heap. Sea-stone, marten and his silver, and you a man who had not sat a horse since harvest. They will sing about the horse. You they will call the Frisian who was on him.
Fourth. The heap by the second ditch. Nobody laughed, and you came in ahead of two kings' sons, who are over there not looking at you.
The horse. Say what you want for him.
He means anything. A horse that has run at a king's burning is worth more than the heap he ran for, and there will be another burning. There is always another burning.
You rode for my brother. While I sit here your boat is a guest's boat at this fort, and your son's after you. Here is my hand on it.
Take the far heap home, and keep the horse
Take the far heap, sell the king the horse, and ask for ground by the lake
Take your heap, and sell the king the horse that came in ahead of two kings' sons
Take your heap and the king's hand, and keep the horse for the next burning

Fourteen sacks of sea-stone, four forties of marten and the dead king's silver go down to the boat, with his bridle on top, which you do not sell. The horse goes aboard last and lies down without the blindfold. The new king takes your hand in front of the fort. The Dane says he has never had a guest who cost him so little and was worth so much.

The king weighs out silver for the horse until the Dane tells you, in Norse, to stop looking surprised. Then the king walks to the shore with a stick and scratches the corners of a house plot next to the Dane's. The heap goes aboard. The grey watches you go, from a king's stable, eating barley.

Six sacks of sea-stone, and for the horse rather more silver than he cost. The king takes your hand as well. It is the horse he wanted, but it is your hand he took, and at this fort that is remembered longer.

Eight sacks, a forty of marten, and a gift of cut silver from a king who admires a man that will not sell. He takes your hand. The grey goes back into the boat. Next burning, the Dane says, walk him two weeks first, and you may not need my scales again.
Neither milk nor mead

They drank mead at the burning and mares' milk at the high bench, as they always have, and then they drank the brew-wife's ale until the cask sucked air. This morning the dead king's brother, who is king now, has sent for her and for you.
A king drinks milk. A slave drinks mead. This is neither. I can give it to whom I like and insult no one. Do you know what that is worth to a man with forty cousins?
He wants a brewhouse inside the palisade and me in it. I said: malt. He said: what is malt. So I shall be here some time.
As long as anyone remembers, a man could say of the Ests that they brew no ale. He will have to find something else to say about them.
Barley was horse feed here at the last moon. This morning it has a price. I would buy before the next fort hears of it.
They have no word for it. They are calling it by their word for mead and pulling a face to show they mean the other one. I shall teach them a better word when I have learned a worse one.
Leave her here with her share and a brewhouse, and take the malt trade
Take the king's thanks in amber now, and his peace on your boat
Ask for the king's hand between his house and yours, and first pick of each winter's amber

The king's men are cutting posts before noon. She has a house inside the palisade, a share, no brother-in-law, and the key of the store where your goods will lie. Twelve sacks of sea-stone and the king's silver go aboard, and an order for twenty sacks of malt at double. She walks you to the boat and tells you which malt.

Thirty sacks. The steward weighs them himself, and the king lays his hand on your stem in front of the fort: this boat owes no gift here. The brew-wife is already arguing with him about where the brewhouse door should face. She seems to be winning.

The king takes your hand at the gate, with the fort for witness. Each spring, when the winter's sea-stone comes in off the west shore, your boat is weighed before the others. Sixteen sacks and his silver go aboard as a beginning. The Dane says he has waited twelve winters for that hand and you got it with a cask.
The store opens
The king burned at dusk. This morning his store is open, the steward sits before it with the Dane's scales, and the lake is full of boats that waited as long as you did.
Now you see what the waiting was for. A year of sea-stone off the west shore, and they sell it in three days, because they want the store empty before the next fort comes to count it.
You came to the wake. You drank. You kept your hands still. What you won at the board is counted. Weigh first.
The cold-wife told him you laid silver by the dead man before anyone asked it of you. That is why he says weigh first. She does not often speak for a stranger.
And sell that horse before you go. There are men here who would give a daughter for him this morning, and he is eating my thatch.
My father's buyers on the Weser will take all the sea-stone one boat can carry, every year. They need a man who knows this lake. I know it now. And I know you.
I am not young, and a house on this beach wants a boat that comes back every year. Yours could be the boat my store waits for. Think about it while he weighs.
Buy at the first weighing, and take the Dane as your man on the lake
Take your winnings in amber, and have the Dane's boy show you every bar from the river mouth to the lake
Go in with the dead Frisian's son: his father's buyers, your knowledge of the lake
Ask the cold-wife's price for a chest of her packing in your hold

Twenty-six sacks at the first weighing, the best of the store, for a hundred pennies' weight and what you won at the board. The Dane puts his hand in yours over the scales. From now on his store holds your goods through the winter, and he buys for you when the price is asleep.

Twenty sacks. Then two days in the Dane's small boat with his boy at the oar: the bars at the mouth of the Wisle, the broad water they call the Ests' mere, where the little river comes in from the east, and which reed bed hides the channel up to the lake. You could find it now in fog.

You cut a stick between you and each keeps half: his buyers, your lake, one boat each, gain and loss shared. Sixteen sacks go aboard and the silver from his father's last sale. He sails west with a bone or a grave to tell his mother of, and your name with it.

Twenty-two sacks, won and weighed. Then the old woman comes down to the boat herself and packs a chest: moss, straw, grey ice, and a layer of something she turns her back to put in. Butter will keep a month in that, the Dane says for her. Do not open it to look. She knows you will.
A handful of the lake
A Gotland boat came in from the east two days before you. By the time you make fast, the bead-makers' row knows what a Frisian did at a king's burning on the Ests' lake.
The Dane who kept the guest house paid the atonement for you. They took his scales, his store and the timbers of his house. He is at Grobin now, weighing for another man.
And they hold strangers to the beach now. No stranger in the fort. No stranger at a wake. No stranger on a horse. No other shore gave us that, and it is gone.
They let you walk to your boat because a thief at a burning is unlucky to kill. Not for anything you said to them.
I do not ask where sea-stone comes from. I ask what it weighs. But I will say this once: you had the whole lake, and you took a handful.
Sell the bead-maker what you know and what you took, and let him do your buying in the east
Pay the Gotlander to show you the Curonians' shore: they have amber too, and have not heard of you
Send the whole atonement east with the Gotlander, and more, in the Dane's name

The bead-maker pays well for what you can tell him: when the store opens, what the gatherers take, which heap is resin. He will buy in the east through other men and work what comes for your house. He weighs the silver twice. He does not offer you ale.

The row pays for what you know of the lake. The Gotlander takes his own pay in the same kind, and draws the Curonians' shore for you in spilt ale on the bench: north past the long spit, five forts, a river with a market up it. They are worse than the Ests, he says. You will get on.

The Gotlander looks at the silver, then at you, then weighs it. At the turn of the year word comes back. The Dane has his timbers and his scales again and will hold your goods. Strangers may ride again. You yourself may come as far as the beach, and no step further, while anyone lives who was at that burning.
Lands to port, lands to starboard

An Englishman is back from the Ests' lake with a string of rough amber round his wrist and a great deal to say. He means to tell all of it to his king. First he wants to tell it to someone who can say whether he has it right.
Seven days and nights from here to Truso, and the ship running under sail the whole way. The Wends' land to starboard. To port Langaland, Laland, Falster and Scania, and all those belong to Denmark.

Then the Burgendas' land to port, and they have a king of their own. Then Blekinge, More, Oland and Gotland to port, and those belong to the Svear. And the Wends still to starboard, as far as the mouth of the Wisle.
The Ests' land is very large, with many forts, and in every fort a king. There is a great deal of honey, and fishing. The king and the richest men drink mares' milk, the poor and the slaves mead.
And no ale is brewed among the Ests. But there is mead enough. I looked. I am a thorough man where ale is concerned.
And they brew ale there, at the one fort, which I had not looked for. They say a Frisian's brew-wife taught them in their grandfathers' time. They are still pleased about it.
When a man dies, his goods are laid in heaps along a mile and ridden for, and the swiftest horse takes the most. Strangers ride for it too, and take it. I saw it done. I did not ride. I have a wife.

They ride for the dead man's goods, I was told. I was not let see it. No stranger goes past the beach there now, for some thief in their grandfathers' time. A Frisian, they say. I do not say he was kin of yours.
They showed me the rise where a Frisian's grey took the far heap, long ago. They still name the horse. Was he of your house? Then I shall say I have met the horse's people.

And there is a kin among them that can make cold, so the dead lie long and do not rot. Set down two vessels of ale or water and they freeze both, summer or winter. I saw the man. He had been dead since the thaw.
He tells it the same way every time, lands to port and lands to starboard, like a man telling knots on a rope. I have stopped mending it. The king likes a thing plain.
Hear him through, and put him right where your house knows better
Tell him what your house knows of the bars at the river mouth, for a price
Let him talk, and tell him nothing: the road is your house's

It takes the afternoon. You mend one thing: which river loses its name to the other where they meet in the mere. He thanks you gravely and tells it wrong again. The clerk, who has it all on wax, lets you take a fair leaf of it for your chest.

He pays without haggling, like a man spending for a king, and the clerk writes down the bars as you give them. Then he leaves them out, because the king will not want bars. You have the silver and a leaf of the telling.

He talks until the light goes and needs nothing from you but your ears. In the morning he sails for England. Whatever is told of the Ests' lake after this will be his telling, and your house will not be in it.

A workshop booth by the landing at Ripa or Sliesthorp, afternoon light through a wattle wall: a Danish bead-maker in a leather apron sits at a low bench among yellow chips, rubbing a lump of raw amber on his wool sleeve; a bowl of water with pieces floating in it, a bow-drill, strings of finished beads on a peg.

The beach at Truso on its lake, a still grey day: a dozen boats drawn up and no goods laid out; on a low rise behind, a timber fort with smoke and many people; in front a broad Dane with folding scales in his belt and beside him a Prussian steward holding out two wooden bowls, one white with milk, one dark with mead.

Inside a dark log house at Truso, light from the door only: a dead king lies dressed on a bench with a sword and spear beside him; frost on the wall posts and the watchers' breath showing; an old woman in a grey shawl sits by two bowls skinned with ice; heaps of amber, furs and a silvered bridle along the wall.

The shingle at Truso, morning sun on the lake: a Prussian woman kneels behind a cloth with three wet shining heaps of yellow lumps; the Dane stands with his scales held up and his eyes turned to the water; far down the shore three small figures rake seaweed with forked sticks.

The Dane's guest house at Truso by rushlight, night: a dead Frisian merchant laid on a bench under his cloak, a small wooden cross on his chest; his young son stands with his hand on the body; in the doorway the Prussian steward and the Dane, and through the door, the dark lake with one fishing boat on it.

Before the fort gate at Truso, bright afternoon: the steward divides goods into five heaps on the grass, amber, bundled furs, cut silver, cloth, a kettle; the dead king's brother, bare-headed with a neck ring, points down a straight road that runs away over a rise; boys lead two horses past.

Behind the landing at Sliesthorp, a windy day: a Jutish dealer holds a lean grey horse by the halter while cart horses stand aside; in the doorway of the alehouse next door a strong Danish woman with her sleeves rolled leans on a mash paddle, watching the skipper and the horse.

The southern Baltic, a low wooded shore to one side, flat evening light: a long low Wendish boat with many oars lies across the bow of a small sailing boat; a man in her bow holds up one open hand; in the small boat a horse lies blindfold on straw among sacks.

The road from the gate of Truso at midday, seen from the gate: heaps of goods at intervals along a straight mile, the smallest near, the largest on the rise; far off a cloud of dust and the first horses; a crowd along the palisade, the Dane and the skipper at the gatepost, women standing by the near heaps.

The morning after, before the Dane's house on the beach: a lean grey horse, still dusty, tied at the door with a ring of Prussians admiring him; the new king holds out his open hand to the skipper; behind, a thread of smoke from a burnt-out pyre and women bent over the ash with rakes.

Inside the palisade at Truso, morning: an empty cask on its side with a ladle on it; the Danish brew-wife, arms folded, faces the new king, who holds a bowl upside down to show it is empty; behind them two men already setting corner posts for a new house; the Dane watching with his hand over his mouth.

The king's store at Truso thrown open, clear morning: sacks and baskets of amber carried out into the light; the steward seated on a stool with folding scales raised, the Dane at his shoulder; a line of foreign skippers waiting, Danes, Gotlanders, a Frisian at the front; the lake crowded with boats behind.

The bead-makers' row at Sliesthorp, a dull day: a Gotland skipper sits on a bench drawing a coastline in spilt ale with one finger; a bead-maker weighs silver without looking up; the skipper of the small boat stands apart with a sack at his feet, and people in the row behind have stopped work to look at him.

The jetty at Sliesthorp, about the year 890, late light: an Englishman of forty with a trimmed beard, a sea cloak and a string of rough amber round his wrist counts lands off on his fingers; a young tonsured clerk beside him writes on a wax tablet; the listener, a Frisian skipper, sits on a mooring post with his arms folded.

Ending picture, the stranger who rode: a grey horse standing alone on a heap of amber, marten skins and cut silver on a rise in the road, a silvered bridle hung on his neck, the fort small in the distance.
Ending picture, the guest who learned: a pair of folding scales in balance, raw amber in one pan and cut silver in the other, on a boat's thwart; the lake of Truso and its fort behind.
Ending picture, ale among the Ests: three bowls on a bench in a Prussian hall, one of white mares' milk, one of dark mead, and between them one of brown ale with a head on it, a ladle laid across.
Ending picture, the thief: an empty beach at Truso with a line of stakes driven between the boats and the fort, and on the near side one small heap of amber that nobody has come to buy.
The fowler's word

A fowler sells duck and teal from a pole on the strand at Gipeswic. He has come down from the Deben, the next river up the coast, and he has something on his mind besides birds. He says it to you because you are a stranger and will be gone on the ebb.
Duck, teal, a heron if your lord is proud. Taken this morning on the Deben, the next river north. The river is full of them since the gale.
You will have seen the hoe from the water, if you have been up there. A long hill over the east bank with humps along its back, like loaves on a board. Those are the old kings. Nobody ploughs there.
The reeve hangs thieves up there now, on one of the smaller humps. He says it saves a cart. They go into the ground beside it, face down, next to the kings. I do not know what the kings think.

The gale put a thorn tree down on the hump at the river end and took the side out with it. I went up for the wood. There is something yellow in the sand under the roots. I looked at it for a while. Then I looked at the gallows, and I came down.
We have a king of our own again, a young one. He strikes pennies with a she-wolf on them. The Mercians let him, so far.
We had a king of our own until Offa had his head off. It is a Mercian's reeve now. He hangs more.
Buy a brace of duck (4 d) and ask him the way in over the Deben bar

He draws the bar in the sand with a duck's foot. Keep the dead oak over the ferry landing, go in on the last quarter of the flood, and trust nothing you saw last year: the shingle moves every winter. The ducks are fat. The men eat them before the boat is afloat.
Ask him whose dead they are

Wuffa's kin, he says. Kings here before the cross came, and one or two after it who were not sure which way to face. His grandmother knew their names in order. He knows the humps. Your lookout, who was a monk's boy once, has stopped pretending not to listen.
Tell him dead kings are no cargo of yours
He shrugs, and sells you nothing. But the men heard every word. On the way back to the boat the Northman asks, of nobody, which way the Deben lies, and the steersman tells him before he has thought.

The strand at Gipeswic on a bright windy morning: a lean fowler with a pole of dead duck over his shoulder points north along the coast; a small clinker boat on the mud behind him, four men turning to listen.
The hoe

The Deben opens two hours up the coast. The flood is making, and the men are looking at you and not at the sail. You go in over the bar and up between the mud banks until the hoe stands over the east shore: eighteen or twenty mounds along the hill's back, and a gallows on one. At the river end a thorn tree lies on its side with its roots in the air. Under the roots the mound is open, like a loaf with the end cut off.
There. Under the root. That is not a stone.

It is a strap mount as long as a thumb. Gold, set with red stones cut in steps, each stone in its own small cell. The sand has run out from around it. Further in there is the green rim of a bronze bowl, and something that was wood.
That is a grave. A man was laid here, with what his people gave him. They gave it to him. They did not give it to us.
A heathen, and gone where heathens go. The gold did him no good. I do not say it would do us any.
The fowler's dead oak was where he said. The reeve's herd is on the far side of the hill, and there is nobody on the river.
Take the gold mount that shows, and nothing more
It comes away from the sand as if it had been waiting. It is heavier than it looks. You wrap it in a rag and put it in the chest under the pennies. Nobody speaks until the boat is over the bar.
Dig with the bailer and your hands for one tide

The sand is soft and runs. In an hour you have the gold mount, a silver buckle black as a coal, and the rim of the bronze bowl with burnt bone in it. Then roof timbers, soft as cheese, and the tide turning. You take the gold and the buckle and leave the bone.

The sand is soft and runs, and it goes on running after you want it to stop. Half the side comes down. When you stand up with the gold mount in your hand there is a herdsman on the far bank, leaning on his staff, in no hurry. He has had a long look at the boat.
Touch nothing. Pull turf down over the break

The Northman cuts turf with his knife and the Saxon carries it. It takes most of the ebb. When it is done the gold is under a hand's depth of grass, and the mound looks only as if a tree had fallen on it. The lookout says a psalm. Nobody tells him not to.

A long bare hill over a tidal river at low grey noon: a row of grass mounds, a gallows on one; in front a fallen thorn tree with its roots in the air over a break of yellow sand; four men standing well back from one small red and gold thing.
Four men and a dead one
That night, at anchor behind the shingle, nobody sleeps. The men have been turning the hoe over since the bar, each by himself. Now they do it aloud.

I will say it plainly. I do not want that thing in the boat unblessed. Take it to the bishop at Dommoc. Gold that goes through a priest's hands comes out a cup for the altar. That is the only clean road I know for it.
We did right. Others will come, and they will not. Tell the bishop at Dommoc. Let him put a cross on that hill and be done with it.

At Ögvaldsnes they laid a king in his ship and heaped a hill over him. My father carried turf to it. So I know a little about hills. I do not like to say this at night. A man who breaks such a hill has the one inside it walking behind him. I have never heard that such a one gets tired.
Put it back and close the hill. That is my advice. It is all the advice I have, and it is cheap.

My father lies under a hill like that, on the Weser. The king's law says I may not, when my day comes. I am to lie in the church's yard among strangers. So do not ask me whose that gold is. I know whose.

The holy Guthlac lived in a hill like it, in the fens. Greedy men had dug it open before he came, looking for treasure. He found devils in it and no gold. Felix wrote that for a king of this very country. The brothers read it to us at Gyrwe.
And there is a song. A dragon lay on a hoard three hundred winters, and a man took one cup from it. One cup. A whole people burned for that.
Give the steersman your word: the bishop will hear of it
The steersman nods once and is asleep at once, like a man who has put down a load. The Northman looks at the water. A cup for the altar, he says. So the bishop is a mound-breaker with clean hands.
Give the Northman your word: the hill is left to its dead

The Northman says nothing. The Saxon grips your arm above the elbow and lets go. The steersman says a word given to the dead about heathen gold is a strange thing to take to confession, and that he will carry it there for you if you like.
Hear them all out, and promise nothing

They talk until the tide turns. Nobody is persuaded. To end it the lookout says the dragon song, as much as he has of it, and it is long, and the men are quiet for it. You have it by heart yourself by the time the anchor comes up.

The boat at anchor at night behind a shingle bank, a horn lantern on the thwart: a grey steersman with a wooden cross at his neck speaking, a dark-bearded Northman looking away at the black water, a big Saxon with his arms folded, a thin young Englishman counting on his fingers.
The third day
The Saxon cannot hold his oar. He is hot, then cold, then hot, and his teeth knock together so that the men hear it from the bow. Nobody says the word mound. Everybody is thinking it.

I will say it, since nobody else will. He is not sick. He is followed. Give the sea something for the one in the hill. A little silver, cut, over the lee side. It need not be much. The dead take payment like anybody else.
We took nothing, so it is not that. I keep telling myself so. Still. A little silver over the lee side never made a man worse.
No silver to devils. We fast a day, we say what prayers we have, and I sign him with the cross. And the lid of that chest as well.

He slept two nights with the marsh fog on him. The brothers at Gyrwe called it the spring sickness and gave warm ale with wormwood. It came every third day, and then it stopped coming. I only say what they did.
I can row.
Cut six pennies and give them to the sea, as the Northman asks

The Northman halves the pennies on the gunwale and drops them over the lee side one at a time, saying something each time that you do not catch. The steersman bails with his back to it. On the third day the Saxon's fever does not come.
Fast a day and let the steersman pray over him

A day on water and prayer. The steersman signs the Saxon's forehead, then the mast, then the lid of the chest. The Saxon lets him, as he once let the Franks. On the third day his fever does not come. The Northman says third days are like that.
Take his oar yourself, and give him warm ale and your dry cloak

You row his watch and your own. Your hands open in two places. The Saxon sweats under your cloak and drinks what he is given, and on the third day his fever does not come. He does not thank you. He scrubs the cloak before he gives it back.

The boat under oars on a flat grey sea: a big man wrapped in a cloak shaking against the mast; an old Northman holding a penny over the gunwale on a knife; the steersman with his hand raised to make a cross.
Old work

A goldsmith has his bench in a lean-to behind the moneyer's house at Dorestat. One of your men has talked over ale, or the man simply has a nose. He asks, without looking up, whether a shipman off the English coast has anything old to show him.

Give it here. I will not run off with it, I have a bad leg. Ah. English work, and old, older than your grandfather. Look at the stones. Cut in steps, every one, with a stamped foil under each to throw the light back. Nobody cuts them so now. The stones stopped coming, and then the hands forgot.

This sat on a king's sword belt, or on the belt of a man a king loved. By weight it is a hundred and sixty pennies: one of gold for twelve of silver. I would melt it by evening. I would be sorry by morning. But I would melt it.

Nothing? Your steersman told the alewife otherwise, or told her you had left it lying. A pity. I had one such piece through my hands as a boy. Red stones cut in steps, foil under them. I melted it. I still think about it.
Do not tell me where. I mean it. If you tell me I must decide whether to tell the count, and I am too old to decide things.
But this much for nothing. Where there is a belt mount there was a belt. Where there was a belt there was a man. And such a man did not go into the earth with one thing.
Sell him the gold mount for melting (160 d)

He weighs it twice, against pennies and then against barleycorns, and pays in good new coin. The bellows are going before you are out of the lean-to. The Northman, who waited outside, asks nothing. He has seen your face.
Ask him about the old gold work, and sell nothing

He talks for an hour. Red stones from beyond the Greeks' sea, split with a hot wire, ground on a wheel no wider than a penny. He has a riddle about what his trade is made of, which an Englishman gave him, and he gives you that too. He takes no pay. He says the talking was pay.
Ask what a whole grave of such work would bring

He puts down his tongs. A sword with gold at the hilt. A purse. Buckles. Cups. If it is a king, a helm. He names a sum, and then names it again more quietly. Come after dark, he says, and by the back, and do not bring the Northman: he frightens my wife. He gives you a riddle a Dane once paid him with, so that you will think of him.

A dark lean-to at Dorestat lit by a small charcoal fire: an old goldsmith with a bad leg holds something small and red-gold close to one eye; fine scales, tongs and a crucible on the bench; a tall Northman waiting in the daylight of the doorway.
The distaff side

An old woman sells wool by the fleece at the edge of the market. She has watched your boat since it came in. When you pass she says, in slow careful Frisian, that she hears you have been on the Deben, and that she had people there once.
My mother's mother was of Wuffa's kin, on the distaff side, which counts for nothing and which I have never forgotten. My name is Leofwaru. I can say the kings back to Wuffa. Nobody asks me to.

The great hill at the river end of the hoe, the long one. They say that is Rædwald, who was washed in Kent and came home and kept two altars in one temple: a big one for Christ and a small one for the old ones. Others say it is his son. The hill does not say.
We have a king of our own again, a young one. Offa of the Mercians watches him as a cat watches a wren.
Offa had our king's head off, and he a guest. Now a Mercian's reeve hangs thieves among my kin and calls the hill the king's. Which king, I ask him.
I have bent my knee to three masters in my time and meant it to none. The reeve hangs thieves among my kin and calls the hill the king's. Which king, I ask him.
Somebody has been at the small hill by the fallen thorn. The reeve knows it. He has put a boy with a horn in the alders, and he is asking after boats.
Tell her what you saw on the hoe, all of it

She listens with her hands flat on the fleeces. When you have done she is quiet a while. So it is open, she says. Well. You told me, which the reeve's men would not have. Whatever you do next, come and tell me that too. I should like one person to.
Ask her to say the kings, and say nothing yourself

Wuffa, Tytila, Rædwald, Eorpwald, and on down through Anna and his holy daughters to Ælfwald, who was the last, and after him strangers. She says them like a woman counting stitches. Your lookout mouths them after her. It costs you nothing, and she is pleased for a week.
Ask her whose the gold in such a hill is now

The king says the king's, she says. The bishop says God's. The reeve says the reeve's, when he thinks nobody hears. I say it is the man's who lies on it, and after him nobody's, like his name. She sells you no wool. She had not meant to.

The edge of an English market under a low autumn sun: a straight-backed old woman in a dark head-cloth behind a heap of fleeces, one hand raised with the fingers spread as if counting; behind her the river and a small boat.
The reeve asks after boats

The reeve of Gipeswic is on the strand himself when you come in, which he is not for most boats. Up the coast, on the hoe, a potter's lad from this town has been hanging for nine days. He was found in the small mound by the fallen thorn, up to his waist in it, with a bronze bowl in his arms.

His name was Dudda and he made bad pots. He dug by daylight, which tells you what kind of thief he was. I hanged him over the place and put him in beside it. He had nothing on him but the bowl. Somebody had been there first.
What lies in the king's earth is King Æthelberht's. I did not make that rule and I do not know who did.
What lies in the king's earth is King Offa's now. All of it, as far as the sea.
What lies in the king's earth is the king's. Ask me next year which king. This year I say Eadwald, and I say it quietly.
What lies in the king's earth is King Coenwulf's.
A herdsman on the Deben saw a small boat under the hoe after the gale. Lapped planks, a tanned sail, four men. He is a herdsman. He remembers things that stand still for a while.
A boat was on the Deben after the gale. Nobody will say whose. Yours lay at my strand that week and went out on the next ebb.
A man who comes and tells me a thing is a finder, and a finder has a share by custom. A man I have to find is the other thing. I have rope.
Tell him all of it, as it happened

He hears it standing. He does not write, because he cannot. He has you say it again before two elders of the town. Keep what you hold until the king's word comes, he says. I know where you sell. He takes half toll of you for two months, his trouble being less.
Say you bought duck from a fowler and sailed for home
He looks at you, and at the boat, and at the men, who look at the gulls. Duck, he says. He has no witness who will swear to a face. He lets the ebb take you.

He lets you finish. Then he has a herdsman's boy brought, who points at your steersman's red cap without being asked. It is forty pennies for wasting the king's reeve's morning, and he says the next sum will not be counted in pennies. There is a watch on the hoe from tonight.
Say it is a matter for the bishop, and that you are on your way to him

He does not like it. A reeve cannot hang what a bishop has his hand on, and both of you know it. Then go to him, he says, and tell him the hill is the king's, cross or no cross. He spits, carefully, not toward you.

The strand at Gipeswic in a cold spring wind: a heavy reeve in a good cloak with a staff, two spearmen behind him; far off up the coast, small against the sky, a hill with a gallows and something hanging from it.
The long hill

The Deben again, on the night flood. From the river you can see what Dudda did before they hanged him: the small mound is half out on the grass. Beside it, at the river end, lies the great one, long and whole, with the turf unbroken from end to end. A boy with a horn is supposed to be in the alders. He is asleep, or he is somewhere else.

Look at the shape of it. No, look properly. Long, and highest in the middle. Earth does not lie like that by itself. There is a ship in that. A whole ship, keel and all, and the man amidships under a roof. I know how it is done.
Then it is the king. The one with two altars.
The small one is spoiled already. What is left in it goes to the next potter. I do not say take it. I say that is how it is.
Turf goes back on quicker than it comes off. I have cut enough of it.
The reeve said a watch. It is one boy. But a horn carries a long way over water at night.
You gave your word about this hill. I remind you of it. I do not hold your arm.
Open the great mound from the top: two nights and the day between

You go in from the top, as down a well, and shore the pit with the bottom boards. Sand, then black wood, then a roof fallen in on what it covered. A helm with a man's face. A sword with gold at the hilt. A buckle as heavy as a quern-rubber. A purse of small gold coins. Silver dishes, crushed, with Greek marks on them. You take what four men can carry down a hill twice. The Northman does not dig. He keeps the watch, and he does not look at what comes up.

A night and a day down the middle of it, and nothing but sand and black wood. In the second dusk the horn sounds from the alders, close. You go down the hill with what you had already lifted from the small mound to pay for the trouble: buckles, a blue glass cup, the gold from a sword. The pit stays open behind you, a spear's length short of whatever is there. The Northman says the dead man's luck held, and sounds glad of it.
Clear what the potter left in the small mound, and go

A blue glass cup, whole, which is a wonder. Two buckles. The gold from a sword hilt, and the red stones out of a pouch lid. A bronze bowl gone green, which you leave to the burnt bone in it. It fills a sack a child could carry. The Northman carries nothing.
Lay back what you took, and turf the break over

It takes the whole ebb. The Saxon cuts and the Northman lays, green side up, tight as a wall. Anything you held goes in first, a hand's depth under. When it is done the Northman pours a horn of ale on it. The steersman, after some thought, says an Our Father, since nobody knows for certain who the man was. Both look satisfied.
Look from the river, and go out on the ebb
You lie under the alders for one tide and look. A hill with a ship in it. Then the ebb takes you out over the bar, and nobody has put a foot on the hoe.

Night on a tidal river under a half moon: a long whale-backed mound black against the sky, a smaller mound beside it torn open and pale; a gallows; the small boat nosed into the reeds, four men looking up the slope.
The last voice

With the land going down astern the steersman ships his oar. He says the thing must be settled before the next harbour, because the men will not sit on it another month. Everybody aboard has a voice. You have the last one.
To the bishop at Dommoc. Say what we saw, give him what we hold, and let him make it clean. A cross on that hill, and no more hanging on it.
Back in the earth, and the hill shut. You all knew I would say it. And if it is too late for that, then nowhere that melts it.
The reeve hangs men over it. Give it to him and you give it to his king. I have seen what kings do with what they are given.
The reeve said a finder has a share. I only say he said it. And a king's leave on a boat is worth more than gold in one.
The goldsmith at Dorestat said to come after dark.
You gave me your word once, behind the shingle.
You gave me your word once. I have not asked what became of it.
I have turned it every way I know. With what is under the boards now, it cannot go back. Not past a watch that is awake. I know it. I say it so that nobody need say it to me.
Back into the earth, and word of it to the old kings' kin

You go in once more on a night flood. What is aboard goes back where it lay, and the turf over it. Then there is only an old woman at Gipeswic to tell. The Northman takes the steering oar without being asked and holds it all the way out over the bar, which he has never done.
To the bishop at Dommoc
The steersman lays the course for Dommoc before you have finished the sentence. The Northman says a bishop is a king with a book, and takes his oar.
To the king's reeve at Gipeswic, for the finder's share
The lookout was right about the king's leave, and knows it, and is not happy to be right. The Saxon rows for two days without a word.
To the goldsmith at Dorestat, after dark
Nobody says anything. That is the men's answer. The steersman lays the course for the Rhine mouth. That night the Northman moves his sea chest to the bow, as far from yours as the boat allows.

The boat at sea in clear evening light, the English shore a low line astern: the steersman with his oar shipped, three men turned on the thwarts toward the viewer, waiting; a sea chest between them with its lid shut.
Green side up

Leofwaru is at the edge of the market with her fleeces, and the fowler is with her. She has heard already: a hill does not get turfed on the Deben without the fowlers knowing by the next tide. She has put on a ring you have not seen before.
Sæwine walked the hoe on Sunday. He says the break is shut, green side up, laid by somebody who has laid turf before. He says he would not find it now if he did not know.

I have nothing a king would call wealth. I have wool rents from three farms, a toft by the quay that my husband left, and this ring, which was my mother's mother's and came out of no hill. Choose. Do not be polite about it.
And I will show you the bar. All of it: the winter channel, the summer one, and where it goes after a north-easter. I have shown nobody. My sons do not want it.
The Mercian will dig it himself one day, or his son will. But not this year, and not because of a Frisian. That is something to have been.
This year a boat of Dorestat lay under the hoe on the Deben. The men took nothing away, and the mound was closed.
Take the toft by the quay

The toft is forty feet of the Orwell's bank, with a hazel fence and a well lined with an old wine cask. She has two elders witness it and puts a turf from it in your hand. With it come six hundred pennies in three kings' coin, the wool rents of two years. The fowler takes you over the Deben bar on the next flood and makes you say it back to him.
Take the ring

She works it off over the knuckle with spit. Gold, plain, with a wolf's head where the ends meet. For your son, she says, or whoever has the boat after you. Tell him whose it was, and that it was given. With it come nine hundred pennies in three kings' coin. The fowler takes you over the Deben bar on the next flood and makes you say it back to him.

The hoe on a clear morning seen from the river: every mound whole and green, the fallen thorn gone for firewood; on the bank an old woman and a fowler; she is holding out one hand with a gold ring on the palm.
A cup for the altar

The bishop of the East Angles receives you in the porch of his church at Dommoc, with the sea loud behind it. He is an old man with ink on his thumb. He has heard the steersman first, which was the steersman's idea. Now he hears you.

When the blessed Gregory sent Mellitus to the English he told him: do not pull down their temples. Cast out the idols, sprinkle the walls, set up altars. A people goes on coming to the place it knows. I have always thought it the wisest letter a pope ever wrote.

So. Gold out of a heathen hill is still gold. God made it before any heathen laid a hand on it. Gold from that hill will be a cup for this altar and a cover for the gospels, and of more use there than it was to him.

And if it is Rædwald: he was baptised, in Kent. A poor sort of Christian, with his two altars. So are most men. I can say a Mass for a poor sort of Christian. I will not say whose it is, and nobody will ask me.
I will have a cross of oak set on the hoe, at the river end. The reeve can find another hill for his rope.
A helm with a man's face. A king's whole gear. I had thought such things were only in the songs my clerks are not supposed to know.
This year word of the old kings' mounds on the Deben was brought to the bishop at Dommoc, and a cross was set up there.
Take the church's freight, and the bishop's hand over the boat

His men will dig the small hill themselves, with a priest standing by, and what they find comes here. To you: six hundred and fifty pennies, paid before the voyage, for the church's wine and wax for a year, and an order for four casks more. He writes three lines to show any reeve of this coast: the boat is on Saint Felix's errand and is to be let alone. The steersman carries the leaf himself and will not let it near the bilge.
Give him the sack, and take his freight and a relic for the mast

He turns the gold in the light for a long time and sets it down gently. A thousand pennies of freight, paid ahead. The leaf that puts the boat on Saint Felix's errand. And a strip of linen that lay a night on Saint Botolph's tomb at Icanho, sewn in a leather bag, to hang at the mast. The Northman looks at the bag. Then he hangs it for you, since he ties the best knots aboard.
Give him the king's gear, and take his freight, a relic, and the cross in your name

It takes two clerks an afternoon to write down what is laid on the porch floor. Fifteen hundred pennies of freight, paid ahead. The leaf. The linen from Saint Botolph's tomb. And on the hoe an oak cross with a line cut in it by your lookout, who asked to do it: that a shipman of Dorestat gave this. The helm the bishop will not melt. He puts it in the chest with the relics and tells nobody why.

The porch of a small stone and timber church above a grey sea: an old bishop with ink on his thumb holding a small gold thing up to the light; the Frisian steersman kneeling; through the door, far along the shore, a new oak cross on a hill of mounds.
The finder's third
The reeve has the king's word, and two of the king's thegns to see it done. A board is set on the strand with a scale on it. Half the town has found a reason to be near.
My men opened the small hill by the fallen thorn on your word. It took them four days and they complained throughout. A cup, buckles, gold off a sword. It has gone to the king.
The sack is weighed and told over before witnesses. A cup, buckles, gold off a sword. It goes to the king.

I have been reeve here eleven winters and I never answered for a helm with a face before. Nor for a hole that size in the king's hill. But the word is that the finder is to be paid and not asked how. So.
The king's word is this. A third to the finder, by weight. And the boat to go free of toll at this strand for as long as she swims.
It is the first gold our young king has had that Offa did not weigh first. He was glad of it. He asked your name.
It goes to Offa, with the rest of what was ours. He will not ask your name. He will ask the weight.
It goes west to the Mercians. It will be rings on the arms of men who never saw the Deben.
At the back of the crowd an old woman with a fleece under her arm looks at the scale, and then at you, and goes home.
This year the reeve at Gipeswic sent the king gold out of the mounds on the Deben, and the finder had his share.
Take the finder's share and the king's leaf

Seven hundred pennies, counted on the board before everybody. And a leaf of parchment in Latin with the king's cross on it and four witnesses' crosses under: this boat pays no toll at Gipeswic. The reeve has a clerk read it aloud, because that is how it is done, and because he wants the town to hear who told.
Hand over the sack for the finder's share and the king's leaf

Eleven hundred pennies, weighed against the sack and counted on the board. And a leaf of parchment in Latin with the king's cross on it and four witnesses' crosses under: this boat pays no toll at Gipeswic. The reeve has a clerk read it aloud, because that is how it is done, and because he wants the town to hear who dug.
Hand over the king's gear for the finder's share, the leaf, and a seat among the king's merchants

Two thousand pennies. It takes the reeve and both thegns to count it, and they count it twice. The leaf with the king's cross: no toll at Gipeswic while the boat swims. And the thegns' word that the king will know your face in his hall and name you among the merchants who are his own. The helm is packed in straw. Nobody in the town has spoken to you since morning.

The strand at Gipeswic at noon: a trestle board with a scale and heaped pennies; a reeve and two thegns with gilded sword hilts; a clerk reading from a parchment leaf; a silent crowd, and at the back one old woman turning away.
After dark, by the back

After dark, by the back, without the Northman. The goldsmith has hung a hide over the door and lit one lamp. His wife counts what you lay on the bench. He does not look at it yet. He is looking at his crucible, which is already hot.
By Martinmas this will be a count's wife's brooches, a ring for an abbot, and the corner pieces of a book at Traiectum. Nobody will know it. That is what melting is for.
One of gold for twelve of silver, less my fire and my silence. My silence is dearer than my fire.
The top piece of the sword I would keep, if I were you. Not to sell. It is the only bit of this a man could hand his son and say what it was.
The helm I do not want to break. It is mostly iron, and it looks at me. Keep it or sink it. Or pay me to do what I would rather not.
Your steersman has gone to the church by the dam and has not come back. The Northman is on the boat with his sea chest packed. He has not said he is going. He has not said he is staying.
Sell it, and keep the sword's gold pommel

Thirteen hundred pennies in three bags, counted by his wife, who is quicker. The pommel he prises off whole and gives back in a twist of wool: gold, with the stepped red stones. By morning the rest is four small bars, and by evening he has sold two. The Northman is still aboard. He says he will stay to the season's end and then see.
Sell the gold and the silver, and keep the helm

Twenty-two hundred pennies. It takes until cockcrow and two crucibles. The Greek dishes go last: he reads the stamps on them with his lips and says a dead emperor's name. The helm goes back to the boat in a sack of bran. On the boat the Northman's place is empty, and his oar is laid along the thwart with the blade toward the land.
Sell it all, the helm too, and have him speak for you at the shipwright's

Twenty-five hundred pennies. The helm he breaks for its silver wire and its red stones, which takes an hour, and which he does with his mouth shut tight. His wife's brother is a wright on the slip below the dam: for a man with this much coin there is a keel's place next winter, and he will say so. On the boat the Northman's place is empty, and his oar is laid along the thwart with the blade toward the land.

A goldsmith's lean-to at night, one lamp and a white-hot crucible: on the bench a helm with a man's face looking straight out at the viewer, crushed silver dishes, a great gold buckle; the goldsmith's wife counting pennies into a bag.
Stones nobody fetches

Behind the dams a quern cutter sits on a pile of finished black stones, cut for the English trade and unsold since the ports were shut. Two skippers stand by him, arguing about whose king a Frisian has.
Forty pairs, dressed and pecked. Cut for the English, who grind finer than we do. They have sat here since the kings stopped speaking. Stone keeps. I do not.
The English used to send word what size they wanted. Now nobody sends word of anything. Six pennies the pair, and I am ashamed to say it.
You have stones aboard already. Then you know what they fetch on this river now. Over the sea is another matter, if anyone lets you land.
The king's order was against the English coming here. The English king's is against Franks going there. Whether a Frisian is a Frank depends on who is asking, and what he is given.
They say it began over a wedding. Kings quarrel about daughters and we cannot sell a millstone. I have stopped looking for the sense in it.
Take four pairs on trust and try the Strand
Buy four pairs at his price, six pennies the pair
Leave the stones and ask what the kings fell out over
Folkmar rolls four pairs down to your boat himself and takes no silver. He says to pay him when the English do. She sits a hand lower in the water.
Twenty-four pennies for four pairs, half what they were worth three years ago. Folkmar says that at Lundenwic no one has seen a new stone since the ban, and that they will pay for the sight.

Nobody at Dorestat knows more than this: about four years ago the Frankish king shut his shores to English merchants, the English king shut his to Franks, and the man to ask is whoever stands on the beach at Lundenwic.
Whose man are you
The king's wic-reeve walks down the Strand with two armed men before your keel has touched. No ship of the Frankish king's people is to land here.
Stay in your boat. Where are you out of, and whose man are you?
Dorestat. Then your king is the Frankish king, and my king's beach is shut to his people. I ask once more, in case the answer has changed: whose man are you?
Black stones. I have not seen a new pair on this beach since the year the order came. My own wife grinds on a stone worn as thin as a dish.
And nothing in her worth the trouble of turning you away. That is almost a pity.
This year my king had the East Angles' king's head struck off. I say so that you know what kind of year it is to ask a reeve for an exception.
Give him a gift and a story: Frisians beached here before either king was born
Lie off the beach three tides and let him see who comes to your boat
Put about and go round by Hamwic, where another king's reeve asks less
The reeve hears the story out, weighs the silver in his hand without looking at it, and says that a Frisian is plainly not a Frank, for a month. You may land. He asks your name twice.
For three tides you lie at anchor and nobody comes but women in small boats, asking the price of stones. On the fourth tide the reeve waves you in. He has counted them too.
You put the helm over. The reeve watches you down the river without a word. A man on the next boat says the West Saxon wic is only half shut, and that Thiadbod of Dorestat keeps a man there.
The size of the gap
At Hamwic a man of Thiadbod's is roping bundles for a party of pilgrims. The bundles are square, and heavy for men who own nothing.
The king here is married to Offa's daughter. So the ban is his wife's father's quarrel and not quite his own. That is the size of the gap, and we live in it.
We go to the thresholds of the Apostles. We have no silver, only our prayers and what is on our backs.
What is on their backs is six English cloaks to a bundle. A pilgrim pays no toll. At the Canche a man of ours takes the bundles and the pilgrims walk on lighter, and holier.
I tell you now, before you say yes: if the toll man there opens one, the cloth is his, and there is a fine, and he remembers the boat.
I hear the reeve at Lundenwic offered you a letter and you would not have it. Good. Letters make peace, and peace closes gaps.
Carry six bundles over to the Canche for a third share
Sell your own goods openly here and leave his bundles alone
Buy the pilgrim ale and let him talk

Six pilgrims and six bundles go over with you. At the Canche the toll man blesses himself as they pass. Your third comes to a hundred and ten pennies, and Hildulf says there is more where that came from.

At the Canche the toll man puts a knife through the rope of the first bundle and six cloaks fall out on the mud. The cloth is the king's. The fine is thirty pennies, and he looks a long time at your boat.
You sell in the open market by the hythe, under the reeve's eye, and pay what is asked. Hildulf shrugs. A woman buys a pair of stones and says she had not thought to see new ones before she died.
He is a weaver's son from up the Itchen and has never been further than this beach. By the third cup he has told you the price of a cloak, who ropes the bundles, and a good deal of English besides.
A hazel rod
The reeve comes to your boat alone, after dark, with a sealed letter and a peeled hazel rod as long as a man's forearm and hand.
You went round by Hamwic. I know. I know most of what goes round by Hamwic. I have come anyway, because your boat is small and nobody watches it.
I want a quiet ship. Not Thiadbod's: everyone looks at Thiadbod's. This letter goes over the sea to the Canche, and no one is to know it went.
There is an abbot there who takes the Frankish king's tolls and is my king's friend. Both things are true at once. Put it in his clerk's hand and no other.
And this. My king wants black stones, and this hazel is the length he wants them. Do not lose it, and do not shorten it to fit your chest.
You have carried bundles for Thiadbod's man. I do not ask. I only say that a letter is lighter than cloth and is paid for longer.
Take the letter and the rod to Quentovic
Take them, and name a price for the risk
Say you carry stones, not kings' letters, and go Thiadbod's way round

The letter goes inside your shirt and the rod under the bottom boards. Before you stow it you cut its length into your own gunwale with a knife: two notches. The reeve leaves twelve pennies for the passage.
Forty pennies. The reeve counts them out slowly and says that he had taken you for a different kind of man, and that it is no matter. You notch the rod's length on your gunwale before you stow it.
The reeve puts the letter back in his sleeve. He says he will find another boat, and that he asked you first. At Hamwic, Thiadbod's man will have bundles waiting.
Whose cloth is that
A long boat with twelve oars comes out from under the land and lies across your course. She has more oars than you have men, and the letter is inside your shirt.
Lower your sail. Whose cloth is that, and whose shore did you leave?
The king's word is that no one from Britain and the English people is to touch the shore of Gaul to trade. I did not make it. I row up and down it.
A Frisian. Every boat I stop is a Frisian, and every one of them has just come from somewhere innocent.
Heave to and show the seal: a letter for the abbot who keeps the king's tolls
Heave to, let him search, and say nothing of the letter
Run for the shoal water where twelve oars cannot follow
He turns the seal to the light, does not break it, and hands it back. The abbot is his own lord. He says he never saw you, and that you should say the same of him.
He does not know the seal and cannot read. He keeps you alongside until a clerk can be rowed out from the shore, which takes until the next day. The clerk looks once and lets you go.
They lift the bottom boards, prod the ballast and find a hazel stick, which interests nobody. Nobody searches a skipper's shirt. It costs you the tide.
You put her over the bank with a hand's depth to spare. Twelve oars draw more water than you do. They stop where the sea turns brown and shout a name after you that is not yours.

She touches on the bank and they are aboard before she lifts. They take the cargo for the king and the letter out of your shirt. The officer says the abbot will have it by morning, with an account of how it came.
The abbot's toll house
At the toll house on the Canche the abbot's clerk holds out his hand. On the mud below lies an English ship with a seal on her hatch and a smell of wet wool.
From the reeve on the Strand. I know the hand. Give it here, and tell me who else has held it since he did.
Your letter came before you, in a king's boat, with a tale about a Frisian who ran. My lord has read both. He found the letter the more useful.
So that is the length a king wants a stone. I had thought a king would ask for something longer.
Forty sacks, shorn at midsummer and sealed in her since Lammas. Put your nose to the hatch. I came over thinking the order was forgotten. It was not.
My lord is roofing two churches. The lead for them lies in the English king's hills and may not lawfully come. He prays about it. He also asks every boat.
Give letter and rod into the clerk's hand, as they were given you
Give them over, and ask the English ship's release instead of thanks
First let Thiadbod's man lift the seal with a hot knife, for silver

The clerk runs his thumb round the seal and is satisfied. Twenty pennies, half the toll for a month, and word that the abbot will answer from his own house on the Seine in three weeks: be at Rotomagus.
The clerk goes in and comes out again. The seal is cut from the English ship's hatch that evening. Her master, Hunberht, says nothing for some time, and then asks your name and your port.
The clerk says the ship is the king's matter and not his lord's to give. The English master heard you ask. He nods to you across the mud. Be at Rotomagus in three weeks for the answer.

Behind the salt sheds Thiadbod's man lifts the wax, reads, and sets it back with a warm blade. Ninety pennies. The clerk runs his thumb round the seal and is satisfied. Be at Rotomagus in three weeks.
Ninety pennies behind the salt sheds. The clerk runs his thumb round the seal, stops, and runs it round again. He says nothing at all. He writes something on his tablet that is not about tolls.
What it was about
