A boat from Saint-Wandrille lies at the quay of Rotomagus. The abbot has come up the river himself with an answer, and with him an English monk who has seen the inside of the abbey's letter chest.
Forgive me. You are the one with the boat? The English king's letters to the abbot lie in a chest at the abbey, a whole bundle, tied. I was let read the outsides.
It was a marriage. The young Charles was to have Offa's daughter. Offa said: then my son has Bertha. The king was somewhat moved, and shut the sea. Now you know as much as bishops do.
I am copying a book for York in a room with no fire. I have written in the margin that the cold is great. It is the truest line on the page.
My clerk has a careful thumb. I will say this once, and name no one: the next seal arrives as it left, by the merits of Saint Wandrille and for forty good reasons.
Here is my answer for the reeve. It says what my king will bear to hear said, which is more than it did a year ago.
And this cord. It is knotted at the length a cloak was when I was a young man. Their weavers send them shorter every year at the same price. Let them lay it on the loom.
Take the answer and the knotted cord back to Lundenwic
Take them, and stay a week for the monk to teach you what a seal says
Take them, and ask a cask of the abbey's wine for the freight
A letter inside your shirt again, and a cord round your waist under it. The abbot gives twenty-five pennies and his blessing in the same movement. The reeve will look for you within the month.
Seven evenings with Sigewine and a wax tablet. You can now tell an abbot's name from a king's on a seal, and he has given you a riddle about a pair of scales to keep you honest. Then down the river.
The abbot does not say no. He never says no at once. A cask is rolled aboard, and he remarks that the saint's wine is usually given and not asked for.
The length of a king's stone
On the Rhine bank at Colonia a stone dealer has heard that a Frisian boat carried a rod over the sea. He would like to see your gunwale, where you notched it.
Roughouts from the pits in the hills, as they have come down this river since the Romans. I do not finish them. I sell them to men who know what the buyer's hand wants.
They say the English king has asked for a length. The man who knew it would have his stones cut and stacked while the rest of us were still hearing that the ports had opened.
Some here say it is not millstones he wants at all, but black stone for a church. I sell both. I would still like the length.
Sell him the length, notch for notch
Keep the length yours: pay him to cut twelve pairs to it and hold them for you
Show him nothing, and ask what the pits send down this year

He lays a stick along your gunwale and cuts it at the two notches. A hundred and fifty pennies, counted twice. By next spring every dealer on this bank will have the length, and he will have had it first.
Sixty pennies down. Gerwin will have twelve pairs cut to your notches and stacked under straw with your mark on them. He throws in a riddle about a whetstone, because a stone man should have one.

He takes it well enough. The pits send down as many as ever, he says, and with no English to buy them the finished stones lie about at Dorestat for whoever will take them: cheaper there now than here.
A knotted cord
You are back on the Strand with the abbot's answer and the cord. Thiadbod's big ship lies on the beach where no Frankish hull should be, and he reaches you before the reeve does.
While this beach is shut, one Frisian ship lands on it, and it is mine. An answer that went astray would be worth a pound of silver to me. I do not ask you for anything. I only say what it is worth.
My man read the first letter on the Canche, so I know what the second one answers. You have sold me half already. The other half is the dearer.
Why do the Franks want them longer? Wool costs what it costs. A longer cloak at the old price is a gift to a stranger. Will the Frankish king send me the wool?
If you have something for me, I will lay it before the king at the right hour. There are wrong hours. I have learned to tell them apart.
The abbot wants lead. There are eight pigs in the king's store that nobody has counted since the ban. If they left as ballast, I would not have seen them go. I am telling you what I would not see.
Give the reeve the answer and the cord
Give them over, and take the eight uncounted pigs of lead as ballast for the abbot
Let the answer go astray into Thiadbod's hand

The reeve takes the letter and winds the cord round his hand. Thirty pennies. He says that kings answer slowly, and that you will hear it on this beach when there is something to hear. Thiadbod has gone back to his ship.
The reeve takes the letter and the cord. That night eight pigs of lead come down the beach on a hurdle and go under your bottom boards. Nobody counts them out either. She rides stiff and low.

Thiadbod weighs out two hundred and forty pennies in a net shed. You tell the reeve the abbot gave you nothing to carry. He asks you twice. The answer does not change. The cord you drop in the river off the Isle of Sheppey.
Rain on an altar
The toll man of Quentovic looks into your boat, sees what lies under the bottom boards, and sends a boy running for the abbot.
Lead. From where? No. I did not ask that. I was told this morning not to ask that.
My clerk had word of eight pigs of lead. I see bottom boards and bilge water. Tell me the rest yourself. I would rather hear it from you than from a toll man.
Saint Peter's and Saint Michael's stand open to the sky. I will not ask any king's leave to keep the rain off an altar.
I have gone to Offa many times for the king. I will go once more, with the reeve's word in my sleeve and a dry roof to show both of them what peace is good for.
Land all eight pigs openly, on the abbot's word
Say the lead is your own cargo and sell it at the smiths' price
Tell him plainly what became of the lead, and stand to hear the answer

Eight pigs go up the bank on the abbey's own cart, in daylight, with the toll man holding the horse. A hundred and sixty pennies and no toll. The abbot says he will cross before the autumn gales and that you should watch the Strand after Easter.

The abbot looks at you, then at the lead, then at the toll man, and says that the toll is a tenth. The smiths pay well. Lead is dear on this shore while the sea is shut. The churches stay open to the rain.
The abbot hears it out. He says that he has been lied to by better men and told the truth by worse, and that the roofs have waited this long. He does not ask you to supper.
The beach is open
A Frankish ship lies on the Strand with her mast down and nobody shouting at her. The abbot of Saint-Wandrille stands beside the reeve, and both of them are waiting for you.
The king my lord is no longer moved. He writes to yours as to a brother. The merchants of each are to have the other's protection, and if they are wronged they may go to the king himself.
It took a wedding that was never held, a hazel rod, a knotted cord and eight pigs of lead. Saint Wandrille did the rest. I would not care to say in what proportion.
You carried the rod, so you land the first stones cut to it. The king has said it. I asked him at the right hour.
I am told there are twelve pairs at Colonia already cut to the length, under straw, with your mark on them. You knew before the kings did. I will not ask how.
And the cloaks will come at the old length. I laid the cord on one myself this morning. It covered the knot. A small thing, but I am an old man and I ride in the rain.
Ask the king's writing: your goods toll-free on the Strand
Ask the abbot instead: a man of yours in his toll house on the Canche
Ask for ground on the Strand, and the first order for the quern cutter of Dorestat
Your twelve pairs lie cut at Colonia: ask the writing, and sell the first stones yourself

Gerwin's twelve pairs come down the Rhine and over the sea under your mark. Eight sell on the first tide at a price nobody argues with; four stay aboard. Fifteen hundred pennies, the king's writing, and the only stones of the right length in England.

A strip of parchment with the king's name and six crosses: your ship and your goods free of toll at Lundenwic. Twelve hundred pennies for stones to come, and both kings' officers know your name. The ports are open a full year sooner than they would have been.

The abbot does not say no. A man of your choosing will sit in the toll house on the Canche and see every cargo that crosses. Fourteen hundred pennies, and an order for more lead, lawful this time. The ports are open a full year sooner than they would have been.

The reeve paces out ground above the tide line and drives four pegs. The first order for stones goes to Folkmar of Dorestat by name. Nine hundred pennies. The ports are open a full year sooner than they would have been, and forty pairs of stones are no longer anyone's shame.
As a brother
The reeve has a letter read aloud on the Strand by a priest who turns it out of the Latin as he goes. It is from the Frankish king to his own, and it speaks of stones.

The Frankish king writes that pilgrims are to go peaceably without any molestation. But any among them not seeking the cause of religion, but that of gain, are to pay the customary tolls in proper places.
And he writes of the black stones. Send a man, he says, to say what kind, and he will have them given and help with the carrying. In return he asks that our cloaks come as long as they used to.
He sent my king a belt, an Hungarian sword, and two silk cloaks. Silk ones, and long, I am told. A king makes his point how he likes.
My king died three days before Lammas. The stones are still wanted. Mills do not mourn. I am still reeve, this week.
The Frankish toll men now open pilgrims' bundles on the Canche. I hear they began with a list of Frisian boats. I did not write it. I was asked to read it.
You asked for my ship on the Canche when you could have asked for silver. I carry wool for half the minsters of Kent. Tell me what you want carried, and where.
You carried the answer: ask to land the first stones, toll-free by the king's writing
You carried the lead too: ask the writing here and a man of yours at the abbot's toll house
Ask only for the reeve's order for stones, paid down, and his pilot to show you the river
Your twelve pairs lie cut at Colonia: ask the writing, and sell the first stones yourself

Gerwin's twelve pairs come down the Rhine and over the sea under your mark. Eight sell on the first tide; four stay aboard. Eleven hundred pennies and the king's writing. The other dealers' stones arrive a month later, a finger too short.

The reeve says the first black stones on the open beach will be a Frisian's, and yours. A strip of parchment with the king's name frees your ship of toll at Lundenwic. Eight hundred pennies paid down, and an order for six pairs at twice the price.

The king's writing here, and by the abbot's word a man of yours in the toll house on the Canche. Fifteen hundred pennies paid down. You have a foot on each shore, and for once both kings are glad of it.
Six hundred pennies down against stones to come. The reeve's own pilot takes you from the Nore to the Strand and back on one tide and names every bank. You will not need him again.
The quarrel outlives the king
Offa is dead and no letter came. At Hamwic Thiadbod has a tally laid out on a cask head, and half of it is in your name.
Offa died three days before Lammas with his quarrel unmended. The abbot's answer never reached him, as you know. The new king has Kent in arms and no hour for letters.
So the beach at Lundenwic stays shut, stones stay dear there and cheap at home, and the gap here stays the size it was. I said a pound. It has been worth more.
The abbot on the Canche has lost two more summers of tolls and knows which boat carried his answer. He names sums and saints in the same breath. You are among the sums.
The quern cutter at Dorestat still asks after four pairs he gave on trust. He has sixty pairs on the pile now. He says stone keeps.
Take your share of the shut years, and a man of your own in the gap at Hamwic
Take it all in silver, with the marks of the Solent creeks, and be seen with neither of them again
Send the abbot word of what his answer said, late, under your own name

Nine hundred pennies, and a man of yours beside Hildulf at the hythe. No letter about black stones is ever written. The ports stay shut for years yet, and you are one of the two Frisians who do not mind. An abbot remembers your boat.
Thirteen hundred pennies, and Hildulf walks you down the shore at low water and names every creek. No letter about black stones is ever written. You do not go back to the Canche if you can help it.

A monk bound for the Canche carries your word, with your name on it. Thiadbod pays you six hundred and says it is the last. The peace is made the year after, with the new king. The old one never read it. The abbot sends back one line: that late is a kind of honest.
A line for us
The kings have made it up. At Hamwic Thiadbod's man reckons the shut years on a tally stick, and a pilgrim has come home from the Canche with nothing on his back.
The Frankish king has written to the English one, and there is a line in it for us. Those not seeking the cause of religion, but that of gain, pay the customary tolls in proper places.
They opened every bundle on the beach. A man from Rome with a bag of relics, they opened him too. I walked home. I have seen the sea now and do not need to see Rome.
Every summer through the gap is on this stick. Your notches are on the left. It was good while kings were angry, and kings are not angry for ever.
The reeve at Lundenwic let some other boat land the first black stones, toll-free, by the king's writing. I hear you were asked first.
They cut one of your bundles on the Canche, that time. Your boat is on the toll man's list there. I would not land at Quentovic in a hurry.
Take your share, and keep a man at Hamwic for honest trade now the gap is closed
Take silver, and what the shut years taught: every creek and bar of the Solent
Pay the tolls you slipped, before the reeve of the wic as witness, and start clean

Eight hundred pennies off the stick, and a man of yours stays at the hythe to buy cloth in the open. The toll men on the other shore have long memories and a list. Your name is spelled wrong on it, but it is there.

A thousand pennies. And you can now bring a boat into any creek between the island and the Itchen at night, on the ebb, without a light. It is an honest skill. It was not honestly come by, and the toll men know it.

You count two hundred pennies of your share onto the reeve's table and name what they are for. He has not seen that done before and calls a second witness to watch. Six hundred left, the creeks in your head, and your name on nobody's list.

At Dorestat they say it again: the Frankish king has shut his shores to English merchants and the English king his to Franks, these four years, over a wedding that was never held. Black stones cut for the English lie unsold behind the dams.
The kings have made peace. The abbot of Saint-Wandrille crossed to King Offa and came back with it. The Strand is open to Frankish hulls, and a Frisian of Dorestat landed the first black stones.

This year King Charles wrote to King Offa as a brother. Pilgrims go free; traders among them pay toll. The merchants of each king have the other's protection. Black stones are wanted at Lundenwic, and long cloaks in Francia.
King Offa died three days before Lammas and no peace was made with the Frankish king. The Strand is still shut to Frankish hulls. Stones are dear at Lundenwic and English cloth is dear on the Rhine.
A Frisian skipper has sent word to the abbot on the Canche of an answer that went astray two summers ago. They say the abbot will cross to the new English king in the spring.

Dorestat, behind the dams, a grey noon: a broad Frisian quern cutter sits on a stack of round black lava stones with a pecking hammer across his knees; behind him two skippers argue, one in a long blue cloak; ships' masts over the roofs.

The Strand at Lundenwic, low water, morning: a small boat nosing the shingle; an English reeve in a green cloak with a gilt disc brooch holds up his rod of office, two spearmen behind him; thatched houses and looms above the beach.

The hythe at Hamwic, afternoon sun: a Frisian factor ropes square bundles onto the backs of four pilgrims with staffs and scrips; one pilgrim stoops under the weight; a beached boat and the Itchen behind.

Night on the Strand, a horn lantern: the reeve alone, leaning over a small boat's gunwale, a sealed letter in one hand and a peeled hazel rod in the other; the skipper cutting a notch in the gunwale with his knife.

The Channel, a brisk grey day, white cliffs low on the horizon: a long twelve-oared boat lies across the bow of a small sailing boat; a Frankish officer stands in her bow with one hand raised; the skipper's hand is at the neck of his shirt.

The Canche at Quentovic, ebb tide, flat light: a timber toll house on the bank, a tonsured clerk with wax tablets holding out his hand; on the mud below an English ship with a wax seal and cord across her hatch, her master sitting on the rail.

The quay at Rotomagus, a cold bright morning: a portly abbot with a silver cross hands down a sealed letter and a knotted cord from an abbey boat; beside him a tall stooping English monk blows on ink-stained fingers; the old Roman wall behind.

The Rhine bank at Colonia, late afternoon: rough black quern blanks stacked like loaves beside a barge; a Frankish dealer lays a stick along the gunwale of a small boat between two knife notches; the Roman walls and river behind.

The Strand, evening, a big Frisian ship beached in the background: a well-fed skipper in a long blue cloak speaks close to the player's ear; a woman at an upright loom holds a short cloak against a knotted cord; the reeve approaches along the shingle.

Quentovic, rain: a toll man lifts the bottom boards of a small boat to show eight dull grey pigs of lead; the abbot stands on the bank under a held cloak, one hand raised toward a roofless church gable behind the houses.

The Strand in spring sun: a Frankish ship beached with her mast lowered and nobody minding; the abbot and the reeve stand side by side, the reeve holding a strip of parchment; the first black stones are rolled up the shingle on poles.

The Strand, a summer morning, a crowd of weavers and boatmen: a priest reads from an unrolled letter while the reeve listens with his rod grounded; at the water's edge a small boat unloads round black stones; one woman kneels to turn a new quern.

A net shed at Hamwic, dusk, one tallow light: Thiadbod in his blue cloak lays out silver on a cask head beside a notched tally; his factor counts; through the door the empty hythe and a single beached ship.

The hythe at Hamwic, a grey morning: the factor splits a tally stick over his knee; a pilgrim with a staff and no bundle sits on an upturned boat; behind them a cut rope and an empty pack frame lie on the shingle.
Ending picture, the early peace: a Frankish and an English ship side by side on the Strand, a hazel rod and a knotted cord crossed on a pair of black quernstones in front.
Ending picture, the peace of 796: an open letter with a hanging seal, a belt, a sword and two folded silk cloaks on a table; through the door a boat unloading black stones.
Ending picture, the answer sold: a knotted cord sinking in grey river water, and far off the Strand with one ship on it.
Ending picture, the runner: a pilgrim's bundle cut open on a beach, six folded cloaks spilling out, a toll man's knife stuck in the shingle beside it.
The weighing

The tribute is being gathered over all England, and the town's share is weighed out on a bench by the water. The reeve's man goes from door to door and from keel to keel. The fleet lies in the river and waits.
Seventy-two thousand pounds from the whole land, and ten thousand five hundred more from this town alone. We held the wall against him all one summer. This is what holding it costs.
Seventy-two thousand pounds from the whole land, and Lunden pays its own on top. Our share is on that bench. It is short, as you can see by my face.
You are a stranger and owe nothing. I only say that the men who pay now will be the men this town knows afterwards.
They told us Michaelmas. Then Martinmas. A man can drink a town dry while he waits to be paid for not burning it.
When it is weighed we go home, all but forty ships. I have a farm in Jutland I have not seen in five winters. I hope my wife has.
Lay down sixty pennies toward the town's share
Sell drink and cloth to the men who are waiting for their pay
Say you are a stranger here, and watch the weighing
The reeve's man cuts a notch for you among the townsmen, and asks how your name is said so that he can say it to the reeve. Sixty pennies go into the scale. They do not move it much.
The shipmen buy on trust against their pay, and the first of them puts thirty pennies in your hand to show the trust is good. Ale and wine will be dear here until the fleet has sailed.

You watch a kingdom being weighed in a fish scale. The man at the beam, to pass the time, asks you a riddle about a thing that was earth once and hid in the earth, and that earth can now be bought with.

A waterside in grey autumn light: a bench with a great balance and sacks of pennies, a reeve's man with a tally stick, townspeople in a line; behind them longships moored in rows across the river, their crews sitting idle on the rowing benches.
Irons for Denmark

The fleet has gone home and forty ships lie below the bridge. A moneyer of the town stands on the hythe with a locked chest and a boy. The king wants English pennies struck among the Danes, and the irons to strike them are in the chest.
Leofstan, moneyer. I am to go to Ripa in Jutland and strike the king's pennies there. The king's ships are all somewhere else. Are you bound east?
You are the stranger who paid toward the town's share. The reeve said to ask you first. He does not say that often.
You sold ale to the fleet in the year of the weighing. Then you know Danes, which is more than I do.
Two irons and a hammer. A man found with these and no leave loses his hand, so I would be glad if nobody dropped the chest in the river.
One king from this bridge to the Sound. A man can sail it now with a full hold and an empty sword-hand. Three winters ago I would have taken that chest from him.
Carry him and his chest to Ripa for forty pennies
Carry him for nothing but his good word at the king's mint
You are not bound for Jutland: ask what the king wants with English irons
He counts out forty pennies of his own striking and looks at each one as it goes. The boy sits on the chest the whole way and will not get off it to sleep.
He says a moneyer's word is the only thing he makes that nobody can clip. The boy sits on the chest the whole way and will not get off it to sleep.
The Danes have silver by the sackful and weigh it out in bits, he says. The king wants them to count it instead, with his face on every piece. A Dane takes him east on the next tide.

A timber hythe on the Thames on a bright morning: a neat man in a town cloak beside an iron-bound chest, a boy sitting on it; behind them the wooden bridge and a row of forty beached warships with their masts down.
One penny on both shores

At Ripa a hearth burns in a shed beside the bishop's church and a hammer rings on iron. The pennies come off the block with the king's head on one face and Ripa's name on the other. The same penny now buys ale on the Thames and on this river.
You see the chest came dry. Hold out your hand. That is the first one off the iron here; I kept it for the boat that brought me.
The shipman from the hythe. I came over with a Dane who sang the whole way. I have thought of your quiet boat more than once.
They still weigh them. I tell them the king has weighed them already. They nod, and then they weigh them.
Half of what the king takes in this town is the bishop's. The bishop says so. The king has not said otherwise, and we take that as a charter.
Bishop Odinkar was schooled over the sea and came home with a taste for Rhine wine at the altar and at table. Jutland grows neither. Six casks, and he pays as a bishop should.
Take the bishop's order: six casks of Rhine wine before next summer
Change your silver for the king's pennies at his table
Ask the moneyer what the Danes make of it
The clerk writes six casks on his tablet and the price beside it: half as much again as the market gives. The nearest vine is on the Rhine. He knows it, and so does the price.
Your mixed silver goes into the pot and the king's pennies come back by count. The toll man here takes them without reaching for his scales, and takes less while he is in a good temper about it.

They say a king's face is a strange thing to put on something a man must cut in half to buy a hen. Leofstan gives you a riddle about the thing they trust instead: twin sisters under one strict law, who favour no man and stand level only when both carry the same.

An open-fronted shed by a small timber church at Ribe, evening: the moneyer at a wooden block with hammer raised, a glowing hearth, a bishop's clerk with a wax tablet, and two Danes at the doorway weighing a new penny on folding scales.
As far as an axe is thrown

The king has given the haven at the Wantsum mouth and its tolls to Christ Church, on both shores. At high water a monk stands in a boat and a ship's boy throws a small axe at the land. Where it falls, the monks' right ends.
From a ship afloat at the top of the tide, as far inland as a small axe can be thrown. The king's own words. We did not ask for an axe; we would have said a bowshot.
It is all in the writing, with the king's cross and the queen's and the archbishop's. A toll without a writing is only a man with his hand out.
Before the monks I paid the king's reeve. Before him, his father. The hand changes. I have never yet seen it close.
They pick the boy with care. Last year's boy could have thrown it to Canterbury. This year's is the cellarer's nephew.
Pay the monks' toll and ask to see the writing
Ask to throw the axe yourself
Ask the ferryman what he paid before the monks came

He holds the leaf where you can see it and reads it out, a finger under each word. The names of the witnesses run longer than the gift. You pay the toll, and you know now what a toll looks like when it has a king behind it.

The axe turns over twice in the sun and stands in the turf a good three paces past the boy's mark. The monk moves his stake without a word against it, and is easy about your toll for the rest of the season.
The axe goes into the water a boat's length short of the shore. The ferryman says the monks should hire you every year. Your crew is still telling it at supper.
The same, he says, to the halfpenny. The king gave away the toll; he did not make it lighter. But the monks write down who has paid, and the reeve never did, so now a man pays only once.

High tide in a wide flat haven under a big sky at noon: a small boat with a monk standing in it and a boy caught in the act of throwing a hand axe toward a low green shore; a ferry and a moored trading ship behind, gulls overhead.
The third toll

On the toll bank below the wall of Cologne eleven people sit on their bundles: English and Danes bound for Rome, and two men of Lunden with cloth. The toll man has taken toll from all of them as merchants. It is the third time since the river mouth.
A pilgrim goes free. A pilgrim with four bolts of cloth is a merchant with a staff. I did not put the cloth on his back.
The cloth is to eat with. It is forty days to Rome from here, and nobody on this river feeds a Dane for his prayers.
A tenth at the count's water. Pennies for the showing at Tiel. A tenth again here. At this rate I shall come to the mountains owning my shoes.
At home we have one king from the Thames to the Sound and one toll at each end. Here every man with a rope across the river is a king.
Wine for a bishop in Jutland? Then you will pay the tenth on it, as bishops' wine has always paid here, and I will give you a tally to say so.
Pay the pilgrims' toll yourself: forty-five pennies
Speak for them: the cloth is their bread, not their trade
Say nothing: count what he takes and cut it on a stick

The toll man gives the cloth back and takes your pennies instead; it is all one to him. The old Dane, Toke, asks the name of your boat and says it over until he has it. You cut the count on a stick: three tolls, and what each took.

You ask the toll man whether he would sell his own dinner. He looks at the pilgrims' feet for a while, gives back the cloth and keeps the merchants' tenth. You cut the count on a stick: three tolls, and what each took.

The toll man hears you out and then charges you ten pennies for showing your own goods on his bank while you talked. The pilgrims go on a bolt lighter. You cut the count on a stick, your ten pennies with it.
You stand by the mooring post and cut notches: three tolls since the sea, and what each took from eleven people. Nobody asks what the stick is for. Shipmen are always cutting something.

A muddy river bank under a high Roman wall on a wet afternoon: pilgrims with staffs and scrips sitting on bundles of cloth, a toll man at a trestle with a balance and a rope strung to a post, river barges moored behind, a shipman in the foreground notching a stick.
The count's water

Since the count beat the emperor's army in the marsh at Flardinga, his men sit at the river mouth and take what they please from every keel bound for England. The merchants of Tiel have sent to the emperor twice. They are loading in one company, and there is room in it.
The emperor sent a duke and a bishop with an army. The marsh kept the army and the count kept the marsh. Now he has a toll and a victory, and we have a grievance.
We told the emperor plainly: if this stands, we cannot go to Britain and the Britons cannot come to us, and then your own tolls at Tiel are worth nothing. He understood the last part.
There are creeks behind the island a small keel can take on the night flood. I say can. The count's men know them too, and if they find you there it is the toll and half again.
We go down together and pay together and drink on it after. The bishop's people say we drink too early in the day. The bishop's people lost the battle.
Go down in the Tiel men's company and pay what the count's men ask: thirty pennies
Take the back creeks on the night tide
Hear the Tiel men out, and cut their count of it on your stick

The count's men take thirty pennies from you and more from the wine ships, and wave the company through by noon. A Tiel man tells you what this does to the price of Rhine wine at Lunden. You cut the count's toll on your stick.

Reeds on both sides and a hand's depth under her. You come out into the open river at first light with the count's fires well astern. You saw his post from behind, and you cut what you saw on your stick.
A boat is lying across the creek mouth with a lantern under a cloak. They are polite about it. The toll, and half again for the trouble of sitting up. You cut it on your stick with the rest.
They give it to you keel by keel: what was taken this year, from whom, and what was only called a gift. It takes a long stick. They say that if the emperor will not hear it, some other king might.

A river quay at dusk with broad Frisian trading ships loading casks side by side; a stout merchant pointing downriver, a skipper drawing creeks in the mud with a stick; far off across flat marsh, a small fort with a fire on its bank.
After the Holy River

This year the king went with his ships to the Holy River, and Ulf and Eglaf came against him out of Sweden by land and by sea. Very many were lost on the king's side, Danes and English both. The fleet is buying bread, and the wounded lie in the boat sheds.
Bread, salt meat, ale, cheese, whatever you have. The king pays a third over the market and pays in his own pennies. Do not ask me how many mouths. Fewer than a month ago.
Who won? The Svear kept the field. The king kept Denmark. You may call that as you like, but I would not call it anything in his hearing.
Godric, of Lunden, a rower in the king's pay. I keep the leg if I keep it dry, the leech says. Four of us from the Thames lie in this shed, and no ship goes home till spring.
They say the river came down on us all at once, timber and all. I did not see it. I saw the man next to me, and then I saw the sky.
Sell the fleet your bread, meat and drink at the king's price
Take Godric and three more home to the Thames, for nothing
Keep clear of a beaten fleet, and listen
The steersman takes all of it and pays ninety pennies over what the market would have given, new coin, counted not weighed. Every keel on this shore will be bringing bread here for a month.

They are carried down on a door, one by one. Godric says the shipmen of Lunden keep a long memory and a short list, and that you are on the list now. Your crew gives up the dry end of the boat without being asked.
You lie off and let others sell. By evening you know who is dead, who is said to be dead, and that the king is going to keep Christmas among the Danes. That is worth carrying home.

A Danish beach under low cloud: battered longships hauled up, one with a split strake; a steersman bargaining over sacks of bread; in the mouth of a boat shed a wounded man on straw, his thigh bound, looking out at a merchant's small ship.
What was taken, and by whom

The king means to be at Rome when the emperor is crowned, and he will not go with an empty mouth. A priest of his household sits in the church porch with wax tablets and asks every shipman what was taken from him on the roads, and by whom.
The king will speak with the emperor and with every lord who holds a road. He wants to know what his people pay, where, and to whom. Slowly, please. I write badly on wax.
Everyone tells me about the barriers in the mountains. I have the mountains forty times over. Was nobody ever robbed on level ground?
You have read a toll writing, I am told. Then say which of these tolls had a king behind it and which only a rope. No emperor will undo his own gifts.
A word, shipman. At Lunden we of Cologne pay our toll, and pepper at Christmas, and no gate is shut on us. If your king shows our emperor a list with Cologne on it, somebody will shut one.
I saw you on the bank with your stick. Two hundred pennies, and the stick goes on the fire. The mountains are grievance enough for one king.
Lay your tally sticks on his table and say all of it, before witnesses
Tell him what the pilgrims say of the barriers in the mountains
Take the Cologne man's two hundred pennies and leave the Rhine off the tablets

He calls two men out of the church to stand by, and you read your notches to him: the place, the toll, the taker. He fills three tablets and asks for your name and your port. The Cologne man leaves before you have finished.

You tell him what the pilgrims told you: the barriers, the snow, the men at each one. He writes a single stroke beside something he has already written, thanks you, and looks past you at the next man.

The stick burns well; it was good dry ash. You give the priest the mountains, like everybody else. The Cologne man pays in his own town's pennies and says there is a place for a sensible man at their board.

A church porch in low winter sun: a tonsured priest on a stool with a stack of wax tablets on his knee, a line of shipmen waiting; at the edge of the porch a well-dressed Rhineland merchant in a fur-edged cloak leans in to speak quietly to one of them.
Palms on their staffs
A Frisian keel out of the Rhine mouth, deep with people. They have dry palm leaves tied to their staffs, and one of them is shouting across the water about the king.
On Easter day, in Saint Peter's own church! The emperor was crowned, and our king walked out beside him, the king of the Burgundians on his other hand. I was behind a pillar, but I saw it.
And he asked for us. For us! That we go and come in peace, no barriers, no toll-takers, merchants and praying men alike. The emperor said yes. An abbot is riding home with it written.
I know that boat! Cologne, the toll bank, forty-five pennies! I prayed for you at the tomb by name, shipman, and I had it right. Come alongside. I have something of yours.
They have told it to me nine times since Tiel. I could say it in my sleep, and I think I have. Take some of them, for the love of God.
Take three of them aboard for the Thames: they have walked far enough
Lie alongside: the Dane from the toll bank at Cologne knows your boat
Wave, and hold your course

You have the whole of it before you raise the land, and you have it a month before any town does. Every weaver's son in England will want to see Rome next spring, and he will carry cloth to pay his way.

Toke hands a small bag across the gap between the boats: a pound of pepper, bought at Pavia with the price of the cloth you saved him. He says the road is open now, and that half of Jutland will be on it by spring with cloth to sell.
The shouting goes on a long time astern. Something about the king and the emperor. You will hear it soon enough, in harbour, with everyone else.

Open sea on a clear breezy day: a broad Frisian ship crowded to the rail with weathered pilgrims, palm fronds lashed to their staffs, one old man standing on a thwart with both arms raised, shouting across the water to the viewer's boat.
The king's letter

This year Abbot Lyfing came home from Rome with the king's letter, and it was read to the English in their own tongue. The king has spoken with the emperor and with King Rudolf, who holds the barriers in the mountains. His people, merchants as well as those who go to pray, shall go to Rome and come home in peace, free of the barriers and the toll-takers.
The king says: I spoke with the emperor and the lord pope and the princes there of the needs of all my people, English and Danes. And they granted it, and set their word to it.
He says also that his reeves shall do no man wrong for his sake, rich or poor. And that he will have plough-alms, tithes and Rome-penny paid before he lands. Kings come home from Rome like that.
You gave the king's priest your word when he asked. It was the word everybody gave. That is how a king knows a thing is true.
Your house is known here for more than its prices. I was told to remember that when the letter came.
The king bids us do right by those who use the sea. A reeve can do right in several ways. Tell me which you want, and ask once.
Ask for the king's writ of protection for your house and keel
Take the writ, and a reeve's man to keep your goods: you paid for others on the road
Ask for ground at the hythe, held under the king's peace
Ask for nothing written: take the road's first fruits, and a man at the hythe

A strip of parchment with a seal hanging from it: the king greets his reeves in friendship and tells them your house and keel are in his peace on both shores. Six hundred pennies come with it, for losses on the roads. The peace is as long as the king.

The writ, sealed, and nine hundred pennies for what you laid out for other people's wounds and tolls. The reeve gives you one of his own men to keep your goods at the hythe between sailings. He says the king likes a debt paid where men can see it.

The reeve walks you along the hythe and stops at a strip between two wine cellars. Twelve feet of waterfront, four witnesses, and six hundred and fifty pennies to build with. Ground does not die with a king.

The first merchants home by the open road sell at the hythe that week, and the reeve sees you served first: six pounds of pepper, a bolt of silk, and silver for the rest. One of his men will keep your goods here. Nothing is written, so nothing can be unwritten.

A crowd before a church door in summer light: an abbot in a travel-stained cloak reading aloud from a long parchment with a hanging seal, a reeve beside him, townspeople, shipmen and a few pilgrims with staffs listening, masts showing over the roofs behind.
The river in the letter

This year Abbot Lyfing came home from Rome with the king's letter, and it was read to the English in their own tongue. It speaks of the barriers in the mountains, as everyone knew it would. Then it speaks of the river road: of the bank at Cologne and the water below Tiel. The abbot looks up from the leaf to see who is listening.
The king says: and I spoke with the emperor of the river also, where my people are tolled three times between the sea and Cologne. And the emperor granted that this too should be amended.
He had your sticks read to him twice on the road, shipman. At Rome he laid them on the table in front of the emperor. An emperor does not often see a grievance he can count the notches on.
The archbishop of Cologne was standing behind the emperor's chair. He said the toll was old. The king said so were the pilgrims.
Of the count at the river mouth the emperor said only that he had sent an army once. But he gave his word for the king's men on that water, and the count will have heard it by now.
Your name is in this, and names travel. The toll men of that river will know the boat that cost them their thirds. Take your reward with that in mind.
Take the emperor's grant: your keel free of toll at Cologne
Take the grant and the king's word that you are worthy of a thegn's right
Take the king's writ of protection, good on the count's water
Ask for nothing with a seal on it: take silver, and ground at the hythe

A leaf in a Rhineland hand, with the emperor's sign at the foot: the bearer and his keel pay no toll at the bank of Cologne. Nine hundred pennies come with it from the king. The toll man there will read it slowly, and then he will read it again.

The emperor's leaf for Cologne, and eighteen hundred pennies. Then the abbot says the old rule aloud before the reeve: a merchant who has fared three times over the wide sea at his own cost is worthy of a thegn's right. The reeve says it has been a good deal more than three.

The king's writ, sealed: your house and keel are in his peace, and the emperor's word stands behind it on the water below Tiel. Eight hundred pennies with it. The count's men will wave you through, and will count your casks as you go by.

Eleven hundred pennies, and a strip of the hythe between two wine cellars, taken before four witnesses. No leaf, no seal. The river road is freer for everyone, and your part in it is a thing people say, not a thing they can find.

A crowd before a church door in summer light: an abbot lowering a long sealed parchment to look straight at the viewer, three notched tally sticks tucked under his arm; a reeve at his shoulder, a Rhineland merchant at the edge of the crowd turning away.
A place at the Cologne board

The king's letter has been read. It speaks of the mountains and of King Rudolf's barriers, and it does not speak of the Rhine. The men of Cologne trade as before, and at Christmas they bring the reeve his pepper, his gloves and his vinegar. They have kept a place for you at their board.
Sit. We said there would be a place, and we of Cologne keep our word, having so few other faults.
Your king got his mountains and our emperor kept his river. Every gate is open that was open before. That is the best kind of peace: the kind in which nothing happens.
I went free through the mountains, as the letter says. I paid twice on the Rhine coming home. Nobody had told the Rhine. Is that wine from there?
Do not mind her. Now: we owe you more than two hundred pennies, and we would sooner pay it in something that lasts. Choose.
Sit down among the emperor's men, and trade as one of them
Ask for a man of theirs at Cologne to keep your goods
Take the rest of what they owe you in pepper, and one of their pilots for the river

They move along the bench. Six hundred pennies, and from now on you buy and sell at the hythe under the emperor's men's law, and bring your share of the pepper at Christmas. The widow finishes her cup and goes out without looking at you.

Seven hundred pennies, and a cousin of his below the wall at Cologne who will keep your goods dry and your name out of the toll man's mouth. The widow finishes her cup and goes out without looking at you.

Five hundred pennies, ten pounds of pepper, and an old pilot of theirs who shows you every bar from Tiel to the wall. No seat. They seem relieved. The widow finishes her cup and goes out without looking at you.

A lamp-lit wine cellar by the hythe on a winter evening: Rhineland merchants on benches at a long board with cups, pepper sacks and a pile of grey gloves; an empty place on the bench; near the door an English widow with a pilgrim's staff watching them over her cup.
One man's peace

This year King Cnut died at Shaftesbury, on the morrow of Martinmas, and they carried him to Winchester. The shipmen of Lunden and the thegns north of the Thames have chosen Harold. The queen sits at Winchester with the housecarls. Harthacnut is in Denmark and does not come.
I am still the reeve. Ask me whose reeve at Easter, when I know. Until then I take the toll in the name of whoever turns out to have been king.
Your writ greets the reeves of a king who is under the floor of the Old Minster. It is a good writ. It wants a living man's word over it, and living men charge.
Your business with the emperor's people is no affair of ours. They say the old king's daughter is to marry the emperor's son. So Cologne at least will stay friendly, whoever sits here.
The leg held. I row for the town now, and it was the town's shipmen who chose this king. I told them about a boat that carried four of us home from the Holy River for nothing.
One peace from the Thames to the Sound, they used to say. It turns out it was one man. He had two sons living, and they will have half of it each, if they are lucky.
Buy the new lord's word over the old king's writing: a hundred and twenty pennies
Let the shipmen of Lunden speak for you: they remember who carried their wounded home
You hold of the emperor, not of a dead king: buy cloth while the English quarrel
Let the old writing lie in the chest: it was one man's peace

The reeve writes a line under the old king's greeting and presses a new seal beside the old one. A hundred and twenty pennies. He says the next king will want as much again, and that it is still cheaper than a toll.
Godric and eleven others come up from the ships and stand in the reeve's door. They do not say much. The reeve writes a line under the old king's greeting, seals it, and waves away your purse.

Nobody in Lunden is sure this month whose toll it is, so the weavers sell low and quickly, and Cologne has heard nothing yet. You fill the hold. An emperor's leaf does not care who is king of the English.

You put the old writing at the bottom of the chest. A priest on the hythe, who has seen four kings buried, writes you out a poem about men who lost everything and outlived it. Each verse ends the same way: that passed, and so may this.

A reeve's doorway on a raw November day, bare trees, a church bell tower behind: the reeve holding an old sealed writ up to the light, a group of oarsmen standing close by with their arms folded, one leaning on a stick; black cloth hung from the church door.
The tribute is weighed out in England: seventy-two thousand pounds, and ten thousand five hundred more from Lunden. The fleet goes home to Denmark, all but forty ships.
The king is sending English moneyers over the sea with their irons. Pennies with his face are to be struck among the Danes, to pass by count on both shores.
The king's fleet met the Svear and the Northmen at the Holy River. Very many were lost on his side, Danes and English. He keeps Christmas in Denmark.
The king's letter is read in England: the emperor and the king of the Burgundians have freed his people, merchants and pilgrims, of barriers and tolls on the road to Rome.
The English king's letter names the river road too. The emperor has given his word against the third toll on the Rhine, for the king's men, and the toll men are not pleased.
The watch roll

On the dam at Dorestat the count's clerk stands on a cask and reads an order of the emperor to anyone who will stop. Boats and men are wanted for a watch on the river mouths. The count walks along the row of keels behind him, and stops at yours.

The lord emperor orders that ships be made ready along the shore of the sea, and that a watch be kept at every harbour and river mouth where a ship can come in. It is not the first time he has ordered it.

The law for you Frisians is simple. Men with horses come themselves. Of the rest, six find the seventh man his bread and his spear, and the seventh goes. I need the seventh. I also need what he will stand in.
The Danish king burned a market of the Wends last summer and carried its merchants home in his ships like hens in a basket. He has more ships than he has uses for.
Count Egbert is building a fort beyond the Elbe this spring. The Danish king will take it as it is meant.
Well, shipman. Your boat is small, but she floats, which is more than I can say for some of what I have been sent.
Put your boat on the watch roll
Pay your part of a seventh man and keep your summer
Say the boat is too small to stop anything, and ask what the watch is for

The clerk writes the boat down under the count's eye, and the toll man is told to go easy on a keel that serves. Your post is the mouth of the Scheldt, at Walichrum, where a man named Gerwin keeps the fire. You are to show yourself there before the summer is out.

Twenty pennies go into the count's chest toward a spear and a sack of bread for a man you will never meet. The clerk gives you a notched stick to prove it. The post is at Walichrum, he says, if you should ever wish to see what you bought.

The count has already walked on. The clerk answers instead, quietly. The watch is a fire on a dune and some boats beside it: at Walichrum, at the mouth of the Maas, at the Vlie. It is for seeing a fleet. What happens after a fleet is seen, the order does not say.
Four boats on the sand

On the highest dune at Walichrum there is a pile of driftwood under a cowhide, kept dry to burn. Below it four boats lie on the sand. Two of them are flat river barges with their noses pointed bravely at the sea.
Four boats. Two were built to carry dung down the Scheldt, and they have not forgotten it. In anything of a wind they go sideways.
The emperor ordered a fleet in the year he rode to Rome. I have had orders every year since. If orders were oak I could plank the sea from here to Britain.
I have a field on the far side of the island. Six neighbours feed me so that they need not come. I am the seventh part of a soldier, and it is hay time.
You are on the count's roll. Good. That makes five boats, and the first that can turn.

If I light that fire, the next fire is lit at the abbey's landing, and by the second night the count knows. By then whoever came is home again and counting. Somebody up the river should be told that. They do not read what I send.
Stand a week on the watch with your boat
Carry his letter up the river: the watch can see a fleet, not stop one
Sell them bread and ale and say nothing about the barges

Seven days lying off the bar in the grey, and seven nights taking turns by an unlit fire. You see fishermen, a porpoise, and a monk in a boat who is lost. Gerwin pays you the count's ration money, twenty-four pennies, and says it is the first week all summer he has slept.

He has it written by the priest on the back of an old tally: four boats, two unfit, thirty men of whom nine have held a spear, and a fire. He gives you ten pennies for the carrying. At Dorestat the clerk takes it, reads it, and puts it with others.
Men on a dune are a good market. They pay thirty pennies for what would fetch twenty anywhere with a roof, and Gerwin thanks you for coming, since nobody else does.
Rope for two hundred keels

The landing is full of ships that are not trading. Men are stepping masts, turning shields over to look at the straps, and carrying bread aboard by the sack. A man with a gilded pin walks down the shingle to see what a Frisian keel is doing among them.
A Frisian keel. The king likes merchants; he sends his messages by them. So I ask as a friend. Whose man are you this summer?
Every rope walk on this coast is sold out to the last fathom. Rope, tar, bread that keeps. The king is buying for two hundred keels, and he pays in silver he took from the Wends.

I know three of those ships. I know their steersmen too. Now look at the sacks going aboard. I gave up counting them. Nobody carries that much bread to cross a bay. That is bread for going somewhere and coming back.

The king says Frisia is his own land and Saxony too, and that the emperor may keep them warm for him. He says he will come to Aachen himself one day and see whether the hall is as big as they tell it.
Buy the ale and let your Dane ask his questions
Sell the king's buyers bread and rope at their price
Say you are nobody's man, and trade as on any other day

Six pennies of ale and one evening. Your Dane listens, and comes back with all of it. Two hundred ships. Not for the Wends this time: west, along the islands, when the barley is in ear and the sea has settled. The king will stay at home. They want silver and cattle, and to be back for harvest.

They take everything in the hold that can be eaten or tied, weigh out a hundred and forty pennies' worth of hack-silver without arguing, and tell you why they are in a hurry: the fleet goes west along the Frisian islands when the barley is in ear. The king's man says he will know your boat again. He means it kindly.
He looks at you for the time it takes to count a crew, and goes back up the shingle. Nobody's man is told nothing. You trade as on any other day, on a day that is not like any other.
A rumour is not a cargo
The mound is at its spring work. Ewes and lambs are out on the salt grass and there is washed wool on every fence. Nobody here has heard anything from the north, and nobody is looking that way.
The count's man was here at Candlemas. He counted our boats, wrote down the number, and went away again. We have not been told what the number was for.
My man went to the host in the Saxon years, and the host kept him. I have forty ewes and no wish for news. News has never once brought me a ewe.
You are standing like a man with a hot stone in his hand, looking for somewhere to put it down.
The sun went dark three weeks after Pentecost, in the forenoon. The old women have been telling us what it meant ever since. They do not agree, so I suppose we shall find out.
Tell them what you heard in the Danes' harbour: two hundred keels, this summer
Tell them to send to the count for men, as the law says
Trade and keep your news to yourself

The law-speaker hears you out and asks one question: who told you. Then he sends boys over the flats to the next mounds at low water. By evening the cattle are being driven inland to the high sand, and the women are taking off their brooches. The best of the silver goes down the well in a pot. It will not stop a fleet. It will leave a fleet less to carry.
A rider goes south with the message, since that is the law. He comes back in nine days. The count is with the host and the count's clerk has written the message down.
You sell what you came to sell, twenty pennies to the good, and they wish you a fair wind. From the water the mound looks as it has looked for three hundred years: a green hump, smoke, and sheep.
Sails to the north

To the north the edge of the sea has gone rough, like cloth with the nap raised. It is sails: more than any trading season ever put on the water, coming down along the islands under oar and sail together.
Sails. I stopped counting at sixty, and I had not come to the end of them.
The king's. Every one of them. Be easy. They want cattle and silver, and they want to be home for harvest. One small keel is not worth an hour of anybody's rowing.
Some of them are eating your bread at this moment. I hope it was good. I do, truly.
Unless she runs. That is the one thing, mind. A boat that runs has something aboard, and young men like a race.
Drop the sail and the mast and lie on the flats until dark
Put her before the wind and run for the river
Stand on, and hail the nearest ship in her own tongue

With the mast down she is a log on a sandbank. The fleet goes by for most of the day, near enough to hear the oars. A gull sits on the stem. When the tide lifts you again it is dark, and the sea is empty and smells of tar.
She runs. Two of them turn after you, and give it up when the water under you goes pale and thin. A boat that draws a hand's breadth less has won, and your crew will be telling it for a year.
She runs, and a long ship with forty oars runs better. They come alongside laughing, take forty pennies' worth of silver out of your chest, weigh it carefully, and tell you that you row like Franks.

The nearest steersman shouts back that they are the king's ships and that the king is at home. Where are they bound? He points with his chin at the islands. Then he asks the price of cloth at Dorestat, hears it, shakes his head, and rows on.
The nearest ship understands you very well. A man who speaks the tongue can also be told plainly what he owes. Thirty pennies' worth, by their weights, and you are let go with good wishes.
A hundred pounds

Three fights have been lost. The Danes have laid a tribute on the whole coast, a hundred pounds of silver by weight, and each mound has been told its part. Emuthon's part is four pounds. That is nine hundred and sixty of the emperor's pennies, from people who keep sheep.
They beat us on Bant. They beat us at the creek. They beat us a third time, when we should have known better. Nobody came. We lit the fire, and it burned very well.
Four pounds. Our silver is on our women's shoulders and in two old graves. I have been speaker here thirty winters and I have never before had to ask whose grandmother was buried with what.
They have my son and eleven more sitting roped on the strand. It is to help us count faster.
It is paid. We paid with silver borrowed up the river against next summer's wool. Then the sickness came and the oxen died, every one. We owe for the tribute and we plough with cows.
We had your word and nine days. The cattle were on the high sand and the pot was in the well. They found less than they came for. They wanted their weight all the same.
The emperor's law has a name for the man who buys a hungry neighbour's goods for less than they are worth. It calls that foul gain. I have not found the law that says what the neighbour is to eat.
Put sixty pennies on the scale as your share, as if you lived here
Buy their cloth for ready silver, at a third of its worth
Keep your purse shut, and carry the women, the children and the ewes up the river

Sixty pennies, counted out on the law-speaker's cloak in front of the mound. Nobody thanks you. Sibrand cuts a notch in the tally of households, between the smith and the widow, and that is where your name now stands.

Six bolts of good Frisian cloth for ninety pennies, the work of two winters. The women carry it down to the boat themselves and stack it properly. It was their own offer, and it is lawful. Sibrand has it written down that it was lawful, with the day and your name.

Two days, three trips up the river to the high ground, with the boat full to the wash-strake of children, old women and ewes. One ewe is sick on your steersman. Tetta counts her flock off at the far end, twice, and says it is all there.
His weights

On the strand below the mound a Dane sits on a sea chest with a small folding balance. The mound's silver goes into one pan and his lead weights into the other. Behind him, by the boats, twelve men sit roped together and look at their feet.
Arm rings, brooches, a cup with a saint on it. Your pennies too. I do not mind whose face they carry. In the pan a king weighs the same as a nail.
My weights are honest. They are only heavier than yours. That is a difference between our countries, and I did not make it.
By his weights our four pounds is nearer five. I said so. He agreed with me, and went on weighing.
I know your boat. Your bread was good, and the rope has held. Sit down.
The king stayed at home this time. He says that next time he comes himself, with all of us, and goes on up the river to the emperor's hall. I only tell you what he says.
Buy the twelve roped men free at his price
Set your own Dorestat pound in the other pan, before everyone
Stand by, watch the weighing, and remember what he says of his king

Eighty pennies' weight for twelve men, which is cheap, and he says so: they are fishermen and would fetch little, and feeding them home costs bread. The rope is cut in one place and they walk up the mound in a line, still tied to each other, because nobody thinks to undo the rest.

You set the bronze pound from your own chest in his pan. It is stamped, and everybody on the strand can see the pan does not move as it should. He looks at it for a long breath. Then he laughs, takes one of his own weights out, and weighs the rest of the mound's silver against yours. It saves them most of a pound.

He picks your bronze pound out of his pan between two fingers, looks at the stamp, and drops it in his purse. A light weight is no use to an honest man, he says. Twenty pennies' worth of bronze and pride, and the weighing goes on as before.

You stand at the edge of it for half a day, as a merchant may, and you hear a good deal. He is called Ketil. The king is Godfred, who did not come and who talks of Aachen. The men like the silver. They are less sure about the king.
The host eats

The emperor has called out the host against the Danish king. Every boat on the river is wanted for bread, every cart is wanted for bacon, and anything an army eats costs half as much again as it did at Pentecost.

Bread that keeps. Bacon. Ale. Each man is to bring three months of food as far as the Saxon march, and the oxen that should haul it are lying dead along the road. So it comes by water, or it does not come.
Mine lay down between here and the ford and did not get up. They say a man from Benevento is going about the country with a bag of dust. I never saw him. I saw the oxen.

The host crossed at Lippeham, a day down the river. The emperor's elephant died there, the one the king of the Persians sent. All at once, between morning and noon. I saw it lying on the bank like a grey barn that had fallen over.
Word has come from the camp on the Weser. The fleet has gone home, and the Danish king is dead. One of his own following killed him. So the host has marched all this way to hear news.
Take the host's order for ship's bread
Hire the boat to the host for a fortnight's carrying
Stay clear of the host, and mark what bread is fetching

Eight sacks of hard bread, wanted here within forty days, at most of its price again on top. The provisioner cuts the tally himself and does not ask where you will find it. He has stopped asking anybody that.

A fortnight under another man's orders, up and down the river with sacks to the gunwale and a soldier sitting on them. A hundred and ten pennies at the end of it, counted out without a word. Your crew say they have carried quieter cattle.

A boat that goes near the host is pressed, and a pressed boat comes home at Martinmas. You keep to the far bank. But you mark the price: ship's bread is fetching nearly half as much again here, and will for a month yet.
Where was the watch?

The emperor's envoys are going down the coast with one question. At Dorestat one of them sits in the count's hall, in the count's chair, with a clerk beside him. The count stands. Shipmen are being called in from the dam, one at a time.

Two hundred ships came, took what they liked, and went home again. The lord emperor learned of it at Aachen from a man on a tired horse. He has had a watch ordered on this coast for ten years. I am to find out where it was.
The Frisians ran. Three times. Ask any man here.
A letter came up from Walichrum on the back of a tally. Four boats, two of them unfit. It was put with others. I have now read the others.
Shipman. You were on the water this summer, and you hold no land from anybody in this room. That makes you the nearest thing I have to a witness.
It is to be written in any case that oak is felled this winter, and ships are built on every river that runs into this sea.
Say what you saw: barges, farmers, and no lord within a day's ride of the boats
Say what the count says: the Frisians ran
Say you carry cloth, not opinions

You say it plainly. A fire on a dune. Barges. Men at hay time who are each one seventh of a soldier. Nobody with a sword and a horse nearer than a day. The clerk writes all the while. The count does not look at you, then or as you go out. He holds your house's debt, and you have just remembered it.

You say the Frisians ran. It is even true: on the third day they ran. The envoy looks at you a little longer than is comfortable and tells the clerk to write it. In the yard the count's man puts forty pennies in your hand, for your trouble in coming up from the dam.
The envoy says that is the answer he has had from every keel on the river, and that the emperor will be glad to know his merchants are so busy. The next man is called.
Three springs
The Danish king is dead by his own man's hand. His nephew Hemming has the high seat and wants peace. At Dorestat three men come to your fire in one week, and each of them has a use for your boat.

Ships are being built at Ganda on the Scheldt, and the emperor means to come and look at them himself before winter. The count wants men there who can tell one end of a keel from the other. He has found very few.
The count is not pleased with you. The envoy is. I should think about which of them lives nearer to your storehouse.
My father says the mound holds its meeting after the shearing. He says to tell you your name will be spoken at it. He did not say how.

Twelve men of each people are to swear the peace on the Eider. I speak Danish, so I go. But I am a Saxon, and a count's man, and neither side believes a word that comes out of me. They want somebody who has sold to both.
It should have been sworn already. The frost shut every road between us and them, so for now each side has sworn it at home, on its own weapons, and hopes the other did the same.
Go to Ganda in the autumn, for the emperor's ships
Go back to the mound at Emuthon after the shearing
Go north with the Saxon, to the swearing on the Eider

The clerk writes your name on a list that is shorter than he would like. Ganda, on the Scheldt, from Michaelmas. If you pass Quentovic on the way, he says, they are short of everything there too, and paying for it.
Sibrand's son nods as if he had been told you would say so. After the shearing, on the green by the creek. He goes back down the river the same day; there are cows to plough with.

The Saxon is plainly relieved. The Danish twelve will ride out from Sliesthorp, he says; be there when the roads open and ask for the spokesman of the king's brothers. Bring something to sell. Nobody trusts a merchant with an empty boat.
The old light

A day up the coast, at Bononia, the emperor's new ships are gathering under the old tower the Romans built. At Quentovic every pitch boiler and rope maker is working for the fleet, and the strand smells like the inside of a cask.
That tower has stood dark since the Romans went home. The emperor has had it mended, and a fire is to burn on top of it every night, for ships to steer by. Ours, he hopes.
The emperor has ordered that when the fleet sails, the lords go aboard themselves. I am a lord. I have been sick since the river mouth, and we have not yet left the river.
Pitch is what they are short of. Pitch, and men who have seen the sea before.
She is to be at Bononia before the emperor is. My steersman is a miller. A good miller. Would you take her up for me? I can pay, and I can keep out of the way.
Take the lord's ship up to Bononia for him
Take the fleet's order for pitch
Sail up at dusk and see the fire lit

Three days. She is long, new, stiff, and leaks at four strakes, and forty men pull forty different strokes. You bring her in under the tower on the evening flood with the lord sitting very still amidships. He pays a hundred and twenty pennies and asks you not to say who steered.
Six barrels of pitch, wanted here within forty-five days, at a good part of the price again on top. The harbour man says the emperor can order ships, but only a pine tree can make them float.

You stand off the cliffs at dusk. The tower is taller than any church, in bands of red and pale stone. A spark shows at the top, then a fire, then a light that lies on the water all the way out to you. Your crew say nothing for some time. Then the steersman says it will make the bar easier, at least.
The ships at Ganda

On the bank of the Scheldt at Ganda the new ships lie in a row, black with tar and still smelling of it. There are thirty of them. Shipwrights, monks, soldiers and the count's men stand about, waiting to be told who is to sail.
Thirty hulls in one year, out of oak that was standing at Easter. Half of them will open at the first hard frost. I have told the count's man. He asked me not to tell anyone taller.
He walked the whole row this morning. A very tall old man who favours one foot and will not be helped. He put his hand on every stem. At the last one he asked who would sail them.
Lords are to sail them, by his own order. Each lord goes aboard himself, with his own men. They are brave, and they have seen the sea from a hill.
I told him what a shipman said at Dorestat last autumn. He asked whether the shipman had anything better to offer than complaint. I said I would ask.
There is one hull over. We laid a keel too many, and I built her my own way while nobody was counting: deep, short, room for cargo. A trader's shape. He will not want her. She does not look fierce.
You have seen the light at Bononia, then. He likes old Roman things that can be made to work again. I wonder whether he counts himself among them.
Take your season's pay, and ask for the spare hull
Tell the envoy your idea: sworn Frisian shipmen on the watch, paid in toll freedom
Pilot the new ships down to the sea, take the count's silver and go home

Six hundred pennies for the season, and the hull nobody counted. Baldric has her written off as spoiled timber and helps you step the mast. The emperor's fleet goes down to the sea with lords aboard and is not much spoken of again. Yours goes down behind it, deep and short, and is the only one of the thirty-one that ever carries a cargo.

You say it to the envoy on the bank. Lords will come when they are called and go when the harvest calls louder. Shipmen live on this water. Swear the Frisian keels to the watch, forty days a summer each, in turns; pay them with freedom from the toll, which costs the emperor nothing he has in his hand. The envoy says it twice over to himself and goes up the row. He is gone until dusk. He comes back with twelve hundred pennies, a writing with a seal that frees your boat of the toll at Dorestat, and the first forty days, which are yours.

You take them down the Scheldt three at a time, with a lord in each stern and a boy in each bow calling the depth. None is lost. The count's man counts out nine hundred pennies and has you entered as the count's shipman: called first when the river needs a pilot, and paid first too. Then you go home, which is what the fleet does soon after.
The thing on the mound

The shearing is done, and the mound holds its meeting on the green by the creek. Peace has been sworn on the Eider. The oxen are dead and the wool is the best in years. Every household stands in its place, and there is a gap in the ring.
This meeting has three matters before it. A boundary stone that walks at night. A cow drowned in a neighbour's ditch. And you.

You put silver on the scale that you did not owe. I notched you into the tally between the smith and the widow. The smith has asked me whether that makes you his neighbour, and what you mean to do about his fence.
He carried my ewes up the river like guests at a wedding. One of them was sick on his steersman. I have brought the steersman a cheese.
My son is standing behind you. He has something to say to you and he will not manage it. He was one of the twelve.
You bought our cloth at a third when we could not say no. It was lawful. We wrote down that it was lawful. I read it out again this morning so that nobody should forget how lawful it was.
You brought the word before the ships came. No count did that. No count has done it yet.

We are done waiting for the emperor's boats. Next time there will be a fire ready on every mound from Bant to the Lauwers, and somebody awake beside it who is not somebody else's seventh man. The mounds are swearing it to each other this summer. What we lack is a keel to carry the word where a fire cannot be seen.
Is it true she can lie flat on the sand with her mast down, and nobody see her? I should like to see that. I mean, not see it.
Take the house plot they offer on the mound
Ask for a sworn man to keep your goods here instead
Swear into their watch: your boat carries the word between the fires, and the boy sails with you

The gap in the ring is yours: a house plot on the south side of the mound, twelve paces by thirty, above every tide anyone remembers. Fourteen bolts of this year's cloth are carried down to the boat to go with it. The coast pays its debts and mends its fences, and waits for the next sails, as it always has.

You would rather have a man than a house. They give you the smith's brother, who can count, and swear him on the meeting's own oath to keep your goods as his own. Six hundred and fifty pennies in silver and cut rings are laid on the cloak: the mound's thanks, weighed on your scale this time.

You swear with them, a hand on the meeting's staff: when a fire is lit, your keel carries the word past the next headland, whatever is in the hold. They give the plot, four hundred pennies in silver, and twenty bolts of cloth, which is most of a year's weaving. Tetta gives the boy. He is twelve, he can swim, and he is to come back knowing every bar from the Ems to the Rhine. That summer there is a pile of dry wood under a hide on every mound between Bant and the Lauwers, and for once the people who built it are the people who will be burned if it fails.
Each after his own custom

A day's ride south of Sliesthorp, twelve Franks and twelve Danes are meeting on the bank of the Eider to swear peace, each side after its own custom. Neither side has ever watched the other swear. Both would like one man there who is believed on the other bank.

Twelve of ours. The king's brothers Hankwin and Angandeo. Osfrid from Skane, and two more Osfrids, so that they can be told apart only by their fathers. They swear as we swear. Yours swear on bones in a box. Somebody must tell each side that the other has truly sworn.
Count Wala leads ours. He is the emperor's own cousin, and he has asked me twice whether the Danes will laugh at the relics. I told him no. I have not asked the Danes.

It has been sworn. Nobody laughed. Now two of ours ride south to the emperor's hall with gifts, and what was said on the river bank has to be said again there in the same words. That is harder than it sounds.
Hemming is dead, and his kin are killing one another for the high seat. What the twelve swore still stands at the gate, for as long as there is anyone alive who remembers swearing it.
I was on your coast last summer, on the king's errand. The king is dead. I have a ship and forty men and no errand. I find I would sooner sell a thing than weigh it.
I still have your bronze pound. I use it. It has cost me a good deal of silver, and men trust me, which is new.
Stand witness for both sides, and ask the freedom of the king's gate for your boat
Ask that the oath name merchants: traders of both peoples to cross with their goods in peace
Let the lords swear, and join hands with the Dane who has a ship and no errand

You stand between the two rows and say to each, in its own tongue, that the others have sworn and meant it. It takes a morning. The Franks give you silver and the Danes give you silver, eight hundred pennies' weight between them, and the spokesman has it said at the gate in the wall that your boat passes without the king's toll. The oath itself speaks of kings and borders. It does not mention merchants. Nobody thought of them.

You ask it of the spokesman first and the count second, so that each believes the other thought of it. That the traders of both peoples may cross the border with their goods, and buy and sell in peace. The Danes add it because their king wants his market full. The Franks add it because it costs nothing. It is sworn with the rest. You have four hundred pennies, six timbers of marten from the king's own store, the freedom of the gate, and a guest's right in any Danish harbour: the first merchant the peace was written for.

While the lords swear, you and Ketil sit on an upturned boat and settle it in fewer words. His ship, your markets. He lays down ten sacks of amber and four timbers of marten as his part, and you lay down what a Frisian knows about Dorestat. You join hands on it before his crew. They cheer, mostly because it means they will be paid.

By the emperor's word the Frisian keels of the Rhine mouths are sworn to the coast watch, forty days a summer each, by turns. A boat that serves pays no toll at Dorestat. The counts are not pleased, and the shipmen are counting days.
The mounds from Bant to the Lauwers have sworn a watch among themselves: a fire ready on each, a man awake beside it, and a keel to carry the word. No count was asked.
It was sworn on the Eider, with the rest of the peace, that traders of the Danes and of the Franks may cross the border with their goods and buy and sell unharmed. Twelve men of each people swore it.

The dam at Dorestat on a grey spring morning: a young clerk standing on a cask reading from a strip of parchment, shipmen half listening; in front, a thick-set Frankish count in a red cloak looking down into a small open boat.

A bare dune at the mouth of the Scheldt under a wide pale sky: a pile of driftwood covered with a cowhide; below it four boats drawn up on the sand, two of them flat river barges; a tired Frankish soldier and a farmer with a spear looking out to an empty sea.

A Danish landing crowded with long ships, bows to the shingle, men carrying sacks and coils of rope aboard and stepping masts; in front, a Dane with a gilded cloak pin talking down to a small Frisian boat; a still, bright evening.

A Frisian dwelling mound in spring sun, seen from the creek: turf houses on a green hump, washed wool over the fences, ewes and lambs on the salt grass; an old man with a staff and a woman with a distaff looking at the merchant; nothing on the northern horizon.

Seen from a small boat lying low among sandbanks: a horizon crowded from edge to edge with square sails and oars, a fleet passing along low islands in hard midday light; in the bow a boy shading his eyes, beside him an old Dane who is not surprised.
