On top of the mound at Emuthon under a low sky: a cloak spread on the grass with brooches, arm rings, a cup and a few pennies on it; an old law-speaker with a notched tally stick; women taking the pins from their shoulders; long ships on the strand below.

A grey strand at low water: a Dane of about forty seated on a sea chest holding up a small folding balance, silver in one pan and lead weights in the other; an old Frisian facing him; behind, twelve men sitting roped together beside beached long ships.

A river bank in high summer, dust in the air: soldiers and carts crowding to the water, sacks of bread passed down into boats, a dead ox lying in its yoke by the road with the carter standing over it; tents and spears along the far bank.

Inside the count's timber hall at Dorestat on an autumn afternoon, light from the door: an older Frankish lord in a travelling cloak seated in the high chair, a clerk writing at his side, the count standing with folded arms; a shipman in front of them, cap in hand.

A winter night at Dorestat: boats frozen in at the dam under snow, a fire in a storehouse doorway; round it a Frankish clerk, a young Frisian in sheepskin and a Saxon in a hooded cloak, each leaning toward the merchant from a different side.

The cliffs at Bononia at dusk from the sea: a tall old Roman tower in bands of red and pale stone, a fire just lit on its top throwing a path of light over dark water; new long ships at anchor below it; a small boat in front, her crew looking up.

The bank of the Scheldt at Ganda on a cold bright November morning: thirty new tarred ships in a row on the grass, an abbey behind; a very tall old man in a blue cloak, leaning on a stick, with his hand on a ship's stem; lords and monks at a distance; at the end of the row one shorter, deeper hull.

The green by the creek at Emuthon in early summer: the households of the mound standing in a ring with one gap in it, new-shorn sheep beyond, the old law-speaker in the middle with his staff, a widow with a boy of twelve; on the mound behind, a pile of wood under a hide.

A flat river bank in a cold spring wind: twelve Frankish lords on one side with a priest holding a small reliquary, twelve Danes on the other with weapons laid on the ground before them; between the two rows a merchant with a Saxon interpreter at his shoulder; horses and a wagon behind.
A man with no kin in harbour

A Gotland trader lies sick of a fever in a host's back room. His ship went east without him nine days ago; a ship does not wait on one man's fever. He has asked the host to find him a man with a boat of his own, who is not of his island and not a Svea. The host found you.
He pays, so he lies here. But he will not see the new moon, and he knows it. He has been asking for a stranger with a boat since yesterday. I do not know why a stranger.
Hegbjorn. Of Gotland. Sit where I can see your hands. A stranger is better: he has no cousin of mine to please.
My farm is Aikgard, half a morning in from the beach at Paviken. Thirty summers I went east for the writing silver. I did not bring it home to look at.
The storehouse with the stone footing. Stand at the south door post. Walk toward the tall stone with the ship cut on it. Twelve feet. Under the boards, a flat slab.
My brother Vivil holds the farm and knows there is silver in it. My daughter Ailikn knows I once walked her to a stone. Neither knows the feet. Vivil would only bury it deeper.
Forty marks, less one, in all. Carry the word to Ailikn. A third is the bringer's, that is the custom. Give me your hand on it and I will tell you the rest.
Give him your hand on it: his daughter shall have the word
Promise nothing, and pay the host for a bed by the fire and someone to sit with him
Hear him out and promise nothing

His hand is hot and dry and stronger than it looks. He does not let go until he has finished. 'In the east pasture old stones stand in the shape of a ship. The stern stone is the tallest. On its seaward side, an arm deep. That is the greater part, and no one alive knows it but you.' Then he asks for water and turns his face to the wall.

The host takes the pennies and moves him to the bench by the hearth, and his wife's mother sits down beside him with her spinning. The Gotlander watches you pay. 'So. You would not swear, and you paid. I have known men who did it the other way.' He says no more about silver.
You hear him to the end and give him nothing but a nod. He looks at you for a long time. 'Twelve feet,' he says again, 'toward the stone.' Whatever else he had to say, he keeps.
What he left

The Gotlander died in the night. The host has laid him in the outhouse and put his sea chest on the table: a folding scale in a bronze case, a bag of weights, a comb, and a stick of yew cut with runes on two sides. He wants his lodging paid and the room back.
He went before cockcrow, quietly. He asked what the wind was. I told him west. He said that was no use to him.
My wife's mother sat with him to the end, as you paid for. He gave her the stick to hold and then took it back.
Eight pennies for the bed and the broth. The chest covers it if nobody pays. A scale like that sells. The stick I would burn.
One of his own rowers was here last night, a Svea, off a boat that came back. He stood in my door and asked what the old man had said to the Frisian. I said I do not listen at sickbeds.
His people burn their dead, I am told. Wood costs. Otherwise he goes in the sand above the tide line with the other strangers.
Pay his lodging and the wood, burn him as his people do, and take the chest for his kin
Pay his lodging, take the chest for his kin, and leave the body to the host
Leave the chest for the lodging. You carry his words, and that is enough

The fire is lit on the shore at dusk, with the wind off the land. A Northman from the next berth comes and stands by it unasked, and says a verse his people say over the dead, the one about what does not die. Afterwards he says it again slowly so that you have it. You put the scale, the weights and the yew stick in your own chest. The host says he has seen kin do less.

The host counts the pennies twice and slides the chest across the table. The scale folds into a case no bigger than your palm. The stick is cut on two sides with runes and worn smooth where a thumb held it. They put him in the sand that afternoon. You are not there.

The host shrugs and carries the chest to the back. By evening a Dane has bought the scale. The stick goes with the comb for a cup of ale, to a man the host does not know. You have the dead man's words and nothing of his to show for them.
A stick of yew

The dead man's stick lies on the thwart beside his scale. It is a hand long, cut on two sides with runes, and worn smooth where a thumb has held it. Two of your men have seen it and have things to say.
I can read that. It's no great boast, mind, any man from north of the Eider can. Look how he cut it, deep, and without haste. A man doesn't cut a market tally that deep.
It is a dead man's word to his child. That is a debt, and we are carrying it. I would no more read it than open another man's purse.
Where I come from they say a man has in the next place what he put in the ground himself. Dig it up and you have made him poor.
Then he would not have told anyone the feet. He told. He wanted it dug.
Have it read aloud, before every man aboard
Spell it out yourself, at night, by the steering oar
Wrap it in the scale's cloth and carry it to his kin unread

He turns it to the light and reads with his thumb, a rune at a time. 'Stern stone. Sea side. Arm deep. Hegbjorn cut this.' Nobody says anything. Then the steersman says, 'Well. Now it is four men's secret, and that is safer than one man's.' He may be right.

Sixteen signs, and some of them do for three sounds. It takes you most of two night watches and a great deal of muttering. Stern. Stone. Sea. Side. Arm. Deep. And a name. You wrap the stick again before the watch changes.

Sixteen signs, and some of them do for three sounds. By the end of the watch you have 'stone' and what may be 'arm' or 'eagle', and a sore head. You know more runes than you did. You do not know what he cut.

You fold the stick into the cloth with the scale and put both at the bottom of your chest. The Northman lifts one shoulder. The Frisian, who has been watching your hands, goes back to his steering and looks easier than he did.
Asking on the beach

Paviken is a beach, a row of boat sheds and the smoke of forges. There is no wall and no reeve, and nobody asks what you carry. You ask a shipwright for the farm called Aikgard. He puts down his adze before he answers, which is not a good sign.
Hegbjorn's. So he is dead. A man does not send a Frisian to ask the way to his own gate.
Follow the stream up to the second ford and keep the ridge on your left hand. His brother Vivil holds the farm. A careful man. He has not sold a sheep he could keep in twenty years.
The daughter is Ailikn. Widowed two winters, one small boy. She lives with her mother's people, the farm with the three ash trees, nearer the shore. She does not ask her uncle for anything.
You are the second this moon. A Svea who rowed for Hegbjorn came off a boat and asked the same. He went up the stream and came down again the same day, not pleased.
Whichever gate you knock at first, the other will hear of it before night. It is not a large island.
Go to the farm and the brother first, as a guest should
Go to the daughter first, as the dead man asked
Stay a day on the beach, buy the wrights ale, and learn how Gotlanders inherit
You take the stream path in the morning. At the second ford a boy with a dog watches you cross and then runs, not toward Aikgard but toward the shore, where three ash trees stand over a roof.

The farm with the three ash trees is small and well kept. A woman of about twenty-five hears you out at the gate without asking you in, then fetches her cloak. 'We will go to my uncle's together. I will not have him say I heard it behind his back.'

Ale loosens shipwrights. A farm here is not cut up: brothers hold it together and the eldest speaks for it. Sons take after the father; where there are no sons, the daughter. Land does not leave the kin. Silver a man earned himself, abroad, is another matter, and they argue about it until the cask is empty. They also say, twice, that no one on this beach has tasted Rhine wine since last summer.
Aikgard

The farm lies half a morning in from the beach: a long house, a storehouse on a stone footing, sheep on thin grass over limestone, and a tall stone by the gate with a ship cut on it. Vivil sets ale and bread before you and asks nothing until you have eaten. Ailikn has walked over from her mother's people and sits by the door with her boy.
Eat first. A man who has come over the sea to my table can tell me my brother is dead when he has had bread.
He came to my gate before yours, uncle. I brought him here myself. Count that for me or against me as you like.
He came to the house first, as is right. I sent for you, niece, within the hour. Nobody will say I did not.
That is his scale. He let me hold the pans when I was small, and I was not to breathe on them.
Thirty summers he went east and I kept his fields with mine. What he brought home he ate at my table and laid under my roofs. It is the farm's silver.
He had one child. He rowed for that silver, uncle; you did not. If he sent a word over the sea, he sent it to someone.
You have been drinking with the wrights, I hear, and know our law now. Then you know that the farm is not divided. Whether a bowl of silver is the farm is what they could not tell you.
Ask the daughter to walk with you to the gate, and tell her alone
Tell the brother, who holds the farm and set the bread before you
Say it once, aloud, to both of them, and let them call neighbours to hear it

At the gate, under the stone with the ship on it, you tell her: the south door post, toward this stone, twelve feet, a slab. She looks at the storehouse and then at the house, where her uncle stands in the door. 'It is under his roof,' she says. 'So I shall have to dig it in front of him.' She does not sound sorry.

Vivil hears it with his eyes on the table. Then he gets up, walks to the storehouse door and stands looking at the floor. Ailikn takes her boy by the hand and goes without a word to anyone. When you leave, Vivil gives you a bundle of fleeces, because a guest is not sent off empty.

Vivil sends a boy to the two nearest farms, and you say it standing, before six people: the south door post, toward the tall stone, twelve feet, a slab under the boards. Nobody moves toward the storehouse. 'The day after tomorrow,' Vivil says, 'in daylight, with these same men.' Ailikn nods. It is the first thing they have agreed on. She brings you a crock of honey when you go.
Under the floor

The storehouse boards are up. Twelve feet from the south door post, toward the tall stone, there is a flat slab, and under the slab a bronze bowl with a wooden lid. Arm rings. Twisted rods. A bag of thin coins with writing on them and no face, many cut in half. It is a great deal of silver. It is not what he spoke of.
Fifteen marks, near enough. At my table, two winters back, he said forty less one. My brother did not say forty when he meant fifteen.
Nor did he keep all his eggs under one hen. He told me that often enough.
You told her and not me, Frisian, on my own ground. I do not forget it. But it came out of my floor, and it stays in my house until better men than us have spoken.
You told him and not me. He would have had it up by night if the neighbours had not seen you come. It was my father's hand that filled that bowl.
The thing meets when the hay is in. Until then the bowl stands on the cross beam, where all can see it and none can reach it without a ladder.
And you, Frisian, will be asked what he said. All of it. Be on the island.
Set up a scale on the door slab and call out every weight for both to hear
Ask for an earnest now, against the share of the man who brought the word
Stand in the door and ask for nothing yet

Ring by ring and bag by bag, with the beam level each time before you speak. Fifteen marks and three ounces. Vivil cuts a notch for each mark on one stick and Ailikn on another, and at the end they lay the sticks side by side. Then each of them puts an ounce in your pan, for the weighing, and neither looks at the other while doing it.

You say it plainly: the bringer's share is the custom, and you have a crew to feed. Vivil looks at Ailikn. Ailikn looks at the bowl. 'A mark and five ounces on account,' Vivil says, 'out of whichever of us wins.' He weighs it himself and is not mean with the beam.

You say it plainly, and it is the wrong morning for plain speaking. 'The hole is not cold,' Vivil says. He weighs out six ounces, with his thumb nowhere near the pan and his face like the slab. Ailikn says nothing at all.

You stand in the door and keep your hands in your belt. When the bowl is on the cross beam and the boards are down, Vivil walks you to the gate and puts two cakes of wax in your arms. 'For the house's candles,' he says, though his own house burns tallow. Ailikn sees it and, for once, seems to think well of him.
Six oars

A six-oared boat has come out from behind a skerry and lies across your bow. No sail, no cargo, six men, and the oars held level. The one in the stern stands up. You have heard of him twice already: in a host's doorway, and on the beach at Paviken.
Frisian! Torkel is my name. Six summers at Hegbjorn's third oar. You sat by his bed. I stood in the door, where rowers stand.
He paid his men when the ship came home. He did not come home. I am owed half a mark, and his brother set a dog on me for asking.
So. You went up to his farm and you came down again. What rides under your deck boards?
Pay him what the dead man owed him: half a mark, weighed over the gunwale
Heave to, lift the deck boards, and tell him who has the silver
Put her before the wind. Six oars tire; a sail does not

You weigh it on the dead man's kind of scale, with both boats rising and falling, and it takes three tries. Torkel bites one piece, laughs at himself and puts it away. 'Six summers, and a Frisian pays me. If they ask at the thing what he said in that room, send for me. I heard him name the girl.' The six oars back water and let you by.

You lift the boards yourself. He looks at wine, wool and bilge water for some time. 'On a cross beam,' he says, when you tell him. 'Under the brother's roof. Then I will never see an ounce of it.' He sits down. The boat pulls away slowly, like men going home from a bad market.

You lift the boards. Two of his men come over the gunwale anyway and go through the hold with their hands. They find no bowl. They find your purse, and Torkel takes out of it what he says he is owed, less than he says, and gives the purse back. 'Now we are even, you and the dead man and I.' It is one way of counting.

The sail fills and she heels and goes. They row hard for the length of ten ship's lengths and gain, and then for another ten and do not, and then the oars come up one after another. Torkel is still standing in the stern when you lose him against the skerries. He will know your sail again.

The wind drops under the land just as the sail fills. For a while it is six oars against a slack sheet, and they come close enough to throw. A stone the size of a loaf takes one of your men on the shoulder before the breeze comes back. Nobody is laughing when you clear the point.
The only witness

The hay is in and the thing has met on the slope above the farms: sixty free men sitting on the grass, their spears stuck upright behind them. The bronze bowl stands on a hide in the middle of the ring. Vivil stands on one side of it and Ailikn on the other. An old man who knows the law by heart asks who heard the dead man speak, and every head turns to the Frisian.
We have no king here to ask, and we do not want one. We have what was said and who heard it. You heard it. Stand where all can see you.
The farm is one. My brother and I never divided it. What lay under the farm's floor is the farm's, and I speak for the farm.
My father had no son. What a man earns with his own oar goes to his own child. My uncle has had thirty summers of my father's fields. I ask only for my father's silver.
I rowed for him six summers and stood in the door of that room. I am a Svea and nobody's cousin here. I heard him say his daughter's name. More I did not hear.
A stranger's word weighs what the stranger weighs. Say less than you heard and we shall know it by winter. It is not a large island.
Say his words as he said them, the hard ones too
Say he named his daughter and no one else
Say he spoke of the farm's silver, and the farm is Vivil's

You say all of it: that he named the farm his, that he said his brother held it, that he said to carry the word to his daughter, and that he said Vivil would only bury it deeper. There is some laughter at that, and Vivil goes red and then, slowly, almost smiles. The old man speaks with four others and comes back. Ten marks to the child. Five to the farm that kept it. Three ounces to the stranger, 'who said a thing that did him no good with either side'.

You say he named his daughter, and you stop there. The old man waits a while to see if there is more. There is not. All fifteen marks go to Ailikn, who pays you two ounces before the whole ring. Vivil pulls his spear out of the turf and walks home without waiting for the other cases.

You say he spoke of the farm's silver, in the farm's storehouse, and you stop there. The old man looks at you for longer than is comfortable. All fifteen marks go to the farm. Vivil weighs you out a mark that evening, generously, and Ailikn passes you on the path as if you were a fence post.
Fifteen of forty

The evening after the thing. Fifteen marks came out of the floor, and at this table two winters ago the dead man spoke of forty less one. In the east pasture, a bowshot beyond the fence, old stones stand in the shape of a ship, bow to the sea. Sheep graze between them. Nobody at the table looks that way, because nobody at the table has any reason to.
Four and twenty marks. That is the weight of a grown man's life on this island, in silver, and it is lying somewhere on my land laughing at me.
He walked me to a stone once, when I was six, and said, remember this stone. I have tried every stone on the farm since. There are a great many stones on this farm.
If it were mine I would not put it back under anything. Twenty-four marks is a ship of sixteen paces with her sail, and a cargo to fill her. Silver in a hole does not have young.
Silver in a hole does not sink either, boy. Ask on the beach how many ships came home last summer and how many went out.
Frisian. You have told us what he said about the floor. Was the floor all he said?
Tell Ailikn where the rest lies, and her alone
Tell Vivil where the rest lies: it is his pasture
Say it at the table, to all three, and say what you would do with such silver
Say you know of no more than the floor, and walk out to look at the evening

You find her at the well after dark and say it, or put the yew stick in her hand and let her read it with her thumb. The stern stone. The seaward side. An arm deep. She is quiet for a moment. 'That stone. I sat on that stone to eat my bread.' Then: 'The night after tomorrow, before light. Bring two men who do not talk.'

You walk the fence with Vivil at dusk and say it, or give him the yew stick and let him read it. He looks out at the stones for some time. 'Under my own sheep,' he says. 'Thirty summers.' He does not ask you to help him dig. He asks you to stay away from the east pasture until he sends for you.

You say it at the table: the stern stone, the seaward side, an arm deep. Then, before anyone can stand up, you say the rest: that it has been in a hole for years and done nothing; that Ottar wants a ship and Paviken builds them; that you can fill her with what the east wants and sell what she brings back on the Rhine. Three shares. It is quiet for a long time. 'He believed him at the thing,' Ailikn says at last, to her uncle. 'So did you.' Vivil says he will sleep on it. He does not say no, and on this island that is a great deal.

You say the floor was all you can tell them. Ailikn looks at you a moment longer than the others. Then the talk turns to the hay. You go out, and your feet take you along the fence toward the east pasture, where the old stones are black against the last of the light.
Her father's daughter

Before light, at the stern stone, on the seaward side, an arm deep: a second bowl, bigger than the first, sealed with pitch. Ailikn has your scale set up on a fallen stone beside it before the sun is over the trees. Her uncle stands at the pasture fence and comes no nearer.
Twenty-four marks and an ounce over. He was never out by more than an ounce in his life.
There is a shore strip next to my mother's people that has wanted a buyer since the winter. And a half share in a ship at Paviken. My son will not row at another man's oar.
On my land! Under my sheep! Thirty summers I kept his fields!
A third is the bringer's. Eight marks. I have weighed it twice; weigh it again yourself. And my storehouse is dry, and nearer the beach than his. Leave what you like in it.
Take the third she weighs out: eight marks
Take four marks and furs from his store, and ask her to carry the other four to the fence herself

Eight marks, in rings and cut coin, weighed three times in all. Your men carry it down to the boat in two bags. Ailikn buys the shore strip before the first frost and her half of a ship before the second. She keeps a corner of her storehouse for the Frisian house from that day. Vivil does not come to the launching. He is said to have dug over half the east pasture that autumn and found a dead sheep.

She looks at you as her father must have looked at a bad bargain. Then she takes four marks in her apron and walks to the fence, and you do not hear what is said there. It takes a long time. When she comes back Vivil is with her, carrying nothing, and he gives you his hand, and says that a man who throws away four marks to mend another family's fence may tie up at Paviken any winter he likes and name Aikgard to whoever asks. She adds two timbers of marten from her father's own store, 'so that nobody says a daughter of Hegbjorn's paid short'.
The farm's silver

Vivil dug alone, at night, and would not have a lamp. In the morning there is a pitch-sealed bowl on his table and fresh turf at the stern stone. He has weighed out five marks for you. The rest he has already carried out of the house, and he has earth on his knees again.
Five marks. A third is for the man who finds. You did not find; you carried. Five is fair for carrying, and I have added wax.
The rest is where a bad year can find it and nobody else can. Not under that stone. I am not a fool. My son will be told when I am as sick as my brother was.
The farm has a strip of shore north of the wrights' sheds. Twenty paces of it are yours, for a boathouse, while your house keeps coming. I will say so before neighbours.
My niece has ten marks of the floor by the thing's own word, or she has nothing by it. Either way the thing has spoken. I owe her a place at my table. I have never denied her that.
Take the five marks, the wax and the shore strip, and ask no more
Take them, and say across his table that a brother's child is owed a marriage portion from it

Five marks, three cakes of wax, and twenty paces of shingle marked with four stones before two neighbours. It is a good morning's pay. On the stream path you meet Ailikn coming up with her boy. She has heard; everyone has. She steps off the path to let you pass and does not answer your greeting. Vivil lives eleven more winters. Whether he was ever as sick as his brother, and whom he told, nobody on the beach can say.

He goes red to the ears. He says a Frisian might mind his own fence. Then he says nothing for the time it takes to drink a horn of ale. Then he gets up, goes out, comes back with earth on his knees for the third time that day, and puts two marks on the table. 'For when she marries again. Not before. Tell her it was my thought.' You tell her it was his thought. She does not believe it, and takes it.

He hears you to the end. 'You have your five marks and your shingle,' he says. 'Do not make me weigh them again.' The neighbours look at the rafters. You take what is yours and go. On the stream path Ailikn steps aside for you and does not answer your greeting.
The stern stone

The ship of stones lies in the east pasture with its bow to the sea, as it has lain longer than anyone can say. The stern stone is the tallest and leans a little. The turf on its seaward side has not been cut in years. From here you can see the farm's smoke, and nobody can see you.
Stern stone, sea side, arm deep. That is this one. We are standing on four and twenty marks, and the only two men who ever knew it are you and a man who is ash now.
Forty less one, he said, and fifteen came up. I'm slow at sums, but even I can do that one. The rest is somewhere under this island, and so's a great deal else, they tell me. Good stones, these.
Before you say anything, hear me. He keeps two dogs. Two. The nights are short at this time of year, and a stranger found digging here is not asked his reasons.
You walk a long way to look at old stones, Frisian. My father did the same, the night before he sailed. I never knew what he saw in them.
My uncle and I have agreed on one thing this year. Five marks from the floor are yours, for the carrying. And this ring, whole. He wore it. Do not cut it.
Lay your hand on the stone, and go down to the boat
Leave it, and give the yew stick to her small son, to keep until he can read it
Send to the boat for the spade and two men, and wait for dark

The stone is warm from the day. You take your hand away and go down to the boat with five marks and a dead man's arm ring, and you do not look back at the pasture more than twice. The sheep graze there for as long as there are sheep at Aikgard. Whatever lies under the stern stone lies there still, an arm deep, on the seaward side.

The boy is four. He takes the stick in both hands and looks at the cuts. 'It is your grandfather's,' you say. 'When you can read it, read it by yourself.' Ailikn starts to speak and does not. At the gate she says, 'Any winter you are caught in these waters, the three ash trees. And my uncle says the same of Aikgard, though he will say it worse.' The boy is already trying the stick against every stone in the yard.
You send a man down the stream path for the spade. It is a long evening. The light goes slowly at this time of year, and the stones seem to stand closer together as it goes.
An arm deep

No moon. The spade goes in on the seaward side of the stern stone, and an arm down it rings on bronze. The bowl is sealed with pitch and takes two men to lift. Up at the farm a dog has started, stopped, and started again.
Careful with it. That is the weight of a grown ewe. So it is two men, and slowly, or one bag at a time and three goings. I cannot make it less. It is a long way to the beach either way.
That dog has our wind. Hear him. If he is loosed we are four strangers in a field with a spade. I have been found in better company, and I would sooner not be found in this.
You gave the old man your hand, I think. Yes. You did. I remember it, so that one of us does.
It is yours to say, not mine. All of it, some of it, or none. But choose quickly. The hole is the only thing here that will not be missed by morning.
Take all of it and be at sea by first light
Take a finder's third, eight marks and one ring, and lay the turf back over the rest
Look at it, seal it again, and fill the hole

Two men on the bowl and two ahead, down the stream bed where the dogs cannot follow a scent. You are afloat before the east is grey. Nineteen marks and more, once the pitch is off, and a twisted neck ring as thick as a thumb that every smith in the north would know. By noon there is a hole at Aikgard and a spade-cut turf, and by evening the whole island knows who walked out to the stones. Do not winter on Gotland.

The dog is loosed while the bowl is still at the fence. It goes over, the lid goes, and four and twenty marks go into the long grass in the dark. You get one bag to the boat, and a man with a torn leg, and a twisted neck ring somebody had the wit to put on his own arm. Behind you there are torches in the east pasture. Vivil will have the rest picked out of the grass by sunrise, and he will know to an ounce what is missing.

You weigh eight marks by feel and a lamp held under a cloak, take one twisted ring for the trouble, and press the pitch back with your thumbs. The turf goes down in the order it came up. By morning the dew has closed over it. Sixteen marks lie there yet. Nobody on the island knows. Three of your men do, and you will hear of it some night when the ale is strong and the pay is late.

You lift the lid a hand's breadth. Rings, coiled one inside another like sleeping snakes, and the thin coins poured over them. You look for as long as it takes to say a short prayer, and then you seal it and fill the hole and tread the turf. In the morning Vivil and Ailikn weigh you five marks for the carrying, and Ailikn gives you her father's arm ring, whole. They think you look tired. The dog knows you and is quiet.
Silver that floats

A new ship lies on the beach at Paviken, home from the east three days, her sail of chequered wool spread on the shingle to dry. Skins are stacked in a new booth above the tide line, and the booth has a Frisian's mark cut over the door. Ottar, Ailikn and Vivil are waiting by the scale. Nobody has dug anything on Aikgard this year except a well.
Out by the long island, in over the lake, back before the first night frost. One man lost to a fever, none to the sea. Your wine went for twice its weight in skins. I should have taken more.

Thirty-nine marks went into her keel, her sail and her cargo. She has brought home more than twice that in skins, wax and silver, and she still floats. I have weighed it three times. A hole never did that.
A ship can sink. I said so and I say so. But I have counted it too, and I will leave the farm's share in her one more summer. One.
A third of the gain is yours, as we said at my father's table. And the booth, while you keep coming. Give me your hand on next summer and I will sail with your goods under my own.
Take your third of the voyage, and give your hand on next summer's
Leave most of your third in the ship for another summer, and take the sable
Take your third in silver, keep the booth, and swear to nothing further

Nine marks of silver and a little over, a timber of sable, two of marten, three cakes of wax, and Ottar's hand, which is as hard as his uncle's was and a good deal cooler. Ailikn cuts three notches in the booth's door post, one for each share. Vivil watches her do it and says the post was sound before. Next spring the ship goes east with Rhine wine under her boards and a Frisian tally stick beside the Gotland one.

You take the sable and two and a half marks to pay your men, and leave the rest in her. Ottar is so pleased that he forgets to be a Gotlander about it. Vivil gives you a long look, the look of a man who has found another fool to share his risk, and then, for the first time, sets ale before you without being the host.

Twelve and a half marks, weighed out on the shingle. Ottar is sorry and does not hide it. Ailikn says only that the booth is yours while you keep coming, since that was said at the table, and that a third share in the ship will not be hard to sell on this beach now that people have seen her come home.
On Gotland they say Hegbjorn of Aikgard's silver was under an old stone all the time, and that his daughter had it up before her uncle was awake. She has bought shore and half a ship.
On Gotland they say Vivil of Aikgard dug up his dead brother's silver one night and buried it again the next, and that not even his dog knows where.
On Gotland they say Hegbjorn of Aikgard spoke of forty marks and left fifteen. His kin have turned over half the farm. The Frisian who brought the word said the floor was all he knew.

On Gotland they say a Frisian who came as a dead man's messenger walked out to the old stones at Aikgard by night with a spade. There is a hole there now. His sail is known on every beach of the island.

At Paviken a new ship is home from the east: built with a dead man's silver, steered by his brother's son, a third of her a Frisian's. There is a Frisian booth on the beach. The old men say it will not last.

A Gotland ship in from the east road had Rhine wine aboard and a Frisian's tally stick beside her master's. They say his house has a booth on the beach at Paviken, which no outland man has had before.

A low back room in a harbour host's house, late afternoon light through a smoke hole: a grey, big-boned Gotlander of fifty-five under a sheepskin on a straw bed, gripping a Frisian merchant's hand; a folding scale and a yew stick on the chest beside him; the host in the doorway.

A harbour shore at dusk, wind off the land: a small pyre burning above the tide line, a Northman standing by it with his hood back; in front, on a table by the host's door, an open sea chest with a scale in a bronze case, a bag of weights, a comb and a rune-cut stick.

Aboard the small boat at sea on a grey, steady day: a broad dark-bearded Northman holding a short yew stick to the light and reading it with his thumb; a broad Frisian steersman looking away over the water; the folded scale on the thwart between them.

Paviken on a bright windy morning: a shingle beach, boat sheds, forge smoke, a half-planked hull on the slip; a Gotland shipwright in a leather apron who has just laid his adze on the strake, pointing inland up a stream.

Inside a Gotland long house at midday, hearth smoke under the roof: a heavy, careful farmer of fifty setting bread and an ale bowl before the merchant; by the open door a young widow in a strap dress with oval brooches, a small boy against her knee; through the door a storehouse on a stone footing and a tall picture stone.

A storehouse with its floor boards stacked against the wall, daylight from the south door: a hole under a lifted limestone slab, a bronze bowl with silver arm rings and a spilled bag of thin coins, many cut in half; the farmer kneeling on one side, his niece standing on the other, neighbours in the doorway.

A low Baltic skerry coast under a white sky, a light wind: a narrow six-oared boat lying across the bow of the small Frisian boat, oars held level; a fair-bearded Svea of thirty standing in her stern with one hand out, palm up.

A grassy slope above farms in late summer afternoon light, the sea a line behind: some sixty free men sitting in a ring with spears stuck upright behind them; in the middle a bronze bowl on a hide, the farmer on one side, the widow on the other, an old white-haired man with a staff, and the Frisian merchant standing alone.

A farm table by the open door at dusk: the farmer, his niece and his son of twenty-two leaning on their elbows; through the door, beyond a pasture fence, a ship setting of standing stones black against a yellow sky, sheep among them, and the merchant looking that way while nobody else does.

The stone ship at first light, mist in the pasture: the widow kneeling at a small folding scale set on a fallen stone, a pitch-sealed bronze bowl open beside her full of coiled silver rings; a fresh hole at the foot of the tall stern stone; her uncle a dark figure at the fence, hands on the top rail.

The farm table in early morning light: an empty pitch-smeared bowl, five small heaps of ring silver and three cakes of wax; the farmer standing behind it with earth on both knees and a spade against the door post; through the door, fresh-cut turf at the foot of a leaning stone.

The stone ship in the east pasture on a long northern summer evening: the merchant with one hand flat on the tall leaning stern stone, uncut turf at its foot; a Norse hand a few paces off with his arms folded; far behind, the farm's smoke, and a woman and a small boy at the fence.

The same stones on a moonless night, seen only by a lamp held under a cloak: two men lifting a pitch-sealed bronze bowl out of a hole at the stern stone, a spade stuck in the turf, the merchant looking over his shoulder toward one small red light at the farm.

Paviken beach on a clear early-autumn day: a new clinker ship drawn up on the shingle, her chequered sail spread to dry; a new timber booth above the tide line with skins stacked inside and a mark cut over its door; a young skipper, the widow with a tally stick and the old farmer with folded arms, waiting by a scale.
Sails in Frisia
A fisherman from the outer coast has rowed two days to sell nothing. He has seen a fleet of the Danes come in among the islands, and smoke behind it.
Long ships, low, with the shields along the side. I stopped counting at thirty because I had started to row. There was smoke on two terps before I lost the land.
There used to be a fire kept ready on the dune and a count's man to light it. Since the emperor's sons took the emperor, the count's men have had other fires to see to.
They did not stay to rob fishermen. They were asking the way. A fleet that asks the way is going to a place, and there is one place up that river worth forty ships.
Nobody on the dams has heard it. A cask of wine is being argued over two berths down, at some length.
He says their swords were good ones. You sold good ones north, once. You do not ask him about the marks.
Take his word to the dams at Dorestat, now, as he gave it
Give him ale and bread and ask it all twice: how many, how laden, which mouth. Then carry it
Finish your business first. Frisia is wide, and fishermen see fleets every spring
You cast off within the hour with a fisherman's word and nothing to hang it on: many ships, some smoke. It is what you have. The dams are a day away.

The second telling is better than the first. Forty hulls or near it, riding light, so they have not filled them yet. They lay in the Vlie on the Thursday. A man could swear to that, and you may have to.
You finish your selling. It was a fair price. The fisherman tells the next boat, and the one after, and by the time you come home his story will be there before you, a little larger.
A fisherman's story
An hour's walk of open bank, a storehouse on every dam, and not so much as a ditch between the river and the richest market in the north. The dams are busy with the summer.
The word reached the dams without you, by a herring boat, two days ago. It has been well laughed at since.
The emperor has been put down by his sons and set up again since last harvest, and one son is still in the field. If I send to say a fisherman saw ships, who do you think will read it?
Forty. Riding light. In the Vlie on the Thursday. That is not a fisherman's story, that is a count. Say it again slowly and I will have it cut on a stick.
I have buried my silver twice in my life and dug it up once. I am not going looking for a spade because a man who sells eels has seen a sail.
In my father's day two hundred ships lay in Frisia and took a hundred pounds of silver, and not one of them came up this river. It is a long river. That is what it is for.
The rich will do as they please with a warning. The poor have no boats. If it is true, tell me today, because it takes me three days to move people who own nothing.
Swear to the king's agent: the count of ships, the day, the mouth they lay in
Cry it on the dams yourself, storehouse by storehouse
Tell the priest, and the women who know which of the poor are truly poor
Say no more. Buy three bolts from a nervous man at twenty pennies the bolt

He has it cut on a stick and sends a rider to Nijmegen, who will arrive too late and be believed afterwards. What matters is that the agent starts loading the king's own chest. The dams see that, and draw their own conclusion.

The first six laugh. The seventh is a woman who was a child on the coast in the year of the two hundred ships. She starts carrying her loom to the boat while you are still talking, and after that it goes down the bank faster than you can walk.

By the fourth dam they have a name for you. It is the name of a marsh bird that shouts before rain. Your own crew hear it and look at their feet. But you said it on every dam, and every dam will remember who did.
By evening the plate is in a farm cart under a load of reeds, and the women are going from door to door among the people who have nothing. Nobody on the dams notices. Nobody on the dams ever does.
He sells you three bolts at less than half their worth and thanks you for it. He has heard something and does not want to say what. Neither do you.
They are past Traiectum
A boy comes running down the bank road from the Traiectum side. They are past the bishop's town with their masts down, rowing. They will be here with the morning.
Half the dams are already empty. Boats have been going up the Lek for three days with looms, casks and children, and the farms inland are full of people who do not know how to milk.
The dams are full. Men who laughed four days ago are throwing cloth into boats that are already too deep, and shouting at each other for the way out.
I have twelve men and a dam four paces wide with water on both sides. They can only come at it from the front. Stand with me, or get out of my light.
I will not tell you it is likely. I will tell you I am too old and too fat to run, and my father built this.
Some of the blades coming up the river were forged on this river. You would know the marks, if you were close enough to read them.
The ships built here on the northern pattern are gone up the Lek already, every one. Nothing on this bank could row like that a lifetime ago.
Load what she will carry, take the neighbour's children, and run up the Lek tonight
Put the house's chest in the ground at De Heul and lie in the alders to watch
Stand on the dam head with Thiadlef's twelve men
You row all night against the stream with four children asleep on the cloth. At first light there is smoke behind you, a thin straight line of it, and one of the children asks whose house that is.

You count thirty-eight hulls from the alders. They work down the dams like men unloading a ship: no hurry, nothing dropped. Nobody looks at a graveyard. By night you have a riddle in your head about a thing that men dig for and hide again, and you know its answer.

A man foraging for pigs walks onto your hand. You leave your cloak and some skin with him and go through the marsh on your belly. The chest is still under its alder. So, for a week, is the feeling in your ribs.

They try the dam head once, find it costs two men, and go to the next dam, where it costs nothing. That is all. Thiadlef's store stands in a row of ash, and there is an arm ring on the planks that nobody comes back for. He tells you a riddle about a shield while his hands stop shaking.

It lasts as long as it takes to say a paternoster. You go into the ditch with a cut you do not feel until evening, and Thiadlef's men pull you out on the far side. The store burns. He says you stood there, and he says it to everyone.
What the fleet left
This year the heathen men came by Traiectum to Dorestat. Some of the people they killed, some they carried off, and a part of the place they burned.
Fewer are dead than might be. The boats that went up the Lek are coming back down full of people, and the ships went home lighter than they came for. They are saying on the dams whose word it was.
The plate of the upper church is back on its altar. It spent the week at Rijswijk in a farm cart, under reeds, and the people with no boats spent it in the same barn.
Your chest is where you left it, under an alder nobody would look at twice. You leave it there. It seems to like the place.
On your own plot the roof is gone from the store and the posts stand. The well is full of somebody's cooking pots.
They took my Hildswith off the bank road. Fourteen at Martinmas. A man saw her put into the third ship, alive and shouting. I am told that is good news.
They sell at Sliesthorp. Everyone knows it. Our own men trade there every summer, and when the bench comes out they look at their feet.
I have a dam head, forty paces of good oak post, and no husband to lie at it. I will not sell it this year. Ask me after the next one.
Tell Thiadlef you will ask after the girl at Sliesthorp
Give thirty pennies for shrouds and bread, and help carry
Buy what is offered behind the alehouse: a silver cup with a cross filed off it, ninety pennies
He nods once. He does not thank you, because you have not done it yet. He tells you what she was wearing, and that she counts things when she is frightened.
You carry eleven to the graves at De Heul before dark. The widow walks beside you for the last three and tells you each one's name and what he owed, so that somebody will know.
It is good silver and heavy. The man who sells it found it in the reeds, he says. The reeds have been generous this week. You wrap it in sailcloth and put it under the bottom boards.
Cloth with the seal still on it
On the landing a Dane sells Frisian cloth by the bolt, a Dorestat seal of lead still hanging from one of them. Behind the cloth, on a bench, sit the people who came in the same ships.
Good cloth. From the Rhine. I did not ask it how it came here, and it has not complained.
That one spins, and she has all her teeth. Her father is a rich man, she says. They all say it. Now and then it is true, and then I am glad I listened.
The third ship. Tell my father it was the third ship. I have a knot in my belt for every day, and I am not going to say how many.
King Horik had no part in it. When the emperor's house fights itself, men sail where they like, and a king cannot stand on every beach. I am told to say so to Franks. You will do.
The king has sent men to the emperor to say the fleets are not his. He also wants to know who killed his last messengers near Cologne. Both things are true. Only one of them is being asked about.
Two Dorestat skippers are selling wine thirty paces off. They have seen the bench. They are very busy with a cask.
Weigh out his price for the girl: a hundred and eighty pennies' weight
Bargain in his own tongue: a father's price, not a market's. A hundred and ten
Buy nothing. Drink with the king's man and ask when ships like those sail again

He weighs it twice on his own scales and once on yours. The girl gets up off the bench without being told, walks to your boat and sits down in the bow facing the water. She does not speak until the landing is out of sight. Then she asks whether the store burned.
In his own tongue he is a different man: a farmer with a debt and two daughters. He comes down seventy and throws in the belt she counted on. She is in your bow before the silver is in his bag.

He drinks your ale and tells you what any Dane could: they go when the sowing is done, they go where it was easy, and nothing on the Rhine was hard. They will go while the emperor's sons keep him busy. The girl watches you leave. You remember what she was wearing.
The third ship
Thiadlef is on his dam head before your rope is. He does not look at you at all until the girl is ashore.
I counted wrong by one. There was a day I slept through.
My father owed nobody on this river, and it took him forty years to arrange. I have owed you since you tied up. I do not intend it to last until dinner.
Here is the price twice over, counted. Or the price once and my order for Rhine wine, which is worth more if you can carry. Choose one and let me sleep.
My father would have asked what you want from me. I am asking what it cost. It is the only difference between us, and I am told it is an improvement.
Take what he counts out: the price twice over
Take the price once, and his order for ten casks of Rhine wine at half as much again
Take nothing. Tell him it was a neighbour's errand
He counts three hundred and sixty pennies onto a cask head and breathes out. You are quits, and he is plainly happier that way. The girl waves from the door of the store.
He counts out the price and cuts a tally for ten casks at half as much again as the market gives. A man does not order wine from someone he means to go on resenting.

He looks at you as if you had hit him. Next morning his own steersman is sitting on your gunwale with his sea chest: a man who can take a boat down the Lek by night with the mast down. Thiadlef has sent him for a season. He has not sent a message with him.
Earth or silver
The men who hold dam heads meet in the upper church, because it is the only roof big enough. There are three opinions, and each of them costs something.
The burned plots are roofed again with new thatch, very yellow. Everyone agrees that they will come again when the sowing is done. Nobody agrees on anything else.
This year the Northmen fell on Dorestat a second time and laid it waste. The emperor was much angered, and came to Aachen, and ordered guards set along the coasts.
The emperor has ordered the coast watched. He ordered it from Aachen. Aachen is nine days from the sea, and the order is travelling at the speed of a bishop.

A ditch and a bank from the old fort to the lower graves. A gate on the bank road. Twelve men who stay awake. Cologne has Roman walls. We have alder posts and a debt to God, and I know which I would rather stand behind.
They want silver. So next time we meet them at the river with silver on a cloth, and we keep our roofs. I have reckoned it. It is cheaper than earth, and nobody has to dig.
A third opinion is not spoken in church. It is a barge at the upstream end of the bank, loading a loom, with her head toward the IJssel.
The shipmen's common chest, a penny a voyage these forty years, votes its whole weight for the bank. Your share is the same, but the ditch will reach the river.
You know what the Danes say about it themselves: they go where it was easy. You say so. It is the only thing said all day that makes Thiadlef stop talking.
Put in the first share for the ditch and the bank: three hundred pennies
Start sending looms, scales and stock up the river to Daventre, a boatload a month
Do neither. Keep the stock short and the boat loaded, and sleep aboard from Pentecost to Lammas

Your silver goes into the priest's box with nine other houses' and the digging starts at the fort end on Monday. The king's agent, who cannot give leave for a bank, finds he can halve the toll of men who are too busy digging to trade. Leave is the palace's to give. Somebody should go to Nijmegen.

The first boatload goes up before the week is out: the big loom, the spare scales, the good cloth. On the dams they watch it go and say nothing to your face. The bench by the fire in the alehouse is a little narrower than it was.
You sell down to what one boat can lift in an hour, and move your bedding aboard. Most of the bank does the same. A market that sleeps in its boats still looks like a market from the river.
A gate on the king's ground
The palace on its hill above the Waal is half empty: the emperor is wherever his sons are. A clerk in the gatehouse has the keeping of what may and may not be built between here and the sea.
A bank I could overlook. A gate is another matter. A gate can be shut against a Dane, and it can be shut against a count. The palace likes to know which the builders had in mind.
You are the one who came with the count of ships in the first summer. It was written down. Very little that is true gets written down here, so we remember it when it does.
There is oak in the king's wood marked for a bridge that will not be built while the emperor's sons are talking to each other. Oak does not improve by lying.
The emperor forgives everyone, in time. He also arrives everywhere, in time. If your town means to be standing when he does, I would not wait for him.
Ask leave for the bank as the man who brought the warning in the first summer
Ask leave, with sixty pennies for the clerk's trouble
Ask nothing. Hear what has been ordered for the coast, and go home

He writes four lines, reads them to you in Latin and then in Frankish, and seals them with the count's seal. Six loads of the bridge oak go down to your boat. He says a gate built of the king's timber is the king's gate, and nobody can complain of that, least of all the king.
The sixty pennies vanish without a sound. The leave is four lines and a seal. He finds three loads of oak that were, on reflection, marked for nothing in particular.

What has been ordered is a watch on every river mouth, kept by the counts, who are all somewhere else with their men. You go home with that. A bank needs no leave to be dug, only to be defended afterwards in a court.
More than twice your hands

Sails under the land to the south, more than you can count on your hands twice, standing in for the mouth of the Maas. One of them hangs back, low in the water, and turns her head toward you. She has more oars than you have men.
Witla is behind those dunes: a market, a landing, a pilot's house. Beyond it is the Scheldt and the fort at Andoverpis. From there to the Lek is two days for men who row like that.
You have casks. We have a thirst and a long row ahead. Sell, and nobody on this water need be unhappy today.
Or run, if you like. We are not here for one small boat. But my rowers are bored, and I cannot answer for bored men.
Put about and run for the Lek with the word: they are on the Maas
Drop the sail, lie under the dunes and count them as they pass
Lie to, sell him two casks of ale at three times the price, and ask where they are bound

She chases for the length of a psalm and gives it up: a small boat with the wind free is not worth a bored crew's sweat. You are in the Lek two tides ahead of them, shouting it at every landing you pass.

She has you inside the hour. They take your bread, your water cask and a man's good cloak, laugh at the rest, and let you go. It is very nearly friendly. The word reaches the Lek a tide behind the smoke.
Mast down, in the lee of the dune, you count twenty-six. By evening there is smoke where Witla was, and by the next evening a second smoke further south. You know before any bishop does.

He pays in cut silver, three times the price, and does not haggle. Witla first, he says, then the fort on the Scheldt, then the Rhine as usual: he says 'as usual'. You have sixty pennies' weight more than you had, and it sits oddly in the bag.
The third summer
Nobody on the dams says 'if' any more. They say 'when they come', and name the feast. Wine and cloth go for whatever a man will give who is fool enough to keep them here.
This year the Northmen burned Andoverpis, and Witla, the market by the mouth of the Maas, and came again to Dorestat and into Frisia.
They remember whose boat came up the Lek shouting, two tides ahead of the smoke. There were very few on the bank road when the ships came, and nothing in the stores worth the row.
The ditch is dug from the fort to the bank road, and the bank is up to a man's chest. There is no gate. A bank with no gate is a hill with a road through it. I need the second share before Pentecost.
And the gate will be the king's oak, hung by the king's leave. I have read the four lines to every man who said it could not be done. Some of them asked me to read it again.
We talked about a bank, two summers ago. There was a great deal of agreement. I buried nineteen people on the strength of it.
I have the tribute chest half full already, from the houses that would sooner pay than dig. Silver on a cloth at the river. They will take it and go. They are merchants too, in their way.
Half your house is on the IJssel already. What is left here fits in two boatloads, and one of them is the cat.
A cask of Rhine wine that was sixty pennies at Easter is offered at twenty-five, on the dam, by a man who keeps looking downstream.
Pay the second share: the gate, the watch-house and twelve men's bread. Five hundred pennies
Take the rest up the river now, and leave the store to the mice
Fill the store while others empty theirs: a hundred and fifty pennies buys what was worth four hundred. Bury the chest first
Change nothing: stock short, boat loaded, one eye on the river

The gate is hung at midsummer: two leaves of oak, a bar a man can hardly lift, and a watch-house over it with a horn. Twelve men draw bread to stay awake in it. From the river the place looks, for the first time, like something that might answer back.

Two boatloads, and the door left open so that nobody need break it. Whatever you paid toward the bank stays in the bank. Thiadlef watches you cast off and says the IJssel is a fine river for people who like Saxons.

The fleet comes, takes what is easy, and does not come as far as your dam. At Martinmas every store on the bank is empty but yours, and the men who sold to you at twenty-five buy back at seventy. You do not smile until you are indoors.

They come before Lammas, and a full store is the first thing they find. What they cannot carry they burn. You watch it from the alders with the smell of your own wine in the smoke. The chest is in the ground. It is all of the house that is not ash.
You change nothing. When they come there is an hour's warning, your boat is loaded, and what burns of yours is a roof. It is not a way to grow rich. It is a way to be here next year.
The gate was shut

This year the heathen men took Walcheren and killed its count, and came up the river to Dorestat as in other years. There was a ditch there now, and a bank, and a gate on the bank road, and it was shut.

They lie two days below the lower graves, looking at it. A man rows up to shout that silver on a cloth would save trouble on both sides. The horn answers him. On the third tide they go down the river, and that evening there is no smoke.
I said silver was cheaper than earth. I was wrong by about the price of my roof, and I have stood on your bank for three nights to say so. Do not ask me to say it again.
The emperor is at Nijmegen, asking his counts why the coast was not kept. They are telling him it could not be done. I am to bring him one place where it was. He will want a name to go with it.
And it was done by his own leave, with his own oak in the gate. That will please him more than the bank does. He can say he ordered it.
He will ask who gave leave for a gate on his ground. I shall say the Danes did, three summers running. I think he will let that stand.
One thing more. A bank is twelve men awake every night from Pentecost to Lammas, for ever. Every house that built it owes a man and his bread. Yours too, and your son's.
Ask the emperor's writing: your house free of the tenth at Dorestat
Ask a seat among the seven who find judgment on the bank
You brought the first warning and you had his leave: let the agent name you at Nijmegen, and ask both

The writing comes down from Nijmegen within the month: your house and its heirs free of the tenth at Dorestat, which the emperor's own merchants pay. The dam heads repay your shares with a third over, fifteen hundred pennies, because a bank that worked is suddenly everybody's idea. The house owes the watch a man each summer.

At the next court you sit with the six who find judgment, on the bench nearest the door, where the newest man sits. The shares come back with interest, twelve hundred pennies, and the agent halves your toll for a year without being asked. The house owes the watch a man each summer.

The agent names you before the emperor, who is glad of one piece of good news and generous with it. The writing frees your house of the tenth; the court makes room on its bench; the bank repays you twice over, twenty-four hundred pennies. In the annals of that year it will say that tribute was taken at Walcheren. It will not say Dorestat. The house owes the watch a man each summer.
Weighed out on the dam head
This year the heathen men took Walcheren and killed its count, and took what tribute they chose. Then they came up the river to Dorestat and took tribute there in the same way.
The bank you paid toward stands to a man's chest and stops at the road. They walked through where the gate was going to be.
Silver now, by weight, and we go down on the ebb with nothing burned. We killed a count on the island eight days ago and a good Dane beside him. We have had enough work for one summer.
I told you. Silver on a cloth. Nobody dead, no roof gone. Ask me next year whether it was cheap, when they come back for the same again. Ask me quietly.
And I still owe you for the third ship. I have not forgotten it for one day. It is like a stone in a shoe.

The emperor has turned back from his road to Rome and is coming to Nijmegen in a rage. He will ask why the coast was not kept. Somebody will tell him the Frisians would not obey. Somebody always does.
There are people on the rowing benches of the nearest ship who are not rowers. Some of them have been there since the island. One or two have been there longer.
Advance three hundred pennies for the houses that cannot find their share, against their pledges
Carry the silver down to the ships yourself, and speak for the people on the benches
Pay your share, and take what Thiadlef has been waiting to offer since you brought his daughter home
Pay your share and no more, and carry bread and ale down the Lek by night to a town with no silver left

Your three hundred makes up the weight. By Michaelmas four of the houses you covered have not redeemed their pledges, and do not pretend they will: twelve bolts of cloth, eight casks of wine, and a dam head whose owner is going to his brother at Tiel. You have a berth of your own. You did not much like the way you came by it.

You stand in the mud with the cloth of silver and say, in the tongue you have of theirs, that a full weight buys empty benches. The chief thinks about it for the length of the weighing. Then he has them put ashore, every one who was taken on this river. The families find six hundred and fifty pennies for you somehow. The dealer's kinsman, who interpreted where your words ran out, says he will keep your goods at Sliesthorp any summer you like.

He has thought about it for three years and says it in one breath: his Hildswith for your heir, nine hundred pennies with her, and the two houses to stand surety for each other's roofs. She is asked. She says she has counted the days on a longer belt this time.

You pay what is asked and not a penny over. Then you spend the season carrying bread and ale down the Lek in the dark, mast down, to a town that has credit and no coin. It comes to six hundred pennies by the first frost. You could now take that river blind, and some nights you did.
A new river
Your looms and scales stand under a hired roof on the IJssel. A boat from the Rhine ties up beside yours, and her skipper tells the bank what this summer cost Dorestat.

They took the island and killed the count, and then they came up to us and did not even trouble to burn. They put a cloth on the dam and we filled it. The emperor is at Nijmegen asking whose fault it is.
They still say on the dams that you were the first to go. They say it differently this year. What do they ask for a roof here?

There is ground by Saint Lebuin's church, dry four years in five. I pace it out, the priest blesses it, and you pay the church a penny a year for ever. It is not the Rhine. Nothing that comes up it is in a hurry.
The Saxons burned this church twice in my grandfather's time. So you need not tell me about leaving. Tell me what you weigh with, and whether your pennies are the heavy ones.
Wine and cloth that would not sell on the dams at any price are dear here, and dearer since the news: every buyer upriver has understood where the stock is going to be.
Sell the stock while it is dear and take ground of your own by the church
Keep the house afloat: sell dear, and leave a sworn man here with the scales and a hired roof
Take two plots side by side, and send the boat back down for Thiadlef's household

The stock goes for seven hundred pennies, and the ground is paced out before the ink of the tally is dry: eighteen paces of bank, a penny a year to Saint Lebuin. You cut the house's mark on the corner post. It is the same mark. It looks strange on new wood.

You sell for nine hundred and build nothing. A man you trust stays under the hired roof with the second scales and a tally of what is his to sell. The house is where its boat is, as it always was, and now it has a door on two rivers.

The boat goes down empty and comes back with Thiadlef in the bow, his household behind him, and his father's door laid across the thwarts. He says nothing for a day. Then he says the posts here are good oak, and that between two houses there is eleven hundred pennies' worth of stock and one boat too many. He proposes to sail the other one himself.
What is in the ground
The posts of your storehouse stand black to the height of a man. This summer the fleet took silver instead of fire, and the houses that kept their stock short have kept their roofs as well.
The chest is under its alder at De Heul, a spade's depth down, where you put it before you filled the store. It is the only thing you did that summer that you would do again.
You asked me once about the dam head. I said, after the next one. There have been three. Name a price and do not make me say it is too low.
I have a roof and half a store's worth of nothing to put under it. You have stock in your head and no roof. I have seen worse matches made in church.
And there is the matter of the third ship. I would be glad to stop owing you. Put your mark on my door and we will call it paid, and I will go on resenting you in comfort.
In the ash where the counting table stood there is a lump of bronze that was a pair of pans, and beside it, baked hard as a brick, the clay box with the weights still in it.
Dig up the chest and buy the widow's dam head at the price she is frightened enough to take
Dig up the chest and build one roof with Thiadlef on his dam: two marks on one door
Dig up the chest, rake the ashes for the house's scales and its stick of names, and build small

She takes the first price you name, which tells you what it was worth. Forty paces of oak post to deep water, and seven hundred and fifty pennies still in the chest. The bank wants timber for a year to come and you have the berth to land it. People are polite about how you got it.

Your mark goes on his door under his father's, and his steersman stops calling you 'the neighbour'. Seven hundred pennies from the chest go into one stock under one roof. He will take the second boat himself, he says, since somebody in this house ought to know what he is doing.

The weights have come through the fire true: you try them against the moneyer's and he cannot fault them. The pans you have beaten out again, a little crooked. With nine hundred pennies from the ground you roof a store half the size of the old one. The scales hang by the door. Your heirs will be told why they are that shape.
A fleet of the Danes is in Frisia, forty hulls or near it, and has burned on the coast. A fisherman who saw it says they asked the way up the Rhine.
This year the heathen men came by Traiectum to Dorestat and plundered it. Some they killed, some they carried off, and part of the place they burned. The people taken are sold at Sliesthorp.
King Horik of the Danes says the fleets on the Rhine are none of his. Dorestat cloth is sold on his landing all the same, and Dorestat people beside it.
The emperor has ordered guards set along the coasts against the Northmen. The counts who are to keep them are away with their men.
A fleet is on the Maas. Witla has burned, and the fort at Andoverpis on the Scheldt. They will be on the Rhine next.
This year the heathen men took Walcheren and killed its count. At Dorestat they found a bank and a shut gate, lay two days before it, and went away with nothing.
This year the heathen men took Walcheren, killed its count, and took tribute there and at Dorestat. The emperor came to Nijmegen, found the coast unkept, and ordered ships built.
A house of Dorestat has taken ground by Saint Lebuin's church at Daventre and sells Rhine wine there. They say it will not be the last.

A river landing in the delta, a bright windy noon in early summer: a sunburned Frisian fisherman in a salt-stiff hooded cloak sits on the gunwale of a small clinker boat, blistered hands open on his knees, talking up at a merchant; behind them casks are rolled along a wattle dam and nobody is listening.

Dorestat from the river, afternoon sun: the long comb of earth-and-wattle dams with thatched storehouses on them and no wall anywhere; in front a Frankish agent with a tally stick, a thick grey Frisian skipper in a shabby blue cloak laughing, and a thin tonsured priest standing a little apart, listening.

The bank road at Dorestat, dusk, a red sky upriver: a barefoot boy running toward us, mouth open; people throwing bolts of cloth into overloaded boats between the dams; on one dam head a heavy grey man with a short sword stands with a dozen men and spears, not moving.

Dorestat, a grey still morning after the fire: black posts where three storehouses stood, thin smoke, a boat coming back full of women and children; in front a grey skipper stares at the river with a child's shoe in his hand, and a young widow sits on a mooring post with her keys in her lap.

The landing at Sliesthorp, flat northern light, low thatched houses and beached ships: a fair-bearded Dane holds up a bolt of grey-blue cloth with a lead seal dangling from it; behind him on a bench five captives, among them a Frisian girl of fourteen sitting very straight, fingering knots in her belt; a king's man with a spear and an arm ring looks on.

Thiadlef's dam head at Dorestat, evening, new yellow thatch on a mended store: the heavy grey skipper kneels on the planks holding his daughter by both shoulders; she is showing him the knots in her belt; the merchant's boat is still being made fast behind them.

Inside the timber church of Saint Martin at Dorestat, daylight through the open door: twenty merchants standing, a priest scratching a line of ditch and bank on the earth floor with a stick, a grey skipper spreading a cloth as if laying out silver, a Frankish agent with folded arms; through the door a barge loading a loom.

The gatehouse of the palace at Noviomagus on its hill above the Waal, a cool clear morning: a young tonsured clerk at a sloping desk with a wax seal and a strip of parchment, an empty courtyard behind him; through the gate, far below, stacked oak trunks on the river bank and a small boat.

The sea off the Maas mouth, hazy afternoon, low dunes along the horizon: a line of more than twenty square sails standing in toward the land; one long ship has turned and rows toward us, shields along her side, a man standing in her bow with a hand raised; in the foreground the stern of a small trading boat with ale casks.

Dorestat from the bank road, a hot hazy day: a raw earth bank chest-high with a ditch in front and a gap where the road goes through, men digging; a merchant selling wine casks cheap on a dam while looking downstream; boats with bedding aboard at every dam head.

Dawn mist on the river below Dorestat: a ditch, a raw earth bank topped with a wattle fence, and a shut two-leaved oak gate with a watch-house and a man blowing a horn; spearmen along the bank, among them a heavy grey skipper; on the water twenty long ships lying on their oars, one small boat rowing back to them.

A dam head at Dorestat, noon, no smoke: a cloth spread on the planks heaped with pennies and cut silver, a pair of scales held by a Danish chief with gold arm rings, Frisian merchants standing in a silent half circle; behind him a long ship with captives sitting among the rowers; an unfinished bank in the far background.

The bank of the IJssel at Daventre, a mild evening: a small timber church with a shingled roof, a man pacing out ground with a measuring pole, looms and a pair of scales under an open lean-to; two Frisian boats side by side at the bank, a skipper telling news with his hands.

A burned plot on a dam at Dorestat, clear cold morning: black posts standing man-high in grey ash, a merchant kneeling and lifting a warped bronze scale pan out of it; a widow with keys at her belt and a heavy grey skipper wait at the edge of the ash; whole roofs on either side.
Ending picture, the bank holds: a shut oak gate in an earth bank at dawn, a horn hanging beside it, and beyond the bank the masts of long ships going away down a misty river.
Ending picture, the tribute of 837: a cloth heaped with silver pennies on the planks of a dam, a pair of scales standing in it, and a long ship's prow above.
Ending picture, up the river: a river barge loaded with a loom, a house door and a cat, going upstream under a grey sky, with a thin smoke far astern.
Ending picture, the storehouse in ashes: a bent pair of bronze scale pans and a box of weights lying in ash between black posts, and beside them a spade and a small iron-bound chest with earth on it.
Money for peace
The heathen army sits on Thanet, and the men of Kent have promised it money to stay there. The reeve is collecting. So is a Dane with a pair of scales.
The men of Kent have promised them money for peace. Every hide pays, and every keel that lies here. I did not make the bargain. I only count it.
They say it buys us the winter. I say a wolf does not sell the sheep it means to eat.
Malt, oats, ale, bread. I pay in silver by weight, and I do not care whose face is on it.
Look at the scales if you doubt me. They are honest. It is the only thing in this army that has to be.
Your boat sits low. I can make her sit higher.
Pay twenty pennies into Kent's share

You pay. Within the month the army steals inland by night, under cover of the peace, and harries all the east of Kent. The money was promised and the burning was done anyway. The reeve does not forget who paid while it still looked like sense.
Sell the Dane your ship's own ale and bread at three times their worth
He weighs out cut silver: half an arm-ring and nine pennies of three kings. Your men drink water as far as the next port and say so. The Dane says his name is Toki, and that an army eats every day.
Keep the hatch shut and watch how he weighs

You sell nothing and learn something. He tests each coin with a knife's point and throws back the bad ones without anger. From his talk the army means to winter among the East Angles and wants horses: fodder will be dear there.

Dusk on the Wantsum shore at Sarre in autumn: an English reeve with a tally stick and a sack, and across a trestle from him a broad Dane holding up a small folding balance; far off over the flat island a line of camp fires under a low red sky.
The king's horses
The great army has taken winter quarters among the East Angles. The king has made peace and given them horses. Outside the town the camp trades like a market, with a Dane at the scales.
The king has given them horses so that they will ride away on them. That is the whole plan. I have heard worse ones.
Somebody will ask me how many they are. I have counted three times and had three answers.
The man from Thanet. Sit down. An army remembers who was there early.
A Frisian. Good. Frisians ask the price before they ask whose side I am on.
Iron. Bars and rivets. We have more keels to mend than this shire has smiths, and the smiths have all gone deaf.
These are my weights: lead, with a piece of somebody's book clasp set in the top so I know them for mine. Silver from the east, silver from the Franks. It all weighs the same.
Sit two days at his scales and learn the weights and the words

Two days. You learn the ertog and the ore, how to nick silver, and what a Dane calls a bad coin. You learn that Toki has a sister's son in the fleet and no wish to farm. Your men are bored and say so.
Take his order: six bars of iron, brought here before the army rides
He gives you earnest silver, a cut dirham and some pennies, and scores the order on a stick in marks you cannot read. Six bars before the army rides, at more than half again the price.
Tell the king's man what you saw of them in Kent

You tell him: the peace in Kent, the money promised, the night ride after. He hears you to the end. 'So they take the price and the goods both,' he says. He pays you for the news and looks no happier for having bought it.

A winter camp outside Gipeswic on a grey morning: a ditch and bank, tents of sailcloth, English grooms leading a string of horses in through the gap; in front a Dane seated on a sea chest with a folding balance and a row of small lead weights on a board.
The strand at York
The army holds York. On the strand by the Foss the people taken in the fighting stand roped in a line, and a dealer walks along it naming prices.
All Saints' day. They were at their prayers or at each other's throats, I forget which. Nobody was on the wall.
They had two kings here and were fighting over which. Now they have none, and it is quieter.
A grown man, forty pennies of your money. A woman who weaves, more. I take silver by weight or wine by the cask.
This one reads. A bishop's school, he says. Sixty, because somewhere there is a priest who will pay a hundred.
I can say the psalter as far as the fiftieth psalm, and I write a fair hand. My master is dead in the church porch. Nobody is coming with a hundred.
Buy the boy free and give him a place in the boat
