Sixty pennies, weighed. The rope comes off. He says his name is Wulfric. He eats like two men, and by the river mouth he is reading your tally sticks aloud and has found a mistake in them.
Buy four of them for the market over the sea
Four, at thirty each for taking them together. They sit in the hold and do not look back at the town. At Sliesthorp they are worth half as much again, and you will know what you carried.
Buy no one; ask who was taken, and carry the names south
The boy gives you eleven names and whose kin they are. You cannot write them, so he makes you say them back until you have them. Somebody in the south will pay nothing for this and be glad of it.

The muddy strand by the Foss at York under the broken Roman wall, a cold bright noon: a dozen roped people, among them a thin boy of twelve with ink on his fingers; a fur-capped dealer points along the line with a stick; smoke over the town behind.
The king is dead

This winter the army rode back across Mercia and sat down at Thetford. King Edmund fought them, and the Danes had the victory and killed the king. At the landing a priest has a sack he will not put down.
Nine days after Martinmas. They killed him and they hold the land, and there is nobody now to give them horses to go away.
How he died I did not see, and I will not tell it as if I had. In a few years everyone will have seen it.
A chalice, a paten, two book covers. I buried them once. The ground keeps things from Danes and from nobody else.
I buy church silver by weight. What it was for does not weigh anything.
You know my scales. Buy from me and not from the men with the axes. I at least give change.
Take the priest and his sack over to Kent

He comes aboard with the sack between his knees and keeps it there. For Canterbury, he says, where there are still walls and an archbishop behind them. He pays in prayers and promises you both kinds are good.
Buy the camp's church silver by weight

Two pieces, a cup with its foot hacked off and a dish with a lamb on it, for their weight in silver and no more. Whole, in a Frankish bishop's town, they are worth three times that. The priest watches you carry them down to the boat.
Hear it told and carry the news
You hear it three times from three men and it has already begun to grow. What does not change: the king is dead, the army will eat the shire bare this winter, and corn is dear.

A frozen landing on the Orwell at first light: a priest in a patched cloak clutching a heavy sack to his chest; a Dane at a trestle with scales, a hacked silver cup in the pan; on the bank behind, ravens in a leafless tree and smoke rising inland.
The golden book

The army has come from Reading to London for the winter, and the Mercians have made peace with it, which means paid. In the camp by the old walls the Dane with the scales has something wrapped in a cloak.
My bishop has let land at Nuthurst go for twenty mancuses of gold to pay his part. He had it written in the charter why, and in which winter, so that nobody later thinks he was careless.
Every keel on the strand pays toward the town's share. Thirty pennies, and you trade this winter under the army's peace, such as it is.
Gold letters on purple skins, and painted men with wings. Nobody here can read it and every man wants to hold it. That is worth something.
Gold for gold. Not silver: I have silver. Somebody among the Christians wants this back more than I want to keep it. Find him.
I show it to you because you know a true weight. The others would cut it up for the clasps.
They are cutting dies down the street for whoever holds the town. A king's name is the cheapest thing on a coin.
Carry word of the book to Kent
He lets you turn three leaves. Purple and white by turns, and the writing like poured gold. You cannot read it either. At Canterbury there are people who can, and who have gold of their own.
Buy it yourself: four hundred pennies' weight of silver

He wanted gold and takes silver, a great deal of it, because silver in the hand outweighs gold at Canterbury. The book goes aboard wrapped in your spare sail. It is the dearest thing you have ever carried, and nearly the lightest.
Pay thirty pennies to the town's share and trade under the peace
The clerk writes you down. The army will drink the town dry by Candlemas, and anyone with ale to sell does well. The book stays in its cloak. Somebody else may carry word of it, or nobody.

Inside the broken Roman wall of London on a winter afternoon: a Dane on a sea chest opening a cloak to show a great book, its page purple with gold letters catching the light; a tonsured clerk with a wax tablet looks away; tents and tethered horses among fallen masonry.
Pure gold
At Canterbury the ealdorman Alfred and his wife Werburg have heard that the heathen army holds holy books. A priest of Christ Church brings you to them.
You know their camp and the man with the scales. We know only that the books are there, and that they are being handled.
My wife and I will not leave holy books among heathens longer than it takes a boat to fetch them. That is all there is to say about why.
Pure gold, our own, weighed here before the priest. Carry it, bring the book, and he goes with you to see both done.
You have it aboard? Then name your price before I see it. Afterwards I shall not bargain well.
The priest you brought over from the East Angles sits at our table. He has told us what kind of man came for him.
Carry their gold to the camp and bring the book back
Werburg counts the gold out herself, thirty mancuses, into a leather bag that the priest ties to his own belt. His name is Hunsige. He has not been in a boat before and means to pray the whole way.
Sell them the book: six hundred pennies, in gold

Twenty mancuses, weighed. More than you paid, and less than the camp would have had from them. Werburg unwraps the book on the table and nobody speaks for a while. The priest washes his hands before he touches it.
Keep the book for a market over the sea

You say it is not for sale here. The ealdorman says nothing. The priest says a good deal, and it will be said again in every minster from here to York. Somewhere in the north a king who cannot read will pay well for gold letters.
Say it is not your errand
They thank you coldly and send for another shipman. Whether he ever sails you do not hear.

A timber hall at Canterbury by lamplight: a grey ealdorman standing, his wife Werburg seated at the table weighing gold coins in a small balance, a priest holding open a leather bag; the merchant in sea clothes just inside the door.
By weight
In the camp at London the gold is laid on one side of the scales and the book on a chest beside them. The priest stands witness. A chief of the army has come to watch, which was not agreed.
Thirty of their gold pieces was the word, and I keep my word, because next winter I shall want to sell again.
The book is the army's, not the weigher's. A priest has come all this way for it. Then it is worth more than was said.
He will take the thirty if you do not flinch. He only wants to see whether you do.
I am here to see it done, and to say afterwards that it was done honestly. I should be glad to be able to say so.
Weigh out the thirty as agreed and take the book

Thirty mancuses, piece by piece. The chief shrugs and goes to find something else to be owed. The priest carries the book to the boat in both arms like a child, and at Fordwic the ealdorman's man pays your passage without being asked.
Beat the price down and keep what you save
You get it for twenty-five, and the priest watches five gold pieces go into your purse. He says nothing. He will say it at Canterbury.
The chief takes your haggling for an insult to his book. It costs the thirty, and forty pennies of your own to smooth him. The book goes home all the same, and the priest saw you try.
Leave the camp with the gold and without the book

On the river you take the bag and put the priest ashore at the first landing. Thirty mancuses is a year's good trading. The book is cut up for its gold before spring or carried north whole, and your name is read out in chapter at Christ Church, though not for prayers.

The London camp at midday, snow on the ground: a folding balance on a chest with gold coins in one pan, the great book lying closed beside it; a Danish weigher, a tall chief in a wolfskin with his thumbs in his belt, and a small priest gripping a leather bag.
The oath on the ring
The army slipped past the West Saxon host into Wareham. The king made peace with it: hostages given, and oaths sworn on their holy ring. At Hamwic the king's reeve wants a man who knows the camp.
They swore on their holy ring, which they have done for no people before. Then they rode for Exeter by night. I should like to know what the ring thinks of it.
We hold their hostages. I am told each is a great man's son. You have sat in their camp: which of these would be missed, and which are grooms in borrowed cloaks?
Their ships met a storm off Swanage. A hundred and twenty lost, they say. The sea is the only ally the king has not had to pay.
I fell behind on the Exeter road with a lame horse. It is the horse I blame.
I held a broken oar from dusk until morning. If your god sent that wind, he was not aiming at me in particular.
You sat at my mother's brother's scales among the East Angles. He said a Frisian learned the weights in two days and the words in none.
Tell the reeve truly which hostages are men of weight

You walk along the hostages with the reeve and say what you know: this one's father commands ships, that one mucks out. He pays you a hundred pennies from the king's chest and writes down which to guard and which merely to feed.
Buy the young Dane out and set him on the road to his kin

The reeve sells him as he would a salvaged spar. The young man's name is Tofi. He does not thank you at length. He says his mother's brother will hear of it, and that in the army a thing heard is a thing owed.
Sell your cargo and stay out of kings' business
The king's host has been in the field since harvest and must be fed. Corn is dear at Hamwic and will be dearer nearer Exeter. That is all of the war that is your business.

The shore at Hamwic on a windy autumn day: a king's reeve in a good cloak with a wax tablet, a row of Danish hostages sitting under guard on a beached boat's rail, one young man with a blanket round him set apart; grey water and a wreck's ribs beyond.
No ale for Yule
The army has gone into Mercia for the winter and sits at Gloucester. Its buyer is in London with a great deal of silver, buying as no camp buys that means to sit still.
Oats, and more oats. Hard bread. Spare girths. Whatever a horse and a rider need for a week on a frozen road.
Ale? No. Where we are going the ale is already brewed. A king's steward has seen to it.
You have not heard me say that. A man who sits at scales all day talks to keep warm.
Winter at home, Frisian. Do not be in Wessex after the twelfth night. I tell you that for nothing, which you know is not my custom.
You bought me off that beach. So: when the Christians are sleeping off their god's birthday, we ride. Keep your boat out of their rivers.
Carry it to the king's reeve at Hamwic
You load nothing and take the ebb. It is a bad season for the Foreland and a worse one for being believed: all you have is a buyer's shopping and a remark about ale.
Sell him the fodder and ask nothing

Every sack of oats on the strand goes through your hands to his, and you take a tenth for the trouble: a hundred and sixty pennies in cut silver. He does not say where the horses are going. You do not ask.
Not your war: lay the boat up for the winter

You winter where nobody is riding anywhere. After Twelfth Night the army comes down on Chippenham, and the king goes into the marshes with a small band. You hear it at Candlemas, from a man who had it from another.

The Thames strand at London in hard frost, late afternoon: sacks of oats stacked high beside a Dane with scales and an open silver chest; a string of pack horses waiting; no ale cask anywhere; breath smoking in the cold.
Before Twelfth Night
The king's reeve at Hamwic is keeping Christmas. The king keeps his at Chippenham. You have a buyer's shopping, a remark about ale, and as much of the reeve's patience as a tide lasts.
Nobody rides at midwinter. Armies sit by their fires until the grass grows. That is how it has been every year of this.
But you told me true about the hostages when I had no way to check it. Say it again, slowly.
And I do not know you. A Frisian who trades in their camp comes to tell me where they will ride. Why should that not be their errand?
You are too late with it. They came down on Chippenham after Twelfth Night, and the king is in the marshes with a few men. I wish you had rowed harder, or that I had listened sooner to somebody.
Tell it all: he knows what your word is worth

He sends two riders before you have finished your ale, by different roads. When the army comes down on Chippenham after Twelfth Night the king is not at table. He is on the hill behind the town with the men of Wiltshire, and the gates are shut.
Swear to it on his relics

You swear on a saint's finger in a silver box. The reeve watches your hand, not your face, and then calls for a rider. When the army comes to Chippenham the king is not there to be taken, and his men are.

You swear. He thanks you, feeds you, and sends nobody. After Twelfth Night the army takes Chippenham and the king flees to the marshes. When you next meet the reeve he remembers exactly what you said, and on which day.
Say nothing after all; sell and go
You talk of the price of corn. Whatever is going to happen in Wessex happens without you.

A reeve's hall at Hamwic on a midwinter night: a Christmas table half cleared, the reeve leaning forward on his elbows, the merchant standing wet from the sea with his hand on a small silver reliquary; through the open door a groom saddles a horse by torchlight.
The king was not at table
This year, after Twelfth Night, the army stole to Chippenham, and the king was there before them with his host; and at Easter they made peace. The reeve has a chest from the king, and a writing.
The king asked who brought the word. I said a Frisian. He asked whether you could be paid or only thanked. I said you were a Frisian.
They gave hostages and swore again, and this time the king chose the hostages himself, from a list. You will know whose list.
They know somebody talked. They do not know who. I would not sit long at their scales.
Take the king's silver and his protection

Six pounds of pennies and sixty over, in a chest two men carry, and a writing which says that you and your heirs trade toll-free at Hamwic under the king's hand, and that whoever harms you answers to him. You cannot read it. Every reeve in Wessex can.
Ask for land by the water in place of half the silver

Three pounds of pennies and thirty over, the same writing, and a plot above the tide line with the king's stake at each corner. The reeve says a man with a house here will be slower to sell news to the other side. He says it kindly.
Not yet: let it lie with the reeve
The chest goes back under the reeve's bed. He says it will keep, and that kings forget more slowly than merchants think.

The hall at Hamwic on a bright summer morning: an iron-bound chest open and full of pennies on the table, the reeve holding out a sealed strip of parchment, the merchant with his cap in his hand; through the door, ships on the Itchen and a peaceful shore.
Written above and below
At Christ Church the ealdorman Alfred and Werburg give the golden gospels to the community. Their gift is being written into the book itself, above and below the gold letters, in plain English.

It says they bought these books from the heathen army with their own pure gold, for the love of God and their souls' need, and would not leave them in heathen hands. It says nothing of boats. Books never do.
The book does not name you. I do. There is gold set aside, and the community has something to add to it.
I told the chapter how the weighing went. All of it. They have decided to be grateful for the book.
Your Wulfric reads better than half our brothers. That is praise of him and a complaint about us.
Stand witness and take what is offered

Forty mancuses from the ealdorman's own chest. The community writes your name among its friends, to be prayed for by name, and at the ealdorman's word the king's reeve lets your keel lie at Fordwic free of toll for as long as your house sails. The book is laid on the altar. It will be read from every month.
Ask one thing more: that Wulfric be freed at the altar as your foster-son

The archbishop hears who paid sixty pennies for a schoolboy on the strand at York and asked nothing for it since. The community doubles the ealdorman's gold: eighty mancuses. Wulfric is freed at the altar with the gospels open, and it is written in the book's margin that he is free and of your house. He reads the line out to you twice.
Not yet: you have a tide to catch
The priest says the gold will keep and the prayers have already started, whether you stay for them or not.

Christ Church at Canterbury, morning light through a narrow window: the great book open on the altar at a purple page of gold letters, a scribe bent over it writing small dark words in the upper margin; the ealdorman and Werburg standing with their young daughter, the merchant a little apart.
Hostages at the Lea

King Alfred and King Guthrum have a peace, and a border up the Thames and up the Lea. No man, free or slave, may go over to the other army without leave. But if they must trade, in cattle and in goods, it is allowed when hostages are given.

Englishmen I cannot send: half would not come back, and the other half would come back with wives. Danes I will not let in. A Frisian is nobody's man. It is the first time I have heard that said as praise.
Leave a pledge with me, so that both sides know you go with a clean back. You have it again when you come over the water with what you said you would bring.
The Frisian. Good. I have land now, and a wife who says it wants ploughing. I would rather buy and sell. Bring cloth. I have horses, and more silver than sense.
On the other bank they still ask who talked before Chippenham. Nobody here knows. Keep it so.
Leave sixty pennies as your pledge and take the leave to cross

A season of crossings: English cloth and wine one way; horses, hides and weighed silver the other; and few others allowed to carry them. Seven hundred pennies clear when the pledge comes back. The reeve gives you a tally cut with the king's mark. It is the whole of the law, and it fits in a purse.
Stand surety for other Frisian keels too, with Toki to answer on the far bank

Your pledge covers four keels, and each pays you for the cover. Toki keeps your goods on the Danish side under his own roof and answers for them with his land. A thousand pennies clear by the year's end. On both banks they begin to say 'ask the Frisian', which is a title of a kind.
Not yet: let others try the crossing first
The reeve shrugs. The river will still be a border next year, he says, and the year after.

The mouth of the Lea where it meets the Thames, a still grey morning: an English reeve at a post on the near bank holding a notched tally, the merchant's boat loaded with bolts of cloth, and on the far bank a Dane with horses on a rope, raising one hand.
The land shared out
This year the army went from Cirencester into East Anglia, and settled the land and shared it out. Toki, who never wished to farm, has a share by the river and no use for it.
They have given me land for fifteen winters at the scales. I asked for silver. They said the land is the silver now.
Our king has been under the water and come up with an English name. He strikes pennies with it. I weigh them like any others.
You sold to us when nobody knew how it would end. There is a plot by the landing with my mark on the post. Put a house on it and we are fellows: your keel, my scales.
The gold book went north with a man bound for Sliesthorp. I hear a king there shows it to his guests and holds it the wrong way up.
Tofi has the next share to mine. He says you are owed a horse. He has no horse. He will.
Take the plot and Toki's fellowship

You strike hands on it before witnesses, in the Danish fashion. The plot is forty feet of river bank with a post on it. Toki weighs out your part of fifteen winters' dealing, nine hundred pennies of cut silver, and loads a second boat that sails when yours does. The English priests of the shire know whose fellow you are.
Take your part in silver, and no land among them

He is not offended. He weighs out fourteen hundred pennies, some of it still shaped like altar furniture, and takes you before the king who was Guthrum, who gives you guest-right in his land: a seat, a hearing, and nobody's hand against your keel. The English priests of the shire know where your silver came from.
Not yet: see first whether their peace holds
Toki says the post will stand. He has put it in deeper than he puts most things.

The river bank at Gipeswic on a spring evening: a new post with a mark cut in it on a strip of bare ground, a Dane grown grey shaking hands with the merchant over it, a plough leaning unused against a new timber house, two boats drawn up side by side.
This year the heathen army sat on Thanet, and the men of Kent promised it money for peace; and under cover of the peace the army stole away by night and harried all the east of Kent.
A great heathen army has taken winter quarters among the East Angles. The king there has made peace and given them horses.
The army holds York. Both kings of the Northumbrians are dead inside the walls, and those taken are sold on the strand by the Foss. A Frisian carries the names of some.
This winter King Edmund of the East Angles fought the army, and the Danes had the victory and killed the king, nine days after Martinmas.
The army swore peace to King Alfred at Wareham on its holy ring, gave hostages, and rode for Exeter by night all the same.
After Twelfth Night the army rode on Chippenham and found the king's host waiting and the gates shut. They say a shipman brought the word.
The tally

The count's steward waits at the dam head with a hazel stick split down its length. His half and yours say the same thing: eight pounds of silver, 1,920 pennies, lent for the boat and due at Michaelmas.
Forty dozen pennies. I cut the notches myself the day the boat was paid for, and I cut them deep. Hold your half against mine. They fit now, and they will fit at Michaelmas.
The count is away with the host. He is home for Michaelmas, and that is the day. I do not move days.
Michaelmas has gone by. The count asks after you every court day, and every court day I tell him the river is long.
He asks back what he lent and not a penny over it. The king forbids more, and so does the Church. So do not be late. A day has no price, and that is what makes it dear.
You are known on the dams, so I will say this once. His people are short of bread-corn, and he wants a hawk from the north to give the king. A man who brought either would find him easier to talk to.
Take your half and say you will be there
Leave twelve pennies for the count's table, as the custom is
Say the boat was never worth eight pounds
A friend on the bank road

Thiadbod, who has the best dam head in Dorestat and a gift for every officer, comes along the bank road in a blue cloak to wish you well. His sister, the widow Thiadburg, watches from her storehouse door.
Two pounds by Michaelmas, in that? I have casks that weigh more than your boat. Still, I began small myself. Smaller than I tell people.
I want six bolts of English cloth, and my own ship is bound up the Rhine. Bring them inside two moons and I pay well over the dam's price. Friends should help each other to their days.
The count eats at my table when he is home. I will say your name to him. Kindly.
My brother gives nothing he has not counted twice. Ask him whose hazel sticks hang in his storehouse. Sibrad had a boat of his own once. He rows my brother's now.
And ask yourself why he sends you to the English for it, when their reeves turn Frankish keels away, and his own ship has not left her post since Easter.
If you are short when the day comes, come to me before you go to him. I lend on goods I can see, and what I am lent I give back.
Take his order for English cloth
Thank him and take no favours
Ask him, before his sister, whose sticks hang in his storehouse
The count's day
The reckoning. In the count's hall the steward lays the two halves of the hazel stick together on the board, and the count looks at you over them.
The halves fit. Forty dozen. Nothing has been cut off.
You are here for the day, shipman. Most are not.
Michaelmas is long past, shipman. I looked for you and saw only my steward's face, which I see every day.
My steward says you left twelve pennies for my table at midsummer. I ate them. They were good.
A count and his whole following were cut down on the Weser this year, and the king has turned back from the Avars for it. I am in no mood for stories. Silver, or what you have in its place.
I ask back what I lent. The king forbids me more and I want no more. But a broken day is a debt of another kind, and that one I may collect as I please.
And hear this, whatever you pay. My people have eaten their seed. Bring wheat up the river before the frost and my steward pays a fair price for it. That is not a favour I ask. It is one I offer.
And if you are ever in the north: he wants a hawk for the king's fist. He has said so every day since Easter.
Count out what you still owe, on the day
Count out what you still owe, late
Ask until next Michaelmas, and offer the boat's work for it
Lay the mooring rope on the board: the boat is his pledge
The hungry winter
The count's steward stands on the bank with a list of the households on the count's land that have eaten their seed corn. He looks into every hold that comes up the river.
Nine score mouths on the count's land, and bread for half of them. What is under your boards?
There was ice in the ditches between the dams this morning. After this the river brings nothing till Easter.
The count pays six pennies the sack for wheat, counted here. On the dams they will give you twelve and bless you for it. I know it. So does he.
That is wheat. I can smell wheat through oak.
No wheat under there. A man cannot eat millstones, though I have seen it tried this year.
You offered the boat's work for your year. This is the work.
They come to the church door at first light and I have nothing to break for them. A sack given there is lent to a lord who has never missed a day.
One thing more, from the count. A man who pays his day can be trusted with stores. When the grass is up the host goes east, and he wants hulls at Daventre. He pays a penny a load.
Sell the count four sacks at his price
Sell four sacks on the dams at the hungry price
Carry two sacks to the church door and sell him the other two
You have no corn to spare
The king's new penny

The mint at Dorestat is striking the king's new penny, broad and heavy, with his name tied in a knot of letters. The count has heard the law from Frankfurt read, and has sent for every man whose stick still hangs in his hall.
Old penny. New penny. Four of the new weigh five of the old and a little over. The fire does not care whose name is on them.
The king says there is one penny now, and a free man who refuses it pays fifteen shillings. So a penny is this. Your stick says pennies, forty dozen of them.
By tale, then. What is cut on the stick, counted out in the new coin.
What he lent was weighed in the old pound. I weighed it. Eighteen score and seven of the new pennies is that weight again. Give him the tale and he has near a third more silver than left his hand.
Do not say the word you are about to say, moneyer. I have asked for pennies. I have asked for nothing the king forbids.
This one sold us wheat at the count's price when the dams paid double. It is on my sticks, so I say it.
And his mooring rope has hung on my wall since the reckoning.
Pay what you owe by tale in the new pennies, and see the stick burned
Have the moneyer weigh out what you owe in new pennies, about three for every four by tale, and pay that
Say you will answer at Michaelmas
The stick for sale

The count is making ready to ride with the host, and he does not mean to leave an open stick behind him. Thiadbod stands at his elbow in a clean blue cloak. On the board lie your tally, a purse and a cask of wine.
The king goes into Saxony after the harvest with two armies, and I go with one. I will not carry a hazel stick to the Saxons.
I ride with the host again, shipman, and your stick has hung a year too long.
Thiadbod offers me forty dozen of the new pennies for it, and a cask for my trouble. A man may sell what is owed him. Match it, or give me a reason.
So the bishop sent you home with a blessing. Blessings take no notches off a stick.
I told you I would say your name to the count. Kindly.
You carried my cloth well. You will carry my wine better.
Six score pennies in my hand now and a third of your next three cargoes, and I pay the count myself. My brother can drink his own cask.
I lend to people who listen. I spoke to you once on the bank road, and you did not.
If you mean to say usury, say it at Traiectum, to the man whose word it is. Not in this hall.
Match the bid: what you owe, in new pennies, and the stick is burned
Take the widow's surety: a quarter of the debt now and a third of three cargoes
Say the bishop will hear of it, and go down to Traiectum
Let him sell it
Saint Martin's man

Inside the old stone fort at Traiectum the bishop hears you between the hours, a deacon with a book beside him. He has waited a long time for a complaint against the count of Dorestat that he could put in writing.
The count of Dorestat and I share a river and nothing else. Sit. Tell it from the day the stick was cut.

To ask back more than was lent is usury. It is forbidden to every Christian, clerk and layman alike, and the king has had it written so. I can write it again, to the count, in a hand he will need a priest to read to him.
A letter holds him to the weight and no more. You would still owe the weight, and you would pay it here, to my clerk, who carries it up the river with the letter. Eighteen score and seven.

Or there is a shorter road. The men of Saint Martin who live on his banks at Dorestat owe the king's officers nothing: no toll, no lodging, no hand on their goods when they die. And Saint Martin has silver enough to buy one hazel stick.

But a man is not a stick. Saint Martin's man carries wax and wine when he is asked, and answers in my hall, not the count's. Think before you kneel. I would rather have a willing boatman than a sorry one.
Kneel, and put your hands between his
Ask for the letter and pay the debt by weight to his clerk
Thank him and go back up the river as you came
Stores for the host
Carts and horse lines on the river bank at Daventre, and one of the count's men counting sacks on a wax tablet. The host goes east into Saxony again, and its stores must cross the river and go up it.
The Dorestat shipman. The count said a small boat that pays her days might come. I did not believe him.
Meal, salt pork and horse-corn, over the river and up the brook as far as she floats. Twelve days of it. The count pays a penny a load, and he pays.
Two armies this year, they say, one from each side, and the Saxons between them like corn between stones.
The king means to be on the Elbe before harvest, they say, and to bring home more hostages than in any year yet.
This year it is ships. Great ones, hauled over dry land like sledges to reach the Saxon rivers. I have seen it and I still do not believe it.
Every year I say it is the last year, and every year the Saxons make a liar of me.
I will not lie to you. If the water falls she stays where she lies until it rises, and the host does not wait to pay.
And if you ever go north, bring the count a hawk. He wants one for the king's fist more than he wants his dinner.
Carry the stores for twelve days
Take his order for salt pork instead
Say the boat has her own summer
A hawk from the north
The count has come down to the dam head himself, which he does not do. Somebody has told him what sits on the perch in your stern.
Take the cloth off her. Slowly. I want to see her before she sees me.
He has not looked at a tally like that in twenty years.
The king hunts from the leaf-fall to Christmas. A count who sets that on the king's fist is asked to sit nearer the fire, and he does not forget who set it on his own.
You paid me on the day, and now this. One day you may want something only a king can give. Ask me then. I will carry the asking.
The dam's price for a hawk like that is ten score pennies. He knows it. He is hoping you will not say it.
Give him the hawk for the king
Sell him the hawk at the dam's price
Keep her for another market
The king's man
Strangers sit at the count's own board, sent to take every free man's oath and to hear any man's wrong. The count stands by the door of his own hall, and every tally stick in it lies on the board.
By the lord king's order every man from twelve years up swears to be faithful to him, and I write the names. After that I hear what any man has to say against any other, count or cowherd.

By the lord emperor's order every man from twelve years up swears to him by name, as a man ought to his lord, and the names are written. After that we hear any man's wrong against any other, count or cowherd.
The lord Charles wrote it to King Offa of the English himself: traders have his protection, and one who suffers wrongful oppression may appeal to him or to his judges. I am one of his judges.
A vassal from the palace with one good horse and a thin cloak. Men like that have been known to ride home with two horses.
An abbot and a count from far up the Rhine, with land enough of their own. The emperor chose such men, they say, because they have no need of gifts.
This is the shipman I spoke of. Ask him what kind of lord I am. I will stand outside while he says it.
Say what you like, shipman. I know who came when I called and who did not.
Some of these sticks the count cut. Some, I am told, hang now in a merchant's storehouse, and went there for a cask of wine. I would like to hear about those from a man who has held one.
Say the count dealt justly with you
Tell him how sticks are sold in this hall
Tell the emperor's envoys how sticks are sold in this hall
A hen at Michaelmas
The king's man has ridden on. The count sends for you, not to the hall but to the bank below it, where a strip of the king's ground runs down to the water between two dam heads.
You could have said otherwise in there and been believed. I know what that is worth, and I know I cannot pay it in pennies. A count who paid for such things would deserve what came to him.
I burned your stick the day it was closed. I have kept the ash of no other.

This ground is mine to give, for the king. Lie here, build here, and bring me a hen at Michaelmas for it. One hen. I like to be reminded of the day. And my table drinks what your boat brings, at my price, which is a good one.
And take this bolt. It came out of the Avars' ring with the rest of what the king shared among his counts. My wife says it is too good for a hall with dogs in it.
Or sit with the seven who find judgment in my court. A man who knows what a day costs should say what other men's days cost.

The king asked who found the hawk. I said a Frisian who pays on the day. He laughed and said there was no such beast. No layman is free of the tenth at Dorestat, shipman. But there was never such a hawk at Aachen either. Ask, and I will carry the asking.
Take the ground on the king's bank
Ask instead for a seat among the seven who find judgment
Ask him to carry your asking to the king: the freedom of the toll
The count's enemy
The hall is quiet. The king's man has finished with the sticks, and the count has come back in from the door to hear what is said of him at his own board.

It is found. A count may not sell a free man's debt for a gift, nor take back more than he lent. Every bought stick is to be burned, and the count owes the king's ban, sixty shillings. It is written, and I carry the writing.
And you will want this. It says you stand under the lord Charles's word, and that whoever lays a hand on your boat answers to him. Keep it dry.
I find the sticks in order and the count within his right. That is all I find.
He does not look at you as he says it. In the yard a boy is leading one of the count's horses round to the king's man's baggage.
You have made an enemy who holds the toll, the court and the levy of this district, shipman. I hope it was worth an afternoon's talk.
They will say the sticks were mine. They always say the sticks were the steward's.
My lord at Traiectum asks whether you would care to tell him what you told the king's man. He says he has a longer memory, and a storehouse inside stone walls.
Take the king's man's letter and carry for the palace
Take the letter, and ask back twofold what was taken from you
Go down to Traiectum, and trade from behind the bishop's wall
Hands between hands

In the small stone church of Saint Martin, inside the fort at Traiectum, you kneel and put your hands between the bishop's. A clerk writes your name under the names of the saint's other men on the banks at Dorestat.
Now you are Saint Martin's, and he has never yet lost a man to a count.
My clerk goes up to Dorestat with the silver in the morning. The count will take it. He will not like the hand it comes from, and that is between him and me, as everything is.
There is a house-place for you on our bank, by the church above the town. No officer of the king lodges in it, and none takes a tenth of what you sell from it. That is in the kings' own writing.
For this you bring Saint Martin what he asks when he asks it, and you answer in my hall. He asks seldom. I ask oftener.
Ask what Saint Martin wants carried first
Ask that a clerk teach your house its letters
Thiadbod's second boat
The count has ridden east with the host. Your hazel stick hangs in Thiadbod's storehouse now, on a peg between two others, and Thiadbod is pouring the wine himself.
There it hangs, between Sibrad's and a Dane's. I do not call sticks in. A man who owes me rows harder than a man I pay.
You lie at my dam head and carry what I load, and a third of what the boat earns is mine until I say otherwise. For that, no toll man opens your hold, and the count's steward forgets your name.
You have carried for me before. You know I pay.
He said the same to Sibrad, word for word. I will stand witness to the third, if you ask me. Then a third it stays.
Drink with him and sail as his second boat
Ask the widow to stand witness to the terms first
This year there is great hunger in the land of the Franks. Wheat brought up the river to Dorestat before the frost finds a buyer in the count's steward.
The host goes east into Saxony when the grass is up. The count of Dorestat wants hulls at Daventre to carry its stores, from Easter to harvest, and pays a penny a load.

Dawn at a dam head at Dorestat, mist on the river: a thin grey steward in a plain brown cloak, notched sticks at his belt, holds out half of a split hazel stick to a young Frisian skipper standing in a small open boat.

Midday on the plank bank road, bright and windy: a well-fed skipper in a long blue cloak with a silver pin stands over the small boat, smiling, one ringed hand on a wine cask; behind him a woman in a white head-cloth watches from a storehouse door, keys at her belt.

A Michaelmas evening in a timber hall, firelight and smoke: the count in a red cloak sits behind a board, a sword across his knees; the steward fits the two halves of a hazel stick together on the board; the skipper stands before them holding a leather purse.

A grey winter morning on the river bank, thin ice in the ditches: the steward with a wax tablet looks down into the open hold of the small boat; behind him thin people wait at the door of a small wooden church, where a priest stands with empty hands.

Noon inside the mint, a charcoal fire glowing: the moneyer in a leather apron holds up a pair of scales, old pennies in one pan and fewer new ones in the other; the count and the steward watch; a guard stands in the bright doorway.

An early autumn morning in the yard of the hall, light rain, horses saddled: the count, cloaked for the road, points at a hazel stick lying on a trestle beside a purse and a wine cask; the rival in his blue cloak stands at his elbow; the widow watches from the gate.

Late afternoon inside the old stone fort at Traiectum, low sun on pale tuff walls: the bishop in a white alb and dark cloak, ring and plain curled staff, sits on a bench before a small stone church; a deacon holds a book; the skipper stands before him, cap in hand.

A May morning on the river bank at Daventre, wet grass and a clear sky: carts, sacks and horse lines along the water; one of the count's men with a wax tablet counts loads into the small boat; a wooden church stands on a river dune behind.

Evening at the dam head, calm and golden: the count himself bends over a white hawk on a perch in the stern of the small boat as the skipper draws the cloth from her; the steward stands behind with his sticks, forgotten.

A summer day in the count's hall, doors open, dust in the light: a stranger in a travel-worn cloak sits in the count's seat with a clerk writing beside him; tally sticks cover the board; the count stands by the door with folded arms; free men wait in a line to swear.

A Michaelmas morning on the river bank, clear and cold: the count paces out a strip of ground between two dam heads; the steward drives in a hazel peg; the skipper stands by with a live hen under one arm.

Late afternoon in the hall, long shadows: the king's man holds out a folded, sealed leaf to the skipper; the count stands apart by the fire, half turned away; the steward kneels at the hearth, feeding hazel sticks to the flames.

Morning in the small stone church of Saint Martin at Traiectum, light from one narrow window: the skipper kneels with his hands between the bishop's; a clerk writes a name on a parchment roll; a wax candle burns on the altar.

Dusk inside a storehouse on a dam head, a tallow lamp lit and rain at the door: a row of hazel sticks on pegs, one newly hung; the rival pours wine into two cups; the widow stands in the doorway; a gaunt oarsman looks up from a coil of rope.
Three roofs

The widow who keeps the storehouse on the dam says the boy of your house knows every knot and one tongue, and that one tongue is a poor cargo. Three roofs would take him: the bishop's school, an English house, a Danish hearth.
Your boy sold my net-mender a dead eel as a sleeping one this morning. He is ready to be taught by someone who is not fond of him.
He is your son, born in the house on the dam, and he has been under every foot on it since he could walk.
He is your sister's son. She died on the mound in the fever year, a skipper brought him down the coast with a bundle and a comb, and the house has no other heir.
Saint Martin's at Traiectum has a school. He would come back able to read what the toll man cuts on his stick. He might also not come back: the bishop keeps the good ones.
Liudger went in at that door a Frisian boy and came out a bishop. I only say what is possible.
There is an Englishman above the Strand at Lundenwic who lodges our people and answers for them to the reeve. English is our own speech with a cold in its nose. He would have it by the second winter.

And there is the Dane at Ripa who speaks for Frisian ships. They foster each other's sons up there and think it binds two houses better than a marriage. Nobody else on this dam would have a Dane's door open to him.
He would come home with their gods on him somewhere. On a cord, or in his mouth when he swears. The priest will see it before you do.
My husband sent ours nowhere. He could gut a herring in the dark and could not ask for bread in any harbour but this one. Send the boy.
Take him to Traiectum, to Saint Martin's school
Take him to Lundenwic, to the English house
Take him to Ripa, to the Dane's hearth
Not this year
The master's bench

Inside the bishop's stone fort the master of Saint Martin's school looks the boy over as a man looks over a plank. He will take him. He asks what the house gives for his keep, and warns you what a good pupil costs a father.
A skipper's boy. Good. They can already count, and they have already been hit.
Franks, English, Frisians and Saxons have sat on that bench. They come in speaking four tongues and go out speaking one, badly.
At table he speaks Latin or he does not speak. For the first month he will be very quiet and very hungry. It passes.
The emperor's council wants the cloister schools kept for boys given to God. This is the bishop's school, not a cloister's. I take whom the bishop lets me take.
The boy has found a wax tablet on the bench and is pressing his thumbnail into it to see whether it holds a mark. It does. He looks at you as if he has found a flaw in a hull.
I tell you now, so that you do not shout at me later. If he is quick, the bishop will want him for the church. A boy who can read finds a boat small.
The church needs wax. For tablets, and for lights. And the master eats.
Give two cakes of wax and sixty pennies
Promise to carry the bishop's letters and bring him wax
Ask him to take the boy for God's sake
A house on the Strand

The Englishman who lodges Frisians above the Strand stands in his door with his own children behind him. He will keep the boy and answer for him to the reeve. He asks what the house gives, and says what a boy turns into here.
So this is the one. He looks like you about the ears. I am sorry for him.
Three nights under my roof and he is mine before the reeve. If he breaks a head, I pay for it first and come to you after. So I will be watching his hands.
First we find him a cloak that covers his knees. Your people sell us those little ones at the price of the big ones. I have not forgotten.
The boy is counting the ships drawn up on the strand below. He gets to forty, loses his place, and starts again without being told to.

I tell you now. At twelve winters the reeve counts him with my household when men are called out. And there are girls on this bank. If he comes home wanting to stay, that is your trouble and not mine.
He will eat like a hound. What comes with him?
Give a cask of Rhine wine for his table and forty pennies
Promise him first choice of your black stones
Say the boy will work for his bread
The Dane's knee

The Dane who answers for Frisian ships at Ripa sits by his fire with his own sons along the wall. Among his people a child is fostered by setting him on a man's knee. He waits to see whether you will ask, or pay, or simply do it.
You have brought me something that eats. Most Frisians bring me something that breaks.
With us, the man who raises another man's son is held the smaller of the two. So think how you do this. My sons are watching, and they will tell it for thirty years.
The boy is looking at the host's sons and they are looking at him. Nobody has blinked. The youngest of them is slowly holding out a piece of dried fish.
I tell you now. At the winter feast we eat horse, and he will sit at my table. He will swear by what my sons swear by, because boys do. What your priest makes of it is between you and your priest.
Well. The fire is warm and the knee is here.
Give a crate of glass for his table and thirty pennies' weight
Promise him the first of your wine each summer
Set the boy on his knee and say nothing of payment
Word of the boy
A skipper in from where the boy is has word of him for you, and gives it at the dam head with his eyes on his own mooring rope. The boy is well. The boy is also in trouble.
I saw your boy. He has grown. He has all his teeth. I was asked to tell you the rest as well.
He spoke Frisian at table. Twice. The second time he was beaten for it, and that night he was found at the river gate with his shoes in his hand, asking which boats went down to Dorestat.
The skipper hands you a wax tablet. There are five words cut in it in a careful, furious hand. He tells you what the master told him: four are right.
The host's nephew called him short-cloak in front of the other boys. Your boy broke his nose. It took two men to lift him off.
The host paid for the nose and says he was owed a laugh that cost that much. But he wants to know what you say, before the nephew's father asks him.
At the winter feast they put horse in front of him. He would not eat it. The men laughed. So he went out and sat in the snow by the boats until morning, and would not come in for anyone.
The host says a boy that stubborn is worth feeding. He also says the boy's feet were white, and that he wants a word from you, since he has only the one foster-son from the south.
And this, for nothing: the Danes' king has two hundred ships out, and they say he means them for the Frisian islands. Sell what you have lying north of here.
And this, for nothing: the old emperor is dead at Aachen, a week before Candlemas. His son has it all now. Charters will want showing again.
Whatever you send, send it by a man who will hand it to the boy and not to his keeper. A boy knows who a thing was given to.
Send him your own knife and one word: hold
Send word to his keepers: do not spare him
Send nothing. He must find his own feet
The school door

Three winters on. The boy comes out of the school door a hand taller, with ink on his thumb, and reads you the letters cut over the church door without being asked. The master stands behind him and does not want to let go.
"It says the house is Saint Martin's," he tells you. "It says it twice. They were afraid somebody would forget."
Your knife is on his belt, the sheath worn pale where his hand rests on it. He does not speak of it. He does not take his hand off it either.
He greets you in Latin first, correctly, and waits a breath too long before he says it again in Frisian.
He reads. He writes a hand I can bear to look at. He argues with the psalms about the price of things, which I did not teach him.
Your wax lit this church through two winters. I told the boy so, each time he thought himself forgotten.
A Bavarian wrote in his word-list that the Romans are fools and the Bavarians wise. That is what comes of learning a tongue from a list. Yours learned it from me.
The bishop has asked about him. I said he belongs to a boat. I said it once. I will not say it for you a second time.
On the way down to the boat he stops at the toll man's bench, looks at the tally lying there, and says quietly: "He has you down for two casks more than you landed."
Thank the master with sixty pennies for the church's lights
Take the boy and go
Leave him one more year
The tide on the Strand

Three winters on. You find the boy at the tide line beating an eel-wife down in her own tongue, and winning. He is a hand taller. The host comes down the bank behind him, in no hurry to give him back.
He sees you, finishes the bargain, takes the eels, and only then comes over. "She had them at three for a penny," he says. "They are four for a penny. Everybody here knows that but the Frisians."
Your knife is on his belt, the sheath worn pale where his hand rests on it. He does not speak of it. He does not take his hand off it either.
He greets you in English first, like a man of this bank, and waits a breath too long before he says it again in Frisian.
He can cheat a Kentishman in Kentish and a Mercian in Mercian. I have nothing left to teach him that I would want taught.
Your wine stood on my table at every feast since. I told the boy whose it was, each time he thought himself forgotten.
My own boy and yours are like two oars on one thwart. If you ever want him set up on this bank, I would not say no. I am only saying it.
The host's son walks down as far as the boat and stands with his hands in his belt. The two of them say nothing to each other for some time, in English.
Thank the host with forty-eight pennies and your hand
Take the boy and go
Leave him one more year
Down the beach

Three winters on. The boy comes down the beach at Ripa among the host's sons and you know him by his walk and by nothing else. He is a hand taller, he speaks as they do, and there is a small bone hammer on the cord beside his cross.
He sees you looking at the cord. "The cross is for the sea off our coast," he says. "The hammer is for the sea off theirs. I asked. Nobody could tell me where the one stops."
Your knife is on his belt, the sheath worn pale where his hand rests on it. He does not speak of it. He does not take his hand off it either.
He greets you in the Danes' tongue first, as a man of this beach, and waits a breath too long before he says it again in Frisian.
He rows. He can find the channel in fog by the smell of the mud. He still will not eat horse. I have stopped asking.
Your glass stood on my table at every feast since. I told the boy whose it was, each time he thought himself forgotten.
My sons go north in the spring for furs. They have a place on the thwart that is his size. I do not ask it. I say the place is there.
The host's sons carry his bundle down to the boat between them, though it weighs nothing. The eldest says one word to him. He says the same word back.
Thank the host with forty-eight pennies' weight and your hand
Take the boy and go
Leave him one more year
His first watch

Dusk, the wind backing, and broken water over a bar ahead. The boy has the steering oar for the first time, by your leave. The steersman says quietly that this is the place to take it back, if you mean to.
That bar is ugly on a backing wind. If she touches, she touches with your cargo in her. I say it once, and then it is your boat and your boy.
I had my first watch at twelve, running from York with half the city behind us. Nobody asked whether I was ready. I do not say that was better.
He has both hands on the oar and his feet planted wide, and he has not looked round at you once. That is either steadiness or fear. From behind they look the same.
His lips are moving. It may be a psalm. It may be the marks for this channel, said over in order. With him it is hard to know.
He is swearing at the bar under his breath, steadily, in English, as the men on the Strand swear at a tide that is late.
He has turned his face a little to feel the wind on his cheek, as the host's sons do, and he is reading the water by its colour and not by the marks.
Leave the oar in his hands
Stand behind him with your hand over his
Take the oar from him
The quarrel

A year on, in the house on the dam, with the boat laid up. He is of an age to answer for himself and he says so. He wants a share, and he wants his own way with it. The widow has come in for a light and is staying for the rest.
"I have been your hand since I could bail," he says. "I pull an oar for a hand's wage and I am told it is all mine one day. When is the day? I would like to know before I am old as well."

"You are cheated at every toll bench from here to the sea, because you cannot read what they write. Let me keep the house in ink. Or let me go back to Saint Martin, where at least they are cheated in Latin."
"Let me winter on the Strand and trade there on my own account, with the host's son. Wine up, wool down. You sell to the English like a man shouting across a river."
"My foster-brothers go north in spring. There is a thwart for me. One summer, and I come home with furs you have never had in this boat. You will not go past Ripa. I can."
"I brought her over the bar at dusk on a backing wind. You were there. You said nothing then, and you have said nothing since."
"You took the oar out of my hands at the bar, in front of the men. I have counted the days since. I can tell you the number."
"I touched her on the bar. Once. I have paid for that strake in my own head every night since. How long do I go on paying?"
"You sent word that I was not to be spared. They read it out to me. I thought you should know that they read it out."
The Franks let a boy answer for himself at fifteen winters. You answered for yourself at twelve, as I remember, and badly. Mind what you say next. He will carry it longer than you will.
The emperor has given each of his sons a portion while he is still alive to see what they do with it. If it is good enough for kings, it is good enough for a house with one boat.
Hear him to the end, and stake him: 120 pennies and a third of the next venture
He sails under you or not at all
Say nothing, and let the widow talk him down
The wrong side of the withy

Coming up to the dam at dusk you took the wrong side of the withy. The steersman laid his hand on the oar and said nothing until she was fast. Now he says it: your eyes are going, and the house must have another hand on the oar.
I will say the worst first. You did not see the withy. Last month you called the seal on the Maas bank a stone. It is your eyes, and they will not mend.
Tonight it was a stick and my hand was near. Next time it is a bank, and it is dark, and I am asleep. So. What can be done about it is in your house, eating your bread.
He is on the dam when you come ashore, with the tally of his own venture in his belt. It came home a third to the good. He has been waiting to see whether you would ask.

He is not on the dam. He went back to the roof that raised him the spring after the quarrel. When you send for him he comes by the first ship, and stands in the door, and does not sit until he is asked.
He is on the dam when you come ashore, and takes your line without a word, as he has every time since the quarrel. He does the work of two men and speaks like half of one.
My husband held his oar till the day he could not find the river with it. Then there was nobody to take it, and you know the rest. Do it while you can still see his face when you do.
The emperor put the crown on his son's head with his own hands, at Aachen, before all his great men. And he could still see.
The young emperor has shared the whole realm out among his sons already, in writing, and he is not forty. Nobody says he was too early. Yet.
The emperor's sons have risen against him this year, they say, because he would not say plainly what was whose. Say it plainly. It is cheaper.
The emperor's own sons have put him down, on a field in Alsace, and his men walked across to them in the night. That is what waiting buys.
Give him the steering oar, before witnesses
Divide the house: two keels, two hearths
Have the house set down in writing
Not yet: one more season
The steering oar

The dam head on a bright cold morning, with the men of the dams called to see it. You unship the steering oar and hold it out across the wale. What is given before witnesses stays given. It remains to say what the old man does next.
The oar is heavier out of its strap than it ever was in it. The loom is worn to the shape of your own two hands. You had not noticed that before today.
He takes it in both hands and does not say thank you. He turns it over and looks at the wear on the loom, and then he sets his hands exactly where yours were.
"I would have taken it from you kindly, two winters ago," he says, low, so the dam does not hear. "I take it all the same."
Let these men remember the day and the hour, and who stood where. Among the Franks they throw a stalk into the heir's lap. An oar is harder to lose.
There. Now you may come and sit in my storehouse door and tell the young ones the river was deeper in your day. I have kept a stool.
The Danes have a verse for it: "A son is better, though late he be born, and his father to death have fared; memory-stones seldom stand by the road save when kinsman honors his kin."
Hand it over, and keep the storehouse on the dam
Hand it over, and ship as his crew for one last summer
Hand it over, give a pound to Saint Martin and go under his roof
The oar is his. Every man on the dams who owed the house came to the ale and settled, so as to start clean with the new master. You keep the storehouse, and the stool in its door.
The oar is his. You pull the bow oar for him one whole summer and are told twice to keep stroke. In the autumn he hangs the old oar over the house door, where every heir after him will duck under it.
The oar is his. You give Saint Martin a pound of pennies and are given a bed, a bowl and a place at the back of the choir. The bishop's men know the house's boat now, and let her lie where she likes.
Two keels

The storehouse floor, swept, with everything the house owns laid out in three heaps and the widow holding the tally. One heap is his, and a keel of his own with it. It remains to say whether two keels are still one house.
Three heaps: cloth, casks, stones, and a small one of silver on top of each. Laid out like this the house looks smaller than it did, and also like more than you ever thought you had.
I have cut the tally three ways and I will swear to each of them. Two thirds stay on this dam. A third goes where he goes. Nobody is to move a cask until both of you have said yes aloud.
"Saint Martin has men who trade for him and pay no bank due here," he says. "I can be one of them, and still land your wax. The bishop gets a merchant who can read. You get a door in the stone fort."
"The host will let me a hearth above the Strand," he says. "Send me your wine and I will send you what it truly fetched. Nobody on that bank will tell a Frisian the price. They will tell me."
"My foster-father will have me land at his beach as one of his own," he says. "What comes down from the north comes to that beach first. I will be standing on it."
He does not look at you while the widow counts. He has brought silver of his own, from the roof that raised him, to buy what you would not give. He means to owe you nothing.
He looks from his heap to yours, and then moves one bolt of cloth from his to yours without a word. "That one was always the house's," he says.
Part as friends: he sails for Saint Martin and keeps your goods at Traiectum
Part as friends: he keeps a hearth above the Strand and your goods with it
Part as friends: he lands at his foster-father's and keeps your goods at Ripa
Let him buy the old boat and his third, and take the tally of it
Two keels, and one house still. He sails with the next fair wind. What he sends back the first season is more than his third was worth, and there is a door open to you now on another shore.
He counts out his foster roof's silver for the old boat and his third, takes his half of the tally stick, and sails. He will keep every bargain the stick names. He will not come to your ale.
The house in writing

A table by the church door with a calfskin leaf pegged flat on it, an ink horn, and the men of the dams standing well back from both. What the house owns, what it owes, who owes it, and whose it is next: all of it is to go down in ink.
Nobody on the dams has done this. Bishops do it, and counts, and the dead. The men have come to see whether a boat can be put on a calfskin, and whether anything will happen to you for trying.
A leaf with witnesses on it speaks in the count's court after every man here is dead. That is all the magic in it. Say the names slowly.
He cuts the pen himself and tries it on his thumbnail. "I will write it so a toll man can read it," he says. "Short words. Their Latin is worse than mine."
He stands at the priest's shoulder and makes him read each line back before the next is begun. He cannot read it. He can count the words, and he does.
Put me down for the storehouse rent, and put down that it is paid to Martinmas. If it is all going in ink, I want my part of it true.
When the names of those who owe the house are said aloud to be written, three men on the dam remember, quite suddenly, that they have the silver at home and can fetch it before the ink is dry.
Let him write it himself, with your share and his in it
Pay the priest sixty pennies to write it
Have it written twice, and lay one leaf in the church's chest: 120 pennies
The leaf is in his hand, with your share and his set side by side, and your mark under it drawn by you. He sews it into a cover of seal skin. It is the first leaf of the house's book.
The priest writes it and reads it back twice. Neither of you can read it. Both of you know now what it says, and so does the dam. It goes into the chest under the cloth.
Two leaves, cut from one skin along a wavy line so that each proves the other. One lies in the church's chest. The toll man hears of it and, for a year, takes your tally as you give it.
At Dorestat a skipper has given his steering oar to his heir at the dam head, before the men of the dams, while he still lives.
A house on the dam at Dorestat has been divided in three heaps on its own floor: the old man keeps two, and the heir has sailed with the third.
At Dorestat a skipper has had his whole house written on a calfskin, debts and all. Three men paid him the same day.

The dam head at Dorestat on a grey summer morning: a stout widow in a brown head-cloth pointing three ways with a tally stick, a thin priest beside her, and at their feet a boy of about ten sitting on a coil of rope, splicing it and listening.

A bare stone room inside the fort at Traiectum, morning light from one small window: a lean tonsured master on a bench, a row of wax tablets on the wall pegs, and a Frisian boy pressing his thumbnail into a tablet while his father stands in the doorway with two cakes of wax under his arm.

The gravel bank above the Strand at Lundenwic at low tide, afternoon, a wind off the river: a broad Englishman in a knee-length cloak in the door of a timber house with children behind him, and a boy in a short Frisian cloak counting the ships drawn up below.

A long Danish house at Ripa by firelight, evening: the host on a bench with one knee turned out, four sons along the wall, the youngest holding out a piece of dried fish to a small Frisian boy who stands very straight beside his father.

The dam head at Dorestat on a raw spring day: a weathered skipper looking down at his mooring rope while he holds out a small wax tablet, the merchant taking it, the widow watching from her storehouse door.

The door of Saint Martin's at Traiectum, a bright cold morning: a boy of about thirteen with ink on his thumb pointing up at letters cut in the stone lintel, his father looking at the boy and not the letters, the master in the shadow of the door behind them.

The tide line on the Strand at Lundenwic, early morning mist: a boy of about thirteen holding up four fingers to an eel-wife with a basket, ships beached behind, the host coming down the bank and the father standing unseen by a boat's stem.

The beach at Ripa in a pale spring noon: four Danish youths and one Frisian walking down the sand in a line, the Frisian known only by a cross and a small bone hammer on one cord, boats hauled up, the father waiting by his own.

The stern of a small open boat at dusk under a torn sky, wind backing, white water over a bar ahead: a boy with both hands on the steering oar and his feet wide, the steersman crouched at the sheet, the father standing a pace behind with one hand half raised.

Inside the house on the dam at Dorestat on a winter night, one tallow light: a youth of fifteen on his feet with his fists on the table, the merchant seated with his back to the wall, the widow in the door with an unlit lamp, snow blowing in behind her.

The channel below the dam at Dorestat at dusk, still water, a withy mark standing on the wrong side of the boat: the steersman's hand laid over the merchant's on the steering oar, the merchant peering ahead, the dam and its lights a blur.

The dam head at Dorestat on a bright cold morning, men of the dams in a half ring: the old merchant holding the unshipped steering oar out across the boat's side, the heir's two hands closing on its worn loom, the priest with a hand raised, the widow with a stool under her arm.

The swept floor of the storehouse on the dam, noon light from the open doors: cloth, casks and quern stones in three heaps with a little silver on each, the widow between them holding a split tally, father and heir on opposite sides, two boats seen on the river beyond.

A table by the church door at Dorestat on a still grey day: a calfskin leaf pegged flat, an ink horn, a hand with a quill, the old merchant making his mark, men of the dams standing well back, and three of them slipping away toward their houses.
An empty house
The widow who keeps the storehouse on the dam stops you at the dam head. She says a house with one man in it is not a house, and offers to ask about a wife for you.
Your father's house has a boat, a bed and one man in it. Who keeps your keys while you are at sea? I looked. Nobody does.
You still owe the Wōkerer. A bride's father minds that less than you think, if you pay on the day. He watches the day, not the purse.
You owe the Wōkerer nothing now. To a bride's father that is worth more than a new cloak.
I know who has daughters between here and the Danes, and what each house is short of. Shall I ask? It costs you nothing but being talked about.
I ask because I would rather lend to a house than to a boat. A boat can sink in an afternoon.
Let her ask
Give her twelve pennies to ask properly
Not this year
Four houses
The widow has asked on the dams and among the ships. Four houses would hear a suitor from Dorestat: a Frisian, a Frankish, an English and a Danish one. Each wants something that is not silver.
I have asked. Four houses would hear you. None is cheap, and each wants something besides the price.

Winaldum, on the mounds past the Almere. A free farmer with sheep, a boat, and a daughter who weaves the cloth the Franks pay for. Her mother's brother must agree; among us he always must. They want wine, and a man who comes back.

Traiectum. The bishop's steward has a daughter. He holds his plot of Saint Martin, so the bishop must give leave, and a priest will ask after your kin to the fourth knee. They want it all written down.

Eoforwic. This one is my own business, and I will tell you all of it if you choose it. A dead man's daughter, an uncle who holds her hand, and a market shut to every Frisian. A marriage might end what silver never has.
I will not send you blind. They may show you the door, or a blade. But no market in the north is richer.

Ripa. The Dane who answers for our ships there has a daughter and no use for priests. With them a bargain is a handclasp before witnesses, and the price is weighed, not counted. Her gods go where she goes. Your priest will have something to say.

You paid me to ask properly, so: the Frisian uncle's wife grinds on a worn-out stone. The steward's daughter can read. The Englishman's niece has waited all her life to be told the truth. And the Dane's girl weighs her father's silver. She will know what yours weighs.
Go to Winaldum, to the Frisian house
Go to Traiectum, to the steward's house
Go to Eoforwic, to the dead man's kin
Go to Ripa, to the Danish host's house
Who speaks for you
A suitor does not ask for himself. Someone must say he will keep her as a wife should be kept, and go surety for it. The widow offers her word and half a tally; the priest offers a letter.
A man who asks for himself is thought to have no friends. Someone must say you will keep her properly, and stand surety that you will.

Hear it all, then. Years ago at Eoforwic my husband killed a nobleman's son in a brawl. Every Frisian in the city took ship that week. The blood-price was never paid. The dead man's daughter was born after. That is who you are asking for.
I can send my word ahead with the next ship, and give you half a tally to carry. They will have the other half. My name is good on the mounds and at Traiectum.
At Eoforwic my name is the worst you could carry. It is also the only honest one. Think before you show them my tally.
At Ripa nobody has heard of me. They know your host, and they know silver. Take my tally if you like. It will do no harm.
I can write to the priest there that you are baptised, free and unmarried, and no kin of hers within the forbidden knees so far as anyone here knows. A letter is believed where a merchant is not.
To Ripa? They would wrap fish in it. Have it if you wish. I will also pray for you; that they cannot wrap fish in.
Carry the widow's half-tally
Give twelve pennies to the church and carry the priest's letter
Speak for yourself
The crew has heard
Word of the match is aboard before you are. The men have opinions, and the steersman knows something of the people you are going to.
So the boat is to fetch a bride. The men want to know two things. Is she heavy, and does her father brew.
Mound people. They will count your sheep before your silver, and you have no sheep.
A steward's daughter. Then everything will be written down, and read back to you later.
Eoforwic. I knew the boy who was on the ship that left there in a hurry. Nobody knew him better. I will take you up the river. I will not go ashore, and you will not say my name.
Danes. They will be polite. You will not know what it cost you until you are home.
And if the house is getting a wife, the men say the house can stand them a cask.
Ask the steersman what else he knows
Stand them a cask of ale and listen
Tell them to mind the oars
The mound at Winaldum

Her father receives you on the house mound, above the salt marsh. Her mother's brother sits beside him and has not spoken yet. The daughter is at the loom in the sunken hut, and the shuttle has stopped.
You are the one from the dam at Dorestat. Sit. You have come a long way across the Almere to look at sheep.
The widow's word came with the last ship. She says you pay what you owe and come back when you say you will. From her that is a long speech.
A letter. Nobody on this mound reads. But the wax on it is good wax, and a priest does not seal a lie for twelve pennies. We take it as meant.
Nobody speaks for you. Either you have no friends or you are in a hurry. Which?
The law is short. Who takes a free woman without the will of those who keep her pays twenty shillings to her keeper. So we are asked first. I am her mother's brother. I am the one you ask.

A pound of pennies to her father, counted on this mound before her kin. A gift to her on the morning after, which is hers alone. And my wife grinds our corn on a stone her grandmother wore hollow. I mention it for no reason.
If he wants to know what the cloth is worth, he can ask the one who weaves it.
The steersman's advice comes back to you: do not praise the daughter. Praise the cloth, and ask what it sells for. They will hear the rest.
Go to the loom and ask her what the cloth sells for
Lay the widow's half-tally in the father's hand
Promise the uncle black stones from the Rhine
Ask plainly and offer the pound
The steward's table
Inside the old stone fort at Traiectum the bishop's steward hears you at his own table. A priest sits by with a wax tablet, to ask after your kin. The daughter pours the ale and stays to listen.
You are the Frisian with the small boat. I have seen your name on the wrong side of the count's tally. Sit down. A debt paid on the day tells me more than a letter would.
The widow on the dam stands for you. She lent to this house in a bad year and was paid. Her word is taken here.
Your priest's letter says baptised, free, unmarried. That spares us a month of asking up and down the river.
Nobody speaks for you. Then you will swear it yourself, with men beside you, and that takes time to arrange.

Now your kin. Your father, his father, and his. Your mother's side the same. And who lifted you from the font. If your people and hers meet inside the fourth knee, or at the font, there is nothing more to say.
The emperor's order is new, but the rule is old: nobody weds until the priests and the elders of the people have asked into the blood.

My terms. A dower in writing, read out before witnesses: it is hers if you die first. The wedding in the open, as the king's law asks of noble and common alike. And the bishop's leave, because I hold my plot of Saint Martin, and so does she.
I will read the deed myself, father. Then nobody need wonder later what the clerk left out.
The steersman's advice comes back to you: wash first, and take wax for the church. A steward notices wax.
Hand the priest your letter
Lay two cakes of wax on the table for Saint Martin's altar
Ask the daughter what a dower should hold
Name your kin and let them ask at Dorestat
The dead man's brother

At Eoforwic a Frisian hull is looked at twice. The man who holds the girl's hand is brother to the youth killed in the year the Frisians ran. He hears you standing, a monk beside him to see it done properly, and the niece at the back of the hall among the women.
A Frisian, asking for a woman of my house. My brother was killed by a Frisian on this strand when I was a boy. Say what you want, and who sent you.
The king took a Mercian wife, to make a friend of Offa. So I am told that marriages mend things. My brother has been dead these many winters and nothing has mended.
The blood-price was paid before witnesses and I gave my hand on it. So I hear you as I would hear any man. That is all it bought you.
Nobody has paid for him. Remember it while you talk.

By the old law of the Kentish kings a maiden is bought with cattle, and the bargain stands if there is no guile in it. If there is guile, she is brought home again and he has his cattle back. We say much the same here, in more words.
He carries a priest's letter from over the water: baptised, free, unmarried. The archbishop's people will want that known before anything else is.
The niece has not been asked to speak. She has moved three places nearer the fire since you began.
The steersman's words come back to you: he will not go ashore, and you will not say his name. Someone on this strand will know his face all the same. A thing told is lighter than a thing found.
Show the widow's tally and say whose house stands behind you
Say you are a merchant of Dorestat, and no more
Ask the monk to lay it before the archbishop's man first
The host's fire at Ripa

The Dane who answers for Frisian ships at Ripa hears you by his own fire. His daughter is at the door with the scales, weighing the day's silver. An old woman has been sent for, to ask by lot whether the luck of the house leaves with the girl.

You are from the dam at Dorestat. Your people have lain at my landing since my father's day and paid what guests pay. Now one of you asks for something I do not sell. Speak. I am listening, and so is the door.
He says it slowly, in the few Frisian words a host needs. The daughter laughs at one of yours and does not say which.
Sigfred is king, and he has not said whom a free man's daughter may marry. So it is my business, and her brothers', and the gods'.

With us it goes so. You name the bride-price. I name what she takes from home. We clasp hands on it before witnesses. Within the year the ale is drunk, and six men see you to her bed, so that nobody can say later it was not a marriage.
Two marks of silver. Weighed. I do not know your king's face, and my scales do not need to.
I cut three twigs from a tree that bears, and mark them. I do not ask whether he is a good man. I ask whether the luck stays.
One thing more. She keeps her gods. If your priests wash her, I will hear of it, and you will not lie at my landing again.
