The steersman's advice comes back to you: do not haggle over her, or they will think you are buying a cow and sell you one. Let the girl weigh your silver herself. She will anyway.
Put your purse on her scale and say nothing
Give the father a cask of Rhine wine and name no price
Offer a mark and a half
The bride-ale on the mound

Her kin stand in a ring on the mound, father's side and mother's. The price is to be counted where they can see it, her hand given, and the ale drunk. Her brother has brought his boat round on the tide.
Here are her kin, both sides. Count it out where they can see. Then I put her hand in yours and you take her home, and it is done before these people and before God.
A pound of pennies, as we said. I have counted the witnesses. Now I count the pennies.
You asked badly when you first came, and I made you wait for it. The waiting was the fine. The price is still a pound.
You promised black stones. I have looked in your boat. A man who forgets a promise to the uncle will forget one to the niece. Come back with them.

Those are Rhine stones in your boat. My wife has seen them. So has every wife on the mound. If they are a gift and not for sale, there is room under my roof for your goods for as long as I have a roof.
No church stands on the mound. A priest has walked a day over the marsh to bless what the kin have already settled, and to see that it is done in the open.
If you are my sister's man, my boat and yours can lie on the same bank. I know the Vlie and the flats. You know the Rhine. Between us that is the whole road.
The bolts in the chest are mine, and they go with me, not with the price. Sell them where cloth is short. Not here, where every hut has a loom.
The cloth in the chest is mine. Father will tell you how much there is. I will tell you if he is wrong.
Count out a pound of pennies before the kin
Count out the pound, and set down two pairs of black stones for the uncle as a gift
Ask for one more season
The deed and the blessing

At the door of Saint Martin's the dower is read out before the bishop's people, the earnest is laid in her father's hand, and a priest blesses the pair. The bishop has given his leave, on a condition.

It is written: to her, if she outlives him, a pound of silver as dower, a third of all they gain together, and whatever he gives her on the morning after. Witnesses, look at it. You need not read it. Look at it.
By our law a bride is pledged with a shilling and a penny, laid in my hand before these men. The dower goes into her own chest today, and I will watch it go in.
The bishop gives leave on one condition. The house you take her to stands under Saint Martin, as mine does: a pound of wax at his feast each year, and his letters carried when he asks.
For that you have a plot on his bank at Dorestat, no bank due is asked of you, and the count's men do not lodge under your roof.

Refuse, and she is still yours; the bishop will not stop a lawful marriage over a pound of wax. Then you deal with the count as before, and I keep a corner of my storehouse inside these walls for your goods.
Take the condition or leave it. But have it written that the storehouse keys are mine while you are at sea. I have kept my father's since my mother died, and he has lost nothing.
I have read it. It is fair. The clerk spelled my name two ways; I have made him choose.
People have come down from both churches to watch. A wedding in the open is the law. It is also the only thing happening in Traiectum today.
Give the earnest, fill her chest, and take Saint Martin's condition
Give the earnest and fill her chest, but keep your house the count's
Ask for one more season
The peace-weaving

Her kin and the archbishop's man stand witness in the wic by the Foss. You are to say before them how you will keep her, what you give for her, and what is hers if she outlives you, and your sureties must be named. The dead man is named first.
Before anything, I name my brother, who was killed here by a Frisian and is not paid for. Now everyone has heard it, and we can go on.
Before anything, I name my brother, who was killed here by a Frisian and paid for at last. Now everyone has heard it, and we can go on.

He is to promise, and his friends go surety, that he will keep her by God's law as a man should keep his wife. Then he names what he gives for her rearing, what he grants her for taking him, and what is hers if she outlives him.
And since he takes her out of this land into another, her kin must be sure that no wrong will be done her there.

You told me the worst thing first, in my own hall. My kin argued for a hundred nights. The women won. A pound and a half, and a plot by the Foss beside mine, where I can see what a Frisian does with it. Whoever touches your house here touches mine.
You let me learn from a wharf-hand whose silver is behind you. I learned it. Two pounds, and be glad it is a price. You may build by the Foss. I will not have my niece's man sleeping on the strand.
You are a stranger, and a stranger pays a stranger's price. Two pounds. You may build by the Foss. I will not have my niece's man sleeping on the strand.
Or the archbishop's man holds a pound for a year and a day. If she is well kept, it comes to her. If not, it comes to me, and so do you.
The old song I gave you says of every grief: that passed over, and so may this. A monk is not supposed to like such songs. I gave it to you so that I need not keep it.
Let my first son have my father's name. Then he will have come home, and my uncle can stop counting.
I have been told what you are. I have not been told who. I suppose there will be time.
Your steersman has not left the boat. From the strand he can be seen in the stern, sitting very still, facing the river.
Promise her first son the dead man's name, and count out a pound and a half
Count out two pounds and name your sureties
Lay a pound in the archbishop's man's hand for a year and a day
Ask for one more season
The handclasp

Witnesses stand round the host's fire at Ripa. The silver is to be weighed, hands clasped on the bargain, and the bridal ale drunk. Then there is the question of whose gods bless it, and what the priest at home will be told.

Here is my hand. Two marks for her. From this house she takes a chest, a loom, and my name behind her on this coast. You may build on my plot by the river and lie at my landing as a son does. Say it back before these men.
You offered me a mark and a half for my daughter. I have told that story at every fire since. It has been worth the other half-mark to me.
The twigs fell well twice and badly once. The bad one was water. Keep her off the sea in the dark of the year.
Now the hammer is laid in the bride's lap and she is hallowed, as the old song says it was done among the gods. Your god's man may stand outside for that part, if his god minds.

My guests tell me your priests call a marriage with one of us no marriage. Ours say the same of yours. So we are even. What you tell your priest is your affair. What is done to my daughter's gods is mine.
Do right by her and by them, and any man of mine on this coast answers for your boat as he would for my own.
At Dorestat the priest will ask whether she has been to the font. The bishops forbid a Christian to wed a heathen. Nobody at Ripa has heard of the bishops.
I will hear your priest out, as a guest hears a host. If he wants to mark me with his cross for that, he may. It is a courtesy. It is not a washing.
My gods come with the chest. Stow them where you like, so long as it is dry.
Weigh out two marks, clasp hands, and let her gods come with her
Weigh out two marks, and ask her to take the sign of the cross as a guest
Pay in Frankish goods: three casks of wine and a crate of glass
Ask for one more season
The morning gift

On the morning after, a husband gives his wife a gift that is hers alone, whatever becomes of him. Every people on this sea has the custom and a word for it. What you give now is what she has if the sea keeps you.
Her kin are waiting outside to hear what it is. They will remember it longer than they remember the price.
Among us it need not be much. It must be mine.
It goes into the deed, under the dower. I will see that it does.
By the old law, if I bear no child, my father's kin have it back. So give me something worth their sailing for.
My mother had a cow and a kettle. She still has the kettle.
The keys of the house, and a third of all you gain together
Sixty pennies in a purse of her own
A pair of brooches from the hold
The keel comes home
A year on. The boat lies at the dam and there is a light in the house. The English have a verse about a Frisian's wife and her man's ship, and for once it is about you.

Dear is the welcome guest to the Frisian wife, when the vessel stands, his ship is come, and her husband to home, her own provider, and she calls him in, washes his weedy garment, and to him gives new raiment; 'tis pleasant on land to him whom his love awaits.
Her cloth is sold before it is off the loom, and her brother's boat has lain here beside yours. The dam says you married sheep. The dam is jealous.
She has read every tally in the house and found two of mine short. I like her. The count's man came for the bank due, looked at Saint Martin's mark on your post, and went away again.
She has read every tally in the house and found two of mine short. I like her. The count's man still comes for the bank due. She makes him wait while she counts it.
A ship of ours lay at Eoforwic all summer and nobody ran. My husband's name was said aloud there and no one reached for a knife. I did not think I would live to tell you that.
She weighs every penny that crosses your threshold, and has caught the moneyer's boy twice. Half the dam is afraid of her. The other half owes her.
She has not come to the font. I have not written to the bishop. Yet. Bring her to stand at the back at Easter, and I can go on not writing.
She let me sign her with the cross, and has stood at the back ever since. She asks hard questions about the bread. I count her a hearer. The bishop need not count at all.
She has held the keys while you were at sea. The storehouse is fuller than you left it, and she has the tally that says whose doing that was.
There is a cradle by the hearth. The widow says the child has your father's nose, and that this is not the child's fault.
Go in
Go in, and count what she has made of her third
First take the widow sixty pennies for her trouble

Evening at a dam head in Dorestat, low sun on the river: a Frisian widow of about forty in a white head-cloth, keys at her belt, has stopped a young skipper beside his small clinker boat; wattle and thatch storehouses on the dam behind them.

Inside the widow's storehouse on the dam, rain outside, one tallow light: she lays four tally sticks in a row on the head of a wine cask, one for each house, while the merchant stands with his cloak still wet.

A dry bright morning outside a small wooden church at Dorestat: the widow splits a notched tally stick down its length and holds out one half, while a priest sitting on the step writes on a scrap of parchment laid on his knee.

At sea under a grey sky, the small boat running before a light wind: the steersman at the side rudder looks straight ahead and says nothing, the mate grins from the oar bench, one ale cask lashed amidships.

A sod house mound above a flat salt marsh at Winaldum, wide sky, late afternoon sun: two older men on a bench by the door, the merchant standing before them, and in the dark mouth of a sunken hut a young woman at an upright loom, her hand still on the shuttle; sheep on the slope.

A timber hall inside old Roman stone walls at Traiectum, daylight from the open door: the bishop's steward at a trestle table, a priest with a wax tablet at his elbow, the daughter pouring ale from a black jug and looking at the merchant over it.

A Northumbrian hall at Eoforwic, noon light slanting through hearth smoke: a tall thegn in a dark red cloak with his hand near his sword hilt, a monk at his side, the Frisian merchant standing alone on the open floor, and a young woman among the women at the back, watching him.

A longhouse at Ripa at dusk, the long fire burning: the Danish host on his bench, an old woman laying three marked twigs on a white cloth, and in the doorway against the evening sky his daughter with folding scales, a small heap of cut silver in one pan.

The top of the mound at Winaldum on a windy bright day: kin standing in a ring, pennies being counted onto a cloth in the middle, the bride with her hand in her father's, a priest muddy to the knee from the marsh, and a second boat drawn up on the creek bank below.

The door of Saint Martin's inside the fort at Traiectum on a still grey morning: a priest reads from a parchment, the steward holds out his open hand for a shilling and a penny, the bride stands beside a small iron-bound chest, and the bishop's people look on from the yard.

The strand by the Foss at Eoforwic under a cold clear sky: the kin in a half circle, the thegn speaking with one hand raised, a monk and the archbishop's man as witnesses, the bride in a cloak pinned with a silver ring; out on the river the Frisian boat, with one man sitting very still in her stern.

Night in the host's house at Ripa, firelight on faces: the Dane and the merchant clasp hands over a pair of scales heaped with silver, witnesses standing round, the bride seated with a small iron hammer laid in her lap and the old woman behind her.

Early morning, pale light through an open door: the new wife sits on the edge of the bed with a married woman's head-cloth on for the first time; the merchant holds out a ring of keys, and a small purse and a pair of brooches lie on the chest between them.

Dusk at the dam at Dorestat a year later, light rain: the small boat made fast, a lit doorway up the bank with a woman in it holding a child, dry clothes over her arm; the widow under her storehouse eave, watching, pleased with herself.
A keel on the sand
The wright at the dam heads has no hull on his slip. He has watched your boat come and go all summer, and he has an opinion about her.
Your boat goes out so deep that the eels look over the rail. A house that loads like that has outgrown four oars.
You went away to think. Thinking is cheap, and my slip has stood empty the whole time you were at it.
A keel ship. Thirty-four feet of keel, forty-six over the stems, a hold for six times what you carry now, and five men to work her.
A pound of pennies now, so I keep the slip for you. Ordered by Martinmas, afloat by Easter. A pound and a quarter more on the day she swims.
You find the stuff. Fourteen oaks from up the Rhine, with the crooked boughs left on. Ten kegs of rivets. A sail from the terp women. I find the hands.

He cuts a hazel stick to the length of his forearm and notches it three times: the width of a plank, the thickness of a rivet's shank, the span between rivets. The stick is the ship, he says. Do not lose it.
They say you owe the Wōkerer. That is between you and him, until he makes it my business.
Count out a pound of pennies as earnest
Offer half a pound and your name
Ask what it will all cost, and go away to think

He counts the pennies twice, by twelves, and puts the stick in your hand. By evening two posts stand in the sand where her stems will be. You have ordered a ship: oak from Colonia, iron from Daventre, a sail from Wijnaldum.
He weighs the half pound in his hand and your name in his head, and takes both. The stick is yours. He says he has built for worse payers, and that most of them paid.

He reckons it on his fingers: the earnest, the oak, the iron, the sail, his wage at the launch. Near five pounds of silver, if nothing goes wrong. He says something always goes wrong. He will ask again while the summer lasts.
Oak across the river
Across the river from the city stand the old fort and the king's estate, and behind them the king's wood. The steward walks you through the oaks with the wright's stick in your hand.
The king wants his woods kept and his clearings cleared. This is a clearing. Every oak you take out of it is one I need not burn.
We fell after midsummer and before Christmas, and when the moon is past her full. A Roman wrote that in a book about war. I have not read it. The oaks seem to have.
Felled, limbed and bound with withies into a raft. Six days down to your dam heads with two of my men on it. They walk home, so feed them well.
Or take what the storm took two winters ago. It lies there dry, and I will sell it for less than half. A wright will tell you why.
I have trees and no axes. Every man who can lift one has gone into Saxony with the king, again. If your crew can swing, they can earn your oak.
My men are home from Saxony and tired of it. If your crew will swing axes in their place for a few weeks, you can earn your oak instead of buying it.
And there is that one. Four men cannot ring it with their arms. Too great to cleave for planks. Hollowed and spread, it is a river ship by itself, and no iron in her.
Buy fourteen standing oaks and the crooked boughs
Take the windfalls: dry, and cheap
Lend your crew to the clearing and take the pay in oak
Buy the great oak and have a river ship made of it here
The steward cuts his mark and yours into fourteen trunks. They will fall when the moon allows and come down on the river. The raft should lie at Dorestat in fifty days.

The windfalls are grey and hard as horn, and they ring when struck. They are bound into a raft within the week. The steward takes your silver and wishes your wright patience. The raft should lie at Dorestat in twenty-five days.

Your men fell oaks for the king for three weeks and curse you for all of them. No silver changes hands. Their hands are raw and the steward has learned their names. The raft should lie at Dorestat in sixty-five days.

You buy the one great oak. A wright of the river bank will hollow it here, through the winter, with fire and adze. The stick in your hand is no use now, and the wright at Dorestat keeps your earnest. Come back in a hundred days.
The raft at the dam head
The raft lies against your dam, low in the water, with a Frank asleep on it. The wright walks its length, strikes each trunk with the back of his axe and listens.
Good oak, and wet, as it should be. Eleven of these will cleave true. Three have a twist in the grain that I cannot wedge out.
This is dead wood. It will blunt every axe I own and split wherever I put a rivet. And three of them are twisted as well.
There is an old keel ship sunk at her post by the north dams. Nobody has claimed her since my father's day. Her knees and floors are grown oak, and sound under the mud.

His men drive wedges into the first trunk. It opens along its length with a sound like ice going on the river, and the two halves lie steaming in the cold. Nobody here owns a saw long enough, or wants one.
So. Three more oaks from upriver, or the old ship's bones, or I build with what came. I will do any of the three. Only one of them will I do without saying so afterwards.
Send upriver for three more oaks
Raise the old ship's knees and floors from the north harbour
Tell him to build with what came

The Frank wakes, takes sixty pennies and the wright's message, and walks south. Three more trunks will come down behind a wine boat. The keel is laid meanwhile, on blocks, with its scarf to the river. The wright wants thirty days before he will talk about her shape.

Your men spend four days to the waist in cold mud at the north dams. Nine knees and six floor timbers come up black and whole. What is left of her settles deeper. The keel is laid. The wright wants twenty days before he will talk about her shape.

The wright looks at you for a while and then at the twisted trunks, and tells his men to cleave them. The keel is laid. He says nothing more that day, and wants twenty days before he will talk about her shape.
Iron from the heath
West of the river the heath smokes day and night. Its iron comes down to the bank at Daventre. The smith takes the wright's stick and turns it over in his fingers.
Brown stones off the heath, and charcoal, and three days of a man's breath. It is soft iron. It bends before it breaks, which is what you want between two planks.
A ship of this notch is two thousand rivets, each with its rove. Ten kegs. A man can carry one keg and will tell you about it afterwards.
Every wright from here to the sea sends me a stick. Yours is the first this year with the notches cut square. He knows what he is about.
The emperor has ordered ships built on every river. His men take iron at their own price and call it service. What I sell you, I sell you today.
My blooms lie at the furnaces, a day's walk into the heath. Carry them down for a week with your crew and I take half the price.
Buy ten kegs cut to the wright's notch
Carry his blooms down from the heath for a week, and pay half
Buy nothing today

He tries a rivet from each keg against the notch before he lets it go. Ten kegs go into your hold, and she sits down in the water under them. They are for the wright at Dorestat when he asks for iron.

A week on the heath with a yoke on your shoulders. The furnace men live in the smoke and laugh at shipmen. Ten kegs for half the silver, and a smith who now calls you by name. They are for the wright at Dorestat when he asks for iron.
He hands the stick back and goes on with his work. The iron will be here next time. He does not promise the price will.
The weavers of the terp
On the terp the looms stand in huts dug half into the ground, where the damp keeps the warp from snapping. The woman who speaks for the weavers hears what you want and looks at her hands.
A sail that size is four women and a winter. You have come at the right end of the year. The looms are warm and there is nothing else to do but talk.
A sail that size is four women and a winter, and you ask in summer, with the sheep to shear and the hay to get in. It will be woven. It will take the same days.
And count six days to the week. The king has sent word that women shall not weave on the Lord's day, nor card, nor shear. He did not say who spins his own cloaks.
Our law prices a weaver's hand with a harper's and a goldsmith's. Break into a weaving hut and you pay with your neck. Remember that when you come to haggle.
Silver is well enough. But a mound in the salt marsh has no stone, no vines and no trees. Good querns and a cask of wine say more here than pennies.
Or take cloak-cloth off the bench today and have it sewn. It is woven for backs, not for wind. It will stretch like a wet stocking, but it is there.
Order the sail: half the silver now, half when it is woven
Pay the first half in quernstones and wine
Buy the cloak-cloth and have it sewn for a sail
Not yet
She takes ninety pennies and ties a knot in a red thread for each of them. The long wool is set aside for you. Come back in a hundred and ten days with the other half.

Two black querns go up the terp on a sledge with half the village behind them, and the cask after. Nobody mentions silver again. The long wool is set aside for you. Come back in a hundred and ten days with the other half.
The cloak-cloth is sewn into a sail in two days by every woman who can hold a needle. It is a handsome blue. The weavers do not say what they think of it, and you have a sail aboard.
She nods and goes back into the hut. A loom does not care when you come, she says, only how long you leave it alone.
Off the looms
The sail lies folded on a bench in the largest hut: fifteen lengths sewn edge to edge, grey as a seal and heavier than a man. It smells of sheep and smoke.
Fifteen lengths, each as long as your mast is tall. The fleeces of a hundred sheep, and only the long outer wool. Count the seams if you like. We did.
Your querns grind fine and the wine was drunk at a wedding. The bride's mother wove the middle length. You may think it the tightest.
A shipman of Dorestat was here at the new moon, one with a dam head of his own. He offered half as much again for it as it lay. I told him it was spoken for. He laughed.
Rub it with mutton fat and red earth before it meets the wind, or the wind will go straight through it. That part is your work.
Pay the second half, as agreed
Pay it, and match the other man's offer as a gift
Say the edge is thin, and offer two thirds
Leave it on the bench until you have the silver
She unties the knots in the red thread one by one as you count. Four men carry the sail down to the boat. It is the terp's own weave, and the wright will know it.

You pay what was agreed and lay the other man's offer on top of it, and say it is for the women. She is silent, which on the terp is praise. The cloaks will be cheap for you this season, and they want four casks of wine and will pay over the price.
You hold the edge to the light and say what you see. She sees it too. She takes two thirds and has the sail carried down, and nobody helps your men lift it aboard.

She folds the sail away from under your hand. It was spoken for, she says, and now it is spoken for again. The shipman of Dorestat has it by the next tide. You will have to find a sail elsewhere, or launch under the old one.
The sail stays on the bench with a clean fleece over it. She will keep it twenty days more. She does not say what happens after that.
The Dane's opinion
The keel and both stems are up and the first strakes are on. A Dane off a Ripa ship that winters at the dam heads has stood before her every morning for a week. Today he speaks.
It is a good trough. My father built ships. He would take two fingers off every plank, a foot off her depth, and give her sixteen oars.
And she would carry four tons where mine carries six, and want twelve men fed where mine wants five. I build for merchants. They count.
Yours carries more. Mine arrives. She goes against the wind on her oars, up any creek, and nothing with a sail alone will catch her.
A ship of that look on this river, with their king and his fleet sitting at Sliesthorp? The count's men will board her first and ask whose she is afterwards.
Your own Northman has come up behind you. He looks along the keel, then at the Dane, and says one word in their tongue. The Dane nods. It was the word for fast.
Choose today. From here on every plank is cut for the one ship or the other. And whichever she is, I want the iron within sixty days, or I go looking for old.
Keep the wright's ship: deep and broad, built to carry
Let the Dane line her off: lighter, lower, more oars
Ask the wright, before his men, what he would take from the Dane

The wright does not smile, but he sends a boy for ale. The Dane lifts one shoulder and goes back to his ship. She will be deep and broad, as she was drawn in the sand. The planking goes on for twenty-five days before he needs the iron.

You give the Dane forty pennies and a chalked line. He walks her length, laying it along the stems, and the wright's men watch their master. The wright says he has built to worse orders. She will be long and low. The planking goes on for twenty-five days before he needs the iron.

The wright thinks, before all his men, and it costs him something. Then: the Dane's way with the top strake, and nothing else. The Dane grins and gives you a riddle of his people for your trouble. She stays the wright's ship. The planking goes on for twenty-five days.

The wright says he would take the Dane's ale and nothing more, and his men laugh too loudly. He does not thank you for asking where they could hear. She stays his ship. The planking goes on for twenty-five days.
The wright will not be hurried
Four strakes a side, and the wright has stopped. He needs the iron now, and you need to know when she will swim. He answers the second question first.
Ninety days, if the frost lets the tar run. Ask me again tomorrow and it is ninety-one.
Ninety days from the day I have the iron. It is not winter, so the men will want to be in the fields, and I will not stop them. Ninety.
Green oak moves as it dries. Rivet it too fast and it tears itself round the iron. I put on a strake, and then I let her think about it.
And today is a feast. There is not a hammer lifted on these dams today, and you are the only man here who has noticed.
No Sundays. The king forbids it, the priest watches the dams from his door, and our own law fines a free man for it. I am a free man.
Your dry oak splits at every third rivet. I bore each hole twice as slowly, and it still splits. I said it would.
The Dane's planks are two fingers thinner than mine. One slip of the axe and the plank is firewood. My men are learning. I am not paying for the lessons.
And you have come without the ten kegs. Then it is the breaking beach, and old rivets cut out of dead ships. Iron remembers every hole it has been in.
Hand over the ten kegs and let him keep his own pace
Hand over the iron and pay for four more men of his choosing
Hand over the iron and tell him to work feast days and by torchlight
Bring no iron: let him cut old rivets on the breaking beach
He has the kegs rolled under the hull and opens one with his own hands. Ninety days, he says again, as if you had argued. She will be ready for the rollers then.
He picks four men off the dams by looking at their hands, not their faces. With ten at the planks she will be ready in sixty days. He does not call it hurrying. He calls it more men.

They work by torchlight and through two feasts, with a boy set to watch the church door. Nobody tells the priest. She will be on the rollers in thirty days. The wright has stopped looking at her seams when you are near.

They work by torchlight and through two feasts. Somebody tells the priest. The fine is twelve pennies and it is yours, read out at the church door. She will be on the rollers in thirty days. The wright has stopped looking at her seams when you are near.

His boys spend a week on the breaking beach with cold chisels, cutting rivets out of dead planks and beating them straight. They are a hundred shapes of brown. She will be ready in ninety days, the wright says, and he does not say for what.
The count at the slip
The count has ridden down to the dam heads with his steward and stands before the hull with his thumbs in his belt. The wright's men have all found work at the far end of her.
So this is where my silver went. A man who owes me builds himself a ship. I have not decided whether that is impudence or good sense.
You owe me nothing, and here you are with a ship on my bank. I like to see it. I like still more to know whose she is.
The king wants boats in Saxony. He has them dragged over dry land from river to river, and he asks his counts where the boats are to come from.
The king has set ships and watchmen at every river mouth against the heathen men. I am to find hulls for this one. I have found one.
The emperor has ordered a fleet built on every river that runs to this sea, and means to come and look at it himself. Every count is counting keels.
The coast must be watched, whoever is emperor. Ships are ordered and ships are not built, and then a count is asked why.

Give her to me for the king's service. I count back all you have laid out, you have a plot at the dam heads, and my hand is over your house. Or carry for me once a year. Or say no. I have heard the word before.
Say she is the house's ship, with respect
Offer one carrying a year at the count's word, for an easier toll
Offer the carrying for a year's delay of the Wōkerer's day
Give her to the count for the king's service
The count looks at the hull a little longer than is comfortable, and says a house should have a ship. He rides back up to the hall. The wright's men come back along the hull one by one.
One carrying a year, when his steward sends: the count's corn, or the count's men. He has it said before witnesses. The toll man will take half from you for half a year. The ship is still yours.
One carrying a year, and for it the Wōkerer's day is put off a year. He cuts a new notch in the tally and does not look pleased to. The ship is still yours.

You give her, there on the sand, before she has touched water. The count's steward counts back nine hundred pennies and paces out a plot at the dam heads. The wright finishes her for the king. You are the count's shipman now, and the toll man knows it.
The launching
She stands tarred black on the slip with her stem to the river. Tallowed rollers lie under her keel, a rope runs to every hand on the dam, and the priest of the upper church has brought his book.
She will weep for a day or two while the oak drinks. Then she will take up and be tight. Do not bail her dry in a fright. Let her drink.
I have put right what could be put right. She is a sound ship. She is not the ship she could have been, and only you and I will ever know it.
Lord, who bade Noah build of wood and carried eight souls over the flood, stretch out your hand over this ship and over those who go in her, and bring them to the harbour they wish for.

My master set us this at school. Long and swift I go, daughter of a fair forest, with a great company crowded close about me. I run many roads and leave no footprint. I never guessed it. I was born inland.
I have cut my mark under her stem, where the water will hide it. I do not do that for every hull.
Your old boat lies at the next post with her four oars shipped. From up here she looks like something the new ship might carry on deck.
Bend on the terp sail, pay the wright and send her down the rollers
Pay the wright and launch her under the sailcloth you have
Pay the wright and launch her under the old boat's sail
Not yet: leave her on the slip

She goes down the rollers faster than anyone meant and sits on the river as if she had always been there. The grey sail goes up and fills. The wright says you may build on your own dam from now on, and he will come to you. The priest gives you his tablet with the riddle on it. Everyone on the dams wants tar.

She goes down the rollers and takes the water with a sound like a long breath. The sail is not the one she was drawn for, and she swims well under it all the same. The priest gives you his tablet with the riddle on it. The house has a keel ship.

She goes down the rollers and floats high and handsome. The old boat's sail on her yard looks like a child's shirt on a carter. She will be slow until she has a sail of her own. But she swims, and she is the house's.
The ropes are coiled again and the priest takes his book home. The wright says a ship keeps on a slip. He also says tallow does not.
A ship before her time
She stands on the rollers, tarred, and to any eye but one she is a ship. The wright has not cut his mark under her stem, and says he will not.
Dead oak. There are splits at the rivets under that tar. I have stopped them with wool and they are still splits.
Three strakes are of the twisted trunks. They sit against their neighbours like a bad marriage. I have made them lie. I cannot make them like it.
Half her rivets came out of dead ships. Some will hold for twenty years. Some for two. They all look alike.
And that sail is a cloak. In the first hard blow it will stretch into a bag, and a bag pulls a ship sideways.
I closed her up by torchlight, on wood that had not finished moving. She will open somewhere. I do not yet know where, and that is what I mind.
She will swim. I think she will swim. She will need bailing every watch and mending every winter, and she will wet whatever lies lowest in her.
Or give me a month and sixty pennies. I take out what is worst and put in what is right. Then I will launch her gladly. Today I launch her because you pay me.
Pay the wright and launch her as she is
Give him a month and sixty pennies to put it right
Not yet: leave her on the slip

She goes down the rollers and floats. Water stands in her by evening, a hand deep, and no deeper by morning. The wright takes his silver and does not come to the ale. The house has a keel ship, and a bailer that will never be dry.

She goes down the rollers, floats, and by dark has filled to the thwarts at her post. It takes a day and a night and every man on the dam to get her dry and stop the seam. The house has a keel ship. Dorestat will not let you forget which one.
The wright has three strakes off her by nightfall, and he is whistling. A month, he says. Come back when the tar is dry and she will be a ship he can stand beside.
She stays on the rollers under her tar. The wright says she will not get better by standing there, and she will not get worse.
The long ship on the Rhine

She is on the rollers, and nothing else on the Rhine looks like her: long, low, sixteen oar ports, her stems a man's height above the rail. Half Dorestat has come to see whether she floats. The other half has come to see what the count's men say.
Sixteen oars and twelve men. You will curse the bread they eat. Then one day something will come over the edge of the sea behind you, and you will bless every mouth.
I have built ships for thirty winters, and this winter I learned something. Do not tell the Dane. He knows it already.
Your toll man came down yesterday and asked whether she was built for the Danish king. I said she was built for a man who dislikes being late.
Think how she looks from a dune. Every watchman on this coast will light his fire when he sees those stems. Hang something Christian where it shows.
She is thin, and thin forgives nothing. With that wood and that iron I would not take her past the river mouth before her first winter's mending. I will not steer her.
My skipper sails for Ripa without me if I ask him. A ship like this wants a man at the steering oar who has stood at one. I have. I know the way in to Ripa in the dark.
Bend on the sail, pay the wright, and ask the Dane to steer her
Pay the wright and launch her
Not yet: leave her on the slip

She slides in and hardly marks the water. The Dane takes the steering oar as a man takes his own cup, and gives you a riddle of his people for luck. With the grey sail up she goes down the river faster than a man can ride the bank. A Frisian wright has built a northern ship at Dorestat, and the Dane will show you the way in to Ripa.

She slides in and hardly marks the water. Your men sit down to sixteen oars and look at one another. The Dane watches from the dam and goes back to his own ship. The house has a long ship, and Dorestat has something to talk about until harvest.
She stays on the rollers. Boys come at dusk to count her oar ports and always make it a different number.
The river ship

On the bank below the old fort lies the great oak, hollowed thin as a shield, spread wide over a slow fire and raised with two strakes pegged with willow. There is not a nail in her. A short mast stands well forward for the tow rope.
One tree, forty-six feet of it. I hollowed her to two fingers and opened her over the fire like a pod. If she cracks, she cracks then. She did not.
The estate's wine goes down the river at Martinmas, and cloaks come up for the household. I would sooner send it in a ship I watched being made.
The emperor has said no new tolls where men only stretch a rope across the water. Some lords along this river have not heard yet. Carry my word and they hear quicker.
Half a pound to the wright and she is yours. Take the estate's carrying with her, and three casks go aboard today on account.
Upstream you haul her by rope from the bank, as everyone does. And at Saint Goar's cell you stop and say the prayer. Frisians have passed it by. The river remembers them.
Pay the wright and take the estate's carrying
Pay the wright and owe the estate nothing
Leave her on the bank until you have the silver

She floats in a hand's depth of water and three casks hardly move her. The steward's boatman shows you the channel as far as the first bend, and tells you the rest as you go. Sixteen bolts of Frisian cloaks are wanted here before the spring, well over the price. The house has turned to the river.
She floats in a hand's depth of water. The steward wishes you a good river and gives his wine to another boat. The house has a river ship and owes nobody for her.
She lies on the bank under wet sacking so that she does not dry and crack. The wright will keep her so for fifteen days. He mentions that sacking is not free.
The ship on the penny
The moneyer's bench in the upper town is bright with new pennies. On one side stands the emperor's name. On the other, where the old dies had a cross or an axe, there is a ship.
New dies, and the name of the town round a ship. A mast, a yard, a steering oar, and stems that turn up. I needed something to look at while I cut it.
I sat two mornings on your dam with a wax tablet. She holds still better than most. If the mast is a little short, that is my hand, not your wright's.
I sat on your dam with a wax tablet. I left out the man bailing. A die has only so much room.
I began with yours. The count's steward looked at the wax and asked whether the emperor's penny was to carry a Danish ship. So the stems came down a little. Hers are still in it, if you know.
When I was a boy, Dorestat's penny had an axe on it. Nobody ever told me whose axe. A ship, at least, everyone here understands.
Give him two worn pennies for the first one struck, and keep it
Ask for it as a gift between neighbours
A penny is a penny
He finds the first one struck, a little off its centre, and takes two worn ones for it. You put it where it will not be spent. An heir will ask one day what ship that is.
He turns the first one over twice and gives it to you, off its centre as it is. Between neighbours, he says, and writes nothing down. You put it where it will not be spent.
You take your change in ships and spend them at the dams before evening. They buy what any penny buys.
At Dorestat the wright at the dam heads has a keel ship on order for one of the small houses. He has been paid in earnest and is cheerful, which is noticed.
A raft of Rhineland oak came down to the dam heads at Dorestat, and a new keel is laid there: thirty-four feet, for a sea-going trader.
A Frisian house at Dorestat gave its new ship to the count for the king's service before she had touched water. The count counted the cost back, and more.
A new keel ship went down the rollers at Dorestat's dam heads and swims. She carries six tons, and the priest of the upper church blessed her.
A Frisian wright at Dorestat has built a ship in the Danish manner, long and low with sixteen oars, for a house of the town. A Dane lined her off. The count's men have been to look.
At Colonia a Frisian house has had a river ship made of one great oak from the king's wood, with no iron in her, and has taken to the river trade.

A late-summer afternoon at Dorestat's dam heads, low sun. In front, an empty slip of sand and blocks, and a broad Frisian wright of about fifty cutting notches in a hazel stick; behind him the player's small four-oared boat, deep in the water at a post, and the long row of timber dams.

An autumn morning in an oak wood across the Rhine from Colonia, mist between the trunks. A Frankish steward in a belted tunic and short cloak lays his hand on one enormous oak; the merchant beside him holds the notched stick. Far behind, the old stone fort and the river.

A grey cold day at the dam head. A raft of oak trunks bound with withies lies low in the water with a Frank asleep on it under his cloak; the wright stands on it with the back of his axe raised to strike a trunk, his head tilted to listen. On the sand behind, men drive wedges into a trunk that is splitting along its length.

The IJssel bank at Daventre under a sky smudged with smoke from the heath to the west. A smith with a leather apron and burnt forearms holds the notched stick against a rivet; ten small kegs stand in a row by his door, and men with yokes come down a sandy track carrying dark lumps of iron.

Inside a sunken hut on the terp at Wijnaldum, dim, lit from the door. An upright loom leans on the wall with its rows of clay weights hanging; a Frisian woman of about forty in a wool dress and head-cloth stands before it looking at her own hands. Through the door, sheep on the green mound and flat grey marsh.

The largest weaving hut, winter light. A great grey wool sail lies folded on a bench, thick as a mattress, its seams showing; the weaver holds a red thread full of knots. Four other women stand along the wall with their arms folded, watching the merchant.

A frosty morning on the slip. The new ship is a keel, two tall stems and three strakes a side, held by props. A lean Dane in a shaggy cloak, a hammer amulet at his neck, points along the keel with his whole arm; the Frisian wright faces him with his adze over his shoulder; the wright's men have stopped work to listen.

Midwinter dusk at the slip, snow on the dams. The hull has four strakes a side and nobody working on her. The wright sits on an upturned keg with his hands on his knees, immovable; beside him a single plank is clamped to the hull, waiting. The merchant stands before him with his breath showing.

A bright cold noon. A Frankish count in a fur-edged cloak, sword at his hip, stands before the half-planked hull with his thumbs in his belt; behind him his steward holds two horses. The wright's men are all crowded at the far stem, very busy. The merchant stands alone between the count and the ship.

An early spring morning, clear, the river high. The finished ship stands tarred black on tallowed rollers with her stem to the water and a grey sail furled on her yard. A priest in a white alb reads from a small book; the wright has one hand flat on her planks; a line of townspeople hold the ropes. The old small boat lies at a post beside her.

A dull day with rain coming. The ship is on the rollers, tarred and whole to look at. The wright stands under her stem with his arms folded and his knife still in his belt, looking at one seam; a boy beside him holds a wooden bailer. Few people have come to watch.

A windy spring day at the dam heads. A long, low ship with sixteen oar ports and stems rising a man's height stands on the rollers among the broad Frisian hulls. The Dane stands at her stern with his hand on the steering oar; the wright looks along her side; a crowd lines the dams, and two of the count's spearmen stand apart, watching.

The river bank below the old fort across from Colonia, late winter, thin sun. A very long, narrow, shallow boat made of one hollowed oak with two pegged strakes lies on the shingle, a short mast far forward; the embers of a long fire smoke beside her. A wright with an adze and the steward stand at her bow; three casks wait on the bank, and the towers of the city show over the water.

The moneyer's bench in the upper town of Dorestat, morning light through a shutter. In front, a spill of bright new silver pennies on a board, each with a small ship on it; an ageing Frankish moneyer holds one up between finger and thumb. Beside him lie a hammer, an iron die and a wax tablet scratched with the outline of a ship.
Short cloaks

On the next dam a man of Thiadbod's is selling Frisian cloaks at the old price. Each is a hand shorter than the old length. Thiadbod, the biggest shipman on the river, stands by in a long blue one of his own and watches who buys.
What is the good of those little napkins? I cannot cover myself with them in bed and when I am on horseback I cannot shield myself with them against wind and rain.
You are the one with the Wōkerer's boat. Every summer the dams have a new man. Most are gone by Martinmas.
You are the one with the small boat that is never empty. I have been meaning to come over.
Wool is dear and weavers are slow. A hand off the length, and no one is colder for it but a tall Frank. Sell as I sell and we both eat.
They tell me your tally with the count is closed. A house that owes nothing is a house worth watching.
Cut your own bolts a hand short and match him
Measure the old length aloud, on your own arm, where his buyers can see
Go across and drink his wine
You sell out by noon, and so does he. The Frank buys from neither of you. Nobody on the dams says cheat. They call it keeping up.

You lay a cloak of the old length along your arm and say the spans aloud, twice. A weaver's wife from the back farms laughs and fetches her neighbours. Thiadbod's man stops crying his price while you are at it. Thiadbod goes on smiling.
His wine is good and his news is a week old: wine was dear on the strand at Lundenwic when his ship left it. It may be dear still. He tells you nothing that he learned this morning.
The king's measure

Corn has had the king's price since the synod at Frankfurt, by the king's new measure, in a full year or a hungry one. Thiadbod's man sells rye at that price to the penny. His measure is a finger short. The buyers who came to your boat last time are on his dam.
Oats one penny the measure, barley two, rye three, wheat four. The king's word from Frankfurt. A dozen grains short is short.
Oats two pennies the measure, barley three, rye four, wheat six. The emperor's word from Noviomagus. And gain made by holding corn back he calls filthy.
You are the one who measured cloaks along his arm. Good. Now let us see whose corn is as long as it says.
The king's price, to the penny. Ask anyone. I would not take half a penny over.
You cut cloth. I cut corn. We understand each other.
A measure is a measure. Mine was on this dam before you could walk it.
Ask the steward to try both measures against the king's
Have your own measure marked by the steward and sell heaped, in the open
Say nothing, and take what you carry down to Traiectum

The steward fills Thiadbod's measure from the king's and has corn left in his hand. He counts the grains aloud, by the dozen. Thiadbod is sorry: an old measure, a careless man. He pays the fine before it is asked. The toll man is told to go easy on you for a while.

The measure on Thiadbod's dam today is true to the brim. Someone told him. The steward tries yours twice, to be fair, finds it true, and goes back to his tallies. You have made an old man walk the dams for nothing.

The steward burns his mark into your measure for twelve pennies. You sell by it heaped, where everyone can see, and lose a little on every sack. He orders rye for the count's household from the one measure on the dams that he need not try.
You say nothing. A bishop's town eats too, and at Traiectum nobody stands beside you with a short measure. Rye and barley fetch more there this month.
The dam head

Your place at the dam is taken. Thiadbod has paid the year for the head where you lay, and his big ship is moored across the mouth of the ditch, so that no small boat goes in or out but under her stern. The Maas pilot is his by the year too. He comes down the planks smiling.
The head is paid to Martinmas. A ship must lie somewhere, and she is long.
Your boat is quick and mine is slow. Carry for me this season. You get my word with the toll man, a place at my dam, and thirty pennies in your hand now.
They say you could buy a second boat. Buy into mine. It is safer to be my friend than my neighbour.
And there is your tally with the count. I could buy it from him at Michaelmas. I could also forget which day Michaelmas is.
The steward and I have made it up. He tried my measure and I gave his lord a hawk. You see how things are mended here.
Take his thirty pennies and carry for him this season
Name the law: no man shuts the public way in a river
Lie inside by the ditch and say nothing
You take his silver and his word with the toll man. For a season yours is the quick one of Thiadbod's two boats. Men on the dams stop asking whose she is.

You say it loud enough for three dams to hear: who shuts the public way in a river pays twelve shillings. Thiadbod laughs, and has his ship warped a length upstream before anyone can be sent for. You have your water back. He has stopped smiling at you.
He asks which river. This is a ditch, he says, between his dam and the next, and his dues on it are paid. Nobody on the dam wants to be the one to disagree with him. You lie inside.
You lie inside by the ditch, where loading takes half a day longer. You say nothing. He notices that too.
The cut rope

At first light your boat is not at her post. The rope is cut clean. She lies a bowshot down the river, driven onto the old dam posts, two strakes stove in and the river in her. The man you left to sleep aboard had been called away to drink on Thiadbod's dam.
It was Meinward, with the split ear, that hauls for Thiadbod. He had a knife out at your post. He went down river at cock-crow on a wine boat, for the Maas mouth.
Cut. A rope that parts has a beard on it. This one is shaved. Two strakes and a rib: six days and thirty pennies, or four days of your own hands and the loan of my adze.
If you mean to take it to the court, shout it now. Men remember what they heard before they had eaten.
You carried for him and then you stopped. Men have had worse for less.
You named the law at him before three dams. This is his answer. It came by night because he could not give it by day.
Raise the cry on the dams now, with the cut end in your hand
Go onto Thiadbod's dam with your men and take a pledge
Mend her with your own hands and say nothing yet

You stand on the dam with the cut end in your fist and shout it: your boat, your rope, last night, and the name the boy gave. Men come out of the storehouses. Nobody answers, and everybody has heard. The wright has her on the bank by noon, for thirty pennies.

You go onto his dam with your men behind you and roll two casks of his wine down the planks: a pledge, until he answers. His cellar men stand aside. The Frisian word is pant. The count's court has another word for it. The wright mends her meanwhile, for thirty pennies.

His cellar men are more than yours and they have staves. You come back along the dam with bruises and no wine. All the dams saw you go armed onto another man's ground. The wright mends her meanwhile, for thirty pennies.

You say nothing. Four days on the bank with the wright's adze and your own hands, and she swims again. The wright says less than he knows. He does say that a wine boat takes two days to the Maas mouth, and that Meinward cannot swim.
The man with the split ear

Witla, the strand at the Maas mouth: boats in the creek, nets drying, a pilot's shed on the bank. This is where the wine boat brought Meinward. The pilot here is old Gerlef, and Thiadbod pays him by the year.
Split ear? He sleeps in my net shed and eats Thiadbod's bread. I was told to keep him here and on no account let him over the water. Odd, for a man they want rid of.
He went out on the ebb with an English boat, days since. Over the water. No Frisian court will hear him now.
The one with the split ear? Gone over the water long since, and the court has sat, they tell me. Then it no longer matters where he went.
I am paid to pilot. I am not paid to lie. I am forty, and I have seen that bar move nine times in fifty years.
I cut a rope. I did not ask whose. Six pennies and bread, and stay in the land, he said. While I am in the land nothing can be asked of him. I do not know what he meant.
Take him, and bring him up the river to the court
Hear him before the pilot and two fishermen, then give him six pennies to go over the water
Leave the man be, and ask the pilot about the bar
He runs for the flats and your men have him before the tide does. He comes up the river in the bottom of your boat, tied, saying nothing. Gerlef watches you go and does not lift a hand.
He is faster over mud than any of you. A fishing boat takes him off the flats and stands out past the bar on the ebb. One of your men has turned his knee. Meinward has left the land.

He says it before Gerlef and two men mending nets: who paid him, how much, and which post. Fishermen forget nothing that costs them nothing. Then he goes aboard an English boat with your pennies in his fist. He has left the land.
You let the man lie. Gerlef talks to the water for a while and then, since you asked, to you: she runs north of the bank since the winter floods, and the old mark on the dune is no use now.
The count's court

The count's court sits under the open sky by Saint Martin's church. Seven sworn men find the judgment and an old Frisian says the law. Your matter is called: a boat cut from her post by night. Thiadbod stands across the ring with five free men behind him.
The king's court. Shipman, say your say and be short. I have a hawk waiting.
The emperor's court. Shipman, say your say and be short. I have a hawk waiting.
I know this shipman, and I think well of him. That is not law, and I do not pretend that it is.
You again. The king's man heard you once. Here you are heard by me.
On other days you sit with the seven. Today another man has your stool, and you stand where the wronged man stands.
Our law is not written. It is in my head, where no mouse has got at it.
They wrote our law down at Aachen, from what men like me told them. They got most of it.
Who takes a man's thing pays it twice, and his own man-price to the king for the peace. Who denies it clears himself with five free men, his own hand the sixth.

Who sets another on: if the doer has fled the land, the setter pays a third or swears. If the doer stands in the land, the setter neither swears nor pays. He bears the wronged man's enmity until he wins his friendship back.
A pledge taken by force we call pant. What spoils while the taker holds it, the taker pays.
I was at Mass. Half the dams saw me. Ropes part, rivers run. I am sorry for his boat, and I said so before he asked.
Bring Meinward into the ring
Charge Thiadbod as the setter-on, with your witnesses; let him swear if he can
Charge him on your own word alone
Take the sixty pennies he offers in the porch and let it drop

Meinward is shown the kettle: a stone to be taken out of boiling water, the hand bound and sealed three nights. He looks at it and tells everything. He owes you your boat twice over and owns a knife and six pennies; the count takes him to work it off on the dams. Then the old man turns to Thiadbod. The doer stands in the land: the setter neither swears nor pays. He bears your enmity, lawfully, until he wins your friendship back. And the old man adds a judgment of his own: a boat at her post is a house on the water, and who looses her by night pays as for a house burned. No one had said that before.

Thiadbod's five come forward to the relics. The fourth stops. He heard what was said about that night, he says, and he has a boat of his own. An oath of five is not an oath of six. Thiadbod pays the setter's third on the spot, two hundred pennies, as if it were a small thing.

Five free men lay their hands on the relics after him, one by one. The oath is whole. By the law he is clean, and you have named a clean man before the court. People look at who stood behind him, and remember.

You have no one behind you. You say it anyway, plainly, and look at each of his five in turn. The youngest will not come to the relics. An oath of five is not an oath of six. Thiadbod pays the setter's third, two hundred pennies, and does not look at the boy.
Your word against six hands. The law is not in doubt, and the seven do not take long. He is clean. The count asks whether you have anything else, since his hawk has waited.
In the church porch, before the court sits, he puts sixty pennies in your hand for the wright. He is sorry for your boat. Your matter is called, and you say you have none.
Thiadburg's storehouse
Thiadburg sends for you. She keeps the storehouse on the dam that her husband built, lends on goods, and is Thiadbod's elder sister. She does not trust him with her keys.
The law says he bears your enmity until he wins your friendship back. He sent me to ask what it costs. I came to see who was asking.
He paid the third and smiled. He has not smiled since. He sent me to ask if that is the end of it.
He swore with five. Two of them owe me silver, so I know what their hands are worth. He sent me to see whether you will be quiet now.
You took his sixty pennies in the porch. He thinks he knows your price. I am not sure that he does.
And his two casks. He counts them twice a day. Keep them or send them back, but he has not stopped counting.
You mended your boat with your own hands and said nothing for forty nights. He does not know what to make of that. Nor do I, yet.
I ask what a thing weighs before I ask what it cost. What does this weigh with you?
Name a price in silver, and take it
Name the price of the friendship the law left open
Ask nothing of him. Ask her for room under her roof
Tell her it stands as it stands
You name a sum. She halves it, you halve the difference, and she counts out a hundred and twenty pennies herself. 'Now he thinks it is over,' she says. 'So do you, perhaps.'
You name a sum fit for a man's friendship. She does not blink. She counts out a pound of silver, two hundred and forty pennies, and says he will call it cheap by Easter.

'Room under my roof, and nothing from him?' She is a little amused. She gives you a place at the dry end, and an order for cloth to go with it. A brother who cannot be trusted with her keys has bought her a new neighbour.
'Then it stands,' she says. 'I will tell him you said it without shouting. That will worry him more.'
A ship on the bank

A big merchant ship lies on a bank where the channel ran last year, heeled over, with casks in the water round her. Men stand on her high side. She is Thiadbod's. The flood is making, and the bank will be under before the tide is half up.
This is the year the storms broke so many ships in the English sea.
The bank was not here at Easter. Ask the pilot. Ask anyone.
I will not ask it of you. You can see what there is to see.
You said yourself that it stands as it stands. I am only telling you how many we are.
We are nine. I can swim. The others cannot.
Take the men off and leave the wine
Take the men off, and four casks for your trouble
Lay out his anchor and try to float her on the flood
Stand off. There are fishing boats; let them earn it

Nine men in a boat built for four. You leave the wine to the flood. One cask has burst on the bank, and it is not wine in the straw: sword blades, greased, bound for the north. Thiadbod sees you see them. He sits in the bottom boards beside his son and says nothing all the way in.

The men come aboard, and four casks after them, over her high side. 'For your trouble,' he says, before you can say it. A fifth cask has burst on the bank, and it is not wine in the straw: sword blades, greased, bound for the north. He sees you see them.

Your steersman lays Thiadbod's anchor out in the deep water from your boat, and his men heave as the flood lifts her. She comes off groaning and swims, leaking, with half her wine. One burst cask is left on the bank, and it is not wine in the straw: sword blades. He pays your men on the spot, with both hands, and does not look back at it.

She lifts, turns, and breaks her back on the edge of the bank. You take the men off with the water at their belts; one of yours is hurt at the rope. The casks go out on the ebb, all but one that bursts on the sand: sword blades in straw. He sees you see them.
You stand off and watch. A fishing boat takes them off at the last of it. The ship stays. Your crew do not talk much that evening. The ones who pray, pray.
The reckoning

Word of the bank reached Dorestat before you did. Thiadbod's wine was bought on trust up the river, and the men he owes have come down to the dams. He and his sister are waiting for you. What the two houses are to each other from now on is settled today.
You took me off the bank. I had your rope cut. Both are true, and I have to stand here and hold both.
You floated her. I would not have floated yours. I have thought about that every night since.
You stood off and watched. I would have done the same. I do not forgive it either.
You saw what was in the straw. You have not said. I count that too.
You took silver for your friendship at my sister's hands. I do not ask for it back. I ask what it bought.
He has a dam head and a name. You have a small boat that is never empty. Put them together or pull them apart, but do it before the count's steward does it for you.
Your cloth is dry under my roof. I say it so that you know I am not only his sister.
Offer him fellowship: two boats, one reckoning
Let the law and his losses run, and be at the steward's sale
Say before witnesses that there is no peace between the houses
He is silent a long while. Then: 'At the next court, in the church porch. Forty nights. I will bring what I have left.'
You say you will be at the steward's sale. Thiadbod nods as a man nods at a price. His son looks at you until his father turns him by the shoulder.
You say it before his sister and the men from up the river: no peace. 'Then say it where it counts,' he says, 'at the court, in forty nights.' He sounds almost glad to know.
Two boats, one reckoning

The porch of Saint Martin's church, forty nights on. Two houses will bear each other's fire and wreck and count the gain of two boats together. The king's law lets men make such agreements, for alms, for fire and for shipwreck. It forbids them to swear to it. Thiadbod wants the oath.
You may agree. You may not swear to it; the king has said so since Herstal. I would rather not hear an oath that I must then say I did not hear.
An agreement without an oath is a rope without a knot. But I have been wrong about ropes.
Half of what she carries is yours while she swims. I have said it before witnesses. Now say yours.
And there will be no more iron in the straw. That was my trade, not ours.
Where I come from we say man is man's delight. We also count the silver twice.
Make it before witnesses, without the oath, as the king allows
Swear it on the altar, each to the other
Make it without the oath, and open the chest to every boat on the dams

Hands, witnesses, a tally split down the middle. From today Thiadbod's boat sails with yours, and the gain and loss of both are counted together. Your share of the first reckoning is seven hundred pennies. The Dane who watched from the dam gives you a stick with a verse cut on it, for luck.

You swear it on the altar, when the priest has found something to do in the churchyard. A sworn band is stronger, and it is forbidden: the count will hear of it by evening and keep it by him, as he keeps everything. Your share of the first reckoning is nine hundred pennies. The Dane who watched gives you a stick with a verse cut on it.

You make it without the oath, and say that any boat on the dams may come in on the same terms: a penny in the chest for each voyage, and the chest pays for fire, for wreck and for the poor at the church door. By Martinmas eleven boats are in. Thiadbod gives what he would give a brother: the Maas marks out of old Gerlef's head, taught to your steersman, and the first reckoning, fourteen hundred pennies. The Dane who watched gives you a stick with a verse cut on it. No one has done this at Dorestat before.
The steward's sale

Forty nights on, the count's steward sells what Thiadbod has to pay what Thiadbod owes: the dam head with its storehouse posts, the last of his wine, and what is left of his name. Thiadbod stands at the back with his son. He is going up the Rhine to the Frisians' shore at Mogontia, to carry other men's wine.
A dam head, six rods by forty. Storehouse posts, sound. Eleven casks: a dozen, less one. Who speaks?
Your claim stands first, by the court's finding. The rest take what is left.
The king's men have asked what a wine ship wanted with iron in her casks. That is not on my tally. I only sell what is left.
Speak up. It is a good dam. I chose it myself.
The hull is still on the bank. The sea did not want her either.
Take the dam head as your price
Take the hull off the bank and have her mended
Let his sister have the dam head, and keep your place under her roof
Take the dam head, and leave him a boat and your wine to carry at Mogontia

The dam head is yours: a place of your own at Dorestat, with three casks and four hundred and fifty pennies over when his debts are met. Thiadbod goes up the river on another man's barge. His son looks back once. He is fourteen, and he has a good memory.

You have her floated off on a spring tide and towed to the wright: a sea-going ship, yours for the mending, and six hundred pennies from the sale besides. Thiadbod watches her come up the river past his old dam. His son watches you.

You speak for Thiadburg, and no one bids against the two of you. She has the dam head she always said was hers. You have the dry end of her storehouse for as long as it stands, a woman there who knows what everything weighs, and seven hundred pennies from the sale. Thiadbod goes up the river. 'She will rob you fairly,' he says.

You take the dam head, and leave him the old wine boat and a third of what he carries for you. He looks at you a long time. 'I would not have done that either,' he says. On the Frisians' shore at Mogontia there is now a man who buys your wine at the press and owes you his bread. Your share of the sale is eleven hundred pennies.
No peace

The court again, forty nights on. You say it before the count and the seven: there is no peace between your house and Thiadbod's. The old Frisian says what the law leaves even to a man at feud. The bishop's clerk from Traiectum is listening too.

A man at feud has peace in church, in his own house, on the way to church and back, on the way to court and back. Who kills him there pays nine times thirty shillings. Everywhere else he looks to himself.
The king wants his shipmen alive and paying toll. Do it on the water, where I need not hear of it.
The emperor's word is that the wronged shall take the price and make a lasting peace. You will hear that again from men less patient than I am.
The emperor's word from Thionville is that feuds are settled, and the stubborn are sent to him. Do not make me send you.
Saint Martin's men on these banks answer to Saint Martin. The count lodges no one on them and takes nothing of theirs. A pound of wax at Martinmas is not much to pay.
This one is Saint Martin's already. Whoever touches him touches the saint. I say it so that it has been said.
I hear him. Let it be remembered, since no one here can write but the clerk.
At home we have a verse about a foe's friends. It is short. Most of ours are.
Put your house and your boats under Saint Martin's hand
Float his hull off the bank and keep her, by the strong hand
Stand alone: arm the crew and hang the cut rope over your door

You give yourself and your boats to Saint Martin at Traiectum: wax every Martinmas, and the bishop's hand over your door. The count cannot lodge men on you or seize your goods, and Thiadbod will not touch what is the saint's. What you took of his on the river this season, seven hundred pennies' worth, you keep. The bishop is pleased. The count is not. Thiadbod's son learns your face. The Dane in the ring gives you a stick with a verse cut on it.

You float his ship off the bank with armed men standing on the sand, and bring her up the river as your own. By the custom of the strand she is wreck. By Thiadbod's reckoning she is stolen, and his sons will reckon it so after him. What you took of his on the river this season sells for six hundred pennies. The Dane in the ring gives you a stick with a verse cut on it.

You hang the cut rope over your own door. Your crew go armed on the dams. What you take of Thiadbod's wine on the river that season sells for a thousand pennies. Nobody undersells you now. Nobody stands very near you either. The Dane in the ring gives you a stick with a verse cut on it.
At the church door

Thiadbod lies in the ground by Saint Martin's, and so does the one who said there was no peace. His heir has the house now, and the feud with it, as you have yours. You meet at the church door, where the law gives even the two of you peace.
They say my house cut your house's rope. Yours always said so. Mine never said that it did not.
I have carried this since I was fourteen. It is heavier than wine and it pays nothing.
The heathen men burn us both alike. They do not ask which house.
You are the saint's and I am the count's. Those two do not love each other either.
In here you have peace, both of you. I would be glad if some of it went out of the door with you.
End it: a marriage between the houses, and the old price paid
Pledge faith and take his price, as the emperor's law orders
Keep it. The rope stays over the door

You pay for the wine and the hull, he pays for the rope, and the two sums cross on the church step and nearly cancel: it costs you a pound of silver. The rest is a marriage between the houses, agreed in the porch, with his dam and yours behind it. The cut rope is burned under the bride-ale. His boat sails with yours from that day.
He counts three hundred pennies into your hand before the priest: the rope, the boat, the years. You pledge faith. It is a lasting peace by the emperor's law, and a thin one by any other.
'Then keep it,' he says. 'I will keep mine.' You go into the church by the same door, one after the other, and stand on opposite sides.

This year, at the count's court at Dorestat, a hired man owned to cutting a boat from her post by night. Thiadbod the shipman, named as the setter-on, neither swore nor paid, as the Frisians' law has it, and bears the enmity of the house he wronged.
This year, at the count's court at Dorestat, Thiadbod the shipman could not find his five for the oath, and paid the setter's third for a boat cut from her post.
This year, at the count's court at Dorestat, Thiadbod the shipman swore himself clean with five free men of a charge about a cut rope.
This year two houses of Dorestat that had been at law made one reckoning of their two boats, against fire and wreck.
This year the shipmen of Dorestat made a common chest against fire and wreck, a penny for each voyage, without an oath, as the king's law allows.
This year Thiadbod's dam head at Dorestat was sold by the count's steward for his debts, and he went up the Rhine to Mogontia.
This year it was said before the count's court at Dorestat that there is no peace between two houses of shipmen there.
This year the heirs of two houses of Dorestat, long at feud over a cut rope, made a lasting peace at the church door.

A dam at Dorestat on a bright, windy morning: a seller holds up a blue cloak that ends at his knee; a tall Frank in a red cloak measures it against himself with scorn; behind them Thiadbod, well fed, in a long blue cloak with a silver pin, watches the player's small boat.

Midday on the dam under a grey sky: the thin old steward pours grain from one wooden measure into another over a cloth and counts on his fingers; Thiadbod stands by with open hands; sacks and a line of farm wives behind.

Evening, low sun on the water: a big merchant ship, twice the length of the player's boat, moored across the mouth of a ditch between two earth dams, shutting in a small boat; Thiadbod comes down a plank smiling, a purse held out in one hand.

First light, mist on the river: a small clinker boat driven onto old black posts, half full of water; in front a hand holds the clean-cut end of a rope; a boy points down the river; a shipwright with an adze looks on.

Low tide at the Maas mouth, wide flats under a pale grey sky: an old pilot with a sounding pole taller than himself stands at the door of a net shed; inside, a young man with a split ear sits on a heap of nets.

Open ground beside a small timber church at noon, a dry wind: a ring of men; the count seated with a sword across his knees; an old Frisian speaking with one hand raised; Thiadbod with five men behind him; an iron kettle steaming over a fire at the edge of the ring.
Inside a storehouse on a dam, afternoon light through the gaps in the planks: bales and casks; Thiadburg, upright, in a white head-cloth with keys at her belt, weighs silver on a small folding scale.

A big merchant ship with one mast, heeled over on a sandbank in a rising grey sea, wind from the west, late afternoon: casks afloat; nine men on her high side, a boy among them; one burst cask on the sand showing straw and iron; the player's small boat coming up under oars.
The dam head at Dorestat in flat late-afternoon light: Thiadbod bareheaded, his rings gone, his sister beside him; behind them strangers from up the river sit on his casks and wait.

The porch of the timber church on a clear cold morning: two men clasp hands over a split tally stick; a priest looks away toward the graveyard; a Dane leans on the fence, watching; below, two boats lie side by side.

The dam head on a grey morning in light rain: the steward stands on a cask with a bundle of notched sticks; bidders in a half ring; at the back Thiadbod and his son with a bundle each, and a river barge waiting.

The court ring by the church under a hard bright sky: two groups of men stand apart; the count on his feet, pointing; between them the old Frisian with both hands raised; a clerk with a wax tablet at the side.

The church door on a still autumn morning, a generation later: two people of middle years face each other on the step, neither armed, a priest in the doorway behind; over a house door in the distance hangs an old grey rope.
Two tallies
Two men sit at the toll bench where one used to sit, each with his own tally stick, and neither looks at the other. The old one you know. The young one wears a sword at a toll bench, which is new.
King Offa died three days before Lammas. I have had no word since from anyone who can tell me to stop, so I sit here, and I cut the notch as I always did.
Kent has a king of its own kin again. Eadberht. The toll of this water is his, as it was his fathers' before any Mercian saw the sea. Pay it here.
They call him Praen. Priest. He was one. I am told a man can put down a book and pick up a kingdom. I have not seen it written where.
The Mercian's archbishop has gone, and nobody drove him. A shepherd who runs before the wolf is seen has told you what he thinks of the flock.
You have nothing aboard. Then for once this bench has nothing to quarrel over. Sit. It is the first quiet hour I have had since the hay.
That is iron under your boards. Do not carry it past Canterbury's landing. The king's steward there pays better than anyone you will find up the Thames.
Pay on the old tally, as you always have
Pay on the new king's tally
Sell nothing today, and ask who is king in Kent
The old man cuts his notch and splits the stick. The young one watches your sail all the way down the channel. Nobody stops you. Somebody will remember.
The young man cuts a new stick, badly, and gives you half. He says the steward at Fordwic is buying spearheads at any price. The old man looks at the water.
You sell nothing, and so owe nobody. By evening you have it from both of them: Offa is dead, a priest is king in Kent, and the archbishop is gone.
What the benches look like
The wic-reeve has heard you came up from the Wantsum. He asks what you saw at the toll benches of Kent, listens, and then asks it again in other words.
You came by Sarre. Who sat at the bench? One man or two? And who sat at the bench at Sarre? I ask twice because the second answer is usually shorter.
The old king is dead and his son is king. The son is not well. I say this to you because the whole Strand says it already.
King Ecgfrith lasted a hundred and forty-one days. I counted. King Coenwulf is no kin of his to speak of, and has Kent to mend before anything else.
No iron goes into Kent from this beach. Corn I cannot stop. Spearheads I can, and I know the weight of a bundle through a sack.
