I hear you paid your toll on the wrong stick. A Frisian cannot be blamed for paying the man with the sword. Once.
I need eyes that pass Sarre and Dofras without being looked at. A Frisian keel is nobody's business. Thirty pennies now, and half toll here while it lasts.
Agree to bring him word of Kent each time you pass
Tell him Kent is quiet and poor, which is half true
Say you are a Frisian and count casks, not kings
He counts thirty pennies into your hand, old king's coin, and tells his toll man to take half from you until midsummer. You have a second trade now. It weighs nothing and it is hard to stow.
He nods slowly. Quiet and poor is what he hoped to hear, and men believe what they hope. He asks it once more, and you say it the same way.
He asks again, and your second answer is longer than your first. He thanks you. He does not offer you the bench by his fire.
He almost smiles. Then count this, he says: no wine has come round by the Wantsum since Lammas, and the Strand is paying a third over for a cask from the Seine.
A new name on the penny
At the landing below Canterbury a moneyer lays a bright penny on your thwart. It carries a king's name you have not read on silver before. Behind him a steward waits with a list.
Read it. EADBEARHT REX. Same dies cutter, same hammer, same arm. Last year I struck for Offa. A moneyer is like a ferry: he serves whichever bank he is on.
Weigh it against one of the old king's heavy ones. Go on. A new king cannot afford a light penny. Only an old king can.
The king's hall wants spearheads. Six bundles, landed here before the leaves are down. I pay near twice what they cost you on the Rhine, in that coin.
The king lived among the Franks when Offa wanted him dead. King Charles fed him. A Frisian is King Charles's man. So we are nearly friends already, you and I.
If iron frightens you, bring wheat. A hall that feeds armed men eats like a minster in Lent, only all year.
I will say what he will not. If the Mercian comes back, the man who landed spears here will be named, and the reeve at Lundenwic keeps long tallies. Corn has no name on it.
Take the order: six bundles of spearheads, landed here
Take an order for corn instead: men eat under any king
Weigh the new penny, praise it, and take no order
The steward notches a stick for six bundles and gives you half. You are Kent's ironmonger until the leaves fall. The moneyer has already turned away.
Twelve sacks of wheat, at half over the price. The steward is not pleased, and not displeased. A man who feeds you is hard to hang.
The penny is full weight and well struck, and you say so. The moneyer is pleased. The steward folds his list. You owe nothing to anyone in Kent, yet.
To the people of Kent
The guest master of Saint-Josse comes down to the Canche with a folded letter under his scapular. It is from his abbot, and it is addressed not to a man but to a whole people.
Abbot Alcuin holds this house by the king's gift, to lodge the English on their way to Rome. Now he writes to the English who stayed at home. To the Kentish. All of them.

He tells them to call their archbishop home. He tells them hardly a man is left anywhere of the old stock of kings, and that a people which keeps changing lords ends with strangers. He is kinder than that. But that is it.
Their king sat at this table once. Odberht, we wrote him down as: a priest, an exile, on his way to Rome with a letter from King Charles. He ate little and asked a great deal about ships.
I am told you carry iron to Kent. Then carry this too. A boat should not bring a land only the things that cut.
I will be honest. There are Kentish boats off the Foreland stopping keels for letters. This one is written to them, not about them. Whether the man with the spear can read is another matter.
Take the letter to Canterbury's landing
Take it, and stay three days to have a copy read to you
Say your boat is searched on both shores already
He gives you the letter, ten pennies for the freight, and a blessing that takes longer than both. It goes inside your shirt, where a king's boat looks last.

For three evenings he reads it to you, a line in Latin and a line in English. You learn the Latin for flock, for shepherd and for folly. The letter goes inside your shirt, and now you know its weight.
He is not angry. He says the letter will find a boat; letters do. You sail without it, and Kent hears the abbot from some other mouth, or does not.
Eight oars off the Foreland
A boat with eight oars pulls out from under the white cliff and holds water across your bow. A man stands in her with a spear grounded on the bottom boards. She has twice your men.
Whose keel, from where, and what is under your shirt? I ask the last because it is always the shirt.
The Mercian's bishop writes to his friends in Kent, and his friends write back. The king wants to read both. That is all this is. Heave to.
A Frisian. You people carry anyone's word for a penny. I do not say it to shame you. I say it because it is why I am out here in the wet.
Heave to and show the letter: it is written to Kent, not to Mercia
Heave to, let him turn the hold over, and say nothing
Bear away for the Goodwin shoals, where eight oars will not follow
He turns it over, finds the word for Kent on the outside, and spells it with his finger. A letter to us, he says, and hands it back as if it might be owed toll.
He cannot read it and will not say so. You lie alongside half a day while a boy runs for a priest. The priest reads the outside, shrugs, and you are let go with the tide lost.
They turn over every sack and sound the bilge with a spear butt. Nobody looks inside a wet Frisian's shirt. It costs you the best of the ebb.
You put her over the tail of the sands with a hand's breadth under the keel. Eight oars stop where the water changes colour. Your men do not speak until the Foreland is astern.
The wind drops and eight oars do not. They take forty pennies for the trouble and break the seal. When they have had it read to them they give it back, looking foolish. It is a letter to Kent.
A letter to everybody
A priest and the king's steward both meet your boat at the landing. Each holds out a hand for the same letter, and each says it is written to him.
It is written to the people. Then let the people hear it. Sunday, at the church door, in English, by me. I have the voice for it, and nothing left to lose but the voice.
A letter to the people of Kent is a letter to their king. He will read it, and tell the people what was in it that concerns them.
The seal is broken. The watch has told me how. I do not hold it against you. I only note that you ran.
Christ Church has been lighter of its silver since the archbishop went. I do not say who carried it out. I say I stayed, and counted what was left.
If it is read aloud, not everyone will like the sound. The last man who said the archbishop's name at that door had a stone for it. I tell you so that you stand to one side.
Have it read at the church door on Sunday, before whoever comes
Give it to the steward, for his king's eyes first
Put it in the priest's hand and go out on the ebb
He reads it twice, Latin and then English. Nobody throws anything. Old men nod at the part about the stock of kings. By evening all Canterbury knows which boat brought it.

At the archbishop's name a stone comes over the heads and takes you on the shoulder. The priest reads on, louder. He finishes. All Canterbury knows which boat brought it, and that her skipper bleeds like anyone.
The steward gives you forty of the new pennies and carries the letter up the hill. What the people hear of it is one sentence, on a market day, and it is not the abbot's.
The priest takes it in both hands. He will read it to those he trusts, behind a shut door. You are out past the Stour mouth before the tide has turned.
In whose coin
The old reeve's bench at Dofras has a new man on it. The king's hall has stores lying on the shingle that must go round to the Stour, and yours is the only keel on the beach.
Forty sacks and nine barrels, from here to Canterbury's landing. One tide round the Foreland. My own boats are out watching for other people's letters.
I will pay in the king's new pennies, a third over the rate. Or in Offa's, if you are fond of the dead, and then it is the bare rate. Or in cloth. The looms here do not care who is king.
Hereberht sat on that bench eleven years. One morning he was not on it. Nobody saw him go, and everybody knows the road he took.
Take the new pennies if you like. But think where you mean to spend them. On the Strand a man was asked last month where he got one, and the asking took all day.
The steward at Canterbury has spoken of you. You are down on his stick already. One more notch will not make you more of a Kentish man than you are.
Do the work for the new pennies, a third over the rate
Do it for old King Offa's pennies, and fewer of them
Do it for cloth off the Dofras looms
Say the tide does not serve, and drink your ale
One tide round, and a hundred and sixty bright pennies with a priest's name on them. They are good silver. Whether they are good company is another matter.
One tide round, and a hundred of the dead king's pennies, worn and heavy. Nobody anywhere will ask you where you got those.
One tide round, and seven bolts of Dofras cloth, the long kind. The alewife says it was her sister's weaving, and that you chose like a man with a wife.
The tide serves well enough and he knows it. He finds a fishing boat by evening. The alewife fills your cup again without being asked.
The answer from Rome
The reeve sends for you to the king's hall in the wic. A tonsured man in a travelling cloak sits by the wall with a book chest at his feet, and lets the reeve do the talking.
The king wrote to the pope about Kent. The answer has come. A priest cannot be a king. The pope has put Eadberht out of the Church, and says the king may put him out of Kent.
The king also asked that my seat be moved here, to London, away from the Kentish. The pope says no. Canterbury it was and Canterbury it stays. I find I am glad, which surprises me.
So the king goes into Kent after the hay, with everything Mercia has. I tell you because by then it will not matter who knows.
An army eats. The corn will go by water, round to the Wantsum, and my boatmen know the Thames and nothing else. You know the swatchways at Sarre. A hundred and twenty pennies now. More on the day.

You had the abbot's letter read at my church door. They know your boat. Then carry one thing more. If he lays the kingdom down before the army marches, the Church takes him back as a penitent, and I will ask the king to spare the land.
You carried the abbot's letter to Kent. I am told few heard it. A letter read behind a door is a seed kept in a bag.
Six bundles of spearheads were landed below Canterbury. I have the count. I do not yet have the name, and I am in no hurry. Names keep.
You paid for your ale last night with a penny I had not seen before. I have it here. Good silver. An odd name on it.
Agree to bring the king's corn boats through the Wantsum when the army goes
Carry the archbishop's offer to Kent: lay the kingdom down, and live
Say little, sail on the ebb, and tell Kent what is coming
Hear it out, and promise nothing to anyone
A hundred and twenty pennies, counted twice. You are to be at Sarre when the smoke shows. The archbishop looks at you once, and then at his book chest.
The archbishop writes six lines, folds them small and seals them with his ring. The reeve says he has seen nothing. Four days to Sarre, and a man there who will know your sail.

You say yes to nothing and are out on the ebb. At the first Kentish beach you tell it plainly: after the hay, with everything. They thank you. It is not news they can use, except to bury their silver.
You hear it out and promise nothing. The reeve is not surprised. On the Strand they are already saying it: the king goes into Kent this summer.
A night at the crossing
After dark a man fetches you to the ferryman's hut above the strand. Inside, by one rushlight, sits a man with a king's ring on his hand and the mark of an old tonsure under his hair.
You will stand there. You will say what you were given to say, and nothing of your own. If he asks for your own, be short.
He writes a good hand, the archbishop. He always did. Penance, a cell, my eyes and my hands left on me. He puts it more gently. I was a priest. I can read between a bishop's lines.
The pope, I am told, sets me beside Julian, who left the faith and took the purple. I left a book and took what was my fathers'. But the pope has the pen.
I have crossed that water once already with nothing. King Charles gave me bread and a letter. It is a hard thing to go back to a table as a guest when you left it to be a king.
Lord, we have spears now, and the men to hold them. The Mercian has a boy's claim and a dead king's debts. Do not hear this boatman.
You, Frisian. You have seen both benches and both halls. If you were a king with one ship's worth of friends, what would you do? Say it short.
Say it plainly: the army comes after the hay, and your boat can be over the water by first light
Remind them whose corn and whose toll Kent has had from you, and put it as a friend
Lay the letter on the table and wait on the strand for the tide; the choosing is theirs
He is quiet a long time. Then he takes off the ring and gives it to the thegn. I will not have Kent burnt for my name, he says. He is aboard before the moon is down, in a plain cloak, facing aft.
The thegn's hand is on his sword before you have finished. The king lifts one finger and it stops. Go back to your boat, he says. I was a priest once. I will not be one twice.

You name the sacks and the tallies. The thegn cannot say you are the Mercian's man. The king laughs, once. Fed by a Frisian and buried by a Mercian: no. He takes off the ring. He is aboard before the moon is down.
They hear you out, because you have earned that. Then the king says a friend's counsel is still a boatman's counsel, and that he will stand. He thanks you. He means it.

You wait on the strand until the flood. Nobody comes down. At Dofras, three days on, they say the king rode west with four men and took ship from the Marsh. His ring was found on the altar at Canterbury.
You wait on the strand until the flood. Near dawn the thegn comes down alone and gives you the letter back, unanswered. The seal has been mended with a thumb.
As far as the marsh

This year the king of the Mercians made inroads upon the inhabitants of Kent as far as the marsh. Smoke stands along the down, and the beach is full of people who have never asked the price of a passage before.
I am Beornheah. I had six hides by the Marsh this morning. I have a wife, two children and nine of my people on this shingle, and you have the only keel that floats.
They took the king at the edge of the Marsh. Bound, on a cart, facing backward. I saw it from the reeds. I did not come out of the reeds. Write that down too, if you are writing.
Frisian. I have a cup with a foot to it and six bolts of cloth and no wish to carry them to Tamworth. Sixty pennies. You will not see that price again.
I will be fair. The cup came off an altar. The archbishop's people are a day behind us, asking after such things. What you do with that is yours.
You are the Frisian for the corn boats. They are lying off the north mouth afraid of the mud. The reeve said you would come. He said it twice.
You told us at midsummer. We buried the silver and stayed with the land. The silver is still buried. I could not tell you now under which ash heap.
You were at the crossing that night. He could have gone. I was one of those who told him to stand. I say it to you because there is no one else left to say it to.
Take as many off the beach as she will carry, and ask nothing
Take the thegn's household over the water for his silver
Buy what the spearman has in his sack
Bring the king's corn boats through the Wantsum, as you said you would
Fourteen people and a dog, the water a hand below the rail. You land them on the Frankish side at dusk. The thegn has nothing to give you and says so, in front of his children.
A hundred and fifty pennies, old coin and new, counted on the shingle while the smoke comes nearer. Thirteen people. The thegn does not haggle. You both remember that he did not.
A silver cup with a foot, and six bolts that smell of smoke. Sixty pennies. The thegn watches from the shingle and says nothing, and goes to find another boat.
You bring eleven corn boats through on one flood, sounding with an oar. The Mercian steward pays a hundred and sixty on the bank. From the water the burning looks like harvest fires.
One tally again
There is one man at the toll bench again, and one tally. Behind him the hall roofs are black rafters, and the first thing he asks any skipper is whether he carries corn.
Cuthred is king in Kent. The king's brother. He did not ask to be. I am his reeve, and I did not ask either. We have that in common, the king and I.
They led the other one bound into Mercia. What was done to him there I did not see, and I will not describe it at a toll bench. He will not sign his name again, nor read it.
The archbishop is home. He walked through his own gate between two rows of people who would not look up. He has ordered corn for them before candles for the church.
The reeve at Lundenwic sent your name ahead of you. He writes that you were useful and that I should say so in a way you can spend.
You carried Abbot Alcuin's letter. The archbishop has a copy of it by his bed. He says the boat that brought it should not pay to tie up under his city.
You carried his offer to Sarre, and it was refused. He does not count that as failing. He says a man who was offered his eyes and chose his crown has no quarrel with the messenger.
You have some of the priest's pennies. So has everyone. The moneyer takes them by weight and strikes them again. Silver does not remember whose face it wore.
Ask the king's writing: one keel of yours free of toll at Sarre, as the abbess's ships are
Take what the archbishop offers the man who carried his word to Sarre
Ask the archbishop's protection for the boat that carried the abbot's letter
Take a burnt toft by the Sarre landing for the asking, and the reeve's order for seed corn

A strip of parchment with the king's cross and four witnesses: one keel of your house passes Sarre without toll, and if she is wrecked or worn out, another in her place. And seven hundred pennies, for corn boats brought through.

The clerk counts out eleven hundred pennies from the archbishop's own chest. Your keel lies free at Fordwic, and your house is written down as under the archbishop's hand. He asks you to pray for a blind man in Mercia.
Six hundred pennies and a leaf with the archbishop's mark: this house's boats are his guests on any water where his name counts. The clerk reads it to you in Latin first, to be sure you follow.

The reeve paces out a burnt toft above the landing and says it is yours if you roof it. He gives you two hundred and fifty pennies on the nail for seed corn, and will pay double for every sack till spring.
What Kent owes
The thegn of the Marsh finds your boat before you have made fast. He has a sea chest, a boy of twelve, and a way of standing that says the chest is all of it.
Kent owes you. The king's steward is dead and his tally with him, so I will pay it. Somebody of Kent should, and I am what is left standing.
They put out his eyes and cut off his hands. A priest's hands. I think of the Mass he used to say. I find I cannot stop thinking of it.
You took my people off the shingle and asked nothing. I had nothing. I have a little now, and I know every creek from the Stour to the Marsh. Half of both is yours if you will have me.
You took a hundred and fifty pennies from me on that beach. It was a fair price. I say fair. I do not say more.
I saw you buy from the spearman. I have thought about it. A man must fill his hold. Still, I saw it.
One thing you should know. The reeve at Lundenwic has your name on the same stick as mine. He is a patient man. Go carefully on the Thames.
Swear fellowship with him: his chest and his knowledge of the coast in a second boat
Take his coaster, got out of the Stour before the burning, against all that is owed
Take the last of his wool and be shown the swatchways of the Wantsum

You swear it on the boat's stem, his hand over yours. Six hundred pennies from the chest go into the common purse. He will sail the second boat, and there is no water between the Stour and the Marsh he cannot take her through at night.

She lies in the Canche with weed on her: a broad Kentish coaster, built for the minster's corn. He gives you her, and two hundred and fifty pennies, and says Kent is quit with you. The boy unships her oars himself.

Thirty bolts, the last cloth of his folds, and a hundred pennies. Then three days in a skiff, at low water, while he shows you where the Wantsum keeps its sand. He names every bank. Some are named for men he knew.
Two tallies, side by side
The Strand smells of wet ash. The reeve has two tally sticks on the table in the king's hall: what you did for his king, and what you did for the other one.
This stick is what you did for the king. This one is what you did for Kent. They are much the same length. I laid them together to be sure.
Half the wic burned this year, and more people than I can count. I have a town to feed and roof, and no time to hang a man who knows where corn is.
And these. Pennies with a priest's name, that came up the river in your purse. I have melted the rest of them. I kept yours.
So. You may be useful to me again, or you may be honest with me for the first time. I pay for either. I pay more for the first.
If you give me names, Kent will know who gave them. Kent is beaten. It is not dead. Their grandsons will have boats.
Buy his silence with names: who in Kent ordered iron, and who paid
Buy the Kentish trader he took at Fordwic, at a tenth of her worth
Say a merchant sells to whoever stands on the beach, and wait
You give him four names. He breaks the second stick over his knee. Eight hundred pennies, and a man of his to keep your goods on the Strand. At Sarre, from now on, nobody will catch your rope.
Three hundred pennies for a sea-going trader with her mast still in her. He says it is the price of a ship nobody else dares buy. He keeps both sticks. She still has a Kentish name cut in her stem.
He looks at you for some time. Then he laughs, the first time you have heard it. Six hundred pennies of earnest for the wic's corn. Use the Wantsum as you learned it. And know I keep both sticks.
Roofs still on
The landing below Canterbury is as it was: thatch on the halls, corn in the ricks, one man at the toll bench. The archbishop has walked down from the city himself to see a Frisian boat come in.
I came home through standing corn. I had expected ash. The king rode in with his army behind him and found nobody to fight, and an army with nobody to fight wants its own harvest.
He is at Saint-Josse, I hear, shaven again, reading. Abbot Alcuin writes that he is a poor penitent and a good librarian. He has his eyes. I think of that more than I thought I would.
Cuthred is king in Kent, the king's brother. The Kentish do not love him. But a king who burnt nothing is easier to pay toll to. I have had no trouble at this bench. None.
There is a matter of six bundles of spearheads. The archbishop has asked me to lose the stick. I have lost it. I am telling you so that you know it was a thing that could be found.
No chronicle will write this year down for Kent, because nothing happened. I count that your doing. Ask me for something. Ask sensibly; I am a Mercian's bishop in a Kentish town.
Ask the archbishop's protection, and a keel free of toll at Fordwic
Ask ground by the Stour and a clerk of the church to keep your goods there
Ask only what the abbess's ships have at Sarre, and give a tenth of the gift to the poor of Kent

Twelve hundred pennies from the church's chest, a leaf with his mark that puts your house under his hand, and a second with the king's cross: one keel free at Fordwic for as long as she swims, and another after her.

Nine hundred pennies, and a strip of ground between the Stour and the road, forty paces by twelve. A clerk of Christ Church will keep the key and the tally. He counts in Latin and cheats in neither tongue.

Six hundred pennies, and sixty of them go back up the hill for the poor before you have closed your hand. He gives you the freedom of Sarre and his protection besides, and says he asked you to be sensible, not holy.

King Offa died three days before Lammas. In Kent a man of the old kin, Eadberht, who was a priest, has made himself king, and the archbishop has left Canterbury. At the toll benches two men sit where one sat.
The pope has answered the king of the Mercians: a priest cannot be a king, and Eadberht is put out of the Church. The archbishop's seat stays at Canterbury. After the hay the king goes into Kent.

This year the king of the Mercians made inroads upon the inhabitants of Kent as far as the marsh; and the Mercians seized Eadberht their king and led him bound into Mercia. Corn is dear on every Kentish beach.

A toll bench on a chalk strand, grey afternoon in late summer: an old toll man and a young man with a sword sit side by side, each holding a tally stick, looking opposite ways; a small Frisian boat nosing the shingle.

The Strand at Lundenwic at low water, a dull morning: the wic-reeve in a green cloak with his rod of office, one hand raised with two fingers up, questioning a skipper who stands in the shallows by his boat.

A river landing below a walled city, clear morning: a moneyer's thick fingers set one bright silver penny on a boat's thwart beside a small balance; behind him a steward with a notched stick, and spears stacked against a shed.

The muddy bank of the Canche at ebb, a windy day: a monk in a black scapular holds out a folded, sealed letter to a skipper in his boat; a small stone cell and a thatched guest hall on the rise behind.

Open sea under a white chalk headland, choppy water and low cloud: an eight-oared boat lies across the bow of a small sailing boat; a man stands in her with a spear upright; the skipper's hand is at the neck of his shirt.

A wooden landing stage on a small river, evening: a priest and a richly cloaked steward each stretch a hand toward the same letter held by a skipper stepping ashore; a city wall and a church roof far behind.

The shingle at Dofras under the cliffs, bright cold day: sacks and barrels piled on the stones, a man at a bench showing two handfuls of coin, one bright and one dull; an alewife in her doorway with her arms folded.

Inside a timber hall, firelight: the reeve standing with an open letter with a lead seal hanging from it; by the wall a tonsured man in a plain travelling cloak sits with a book chest at his feet, watching the skipper.

A ferryman's hut at night, one rushlight: a man of about forty with a gold ring and a half-grown tonsure reads a small letter; an armed thegn stands behind him, hand on hilt; the skipper stands by the door, rain on his cloak.

A Kentish beach at noon, smoke rising in three columns from the down behind: a crowd of men, women and children with bundles at the water's edge, a thegn holding a child; to one side a spearman with a sack; one small boat.

The toll bench again, autumn, thin sun: one man, one tally stick; behind him black roof timbers against the sky and a clerk in a dark gown with a strip of parchment; sacks of corn being carried up from a boat.
The quay at Quentovic in drizzle: a tall weathered thegn in a patched cloak stands by a sea chest with a boy of twelve; behind them a broad Kentish coaster lies on the mud with weed on her planks.

A table in a half-burnt hall, grey light through a gap in the roof: two tally sticks laid side by side, a few bright pennies between them, the reeve's hands flat on the table; charred posts and the river beyond.

The river landing below Canterbury, a golden harvest evening: thatched halls whole, corn ricks, the archbishop in his pallium walking down the path with a crozier toward a small Frisian boat; one toll man at his bench, half asleep.
A strip of parchment with a king's cross and four witnesses' marks, lying on a charred beam.
A man's hand over another's on the stem post of a boat, grey Channel water behind.
Two tally sticks of the same length tied together with a cord, hanging on a nail in a reeve's hall.
A gold ring left on a bare altar cloth, morning light from a small window.
A strip of gilt

On a dealer's cloth, between a cup and a little box shaped like a house, lies a strip of gilt bronze worked in knots, with four rivet holes and no rivets. It was made to be fastened to something flat.
Western work. A man came home from over the sea with a chest of it, and none of it any use on a farm. I buy what the women do not want.
That strip came off a board. The board was the lid of a block of calfskins, sewn at one edge, with small black marks on every skin and pictures on some. He broke the gold off and kept the skins.
The round piece with the stone in it his wife took, and had a pin put on the back. The women like the knots. The men ask what it weighs.
He showed the skins here at the end of summer. Nobody bid. What would a man do with them? But he would not burn them either. He lives west, on the sound where the ships go north.
Buy the strip for twelve pennies' weight
Leave the strip and ask where the skins went
Sit down with him over ale, in his own tongue
He weighs your silver against a lead weight, twice, and wraps the strip in a dock leaf. It is lighter than it looks. Whoever made it took a month over a thing no wider than two fingers.
West, he says again, on the Karmsund: a hall on the point, and a big man with red in his beard. He does not say the name, and you do not think he has forgotten it.

By the second horn he has said it. Thorleif, at Ögvaldsnes. He wants swords and a second ship, and has no use for prayers. 'He calls it a good landing. He had four men to bury after it, so judge what he calls a bad one.'
What is gone
The bishop stands in a church with its doors off and counts on his fingers what the heathen men took. He has done it before; he does not need to think.
The silver from the shrine. Two cups and the plate of the altar. The cloths. The brethren they killed. The boys they took. And a gospel book.

Not the great book. That one they did not find, God be thanked. The book of the daily altar, that went out to the sick and round the fields on the Rogation days. Wigfrith wrote it, in Bishop Æthelwold's time.

You would know it. On the first leaf of John there is a hole in the skin the size of a pea, where the calf had a scar, and Wigfrith wrote round it. On the last leaf he asks a prayer for himself, by name.
He turns the strip over twice. 'This was on the lower edge of the front board. I have had my thumb on it every Easter since they made me bishop. Where did you buy it? No. Tell me slowly.'
You have seen a piece of it? In a market, on a cloth, beside a cup. Yes. That is how it would be.
The boys first, if you hear of them. I have their names. Alcuin writes that he will speak to King Charles for them. A book does not lie awake at night. But ask after the book also.

I cannot pay as a king pays. Wax, some wine when we have it, what silver they left, and what our estates send at the feasts. And the saint does not forget who served him. That is not nothing, on this coast.
Say you will keep your eyes open in the north
Put the gilt strip in his hand
Ask what the altar is short of, and take his order for wine

He nods as a man nods who has been promised things all summer. Then he tells you the boys' names, one finger each, and makes you say them back. At Eoforwic, he says, a scribe of the minster can tell you what such a book is worth, so that you are not cheated in either direction.

He will not give the strip back, and you had not thought he would. A brother brings a cake of wax down to the boat: it is what the house has today. The bishop walks with you as far as the sand and tells you the marks of the book again.

Four casks of Rhine wine, for the altar and for the sick, before the second winter. The price will come from the house's farms on the mainland, and it is a good one. He tells you the marks of the book while a brother cuts the tally.
A herd of calves
In the minster's writing room a scribe hears your errand from the island without looking up, finishes his line, wipes the pen and then tells you what a book is.
A gospel book is a herd of calves. A hundred skins for a middling one, more for a great one, and each skin scraped, stretched and ruled before a word goes on it.

Then a year of a man's eyes. Then the colours, which come further than you do. So: to its own house it is worth whatever the house has. To another church, a farm. To a heathen, the weight of its mounts.
That is your luck, if you find it. He will have sold the gold already and will think the rest is rubbish. Do not correct him until you have paid.
Alcuin's letter to the king was read here before the whole household. We made copies. It says the sack of Saint Cuthbert's church is a judgement on us. The king did not enjoy it.
You are a Frisian. Frisians are remembered in this city. I would not stand long by that window.
And shut the door. The cold is in my thumb. Nobody writes that at the end of a book, but every book has it in it.
Stay three days and learn to tell a gospel book from a psalter
Take the writing room's order for colours
Ask only for a copy of Alcuin's letter, to show whose errand you are on

Three days on a bench with books you may not touch. By the end you know the four beasts of the four gospels, where each book begins, and what the red letters are for. He sends you off with a riddle about a thing that was killed, soaked, scraped and dressed in gold, and says a merchant ought to get it in one.

Red lead, the yellow that looks like gold, and the green if you can get it dry: he cuts the order on a tally and gives you a copy of Alcuin's letter to wrap it in. 'Read it if you can. If you cannot, carry it as if you could.'

He gives you a copy from the pile without a word and goes back to his line. At the door he says, to the page and not to you, that the first leaf of John is where a liar's book and a true one part company.
The hole in the page
The English lookout has been quiet for a day, which is not like him. At the evening meal he says he has seen the book you are asking after.
I was nine. My brother was given to the island and we went up with him for the feast. They carried it round the fields, and he was let hold the cloth it lay on. He was sick with pride.
There is a hole in one leaf. The scribe wrote round it, like a stream round a stone. The brothers showed it to all the new boys. It was the only joke in the house.
If we find it: a wet book is a ruined book. The skins swell and the colours run. In this boat there is one dry place, under the stern board, and it has your spare boots in it.
They took him too. He was twelve. I do not ask you to look for him. I only say that the book and the boy went in the same ship.
Have him sew a sealskin wrap and clear the dry place under the stern board
Have him teach you the first words of John, to test any book you are shown
Tell him a lookout looks at the sea

He sews it double, hair side in, rubbed with tallow, with a flap that folds twice. Your boots go forward with everyone else's. The steersman says the boat has a chapel now and asks who is to sweep it.

'In principio erat verbum.' He makes you say it until it stops sounding like a cough, and draws the shape of the great first letter on his wax tablet. Now you can find the leaf yourself, in any house, with nobody's help.
He goes forward and looks at the sea. He looks at it very thoroughly for two days and reports every gull.
A box of skins
A big red-fair man has a thing to show to anyone who trades with Christians: a block of sewn calfskins without boards, the first leaf a page of knots in red, yellow and green.
We had a good landing once, west over the sea. A low island, a house full of men who do not fight. This was in it.
Ketil talks. I knew a Frisian would come asking before the Frisian did.
The gold I took off. The skins I kept. Look at that: a man made that with a feather. I have a smith who could not do it with a chisel.
You turn straight to one leaf and put your finger through a hole in it. So it is the one you want, and you know it is. That was honest of your finger. It has cost you the haggling.
You turn the leaves like a man looking for something and not finding it. One box of skins looks much like another, they tell me. This is the one I have.
The woman at the loom wears a round gilt mount on her cloak, with a clear stone in the middle. She sees you look. 'It was on the lid. He says the lid was ugly. It was not.'
Two swords, Frankish, with the hilts on. Or silver in the scale until I say stop, and I stop at about the weight of a good axe head. Not prayers. I was offered prayers on the island, loudly.
It sleeps in the chest by my bed, and my hounds sleep on the chest. I say so because some guests are forgetful.
Weigh him out three hundred pennies of silver
Give him two Frankish swords for it
Tell him what it is and whose, and leave it on his chest
Say nothing, and come back for it after dark

The pennies go into his scale as plain metal; he does not look at the king's name on them. When the pan drops he says stop, and laughs, and adds one more with his own finger. The book goes down to your boat in a flour sack.

He draws each blade, bends it against his knee, and listens to it. Then he puts the book in your arms himself, as a man hands over a child he was minding. 'I hope your god reads better than I do.' You do not ask where the swords will go next summer.

You tell him: it is the word of the Christians' god, written for one house, and that house would give more for it than any market. He hears you out. 'Then it will not go for skins. I will send it south with the autumn lot and see who weeps most.' He has ale brought, and it is good ale.

The hounds know your smell from the afternoon and the man sleeps like the just. You are at sea before the tide turns, with the book between your feet. Behind you a horn blows once, and then for a long time.

The hounds are quiet until your hand is on the lid. His men throw you down the beach and your crew after you. He does not kill a guest, he says, but he may improve one. From the door he calls that the skins go south to Asulf with the autumn lot, if you would like to try buying next time.
Green water
The wind backs and hardens in the afternoon. The steersman looks at the sky to windward and then at the bundle of calfskins in the bottom of the boat.
She will take water over the quarter before dark. That is the worst of it. The rest is only work. Say now where the skins ride.
The boy's sealskin is tight; I tried it with a bucket. Under the stern board it will be drier than I am.
A flour sack keeps out flour. If we drive her, the sea chooses. If we lie to, you choose, and we lose the day.
Shorten sail, lie to, and hold it on your knees under the tilt until it blows through
It rides in the sealskin under the stern board: sail on
Wedge it under the thwart with the spare sail over it and drive on

A night with the sail down and the book in your lap, like a man nursing a goose. By morning the wind has gone round and the skins are dry. The crew have a new name for you and use it only among themselves.
Twice the sea comes in green over the quarter and runs out through the bailing. When it is over the lookout opens the flap with clean hands. Dry as a bone. He is unbearable about it for a week.
She takes one sea aboard and shakes it off. The sail over the bundle is wet through, and under it the sack is only damp at one corner. The steersman says nothing, which from him is praise.

The third sea fills her to the thwarts. When you can look, the bundle has been lying in water. The leaves at one edge are swollen and the green has run on the pages of Mark. It is still a book. It is not the book it was this morning.
The same square sail
A sail lifts astern at first light and does not fall behind. By mid morning there are shields along her side and a big man standing in her bow, in no hurry.
Striped, red and undyed. I know that sail. I have known it since I was told of it. Blessed is the man... no. I cannot think of the rest.
Frisian! You left in the night and forgot to pay. I came to remind you. It is no trouble; I was sailing this way.
The price was an axe head of silver. Now it is that and the price of my night's sleep, which I value. Or give me the skins back, and we have both had a sail.
Or run. There is shoal water under your lee and you draw less than I do. If I catch you I take the skins and leave you the boat. A story needs a living man to tell it.
Lie to and weigh out his price, with the price of his night's sleep on top
Run for shoal water, where her keel cannot follow yours
Lie to and hand it back over the gunwale

He weighs it on his own scale across two gunwales in a swell, and does not spill a penny. 'Now it is bought. Tell them on your island that Thorleif sells, and that he was not asked first.' His ship goes about and is gone before noon.

You take her in over the bank with a hand's breadth under the keel and the sounding pole going. He follows until his steersman shouts, then lies to and watches you go. He lifts one hand. You think he is laughing.

The bank is not where it was. She touches, and by the time she floats he is alongside. They take the book, a cask and a tooth from the mate, and leave the boat, as he said. 'It goes to Asulf at Sliesthorp with the next lot. Bring silver. It is easier on the hounds.'

He takes the bundle in both hands and looks into the sack to see that it is the same one. 'You came a long way to carry my goods for me.' His crew laugh; yours do not. He says it goes south to Asulf with the next lot, and that buying is permitted.
Asulf's lot
On a bench outside the dealer's pen, with a sealskin, two cups and a bell without a tongue, lies the block of calfskins. A spare, pale-eyed Svea is counting its leaves for the second time.
From Thorleif, with the autumn lot. He says a Frisian told him what it is, and to ask more than skins are worth. You are a Frisian.
From Thorleif. He says you know this piece, and the way to his bed in the dark. Here you may look at it by day.
Two hundred and fifty-eight skins. I counted two hundred and fifty-eight before. Eight ounces. Scraped clean, they will take a tally as well as new skin.
Or not scraped. I have a man at home who reads such marks. He is English. He might be worth more with something to read.
Fifteen ounces takes it now. Or two Frankish blades: a blade buys me more people than silver does. I do not haggle twice.
A Christian I may not sell south to the Franks. A Christian's book I may sell to anyone. I did not make the law. I only notice it.
Outbid the Svea: fifteen ounces, two hundred and fifty pennies' weight
Give the dealer two Frankish swords for it
Tell the Svea truly what a house of monks would give for it, and let it go east

Asulf cuts nothing from his arm ring today. The Svea closes his scales, puts them back in their bronze case, and says that he had only bid for the skins. He watches the book all the way down to your boat.

Asulf looks along each blade and sets them inside the pen door, out of the damp. The Svea counts something on his fingers and stops. The book is yours. Somewhere east of here two swords will be turned into people.

You say it plainly: its own house would give a farm for it; a king might give more. The Svea repeats this back to you slowly, and is silent, and then bids twenty ounces. Asulf takes it. 'He will hear of this in the west,' he says. 'Thorleif pays for a true word. Go and see him next summer.' The book goes into a fur bale for Birka.
Low water
You carry the bundle up from the boat over wet sand. Word has run ahead of you: the brethren are standing outside the church, and nobody speaks.
The bishop does not take it at once. He opens it where it lies in your arms, turns to one leaf and puts his little finger through the hole. 'Wigfrith,' he says. 'You careful, careful man.'
I am Ecgberht. Bishop Higbald died in May, before Whitsun, and he asked after this in his last week. Let me see the first leaf of John. Yes. He described it to me, in case.
The old brothers have told of this book since before I took vows. There should be a hole in one leaf. There is. I did not truly believe in the hole until now.
It has been in the sea. Mark has run. Well. So have we all been in the sea, these years, and we are still read from.
How did you come by it? I ask because of your face. Then there will be a sail, some morning. We know what that is. I do not say you did wrong. I say I will not be able to help you with it.
You have brought it again. Am I to look at it again, or is it staying this time?
I have nothing in my hands today but this. Come at the saint's feast in spring, or at Aidan's at the end of harvest. The estates will have sent by then, and the king's rock will have heard.
Lay it in his hands and ask nothing
Give it over, and ask back what it cost you and a fair freight
Let him see it, and carry it back to the boat: others will pay more

You put it in his hands and step back. He stands holding it as if it weighed what the altar weighs. A brother begins a psalm and the others take it up, badly, because some of them are weeping. Nobody thanks you. It does not seem to be that kind of thing. Come at the feast, the bishop says at the boat: the saint pays his own debts.

You name what it cost and what the carrying is worth, and he nods at each sum: this is a language he was afraid you might not speak. 'That is fair, and it will be paid. Come at the feast.' The book goes into the church. The brethren sing over it, and one of them brings your crew a cheese.
He closes the book himself and puts it back in your arms. 'York has silver. The Franks have more. I know what I have.' He walks you to the sand, because you are a guest. The brethren do not.
On the altar
On the feast the book lies open on the altar at the first leaf of John. The brethren from the estates are here, and a thegn from the king's rock, and a merchant who is asked to stand at the front.
The heathen men took this from us. A shipman of Dorestat went north after it and came back. I do not know that such a thing has been done before. Write the day down.
He asked nothing for it. I have told him that will not be allowed.
He asked what it cost him and a fair freight. That is a merchant's honesty, and I wish more lords had it.
It came home marked by the sea. We will not mend those leaves. Let whoever reads Mark here remember how it came back.
We saw their sails from the rock that day, and we did not come. I have brought silver. It does not mend that. I have brought it anyway.
One thing more. The saint's peace runs to the tide line. Past it there is a man with a striped sail who thinks he is owed. Pray; and keep a lookout.
Here is what we have: the silver that York collected and the king's rock has added, wax from our farms, ground on this island, and what a saint can give. Say which.
Take what he offers the giver: your name in the book of life, a cloth from the saint's coffin, and the carrying of the house's wine
Take the ransom: York's collection, the thegn's silver and the house's wax
Ask for ground instead: a boat strand and a storehouse inside the harbour sands

Your name is written among the friends of the house, to be read at the altar while the house stands. A strip of the linen that lay on Cuthbert's coffin is folded into your hand. The thegn presses his silver on you all the same, and the bishop will have his wine from no other boat. On this coast, from now on, you are Saint Cuthbert's man.

Nine hundred pennies' weight, some of it cut plate, and ten cakes of wax carried down by brothers who will not let your crew lift them. Your name goes into the book of life with the rest. It is the best freight you have ever been paid, and the bishop looks as if he thinks it cheap.

He walks the ground with you at low water: a strip above the tide inside the sands, where a boat lies easy in a west wind, and leave to build on it. A brother cuts the bounds on a stick. A Frisian has a strand on the bishop's island. The thegn says he will tell the king before the king hears it from someone else.
A house with walls
The scribe has told his lord what lies in your boat. The archbishop comes down to the staith himself, which he does not do for wine.
The island's hand, sixty or seventy years old. And there is the hole. I am sorry. I had to tell him. He is my lord, and I am fond of eating.
The island could not keep it once. It has no wall, no ditch and no spears, and the same ships are at sea this summer. Here it would lie behind stone, with the best books north of the Alps beside it.
I hear you carried it up their sand and down again. So you are a man who can be talked to.
I will pay as the island cannot. Silver, weighed here today. A clerk of mine to keep your goods and write to you by every ship. Or ground by the river, if you would rather have land than a man.
The scribe says nothing. He holds up his ink-stained thumb behind his lord's back and moves it upward, twice.
The island's bishop will write to me. He will write very well. I shall answer that the book is safe, and that is the end of what he can do.
Sell it for his first price in silver, and a clerk of the minster to keep your goods here
Name the price the scribe taught you: a herd, a year and the saint's name
Sell it for less silver and a house plot by the Ouse
Say it is not for sale here: it goes to the island

Twelve hundred pennies' weight is counted out on the staith, and a young clerk is told that he keeps a Frisian's goods from today. The book goes up to the minster under a cloth. On the island they will hear of it within the month, and they will know who sold it.

You name the herd, the year and the saint, and what each is worth, in that order. The archbishop looks at his scribe, who is looking at the river. Seventeen hundred, and the clerk. 'You have been to school,' the archbishop says. 'I wonder where.' On the island they will hear of it within the month.

Six hundred pennies' weight, and a strip of ground between the street and the Ouse with leave to build and to draw up a boat. The reeve marks the corners. The book goes up to the minster under a cloth. You have a house in the richest market of the north, and a bishop further up the coast who will not forget how you came by it.

'Then carry it carefully,' the archbishop says, 'since you carry it for nothing.' He goes back up the hill with his thegns. The scribe stays a moment and says the island has a friend he had not expected, and that there is still some of the bread left from noon.
The king's alms
A tall stooping monk in a patched cowl has been asking along the bank for a ship that goes north. He sees what you carry before you have said a word, and sits down on a mooring post.
Forgive me. I am not often short of breath on dry land. Is that from the island? May I see the first leaf of John? Only that one. Thank you. Yes.
I carry my master Alcuin's answer to the bishop. He promised to speak to King Charles for the boys who were taken, and he has spoken. I have a bag of the king's alms for ransom, and nobody to ransom.
My master has Saint Martin's at Tours now. He would have this copied before it went home, and then he would send it home. He is like that. It makes him expensive to serve.

A book is not a boy. But it was carried off by the same hands, and alms given for the one may honestly buy back the other. Let me take it north as the king's gift. You would be paid here, today, in full.
And the abbot who keeps the toll here does what my master asks. A man who brought this out of the north should not pay a tenth on this bank again. I can have that written.
I will be honest. I am a bad sailor and the book would be safer with you. But it would come to the island as your gift then, and not the king's, and kings count such things.
Give it into his hands for the king's alms: he will take it to the island as King Charles's gift
Take part of the alms toward what you paid, and Alcuin's letter, and carry the book home yourself
Let him read in it for an evening, and decide nothing

He counts out a thousand pennies as if each one hurt, and has the abbot's clerk write that your boat goes free of the toll at Quentovic. Then he wraps the book in his own cloak and goes to look for another ship north, apologising to the skipper before he has found him. The island will have its book back from the hand of the king of the Franks, and will know whom to thank.

He weighs out a hundred and fifty pennies toward the ransom and gives you his master's letter to carry with the book. 'Then it is your gift. I shall tell him so. He will be pleased, and then he will ask why I am not on your ship.' He is still explaining why not when you cast off.

He reads by a rush light at the hospice, aloud, following the line with a straw so as not to touch the skin. You follow some of it. Twice he stops to tell you that the cold on this coast gets into a man's knees. In the morning he gives the book back with both hands.
A true word
The big red-fair man sees your sail before you see him, and sends a boy down to say there is a place for you on the bench and that nobody will ask what you paid for it.
Twenty ounces, Asulf had for my box of skins. From a Svea. Nobody has had twenty ounces from a Svea since the gods were young. He says it was your word that did it.
We have met by night, you and I. This is better. There is more light, and the hounds are fed.
The woman has the round mount on her cloak still. 'He says you told the Svea what the lid was worth as well. Nobody will have that from me. It will go into the ground with me.'
The skins are at Birka. They say the Svea has an Englishman who reads them aloud to him at night. The Svea understands none of it and will not miss an evening. Explain that to me, if you can.

I pay for a true word. It is rarer than a book. Walrus tooth and a guest's seat here; or my sister's son, who has a boat and wants a partner with silver; or your share on the scale, and my steersman shows you the sound.
Take his gift of walrus tooth, and a guest's place in his hall and on his coast
Lay goods together with his sister's son, who has a boat and no silver
Take your share by weight and the marks of the sound, and carry word to the island of where its book lies

Eight tusks from the far north, each as long as your forearm, and his word before the whole bench that your sail is a guest's sail from here to the mouth of the sound. It is a strange thing to have the friendship of the man who emptied Saint Cuthbert's church. It will keep his ships off yours, and perhaps his friends' ships too.

The young man has a good boat, a quick tongue and five bundles of marten that are yours to sell for the common stock. You swear it with joined hands before the bench. In the Christian ports they will ask whose kin your partner is, and you will have to decide each time how much to say.

Six hundred pennies' weight in cut silver, and three days in his steersman's boat learning the Karmsund: the rock that shows at half tide, the two cairns in line, where the stream turns. And a thing to tell on the island: the book is whole, it is at Birka, and it is read. It is not what the bishop prays for. It is more than he has now.

A gospel book that the heathen men carried off from Saint Cuthbert's island has come home. A Frisian shipman of Dorestat found it in the north and brought it over the sand at low water. It lay on the altar at the feast.

The archbishop at Eoforwic has bought a gospel book that was taken from Saint Cuthbert's island, from a Frisian shipman who had it in the north. The island's bishop has written to ask for it. The book is in the minster.

King Charles's alms have bought back a gospel book that the heathen men took from Saint Cuthbert's island. Alcuin's monk is carrying it north. A Frisian of Dorestat found it and goes free of the toll at Quentovic for it.
They say in the north that a Svea paid twenty ounces of silver for a Christian book without its boards, on a Frisian's word of what it was worth, and took it east to Birka in a bale of furs.

A northern beach market on a grey late-summer afternoon: a dealer squats behind a cloth on the shingle with a silver cup, a small house-shaped box and a narrow strip of gilt bronze knotwork on it; a merchant's hand reaches for the strip; tents and drawn-up boats behind.

Inside the wooden church at Lindisfarne, morning light falling through the doorway where the doors have been torn off: a gaunt old bishop with a plain wooden staff counts on his raised fingers; behind him a bare altar and an empty book stand.

The minster's writing room at York on a cold bright day: a scribe at a slanted desk by a small window, pen lifted, breath showing, ruled calfskin before him and horns of red, yellow and green colour; a Frisian merchant in a short cloak waits by the door.

Evening at sea in a small open boat under a brown sail, low sun, calm water: a thin English youth holds up a wax tablet on which he has drawn a page with a small round hole in it; the steersman and the skipper lean in over their bread.

A Norse hall on a bright summer day, the door open on a sound with a ship drawn up: a big red-fair chief holds open a book without covers at a page of red, yellow and green knotwork; two hounds lie on a chest behind him; a woman at an upright loom wears a round gilt mount as a brooch.

The small boat hard pressed under a dark afternoon sky, a green sea breaking over her quarter; the skipper crouched under the tilt with a wrapped bundle held against his chest; the broad steersman braced at the steering oar, looking to windward.

Clear mid morning on a grey-blue sea, seen from the small boat's stern: a longship close astern under a red and undyed striped sail, shields along her side, a big man standing easy in the bow with one hand raised; pale shoal water to leeward.

Sliesthorp in spring under a flat white sky: a bench outside a wattle pen with a sealskin, two cups, a tongueless bell and the coverless book on it; a spare pale-eyed Svea in a fur-trimmed cap counts its leaves with one finger while a stout Dane with a plaited beard and a hazel switch watches him.

Low water at Lindisfarne, wet sand shining under a wide pale sky: a merchant walks up from a beached boat carrying a bundle in both arms; ahead, monks in undyed habits stand silent outside a wooden church with no doors, the old bishop a step in front of them.

The church at Lindisfarne on a feast day, new doors standing open, candles lit: the book open on the altar at a great decorated first letter; the bishop beside it, the brethren crowded behind, a thegn in a dark red cloak with a bag of silver, and a Frisian merchant standing at the front, ill at ease.

The river staith at York on a clear afternoon: an archbishop in a rich dark cloak, armed thegns at his back, stands over a small Frisian boat pointing at a wrapped bundle in the skipper's arms; behind him a scribe looks away at the river; the stone minster on the hill.

The river bank at Quentovic toward evening, soft light, ships moored along the timber bank: a tall stooping monk in a patched black cowl sits on a mooring post with the open book across his knees and a leather letter case under his arm, a small bag of coin on the ground at his feet.

The Norse hall at night, long fire burning, guests on the benches: the red-fair chief stands and holds out a walrus tusk to a Frisian merchant in the guest's seat; the woman beside him wears the round gilt book mount on her cloak; through the open door, the sound in the last light of a northern summer night.
Word from the islands
A man with a burned hand is asking along the landing for your house by name. He is off the islands. He was your brother's neighbour, and he has been walking for nine days.
Nobody counted them. The sea was ships from one sandbank to the other. We stood against them three times. After the third time there were not enough of us to stand, so we paid.
Liafbern was alive when they rowed him off. I saw that. He was sitting up and he was angry, and they do not carry off the ones who will not last.
The boy went in another ship. Wibern. He did not cry out. He was holding on to a sheep, and they took the sheep as well.

The king is on the Aller with the whole host, waiting for the Dane to come and fight. The Dane is dead. His own man killed him. And the great beast the Saracen king sent died at Lippeham. It has been that kind of summer.

There is a peace now. Twelve of ours and twelve of theirs swore it on the Eider. I have not heard that anybody's kin were in it. A hundred pounds of silver went north, and that is all that went either way.
Give him bread, a place by the fire and six pennies, and hear all of it
Ask the count's rider whether the king will buy the taken back
Thank him and say nothing more

He eats slowly, like a man who has taught himself to. The ships went home by the north, he says, heavy. What the Danes take alive they sell at the new market on the Slie, where their king set the merchants down. Then he sleeps where he sits.

The rider laughs, not unkindly. The king is building ships at every river mouth and has no penny over for people. 'If a man wants his kin, he goes and gets them. The Danes sell at Sliesthorp. They will sell to you as soon as to anyone.'

He nods, and goes on down the landing to find the next house on his list. He has eleven. You stand a while. Your brother's mound is by Doccinga, and somebody there will know more than a neighbour could see from a ditch.
The mound by the creek

The byre is black posts. The house stands, because it was raining. Your brother's wife is at the loom as if nothing else could be trusted to stay where it is put. The priest has walked over from the church with a wax tablet.
They did not want me. I was under the boat with the little ones and the Danes were in a hurry. I have thought about whether to be glad.
You will know him. The front tooth he broke on your father's oar. The white scar across the left hand from the eel spear. If they have cut his hair he will be in a worse temper than the tooth.
The boy has my band for a belt, red and undyed, the goose-foot pattern. Nobody else weaves it with the feet turned in. I did it wrong the first time and kept doing it.
Forty-three from these mounds. I am writing them all, because God knows them and I would like one other to. A list is a small thing. Kings have been moved by smaller.

In England once a taken man's bonds fell off him each morning. His brother, a priest, thought him dead and said Mass for him at that hour. In the end they sold him to a Frisian. We come into every story sooner or later.
Have the priest write down every name the islands lost, and carry the list
Take the silver the mound has dug up for the buying back, and give your word on it
Take only the end of the band she wove for the boy's belt, and promise nothing

It takes him until dark. Forty-three names in a small square hand, yours two among them, on a strip of calfskin he had been keeping for something better. He says there is nothing better. He will say the Mass for all of them, each morning, and see what falls off.

Frethburg lifts a hearthstone. Ninety pennies' weight in cut silver and old thin coin, some of it your mother's. Three neighbours watch you take it, which is what they came for. You say that you will bring them back. It sounds larger said aloud.

She cuts a hand's length from the end still on the loom and knots it so it will not run. 'Promise nothing,' she says. 'I have had promises. Show him that, and he will know I am alive, and that is as much as I can send.'
A man who remembers every sale

Asulf's pen is a fenced yard with a roof along one side and a trough. He feeds his lots; it is cheaper than burying them. He has a hazel switch in his hand and a row of notched sticks on a peg, one for each ship that sold to him this year.
The island lot. Nine ships sold to me. A man with a broken tooth who would not stand when he was told. A boy who came with a sheep. I do not forget stock. It would be bad for the trade.

I split it. Grown men go south: a Saxon walks them to the Rhine, and Franks from a town called Verdun buy there for Spain. The young go east. A Svea took the boy to Birka. Two roads. You have one boat.
The king who sent the ships is dead. His own man did it. I mention this so that you know there is nobody to complain to.
I have heard what was sworn on the Eider. I was not asked. Your two were sold out of the kingdom before any oath, so the king pays and I do not. That is a good oath. I could live under more like it.

He sells my people by the dozen and yours by the one, and he has never told a lie about either. The south road is the short one. The Verdun men do not keep a lot through a winter. They would have to feed it.
Lay a Frankish blade on his table for the whole telling and his own stick
Weigh him two ounces of silver for the telling and his stick
Carry water in his pen for a day, and listen

He bends the blade against his knee and lets it spring. Then he talks for as long as it takes to drink a horn. The Svea is Ingimar, with a farm behind the town at Birka. Asulf cuts you a stick with his mark and the price he was paid, and says he will send word east that the boy is asked for.

He weighs it himself, on his own scale, and gives back a clipping that was over. The Svea is Ingimar of Birka; the Franks buy at Mainz, in a yard by the Frisians' houses. He cuts a stick with his mark and the price he was paid. 'They know my mark. It saves talk.'

Forty buckets from the well to the trough. Nobody in the pen looks at you. At dusk Asulf tells you the two roads anyway, in as many words as there are roads. The Wend walks you to the gate and adds the names: Ingimar at Birka. A yard at Mainz, by the Frisians' houses.
Twelve and twelve

The town is full of horses. A day's ride west, on the Eider, twelve great men of the Franks and twelve of the Danes are to swear the peace the kings made over the winter. A Frankish clerk is buying fish and writing down what it cost. One of King Hemming's men is watching him write.

Count Wala leads ours. The king's own cousin. Theirs are led by two brothers of their king. Twenty-four great men, and I am the one who has to find them all dry fish in a town that sells mostly people.
A list? Written? Give it here. My count can do nothing with a man weeping on a riverbank. A list he can read out, and what is read out before twenty-four witnesses has to be answered.
You have kin who were taken. So has half that coast. My count cannot swear to a sorrow. If you had names, written, that would be another thing.
What was taken was sold. What was sold was sold again. A king can give back what is in his hand. This one is new, and his hand is not yet full.
Hemming wants the peace more than your king does. He has brothers. If somebody asked a thing that cost him little and looked like much, I would not say he would refuse it.
Give the clerk the list of names, and forty pennies to see it reaches his count
Ride to the Eider and say it yourself, in their tongue, before both twelves
Stand in the crowd and watch them swear

Three days later the clerk finds you on the jetty, pleased with himself. The count read the names out, all forty-three. A brother of the Danish king said that a king who keeps another king's farmers looks poor. It was sworn with the rest: those still in the kingdom go home by Lammas, and the price is made good for those sold out of it.

The list was read. The clerk says so twice. It was not sworn: there was the border to settle, and the winter had been long, and the great men wanted to go home. King Hemming's man cuts you a stick with his king's mark. 'Show the dealers this. It is not an oath. It is a king looking at them.'

You say it badly and they understand it. Forty-three farmers, by name, off islands that have paid their hundred pounds. Count Wala looks at you for some time. A brother of the Danish king laughs and says the Frisian has a point and a bad way of making it. It is sworn with the rest.

They swear on their weapons, the Danes and the Franks alike, on a wet meadow by a brown river. It takes less time than unloading a boat. The border is the Eider. Nobody says a word about anybody's kin, and by evening the horses are gone.
One who crossed himself
The road from Saxony comes down to the water here, and whatever walks it crosses in this man's boat. He counts everything he carries, because he is paid by the head, for oxen and for people alike.
Twelve on a rope and a Saxon with a stick. Three weeks back, or four. He paid for twelve Wends. I do not ask what a thing is. I ask how many.
When we pushed off, one of them crossed himself. Forehead, breast, shoulders, the way my mother does it. Wends do not. I noticed it, and then I had the current to mind.

They sell at Mainz, before the archbishop's steward. It has to be before somebody: that is the old king's law. If a man stood up there with a witness the steward knew, the Saxon's oath would not be worth the breath.
Pay him thirty pennies to come up the river and say it under oath
Ask him what else the road has brought down, and go on

He leaves the ferry to his son, who is pleased, and comes aboard with a loaf and a clean shirt for the oath. He has carried the archbishop's own oxen over this water for twenty years. 'The steward knows my face. He owes me for a calf.'

Oxen, he says, and Saxon horses, and fewer cloth boats than any year he remembers: the Frisians are late, and the Mainz men are paying over for a good cloak. He wishes you luck with your Wend. He says it as if he knows it is not a Wend.
Eleven Wends and a Frisian

A walled yard behind the Frisians' quarter. Twelve men sit along the wall with a rope through their belts. Eleven are Wends. The twelfth has a broken front tooth and a white scar across his left hand, and he has seen you and is being careful not to look.
Twenty-five shillings for that one. He is strong and he has all his fingers. In Saragossa they will give me three times that, and I have to walk him there and feed him. You see I am not a hard man.
The drover swore the whole rope heathen, on relics, before I paid. A Wend who has learned to make the cross is still a Wend. I have had them recite the whole Creed when they see the mountains.
You took your time. I have walked from one sea nearly to another, and I can tell you the middle of the world is mostly mud. Is the boy with you?
A lot is sold before me or it is not sold. Heathen men of the marches, yes. A free man of the king's own Frisians, no: the law of his country says who sells him out of it pays as for a killing.
My lord Riculf has ruled this church since before you had a beard. He does not like oaths sworn lightly in his court. He likes Verdun's merchants a little less.
My lord Haistulf is new in the chair and wishes to be known as careful. Bring me an oath I can stand behind, and he will be pleased with us both.
I know that ferryman. He has never lied to me about a head of cattle in twenty years, and he complains so much about what I owe him that he must be honest.
Buy him at the Verdun man's price
Swear him a free Frisian before the steward, with the ferryman's oath beside yours
Swear him a free Frisian with your crew as oath-helpers
Kneel to the steward and ask for the church's alms for the taken

Three hundred pennies, counted twice on a plank. Gundbert unties the rope himself and wishes you both health. Your brother says nothing until the gate is shut behind you. Then he says that he was worth more, and that he will pay it back, and that you are not to tell his wife the figure.

The ferryman swears to the cross made on the water. You swear to the tooth and the scar. Your brother says the Our Father in his own bad Latin and then, unasked, the names of your father's cows. The steward rules him free. The drover is gone, so the Verdun man pays the wrong, and pays it looking at you.

Your crew swear one after another that you are a man whose oath stands. Your brother says the Our Father, and then the names of your father's cows. The steward listens to the cows with more attention. He rules him free, and has the Verdun man weigh out the wrong. Gundbert weighs it slowly, so as to remember.

The steward asks which of your helpers knew this man before the raid. None did. The oath falls. He is sorry; he believes you; belief is not law. He buys your brother himself with the altar's silver, for the love of God, and writes your name in the church's book of what is owed.

You kneel on the stones of the yard in front of eleven Wends, your brother and a man from Verdun. The steward lets you stay there a moment longer than he need. Then he pays from the alms for the taken, and says the altar wants four cakes of wax within the year, and that he will know your boat.
An empty yard

The yard behind the Frisians' quarter has been swept. There is a ring in the wall and nothing tied to it. The archbishop's steward remembers the lot: it was sold before him, as the law asks, and nobody stood up to say a word.

Twelve heads, sworn heathen. One had a broken tooth and looked at me as if I should know better. I did not know better. Nobody was there to tell me. That is what the law is for, and that day it had nothing to work with.
Up the Mosel road to Verdun. From Verdun they go down the rivers to the south sea, and over the mountains to the Saracens. What a boat can follow ends here, at this wall.

I carry wine to Metz and Verdun every season and I know which houses buy men. For a pound of silver I will ask, and buy if he is there to buy. If he has gone over the mountains, you will have paid for an answer.
There are Masses at Saint Alban's for those who are away and cannot come back. The living are named in them. It costs a candle. I do not say it is the same as a rope cut.
Send a pound of silver after him with the carrier, and the marks to know him by
Ask for the archbishop's letter to the bishop of Verdun, and owe the church for it
Pay for a Mass at Saint Alban's, and turn the boat

The carrier ties the silver into his own belt and says the marks back to you: the tooth, the scar on the left hand, the temper. He goes at first light with six mules. 'After the vintage I come down again. Or he comes down without me. You will know at your own door, or you will not.'

The steward writes it himself, a hand's breadth of careful Latin, and seals it. One bishop greets another and asks after a free Frisian wrongly sold. It will go with the next clerk who rides west, which may be a month. 'A letter is slower than a rope of men. I tell you now so that you do not tell me later.'

You buy the candle. The priest at Saint Alban's asks the name, and writes it among the living, between a tanner's son gone to Rome and a woman nobody has seen since the flood. Then you go down to the boat. The river runs the right way for once.
The boy with the sheep

Holmfast walks you over the hill behind the town to a farm above the water. A boy is driving sheep off a boat's nets with a stick. He has grown a hand's width and his hair is cut the Svea way. He sees your cloak before he sees your face, and stops.
One boy. Frisian. Ten winters, now eleven. Bought at Sliesthorp by Ingimar for one mark less an ounce. I said I would show you the farm. I have shown it. That is one thing done.
He is a good boy. He does not steal and he is not sick. He talks to the sheep in his own tongue and they have started to listen. I would as soon keep him.
But kin is kin. A mark of silver, weighed. I paid less, and he has eaten since. Or wine: I have a daughter to marry and nothing in the house fit to pour.
He has a stick. I know the mark. The stick says a mark less an ounce and somebody's word behind it. Ingimar: the stick is the price. I say it twice. The stick is the price.
Is my father on the boat? No. Then where is he? You can tell me. I know how many they got for me.
Weigh out a mark of silver for him
Show the stick, and pay what he gave and no more
Give three casks of Rhine wine for him
Give your hand to carry his skins to Sliesthorp this summer for nothing

Holmfast holds the scale so that neither of you has to. A mark, level. Ingimar gives the boy the stick he herded with and tells him the sheep will miss him, which may be true. Then he asks what Frisian cloth costs where it is made, and orders six bolts for the wedding.

Ingimar turns the stick over, finds the mark, and breathes out through his nose. Seventy pennies' weight, and not a clipping more. He takes it well for a man who has just fed a boy a year for nothing. He orders six bolts of cloth, and you understand that the cloth will not be cheap.

He has the casks rolled up to the house before he says yes. He tastes one, counts them twice, and weighs you back forty pennies: nobody at his daughter's wedding is going to say he took a boy's price twice over. The boy carries the stick down to your boat and will not put it down.

You give your hand on it in front of Holmfast, who counts it as he counts everything. Eleven bales to Sliesthorp, unpaid, before the nights draw in. Your crew look at the bales and then at the sky. The boy gets into the boat without being told and starts to bail, though she is dry.
Gone with the summer ships

The farm above the water is shut and the boat shed is empty. Holmfast has the reckoning ready before you ask: the shipman went east after midsummer with four in the boat, and one of the four was a boy who bails.
Ingimar. One boat, four in it. Three men and a boy. East, after midsummer. You are late. I do not say it to wound. I say it because it is the first number.
He winters at Aldeigja and comes back with the skins when the ice goes. Or he goes on south from there with the ones who go south. Then the boy goes where the boat goes.
I go east myself at the next midsummer. A mark and a quarter: a mark for the boy, a quarter for me. If Ingimar will not sell, or the boy will not come, I keep the quarter. I say it now.
That is weaving. Goose feet, turned in. I will carry it for nothing. It weighs nothing. But a strip of wool does not buy a boy from a man who has taught him to steer.
Weigh Holmfast a mark and a quarter to buy the boy at Aldeigja and send him west
Send the end of his mother's band east, and let him choose
Ask Holmfast to say the boy is remembered, and turn the boat

He weighs it, says the weight, and has you say it back. A mark and a quarter, the boy Wibern, to be put on a westbound ship at Birka with food for the passage. 'A winter and a sea. Look for him at your own landing after the next harvest. If you do not see him, you will see me, with the mark.'

He winds the strip round two fingers and puts it inside his scale case, where he keeps nothing that is not silver. 'I will give it into his hand and say whose it is. After that it is his reckoning, not mine. He is eleven. At eleven I had been to Gotland twice.'

Holmfast repeats it: the boy Wibern is remembered at his mother's hearth. He will say it once, in Frisian if he can get his mouth round it. He does not say it is a small thing to carry, and you find that you are grateful.
Two at the table
