There is a new byre on the mound, built of driftwood and one good oak post. Your brother is roofing it. The boy is handing him turves and speaking to the dog in the Svea tongue. Frethburg has set four bowls and is looking at them.
I set two bowls for a year. Then one day I set four, by mistake, and that was the day the boat came up the creek. I do not say it means anything. I shall go on setting four.
I know what a man costs now, which is more than most can say. I know what I cost and what the boy cost, and I am going to pay both, so do not start.
And the archbishop's wax. I was bought with altar silver like a candlestick. We will take him his four cakes, and a fifth so he cannot say Frisians count short.
That Verdun man will know your sail. He weighed that silver out like a man pulling his own teeth. I would stay off the Mosel wine for a year or two.
The Svear steer with the wind behind the ear and do not look at the land at all. I can show you. Ingimar said I had the hands for it. He said it to the sheep, but I was there.
One purse and two boats: take your brother as a sworn partner, and the boy to bail
Leave them the land; take the mound's weaving for the house, year on year
Take nothing: kin is not cargo

You swear it at the church door, hand on the post, the priest for witness: one purse, two boats, losses shared. The mound lays down its silver and twelve bolts of the red cloth. Your brother has walked across the world and says he would sooner sail the rest. The boy is in the bow before the cloth is stowed.

Your brother stays on his land, and nobody who has seen him roof that byre would move him. The mound's looms weave for your house first from now on, and Frethburg sets the price, which is fair and will stay fair. The boy is to come to you at fourteen. He has counted the years on his fingers twice.

You say it and mean it. In the morning there is silver under your rowing bench and ten bolts of cloth on top of it. Your brother is marking out ground beside his house with four pegs. 'A store. Yours. I am not asking.' He has his sea bag with him, and the boy has made himself one out of a sack.
The father's bowl
Your brother is mending a net on the bench by the door. He works as he always did, quickly and without looking. There is a small wooden bowl on the shelf above him that nobody has moved.
I am home. I say it each morning to see if it has become true. The byre is up. The eels are running. I have every thing I had before but one.

On a river in the east, with a Svea who feeds him and has taught him to steer. I have been a head on a rope. He is better off than I was. I tell myself that, and it is true, and it does no good at all.
Nobody can tell me where. East. That is a direction, not a place. I look at the sea in the mornings as if it might have an opinion.
Leave the bowl. He will be twelve at Martinmas, and then thirteen, wherever he is. I can count as well as any Svea.
One purse and two boats: take your brother as a sworn partner
Give him your hand on it: the summer the house sails east, he is in the boat
Leave him to his land; take the mound's weaving for the house

You swear it at the church door: one purse, two boats, losses shared. The mound lays down its silver and eight bolts of cloth. Your brother is a good hand in a boat and a silent one now. Whenever a ship comes in from the north he reads her crew, man by man, and then goes back to work.

He takes your hand and holds it too long. 'The summer you go. Not the summer after.' Frethburg cuts a new length of the goose-foot band and gives it to him, not to you. The silver and the cloth are in the boat already. It seems they were always going to be.

He will not leave the mound again, and says so before you ask. Frethburg's looms and her neighbours' weave for your house first from now on. Fourteen bolts go down to the boat. Your brother carries the last one himself and stands on the bank until the creek turns.
His father's knife

The boy is cutting reed on the creek bank with a knife too big for his hand. It was found in the ash of the byre. He has ground the burn off it himself. He does everything now as if somebody were about to tell him to stop.
It is his. I am keeping the edge on it. If he comes back and it is dull he will say I was badly brought up, and that would fall on him, so.
I am not a widow. The priest says so and the law says so. I have a husband in a country where they do not have winter. I have decided to think of him as warm.
Men have come back from the Saracens. I will not tell her how many years it took the ones I have heard of. She has not asked, and she is a woman who asks what she wants to know.

He is named at Saint Alban's among the living, I am told, and here each morning. If bonds can fall off in England they can fall off in Spain. I have not found the place where it is written that they cannot.
Take the boy into the boat and the house, before witnesses, as your own
Stand guardian of his father's share until he is a man, and build a store on it
Leave him with his mother; take the mound's weaving for the house

You set him on your knee before the neighbours, which is how it is done, and he is too big for it and bears it. The mound lays down silver and eight bolts of cloth for his keep. Frethburg ties his belt herself. In the boat he steers with the wind behind his ear and does not look at the land.

The neighbours witness it: his father's share is his, and yours to keep for him until he can carry a spear to the muster. You pace out a store by the creek. The boy paces it after you, checking. Silver and ten bolts of cloth go down to the boat as the first year's reckoning.

She needs him and he knows it, and that is the end of the talk. The looms of the mound weave for your house first from now on. Thirteen bolts go into the boat. The boy hands them down one at a time, and counts aloud, in two tongues.
The empty bench

The neighbours have come up the mound in their good cloaks. Nobody has died, so it is not a burial, and nobody knows what else to call it. The priest has the tablet with the names. Your brother's place on the bench has a folded cloak on it.
I wove that cloak for him while he was gone. It was something to do with my hands. Now it is done, and it fits a man who is not here, and I find I cannot cut it down for anyone else.
You took our silver and gave your word. I do not ask for the silver. I ask you to remember that there were three of us who heard you, and that we are still here.
The law does not know what to do with a man who is neither here nor dead. His share cannot lie idle. You are his brother. It comes to you, unless you say otherwise before these people.
The boy lives. Remember that when you choose. A Svea's boy on a far river is still his father's son, and might one day walk up this mound with a beard and ask whose store that is.
Take your brother's share of the mound, as the law gives it
Leave the land to Frethburg; take her weaving for the house
Give your share to Saint Boniface's church, for a Mass for the two of them every year

The neighbours witness it without a word, and it is yours: a strip of the mound, a share of the creek, room for a store. The kin count out what the land owes you in silver and cloth. Frethburg hands you the folded cloak with the rest. 'It goes with the share,' she says. It fits.

You say it before them all: the land stays where the loom is. Somebody's grandmother says 'well', which on this coast is a speech. Frethburg's cloth comes to your house first from now on. Fourteen bolts are in the boat by evening, and the cloak stays on the bench.

The priest writes it on the tablet under the forty-three names: a share of the mound to Saint Paul and Saint Boniface, and a Mass each year on the day of the raid. The neighbours bring cloth down to the boat, a bolt from one house, two from another, until you stop them. On every landing of this coast you will be the church's man now.
The boats from the Eider

There is smoke from every mound along the creek. The boats came at Lammas: thirty-one people of the forty-three on the priest's tablet, thin, and counted off the gunwale by a Dane with a tally stick. He is still here. He has a bag of weighed silver for the names that could not be found, and two of those names are yours.
Thirty-one. I read the names and they answered. I have said Mass for a good many years and never had the dead answer before. They were not dead, but I had begun to read them that way.

Thirty-one in the boats, and my two walked in by another road, because you fetched them. The Dane has silver for them all the same. Take it. Somebody should be paid for this year, and it had better be us.
Every mound on this creek got somebody back, and I have one of my two. I stood on the bank and counted the boats in with the rest. I was glad for them. I want that known, since I did not look it.
Thirty-one came up the creek and neither was mine. I baked for the ones who came. It is what there was to do. They ate it all.
Two names sold out of the kingdom before the oath. The king makes good the price, and the same again, because he is a new king. Whether you have found them since is not my reckoning.

The king heard how the names came to be read. He says a Frisian who can make twenty-four great men listen should sell his cloth at Sliesthorp and pay no man for the leave. I have his mark here, if you want it.
Take the silver for your two names, and the Danish king's peace for your boat at Sliesthorp
Take the silver, and your brother as a sworn partner in a second boat
Have the silver shared among the mounds that got nobody back
Take what is counted out for your two names, and nothing else

He counts the silver onto your thwart and cuts a stick with a mark you have seen once before, on the Eider. 'Show that at the jetty. You pay nothing there while this king lives, and I would not wager on the next.' The mounds send cloth down after him. The people of the creek have started calling you the one who speaks.

Your brother watches the Dane count the silver and says that it is the first time he has seen his own price paid in the right direction. You swear it at the church door: one purse, two boats. The islands have already decided who speaks for them at the count's court, and did not think to ask you.

The priest reads the twelve names that did not answer, and the silver is weighed out mound by mound. By evening there are sixteen bolts of cloth in your boat that you did not ask for, and the creek's whole people on the bank. When the count next wants a man to speak for the islands, they will send you.

You take the two prices and the cloth Frethburg presses on you, and leave the rest of the bag where it is. The Dane shrugs, and goes home on the ebb. But a thing done before twenty-four great men cannot be undone on a creek bank, and the islands call you their spokesman from that day.

Two hundred ships of the Danes were on the Frisian islands. The Frisians stood three times and then paid a hundred pounds of silver. People were carried off alive. The king is building ships and buying nobody back.
The peace is sworn on the Eider, twelve great men of the Franks and twelve of the Danes, on their weapons. The river is the border. Nothing was said of the people taken from the islands.

The peace is sworn on the Eider, and with it a new thing: the Danish king gives back the islands' people still in his kingdom by Lammas and pays the price of those sold out of it. A Frisian merchant brought the names.
A man of the islands and his son are home, one fetched from a Verdun merchant's rope at Mainz and one from a Svea's farm at Birka, by the same Frisian boat. Nobody on the coast has heard the like.
A Frisian taken from the islands is home, fetched off the road to Spain by his own brother. His son is still in the east with the Svear.
A boy taken from the islands is home from Birka, fetched by his father's brother. The father was sold south past Mainz and has not been heard of.
The mounds by Doccinga have held a day for those taken by the Danes and not come back. Forty-three names were read at Saint Boniface's church.
Boats came from the Eider at Lammas with thirty-one of the islands' people, given back under the peace, and silver for the rest. The mounds by Doccinga are smoking again.
The king has sent farmers home to the Frisians and paid for the ones he could not find. The dealers do not like it. A Frisian sells cloth on the jetty under the king's own mark.

A Frisian landing on a grey summer evening, the tide out: a thin man with a rag-bound burned hand stands asking at a boat's side; behind him a Frankish rider waters a tired horse; smoke far off over the flats.

A dwelling mound in the salt marsh under a wide white sky after rain: burned byre posts in front, a low turf house behind; in its doorway a woman at an upright loom with a red and white band on it; a tonsured priest in a seal-skin cloak writing on a wax tablet.

Sliesthorp, a wattle-fenced yard behind the booths at noon, autumn: people sitting under a lean-to roof by a water trough; in front a stout Dane with a plaited beard and a hazel switch, notched sticks hanging on a peg; a wide-faced Wend in a fur-edged cap at the gate.

A wet spring meadow by a brown river, low cloud: two lines of twelve cloaked men facing each other with swords and spears held upright, horses behind each line; in the crowd in front, a young Frankish clerk holding a strip of parchment.

The Rhine at the Ruhr's mouth on a windy afternoon: a broad flat ferry at a muddy landing where a rutted road comes down from the east; the ferryman, grey and thickset, leaning on his pole and making the sign of the cross to show what he saw.

Mainz, a walled yard in hard midday light: twelve men sitting along a wall with one rope through their belts; one has a broken front tooth and looks away; in front a well-dressed merchant with open hands and an older steward with keys and a staff.

The same yard at Mainz, empty and swept, late-autumn rain: an iron ring in the wall with nothing tied to it; the steward in the gateway under his hood; beyond the gate a carrier loading wine casks on mules.

A farm on a rocky hill above Birka's bay, bright early-summer morning, birches: a boy of eleven with cropped hair and a herding stick among sheep on spread fishing nets, a red and white woven belt at his waist; a spare Svea trader pointing; the farmer with folded arms.

The same farm above Birka, shut, on a still grey day at summer's end: a barred door, an empty boat shed with the rollers lying in the grass; the Svea trader holding a folding scale; far out on the water one small sail going east.

The mound at Doccinga on a clear evening: a new byre of driftwood, a man with a broken tooth on its roof laying turf, a boy handing turves up and a dog watching him; in the house doorway a woman with four wooden bowls.

The house door on the mound, low morning sun: a man mending a net on the bench without looking at his hands, his eyes on the sea; on a shelf above him one small wooden bowl; a woman in the dark of the doorway.
A creek bank below the mound, a windy bright day: a boy cutting reed with a man's knife too big for his hand; his mother on the slope above with a bundle of wool; the priest beside her looking south.

Inside the turf house, daylight from the door and the smoke hole: neighbours in their good cloaks standing along the walls; a bench with a folded new cloak on it and nobody sitting; the priest holding a wax tablet; a woman with her hands still.

The creek at Doccinga at high water on a warm Lammas evening: smoke rising from every mound to the horizon; two long Danish boats at the bank, thin people being helped ashore; a Dane with a tally stick and a leather bag in front, the priest reading from his tablet.
The first tribute
The reeve has a table set up on the strand and a list of hides. Ipswich has been plundered, the ealdorman is dead at Maldon, and the king's council has agreed to pay the fleet ten thousand pounds.
Ten thousand pounds. I have done the sum three ways. It comes to so much on every hide, and the hides that were burnt pay the same as the hides that were not.
The archbishop gave the counsel. I do not say he was wrong. The ealdorman gave them spears instead, the day after Saint Laurence, and the monks of Ely buried what the ships left of him.
Ninety-three ships. I counted to forty and then they were in the street. They took my man off the fulling floor with his hands still wet.
They do not keep the people. They sell them over the water, where the duke's town is. If you go that way, he is called Leofric, and he limps on the left.
You hold no hide here and owe nothing. I only say that a boat which paid when it need not is a boat I will know again.
Put forty pennies toward the town's share, though no hide here is yours
Buy the chalice the minster must sell to find its share (150 d)
Pay nothing, and ask where the ships took their people
He counts the forty twice and cuts your mark on the town's stick, among men who were born here. It will go to the ships with the rest. He says your toll can wait a while.
The priest wraps it in a sack himself and does not look at you. It is good work, and it cost you less than the silver in it. There will be more of this for sale, every year they come.
You pay nothing. By evening you know what everyone knows: the ealdorman is dead, the king will pay, and the people the ships took are sold at Rouen.
Sold at Rouen
On the duke's quay a man of the fleet is selling eleven people on a rope and a heap of English cloth. Their speech is the speech of Ipswich.
Fifty each for the men, less for the women, nothing off for the lot. The cloth is good. The cross is silver right through; I bit it.
Leofric. A fuller, from the street by the river. I limp, but I can tread cloth all day. Tell the buyer that. I would sooner go to a man who wants cloth trodden.
The duke takes his toll on what is sold on his quay. He does not ask where a thing was before it was on his quay. Nobody could run a harbour that way.
Yes, there was a bishop from Rome here before Lent, and oaths. The duke will not shelter the English king's enemies. These men are not sheltering. They are selling, and then they go.
Buy the fuller and the two women free and carry them home (150 d)
Tell the duke's man what was sworn in this town on the first day of March
Buy the cloth and the altar cross, and ask no one whose they were (80 d)
Look, remember the faces, and walk on

A hundred and fifty pennies for three. The dealer cuts the rope with the same knife he eats with. The fuller sits down in your boat and treads the bottom boards all the way down the Seine, from habit.
You say it loudly, in front of a canon. The duke's man goes red, then goes away, then comes back with three people and no bill. He says the duke keeps his oaths. He does not say which eight are left.
He hears you out and asks whether you are a bishop. Then he asks what you carry and whether the toll on it is paid. The dealer spits near your shoe. The rope goes up the hill.
Six bolts of good English broadcloth and a silver cross with a saint's name scratched on the foot. Eighty pennies. It is the best bargain on the quay and you do not feel clever.
You look at each face long enough to know it again, and walk on. There is nothing here that a merchant is obliged to do. You notice that you have told yourself so.
The song of the fight
Ipswich has new thatch on half its houses. In the alehouse a grey man is singing how the ealdorman stood at the causeway, and the mass-priest is waiting for him to finish so he can ask you for money.
Three men could hold that causeway, and three did. Then the ealdorman gave them leave to cross and fight on firm ground. I was there. I have made it sound better than it looked.
He is home. He trod cloth yesterday for the first time and fell asleep standing. The street has put something together for you. Do not say no to it; they have little else to be proud of.
No word of mine. The priest says to pray, and the reeve says to pay, and I do both. If you pass Rouen again, he limps on the left.
There is talk that our altar cross was seen on a Frisian boat at Rouen. I do not ask. I say only that Saint Mildred's name is scratched under the foot, if anyone should look.
They will come again and the king will pay again, and the minster has sold what it can lift. Lend us a hundred pennies. I cannot name the day. I can name you at the altar.
Take what the fullers' street has gathered for you
Lend the minster a hundred pennies against its next tribute, with no day named
Buy the singer his ale and hear the song to the end

A hundred pennies in a stocking, most of them clipped, and eight bolts of their own cloth, fulled twice. The reeve says your boat pays half at his table until he is told otherwise, and he is seldom told anything.
The priest writes it on the flyleaf of the gospel book, which is where this minster keeps what matters. He reads it back to you in Latin, slowly, and you find you follow most of it.

It takes the whole evening. The old retainer says his heart must be the harder as his strength grows less, and the room goes quiet. A clerk writes it out for you after. It ends in the middle, as the fight did.
London holds

There are scorch marks on the river wall and a burnt longship on the mud below it. London held. The fleet has gone round to Southampton for the winter, and the king has agreed to feed it and pay it sixteen thousand pounds.
The Nativity of Saint Mary. Ninety-four ships and two kings in them. They tried the wall and then they tried fire. We gave them more harm than they thought any townsmen could.
So we won, and now we pay. I have asked three men to explain it and each of them told me to lower my voice.
They are to be fed out of all Wessex until spring, and they eat like men who did not grow it. I need flour and ale at Southampton, and I need it in boats they will not burn.
You are the boat that paid on a stick three years ago with no hide to pay for. It is written down. Not much that is written down in my hall is to anyone's credit.
A foreign keel is the thing. They have sworn peace to every merchant ship in a river mouth. I would rather try that oath with your boat than with one of ours.
Take the king's load on trust: ten sacks of flour and six casks of ale for the fleet at Southampton
Lay sixty pennies on the reeve's table toward London's share
Sell what you came to sell, and ask only what an army with silver is short of

Ten sacks and six casks come down to you on Londoners' backs, counted by a clerk. It is the king's food until it is in a Northman's hands. The reeve says the price is paid at the other end, for a whole load.
Sixty pennies on the table. The reeve looks at them and then at you, and has your boat moved up to the good end of the hythe. The toll man is told something behind his hand.

The lighterman tells you for nothing. Drink, he says. Ninety-four crews with a king's ransom and the ale at Southampton ran out at Michaelmas. Wine too, if you have it. They have stopped asking what things cost.
The winter camp
Ninety-four ships lie drawn up along the Itchen under tilts. Their crews have been paid in new pennies, and Southampton has nothing left that a man could want to buy.
Look at it. A sack of little kings, all the same king. I cannot eat them and there is no woman here will take them. Have you anything in that boat? Anything.

Olaf has gone inland to the English king, with their hostages in our ships to keep him safe. They put a bishop's hands on him. He has promised not to come back as an enemy. He means it, which surprised us.
Toke, Asgot's son, of Hedeby. I do not row for them. I came behind them with a boat of whetstones and combs, and I have sold the lot, and the boat.
They have sworn peace to every merchant ship in an English river. Think what that is worth. A man could live here. I have looked at London twice now, once from the wrong side of the wall.
I have heard of you. The Frisian who loads what a paid fleet buys. There are two of us, then. It is not a trade a man boasts of on either shore.
Hand over the king's flour and ale whole, and take the king's price
Give the fleet first pick of your hold, and take a purse for it on top of the price
Sell nothing yet. Sit by the Hedeby man's fire and learn how he talks to them

The king's reeve at Southampton counts ten sacks and six casks and seems surprised by the number. A hundred and sixty pennies. The Northmen offered you three times that on the way up the river, and he knows it.

They go through your hold like heirs through a dead man's chest. A purse of two hundred and twenty on top of whatever the market gives you. On the bank an English reeve's clerk is writing something down.

By midnight you can ask a price in his tongue, refuse one, and insult a steersman without being killed for it. He says wine at Hedeby will be dear all next year: these men are going home thirsty and rich.
A ship going home heavy
A longship comes down on you under a striped sail, deep in the water for her kind. She does not shorten sail and she does not take her shields off the rail. Somebody aboard is singing.
Merchant! Hold your course, we are not working today. We have been paid. I never thought I would shout that across water.
There is a peace sworn for boats like yours. I was there; I could not tell you all of it. Something about river mouths. This is not a river mouth, but I am in a good temper.
What we have not got is anything to drink. Sixty men, a chest of English silver, and a water cask. Name a price. No, do not; we will name it. You will like ours better.
Close and pass a cask of ale across; let them name its price
Heave to and ask where they will spend it
Bear away. A sworn peace is a long way from here
The cask goes over on a line. A hat comes back with seventy pennies in it, all with the same king's head, and the hat. They are singing again before you have your sail drawing.
Hedeby, says the steersman, all of it, by Yule. Wine first, then silk for his wife so that she will forgive the wine. He waves. Sixty men wave. It is an odd thing to see from that kind of ship.
You bear away and she lets you. Somebody aboard shouts something that makes the rest laugh. Your men pull as if they had not heard it.

She is alongside in the time it takes to say a Paternoster. The steersman is hurt that you ran. He takes twenty pennies as a pilot's fee for showing you how a ship should be sailed, and gives you back your painter.
Pennies in the north

At Hedeby a fisherman pays for a knife with King Aethelred's head. Men home from England are buying everything twice, and by the south jetty an Englishman is striking pennies for the king of the Danes.
Asgot. I have sold here forty years by weight. Now boys come home with sacks of coin and pay what is asked. Everything is dear and nobody is richer, except the ones who sell drink.
You are the Frisian from the winter camp. My son speaks of you. He has gone back to England with a new boat, to live there. Among the people who paid. I told him what I thought of that.
I have a son in England. Not with the ships. Selling combs, in London, to the people the ships robbed. If you lie there, ask for Toke by the hythe, and tell me if he is fat.
It is King Aethelred's penny with King Swein's name. Same cross, same weight, near enough. He wanted a coin like the ones he was paid in. I cut dies. It is not for me to say it is strange.
I had a bench at home and a king who changes the coin every six winters and fines you if the weight is off. Here nobody has ever seen a fine. I do miss the ale.
Take Asgot's order: eight casks of Rhenish wine before the next winter, at his price
Sell into the silver: let the men home from England bid against each other
Weigh one of the new Danish pennies against an English one, and say what you find

Eight casks of Rhine wine, before the ice. He names a price near double the market's and seems to think he has cheated you. He has not bought by the cask before. His son told him it was how it is done now.

You say a price for a joke and a boy with a new sword pays it. By noon you have a hundred and sixty pennies more than your goods were worth. Asgot watches from his door and says nothing a merchant could argue with.

They balance, near enough. The moneyer is pleased somebody checked. He says cloth is what he would bring here: every man home from England wants a cloak cut the English way, to show where he has been.
The house by the hythe
At Billingsgate the toll is called out by the size of the ship. Behind the hythe a Dane has built a house in the English manner, with a storehouse he cannot fill alone and a wife who keeps the tally.
Small boat, a halfpenny. A boat with a sail, a penny. A keel, four. The emperor's men trade as the Londoners do, and you are one, I am told. Rouen pays more, and they complain in better wine.
The winter camp! You sat at my fire and I had sold my boat. Look: a house. A wife. She is English and so is the roof. Come in before the reeve counts you twice.
You are the Frisian they talk of on the hythe. Toke, Asgot's son. I came here behind a fleet and stayed for the peace. Come in. My wife says a guest who stands in the door lets the heat out.
You saw my father? Did he ask if I was fat? Tell him yes. Tell him the English feed a man well when he pays the toll and goes to church, and that I do both.
He cannot read the reeve's stick, so I do. He cannot hear when a Londoner is cheating him, so I do that too. He says I am his best bargain. He has not seen what my brothers think of it.
The store is too big for me. Take a share. Or stand for me before the reeve: a foreigner needs a man to answer for him, and a Dane needs one more than most. Or only eat.
Go shares in his storehouse (120 d), and take his first order
Stand surety for him before the reeve: your name beside a Dane's on the stick
Pay your toll, eat at his table, and keep your name off other men's sticks

A hundred and twenty pennies and your hand on it. Leofflaed cuts a tally in three parts, one for herself. Toke orders ten casks of Frankish wine on the spot, at a price she corrects downward, and still a good one.

The reeve cuts your mark beside Toke's and looks at you a moment longer than he need. It costs nothing unless Toke runs. Toke sends his own lighter to bring your goods ashore, and the toll man looks at lighters less.
You pay your toll and eat his pork. He is a little hurt and too well mannered to show it for long. The children speak English to their mother and Danish to the dog.
Who deals with Danes
The reeve is going from keel to keel with a clerk and a wax board. He is not asking what you carry. He is asking who you sell to, and what tongue they answer in.
Pallig had the king's land, the king's gold and the king's hand on it. This summer he took every ship he could gather and went over to the army. Now tell me again how well you know your Dane.
Twenty-four thousand pounds this time. I carried London's part of it down to the ships myself. They weighed it. They always weigh it. I should like, once, to be the one holding the scale.
It used to be they cursed the ships. Now they curse the Dane three doors down who sells them combs. I pour for both. I would be gone before the dark evenings, if I were three doors down.
The king has a new lady from over the water. The duke's daughter, from Rouen, where our people are sold. They say it is to shut that harbour to the ships. I say she is young and it rains here.
My children were christened in that church. I pay the toll, and the tribute too, on this house, to keep off my own cousins. What more does a man do to belong to a place? I ask you honestly.
And you. You sold to them. It is on a board somewhere; I have seen it. I do not say it was against any law. I say I have seen the board.
Vouch for Toke: he pays his toll, hears Mass and has children baptised here
Say little to the reeve, and tell Toke to sell up and be over the sea before winter
Give the reeve the names of the Danes you deal with, and take what he pays for them
Say you sell wine, and everyone who has a mouth buys it
The reeve listens to the end. He has the clerk smooth the wax where Toke's name was, not all the way. He says a man with a surety is a man he need not think about this month.
The reeve listens to the end, and then has the clerk write your name under Toke's. He says Pallig had sureties too, and better ones. Toke grips your arm afterwards and cannot find the English for it.

He laughs, and then he does not. He will not go: the house, the wife, the peace he was sworn. But he sends his silver and his eldest boy to his father at Hedeby, and has a boat kept ready by the hythe.
You give him six names. He knew four. He pays sixty pennies for the other two and tells the toll man to go easy on you. Toke's is one of the four, you tell yourself, which is true.
The reeve says that is what the last Frisian said, and the one before him. He moves on to the next keel. The clerk writes something. With a wax board you cannot tell how much.
The king's writ
Two days after Martinmas is Saint Brice's mass-day. A priest who writes for the reeve comes aboard after dark, will not sit, and tells you what the king's writ says is to be done on it.
I wrote the copies myself, so I am not guessing. On Saint Brice's mass-day, all the Danish men who are in England. Every reeve has it. I am a priest and I am telling a Frisian, God forgive me.
The king has been told they mean to kill him and then his council and take the kingdom. Told by whom, the writ does not say. It says weeds among the wheat. It is well written.
There is a woman in the reeve's guest house with a boy. Pallig's wife. The king of the Danes' own sister, held for her husband's oath, and he broke it. Nobody has said she is to be spared.
You told me before winter. I said the peace was sworn. The boat is by the hythe, as you said to keep it, and it is too small. Yours is not. I am asking.
The priest came to me first. I have a wife they will not touch and sons they will. I know the man on the guest-house door; he drinks my ale. I have no boat that can cross in November. You have.
The reeve has a list. Some of it is in your hand, or near enough. I thought you should hear the writ from someone before you heard the bells.
Go with Toke to the reeve's guest house, bring out the king of the Danes' sister and her boy, and drop down river on the ebb
Take Toke and his sons aboard under the tilt and sail before the bell for prime
Keep your men aboard, your hatch shut, and your boat where she lies

The door-ward takes Toke's purse and finds he needs to visit the privy. A tall woman walks out with a boy by the hand as if she had ordered the boat. You are past the bridge before the tide turns, and an outlaw in England by morning.

A different man is on the door tonight. He has a club, and then friends. It costs you a hundred and twenty pennies and a cut scalp to be only a drunk Frisian at the wrong house. You get Toke and his boys down river. The door stays shut.

Toke and the boys lie under the tilt among the casks. Leofflaed stands on the hythe with the youngest and does not wave, because a wave is seen. You are off Thanet when the bells begin, too far to hear them.

You double the lines and keep the men aboard. Two days later the bells ring for the mass of a bishop of Tours, and there is running in the lanes, and then less. Nobody comes near your boat. You are the emperor's man.
Brice's morrow
There are goods laid out on the hythe with nobody standing behind them: sea chests, a balance, cloaks, a child's shoes. The reeve is selling them for the king. Nobody is bidding much.
The king's goods, by forfeit. I am told to sell them. I did what the writ said and no more than it said, and I will thank you not to look at me as the priest does.

Word from Oxford. The Danes there broke into Saint Frideswide's and barred the doors, thinking a church would hold. The town burned it over them. Church, books and all. The king will have to build it again.
He is over the sea, then. Do not tell me where; I am asked every day. I have the house and the youngest, and brothers who have remembered I am English. I keep the tally. There is nothing on it.
They took him at the hythe, with the boat ready and too small. He said the peace was sworn. He said it in English, so they would understand. That is his balance, on the cloth there.
They are in a pit beyond the wall. I have asked the bishop whether baptised men may lie so. He has not answered, and I do not think he is going to.
Bid for the lot: ivory, cloth and brooches at a hundred pennies
Buy nothing. Give the priest thirty pennies for graves and Masses, whoever they are for
Buy nothing, say nothing, and carry the news where it is not yet known

Two pair of walrus tusks, six bolts of cloth and three pair of brooches of Jutland work, for a hundred pennies. The reeve is glad to see them gone. One of the brooches has a name cut on the back in runes.
Thirty pennies. The priest says it will buy a corner of churchyard and a month of Masses, and that he will not write down for whom, and that God reads without a list.
You load what you came for. On every quay from here to the Rhine they will ask if it is true, and you will say yes, and they will ask how many, and you will say that nobody counted.
What the silver bought

At Hedeby they are tarring hulls in the cold, which nobody does without a reason. The king's ships go to England after the lambing. Old Asgot has a table laid in his house by the south jetty, and a reckoning to make with you.

The king goes himself this time. Before, he went for silver. Now he has a reason he can say aloud at a feast. The English king has given him that for nothing, after paying so much for everything else.
My son is in the next room, complaining about the ale. You brought him in November, in that. I have counted what I owe you several ways and it comes out more than I have.
My son went to live among the people who paid. I told him what I thought. I was right, which is no use to me. His silver came home. He put my name on the bag, in English letters.
I had a house there. I have a wife there. When the ships go I will not be in them. But when England has one king over both shores, and it will, I am going home to Billingsgate. Come in with me.
A man showed me a brooch you sold. It has a name on the back that I cut myself. I am not accusing. I am telling you that things bought on that hythe can be read here.
Twelve winters you have sold where our silver went. I do not blame a merchant for the weather. Let us settle. I am old and I would rather owe God than a Frisian.
Swear fellowship with Toke: one purse, two boats, and his father's store at Hedeby for both
Buy the ship Asgot had built with English pennies, for what the timber cost him (300 d)
Take your reckoning in pennies, and the strip of ground beside his jetty

You and Toke lay hands on one purse before witnesses. Seven hundred pennies go into it from Asgot's chest as his son's share. Toke takes your old boat. The old man keeps the store and the key, and counts in his sleep.

She was to be Toke's. Sixty feet, oak from up the Slie, a hold a man can stand in. Three hundred pennies, which is the timber and not the work. Asgot says a ship should not lie on a slip waiting for the dead.

Nine hundred pennies, every one with the English king's head, and a strip beside the jetty marked with four pegs. In London a reeve has your name on a board. Asgot says boards burn, and that he has seen London tried.
An empty hythe

Billingsgate has room at it, which it never had. The Danish keels did not come this year. The reeve stands at the head of the hythe with his stick and counts the boats that did, and yours is one of them.
No whetstones. No ivory. No tar; I have a bridge that wants tar. The king was told the Danes meant him harm. Nobody told him who brought the tar.
Swein is coming, with everything. It is said his sister was among them. I do not know. I know he would come for less. We paid three times so that he would not, and then we did this.
You paid when you owed nothing, or carried, or lent, or bought our people back. It is written in three hands on three boards, and for once I have been told to read them all.
Your name is under a Dane's on one of my boards. I have rubbed it thin. I have not rubbed it out. A reeve who rubs things out is asked what else he has rubbed.
The storehouse stands. Your mark is on the door post beside his, and nobody has dared take the door. I can keep a tally for two houses as well as for one. Better; there is less talk at table.
I need keels. The king needs toll. London needs wine before Lent. You are the emperor's man, and nobody has a writ against Frisians. Ask for something while I am still frightened enough to grant it.
Ask the king's writ: your house to trade here as the Londoners do, free of the toll at this hythe
Take what the reeve offers the man who gave him names: a dead Dane's toft behind the hythe
Keep the share in Toke's storehouse, with Leofflaed to hold the key and the tally for both houses
Ask nothing of the king. Carry what the Danish keels used to carry, and learn the river from the lightermen

A strip of parchment with a seal on a tongue of it: the king greets his reeve and his bishop kindly, and your house trades at Billingsgate as a Londoner. Eight hundred pennies come with it, part of them a minster's debt, paid by the king.

Six hundred pennies, and a toft with a house on it in the English manner, built by a Dane. The hearth is still laid. The neighbours watch you take the key and go indoors. Somebody has cut a mark on the door post and somebody has tried to plane it off.

Leofflaed sells off the stock nobody will come for and counts seven hundred pennies across to you, to the farthing. She keeps the key. She says a widow's house or a wife's, it is a storehouse either way, and wine does not ask.

The reeve pays six hundred pennies ahead for freight and orders twelve casks before you can sit. An old lighterman takes you up to the bridge and down to the Nore at low water, and shows you every shoal the Danish pilots knew.
The king's sister
A man of the king's household is waiting on the jetty with twelve others and a led horse. He looks first at the woman and the boy coming up your gangplank, counts them, and only then looks at you.
Two. We had word of the writ a week ago, from a ship that left before it. The king had already said what he would do about his sister. Now he will have to think of something else to say.
I was a hostage four years and nobody was unkind. Then one evening the woman who brought my bread would not look at me. I knew before the Frisian knocked. I had the boy's shoes on already.
My husband broke his oath and I was the pledge for it. By their law they had a claim on me. I will say that to my brother. He will not want to hear it, so it must be said first.
My wife is on the other shore with our youngest. She is English; they will not touch her. I say that every hour. When there is one king over both shores I am going home. Until then I can sail a boat.
The king goes to England after the lambing. He was going in any case; they pay too well. But he goes for silver and not for blood, and men who are paid go home. Remember that you did that.
The king does not owe merchants. He has told me to say that, and then to ask what you want, and to give it. He would like it to be something he can give before the ships sail.
Ask to be the king's guest: his protection on your house, and your keels free of toll at Hedeby
Ask for a ship of the king's own building, and Toke to sail your old one beside her
Ask only that when his ships go to England they keep what was sworn in 994: peace for a merchant keel in a river mouth

Fifteen hundred pennies, weighed, not counted. A rune stick with the king's mark that every toll man from the Slie to the Limfjord can read: this house is the king's guest, and its keels pay nothing at Hedeby. No English reeve will ever read it kindly.

A thousand pennies and a ship off the king's own slip, sixty feet, new sail, never launched in anger. Toke takes your old boat and swears fellowship on her stem. He names her for his wife, in English.

The king's man is silent a while, then says it will be told to every steersman. Eight hundred pennies and the king's guest-right come anyway. Gunhild takes a gold ring off her hand, the one they did not take in four years, and says it is for your daughter's daughter.

This year was Ipswich plundered; and very soon afterwards was Alderman Britnoth slain at Maldon. The king's council has agreed to pay the fleet ten thousand pounds, on the archbishop's counsel. It is the first time. Every hide pays.

People taken at Ipswich are sold on the duke's quay at Rouen, a few months after the duke swore before the pope's bishop to shelter none of the English king's enemies. The duke's toll is paid on them.

This year came Anlaf and Sweyne to London, on the Nativity of St. Mary, with four and ninety ships. The townsmen drove them off. The army winters at Southampton, fed out of Wessex, and is paid sixteen thousand pounds.

The king of the Danes is striking pennies with his own name, copied from the English king's and cut by an English moneyer. They weigh the same. At Hedeby a man may now pay by count, if the seller is young.

At Billingsgate in London the toll goes by the ship: a small boat a halfpenny, a boat with a sail a penny, a keel four. The emperor's men trade there as the Londoners do. Danes have houses by the hythe.

This year the English king ordered all the Danish men who were in England to be killed on Saint Brice's mass-day, two days after Martinmas. At Oxford they were burned in a church. No Danish keel lies at Billingsgate.

A grey strand below a half-burnt town, late summer, low cloud: a reeve at a trestle table with tally sticks and a small heap of pennies; a woman in a fuller's apron beside him, pointing out to sea; charred roof timbers behind.

The stone quay at Rouen under a square church tower, bright cold morning: eleven men and women tied on one rope, a heap of folded cloth with a small silver cross on top, a bearded seller with an arm ring, a well-dressed Norman steward looking away.

Inside an alehouse by firelight, evening: a grey-haired man with a scarred hand sings with his eyes shut, a small harp on his knee; listeners on benches; a priest waiting by the door post; new pale thatch seen through the door.

The river wall of London at low tide, autumn sun: old Roman stone with black scorch marks, the burnt ribs of a longship on the mud, a reeve with a staff talking down to a skipper in a small boat; the timber bridge far behind.

A river bank in winter dusk, light snow: a long row of longships drawn up under tilts, cooking fires, men throwing dice for heaps of pennies; in front a young Danish trader in a good cloak by a fire, a cross and a hammer on one cord at his neck.

Open sea, fresh wind, broken sunlight: a longship under a striped sail, low in the water, shields on the rail, running down on a small merchant boat; her steersman standing with one arm raised and his mouth open, shouting; men laughing behind him.

The south jetty at Hedeby inside its earth wall, clear noon: an old Danish merchant in his doorway with folded arms; in front a moneyer at a block with hammer and die, one bright penny held up between finger and thumb; young men with new swords crowding a stall.

The hythe at Billingsgate, a busy morning: keels and small boats nosed to a timber wharf, a reeve calling the toll with his stick raised; behind, a new timber house with an open storehouse door, a Dane in it with a child on his arm and his English wife holding a tally.

The hythe on a dull wet afternoon: the reeve leaning over a boat's side, a clerk at his shoulder writing on a wax board; an alewife watching from her door with a jug; in the background a Danish merchant standing very still among his bales.

The deck of a small boat at night under a tilt, one horn lantern: a priest standing bent under the canvas, speaking; the skipper seated on a cask; in the gap of the tilt a Dane's face lit from below; dark river and a few lights of London behind.

The hythe on a still grey November morning: goods laid out on cloths with nobody behind them, a sea chest, a folding balance, cloaks, a pair of child's shoes; the reeve standing over them with his stick; a woman at the edge, hands wrapped in her apron.

Hedeby in winter, hard frost, smoke going straight up: men tarring longship hulls on the shore; in front a table laid in an open doorway, an old merchant at it with a bag of pennies and a balance, an empty stool across from him.

Billingsgate in spring, thin sun: a long timber wharf with only three boats where thirty lay; the reeve alone at its head with his stick; mooring posts in a row, each with nothing tied to it; the bridge and the wall behind.

The jetty at Hedeby, cold bright morning: a tall woman in a travelling cloak walking up a gangplank holding a small boy by the hand; a king's man with twelve armed men and a led horse waiting; the skipper behind her, still in sea clothes.
A leather bag of English pennies spilled on a table, every one showing the same king's head, with a Danish folding balance beside them.
A row of empty mooring posts along a wharf at low water, one small Frisian boat tied to the last.
A woman's hand and a child's hand together on a ship's rail, a gold ring on the woman's finger, grey sea behind.
Two monks and forty books

Two monks stand among the merchants who are making up a convoy for Birka. They have the emperor's gifts for the king of the Svear in sealed chests, and more books than most men here have seen in one place.
God keep you, shipmaster. I am Anskar, a monk of Corvey. They tell me you know this water, and that you do not charge a monk double. One of those may be true.
Men of the Svear came to the emperor and said their people would hear priests, and their king would allow it. So the emperor looked for someone to send. Nobody else stood up.
I am Witmar. I keep the books. Thirty-nine. Brother Anskar says nearly forty. He counts souls the same way.
The emperor's gifts and the book chests go in the big ship; she has the room. We two weigh little and eat less. It is Lent with us most of the year.
The merchants sail together when the wind serves. Will you take two of us aboard? We can pay a fare, and I am told I row badly but willingly.
Take the two monks aboard and sail in the convoy
Sail in the convoy, and let another hull carry them
Wish them a fair wind and go about your trade
Witmar counts the fare into your hand twice. Anskar comes aboard barefoot, sits where he is told and asks the name of every rope. The chests go into the big ship, and he watches them go.
A Dane with a broader hull takes the monks. You are one sail among the rest. Anskar lifts a hand to you across the water each morning, as if you had agreed to something.
He thanks you as though you had said yes. The convoy is still gathering. The book chests sit on the jetty under a hide with Witmar on top of them.
Sails out of the haze

Half-way, with land low to one side, the lookout counts sails coming out of the haze that are not the convoy's. They are long, low and under oars as well. The big ship with the monks' chests is the slowest hull among you.
Seven. No, nine. They have their masts down and they are rowing at us. Nobody rows at a stranger to ask the price of salt.
The merchants are shouting from hull to hull. They mean to close up round the big ship and fight. There are a good many of them, and they have done it before.
The books are in that ship. I ask nothing of you that you would not do for your own cargo. I only tell you where they are.
There is a beach under that low point, an hour off. And there is open water astern. Say which, while saying still counts for something.
Close up on the big ship and fight beside the merchants
Lay alongside her, take off one chest and run for the beach
Leave the convoy and run while they are busy with it

They come on twice. The first time the merchants beat them off, and the second time also, which nobody had looked for. By evening the long ships are hull down. The chests have not left the big ship. Witmar counts the books anyway.

The first attack is beaten off. The second is not. The merchants lose the ships and all that was in them and wade ashore with their lives. The emperor's gifts go north in a stranger's hull, and the books with them. Anskar says they will go on by land.

You touch the big ship long enough for two men to swing one chest across, and then you are away for the beach. Behind you the fight is lost. On the sand Witmar opens the chest: six books, a psalter on top. He says six is a number too.

A long ship is alongside her before you are. An oar is broken, a man is hurt, and what you had in the stern locker is gone with a boathook. You reach the beach with nothing of theirs. The monks walk up it after you, wet to the chest.

You put the helm over and the wind takes you clear. Nobody follows a small boat when a big one is to be had. That night the crew are quiet. Word comes later: the merchants lost everything, and the monks went on to Birka on foot.
The king asks his friends

The king of the Svear is on the island, and the prefect of the town has brought the two Frankish monks before him. The king has heard them. Now he looks along the bench at the merchants who came by the same road.
I am Herigar. I keep this town for the king. The Franks' king has sent ours a sword-belt, cups and a whole chest of calfskin. The king likes the belt. He is thinking about the calfskin.
I am Herigar. I keep this town for the king. Two envoys have walked in from the south with an emperor's greeting and no gifts. Such a man is a beggar or a brave one. The king wants to know which.
They say one small boat got clear of that convoy with her cargo whole. It is a good boat that knows when to leave. I say nothing against her master.
We lost what we were given to bring. We were not sent to bring cups. Tell him that, if he asks you. He will not believe it from me.
Six books, shipmaster. You have never seen Brother Witmar happy, so I tell you: that was it.
I am Bjorn. I have heard them. I will ask my friends what they think, and the men who trade in the south, who have seen this god at home. Then I will say whether these two may talk here.
You are of Dorstadt. Our men go there. Some come back with a new god and some with a cough. What do you say of it, in a few words? The king dislikes many.
Set a cask of your wine before the king, in the emperor's name
Say what you know: Dorestat trades under this god and does not starve
Leave kings and monks to each other and ask the price of cloth

The king has the cask broached where he sits. He drinks, and has Anskar drink from the same cup, and says an emperor who sends this may send his talkers too. Herigar tells you quietly that your ship will not be looked at hard this summer.

You say it in a few words. The king nods at the number of ships you name, not at the god. He gives the monks leave to stay and to speak, to those who want to hear. Herigar wants to hear, it turns out.
Herigar laughs and tells you: the good coloured cloth is short this year, and the women of the town know it. The king gives the monks leave without your help. He had mostly decided.
Calfskin with marks on it
A dealer has amber laid out on a square of pale skin with black marks in rows. Behind him, under a hide, lies a heap of the same: books with the boards torn off.
Good skin, scraped thin. It keeps the damp off amber. The marks do no harm. I had a man look, and he said they are not runes, so nobody is cursed.
They came with boards on, and some of the boards had bronze on them. The men who brought them kept the bronze. That is all I know of the men who brought them.
Eleven are whole inside. The rest got wet and stuck together like a bad cheese. I sell those by the leaf, for wrapping.
For the heap, silver to the weight of ninety pennies. You look at it as if it were worth more. If it is, you had better not say so until you have paid.
Buy the heap for 90 d, to carry back to the monks
Buy the heap for 90 d, and sell the best book in Francia
Tell him who would pay for them, and keep your silver

He weighs your silver and helps you carry the heap down in two hides. He throws in the leaf the amber sat on. Aboard, you find a name written small inside one of them, and a count in another hand: thirty-nine.

He weighs your silver and helps you carry the heap down. One gospel book is sound from end to end, and an abbot will pay a herd of calves for it. The rest you stow dry all the same. It seems wrong to wrap fish in it.

You tell him: a monk called Anskar, among the Danes or at Hammaburg, and he pays in silver for what the sea took. The dealer covers the heap again and moves it in from the door. He does not thank you, but he gives you a piece of amber for the walk back.
A church on Herigar's land
On the prefect's own ground behind the town stands a small new house of upright timbers with a cross cut over the door. Herigar is counting what it lacks. The Frankish monk is packing to go home.
I went into the water this spring and came out Herigar still, only wetter. This is my father's land. Nobody can tell me what I may build on it. Several have tried.
It lacks wine. The monks say their god will not be met in ale. Four casks of the Rhine sort, before the lake shuts next year. I pay over the market, since there is no market.
Two winters, shipmaster. I go home with a letter from the king, cut in his own marks by his own hand. Nobody at the emperor's court can read it. I can tell them what it says.
They tell me you have a heap of wet calfskin aboard that you paid too much for. Brother Witmar has not slept since he heard.
I was a boy on Lindisfarne when the ships came. I have tallied furs here for thirty winters. I can still say the psalms. I had forgotten that I could until that monk began one and stopped.
His master would let him go for the price of two thralls, since he is old and only reads. The monk has spent his silver on boys. He looked at me. I looked at you.
Take his order for Mass wine and nothing more
Lay the books without boards on the altar step
Give the monk passage south with the king's letter
Buy the Englishman free for 96 d and give him a place aboard
Herigar strikes your hand on it before witnesses: four casks, before the ice, at half as much again as wine fetches here. He says a church is like a ship. The hull is the cheap part.

Witmar goes through the heap on his knees and says the names of the books aloud like a man finding his children. Eleven whole. Anskar has Herigar weigh you two hundred pennies of silver and will not hear of less. Witmar teaches you the letters of your own name while he counts.

Anskar comes aboard with one sack and a flat stick wrapped in cloth. At sea he unwraps it and shows you the king's marks, and tells you what each one says, and you find you remember some. The fare is paid at parting, with a blessing you did not ask for.

His master takes the silver and the Englishman takes nothing with him but a stick he holds like a pen. Aboard he reads your tallies, finds two mistakes, both in your favour, and tells you so. He says his name is Tidwine. He has to think first.
No priest at Birka
The church behind the town is shut and its door is nailed. The prefect still wears his cross outside his cloak. An old woman in a good gown has sent to ask whether your ship carries wine.
They rose in a crowd. They killed the bishop's nephew Nithard in the house, bound the bishop and put him and his people out of the land. Then they went home and felt better for a week.
It was not the king's doing. Remember that. Here a crowd can do what a king cannot, and afterwards nobody did it.
I still speak at the thing. Last time it rained on all of them and not on me and my boy. They said it was the wind. It was a very narrow wind.
Your house brought the wine for the first Mass said on my land. I do not forget who came when it was easy. Now it is not easy.
I am Frideburg. I am old and there is no priest. I want a cask of wine to keep by me. When I am dying they are to put some in my mouth and commend me to God. I have told my daughter twice.

The bishop will not come back, and I do not blame him. But there is the other one, Anskar, among the Danes. Somebody must tell him there are Christians here who will die unshriven. I cannot leave the town.
Sell Frideburg a cask to keep for her last hour
Promise to carry Herigar's word to the archbishop
Say a trader has no part in a town's gods

She has the cask carried to her house and set on a shelf where she can see it from her chair. She pays without bargaining, which nobody in Birka has done before, and tells you she intends to keep you waiting for news of it.
Herigar gives you no letter, since nobody here can write one. He gives you a small silver cross from his own neck to show, and the words to say. You are to say them the same way each time.
Herigar says that is a trader's answer and he has given it himself, about other men's troubles. He sees to your berth as fairly as before. He does not ask you to eat.
The book on the fence

On the road up from the jetties a book hangs on a fence, tied with a cord, in the weather. People walk on the far side of the road. A grey man stands at his door across the yard and watches who stops.
My son brought it home when they broke up the bishop's house. Everyone took something. He took that. It had a clasp, and he thought his mother would like the clasp.
His mother is dead. He is dead. My daughter is dead. The cattle went after. I had a good farm two winters ago, and you can see what I have.
I asked a man who knows such things which god I had angered. He asked them all. Every one was content with me but one, and that one I had never met. He said something of that god's was under my roof.
So it hangs there. Anyone may have it. I have said so to everyone who passes. If you take it I will give you silver to carry it far. I do not sell it. Understand me. I do not sell it.
Untie it and carry it to the Christians of the town
Untie it and put it in your own chest to sell in Francia
Walk on the far side of the road like everyone else

The cord is stiff with rain. He puts cut silver in your hand before you have it loose and goes in and shuts his door. In Frideburg's house a man who can read a little reads it aloud to the rest, slowly, a psalm an evening. He shows you where the words begin.
He pays you to take it, and you take it further than he thinks. It is a psalter, hardly spoiled. The crew find out what is in the chest by the second day and steer as if the boat were made of eggs.
You go by on the far side. The grey man watches you all the way down the road. The book turns a little on its cord in the wind off the lake.
Thirty-two ships in the sound

Ships fill the sound: twenty-one of the Danes and eleven that belong to a king the Svear put out. The king who rules is far away. The townspeople have gone up to the fort on the rock, and the merchants are told what peace will cost.
King Anound was driven out of this land and has come to see it again. He has brought friends who were promised a rich town. He can ask them to leave it standing. They will want to know why.
A hundred pounds of silver. That is the why. The town has not got it. The merchants in harbour have, between them, and they are in harbour. You see how it stands.

Up at the fort they are killing beasts to every god they can name. I told them: you have vowed and given to those for years, and here are thirty-two ships. Vow to mine for once. They laughed. The Danes have not left, I notice.
Your share is small. You may pay it and be thanked. Or you may stand by me when I say it again to their faces, and be laughed at with me. I do not advise a third thing.
Weigh in your share with the merchants: 60 d
Stand by Herigar when he tells them to vow to Christ instead
Slip the mooring after dark and go out by the narrow sound

The silver goes out to the ships in sacks. The Danes say it is too little: any one merchant here has more. Then they throw lots, as they do, and their gods will not let them touch the place. Another lot sends them off against a town of the Slavs, a long way east. Herigar notes who paid.

They laugh at the two of you. Then, because nothing else has worked, the townsmen vow a fast and alms to Herigar's god. The Danes cast lots on whether to sack the town, and the lot says no. They cast again, and it sends them east against the Slavs. Nobody laughs at Herigar that week.

No moon, and the narrow sound is all rocks, but your men find it. By first light you are in open water with the hold whole. You hear later that the town paid, and the lots sent the Danes elsewhere. Nobody at Birka remarks on who was missing.

A guard boat lies across the narrow sound. They take what silver is to hand, crack a man's ribs with an oar and send you back to your berth. Herigar says nothing about it. He had advised against a third thing.
A hermit for Birka

By the new church at the harbour a greying bishop in a plain cloak is asking the shipmasters which of them goes to the lake of the Svear. Beside him stands a thin man with a sack, who looks at the ships as a man looks at a tooth-drawer.

Nearly seven years Birka has had no priest. There are Christians there who were baptised by my hand, and they are growing old. I cannot go myself this year. King Horik has only just let me have a roof here.
Herigar's cross reached me, and his words. You said them the way he told you to. I could hear him in it. It is why this man is standing here with his sack.

Some of the books the sea took came back. A dealer sent word that he had heard I pay. I bought my own psalter from him, and I think he had sold it to me once before. Nearly forty. Witmar always said thirty-nine.
You still have those books without boards? Then keep them dry as far as Birka. They were on their way there when they were stopped. It has only taken them twenty years.
I am Ardgar. I lived alone in a cell and was content. The bishop says God wants me in a town full of fur dealers. I have asked God about it and so far only the bishop has answered.
He needs a place in a ship, and a master who will see him ashore at Birka and into Herigar's hands. He eats almost nothing. He will tell you so himself, more than once.
Carry the hermit to Birka and take no fare
Carry him for the fare
Tell him your hull is full this voyage

The bishop does not press the fare on you twice. He marks you down somewhere behind his eyes instead. Ardgar comes aboard, finds the least comfortable place in the boat by himself and seems easier there.
The bishop counts out the fare in the new pennies of this place. Ardgar comes aboard, finds the least comfortable place in the boat by himself and seems easier there.
The bishop thanks you and turns to the next master along the jetty. A Dane takes the hermit two days later. You hear he was seasick as far as the islands and prayed the rest of the way.
The archbishop wants a ship
The archbishop is going to Birka himself, twenty days by sea, at past fifty. With him are a young priest and a man of King Horik's who carries the king's token in a bag round his neck.
Herigar is dead. He had the sacrament from Ardgar's hand at the last, and Frideburg after him, and then Ardgar came home to his cell. So Birka has no priest again and no Herigar. I am going myself.
He died with a priest beside him because a ship carried one there. I have not forgotten whose ship.
King Horik sends his own man with me, and his token, to King Olaf. He bids the man say he has never in his life seen so good a man as I am. I told him kings should be careful what they swear to.
I am Erimbert. Bishop Gautbert is my uncle. He was bound and put out of Birka, and my cousin Nithard was killed there. My uncle says it is not fitting that he go back. So he has sent me.
The last time I went I trusted to a convoy and a great many merchants. This time I would rather have one master who knows where the beaches are.
Twenty days, if the wind is kind. Three of us and what a church needs. Will you take us? I row no better than I did.
Take the archbishop, the priest and the king's man aboard
Take them, and buy a small bell for Birka at your own cost
Sail in company and carry only their stores
Say you are not bound that way yet

The king's man sits in the bow with his hand on the bag at his neck. The young priest is sick over the lee side with great patience. The archbishop asks the name of every rope, and this time remembers them.

A founder in the town has a hand bell of bronze he made for a Frisian who never came back for it. You pay him and wrap it in sheepskin so it will not speak at sea. The archbishop looks at the bundle and then at you, and says the heathen think such a thing unlawful. He does not say leave it.
They take passage in a bigger hull, and you carry their meal, their wax and their altar cloths, and keep her in sight. The archbishop lifts a hand to you across the water each morning.
He says he will be here some days yet, since King Horik's man is still taking leave of his wife. The young priest looks relieved at any delay at all.
A new god, or King Eric

Birka is talking of one thing. A man has stood up and said he sat at the gods' own meeting, and brings their word. The archbishop's friends tell him to buy his life and go. He has asked the king to eat with him instead.
You have heard what the man said. He was at the meeting of the gods who own this land. They say: we gave you peace and good years for a long time, and now you grudge us our due.
And they say: if you must have more gods, and we are not enough, we will take Eric who was your king into our number. He can be your new god. At least he knows the way here.
My friends here tell me to give the king all I brought, as the price of leaving alive. I have given it to him as a gift at his meat instead. It is the same silver. It reads differently.
I am Olaf. I liked your meal and I like your Danish king's word of you. But priests were here before, and the people drove them out. Not the king. The people.
So I will ask the gods by lot whether they allow it. Then I will ask the people at the thing. That is our custom. Here such things rest with the whole people and not with the king.
You are of Dorstadt, and the people will look at you when it comes to talking. They trust a man who sells them cloth above a man who sells them heaven. Which way will you talk?
Tell the king's men what the cross is worth on the Dorestat road
Drink with the men who want King Eric among the gods
Ask the king what a stranger may keep on his own plot

You tell them plainly: at Dorestat a baptised Svea eats with the merchants and a heathen one eats with his crew, and prices are made where the merchants eat. They follow that better than the archbishop's sermon. He does not seem to mind.

They are good company and they pour well. King Eric was a fair judge of a horse, they say, and will make a sensible god. Before the night is out one of them has offered you marten skins at a price for friends. The archbishop sees who you sat with.

The king thinks about it. A man's plot is his own, he says, inside his fence, so long as he pays his due for it. Herigar built on his, and nobody could stop him. Whether a stranger may have such a plot is for the thing. He looks at you with more interest than before.
The lot in the open field

The king and his chiefs have gone out to the open field, as the custom is. An old man shakes cut slips of wood in his two hands over a white cloth. The question has been said aloud: do the gods allow the Christians' worship here.
Stand back from the cloth. All of you. The gods can see over your heads, but I cannot.
Whatever falls, falls. I will carry it to the people as it lies, and I will not be asked to throw twice because some man dislikes it.
I have fasted three days over this. Now it comes down to how an old man opens his hands. I do not complain. The apostles drew lots for the twelfth of their number.
I have thrown for kings and for a man who had lost a pig. The slips do not know the difference. People always ask me whether they do.
Stand among the merchants and watch it fall
Vow alms for the poor of Dorestat, aloud, whichever way it falls
Send the thrower 80 d beforehand, to see the slips fall kindly
Send him 80 d to let it fall against the stranger god

The slips lie on the cloth. The old man bends, looks a long while, and stands up with his hand on his back. The gods allow it, he says. The king lets out his breath. The matter goes to the thing in two days.

The slips lie on the cloth. The old man bends, looks a long while, and stands up with his hand on his back. The gods do not allow it, he says. Nobody speaks. The archbishop bows to the king as if he had been handed a cup.

You say it aloud, with the amount, and the merchants turn to look. The thrower says the gods of this field take no interest in the poor of Dorestat, but that it was handsomely said. Your crew stand a little straighter. Then he opens his hands.

The old man took your silver the night before without a word and throws today without a glance at you. The gods allow it, he says. You will never know what you bought. He is the only man in the field who looks entirely at ease.

The old man took your silver the night before. Today he lays it on the white cloth beside the slips, in front of the king, and says a stranger tried to help the gods make up their minds. Then he throws. The gods do not allow it. The king does not look at you at all.

The old man took your silver the night before without a word. The gods do not allow it, he says. Your friends of the other evening are careful not to smile. The archbishop bows to the king as if he had been handed a cup.
The old man took your silver the night before without a word. The gods allow it, he says, and looks straight at you while he says it. He keeps the silver. There is nobody you can complain to.
The old man at the thing

The king's crier has said it before the whole people: the lot allows the Christians' worship, and the king asks what they will have. The shouting goes on a long time. Then an old man gets up, and they let him speak because of his years.
Hear me, king and people. Many of us know this god. He helps those who hope in him. More than one man here has called on him in danger at sea, and is here to be shouted at.
Some of us went to Dorstadt and took up this worship there of our own will, because we saw it was of use. We sailed a long way to get it.

Now the way there is beset with pirates, and a man may lose his ship going. Why then do we refuse at our own door what we went so far to find? If our own gods are slow, it is good to have this one's favour as well.
You have heard the lot and you have heard him. Is there a man here who has been where he speaks of, and will say whether it is so?
The thrower wears a new arm-ring today. I do not ask where a poor old man finds silver. I only say I would rather have lost honestly, and I think you know it.
Stand up after him: you are of Dorestat, and it is as he says
Lay the book and the bell before them, and say what your house has carried
Ask the thing for the church on your own plot, as Herigar had his
Stand up and count out what the last priests cost this town

You say it in few words: there are churches at Dorestat and ships at Dorestat, and the one has not sunk the other. The people shout their yes. The king gives a hall of his own to be the church, and the archbishop buys a plot beside it for the priest. Its storehouse has room for your goods.

You lay the book on the ground before them, and the bell on the book. You say where each has been, and who was carried, and who stood where. Then you ring it once. The heathen hold a bell unlawful. Nobody moves to stop it. The king says he will hear that sound again, and the people shout their yes.

You ask for no new law. A plot inside a fence, held of the king for the common due, and a priest kept on it at your cost, for any trader who wants him. The thing likes it: no hall of the king's, no bishop's man answering to no one. The traders who go south pay in furs for their share. The archbishop thanks you carefully.

You count it out for them on your fingers: a bishop's nephew dead in the house, a farm emptied over one book, a hundred pounds of silver to thirty-two ships. The old man calls you a seller of both sides. The people shout their no. Your friends bring furs to the jetty after dark. The archbishop goes home in another ship.
The gods say no

The slips fell against it, in front of every chief. The king has sent the archbishop a ring and a courteous word, and the word is no. An old man of the town has come down to the jetty and is angry with all of you.
I cannot carry to the people a thing the gods have refused. I told him so before I threw. He is a good man, and my brother the Danish king was right about him. He must go home.
And tell the Frisian that at this market we weigh silver in the open, on a scale, where both sides can see the pans.
I was robbed coming here the first time and came on. This time nobody has robbed me. I have only been told no, politely. I find that I do not know what to do with it.
Slips of wood! I have called on that god in a gale off the Danish islands and I am standing here. I would have said so at the thing, if there were to be a thing.
Herigar asked no lot. He built on his own land and let them talk. The gods were asked about the whole town. Nobody has asked them about one man's fence.
Carry the archbishop home, and say nothing clever on the way
Ask the king to throw once more, on a smaller question: a stranger's own plot
Bring the old man before the chiefs, lot or no lot
Take the thanks of the men who wanted it so

Twenty days back. He is silent for the first three, and then asks the names of the ropes again, to be sure. At Sliesthorp he weighs you the silver that was meant for a priest's house, since no priest will need it, and says that whoever touches you or your goods in his see touches him.

The king does not throw twice on one question. This is another question, he says, and a small one, and has the old man shake the slips again. A stranger may keep his own god inside his own fence. The traders who go south pay in furs for their share of it. The archbishop sails home with half of what he came for, and it is in your name.

The king hears you out and says he told everyone beforehand that he would not be asked to throw twice. He is not angry. He is finished. The archbishop goes home, and on parting weighs you the silver meant for a priest's house and takes you under his hand, because you tried.

The old man does not ask leave. He walks in among the chiefs and tells them about the gale, and the islands, and who he called on. Then he asks which of them wants to tell the seamen of Birka that they may not thank the god who brought them home. The king puts it to the thing after all. The people shout their yes.

The chiefs hear the old man with respect and do not change their minds. The gods were asked, and answered. The king is short with you for pressing it. The archbishop goes home, and on parting weighs you the silver meant for a priest's house and takes you under his hand, because you tried.

They come down to the jetty after dark with sable, which they do not sell to strangers, and the word that a plot by the stone jetties is yours when you want it. The archbishop sails in another hull. He does not look across.
