This year the Svear asked their gods and their people, and both said that the priests might stay. Erimbert kept the church at Birka. The archbishop went home in the same ship. After his death no priest came for seventy years.

This year the Svear asked their gods and their people, and both said that the priests might stay. A bell was rung at Birka before the whole thing, and the king had it hung. When the archbishop died the church on the island did not shut, for the traders had come to tell the hours by it.

This year the Svear would have no bishop's church, but let a Frisian keep a priest on his own plot at Birka for any trader who wanted one. The archbishop called it half a loaf. It was still there when he was dead, since it belonged to a house and not to a see.

This year the Svear sent the archbishop home and took their dead king Eric among their gods. No priest came to Birka again in that age. A Frisian house had a plot by the stone jetties there, and bishops on the Rhine knew its name.

This year the lot fell against the Christians at Birka, and the archbishop went home in a Frisian's boat. The Svear took their dead king Eric among their gods. The archbishop did not send again, but he kept his hand over the house that carried him.
At Birka the lot and the thing have both allowed the Christians' worship. The king of the Svear has given a hall for a church, and a Frankish priest stays there.
A bell has been rung before the thing at Birka and the king of the Svear has had it hung in the new church. Men who go to Dorstadt say the lake is a Christian's road now.
The Svear would have no bishop's church at Birka, but a Frisian keeps a priest on his own plot there, and any trader may hear Mass inside his fence.
The Svear have sent the archbishop home from Birka. They say their dead king Eric sits among the gods now, and that they had gods enough.

A spring morning at a timber jetty, hulls being loaded for the north. Two young tonsured monks in black habits: one thin and barefoot, talking to a shipmaster; the other sitting on a stack of iron-bound chests under a hide, counting on his fingers.

Open sea in thin haze, a low shore to one side. A huddle of merchant ships round one big slow hull; out of the haze long low ships under oars with their masts lowered. In the near boat a monk stands, looking at the big ship.

A dim hall on Birka by firelight. A king on the high seat with a cup; before him two travel-worn monks with mud to the knee; a broad man with keys and a staff standing between them and a bench of merchants. All eyes on one Frisian on the bench.

A beach market under a grey sky. A dealer squats behind a square of written parchment spread with lumps of amber; behind him a hide half pulled back from a heap of books with their boards torn away, the leaves cockled by water.

Summer on Birka, behind the town. A small new church of upright split timbers with a cross cut over the door; a heavy man counting on his fingers at the doorway; a monk tying a sack; an old thrall in a rope collar holding a stick like a pen.

The same small church years on, weathered, its door nailed shut with a plank. A grey-bearded man with a silver cross worn openly stands before it in the rain, dry. At a house door behind, an upright old woman in oval brooches and beads.

A muddy road up from the jetties on a wet, windy day. A book with a clasp hangs by a cord from a wattle fence; passers-by keep to the far side; across an empty yard a grey man watches from the door of a house with no smoke.

Evening over the sound at Birka: the water crowded with thirty ships, shields along their sides. On the stone jetty a line of merchants weighing sacks of silver on folding scales; above the town, the fort on its rock, with fires and people on the rampart.

The harbour at Sliesthorp on a bright day, a new plank church by the water. A greying bishop in a plain cloak speaks to shipmasters on the jetty; beside him a gaunt hermit with one sack eyes the boats with dread.

A small boat being stowed at Sliesthorp in early summer. The old archbishop steps aboard with a hand from a sailor; a pale young priest waits behind; a Danish king's man with a bag at his neck; in the hold, a bell wrapped in sheepskin.

A feast in a hall on Birka at night. The archbishop serves the king of the Svear at his own table, gifts laid out between the dishes; down the benches chiefs lean together and mutter; one of them is looking at a Frisian merchant, a horn held out.

An open field outside the town under a high pale sky. A ring of chiefs and a king stand back from a white cloth on the grass; an old man holds cut slips of wood in his cupped hands above it; the archbishop apart, head bowed.

The thing at Birka at midday: a great crowd on a slope, the king on a stone, a crier beside him. One very old man is on his feet with an arm raised, speaking; the crowd has gone quiet. At the edge, the archbishop and a Frisian merchant.

The stone jetty at Birka on a grey morning. The archbishop sits on a sea chest with a gold ring in his open hand, looking at it; a king's man walks away up the jetty; an old townsman shakes his stick at a moored Frisian boat.
A bad hour
The wind has backed and the sea comes over the quarter faster than two men can bail. The steersman and the hand each say what a man does now, and they do not say the same thing.
The worst first. She will not take much more of this.
Now what can be done. Promise Saint Martin a candle as long as her keel, and say it aloud so the men hear it.
Saint Martin's house is a long way off, and no road to it from here. The sea is here. It is in the boat with us. Promise it a share of what it lets you keep. My people do, and I am still above it.
He means his devils.
I mean whoever is listening. Somebody is. Somebody always is. Only say something, and say it now. A man who bargains gets a better price than a man who begs.
Vow Saint Martin a candle the length of her keel
Vow the sea a share of what it lets you keep
Promise nobody anything, and bail

You shout it into the wind: a candle the length of her keel, to Saint Martin at Traiectum. The steersman crosses himself with his free hand. Toward morning the wind goes round, and she is still afloat.
You say it to the water: a share of whatever comes safe to land. The hand pours the last of the ale over the side and says nothing. Toward morning the wind goes round, and she is still afloat.

You promise nothing and bail until your arms give out. Toward morning the wind goes round, and she is still afloat. Neither man thanks you for it. Both of them look at the sky as if it had been owed something.
What the dune gave up
The gales have cut a slice from the dune west of the houses. A grey stone the height of a child stands half out of the sand, and a woman with sheep is looking at it as she would at a stranger's dog.
It comes out after a hard blow, and the sand has it back by midsummer. My mother saw it twice. Do not ask me who she is. Nobody here knows.
A woman sitting, with a basket of apples on her knee. A dog. Under her foot, the front of a ship. And letters, for those who have letters.
There are green coins in the sand by her, with heads on them. And three little silver ones, of the kind my grandfather was paid in. Somebody laid those there, and not so long ago.
There was another one, by the creek. The bishop broke it in my mother's mother's time. Its keeper hit him with a sword and was dead in three days. So we are Christians here.
You promised the sea a share. I have not forgotten it. Now the sea shows you where other men paid theirs.
Look, a ship under her foot. Somebody thanked her for a cargo once, and a good cargo, if it paid for a stone. He won't have been the only one who meant to.
Cut the letters on a tally stick, as they stand
Lay a penny in the sand with the others
Pick the silver out of the sand
You cut the letters into a hazel stick, stroke for stroke, without knowing one of them. The woman watches. She says the bishop's clerk does it faster and understands as little.
You press a penny into the sand beside the three. The woman says nothing. Later a boy brings a cheese down to the boat and will not say who sent it.
You sieve the sand through your fingers: three thin pennies, and a handful of black ones that scrape white. Twenty-four pennies by weight. The woman calls her sheep and goes without a word.
Whose stone
A quiet watch. The steersman and the hand have been not speaking about the stone since Walichrum, and now they are speaking about it.
It is an idol. The priests have a list of such things, stones and springs and the rest, and what is to be done with them. You tell a priest. He breaks it.

No, no. It's a tally, that's all it is. A man promised something in bad weather and paid when he came home, and he had it cut in stone so nobody could say he hadn't. I thought Frisians liked a paid debt.

East of the Lauwers there is an old law for the man who takes from a god's house. They lead him down to the sand the tide covers. I do not say it is still done. I say nobody there picks up silver beside a stone.
And we have silver aboard that was picked up beside a stone.
Here's one for the watch, and I have all of it, for once. What is owed to nobody you can see, and still falls due?
The tithe.
A vow. But yours is a good answer. A good one, mind.
The steersman is right: a priest should hear of it
The hand is right: it is a paid debt, and not ours
Tell them both to mind the sheet
The steersman nods and says no more about it. The hand goes forward and coils a rope that was coiled already.
The hand says nothing. The steersman says he will pray for the boat, and it sounds like a warning.
They both look at the sheet, which is where it should be, and then at you. The hand laughs first. The question is still aboard in the morning.
For goods kept safe
A priest of Saint Martin's has heard that a Dorestat boat lay at Walichrum when the dune opened. He has a wax tablet with him, and he asks what you saw.
You cut them as they stood? Good. Most men bring me what they think a thing says.
Our clerk was on the island for the tithe lambs and copied it. I want a second pair of eyes that were there. Was there a dog?
DEAE NEHALENNIAE OB MERCES RECTE CONSERVATAS. To the goddess Nehalennia, for goods kept safe. Then a man's name: Marcus Secundinius Silvanus, a dealer in pots with Britain.
And four letters at the foot: V, S, L, M. He paid his vow, gladly, as was due. A merchant on your own road, thanking a devil with a basket of apples.
I have not met her name in any book we have. That troubles me less than the three silver pennies. Those are not Roman. Somebody's grandfather laid them there.
Your steersman says you owe the saint a candle the length of your keel. Saint Martin is patient. He is also exact.
And I am told you promised something to the sea. To the sea. As if it kept a tally.

The blessed Willibrord broke one on that island with his own hands. This one should not stand till midsummer for fools to lay pennies at. Be there in spring. I will send a clerk. See that it is ended decently.
Pay for the candle: wax the length of her keel
Take his errand to the island, and promise no more
Thank him for the reading; you carry goods, not mattocks

The wax is weighed and paid for, and the chandler measures your keel with a knotted cord and whistles. The candle will burn at the saint's altar from his feast until it is gone. The priest orders more wax of you, since you now know the price.
You say you will be at the island in spring and will see what is done. He writes something on his tablet. Then he asks whether you carry wax, and at what price.
He looks at you for a while, and then thanks you for coming. "I shall send a clerk with a mattock. You may at least not stand in his way."
Winter's start at Hleidr
A Danish skipper who knows your hand of old is loading for the islands. His lord keeps the feast at winter's start in the hall at Hleidr, and the hall is short of drink.
So this is the Frisian. Your hand tells me you made a promise in bad weather. Everybody has. Not everybody is asked about it afterward.
My lord kills a horse at winter's start and feeds the district. The meat is boiled, the ale goes round, a share is set aside. That is all it is. Strangers make more of it than we do.
Every ninth year it is a great one, they say, and a stranger does well to be elsewhere. This is not that year.
He wants wine on the table for the ones who count. Six casks from the Rhine, here on this jetty, before the first frost. I carry them over with mine. He pays like a lord, which is late and too much.
A share promised to the sea is paid where the sea is honoured. I know of no such place in your country. Not one. I know of one in his.
Go and see it once. I would, in your place. You sell to these people, and it helps to know what they do when they're not buying.
Take the order for the wine, and the seat that goes with it
Ask to come as a guest and carry nothing
Wish his lord a good feast and say you winter at home

He spits in his palm and you strike hands on six casks. "There is a seat for the man who brings the drink. Low down, but under the roof." He adds that wine at Hleidr is worth half as much again until the feast is over.
"Then come with empty hands and a good appetite. There is a seat, low down, but under the roof." He adds, for nothing, that wine at Hleidr is worth half as much again until the feast is over.
"A man should winter where his hearth is." He does not sound offended. "The seat is kept all the same. My lord keeps more seats than he fills."
A swell with no wind
The air is still and the sea is not. A long swell comes in from the north-west under a sky the colour of a knife, and both your men have stopped what they were doing to look at you.
No wind, and a swell like that. I have seen it twice. Both times there was a man aboard who owed something.
The candle is not burned. I am the steersman. I say what I see.
You said a share. A share, that was the word. I heard you. So did it.
The sea counts slowly. It does count.
This is not the first time I have had to say it.
Put a purse over the side, now, whoever is owed
Say the vow again, aloud, with a day on it
A swell is a swell. Shorten sail and stand on
Forty pennies in a knotted cloth goes over the side and is gone without a splash you can hear. The hand breathes out. By evening the swell has flattened, and there is a small honest wind.
You say it again, aloud, and put a day on it: before four moons are out. The men go back to their work. The swell runs on under you till dark, and then it is only sea.
You shorten sail and stand on. The gale passes north of you in the night with a noise like carts on a bridge. In the morning the men are quiet and do not meet your eye.
The gale that was behind the swell finds you at dusk. It takes the water cask, a spar and most of a night. Thirty pennies will make it good. Neither man says he told you so, and both of them could.
The grey from the lord's field
The hall at Hleidr is full to the doors and smells of boiled meat and wet wool. The lord's steward finds you a place on a bench near the bottom, and a bowl is coming down the table toward you.
You are the Frisian the skipper spoke for. Sit there. Nobody here will ask what you believe. They will see what you eat.
It is the grey from the lord's own field. He was a good horse. A share has gone where shares go, and the rest is for the district.
You have wine aboard, I hear. The lord says the Rhine's is thin. He has never yet sent a cask back.
Eat or do not eat. That is yours to say, not mine. But decide before the bowl reaches you. A man who looks into the bowl and thinks is remembered longer than either.
Your steersman's stayed with the boat. He says somebody should, and he's right, mind.
Eat what the hall eats
Take bread and ale, and pass the bowl on with both hands
Thank him, and eat aboard with the steersman

It is dark meat, sweet, boiled soft. You eat it with your fingers like everybody else. The man beside you shifts along the bench to give you room, and that is all that happens. Somebody will tell it at home.
You take bread and a horn of ale and hand the bowl on with both hands. The bench laughs. An old woman across the table says the Christians fast so often it is a wonder they have the strength to row.
You eat cold bacon aboard with the steersman, who says the blessing twice. Light and noise come down from the hall half the night. In the morning a boy is sent to fetch you up to the yard.
Three slips of wood

In the morning an old man of the district sits in the yard with a white cloth on his knees and three slips of wood. He lifts one for anybody whose question can be answered yes or no. The hand has told him yours.
You promised a share in a storm, and you are not sure it was heard. That can be asked.
You promised your own god's man a candle, and you want to know whether the ones here mind. That can be asked.
You promised nobody anything and came through, and it sits badly. You want to know whether something is owed. That can be asked.
I lift one slip. It says yes or it says no. It does not say why, and neither do I.
If you are paying, the share goes into the water off the point, not into my hand. I am told the Christians do it the other way.
He is the one the lord asks before he sails. The lord himself. I have seen the lord stay home.
Give the share to the water off the point
Put the question, and watch him lift a slip
Tell him you came to sell, not to ask

Forty pennies of cut silver, weighed and knotted in cloth. You wade out off the point to the knee and let it go. The old man nods once. The hand says, in your own tongue, that it is done and well done.
He moves the slips about under the cloth and lifts one. "Yes." He puts it back with the others. That is all of it. The men are easier on the way down to the boat.
He moves the slips about under the cloth and lifts one. "No." He puts it back with the others. He will not lift a second, and he will not say what you should do about it.
"Then sell." He is not put out. "The lord's hunters are down from the woods with marten and want it gone before the snow. They will take a low price this month." It is true.
A priest hears things
The priest of Saint Martin's has a small book open on his knee and a finger in it. He has had word of you from the island, or from the north, or from your own steersman's face.
You ate horse at a heathen table. The blessed Boniface had it from the pope himself that this is unclean. Men come home from the north and think nobody saw.
You gave silver to the sea for a promise. Silver that might have fed the poor of Dorestat, of whom there is a multitude.
You laid a penny at that stone. So there are four silver ones now.
You took silver from the sand beside it. I do not grieve for a devil's purse. But the islanders say you robbed her, and they say it as Christians should not.
The book gives a term for each thing. I have added it up. Forty days on bread, salt and water, and no meat before Easter.
Or the term may be turned into alms. It is done everywhere. I do not like it, and I take it. Forty-eight pennies, to the poor, through my hand.
Take the forty days
Turn the term into alms
Say he has been told sailors' stories
Forty days of bread and salt. You trade thin and sleep badly, and the steersman keeps the fast beside you without being asked. At the end of it the priest gives you his hand.
Forty-eight pennies on his table. He counts it, writes it down, and says the poor will pray for you by name. He does not say he thinks better of you.
"Sailors' stories," you say. He closes the book on his finger and looks at you a long time. "Then I was told wrong." He does not believe it, and he cannot show otherwise.
"Sailors' stories," you say. "Your steersman came to me on Sunday," he says, "for himself, and wept for you." He closes the book. He will know your sail when he sees it.
Before midsummer
The stone stands clear to its foot. The sheep woman is there with two neighbours, and a young clerk from Traiectum with a mattock and a mule. Everybody has been waiting for somebody else to begin.
By midsummer the sand takes her back. It always has. I would let it. But nobody asks me.
The priest's word is that it is to be broken, or else signed with the cross and made honest. Whatever lies under it is the church's and the king's. He said you would know which.
I am sent to see it and say what I saw. I was not sent to lift a mattock alone among these people.
My neighbours say stand her up and leave her be. Skippers ask after her already. One from over the sea left apples.
You have paid for that night. This is not your debt now. That is the best time to decide a thing.
I was beside you that night. Whatever you do here, do it as a man who was in that storm.
Take a shovel and give her back to the sand
Set her upright on a footing of turf, facing the sea
Have the clerk cut a cross on her and bless the ground
Take the mattock

You take the shovel from a neighbour's hand and begin. After a while the women help, and then the clerk, who is young and has nothing else to do. By evening there is a hump of sand, and after the next blow not even that.
It takes six people and the mule to walk her upright onto a bed of cut turf. She faces north-west, where the weather comes from. The clerk will not touch the rope. He rides for Traiectum before dark.

The clerk cuts a cross above her head with a chisel, deep, and says the words over the ground with a bowl of salt and water. The islanders watch. One of the neighbours asks if it is a church now. He says it will be.
It takes eleven blows. The apples go first. Under the foot of the stone the sand is green, and then it rattles. The clerk goes down on his knees in it. The sheep woman has already gone.
Midsummer sand

The dune is whole again. Where the stone stood there is marram grass and a sheep track. The sheep woman has her neighbours with her, and something to say to the Dorestat man who used a shovel when he was handed a mattock.
The clerk went home with nothing to break. The Danes who call here saw nothing to ask about. We are left alone. That is all we wanted.
We have no silver to speak of. We have cloth. Fourteen bolts, from every house a share. Do not say no. They have already argued about who gave most.
And we know this water. The banks off the point have drowned better boats than yours. My brother will take you through on the ebb until you can take yourself.
If you want wool kept dry here and a true tally cut, there is a house. That we do not offer to everybody.
She will come out again after some hard blow. Not in my time, I hope. Let whoever finds her then have as much sense.
Take the cloth, and go out with her brother on the ebb
Take both, and ask for the house she spoke of
Say a shovel of sand is not a debt; take the pilot's teaching only
Fourteen bolts go aboard. For three ebbs her brother stands at your shoulder and names every bank and gut from the creek to the open sea, and makes you say them back.

Fourteen bolts go aboard, and over three ebbs her brother teaches you the banks. The house is the third from the creek, dry, with a loft. Her sister's husband will keep your wool there and cut a tally you can trust.

She looks at you as she looked at the stone. Then she sends her brother down to the boat anyway, and he teaches you the banks over three ebbs. The cloth stays. The island tells the story for years, and in it you are taller.
The stone under the altar

A chapel of turf and oak stands on the dune at Walichrum now, and the stone with a cross cut in it is the foot of its altar. At Traiectum the bishop has asked for the man who would not let it be broken and would not let it be bowed to.
The islanders already say the blessed Willibrord bled upon that stone. He did not. I have stopped correcting them.

Pope Gregory wrote to the English that a well-built shrine should be cleansed and kept, so that people come to the place they know and find God in it. You did as the pope advised, without having read him.
I wanted it broken. I was wrong, and I have said so, once.
He paid the saint his candle too, to the inch. I measured the keel myself.
Saint Martin has wine from his own slopes and a seal that toll men can read. You shall have some of each.
Take the wine, the silver and the seal
Take them, and ask for a chip of the stone for the house
Ask only that the boat be blessed

Eight casks from the church's cellar, twelve score pennies, and a strip of parchment under Saint Martin's seal that says you carry for the church. The toll man at the bank looks at the seal twice and waves you through.

The bishop sends for the flake the chisel struck off when the cross was cut. It is the size of a thumbnail, sewn in linen. "It lay under a devil and now it lies under an altar. Keep it in the house, and tell the story straight." The wine, the silver and the seal come with it.

He comes down to the bank himself and signs the boat from stem to stern with a wet branch. Then he gives you the seal anyway. "A man who asks for nothing must be given something, or he becomes hard to bear."
Apples in the sand

She stands on a footing of turf with her back to the houses. There are apples at her foot, a cheese, a string of beads, and more silver pennies than there were. A Danish ship lies off the beach, and her skipper is wading ashore with something wrapped in cloth.
They come now. English, Franks, your Danes. Nobody says a name, because nobody has one. They put a thing down and go.
The clerk came back once and counted what lay there. Then he went away again. I think he was told to count.
The lord at Hleidr has heard there is a place on the Frisian side where a seaman can pay what he promised. He finds that a civil thing in a Christian country. He asked who was behind it.
He sends a ring from his own arm, to be kept whole. And four hundred pennies by weight, and marten, because a lord's thanks should be heavy.
And he says this. Lay your goods with his, and two keels go where one went. We call it a fellowship.
The priest at Traiectum knows your name. I would not sell wax there this year.
Lay your goods with his lord's: two keels where one went
Take the ring and the partnership, as a man whose word was good
Take the ring and the lord's thanks, and keep your own keel

You strike hands over the silver, and witnesses are called up from the beach. The ring goes back to Hleidr with your thanks: a man does not take a lord's ring and his goods both, unless his word is known. The second keel sails in spring.

The skipper has asked about you along the coast. What he heard was that you paid what you promised, to the one you promised it to. "Then both," he says. The ring goes on your arm, and witnesses are called up from the beach.
You take the ring, the silver and the furs, and say your own keel is enough for one house. He is not offended. "Then show the ring at any jetty of ours. They will know whose friend you are."
Two parts to the king

Under the stone lay a pit of coin: green bronze by the basket, blackened silver, and three thin pieces of gold. It has been weighed at Traiectum before the count's man, and the weights checked twice by people who do not trust each other.
Two parts to the king, as when Liudger broke the shrines in the east. One part to Saint Martin. The finder is paid out of Saint Martin's part, not the king's. I say so in case there is doubt.
The islanders will not sell you a fleece this year. They will come round. People do, when the thing is gone and the sky has not fallen.
The bishop puts his hand over you for this. In his courts, and against other lords' men, you are Saint Martin's.
I had the face of the stone brought here before the rest was burned for lime. I looked for her name once more in our books. It is not there. Now it is nowhere.
I will row for you. I will not leave you short of a man. Do not ask me to sit near you in the next storm.
Take the finder's share and the bishop's hand
Give your share to the poor of Saint Martin's
Send half your share back to the island, for their broken dune

Two pounds and eight ounces are counted out to you by tale: six hundred and forty pennies, some so old the heads are worn to thumbs. The count's man watches every one. The king's part goes up to Noviomagus under guard.

You push the silver back across the table. The priest is silent, then sends for the bishop. You leave with no pennies, the bishop's hand over you, and Saint Martin's seal for the toll man. The poor of the church eat meat on a Sunday and are told whose it was.
You take half, and send half down the river with a man you trust, for the island, with no message. At the next shearing a boy brings a fleece to your boat at Walichrum and names a fair price.
This year the gales cut the dune at Walichrum, and a stone of the old people stood out of the sand: a woman seated, with a dog and a basket of apples. Nobody there could say who she was.
At Walichrum the sand has covered the stone again before midsummer. The bishop's clerk came home with a clean mattock.
This year a chapel was raised on the dune at Walichrum, over a stone of the old people that the bishop's clerk signed with the cross. The islanders say the blessed Willibrord bled on it.
On the dune at Walichrum a stone of the old people stands upright, and seamen of every people lay apples and pennies at it. The priests at Traiectum are not pleased, and the stone is still there.
This year a stone of the old people was broken on the dune at Walichrum, and a pit of old coin found under it. Two parts went to the king and one to Saint Martin.

A small open boat in a gale at dusk, the sail down to a rag, green water coming over the quarter. A broad Frisian at the steering oar with a wooden cross at his throat is shouting; a broad dark-bearded Northman bails with a bucket and looks at the sea, not at him.

A fresh-cut dune face on a grey morning after a gale. A weathered limestone altar stands half out of the sand: a seated woman, a basket of apples, a dog, a ship's prow under her foot, worn letters below. A woman in a dark hood with sheep behind her looks at it; small coins lie in the sand.

The boat under easy sail on a calm evening, low sun. The steersman at the oar and the hand on a thwart are turned toward each other, the one pointing aft toward land already out of sight, the other holding up a notched tally stick.

The porch of a timber church at Traiectum in thin autumn light. A tonsured priest in a dark tunic holds a notched hazel stick close to his eyes in one hand and a wax tablet in the other; the merchant waits, cap in hand; the river and a moored boat behind.

A plank jetty on the river at Ripa under a wide pale sky. A heavy Danish skipper in a blue cloak sits on a cask with his hand out to strike a bargain; the grey-haired hand stands beside him with folded arms; beads and combs on a stall behind, a ship loading.

A windless afternoon at sea under a hard steel-grey sky. The sail hangs slack while a long oily swell lifts the boat. The steersman and the hand have both stopped work and are looking straight at the viewer.

Inside a great timber hall at night, seen from a low bench by the door: a long fire, smoke under the roof, crowded tables, a wooden bowl of dark boiled meat being handed down the table toward the viewer. A steward with a staff stands near; far off at the high seat a lord drinks from a glass cup.

A fenced yard beside the hall on a cold bright morning, frost on the grass. An old man in a grey cloak sits on a stool with a white cloth over his knees and three small slips of wood on it, one lifted between finger and thumb. The fjord lies behind, with a low point running out into it.

A bare room by the church at Traiectum, lit by one small window. The priest sits with a small book open on his knee and one finger in it, looking up without expression. The merchant stands. A balance and a few pennies lie on the table between them.

The dune in early summer, larks up, the sea pale behind. The stone stands clear to its foot in a scoop of sand. Around it, apart from one another: the sheep woman and two neighbours with a wooden shovel, a young tonsured clerk holding a mattock beside a mule, and the grey-haired hand with his thumbs in his belt.

The same dune at midsummer, whole again, marram grass and a sheep track where the stone stood. In front, bolts of grey-blue cloth stacked on the sand by the beached boat; the sheep woman with her arms folded; behind her a man points out over the banks, where the ebb shows brown water.

A hall of the bishop's house at Traiectum. An old bishop in a white alb and dark cloak, with a plain curled staff, holds out a strip of parchment with a wax seal hanging from it; the priest stands a step behind; wine casks are being rolled past the open door toward the river.

The stone upright on a bed of turf at the top of the beach, facing a bright windy sea. Apples, a cheese, a string of beads and small coins lie at its foot. A Danish ship lies off; her skipper wades ashore holding up a silver arm-ring; the sheep woman watches from the side.

A table in a storeroom at Traiectum by lamp and daylight. Heaps of green bronze coin, a smaller heap of black silver, three gold pieces set apart; a balance; the count's man in a good cloak with his hand flat on the largest heap; the priest holding a broken piece of carved stone with part of a basket of apples on it.
Three for the Apostles
A widow, her mass-priest and a girl wait above the tide line with staffs and bundles. They want a keel to Cwantawic, and the priest keeps his back to the road.
We are three for the thresholds of the Apostles: myself, my mass-priest and the girl. We want a keel to Cwantawic. After that we have feet.
My husband is three winters dead and the sea has my son. I have prayed for them in every church in Kent. There is one church left that I have not tried.
We came up to the Strand to find a ship. In Kent every keel is counted out and counted in, and I did not care to be counted.
Two skippers have said no since Sunday. One looked at the reeve's house before he said it.
God keep your boat, shipman. I can pull an oar, if that changes the reckoning.
Take them for a fare: ten pennies a head
Take them for nothing but a prayer at the tomb
You are not bound that way: hear their road and wish them a keel
The widow counts thirty pennies into your hand without haggling. The girl is sick before the boat is off the shingle. The priest sits in the bow and watches the shore until there is none.
The widow says your name over twice so as to have it right when she gets there. The crew find room. The priest sits in the bow and watches the shore until there is none.

They mean to walk from the Canche to Rome before the snow shuts the mountain. The widow says the ports of Kent are watched for people who leave without the king's leave, and looks at her priest when she says it. You hear later that a Frank took them over on the next tide.
A priest who pulls an oar
Mid-channel the wind drops. The widow's priest takes an oar unasked and pulls it like a man raised to it. When the bread goes round, the widow serves him before herself.
He is a priest right enough. He says the hours under his breath and gets them right, which is more than our own priest did at Gyrwe.
But a lady does not hand her mass-priest the bread first. She did it without thinking. People only do that for one kind of man.
My father thought a boy should know a boat, a horse and a psalter. I kept two of the three.
He is my priest. That is what he is on this boat.
Ask him straight who he is
Say nothing and watch what the widow does
Leave him be and ask the widow about her road

A priest, he says. Then, since there is water all round: a priest whose father's father sat in the king's seat at Canterbury, before Kent had a Mercian for its king. King Offa would like him nearer to hand. He asks you to have forgotten it by the Canche.
When the coast of Kent goes under the sea's edge the widow bows her head to him, not to the shore, and he lets her. Your lookout sees it too. Whatever the man is, Kent used to bow to it.
The widow sleeps. The priest pulls his oar. The girl is sick again. You learn nothing, which is what they paid for.

Eleven weeks' walking, she has been told, if nothing goes wrong: Saint-Riquier, Saint-Denis, the long plain, then the mountain of Jove, which is crossed before the snow or not until after it. Then Pavia, where everything is for sale, and Rome. By Saint Peter's there is a street of English with a church of their own. You can die there among people who understand what you say.
A priest without a letter
At the toll house on the Canche the clerk waves the widow and the girl through without looking up: pilgrims pay nothing. Then he looks up, and asks the priest for his bishop's letter.
Pilgrims for Rome pay no toll, at this house or any bridge or ferry in the kingdom. That is old King Pippin's law. I did not make it.
But a priest away from his own church carries his bishop's letter, or nobody is to take him in. That is the present king's law. I did not make that either.
And since the two kings wrote to each other I am to open pilgrims' bundles as well, for cloaks. Your people have made my mornings longer.
You brought them over, Frisian. Do you speak for him?
The man who brought them put them on the bank and went out on the same tide. So nobody speaks for him. Unless you do; I saw her greet you.
I had a letter. It went into the water at the beach, with one of my shoes.
My bishop is King Offa's man. He would have written me a letter, and it would have been to the king's hall at Tamworth.
He is my mass-priest and says the office for my dead. I answer for him. Write my name down, if you want a name.
Swear that he is the widow's priest and no trader
Lay fifteen pennies on his table for the trouble of not writing
It is not your business: let him write the name down

The clerk takes your oath the way he would take it for your own goods, and puts his stylus down. He says a skipper who swears for strangers ought at least to have his cargo looked at kindly, and tells the toll man so.
The clerk hears the oath out and writes all the same: a priest of Kent, no letter, sworn for by a Frisian. He reads it back to you. He says it is nothing. The abbot only likes his tablets full.
The clerk looks at the fifteen pennies and then at the ceiling. He smooths the wax with his thumb. He says three pilgrims passed, he thinks, or it may have been two.

The clerk writes: a priest of Kent, no letter. He asks the name and the priest gives it: Eadberht. The tablets go to the abbot at the month's end, and the abbot is the English king's friend. The priest watches the stylus as if it were being used on him.
The saint's guests

A league down the bank the cell of Saint Josse takes in whoever comes over the sea. Pilgrims sit along the south wall with their staffs. The widow counts her silver twice, and it is the same both times.
King Charles gave this house to my master Alcuin so that pilgrims should be fed. He did not give a mule with it. I mention it because everybody asks.

A company leaves on Monday for Saint-Riquier and Saint-Denis. With a mule she keeps up with it and is over the mountain before the snow. On foot she winters on this side, and people who winter on this side mostly go home.
Martin, the abbot's own priest, lies sick in our guest hall this autumn. We are short of everything but patience, and I am watching the patience.
They say our saint's hair still grows in his coffin, and that his keepers cut it. I keep the guests. Nobody has handed me the shears.
I have enough to reach Rome, or enough to come back from it. I had not reckoned what a mule costs among the Franks.
Lend her sixty pennies for a mule, to be settled when she comes back
Give the cell twelve pennies for the pilgrims' pot
Wish her a dry road: the monks will see to her

The widow takes the sixty pennies and cuts a tally for them herself, badly. She says she will pay you in whatever Rome sells that Kent does not. The guest-master says he has seen that promise kept about one time in two, and that the other time is not the pilgrim's fault.

The guest-master puts the twelve pennies in the pot box and says the house pays its debts in what it has. What it has is a riddle of Bishop Aldhelm's about a tower that shows ships their road. He says there is such a tower a day north of here, and it has been dark longer than anyone has been alive.

The widow thanks you for the crossing and goes in to supper. The guest-master walks you to the fence. If you come this way again, he says, bring wax: the saint's lights eat it and the house will pay over the common price until Martinmas.
Half a penny
At dusk the priest walks you back along the bank. He is going no further than the Frankish king's hall, he says: Rome will wait for him. He holds out half of a cut penny.
This is a penny of King Ecgberht, the last king Kent had of its own. You will not have seen many. A man at Dofras has the other half.
His name is Heahstan and he buys wine for a thegn's hall. Put it in his hand and say: the priest is over the water. Nothing else. He will know how much that is.
You know what I am. So you know why it cannot go by a Kentish boat.
I am a priest. I was born something else as well, and King Offa remembers which. That is as much as is good for you.
My name is on that clerk's wax now, and wax travels. So it must go soon.
Take the half penny
Take it, and ask what a king's kinsman pays a ferryman
Give it back: you carry goods, not kingdoms
The half penny weighs nothing. He closes your hand over it with both of his, the way a priest does with something else, and walks back toward the cell without looking round.

He gives you twenty pennies, which by the look of his purse is most of them. When Kent has a king again, he says, your keel will pay nothing between the two Forelands. He has nothing else to promise with, and says so.
He closes his hand on it. Then you carried a widow's priest over the sea, he says, and that is all you did. He does not seem angry. He seems to be counting who is left to ask.
Two men on the shingle
At Dofras a steward is buying wine on the shingle and taking his time over it. Twenty paces off the king's reeve is asking each skipper whom he carried over this summer.
The king wishes to know who leaves Kent without his leave. Priests above all. I only ask the question. I am a Kentish man myself, as people keep reminding me.
There is silver for a true answer. The king's silver, not mine. I would not spend mine on it.
A tablet came over from the Franks' toll house with a Kentish priest on it and a Frisian keel beside him. No letter, it says. I thought you might help me read it.
I buy for a hall that used to drink with kings and now drinks with whoever calls. Show me what you have, Frisian. Slowly; I am old.
Bargain with the steward over wine you have not got, and pass the half penny with the handshake
Tell the reeve whom you carried, and show him the half penny
Do neither: the half penny goes over the side at the first deep water

You say the words into the handshake. Heahstan's face does nothing at all. He pays forty pennies in front of everyone for two casks of Frankish wine that you are to bring him before the winter, and complains of the price loudly enough for the reeve to hear.

The half penny goes across. So does the reeve, a moment later: he has seen a handshake that lasted too long. He finds nothing on either of you, because Heahstan has swallowed it. He takes twenty pennies from you for selling unwitnessed, and he will know your boat again.

The reeve turns the half penny over for some time. He says he had hoped nobody would answer. Then he counts out a hundred and twenty pennies, the king's, exactly. When you look round the steward has gone, and has left his wine standing on the shingle.
You tell the reeve you carry wine and stones. You tell the steward the price of wine. Off the South Foreland the half penny goes into forty feet of water, where the last king of Kent can keep it.
Word from the thresholds

A Northumbrian monk with sore feet and a satchel of letters finds your boat. He has walked from Rome by Tours, and one of his messages is by word of mouth, for the Frisian who carried a widow of Kent.

She reached Rome. The girl did not come away from it: the fever in that city takes the young ones first. She lies in the English quarter by Saint Peter's, where our people have their own church and their own graves, and need both.
The widow has it too, the kind that comes back every third day. On the days between she is well and does everything she went there to do. She has done most of it twice.
She will start north when the mountain opens. Look for her at Saint Josse about four months from now. If your boat is not there she will wait. She says she has learned how.
I was to tell you, in these words, that it was a good mule.

There are Frisians there as well, with a house of their own under the hill. At the tomb of the Apostle one of them asked me what herring was fetching at Dorestat. I did not know. He was disappointed in me.
The old pope died at Christmas. The new one is called Leo, and the Romans have not yet made up their minds about him. When Romans make up their minds it is as well to be elsewhere.
Send forty pennies south by the next company, for her road home
Send word only: the boat will be at the Canche
Promise the boat, and ask him what became of the priest

The monk sews the forty pennies into a hem for the next company going south and writes her name on a scrap to go with them. He says about half of what is sent that way arrives. He says it as a man who has thought about which half.
The monk repeats the message until he has it: the boat will be at the Canche. He says it is the shortest letter he has carried this year and the only one he has understood.

The priest left the company at Saint-Denis and went to the king. King Charles feeds a number of Englishmen who cannot go home, the monk says; King Offa has asked for them more than once, and is answered politely. For the asking he gives you a riddle he has no room to carry: Bishop Aldhelm's, about a chest full of books that has never read one.
What she brought back
The widow sits against the south wall of the cell with her staff across her knees. She is half the weight she was. The girl's bundle lies beside her own.
This cloth lay a night on the Apostle's tomb. They weigh it before and after, and it comes up heavier. I watched the scale myself. I do not understand it and found I did not need to.
At Pavia I sold the gold-worked bands I took for the road, and bought what a Kentish church cannot get: pepper, incense, a little silk for an altar. Everyone does. The Lombards have a street for us.
And I have a fever, the girl's shoes, and the right way to sing the Alleluia, which is not how we sing it at home. I have been asked what a pilgrim brings back. That is the list.
I owe you a mule. It died under the mountain, on the way back, so it did all that was asked of it.
Your forty pennies found me at Saint-Maurice, under the pass. I ate them. I thought you would rather know that than be thanked.

A sealed leaf was left here at Candlemas by a priest from the king's hall, for the first of Kent to come back this way. She is the first. I gave it to her this morning, and she has been holding it like a hot dish since.
Take her home, and take the pepper and incense she offers against the mule
Take her home for a length of the silk
Take her home for nothing

She measures out two bags of pepper and two of incense on the guest-master's scale and will not be told it is too much. A debt carried over the mountain grows, she says. She comes down to the boat on the monk's arm.
She cuts you a length of the altar silk without a word and folds what is left smaller. It is good silk. She comes down to the boat on the monk's arm.
She says nothing for a while. Then she says she has met four kinds of people on the road and had begun to think there were only three. She comes down to the boat on the monk's arm.
The third day
Off the Frankish shore the widow's fever comes back on its day. She lies under the bottom boards with her teeth shut and shakes the boat. The crew look at her, and then at you.
It is the third-day fever. The brothers at Gyrwe had it from the marsh. It does not pass from one man to the next. I think it does not.
You think it does not. Well. She walked to the end of the world and back for a rag. I would not put her ashore, not her. I would not sit next to her either.
It will be gone by dark. It always is. Sail your boat.
Put your own cloak over her and hold the course
Let the lookout ask her to lay the cloth against the mast
Heave to, rig the sail over her and lose the tide

You steer in your shirt until dark. The crew say nothing about it, in the way that means they are saying a good deal. By dark the shaking stops, as she said it would, and she hands the cloak back folded.

She has the cloth held to the mast for the space of a psalm. The wind comes round fair before the psalm is done. Ravn says winds do that. He says it quietly, and afterwards he is seen to touch the mast in passing.
She has the cloth held to the mast for the space of a psalm. Nothing changes but the light. Ravn says nothing in a way that everyone hears. The fever goes at dark, as it always does.
The sail comes down and goes over her like a roof. The boat lies beam on and rolls for half a day. Nobody complains: a crew will forgive a lost tide sooner than a sick woman left in the wet.
The sealed leaf

At Sarre the widow kneels on the strand until the nun from the ship-house lifts her up. Then she takes the priest's sealed leaf out of her bundle and asks you what to do with it, because she can no longer tell what is a pilgrim's business.
He asks me to see it to Heahstan's lord. I have carried heavier things further, and none I liked less.
I went to pray for two dead. I think this leaf is for making more. But I served him the bread first, on your boat; you saw me. So I am not the one to judge it.
They tell me at the toll that Kent has a king, and that he was a priest. Then the leaf is late, and I still know whose hand it must go to.
They tell me at the toll how it ended, and what was done to his hands. Then this is a letter to nobody. I would still like it somewhere that is not my bundle.
If it is given into the abbess's hand it goes into the house's chest with the old kings' charters, unopened. What goes into that chest stays there. We have kept worse things than a letter.

I hear a widow has come home from Rome. The king is glad of every pilgrim's safe return, and of anything a pilgrim may have been given to carry. I have a horse, and I can wait as long as the ferry can.
See the leaf over the ferry to the hall it is meant for
Take the leaf over the ferry yourself, under the eyes of the king's man
Give the leaf to the king's man
Tell her it is no pilgrim's business, and let the abbess's chest have it

The ferryman takes it over inside his shirt with a load of oysters and comes back without it. He asks no question and is given a penny for that. The widow watches the far bank until the road is empty.

You cross with a cask on your shoulder and the leaf under your belt. The king's man watches the cask the whole way over. On the Canterbury side a boy takes the leaf from you and is gone into the saltings before you have set the cask down.

The king's man rides down into the ford and has the ferry held. Before he reaches it the leaf is over the side, and the Wantsum takes ink as readily as anything else. He fines you thirty pennies for crossing without the toll man's word, and looks at the water for some time.

The king's man breaks the seal there on the strand and reads standing. He counts two hundred pennies into your hand without looking at them. The widow does not speak to you. The nun takes her up the bank, and neither of them turns round.

The widow lets out her breath. The nun takes the leaf between two fingers and carries it up to the ship-house as if it might spill. On her way she has a word with the toll man about your keel, and he finds he can count it at the half for a while.
The priest is over the water

This year King Offa died, three days before Lammas, and before the corn was in Kent had a king of its own again. The men at the toll post say he was a priest. A steward is waiting on the strand with a horse for you.
He came ashore with nine men. By the second Sunday he had the hall at Canterbury and the archbishop had taken ship. The archbishop was King Offa's man and nobody had to tell him so.
The leaf told six halls to be ready and for what day. They were ready. I am not a young man and I rode all night, and I would do it again.
I told you once that you had carried a widow's priest and that was all. I was wrong, and I have seldom been so glad of it.
I have had pennies struck with my name on them. A king must, or he is only a man in a hall. Take some. The silver is good, whatever comes to be said of the name.
I promised your keel something on the bank of the Canche, when I had nothing. I have it to give now. Hold me to it quickly.
They will say a priest threw off his gown to put on a ring. It is true. Kent had nobody else left to ask.
Ask for his writing: your keel free of toll in the Wantsum
Take the writing and a place among his men, as the one who carried the half penny and helped the widow
Take his new pennies and Heahstan's friendship, and nothing with your name on it

A clerk writes it while you wait: this man's keel passes Sarre and Fordwic without toll, as the old kings granted to the minster's ships. The king makes his cross under it. Six hundred of the new pennies go into your chest. Your name is on a king's writing, in a year when Kent has changed kings once already.

The king has the writing made, and then has you sit at his table, three places down. Heahstan says the men above you have land and the men below you have swords, and that you are the only one who came by boat. Twelve hundred pennies, and a name the Kentish will know as long as this king sits there.

The king laughs for the first time and says a Frisian is a hard man to reward. Nine hundred pennies, new from the die. Heahstan walks you down to the boat: whatever you leave in his storehouse at Dofras will be there when you come back, and so, he hopes, will he.
Kent kept quiet
This year King Offa died, three days before Lammas. In Kent, where men had waited ten years for that day, nobody stirred. The reeve has a bag for you that has been sealed for some time.
There were six names in that leaf. The king had the men brought to him before he died, and their sons with them. He killed none of them. He was old and wanted it quiet.
So when he died there was nobody in Kent to light the fire, and a priest at the Frankish king's table with no one to come home to. He is there yet. I am told he says Mass well.
The new king has not needed to bring an army into Kent. He has you to thank for that and does not know your name. I have kept it so. You may thank me or not.
The widow went into the minster on Thanet. She does not ask after you. In Kent they do, now and then, and I would beach elsewhere than the Wantsum for a year or two.
Take the bag, and the king's protection for your house
Take the bag, and ask for ground on the Strand at Lundenwic
Take the protection, and send half the bag to Saint Josse for the men who cannot come home

Eight hundred pennies, and the reeve's word before witnesses that your house and its goods stand under the king's hand in every Mercian port. No fire was lit in Kent that year or the next. Nobody will ever be able to say what that was worth, which the reeve says is the best kind of service and the worst paid.

Six hundred pennies, and the reeve paces out a plot above the Strand himself, twelve of his rods by four. He drives the corner stakes with his own heel. He says it is good ground, and that he would not tell the neighbours how you came by it.

You keep four hundred and the king's protection. The other four hundred go over the water to the guest-master at Saint Josse, for the Englishmen who eat at the Frankish king's table and cannot go home. He sends back no thanks, only a tally with the sum cut in it, exactly.
Written in the book
The widow has given her land to the minster and taken the veil there. The nun who keeps the ships comes down to your boat with a tablet, a purse and a folded strip of cloth.
She has sold her husband's horse and his war-gear and says the price is yours. I told her it was too much. She told me I had not been there.
The leaf is in the chest. Nobody has opened it, and nobody will in my time. I have written on the lid what it is, in case the next keeper is curious, and what I think of curiosity.
You sent the leaf over the ferry, I know. It came to whatever it came to without you. That happens to most letters.
Kent has a king of its own this year. It did not need that leaf to get him. It will need a great deal more than a leaf to keep him.
They took the priest who was king, down in the Marsh, and led him into Mercia bound. I pray for him. I also count the house's ships each evening, and all of them are there.
I have the fever still, every third day, and have stopped minding it. The sisters have learned the Alleluia my way. Come and be prayed for when you pass; it costs nothing here.
Take the purse, and ask that your keel sail under the abbess's cross
Take the purse, and the strip of the cloth for under the mast
She says the one who asked no fare is to have both, and the minster's wine to fetch
Ask only that your dead be written in the minster's book

Six hundred and fifty pennies. The nun nails a small wooden cross to your stem herself and enters your keel on her tablet among the house's ships. The old king's charter allows the minster a ship in place of one worn out, she says, and the toll man has never yet won an argument with it.

Six hundred and fifty pennies, and a strip of the cloth two fingers wide, sewn into a linen bag. It goes under the mast, where a coin goes when a keel is new. The crew watch it go in. Even Ravn finds something to do nearby.

Twelve hundred pennies, the cross on your stem, the strip of cloth under your mast, and the minster's order for six casks of Frankish wine at better than the common price. The nun reads the list out twice, as if hoping to find a mistake in it. The widow, she says, was very exact.

The nun writes your father's name and your mother's on her tablet and asks how they are said. They will be read out at Minster with the house's own dead, each year, for as long as there are sisters to read. She leaves the purse on your thwart all the same: six hundred and fifty pennies. The widow said you would try to refuse it.
After the Marsh
This year King Coenwulf laid Kent waste as far as the Marsh, took the priest who was its king, and led him bound into Mercia. At the toll post a Mercian sits beside the toll man with a list.
They put out his eyes and cut off his hands. A priest's hands. He can be neither king nor priest now, and that was the thought behind it.
King Coenwulf's brother has Kent. Every writing the priest gave is void. Some men's names are on those writings, and I have them here.

Yours is one. A keel free of toll in the Wantsum. The new king may be brought to say the same thing in his own name, for a hundred and fifty pennies. He is a reasonable lord, and new, and short of silver.
Yours is not. You had his pennies, I am told. So did half of Kent. We are melting them.
They say he is alive, in a minster in the west, and that somebody feeds him. I do not ask who says so.
Buy the new king's word over the old writing: a hundred and fifty pennies
Let the writing lapse and keep your silver
Say that you sold the man wine, like half of Kent
Ask where the priest is kept, and send thirty pennies for his keep

The Mercian scrapes one king's name off the leaf and writes another over it. The cross beneath is new and the words are the same. Your keel still passes free. The toll man says a writing is like a boat: it is the same boat, whoever is steering.

The Mercian draws a line through your name and looks almost sorry: it was a good writing. From today your keel pays at Sarre and Fordwic like any other. The toll man holds out his hand, to show there is no ill will in it.

The Mercian runs his finger down the list twice and does not find you. He says a man who takes pennies and no parchment has either no ambition or a great deal of sense. The toll man says that with Frisians it is hard to tell.

The toll man knows a carter who knows a monk. Your thirty pennies go west with a load of salt. Some weeks later word comes back the same way: the man they keep there could not see who had sent it, and asked to have the name said twice.

Offa, king of the Mercians, is dead, and the Kentish have taken a king of their own kin, Eadberht, whom they call Praen, the priest. The archbishop has left Canterbury. English ships are slow to sail until it is known whose toll is whose.
Offa, king of the Mercians, is dead. Men looked for a rising in Kent and none came: the Wantsum ports trade as before, and the Mercian reeves sit where they sat.

A shingle strand in Kent, a bright windy morning: a thin widow of about forty-five in an undyed cloak and linen head-cloth, a staff in her hand and a roped bundle at her feet; beside her a girl of fifteen; a little apart, a tonsured man in a plain dark gown with his back to the track; a small beached boat in front.

Mid-channel in a flat calm, noon, the sail hanging: a tonsured priest pulling an oar with a rower's back; the widow holding out bread to him first; in the bow a young English lookout watching the two of them instead of the sea.

The toll house on the Canche, grey morning light through open doors: a Frankish clerk at a long table with wax tablets, his stylus pointed at the priest; the widow and the girl already past him in the doorway; a balance hanging from the beam.

The cell of Saint Josse, late afternoon sun: pilgrims with staffs sitting in a row against the south wall of a small church; an English monk carrying a pot of pulses; the widow counting pennies in her lap; dunes and the river mouth behind.
The bank of the Canche at dusk, the tide out: the priest holding out half of a cut silver penny on his open palm to the skipper; beached boats and one lantern behind them; the first stars.

The shingle at Dofras under the grey Roman wall, overcast noon: in front an old steward tasting wine from a horn beside casks; twenty paces behind, a reeve with a rod of office questioning a skipper; the skipper of the small boat between them, one hand closed.

A jetty at a Frankish river port, a wet afternoon: a lean Northumbrian monk sitting on the boat's gunwale with his shoes off and a satchel of letters on his knees, talking; the skipper listening with a rope in his hands.

The south wall of the cell of Saint Josse, clear morning: the widow, grown gaunt and brown, sitting with her staff across her knees; two bundles beside her, one small with a pair of girl's shoes tied to it; in her hands a folded cloth and a sealed leaf of parchment; the guest-master standing by.

The open boat under sail off a low shore, late afternoon, a grey chop: the widow lying under a cloak on the bottom boards, shaking; three crewmen turned toward the skipper at the steering oar; a strip of pale cloth in her fist.

The strand at Sarre, evening light on the mud: the widow on her knees being raised by a nun in an undyed gown; in the widow's hand a sealed leaf held out to the skipper; on the bank above, a horseman sitting still beside the toll post.

A timber hall in Kent by firelight, a harvest evening: the priest of the boat, now in a red cloak with a gold ring on his hand and his tonsure growing out, pressing a handful of new pennies on the skipper; an old steward smiling behind; spears stacked by the door.
A reeve's house above a beach, a dull still afternoon: a sealed leather bag on a table between the reeve and the skipper; through the open door a quiet strand with boats unloading and nobody armed.

The abbess's ship-house at Sarre, a clear cold morning: a nun with a wax tablet handing down a purse and a folded strip of cloth into the boat; on the bank above, a veiled widow leaning on a staff, one hand raised.
The toll post at a Kentish landing in autumn rain: a Mercian in a good cloak sitting beside the grey toll man with a parchment list on his knee, his finger on a name; smoke on the skyline inland.
A silver penny with a king's name on it lying beside half of an older cut penny, on a boat's thwart; behind, a Kentish strand with a hall's smoke rising.
An empty beacon stack on a chalk headland at sunset, unlit, the firewood grown over with grass; below it a calm strait full of ordinary sails.
An open book of names on a lectern in a small wooden church, a nun's finger on a line; through the door a boat with a little cross on her stem lying at a strand.
The man who watches the bar
The pilot of the Maas mouth sits in the door of his net shed and watches the bar. Skippers offer him silver to take them over it. Nobody asks him how he knows.
She runs north of the bank since the floods. You came in on last year's marks with a hand's breadth under you. I watched. I do not often get to watch that twice.
Do not ask me to take you out. Thiadbod's ship is looked for, and he pays me by the year to be free for her. I never said I liked it.
Four ships wait on this ebb and each master has a purse out. They all want to be taken over. Not one of them wants to know where she went.
The post stands well clear of the ridge end this morning, father. Anybody can see that.
Grandfather, why do the gulls stand in a row out there, when there is all that water to sit on?
Because they have something to stand on. That is the first question anybody has asked me this year that was about the water.
Sit down and ask where the channel went this winter
Offer him forty pennies to show you the marks
Carry his pole and line down to the boat, row for him, and say nothing

He talks until the flood is half made: where the old channel filled, where the river cut a new one, which bank is walking south. He does not look at you once. When you get up he says: come again when you have sold your cloth. I have more water than this.

He looks at the forty pennies as a man looks at a fish he did not order. Thiadbod offered a pound, he says, and I told him what I tell you: it is not for silver. Sit down or go away. You keep your pennies.

You row him out and back through one tide while he sounds for a wine ship. He says nothing to you that he does not say to the water. On the strand he counts six pennies of the fee into your hand and says: you pull evenly. Come again.
The far mark
A wine ship stands in for the bar. The pilot asks you, as if it did not matter, whether the post on the dune is open of the ridge yet. It has been open for some time.
The far mark is soft this year. It is the haze. It was the haze last year too.
That will be the red sail from Colonia. No? Striped. Then it is the light. A striped sail looks red in this light.
What a lot of room there is between the post and the ridge today. And a striped sail coming in, a hand north of where she should be.
I talk too much. Everybody says so. It is a great help to him.
You asked me about the water. So I ask you about the mark. That is all it is.
Say what you see, the way his daughter does: as if by chance
Tell him plainly that you saw him miss it
Say nothing here, and sell the word in the ale-houses up river: the pilot of the Maas is going blind

You remark on the post, the ridge and the striped sail, to nobody. He brings the ship in by what you say and what the pole tells him, and she never touches. Afterwards he says a Dane once paid his fee with a riddle about fog, and gives it to you. It is as near as he comes to thanks.

He says nothing for the length of a tide. Then: so you know what I am selling, and why I am in a hurry. He is short with you until dark. In the morning he is plainer with you than he is with his own daughter.

Three skippers at Dorestat pay ten pennies each to know it before the others do. One of them is Thiadbod's man. At Witla the pilot's daughter hears who brought the word up the river before your boat is back in the creek.
Not silver
After Michaelmas the wine ships stop coming and the pilot has time. He has you sit on the net pile and says what he wants for the marks. It is not silver.
My father had the Maas from his father. I had the Vlie from my wife's father, with her. Each of them told one man. A thing two men know is a thing for sale.
My price is three things. A spring, a summer and an autumn of your boat, when I say and not when the market says. Your mouth shut about my eyes. And the boy.
He is too young to carry it and I am too old to wait. So you carry it. When he can hold the pole you put it in him, all of it, and you ask him nothing for it.
You said it to my face, about the mark. So I need not pretend with you. That saves a tide.
Somebody sold my eyes in the ale-houses up river. I do not ask who. I ask you to swear, and I will listen to how it sounds.
I am forty. I have been forty for some time. There is no hurry, except that there is.
The pole, yes. Not the sea. Teach him the bar and leave him the shore to sleep on. That is my part of the price, and nobody asked me for it.
Swear it at the cross on the ridge, with your hand on his pole
Give him the three seasons, and swear nothing about a boy you hardly know
Swear it, and pay Thiadbod back his year so the old man is nobody's but the water's

You swear at the cross with the wind taking the words, your hand on the notched pole and his hand over yours. He gives you a riddle to hold until spring: the answer, he says, is the only friend a ship has on this coast. Then he says: after Easter, on the first quiet ebb. Bring oars.

He thinks about it for as long as it takes to mend a mesh. A man who will not swear will at least not lie to me, he says. You will have the water. The boy we will see about. After Easter, on the first quiet ebb.

You swear at the cross, and you count sixty pennies into his hand to send up the river: what Thiadbod pays for a year of him. He holds them a long time. Twenty years I have been rented, he says. I had forgotten I was for sale back. He gives you a riddle to hold until spring, and his daughter sends ale after you to the boat.
After the floods
The winter floods have moved the bar again. On the first quiet ebb after Easter the pilot goes out to find where the channel went, and this year he takes you to be his eyes.

Forget marks. Marks are what is left over afterwards. First the pole. Then the lead, and look what the tallow brings up: grey sand is the bank, shell is its edge, black mud is the old channel and she has left it.
Where gulls stand at half ebb there is a hand of water. Where she is brown and smooth she runs deep. Where she wrinkles with no wind on her, keep off.
And she is deepest here when a full moon stands in the south-east. That is the one thing my father told me that is still true.
Seven hands. Seven. Six and a thumb. Grandfather, it goes shallow the wrong way round.
Pilot! I have forty casks of the bishop's wine and I have been looking at your beach for two days. A full fee to whoever brings me in before I drink the cargo.
You may take him in if you think you have her. But if you put him on the bank it is my name that lies on the strand, not yours. Say now if you are not ready.
Take the pole yourself, and let him say what the tallow means
Row for him three ebbs and learn by watching
Bring the wine ship in yourself, under his ear, for the fee

You sound and call; he names what you bring up before you have finished saying it. By the turn of the tide you have her: a crooked road of brown water north of the bank, eight hands deep. He takes two ships over it that evening and gives you twenty pennies of the fees. You found her, he says. I only recognised her.

You read shell where there was sand, and your own boat sits down on the bank and starts a plank. Fifteen pennies to the wright, and the crew look at the sky. The old man is not angry. Now you know what sand feels like through a pole, he says. Again tomorrow. You find her on the second ebb.

For three ebbs you row and he sounds and the boy calls the notches. You say nothing and miss little. It takes longer this way, and nobody goes on the bank. On the third evening he has you point to where she runs, and you point, and he says: north of that. But not much.

You stand in the wine ship's bow with the pole and the old man stands behind you with his head on one side, listening to the water along her planks. She comes over the bar on the last of the flood and never touches. Her master pays ninety pennies and rolls a cask down the plank after them. The old man says: do not tell me you were not afraid. I could hear it. Good.

She takes the bank a ship's length short of the deep and sits there a whole tide with forty casks in her. Nothing is broken but the day. You pay her master thirty pennies for it, and on the strand they say the old pilot put a wine ship ashore. He lets them say it. You sound the bar again, and this time you have her.
Rented by the year
On the dam at Dorestat Thiadbod is friendly, which is how you know he wants something. He has heard that his pilot has taken a pupil.
I pay Gerlef by the year. A man I pay by the year does not give away in spring what I paid for in winter. You see how it looks, neighbour. I only say how it looks.
You sent me back his year. Sixty pennies, in a cloth. It was neatly done. I counted it twice, to be sure I was not being thanked.
So let us be plain. What he puts in your head, you put in my steersman's. A hundred and fifty pennies today. And when you have the Vlie as well, something better than pennies.
They say in the ale-houses his eyes are going. Then he is selling a cask with a hole in it, and you and I should agree a price before the news is any older.
I can learn a bar in a tide. It is only water.
Tell him the marks were never his to buy and are not yours to sell
Take the hundred and fifty pennies, and promise him the marks when you have them all
Say the old man teaches nothing: he only talks to the water

Thiadbod goes on smiling, which costs him something. As you like, he says. I rented a pilot for twenty years and never once thought to ask him anything. It seems that was the cheaper way to get it. He does not offer you ale.

A hundred and fifty pennies, counted on a cask head, in good new coin. Thiadbod's steersman watches them go into your purse as a man watches his own dinner carried past. When you have the Vlie, says Thiadbod. I am patient. Ask anyone I have lent to.
Thiadbod laughs. Then he talks to it for a long time, he says, with you sitting in the boat. He lets it lie. He is not deceived, only put off, and he has time.
North along the dunes

Between Whitsun and Lammas the weather is as steady as it gets. The pilot stands on the strand with his pole and a bag of bread. The Vlie, he says, is three days north with the dunes on your right hand, and he has not seen it in twelve years.
I had the Vlie from my wife's father, on the Westflinge side. She is dead and so is he. If the water there has moved since, nobody thought to send me word.
He does not go out alone at dusk any more, and now he is going to the Vlie. Bring him back before Lammas, and bring him back dry.
I can call the lead. I call it better than he hears it. Ask him.
There is the inside way: up the river, down the Vecht, over the Almere. Sweet water and no bar. Saint Boniface went that way to be killed. You learn nothing on it.
Take the old man and the boy, outside along the dunes
Take the old man outside along the dunes, and give his daughter your word on Lammas
Take him by the inside way: up the river, down the Vecht and over the Almere

The boy is in the bow before anybody has said yes. His mother stands on the strand with her arms folded and does not wave. The old man sits in the stern with his face to the wind and says: north. Keep the dunes where you can count them.

You give your word on Lammas and she takes it as she takes a penny, looking at both sides. The boy is left on the strand with the old pole. The old man sits in the stern with his face to the wind and says: north. Keep the dunes where you can count them.

His daughter kisses your sleeve. The old man gets into the boat as a man gets into a cart. Up the river, then, he says, with the cows. You will see the Vlie from behind, like a thief. He does not say the verse of the dune marks on a river, and you do not hear it.
The verse of the marks
The dunes go by on the right hand, one pale hill like the next. The old man cannot see them. He says them in order, in a verse, and after each line he asks you whether it is there.

The post on the ridge, and the Maas behind you. A day of white dunes with never a tree. A stone in the surf that the giants squared, where the Rhine goes out tired. Kinnem's sand, and the saint's roof behind it. Then the dunes lie down and the land goes low: that is the door of the Vlie.
A verse, because a verse can be said in the dark and in a gale. And because when a line is lost you can hear the hole. Nobody can tell when a list is short.
The stone. Is it there? Say what you see, not what I said.
It is there, grandfather. But there is white water a long way south of it. More than is in the verse.
If there is white water south of the stone, the Rhine is shutting her door. My father took ships in there. That is why the line says 'tired'. One day it will have to say 'dead'.
Say the verse back to him, line by line, until it holds
Cut the marks on a yew stick at night, where he cannot see you do it
Hold your tongue, steer, and learn the shore with your eyes

You have it by the time the saint's roof is abeam: five lines, each with a thing in it you have now seen. He has you say it once more with your eyes shut. That is how I say it now, he says. It is no worse.

You lose the third line, then the fourth, then the third again. He has you say it nine times. By the ninth the whole crew has it and the man at the bailer is saying it under his breath. Good, says the old man. Now it is in five heads and I must drown four of you.

At night under the tilt you cut it small along a yew stick: post, dune, stone, roof, door. The knife is quiet. In the morning he says: you were cutting something. A tally, you say. He turns his face to you. I am going blind, he says, not deaf. A tally does not take that long. He says no more about it.

You let the verse go by like the dunes and learn the shore itself: the stone in the surf, the white water south of it, a small grey roof behind Kinnem's sand, the place where the land lies down. He knows you are not saying it. Eyes are good, he says, while they last.
Her door has moved

The Vlie is a narrow water between the Frisian shore and Wiron, with the lake behind it. The old man says the channel lies under the eastern bank. A fisherman mending an eel trap says it has lain under the western one since before his son was born.
Under the west bank, and narrower every year. The king's man takes his tenth from every keel that finds it. The keels that do not find it pay the mud.
Twelve years. I gave you a verse and the last line of it is a lie. Do not be kind about it. I do not know this water.

The king's tenth, and of that a tenth to Saint Martin at Traiectum. His boat comes for it after harvest and goes aground every second year. Find her a road and the saint will not be the only one grateful.
