Good. Now you can learn the only part worth having. Not where she is. How to ask her.
A verse goes bad like fish. I should have told you that when I gave it to you. I did not know it myself until this morning.
Try my old marks if you like. You will find out the hard way how many of them still stand. I would not. But I am not the one who is learning.
Lie here three tides and find the channel yourself, with pole, lead and tallow
Pay the fisherman twenty pennies to take you through and name his marks
Try the old man's marks, to learn how much of the verse still stands

Three tides. Grey sand, grey sand, shell, then black mud, and the water going brown and smooth along the western bank. You find her without one mark that anybody gave you. The old man sits in the stern and says nothing at all, which is new. Saint Martin's boat comes down on the fourth tide and you take her through. The toll-gatherer pays forty pennies, halves your toll until autumn, and asks for four casks of wine by a keel that will not sit on his doorstep.

The fisherman takes you through in the time it takes to say it: the dead alder, the trap stakes, the hut with one wall. You have this year's road for twenty pennies. The old man says: now you know where she is. Ask him where she will be after the next ice. He will not know either, but he will not be surprised.

The eastern marks are gone or lying, and you know it within a ship's length. So you stop trusting them and feel for her with the pole, across the stream and back, as he taught you on the Maas. She is under the west bank. The old man says: one line of mine was still true. Which? None, you say. He laughs for the first time since Witla. The toll-gatherer pays forty pennies for the saint's boat brought through, and orders wine.

The old marks put you on the mud at the top of the tide, which is the worst time for it. You sit there until the next one, through a cold night, with a cask stove and thirty pennies of goods spoiled. The old man does not speak. At first light the fisherman hauls you off and names his marks for nothing: he says he has not had so good a night's watching in years.
The tide in a book

At Saint Martin's the schoolmaster has heard that a shipman knows why the saint's boat goes aground at Medemelacha. He has a book open at a page about the moon and the sea, and a boy beside him with a pen.

Bede the priest wrote it at Jarrow in my grandfather's day. The sea follows the moon, and each day the flood comes later by four parts in five of an hour, as she does. He says every shore has its own hour and the men who live on it know it. He did not write the hours down. Nobody has.
You carry in your head what he left out. Say it, and the boy will write it on the last leaf, after the tides. Saint Martin's boats would stop feeding the mud.

It is no heathen craft. Saint Paul's shipmen let down the lead and found twenty fathoms, and a little further on fifteen. It is in the Acts. They also wished for the day, which I take to be the oldest prayer at sea.
This parchment is hairy and the ink is thin. But I can write 'sand'. I can write 'mud'.
You swore to tell one boy. I ask you to tell one book. A book does not gossip. It is, I grant you, easier to carry off.
Say the marks, bar by bar, and let the boy write them
Give them only the hours: where the moon stands at high water on each bar, and no marks
Say it is in your head on loan, and not yours to put on a leaf

You say it and the boy writes it: a rough leaf for now, in a hand like a row of fence posts, to be made fair later. The schoolmaster reads it back to you in Latin and you know your own bar by the sound of it. The cellarer sends sixty pennies. Walking down to the boat you find you have learned what 'arena' is, and 'lutum'.

The moon in the south-east for the Maas; a little later for the Vlie. The hours belong to no man: any fisherman has them. The boy writes two lines under Bede's page and the schoolmaster is as pleased as if you had given him a relic. He reads you the whole chapter in return, slowly, and the cellarer sends thirty pennies.

The schoolmaster shuts his mouth on what he was going to say, and then nods. A thing held in trust, he says. We have a word for that too. He reads you Bede's page on the sea and the moon all the same, slowly, putting each sentence into Frisian, and asks nothing for it.
A space beside the Maas

The count has a list of the river mouths between the Sincfal and the Vlie, and beside each a space for the name of a man who can take the king's boats in. Beside the Maas the space is empty, and somebody has told him about you.
Shipman. The Maas mouth. I am told one old man knows it, that Thiadbod rents him, and that you are learning it for nothing. That is three things I dislike, in one breath.
In the Lent before he went to Rome, the lord king rode the shore himself and ordered ships and a watch against the pirates. A watch that cannot cross its own bar is a row of men looking at the sea.
The king's toll boat at Witla went on the bank twice last year. The second time the toll was in her.
Put your name in the space. Teach two of my men the bar. A hundred pennies now. Later, when I am asked who keeps the king's river mouths, I say your name and not Thiadbod's.
You Frisians say you need follow the king no further than the Weser and the Vlie, out with the ebb and home with the flood. I am asking you to go as far as your own doorstep.
Put your name beside the Maas, and take the hundred pennies
Say the marks are the old man's to give, and the old man is not giving
Say the bar moves every winter: let the king's men come at Easter and sound it with the rest of us

The clerk writes your name beside the Maas, and after it a word you cannot read. A hundred pennies are counted out from the toll chest. The count says: when you have it all, shipman. I can wait a year. The king is said to be less patient than I am.

The count looks at you as at a horse that has stopped. An old man on a beach, he says, and the king's ships wait on his pleasure. He does not threaten. He has the clerk leave the space empty, which is worse.

The count breathes out through his nose. The clerk, who has been at Witla, writes one word in the space. What have you written, says the count. 'Moves', lord, says the clerk. It is the truest thing on the list.
The first winter he has not sounded
The pilot does not get up when you come to the shed. He turns his face to the sound of your feet in the shells and says your name. The pole stands against the wall with this year's notches uncut.
It went at Michaelmas, between one tide and the next. I can still tell flood from ebb by the sound. That is not enough to take a ship in on.
You have all I had, and the one thing I did not have until the Vlie showed it to me: that the verse goes bad. Now. Three men have asked me whose the marks are. I told each of them: ask him.

You stayed away, and I could not wait for you. Sit. What I cannot show you I will tell you from here, and you will have to go and see how much of it is still true. It is not the way I meant. Then: whose are they to be?
You swore to me with your hand on the pole. I am not reminding you. I am only saying where the pole is.
And you have a stick. I heard the knife, the second night. I have been waiting ever since to hear what you would do with it.
Wilsuit says the priests at Traiectum have me on a leaf. An old man, pressed flat. Well. It is done. What is left is whether it is done properly.
The boy asks after you every time a sail shows. He has outgrown two poles since you first came.
I sounded the bar myself after the last gale. I found two channels. I think one of them is wrong, and I do not know how to ask him which.
Keep faith: come back for the spring sounding and put all of it into the boy
Have it written, the bars and how to find them, so that it cannot die in one head
Tell him the marks will have a master up the river: the count, or Thiadbod

He nods once, towards the bar. After Easter, then, he says. The first quiet ebb. The boy will hold the pole and you will row, and I will sit in the stern and be in the way. His daughter puts a bowl in your hands before you have asked for one.

He is quiet a long time. A leaf does not move, he says, and she does. But a leaf does not go blind either. Do it, then. Only have them write at the top, before anything else: she moves. If they will write that, I do not mind the rest.

He does not turn his face away, since it makes no difference to him where it points. So it was for sale after all, he says. I held it forty years and never found that out. His daughter takes the bowl she had brought you back into the house. The boy is sent to look at the nets.
The pole changes hands

On the first quiet ebb after the floods a boat goes out to the bar at Witla: the grandson in the bow with the pole, you at the oars, and in the stern a place for the old man, if he is still above ground to sit in it.
Do not tell me what you see. Tell him what to ask. I am only here for the air.
Grey sand. Shell. Shell. Black mud: she lay here last year and she has gone. She is north of us. Is she north of us?
Sound it twice, boy. The first time is for the river. The second time is for you.

He died in the hard frost after Martinmas, sitting with his face to the bar. He said your house asked about the water first. It was the best he said of anybody. Then he said: if that one comes, he knows where the pole is.
What he did not get to put in you, I can. And what you saw that he could not, you can put in me. It is the same water.
He has the pole and he sleeps at home. That is the bargain I wanted, and I did not think a merchant would be the one to keep it.
I know who carried the word about his eyes up the river. I have not told the boy. See that I never have a reason to.
Give the boy everything you have, and take your half of the season's fees
Give him everything, and stand at the cross as his foster-father in the craft: your house and the pilot's, one kin
Take the marks as your wage, pilot for yourself this summer, and leave the boy to what the old man told him

From Easter to Lammas you and the boy take every keel that asks, he with the pole and you behind him saying less each week. By Lammas you are saying nothing. Your half of the fees is three hundred pennies; the skippers' thanks are four casks of wine and six bolts of cloth. The Maas mouth and the Vlie are yours to cross without asking anyone. On the strand they have stopped calling him the old pilot's boy.

At the cross on the ridge, before the priest and the strand, you take the boy by the hand and say that his house and yours are one kin in the craft: what one knows the other is owed, to the last heir. All summer you and he take every keel that asks. Five hundred pennies, six casks and eight bolts are your part. The old man's lead is put into your hand, the tallow still in its foot. Keep it, the boy says. I have the pole. It ought to be in two houses.

You take the ships in yourself that summer, for the whole fee: six hundred and fifty pennies by Lammas, and a lead and line of your own. Nobody on the strand has stopped you and nobody on the strand speaks to you. The boy sounds the bar with what a blind man could tell him and goes on the bank twice before he has it. He will be a good pilot. He will not be your friend, and neither will his mother.
The leaf after the tides
In the writing room of Saint Martin's a leaf lies ruled and empty at the back of the book of times, after the chapter on the sea and the moon. The schoolmaster asks what, exactly, is to go on it.

Nobody in the North has written a shore down. The Greeks did it for their own sea, I am told: we have the word for such a book and not one of the books. This will be a single leaf. I should like it to be a true one.
Your stick is very well for a man who reads sticks. I can make out 'dune'. Read it to the boy, and slowly.
Thank God it is one leaf. My hand is tired of the moon.
One thing troubles me. You say the bar moves each winter. Then what I write at Martinmas is false by Easter, and a false leaf in a true book is worse than an empty one.
Unless we write what you say you learned at the Vlie. Not where the channel is. How a man asks the water where it is.
Write whatever keeps my boat off the mud. I will pay for the calf.
Dictate the verse and this year's marks, bar by bar
Dictate the way of asking the water, and a rule: a brother sounds each bar at Easter and amends the leaf
Dictate it, and have a second leaf made for the boy at Witla, so the pilot's house has what the saint has

The verse, the post, the stone, the roof, the western bank of the Vlie: one leaf, in a fair hand, with 'she moves' at the head because you promised. The cellarer pays five hundred pennies, six cakes of wax and two bundles of parchment, and you carry away a copy. The saint's boats cross without a pilot that year. The year after, one of them goes on the bank with the leaf open in the steersman's hand. At Witla nobody asks you in.

It takes four days and the boy's hand cramps twice. Pole, lead and tallow, and what each colour of the bottom means. Birds at half ebb. Brown smooth water and wrinkled water. The moon's place for each bar. Last, the rule: at Easter a brother goes out, sounds, and writes what he finds beneath what the last man found. The schoolmaster says it is the first book he has known to admit it will be wrong. Seven hundred pennies, eight cakes of wax, a book for your chest, and the bishop's word that you are Saint Martin's man. At Witla they see the saint's own men sounding the bar, and draw their own conclusion.

Two leaves, the boy writing both and complaining through each. One stays in the book of times. The other you carry down the river in oiled cloth and put into the grandson's hands. He cannot read it. His mother says: then the priest reads it to him at Easter, and he tells the priest where it is wrong. That will do them both good. She keeps your goods on the strand from that day, and counts them. The cellarer's four hundred pennies, wax and parchment are the smaller part of it.
A master for the water

On the dam at Dorestat the marks of the Maas and the Vlie are waited for. The count has a list with a space on it. Thiadbod has a steersman who learns a bar in a tide. Whoever has paid you expects to be told.
The space beside the Maas is still empty, shipman. I have been asked about it by a man who does not like empty spaces, and he was not asking kindly.
A writing for the king's post at Witla: your keel passes untolled for as long as you keep the king's boats off the bank. It lasts as long as you do, and as long as you come when you are called.
A hundred and fifty of my pennies have lived in your purse a long time. I should like to hear them say something.
Twelve hundred pennies more, and the lower end of my dam head: the dry end, with the shed on it. For water. My father would have had me bled.
And the old man? He has an alehouse and a grandson. Most men end with less.
Teach the count's two men the bars, and take the king's writing
Teach Thiadbod's steersman, and take the silver and the dry end of the dam head
Tell them both the old man went blind and the marks went with him, and go down the river to the boy

Two of the count's men row with you for a month, Franks who say 'it' of the river. They learn enough. Your name is written beside the Maas and beside the Vlie; you are given seven hundred pennies and a writing with a seal, and the toll man at Witla lets your keel by with his mouth shut. When the king's boats come to the bar it is you who are sent for, in whatever season it is. On the strand at Witla the old man's grandson is told he may sound the bar when the king's pilot does not need it.

The steersman does not learn it in a tide. He learns it in six weeks, and badly, and that is enough for Thiadbod, whose ships now cross the bar when they please and whose rivals wait. Twelve hundred pennies are counted out on a cask head, and you are walked along the dry end of the dam and shown where your posts may go. At Witla the pilot's house has the old pole and the water has an owner. They do not say which they think is worth more.

You tell them the old man's eyes went and the marks with them: he could not show what he could not see. Thiadbod does not believe a word and cannot prove one. The count has the clerk draw a line through a name. Neither asks for his silver back, since asking would be admitting what it was for. You go down the river. The spring sounding is still to come, and the boy is waiting with the pole.
The pilot of the Maas mouth is going blind, they say at Dorestat. Skippers bound for the sea talk of going round by Walichrum.
There is a new pilot on the bar at Witla: the old man's grandson, with the old man's pole. He sounds everything twice.
At Saint Martin's they have written the bars of the Maas and the Vlie on a leaf, after the chapter on the tides. The saint's steersmen are learning to read.
The count has named a king's pilot for the Maas mouth, a merchant of Dorestat. The pilot's house at Witla was not asked.
Thiadbod's ships cross the bar at Witla without waiting for a pilot now. Everybody else's wait as before.

The door of a turf-walled net shed above a tidal creek on a grey spring morning: a wiry old man in a salt-stiff hooded cloak sits on the sill looking out to a white line of breakers, a notched pole taller than himself against the wall; a woman with a dipper and a small boy stand by; boats sit on the mud below.

A turf mound at the seaward end of a low ridge in hazy noon light, a tall post with a cross-piece on it; the old pilot shades his eyes and looks slightly the wrong way; his daughter beside him points with her chin at a striped sail standing in over brown water.

Inside the net shed on an autumn evening, rain at the open door: the old pilot on an upturned basket holding up three fingers, a merchant sitting on a pile of tarred net, the sounding pole between them, a rush light, his daughter in the doorway with her arms folded.

A small open boat on a river bar at low water on a cold bright spring morning: a merchant in the bow pushing a notched pole into brown water, an old man in the stern with his head on one side holding up a lead with grey sand stuck to its foot, a boy counting on his fingers; gulls standing in a row on a sandbank; a wine ship at anchor outside.

The timber dam at Dorestat on a fine afternoon: a well-fed man with a combed fair beard and a long blue cloak with a silver pin counts pennies onto a cask head, smiling; a young steersman behind him with his thumbs in his belt; a big ship alongside and a small one beyond her.

A creek strand at early morning in summer: a small boat afloat with her sail bent on; the old pilot wading out to her with a pole and a bread bag; his daughter on the sand with folded arms; a boy already half over the bow, looking back at her.

A small boat under a square sail running north in a light summer breeze, a long line of pale dunes on her right hand; far off, a dark squared stone ruin standing in white surf; an old man in the stern with shut eyes and one hand raised, counting lines on his fingers; the steersman looking at the shore.

A narrow flat water between two low green shores under a wide grey sky, a row of thatched houses on a peat bank behind; an eel fisher on the bank mending a wicker trap and pointing west; in a small boat the old pilot sits bowed with his pole across his knees while a merchant looks from one bank to the other.

A plain timber writing room with one small window, afternoon light on a sloping desk: a tonsured schoolmaster with his finger on an open book that shows a drawn moon; a boy scribe with a quill and an ink horn; a merchant in a sea cloak standing, his cap in his hands, sand on the floor from his shoes.

The count's hall at Dorestat by day: a thick-set man with a long moustache and a red cloak pinned on the right shoulder holds out a strip of parchment; a clerk at his elbow with a pen points to an empty place on it; a merchant before them, a toll chest open on the table.

The net shed in low winter light, snow on the turf roof: the old pilot sits inside the door with his face turned towards the listener and his eyes on nothing, hands open on his knees; the pole against the wall; a tall boy outside holding a newer pole; grey sea and the white line of the bar beyond.

A small boat on the bar at Witla on a still spring morning after rain: a long-armed youth in the bow with the old notched pole, a merchant at the oars, and in the stern an old blind man with his face lifted to the wind (or an empty thwart with a folded cloak on it); the ridge, its cross and the mark post behind.

The writing room of Saint Martin's by candle and window light in late autumn: a boy scribe bent over a ruled leaf at the back of a thick book, the schoolmaster reading over his shoulder, a stout cellarer with keys in the doorway, a merchant dictating with a yew stick in his hand; cakes of wax stacked by the wall.

The dam at Dorestat under a windy sky: the count in his red cloak with a sealed writing on one side, the rich skipper in his blue cloak with a heap of pennies on a cask head on the other, a merchant between them looking down river; far off down the water, very small, a boat with a single figure holding a pole.
The box from the Main

A young deacon has come down the river from the Main with a box sewn in waxed linen, about as long as a man's arm. He does not put it down to talk. He is asking along the shore for a Frisian who knows the Scheldt.

They say a Frisian will carry anything anywhere if you name the tide. I need Ganda, on the Scheldt, where the Lys comes in. Fifteen days by boat from our house, my lord reckons it. My lord has never rowed it.
I came down the Main this morning on a grain boat. Her master crossed himself when I stepped off. I do not think it was for my sake.
The wine boat that brought me from the Main goes no further. Her master says the sea is for Frisians and fools, and he was not sure which I should look for first.
One box. It does not eat, it does not spoil, and it does not go under the ballast. It lies where I lie.

My lord is abbot at Ganda and is never there. He is at the palace. He writes. The steward at Ganda has a letter by now saying a boat is coming, so somebody will be looking out for you, which I am told is rare for a Frisian.
Name a freight: thirty pennies now and ninety at Ganda
Ask what is in the box before you name anything
Carry him and his box for nothing, for your dead
He counts thirty pennies out of a purse that has more in it than a deacon's should. The box goes under the stern board on a folded sail. He sits down on the board, and that is where he stays.

He says his teacher answers every question with another, and gives you one about a thing that opens and shuts a house. Then he tells you plainly. Two martyrs of Rome, Marcellinus the priest and Peter who drove out devils, or as much of them as his lord can spare for Ganda. The freight is thirty now and ninety there.

He looks at you for some time. Then he says he will write your father's name and your mother's on the list for the altar at Mulinheim, and asks how they are spelt. You do not know. He says the saints will.
The man from Soissons

A priest in a good cloak has been waiting where the boats lie. He knows what you carry and from whom. He waits until the deacon has gone up the bank to find bread, and then he comes down the plank as if it were his own.
A box in waxed linen, a deacon who sleeps on it, a Frisian boat bound for the Scheldt. You people think a river keeps secrets. A river is a road with ears on both banks.

Gozhelm, of Saint-Medard at Soissons. The holy Sebastian came to us from Rome two years ago, by the pope's own gift, and the sick have not left our door since. A house with one great saint soon finds it needs another.

A priest of ours went to Rome with the notary and came home with a share of Marcellinus. After Easter our abbot was made to hand it back at the palace, in front of everyone, to the little man who is abbot of Ganda. My house has not forgotten how that felt.

A boat can lose her way in the mouths of the Scheldt. Nobody blames a boat. Bring the box up the Seine to the landing of Saint-Denis, and the cellarer will count you two thousand pennies and will not ask what road you came. Here is a hundred and twenty, so that you think about it.

And do not say theft to me. If the martyrs did not wish to go, no man could lift them. That is known. The notary lifted them out of their own tomb by night, and they came. Ask yourself what that tells you about them.
They tell me you asked no freight. Then you are a pious man, and a pious man should want the martyrs where the most people will come to them. Ganda is a marsh with sheep on it.
Send him off, and tell the deacon when he comes back with the bread
Take the hundred and twenty, and say you will think about it
Hear him to the end, take nothing, and say nothing to anyone
He takes it calmly and puts his purse away. The deacon, when he hears, takes it less calmly, and eats his bread sitting on the box. That night he sleeps with one arm through the cord.

A hundred and twenty pennies, good ones, new from the palace mint. He does not ask for your word and you do not give it. When the deacon comes back with the bread the priest is looking at another boat, and you are coiling a rope.

He talks well. Before he goes he tells you, for nothing, that the abbot's cellarer is paying a fifth over for Rhine wine against the fair of Saint-Denis. It is the kind of thing a man says to be remembered kindly. It is also true.
What the box does

The men know what lies under the stern board. Nobody told them. The boy has a fever from the river and lies under the fore thwart with his teeth knocking, and the others have been talking low since noon.

The grain boat's men told it at the Main mouth. Where that box lay first, up in the hills, it sweated blood for days, and men dreamed the saints wished to be somewhere else. So they were moved. I would like to know where they wish to be now, before we are over the bar.
The boy asks only to lay his hand on the linen. He says he will keep his eyes shut while he does it.

They are not cargo, and they are not a charm for boatmen. But I say the office beside them at dusk, and a man who stands near while I say it does no wrong. I cannot stop a sick boy from standing near.
And somebody at the last landing gave you silver for nothing. I have steered long enough to know what nothing costs.
You sent that priest up the plank faster than he came down it. The men saw. It is why they are asking you and not just doing it.
Let the deacon say his office at the stern, and the men stand near
The box is freight. Nobody goes near it but the deacon
Wait until the deacon sleeps, and lift the linen yourself

The deacon sings thinly and the men do not know the words. The boy lays two fingers on the linen and takes them away as if it were hot. By the middle of the night he is asleep and wet through, and in the morning he asks for bread.

The deacon sings thinly and the men do not know the words. The boy lays two fingers on the linen. The fever takes its own time after that, as fevers do, but the men pull better for having stood there.
The men say nothing, which is how you know what they think. The deacon thanks you. The boy sweats it out by himself under the fore thwart.

Inside the linen is a box of plain oak, and in the box two bundles in red silk, each no bigger than a loaf. A strip of parchment is tied to each. You can make out an M on one and a P on the other, and after that a clerk's small hand. You sew the linen shut with sail twine. It is neat work, for a sailor.
The seller of bones

A man with a mule's pack and a southern way of talking is selling from a cloth on the landing: a tooth, a knot of hair, a splinter of bone. Each has a name on a strip of parchment. He looks up before you have said who you are.
Felicitas, a rib. Dust from the grave of Agnes, cheap, because dust goes a long way. A pope's finger, the name is a little rubbed. All from Rome. I was there when they were lifted. I held the lamp.
You are the boat with the box. Do not look surprised. Since the notary came over the mountains with his two martyrs, every man on this river who owns a spade is a deacon of Rome.

For a boatman I have something useful. Two bundles in red silk, the labels blank, the weight of two small men. Twelve pennies. I do not ask what a box ought to weigh. I only know that boxes get weighed.
Yes, yes. The old emperor's law. No false names of martyrs, no wanderers deceiving the people. I have heard it read out in six towns. In all six I was selling by the church door while they read it.
A priest in a good cloak asked me this morning what a Frisian boat costs. I said it depends who has already paid for it. He did not laugh. You might.
Buy the two blank bundles (12 d)
Buy the rib with a name on it for your own chest (60 d)
Tell him the deacon has a bishop's ear, and watch him pack
Two bundles in red silk go into your sea chest under the spare line. They weigh what he said. Whose they were he does not say, and it is likely he never knew. A graveyard is a graveyard.

Sixty pennies for a rib the length of your hand and a strip of parchment that says FELICITATIS. He swears to it by three saints, all of whom he has for sale. It may be hers. A bishop could say, if a bishop were asked.

He has the cloth rolled and the mule loaded before you have finished the word bishop. Over his shoulder he says the canons at Ganda are paying anything for wax, since candles go with saints, and that he at least sells what he says he sells: bones.
The blind man of the coast

A blind man is led down to the boats by a child. He has heard that saints are going up the river, and he stops at every stern and asks whether this is the boat. The boatmen say no and look away, though he cannot see them do it.
Germar is my name. I am from the coast here. Six winters I have been blind. They say holy men are going up to Ganda in a boat. Is this the boat? Nobody will tell me, and I cannot look.
I have one penny, and I can bail. I bail well. A blind man is never surprised by water.

My lord wants the name of everyone who comes to them, and where they are from, and what ailed them, and the day. He means to write it all down. Take this one, and I have the first name on the list before we are even there.
You sent the priest of Soissons away without being asked. I think you can be trusted with a blind man.
Take him aboard for nothing
Take his penny and set him to bail
Tell him it is some other boat
The child hands him over the side like a parcel and runs. He finds the bailer by feel and sits with it in his lap, facing the stern. He does not ask where the box is. He seems to know.
You take the penny. It is an old light one, worn nearly smooth. He bails as he said he would, without being told when, and the men stop minding him by the second tide.
He thanks you and goes on down the line of boats, asking. The deacon watches him go and says nothing, and writes nothing.
The ebb

The deacon has gone up to the church to hear the office and will be an hour. It is the first time he has left the box. It lies under the stern board. The ebb has begun to run, and the priest of Soissons stands on the strand with a horse and a servant, a little way off, like a man admiring the view.
An hour. The tide is with you and the wind is fair for the west. By the time he has said his Amen you are a sail. Up the Seine to the landing of Saint-Denis, and ask for the cellarer.
You took my hundred and twenty on the river. I did not give it for your thinking.
You took nothing from me on the river, and I respected that. Now I am offering two thousand, and respect is finished.
Three hours of ebb yet. I say only what the water is doing. What we do is yours to say.
In your sea chest, under the spare line, lie two bundles in red silk with their labels blank.
The blind man sits in the bows with the bailer in his lap. He has turned his face toward the strand, where the voices are.
Wait for the deacon. There will be another ebb
Cast off on the ebb with the box aboard
Tell him to come to the boat after dark, alone
Go up to the church and tell the deacon who is on the strand

You sit on the stern board yourself, for once, and watch the ebb go to waste. The priest waits a while, then mounts. The deacon comes down the path wiping his mouth and finds everything as he left it, and does not know there was anything to find.

If there is anyone aboard who is not yours, he is handed onto the sand first. Then the line comes in and she takes the ebb. Nobody speaks. From the water you can see the church door, and it stays shut a long time. When it opens you are too far off to tell one man from another.
He looks at you, and then at your sea chest, though he cannot know what is in it. He says he will come when the fort has shut its gate, and that he will bring what a horse can carry.

The deacon finishes the psalm first. Then he goes to the count's man at the gate. The priest of Soissons shows a letter with the archchaplain's seal on it, and nobody there dares hold him. He rides. But his name is written down, and yours is written beside it, on the other side of the page.
Two boxes

After dark. The deacon sleeps inside the gate. Under the sail on the bottom boards lie four bundles in red silk, two with names on their labels and two without. The priest of Soissons has brought a lamp he does not light, and a bag that he sets down carefully.

I will not count them and I will not look. What I do not see I need not confess. Put two in my hands and I will put the bag in yours. Nine hundred. The rest was for the Seine, and you are saving me the Seine.
Labels are for clerks. Our cellarer writes a fair hand, and he knows the names.
You have seen the true labels by daylight: an M, a P, and a clerk's small hand. Even in the dark your fingers know which pair has writing on it.
You have never seen inside the linen until now. Two of the four have a strip of parchment with writing on it. That is all there is to tell them apart.
Give him the two you bought. A blank label is his cellarer's business
Give him the martyrs, and tie their labels to the two you bought
Give him nothing. Sew the linen shut and send him up the strand

He takes the two bundles against his chest like a man carrying a child out of a fire, and hands you the bag without letting go of them. The martyrs go back into their oak box. You sew the linen with sail twine by feel. Somewhere west of here a great abbey is about to receive two strangers with honour.

The knots on the labels are a clerk's knots and take longer than they should. Then it is done. He goes up the strand with the martyrs against his chest. In the oak box, under the abbot of Ganda's seal, two strangers lie with borrowed names. The men were told to sleep. You do not think they did.

He stands a while with his bag. Then he says that a man who will not sell is only a man who has not heard the right price, and that he has no more prices. He does not ask for his earnest back. It is not a debt a man can take to court.
Weather in the mouths
The wind backs and hardens, and the sea goes the colour of lead over the banks. There is white water where you have never seen any. The men look at the stern board more than at the sky.
This is only weather. I have had worse with a cargo of cheese, and nobody said the cheese was angry.
At the Main mouth they said the saints sweat blood when they are where they do not wish to be. I am not saying this is that. I am saying the men are saying it.
Skipper, if we vowed them a candle. A big one, the weight of the boy. They could not take that badly.
Or if we put about. There is still a Scheldt behind us.
I slept that night at the landing, as I was told. I sleep lightly. I will say no more about it than that.
Shorten sail, keep the lead going, and lose a day
Stand on under full sail
Vow the martyrs a candle of the boy's weight, and lay by 24 d for the wax
Put about for the Scheldt and take the box where it was sent

A reef in the sail, a man in the bows with the lead, and the banks felt out one by one like stairs in the dark. It costs a day. By evening the wind has gone round and the men have stopped looking aft.

She goes through it with her lee rail under and comes out the far side into flat water and a clearing sky. The steersman says nothing. He has the look of a man who would like it known that he said nothing.
A sea comes aboard over the quarter and takes a man off his feet against the thwart. Ribs, most likely. The box does not shift. Nobody finds that a comfort.

You say it aloud at the stern with your hand flat on the board, and count twenty-four pennies into a rag where the men can see. The wind does not drop. The men do not need it to. They needed something to have been said.

She comes round heavily and takes the wind on the other side. Nobody cheers. One of the men begins to sing, badly, something the deacon sang. Whatever the priest of Soissons gave you he will not see again, and neither will he see the box.
A letter on the coast

The toll man has a clerk beside him today, and the clerk has a letter. A deacon on the Scheldt has written to every bishop between the Rhine and the Seine about a Frisian boat and a box in waxed linen.
I take the king's tenth on what is sold. Nobody sells saints, or nobody says so, and I have no tenth in this. But the bishop's clerk has a letter. He reads. I do not.
A boat of the Frisian build, four men. A box so long, sewn in waxed linen, under the seal of the abbot of Ganda. Carried off on the ebb while a deacon sang the office. Lift your stern board, shipman.
Unless you are bound for some landing I should know of. Boats have passed here on a great man's name before now. I am told to look. I am not always told to find.
I know this boat. She has paid her tenth here like a Christian. That is all I will say for her, and I say it only because it is true.
Say whose landing you are bound for, and let the archchaplain's name do the rest
Forty pennies for the clerk's poor, before the board is lifted
Lift the board. Say the deacon missed his tide, and that you will carry the box back yourself

You say the landing of Saint-Denis, and whose cellarer waits there. The clerk folds the letter along its old folds. He says the boat he was told of had a red sail, he is almost sure. Yours is brown. Anyone can see that.

The clerk says any Frisian can say a great man's name. It takes a hundred pennies and an hour before he agrees that the name may be the right one. He writes down your boat all the same, the strakes and the patch in the sail, and puts it in with the letter.

The clerk's poor are many, he says, and thanks you on their behalf. The letter goes back into his sleeve. The toll man looks at the river through all of it, as a man looks who means to have seen nothing.

You lift the board yourself. The clerk looks at the seal and does not touch it. He says the deacon's letter asks only that the box come to Ganda, and does not say in whose boat, and that he sees no reason to write more than he was asked. It is a long way back, and you have time to think on it.
The bank at Ganda

Where the Lys runs into the Scheldt the canons of Saint Bavo stand on the bank with candles lit in daylight. Boys run along the water ahead of you, shouting. Somebody has been watching this river for days.
Erembert, the abbot's steward. We have had the letter a week, and the boys have been on the bank since. You are the first boat they have not been wrong about.
I came by land, on a borrowed mule, with a letter written out for every bishop on the coast. I see I need not send the rest of them. I will say what happened, and I will say that he came back.
This is the shipman I wrote of. He was offered two thousand on the strand, and he came up to the church to tell me in the middle of a psalm.
And he asked no freight. Write that down too. No, write it somewhere the abbot will read it.

The blind man Germar, from the coast by the Scheldt mouth, was led into the church behind the box. Before the office was sung through he said he could see the candles, and after a while the men who held them.
The blind man Germar was led into the church behind the box and stood through the office with his face turned to the candles. Afterwards a canon led him out again, by the sleeve.

The freight I can pay from the chest. More than that is the abbot's to give, and the abbot is at the palace. Come again when two moons have gone. A letter to the palace and back takes that long, when he answers at all.
Carry the box up to the church with your own men
Hand it over at the bank and see to your boat
Lead the blind man up yourself, behind the box

Four Frisians carry it up from the water on two oars, as you would carry a hurt man, and the canons sing in front and do not know what to do with their hands. The steward counts ninety pennies into yours at the church door. Your men talk about it for a year.

The canons take it from you at the water's edge, and it is gone up the bank among the candles before your line is fast. The steward counts out ninety pennies. The boat needs bailing. A boat always does.

He holds your sleeve the whole way up, and lets go of it at the church door without being told he is there. The steward pays the ninety pennies and asks the blind man's name and yours, and has both written down, though only one will be kept.
The abbot's answer
The abbot's answer has come from the palace. The steward reads it to you standing, because it is short. Behind him a canon is writing names on a sheet: who came, from where, and what left them.
He writes: pay the Frisian well, in good silver and all of it, and ask him what he would have besides. He says the part about the silver twice. He always says the part about silver twice.

A girl from Furnes who was blind. A man from Alphen who left two crutches at the door. Two of our own people from the abbey's land. I have the days for all of them. It goes to the abbot when the feast of Saint Bavo is past, and he will put it in a book.

The deacon told the abbot all of it, the ebb and the turning back. The abbot writes that a greater man's priest did worse and was forgiven in front of the whole palace. But he does not offer you land.

And for the matter on the strand he has spoken to the emperor's people. There is a writing being made this year for merchants who serve the palace: its bearer goes free of toll, save at Quentovic, at Dorestat and at the mountain passes. Your name can stand in one.
The deacon says the linen was sewn with sail twine when it came. I told him boats are wet places and things get mended in them. I would as soon not hear whether I was right.

This year the bones of the holy martyrs Marcellinus and Peter, which Ratleic the notary had brought out of Rome, came by boat to the house of Saint Bavo at Ganda, where the Lys meets the Scheldt. Many sick were healed there until the eve of Saint Bavo's feast.
Ask for a plot on the bank by the lay village
Ask for a cloth that has lain on the martyrs
Ask for your name in the emperor's writing, and the plot besides

Seven hundred pennies, and a strip of the bank between the abbey and the village, paced out by the steward himself with a boy carrying the pegs. A yearly rent in wax, which he asks you to begin on at once: six loads, at half again over the price, because the candles do not stop.

Six hundred pennies, and a square of white linen that lay a night and a day on the martyrs' bundles. The canon folds it into a little bag of red silk and ties it with a clerk's knot. It weighs nothing. Your men will not let it be stowed anywhere but the stern.

Fourteen hundred pennies, the strip of bank, and a promise that is kept before winter: a sheet with the emperor's name at the foot and yours in the middle, spelt as a Frank would spell it. The steward says a toll man who cannot read will still know the seal. He adds that the archchaplain's people also know your name now, and will for as long as he is archchaplain.
The abbey does not ask
At the landing of Saint-Denis the cellarer has a cart waiting with a white cloth in it. He does not ask what road you came. He asks only whether the seals are whole.
Whole. Good. The abbot of Ganda's own seal. He will know it again when he is told where it lies. That is a matter between great men, and you and I are small ones, God be thanked.
It will be written that the martyrs turned a Frisian's helm with their own hands, wishing to rest beside the holy Sebastian. I have the first lines already. You are in it, as a wind.
Two thousand, as was said. Or less, and a place on the abbot's ground at the fair. The abbot holds the fair's tolls. A man of ours pays them, in a manner of speaking, to himself.
The clerk on the coast wrote down your boat. Let him. A letter against a man of the archchaplain's goes into a chest and stays there.
You see I was right to give you the hundred and twenty. A man thinks better with silver in his hand. I have always found it so.

This year the bones of the martyrs Marcellinus and Peter, sent by boat to Ganda, came instead to the house of Saint Medard at Soissons. The abbot of Ganda complained of it at the palace and was not heard.
Take the two thousand, and the abbey's name over yours
Take thirteen hundred and a plot on the abbot's ground at the fair
Take six hundred for the freight, and ask that the monks name you in their prayers

Two thousand pennies, counted in tens on the tail of the cart, beside the box, with the white cloth turned back so that it should not be touched by money. The cellarer says you may call yourself Saint-Denis's man on this river and that the toll men will know what it means. On the Scheldt it will mean something else.

Thirteen hundred pennies and four pegs in the abbot's field, where the booths stand at the fair in the month of the vintage. He wants three casks of Rhine wine from you before the next one, and will pay well over the price. The cart goes off at a walk. Nobody on the landing kneels, since nobody has been told.

The cellarer counts out six hundred and waits for you to ask for the rest. When you do not, he looks at you for the first time. He says he will have your name read with the benefactors, and that he has known the house pay two thousand for less. The men pull easier going down the river than they did coming up.
Two saints

The abbot's answer has come from the palace, and with it news from the west: the house of Saint Medard at Soissons is showing the people the martyrs Marcellinus and Peter. The steward does not know what to think. You do.
They cannot lie in two places. The abbot writes that he took them back from Soissons once already, after Easter, with his own hands, and that he is too old to do it every year.
Let Soissons show what it likes. The blind see here. A girl from Furnes, a man from Alphen with two crutches. I have a sheet of names, with the days.
It is strange. The pedlars say there are healings at Soissons. Here we have had candles and crowds, and nothing I can write down.
The deacon says the linen was sewn with sail twine when it came. I told him boats are wet places and things get mended in them.
Whatever Soissons has, you brought us what you were given, under the seal. The abbot says pay the Frisian in good silver. So.
This year the martyrs Marcellinus and Peter came to Saint Bavo at Ganda, and the same year the house of Saint Medard said that it had them. Each house wrote down its own miracles.
This year two houses said that they had the martyrs Marcellinus and Peter. The healings were at Soissons.
Take the steward's silver, and keep the finger bone you held back
Tell the steward everything, and lay the Soissons silver on the altar (900 d)

Six hundred pennies from the steward, on top of nine hundred from a bag in the dark. And in a twist of red silk in your sea chest, one small bone that came out of the bundle marked P and never went back. Two abbeys have a saint each. You have a secret, and a finger of Peter who drove out devils, and you will have to decide for yourself what the two are worth together.

The steward sits down. When you have finished he is quiet for a time, and then he sends the canon out. The nine hundred goes on the altar in its own bag. He pays you the six hundred anyway, because the abbot's letter says to, and he says that a man who will tell this at Ganda can tell it at the palace if he is asked, and that the abbey looks after its witnesses. What the abbot does about the boxes is the abbot's affair.
The book

A monk is copying a new book in the porch for the light: the abbot Einhard's own account of how the martyrs came out of Rome and what they did afterwards. He reads a little of it aloud to anyone who stands still.
Four books of it. The notary at the tomb by night, the priest of Soissons with his hand in the box, the blood, the dreams, the blind, the lame. He leaves out nothing that happened on land.
The boat to Ganda? They came there, he says, and the day. No shipman's name. A notary has a name. A blind man has a name. Boats arrive.
Of the box that went to Soissons he writes with great anger and very little ink. He names a wind, and Frisians in general.
He has heard that Soissons shows the same martyrs. He writes that God knows where his saints lie, and that he, Einhard, also knows.
And the archchaplain is archchaplain no longer. He stood with the emperor's sons in the year of the troubles and lost his abbeys for it. They say he will have some of them back. Great men float.
The abbot himself was here in the spring, sick, and could not ride. He had the sheets of the cures brought to his bed and corrected the Latin.
Ask him to read the part about the river again
Pay him to copy the leaf with the blind man of the coast on it (20 d)
Send three hundred pennies to Ganda for a lamp before the martyrs, wherever they lie

He reads it again, slowly, a finger under each word, and puts it into your tongue after. You begin to hear where one word stops and the next begins. When he tires of it he asks you a riddle about a chest that is full of wisdom and has none itself, and goes back to his ruling.

One leaf, ruled and written in an afternoon: Germar, blind, from the coast of the Frisians by the mouth of the Scheldt, and the day he saw. The monk points to the place where it says they came. That, he says, is you. It is the word for arriving.

The monk writes it down as given by a shipman for the lamp of the martyrs, and asks which house you mean. You say Ganda. He says oil burns the same before any box, and that the martyrs at least will know where to look for it.
The bones of two martyrs of Rome have come by boat to Saint Bavo's at Ganda. They say the blind see there.
The martyrs that the abbot of Ganda sent to his own house have turned up at Soissons. They say a Frisian boat lost her way in the Scheldt, and found it again in the Seine.
A river landing under a Roman wall on a spring morning; a thin young deacon holds a long box sewn in waxed linen against his chest and talks up to a Frisian in a small boat; grain sacks behind him.
The same boat at a busy landing, grey noon; a well-fed priest in a good dark cloak sits on the gunwale holding out a small purse; far up the bank the deacon walks away with his back turned.

The boat under sail at dusk on a wide river; the deacon stands at the stern singing over the stern board; a sick boy reaches two fingers toward the linen; the steersman watches the box, not the river.
A cloth spread on a muddy landing in flat afternoon light; small bones, a tooth and a knot of hair, each with a parchment strip; a lean southern man with a mule holds up two bundles of red silk.
A beach of drawn-up boats under dunes, a windy bright day; a blind man in a short Frisian cloak, led by a small child, turns his face up to a boat's stern; boatmen look away.
The boat afloat at the edge of a wide strand, the tide running out past her; on the sand a priest stands beside a horse and a servant; up the path, small, a church with its door shut; evening light.

Night in the bottom of the boat under a slack sail; four bundles of red silk side by side on the boards, two with parchment labels; a merchant's hands above them; the priest's shape against the stars, a bag at his feet.
The small boat hard pressed among sandbanks under a lead sky; white water on the shoals; three men looking back at the stern board instead of ahead.
A riverbank landing on the Channel coast, cold morning; a toll man with a tally stick looks at the water; beside him a young clerk reads from an unfolded letter and points at the boat's stern.

Where two rivers meet, bright July noon; canons in white stand along the bank with lit candles; boys run in the shallows; the small boat comes in with the long box at her stern and a blind man in her bows.

ENDING, Saint Bavo: inside a low stone church at Ganda; the box under a cloth before the altar among many candles, two crutches leaning by the door; the steward reads a short letter to a Frisian while a canon writes a list.

ENDING, Soissons: the landing of Saint-Denis in autumn light; an ox cart with a white cloth turned back from the sealed box; a cellarer counts pennies in tens on the cart's tail; the priest of Soissons smiles; nobody kneels.

ENDING, two saints: the steward's room at Ganda; he holds one letter in each hand and looks from one to the other; the Frisian stands before him with a closed face and one hand shut on something small.
A church porch in clear morning light; a monk at a sloped desk copies from one book into another, a finger on the line; a merchant stands listening with his cap in his hand; the river beyond.
The wax booth

A Wend sits before a stack of wax cakes, each as big as a loaf and stamped with a thumb. He has a tally in his hand and a Saxon beside him to carry his words, and he has been watching your boat since she came in.
He says: sit. He says a man who stands before a Wend's booth is either buying or counting, and he would rather you were buying. His name is Dragomir. Mine does not matter. I am the mouth.
He says: this is his booth, the third from the water. His father's was the fifth. A family that moves two booths nearer the water in one lifetime is doing well enough.

He says: he is here for one moon with wax, because the Danes pay in silver and his own people pay in more wax. His booth is at Reric, on the Wends' shore, the third from the water. Any child there will show you.

He says: you come from where the iron is good. Axes, adzes, shears, knives that keep an edge. Our smiths make iron out of bog and it shows. Bring him tools from the Rhine and he will pay in wax and marten, and you may choose the skins yourself.

He says: your emperor has given our prince the Saxons' land beyond the Elbe. It is good land and it has not seen a plough for four years. He wants ploughshares, axes, sickles. He will pay in wax and marten, and you may choose the skins yourself.

He says: your emperor has also said that your merchants may come no nearer to us than Bardowick, and may bring no blades. He says a ploughshare is not a blade. He says also that a boat does not pass through Bardowick. He asks if he has understood your law.

He says: you will pay toll here to Prince Thrasco's man, and Thrasco's man sends a part of it over the water to the king of the Danes, so that the Danes go on thinking this beach is worth more to them whole. He says it has worked so far.
Take his order: six crates of Rhineland tools, brought to his booth at Reric
Buy three cakes of his wax now (75 d) and promise nothing
Buy nothing, eat at his table and learn ten words of his tongue

Dragomir cuts a notch in his tally and breaks the stick down its length. He keeps one half and gives you the other. Six crates of tools. He names no day: a Frisian comes when the wind lets him, he says, like weather.

Three cakes at twenty-five pennies, weighed on his scale and then on yours. The scales agree, which surprises both of you. The Saxon says his own people have a riddle about what the bees carry home from the groves, and gives it to you for nothing, since you bought.

Millet, smoked eel, honey in the comb and a sour drink you do not ask about. By the end you can say bread, salt, boat, wax, how much, too much, and four words the Saxon will not put into Frisian. Honey is cheap on this shore once the bees are taken, and he tells you when that is.
Iron for wax

Dragomir's booth is the third from the water at Reric: a sunk floor, a roof of reed, a stack of wax as high as a man's belt. He knows your boat before she grounds, and by the time you have her made fast his wife has set out bread and honey.
I have learned Danish since you saw me. It is easier than keeping a Saxon. I have my half of the stick. Have you the other half, and what goes with it?
The Frisian who buys nothing and remembers the way back. I have learned Danish since you saw me. It is easier than keeping a Saxon. Sit down.
My brother has land over the Elbe now, Saxon land. He cut the first furrow with a share made of bog iron and it bent like a wet reed. He has spoken of nothing else since.
A tenth of what you sell, for Prince Thrasco. Of that tenth a part goes over the water to the Dane. We pay a wolf to stay a dog. It is cheaper than a wall.

The Dane king lay at the Slie with all his ships and all his horses, the summer your emperor wanted to talk to him, and would not go and talk. A man who will not talk has decided something. I should like to know what.
We do not swear quickly here. A man who swears quickly has done it before. When we do swear we swear over water, because water goes everywhere and tells everyone.
Hand over six crates of tools for six cakes of wax and a timber of marten
Give him two crates as a guest's gift and ask no price
Tell him plainly you have brought no iron, and eat his bread

He tries every edge on his thumbnail and every axe on the doorpost, and is in no hurry. Then six cakes of wax and forty marten skins on a cord, and he lets you choose the skins as he said. The two halves of the tally go into the fire together. Among the Wends, he says, that means the next bargain needs no stick.

He looks at the two crates a long time. Then he fills a bowl from the bay, sets it between you, and says over it that your boat has a booth at Reric as long as his has a roof. His wife sends three crocks of honey down to the boat. He teaches you the words for what he swore, so that you know what you are held to.
He nods. 'A man who says he has nothing has at least that.' You eat his bread. Tools are still wanted on this beach, and still dear.
Ships called out

There are more hulls on the strand than the trade can account for, and the men tarring them are not shipmen: they hold the brush like a spear. Shields are stacked under a sail. Asulf the dealer is buying rope by the coil and paying without weighing twice.
Rope. A man in my trade never has enough rope in a year like this one. I will say no more than that. It would not be useful to me to say more.
You trade east, I think. You know the Wends' beach, the one with the wax. It is a good beach. I have always said it was a good beach.
A Frisian. Then you are the emperor's man, whether you know it or not. Sell your wine. Count your pennies. Do not count ships.
If you have bread or ale aboard, sell it today. A fleet eats like a fire. By the new moon they will be gone and you will be feeding it to pigs.
Stand Asulf a jar of ale (15 d) and ask where a man buys so much rope for
Ask the king's man to his face where the ships are bound
Ask nothing: an army eats, and you have things to sell

Asulf drinks slowly. 'The king goes against the Wends as soon as the hay is in. The Wilzi go with him for nothing: they have hated Thrasco's people longer than we have. There will be strongholds, and I will need the rope. And last of all the beach. The king says a market that pays him a part can pay him the whole, nearer home.' He puts the jar down. 'You did not hear it from me. You heard it from the ale.'

He laughs, which you had not expected. 'East. The Wends. Everyone on this strand knows it but the Wends.' Then he looks at you again. 'You trade on their beach. The king will want to know which booths are worth the carrying and which have a chest under the floor. A man could walk that beach before we come, and count. He would not be forgotten when the taking is shared.'

'Whose man asks?' Two of his fellows have come up behind you. It takes two ounces of silver, cut from your own purse and laid on his palm, to make you a wine seller again. But a man does not guard a secret so hard unless it lies near, and he looked east when he said it. East is the Wends, and the Wends have one beach worth the trouble.
Bread and ale are going at half as much again as they should, and nobody haggles. You sell and ask nothing. The ships are somebody else's business.
A word on the beach

Reric trades as it always has: wax, furs, people, pitch smoke, a Saxon quarrelling over a weight. Children are catching crabs under the boats. You are the only man on the beach who knows what the rope at the Danish landing is for.
You have a face like a man with a stone in his shoe. Sit. Eat first. Whatever it is will still be true after bread.
The Frisian. You look at my booth the way a man looks at a horse he has heard is sick. If you have something to say, say it in Danish. I have enough of it now.
A quiet summer. The toll is good. The Dane's part went over the water at the last full moon, as always, and his man took it and said nothing, as always.
If there is trouble it will come by land, from the Wilzi, as it does. The prince is watching the east. Nobody comes at Wends from the sea. What would they want? Wax?
Tell Dragomir alone, after dark, and let him do as he thinks best
Say it aloud before Thrasco's man and the whole beach
Walk the beach and count the booths for the king's man
Say nothing, sell out your cargo and be gone before the moon changes

He hears it through without moving. 'I cannot go. If I go, my neighbours ask why, and then the prince's man asks, and then I am the Wend who ran from a Frisian's story. But wax can go.' Before light, six cakes of his best wax and three cords of marten are under your boards. 'Sell it in the west. Keep the silver. If you are right I will need it. If you are wrong, bring it back and I will laugh at you every year until one of us is dead.'

Thrasco's man hears you out with his arms folded. It is an old woman who settles it, a seller of combs: she says the Dane's man took the toll at the full moon and did not count it, and a man who does not count what he is given expects to come back for the rest. Nobody laughs after that. For three nights boats go out loaded and come back light. The way behind the island is narrow and they show it to you, since you may need it too.

Thrasco's man says it loudly, for the beach: a Frisian is the Franks' man, the Franks want this trade at their own posts on the Elbe, and here is a Frisian with a tale to empty the beach. Men turn back to their scales. Only Dragomir comes to the boat after dark, with six cakes of wax and three cords of marten. 'I do not know if you are right. I know you had nothing to gain by saying it. Sell these in the west and keep the silver for me.'

Forty-one booths. Nine with a chest that has a lock. Eleven boats fit for the open sea. Two storehouses the prince's man keeps for the toll. You cut it on a stick in your own marks. Nobody asks why a Frisian walks so slowly. Dragomir's wife gives you a honey cake as you pass.
It is not your beach and they are not your people. You sell the last of the wine a little dear, because you are in no mood to haggle and it shows, and take the boat out on the morning wind.
Sails in the bay

At first light the bay is full of ships, more than you have seen in one water. There is no fight worth the name. By noon the king's men are going from booth to booth with a tally, and wax, furs, scales, looms, anvils and people are going down to the water. The king sits his horse on the rise behind the beach in a red cloak and watches it done. He does not come down.

Hear the king's word. This market is closed. The king has a better harbour for it, at the head of the Slie, and every merchant here is his guest there from today. You will load what is yours. What you cannot load will burn.
The king has had a part of this beach's toll for many years. He has thought about it, and he finds he would like all of it.
The Frisian with the stick. Forty-one, you said, and nine with locks. We found the nine. Load beside the king's ships, and stay near me.
A Frisian boat. The emperor's man on the Wends' beach. The king's word is for every merchant here. I did not hear him say 'except Frisians.'

They hanged Godelaib. A chief, taken by a trick and hanged like a thief. Thrasco is gone, nobody knows where. The Dane lost a brother's son at one of our strongholds, and he is making the beach pay for the boy.

The boats are behind the island, and the chests, and the old woman with the combs. There is nothing in my booth but a broken pot. Let him burn the pot. Come now, the way is narrow and the tide is going.
Take the king's peace: load where his men point and sail with the fleet
Slip the cable in the dark and row for the open bay
Say a Frisian is no Wend, and lay five ounces of silver (60 d) on the king's tally
Lie behind the island with the Wends' boats until the smoke is gone

You load. A king's man cuts a notch for your boat on the same stick as the Wends' boats, between a honey seller and a man with two looms. Behind you the reed roofs go up one after another, quickly, the way reed does. Nobody on the water looks back for long.

No moon, the ebb running, rags on the oar looms. A guard ship lies across the channel with a fire in a pot on her foredeck, and the men round the fire cannot see past it. You go by so close that you hear one of them say the Wends' ale is thin. By first light there is open water under you and smoke behind.

The guard ship is not where she lay at dusk. She is across the channel, and her men are awake. Somebody's spear shaft finds your ribs. The steersman takes four ounces of your silver, for the king's trouble, and sets you back in the line. 'You go to the Slie. Tonight or tomorrow. Tomorrow you keep your teeth.'

He weighs the silver in his hand, not on a scale, and looks up the rise. The red cloak does not move. 'The king gives the Frisian leave to go where he likes. The king says also: there is no market here now. When the Frisian wants wax, he will find it on the Slie.' The notch for your boat is cut off the stick with a knife.

Two days in the reeds with forty Wend boats, no fires, the children kept quiet with honey. On the second evening the smoke comes over the island, low and brown. On the third morning the bay is empty. The king has burned forty-one roofs and a broken pot, and has carried nobody to the Slie.

On the second day a Danish boat noses round the point, eight oars, looking for somewhere to water. She sees you before you see her. Her steersman looks at forty hidden hulls and then at the silver you are holding up. He takes the silver. He is a man with a farm, he says, not the king's dog, and he has seen nothing but reeds.
News from the east
A shipman in from the Baltic has news. He has told it four times today and is glad to tell it a fifth, with his hands.

This summer the king of the Danes went over the water against the Wends with all his ships. He took strongholds and hanged a chief, and he lost a brother's son doing it. And before he went home he burned the market at Reric to the sand.

He did not kill the merchants. He put them in the ships, with their scales and their wives, and set them down at the head of the Slie. He says it is their market now. A man steals a hive that way: he takes the bees and burns the tree.
Some got their goods out beforehand, they say. Sent them west in a stranger's boat. I should not like to be that stranger, or else I should like it very much. It depends on the stranger.
And he is building a wall. From the one sea to the other, they say, with one gate in it for carts. I have not seen it. I have seen the men digging.
And the Wends' prince is dead, Thrasco. He came back, and the Dane's men killed him on that same beach. So there was still something there to come back to.
Ask after a Wend named Dragomir, with a booth third from the water
Buy four cakes of wax from him (80 d), and do not ask whose it was
Hear him out and say nothing

'Third from the water? There is no third from the water. There is no water's edge with a booth on it.' He thinks. 'They are all at the Slie now, those that lived. Ask there. Ask for the Wends' strand. You will smell the wax.'
Twenty pennies the cake. Each has a thumb pressed into it, the way one man on that beach marked his wax. You do not look at the thumb for long.
You hear him out. Wax is cheap on the Slie this season, he says, with so much of it come in at once and so few of its owners in a state to haggle.
In the king's wake

The fleet goes north along the land in a long line: the king's ships, then the Wends' own boats rowed by their owners, low in the water with everything they have. The guard ships keep the outside of the line, like dogs.
Frisian! Close up. A gap in the line is a thing I have to explain, and I do not like explaining.

Look there, and do not stare. The ship with the shields turned inward. That is Reginold going home, the king's brother's son. He went first up a wall. The king liked him better than his own sons, they say. I have heard it from more than one. It is why the beach burned so thoroughly.
Now, that guard ship. I know her. Her steersman is from my fjord, and I know him too. He counts well at noon and badly at dusk. He always did.

A sail astern, off the point. One of theirs. She has seen us, and she has twice our oars. Now, there is shoal water to the south that would take us and not her. I am nearly sure of it. Or there may not be. It has been some years.
You there, the small boat! Every hull in these waters goes to the Slie this week. King's word. You seem to be going somewhere else.
Keep your place in the line
Drop astern at dusk, a boat's length at a time, and turn away with the dark
Run for it over the shoal water where she cannot follow
Heave to and say you are bound for the Slie like all the rest
You close up. The Wend in the boat ahead has a loom lashed across his thwarts and a goat standing in the bows. The goat looks at you all the way to the Slie.

A boat's length. Another. The guard ship's steersman counts the line at dusk and gets the number he wants. When the last light goes you put the helm over and let the land breeze take you. In the morning there is nobody on the water but gulls.

He counts better at dusk than Ravn remembered. The guard ship comes down on you under oars, and a spear stands in your planking a hand from the steersman's knee. It costs you a gift to have it called a mistake. She rows beside you from there to the Slie.

The shoal is where Ravn said it might be. You go over it with a hand's depth to spare and the lead going all the time. The guard ship stops at the edge like a horse at a ditch. Her steersman shouts something. The wind is the wrong way to hear it.

There is a shoal, but the tide is over it, and she comes across after you without slowing. Twice your oars. Her steersman takes four ounces for making him sweat and puts you in the line behind a boat full of looms. 'Next time, be a faster boat.'

You back the oars and wait for her. 'Bound for the Slie, like everyone. We lost the line in the dark.' He looks at your boat, which is too small to be worth his doubt. 'Then find it again. That way.' He has forgotten you before you have the sail up.
Set down

On the strand at Sliesthorp the king's men are pacing out plots with a knotted rope and driving hazel rods at the corners. The people of Reric sit on what they carried and wait to be told which rods are theirs. Up the slope, men with spades are standing in a line that runs out of sight to the west.

Each merchant has a plot, four rods by eight, with its short end to the water. Build on it before the frost and hold it over the winter and it is yours by the king's word. Leave it empty and it goes to a man who wants it.

The king is closing his border with a wall, from the eastern water to the western sea. One gate in it, for carts and riders. Every leader has his length to build, and every guest of the king owes days on it, or the price of a man's days.
So. You were right, and I am alive to say it. I will not ask about the wax today. A man who asks on the first day has already decided he was robbed.

I have a scale, a wife, and a tally with nothing to count. The Dane calls me his guest. In my tongue we have the same word for guest and for stranger. In his, I think, there is one for guest and cattle.
You were not there. Good. One fewer to feed on the way.

Not everyone from that shore came as a guest. Those taken at the strongholds are mine to sell. There is a boy in the pen, ten winters, who says his mother's brother is a merchant on this strand. They all say that. This one may be right.
Forty-one booths, I hear, and nine locks. That was neat work. The spokesman has not forgotten it. Nor have I. I like a man who counts.
Have a rod driven for yourself: a plot of the king's, and your days owed at the wall
Tell Dragomir his wax and furs are safe in the west and will come back to him as silver
Buy his sister's son out of Asulf's pen (90 d) and bring the boy to him
Go to the spokesman and ask what a count of forty-one booths is worth

Four hazel rods and a notch on the king's tally: a Frisian's plot between a honey seller's and a comb maker's. You owe six days at the wall, or a man to do them. Hold the plot over the winter and come back when the ice is out of the Slie.

He looks at you for the time it takes to count to ten. 'You came here to say it. You could have sailed past the mouth of the Slie and I would never have known whether the sea took you.' He asks for no oath. 'You came back. That is the oath.' Come again when the goods are sold, he says. He is not going anywhere.

Asulf names seven and a half ounces and does not say it twice. The rope comes off. The boy's name is Ratimir and he does not speak until he sees his uncle, and then he does not stop. Dragomir puts his hand on the boy's head and looks at you over it, and says nothing for some time. Come back in the spring, he says at last. He will have thought of what to say.

'When the taking is shared,' the spokesman says. 'After the wall is begun. Two moons. You will be called after the ships' leaders and before the cooks.' When you turn round, Dragomir is standing by his rods. He has seen whom you went to, and he has worked out the rest.
Word by merchants
The king's spokesman comes down to your boat himself, which he has not done before, and sends his men out of hearing. He has washed and put on a clean shirt. It is that kind of errand.
The border is shut and envoys do not cross it. Merchants do. A merchant can walk into a count's hall with a king's words in his head and nobody has to say that an envoy was received.

Say this at Dorestat, to the count, for the emperor. The king of the Danes has heard that the emperor is angry because he led his army against the Wends last summer. The king wishes to clear himself. It was the others who first broke the peace. Let counts from each side meet beyond the Elbe, at the border, and what was done wrong on either side be put right.
There is a piece of an arm-ring for the carrying. More, if an answer comes back by the same boat. The king remembers who is useful. He also remembers the other kind.
If you carry his words, carry six of mine. Tell the Franks: the Wends on the Slie are held, not settled. They gave our prince a sword once. Let them remember whose merchants these are.
Carry the king's word to the count at Dorestat, as it was said and no more
Carry the king's word, and Dragomir's with it: that the Wends on the Slie are held, not settled
Say you sell wine and are nobody's mouth
He has you say it back twice. Then a piece cut from a silver arm-ring, three ounces and a little, still warm from his arm. 'The count at Dorestat. Not his clerk.'

The spokesman has you say his words back twice and gives you a piece of an arm-ring for them. Dragomir gives you nothing and has you say his back once. Two messages in one head, and only one of them paid for.
'Then sell wine,' he says, and goes back up the strand. He will find another boat. With the border shut there is not much wine on the Slie this year, and what there is goes dear.
The count's hall

The count hears you standing, in the hall above the river, with a clerk at his elbow who writes on wax and does not look up. Through the door you can hear the toll being argued on the dam, as it is every day.
He sends me a wine seller. Not a kinsman with a white shield. A wine seller. So he wants to be heard and does not want to be seen asking.

It will go to the emperor. I think he will send counts to meet theirs, since it costs nothing, and I think nothing will come of it. A man who builds a wall first and asks to talk afterwards has finished talking.
And what did the merchant see, on the way to being given these words? A wall? How long? How many gates? Ships, drawn up or in the water? We have men who are paid to find out such things and do not.
'Held, not settled.' That is well said for a Wend. Thrasco is the emperor's friend and those are Thrasco's people. It will go in the same letter. I do not say anyone will ride for them.
Give the king's words as they were given, and nothing of your own
Give the words, and then everything you saw: the wall, the one gate, the ships on the strand
Say you were given words for the count and would as soon be rid of them: let the clerk have them, and go

You say it as it was said. The clerk's stylus stops when you stop. The count has five shillings counted out for you and tells the toll man that your boat is to be dealt with gently until Martinmas. 'A man who brings a message and adds nothing to it. I had heard there were such men.'

You tell it all: the turf wall and the men on it, the one gate, the plots on the strand, the hulls you counted without meaning to. The clerk fills three tablets. Ten shillings from the count's own purse, and the toll made light for half a year. As you go out the clerk is already reading it back to a man you do not know, and you think of how many people can read wax.
You say the words to the clerk in the doorway, once, quickly, the way a man puts down something heavy. The count does not get up. You are back at your boat before the tide turns.
The king's new town

A winter has gone over the rods on the strand. There are roofs between them now, a plank road down to the water, a jetty begun, and smoke from forty hearths that burned last year on another shore. Up the slope the wall is a green bank with a ditch before it, as far as you can see.
You held your plot. Not all did. The king said the first comers would be remembered, and I am the one who does his remembering.

A count's clerk at Dorestat has three tablets about our wall, I am told, and they are in your words. You may keep your plot. The king's word is the king's word. But a man does not get the king's gift for counting the king's ships.
