So we are neighbours, Frisian. I did not choose my plot and you chose yours. It is the only difference between us, and it is a large one. Still, the wax sells. The Dane was right about the harbour. I hate him for that as well.
Six cakes of wax and three cords of marten went west in your boat. I see you have a plot and a new roof. I do not ask. I only count, and I am a patient man.
Thrasco is dead. He came back to our beach, to what was left, and the Dane's men killed him there. So there is nobody now to ask for us.

The king is dead, by one of his own house. Hemming his brother's son has the kingdom, and twelve of ours have sworn peace with twelve Franks on the Eider. The gate is open. The town stays where it is. A dead king's word still holds a plot.
Hold the plot by the king's word, free of the landing gift, as the first comers were promised
Build on the plot: a house and a store among the Wends' booths
Sell the plot to a Saxon who wants it more, and stay a guest

He says it before witnesses on the strand, which is how a thing is written here: the Frisian's boat owes no gift at this landing, by the king's word, while his house holds the plot. A winter's trade off the plot comes to three hundred pennies by weight and four cords of marten. At Dorestat they will say you are the Dane's man. For a year or two they will be right.

Oak posts, wattle, a reed roof, a store with a door that locks. Four hundred pennies by weight from the winter and eight cakes of wax owed you by neighbours who paid in what they had. A roof of your own on the Slie, on ground a king took from nobody in particular. At Dorestat they will say you are the Dane's man.

A Saxon with two sons pays seven hundred pennies by weight for four hazel rods and the right to stand between them. You keep a guest's seat at the landing and owe nobody days on a wall. Nobody in Frisia can say whose man you are, which in these years is worth something.
Faith kept

Dragomir has a roof on the Slie now, lower than the one that burned. He sets out bread and honey as he did at Reric, and talks of the weather, and does not ask the question he has waited two hundred days to ask.
Eat. I have told my wife every week that the Frisian will come. She has told me every week that the sea is wide and silver is heavy. One of us is about to be unbearable to live with.
The boy eats like a wolf and has learned to swear in Danish. My sister is alive. She walked eleven days to find out whether he was. You did that, and I have still not thought of what to say.

My kin's wax came round this autumn in Holmfast's boat, the Svea. He weighed it three times and charged me for two. So I have goods again, and a strand to sell them on, and no boat I would trust past the point.
I want a way home that does not go through the Dane's gate. A boat does not go through gates. You have a boat, and I have what goes in one.
He will not say it, so I will. We had nothing when they set us down. If we have something now it is because one stranger did what he said.
They killed Thrasco on our beach, the Dane's men, when he came back. I have no prince now. I have a partner, if he will have me. It is a smaller thing, and it is more use.
Count out the whole price of his goods (480 d) and take nothing for the carrying
Count out the price less a fair freight (360 d)
Say the boy was a gift, and ask what a Wend and a Frisian might carry together
Tell him the silver is not all there yet: give him your hand on it, and a year

Forty shillings, counted onto his table in fours. He weighs none of it. 'And the freight?' There is none. He is quiet. Then he fills a bowl with water and swears over it, slowly, as his people do when they mean it: half of what his boat carries is yours, half of what yours carries is his, for as long as both float. Eight cords of marten, ten cakes of wax and four sacks of amber go down to your boat as the first lading. His wife takes a ring of twisted silver from her temple and puts it in your hand. It was on her head when the beach burned.

Thirty shillings on the table and ten kept for the carrying. He nods: it is what he would have asked himself, and he says so. He swears partnership over a bowl of water, and five cords of marten and six cakes of wax go down to your boat. 'A fair man,' he tells his wife in his own tongue. You have enough of it now to know he said fair, and not more than fair.

'A gift.' He says the word in Danish and then in his own tongue, to hear whether it means the same in both. Then a bowl of water between you, and the oath: half of his lading yours, half of yours his, while both boats float. Four cords of marten and six cakes of wax go down to your boat that evening. The boy carries the wax and will not be helped.

He looks at your hand before he takes it. 'A year. I have waited two hundred days; I know how to do it now.' He will keep a corner of his store for your goods meanwhile. It is a kindness, and it is also a place where he can see them. His wife does not come out to see you off.
Reric holds

A Wend boat lies at the landing with new wax in her and a face you know at the steering oar. Dragomir has been asking for a Frisian boat at every beach for a month, and has a speech ready that he does not, in the end, make.
There. I told them: a small boat, a Frisian, a man who looks as if he is adding something up. They said that is every Frisian. But here you are.
You see? Third from the water. The posts are new and the reed is green, and the pot is mended. Sit. This time you will eat until you cannot stand.

He burned forty-one roofs. A roof is reed, and we have reed: the place is named for it. He found nine chests, as someone must have told him he would. There was sand in them. He stood on the rise a long time, they say. Then he went home.

I called you a tale-bearer in my heart, Frisian, before the old woman spoke. I say it aloud now so that it is not between us. The beach owes you. A beach pays slowly, but it does not forget where it stands.

The Dane knows a stranger warned us. He does not know which stranger. I would keep clear of his landing until he is tired of asking. Kings tire. Or they die. This one has many friends who would be glad of either.
They say he had plots marked out on the Slie for us, with rods. A whole strand of rods, and nobody to stand between them. I should like to have seen it.
Take what the beach offers: a booth in your own name, third from the water, and Dragomir's hand as a partner
Take no ground on a beach a king has marked: a partner, and a lading
Ask only for what you used: the way through the shoals behind the island

The beach gives you the plot beside Dragomir's, which makes it third from the water and his the fourth. He says nothing about that, and it is the largest gift of all. Eight cords of marten, twelve cakes of wax and eight crocks of honey, brought by forty-one households, each a little. Dragomir swears partnership over a bowl filled from the bay. The Danish king will hear a Frisian has a booth at Reric, and will draw his own conclusion.

'Wise,' says Thrasco's man. 'He came once.' Dragomir fills a bowl from the bay and swears: half his lading yours, half yours his, while both boats float. Ten cords of marten and eight cakes of wax go into your boat, and his boat follows yours out past the island the next morning.

They laugh, and load you all the same: six cords of marten and six cakes of wax. And an old Wend sits at your steering oar for a month and takes you through every gut and over every bar of the bay, at every state of the tide, until you could do it in fog. You come out of it knowing the water and most of his tongue.
The finder's share

The taking of Reric is shared out on the strand, by tally, with a scale on a tripod. The king's spokesman calls the leaders of the ships first, then the men who were useful. The Wends watch from between their rods. They have not been asked to, and nobody has told them to stop.
The Frisian who counted. Forty-one booths and nine locks, and it was as he said, to the booth. The king does not forget a true count.
There is silver, by weight. There is a Wend boat by the rods there, sound, whose owner will not be needing her to go anywhere. Choose. Not both; you are useful, you are not a ship's leader.
Or take all silver, and put your goods in my store. My man watches it day and night; he has to, for the pen. You count and I keep. We need never like each other.

I gave you bread. My wife gave you a honey cake while you were counting us. I will not swear anything about you, Frisian. I will only tell it, over water, to every Wend who comes to this strand. Water goes everywhere.
Take the Wend boat drawn up by the rods, and fifty ounces of silver
Take silver, and Asulf's offer: a corner of his store and his man to watch it
Take the silver and the king's peace, and nothing that had an owner you knew

Fifty ounces on the scale, and the boat: clinker-built of oak, pegged with wood in the Wends' way, sweet in her lines. Her owner stands between his rods and watches you run your hand along her strakes. He rowed her here himself. No Wend on the Slie will sell to you or buy from you after today.

Seventy-five ounces on the scale. Asulf shows you your corner: dry, barred, and one wall away from the pen. You can hear them through it. 'You stop noticing,' he says. No Wend on the Slie will sell to you or buy from you after today.

A little under sixty ounces, and the spokesman's word before witnesses that the Frisian's boat goes in the king's peace wherever the king's ships are. You leave the boat where she lies. It makes no difference to her owner, or to what he tells the others over water.
This year the king of the Danes burned the Wends' market at Reric, and put its merchants in his ships, and set them down at Sliesthorp.
The king of the Danes came to the Wends' market at Reric with his ships and found the booths empty. He burned them and went home. They say a stranger warned the beach.
The merchants the Danish king carried off from Reric have roofs at Sliesthorp now and a plank road to the water. There is a Frisian plot among them.
A Wend of the Slie and a Frisian shipman have sworn partnership over water. The Wend says the Frisian carried his goods out of Reric before the fire and brought back the price.
The Wends are trading at Reric again under new reed. The strand the Danish king marked out for them at Sliesthorp stands empty, and wax is dear there.

A beach market on a summer afternoon: a wide-faced Wend in a fur-edged cap sits before a stack of round wax cakes with a wax tally in his hand, a thin Saxon crouched at his shoulder; behind them sunk huts with reed roofs and boats drawn up on the sand.

Inside a sunk booth at Reric, light from the door: the Wend tries an axe edge on his thumbnail, crates of iron tools open on the floor, a bowl of water between him and the merchant; his wife, silver rings at her temples, sets down bread and honey.

A Danish strand in spring under a grey sky: a row of long hulls being tarred, shields stacked under a sail, a stout dealer with a plaited beard and a hazel switch counting coils of rope while a king's man with a spear looks straight out at us.

The beach at Reric at dusk in early summer, calm: booths, cooking fires, children catching crabs under the boats; in the foreground the Frisian and the Wend stand close and speak low, an island dark across the bay behind them.

Reric at noon in high summer: the bay crowded with striped sails and long ships, armed men carrying wax, looms and chests down to the water, the first reed roofs alight; on the rise behind, small and still, a horseman in a red cloak.
A landing on a windy autumn day: a shipman tells his news with both hands spread wide to a ring of listeners; at his feet a few cakes of wax, each with a thumbprint; grey water and one sail behind.

Evening at sea, low red light: a long line of ships going north along a flat coast, a Wend boat ahead with a loom lashed across her thwarts and a goat in the bows, a guard ship with shields along her side keeping the outside of the line.

The strand at Sliesthorp on a dull late-summer morning: two king's men stretch a knotted rope and drive hazel rods, Wendish families sit on bundles and looms waiting, a rope pen of captives to one side; up the slope a line of men with spades.

A spring morning at the jetty at Sliesthorp, mist on the water: a Dane in a clean shirt and a good cloak stands close to the merchant at the boat's side, cutting a piece from a silver arm-ring; his armed men wait out of hearing.

A timber hall at Dorestat, daylight through the door: a grey Frankish count on a bench leans forward, a tonsured clerk beside him writes on a wax tablet without looking up, the merchant stands before them cap in hand; the river and masts beyond.

Sliesthorp a year on, a bright cold morning with the ice just gone: new wattle houses in rows with their short ends to the water, a plank road, smoke from many roofs, a Frisian boat at a half-built jetty; a green earth wall along the skyline.

A low new house on the Slie, firelight: pennies counted out in fours on a board, a bowl of water between the Wend and the Frisian, the Wend's hand raised over it; his wife holds out a ring of twisted silver wire, a boy watches from the door.

The beach at Reric in clear autumn light: black burnt posts and beside them new booths under green reed, forty boats coming in from behind the island, people carrying wax ashore; a Wend and a Frisian stand at a booth third from the water.

The strand at Sliesthorp, a flat grey afternoon: a scale on a tripod heaped with cut silver, the king's spokesman holding a tally, a Wendish boat drawn up by hazel rods; between the rods a Wend stands with his arms at his sides and looks at the merchant.
A stick from a guest

A Danish skipper in from Ripa walks the dam asking which boat is the Frisian's with the Northman in it. When he finds yours he holds out a stick of ash wood, a hand long, squared, and cut with runes on all four sides.
I was asked to put this in your hand. Not your man's hand. Yours. I was told to say that twice.
Who sent it? A guest. That is the name he gave, and at my age I do not ask a man for a second one.
When you know what it means, say it to the carter at the landing at Ripa. The one with the two red oxen. He will know if you are right. He knows very little else.
Old cutting, this. Look at that sign, the one like a gate with a bar across. Nobody under fifty cuts it so. It says a man went out from home and saw a way of ways.
You had the first one from me, and you got it, and I was glad of that. This is the second. It is not from me. Somebody has been counting.
Take the stick and put it in the chest
Have Ravn read it to you, sign by sign
Say a Frisian carries cloth, not kindling
The stick goes into the chest with the tally sticks, and looks much like them. The Dane nods and goes back to his hides. Ravn watches him all the way down the dam.

Ravn reads it with his thumb, one sign at a time, and makes you say each sound after him. It takes until the tide turns. You know six runes now and one riddle. He does not tell you the answer and he does not say whose hand cut it.
The Dane shrugs and lays the stick on your thwart anyway. "Then burn it," he says, "and say at Ripa that you were cold." It is still there in the morning. Nobody aboard has burnt it.
The carter at the landing

At the landing at Ripa a carter stands by two red oxen with nothing in his cart. He looks at the stick in your belt before he looks at your cargo, and then he looks at the sky, like a man who has been told not to speak first.
Three Frisian boats since the spring and none of them had a stick. I had begun to think he had sent it by a fool.
This is how it goes. You say the answer. If it is right I give you what he left and the next stick. If it is wrong I still give you the next stick, but I am allowed to laugh.
You have the look of a man who knows. Go on. I drive over one twice a day, so do not try to tell me it is something else.
You have the look of a man who has carried a thing a long way without opening it. Well. That is my trade too.
Give him the answer
Buy the ale and let him say it himself (4 d)
Say you do not know, and help him load instead

He slaps the near ox for joy. Out of his shirt come a twist of silver wire, weighed against your own pennies at twenty, and a second stick, shorter, about a beast with too many legs. "And sell your cloth here, not further north. They are short of it till the moon turns."

He drinks your ale and says the answer with his mouth full of bread, so that you are not sure of it even now. Then he gives you the second stick. "He did not say you had to be clever. Only that you had to come."

He laughs, as he was allowed to. You load his cart with another man's hides for an hour. At the end of it he puts the second stick in your hand. "A man who will carry what he does not understand. He will like that, or he will not. I never knew which."
A hail across the water
A Norse ship alters course to pass close under your lee. Her master stands on the stern with one hand on the stay and a stick in the other, and shouts a question over the water.
Frisian! I nearly ran you under. I have been looking for you in this since the morning, which is a joke, and you will see why when you read the stick.
Frisian! One small boat, four men, a Northman at the sheet. He said I could not miss you. He was wrong by nine days.
The carter's one first. Four that walk and four that hang. Shout it, and shout it right, and I will throw you something that shines.
I am for the Slie. The ferryman there has the next, and he is slower than I am. Take wine if you have it. They are drinking water and calling it a virtue.
Shout the carter's answer across
Close with him and take the stick by hand
Hold your course; a strange ship is a strange ship

He roars it back to his own crew, who cheer as if they had bet on it. A ring of silver wire comes over the water and Ravn takes it out of the air. The stick follows, tied to a net float. It is about a huge thing that fears nothing but the wind.

The two hulls touch and part. He hands the stick down himself. "You did not answer. I do not blame you. I shouted mine wrong at the first man too." His ship is a spot on the sea before you have the sail drawing again.

You hold your course. He passes a boat's length off, laughing, and throws the stick. It lands in the bilge. "Careful is good," he shouts. "The old man was never careful and look at him now." He does not say what there is to look at.
The ferry on the Slie

The ferryman on the Slie pushes your pennies back across the thwart. He wants a word from you instead, and under his seat, tied to the rib with tarred cord, there is a small bag that hangs as silver hangs.
No fare. I have been paid for you already, and overpaid. Sit. The crossing is as long as I choose to make it.
You have met a carter, a shipman and me. Did you not wonder? We all sat on one bench when we had hair. The low bench, by the door, in a hall you will see soon enough.
He calls himself Gest on the sticks. A guest. It is not his name. His name you can earn. He taught the four of us to hold a hundred verses in our heads, and we have each kept about six.
There are more spears than merchants on this shore since King Godfred came with his ships. I row them over all the same. A spearman's backside is as heavy as a trader's and pays worse.

After me it is Zealand. Go up the long fjord to Hleidr and ask for the man who cannot count the king's swine. Do not ask at the hall. They will send you to the skald, and the skald will send you home.
Tell him what swallows water and woods and fears the wind
Take the other oar for a day and listen
Pay him to say plainly where the sticks come from (10 d)

He ships his oars in the middle of the water and cuts the bag loose. Ring silver, hacked small: it weighs out at a hundred and twenty pennies. "He said the one who got this far was to be paid as a man is paid, not as a boy." The next stick is about brides in white hoods. He talks Danish at you the whole way back and by the far bank you are following half of it.

You row. He talks. Eleven crossings, a horse that will not board, two fights about the fare. By evening you have a blistered hand, a share of the day's takings and more Danish than you came with. He gives you the stick about the white-hooded brides. The bag stays under his seat. "That was for the answer. This was for the back."

He takes your ten pennies and weighs them, since he does not trust a king's face on silver. "From Hleidr. From an old man by the mounds. There. You have bought with money what the others earned, and it is worth what money is worth." He gives you the stick all the same.
The hand at the cutting

On the night watch Ravn lays the four sticks side by side on the thwart and runs his thumb along the cuts, as a man feels a blade he once owned. He has known whose hand it is since Dorestat. Tonight he looks as if he might say so.
This sign, look. The gate with the bar. I cut it so myself. I cut it so because the man who taught me did, and I was beaten when I did not.
Hroald. He sat at the king's feet at Hleidr and held the old words. Who begot whom. Which verse goes after which. What was sworn, and by whom. Not a skald. A skald makes. Hroald kept.
We had that word at Gyrwe. Thyle. In the old songs he is the man who sits at the king's feet and remembers what everyone else in the hall would rather forget.
I was the best he had. He said so once, to someone else. Then one Yule he asked me a thing before the whole hall, and I answered it. That was the mistake. Not the answer I gave. That I gave one.
Ask him what the last question was
Take his watch at the oar and let him talk or not
Tell him a hand does not keep a secret from the man who pays him

He cuts it for you on the back of a tally stick by the light of the lamp, and reads it out once. It is about what a father said in his dead son's ear. "I said something clever. The hall laughed. Hroald did not. I took ship in the spring and I have not been up that fjord since."

You take the oar. For a long while there is only the water. Then he tells it, all of it, to the sea rather than to you: the bench, the Yule, the question about the father and the dead son, the laughter. Before light he cuts the question on a stick and puts it in your chest himself. "So that there are two of us who cannot answer it."

He looks at you for the time it takes a wave to pass under the boat. "Hroald. Salhaugar, by Hleidr. There is your wage's worth." He gathers the sticks, gives them back to you, and takes the bow watch though it is not his turn. The rest he keeps.
Where the king's swine root
Below the great hall at Hleidr the steward bars the path with his staff. Behind him a swineherd is counting pigs out of a pen, aloud, and does not get the same number twice.
A Frisian with cloth is welcome at the landing. A Frisian with sticks wants something at the hall, and at the hall I am the door.
The ferryman's one, then. The brides who walk the reefs. Old Hroald said that whoever came would know it, and that if he did not know it I was to feed him and send him down the fjord again.
Ten tongues. No. Twenty eyes, that is right, I counted the eyes. It walks, the old man says, and I am to ask what it is. I have it in the pen and I still do not know.
The king drinks here in three nights. Strangers sit by the door and are asked things. If you want the old man, that is the road to him. He does not see anybody the hall has not laughed at first.
Name the white-hooded brides for the steward
Help drive the pigs to the oak wood, and hear his riddle on the way
Give the steward a guest's gift (20 d)

The steward lifts his staff. "By the door, in three nights. Bring your own knife." The swineherd gives you his riddle in a rush, wrong the first time. And a boy brings a broken stick from the midden behind the hall, with the first words gone. "The old man threw that one away himself," the steward says. "So it is likely the best."

Two days in the oak wood behind the king's pigs. Aldger says nothing about it, loudly. The swineherd tells you his riddle nine times, and on the way home he speaks to the steward, who looks at the mud on you and finds a place for you at the feast after all. It is five nights off now, not three.

The steward turns your gift over, finds nothing wrong with it, and is a little disappointed. "By the door, in three nights. I have let in worse for less." The swineherd shouts his riddle after you down the path.
The low bench

You are seated on the low bench by the door, far from the fire, where the draught is. The king is a shape beyond the smoke with gold on his arm. His skald walks the length of the hall with a full horn in his hand and stops in front of you.
This is the bench. Every man the old one taught sat here first. Mind the third plank. It has been loose since my father's day.
A guest from the south, with a chest full of old Hroald's kindling. Then tell the hall what the swineherd has in his pen: ten tongues, twenty eyes, forty feet, and it walks.
He is not here. He does not come since his son died. He kept what other men made, and called it a craft. I make new, and the king pays me for it, and I am told that is the lesser thing.
King Sigfred likes an answer given quickly. He has waited on Franks at their assemblies and says he is done waiting.
King Godfred is listening. He likes to know what a Frank's merchants are made of before he meets the Frank.
The rule of the bench is older than I am. Answer, and something comes down the hall to you. Fail, and this horn does, and you see the bottom of it before you sit.
Answer the swineherd's riddle before the whole bench
Say you cannot, and drink the horn dry for it
Buy the skald's own riddle of him, and ask where the old man sits (12 d)

You say it. There is a silence the length of a breath, then the benches beat the boards. Something bright passes from hand to hand down the hall: an arm-ring off the king's own arm, a hundred and fifty pennies by weight. The skald sets you one of his own to take away, two meanings in every word, and says quietly: "South-east, a morning's walk. The farm by the mounds. Go in two days. He sleeps after a feast he was not at."

The horn holds more than it looks. You see the bottom of it, and then the roof, and then the faces of your crew. The hall likes a man who pays what he owes. The skald, in a good humour, sets you a riddle of his own for the road and tells you where the old man lives. You will remember that part tomorrow, when Ravn tells it to you again.

He takes your silver across the palm of his hand, as he would from any buyer. The riddle he sells has two meanings in every word. "Hroald is at Salhaugar, a morning's walk to the south-east. Tell him his sticks reached the hall. Tell him the hall had other things to talk about."
Salhaugar

At the farm by the mounds an old man sits on a bench in the sun with his face turned a little to the wrong side of you. His eyes are white. A grey stone as long as a man lies by the door, and nothing is cut on it.
A Frisian. I could smell the tar and the cheese from the gate. Sit. I am Hroald. I was the mouth of this hall for forty winters, and now I am an old man who sends sticks to strangers.

Gunnvald had the seat after me. My son. He held everything I gave him and never once got the order wrong. He died at the winter nights with a cough, in bed, like a farmer. That stone is his. I cannot see to have it cut.

What I know is in one place, and the place is seventy years old and coughs too. So I cut riddles and sent them out by men who owed me, to see who would carry a thing from port to port for no pay he could name. A head like that holds. I hoped for a Dane. One takes what washes up.
And he is with you. I know that step. He put his feet down just so thirty winters ago, walking out of the hall. Stand where you are, boy. I am not done with the Frisian.
A man with no stone is gone when the last one who knew him is gone. He wants the name set up. That much any crew with rollers could do for him. We have rollers.
Master, he has it all by heart and nowhere else. At Gyrwe we would call that a library with one candle in it. Calfskin, scraped. I could write it as he says it. I could try.

I can pay. Gunnvald had rings from two kings. He is lying with the best of them, in the new mound, and the rest are in the house. I tell you so you know I am not a beggar. I am told I should not tell people.
Offer your crew and your rollers to set up the son's stone
Say his pupil is standing behind you
Say what is cut in stone lasts, and so does what is written on skin (40 d for calfskins)
Say little, and mark which mound is the new one

"So. Not a head. A back." He is quiet, and then he laughs, the first time. "I asked the sea for a pupil and it sent a carter. Good. There is a man at the hall who cuts. Come again when the moon has been full twice, and bring your rollers."

He turns his white eyes to where Ravn stands. Nobody speaks. "He answered what should not be answered." "He has had thirty winters to think about it," you say. The old man breathes out. "Then let him winter here or come back to it. After Yule, when the days turn, I will ask it once more before the hall. Once." Ravn has not moved. He looks like a man who has been handed something hot.

"Words on a dead calf." He spits. "They will lie there and not say themselves. Nobody will know how the voice goes." Then his hand finds the uncut stone by the door, and stays on it. "But I am having a name cut in a rock so that it lasts. So I am a fool either way. Buy your skins. Have them scraped over the winter. Come when the ice is off the fjord and bring the boy who scratches."

You say what a guest says, and little of it. On the way out you count the mounds. Five old, grown over with thorn. One new, on the south side, where the turf has not knitted. Ravn sees you counting. He does not speak on the walk back.
The new mound
No moon. The new mound is the one on the south side, where the turf has not knitted. There are two wooden spades in the boat for digging ballast, and so far the farm's dogs are quiet.

I will say it once. He will know by the morning. A blind man hears his own ground. And every Dane from here to the Slie will know by the autumn. They will not come for you with spears. They will only stop seeing your boat.
Heathen or not, he is a dead man in his grave and we are four men with spades. I have robbed nobody yet, living or otherwise. I would have liked to die able to say so.
I will not carry one. Not into that ground. I will not stop you either. Those are the two things I can do, and I am doing both.
Dig, quickly, and be down the fjord before light
Pour the ale you brought onto the mound instead, and go
Put the spades back under the thwart and say it was a walk

The turf lifts like a lid. Charred wood, a clay pot, and beside it, not burnt, what the father could not bring himself to put on the fire: rings, twisted and plain, and one broad arm-ring cut with a row of small horns. It weighs out later at eleven hundred pennies and more. You are down the fjord before the cocks. Nobody aboard says a word until the open sea, and then it is only the course.

The dogs. Then torches, and housemen with staves who know their business. When it is over you are on your knees in the yard and the old man is standing over you in his shirt. "I counted your steps going out, Frisian. You counted my mounds." He takes forty pennies for his men's trouble. "And you will haul my son's stone. With that back. Come when the moon has been full twice. You will come." You will.

You pour the ale out on the raw turf, all of it. Aldger looks away and crosses himself. Ravn says something short in his own tongue. Then you go back to the boat. In the morning Ravn says, to nobody: "He needs men with rollers for that stone." It is settled as easily as that.

"It was a walk," you say. "A long one, for a man carrying spades," says Aldger. The spades go back under the thwart. In the morning you send word to the farm that a crew with rollers is at the old man's service for his stone.
Gunnvald's stone

The carver has done. Two rows of runes down the face; above them three horns locked into one another, and a wheel-cross with four bent arms. The stone lies on your rollers at the foot of the mounds, and a hole has been dug for it.
I will read it as it stands, so no man says later it reads otherwise. Gunnvald's stone, Hroald's son's, thul at Salhaugar. I was not told to cut more. I asked.
Put my hand on it. Yes. The gate with the bar across. He has cut it the old way. I told him to. Let them wonder at it when I am gone.
You came. A man who has been in my son's mound to his elbows and still comes back when he is bid. I do not know what you are, Frisian. But you are not a liar. Lift.
That is all of it. His name, mine, the seat, the place. What we held between us is not on it. A stone is not big enough, and no one left has the head for it. So. A name. It is more than most get.
It will stand when the hall has fallen in. Somebody will stop at it and say the name aloud, not knowing who he was. Gunnvald, he will say, and walk on. That is the use of it. It is not nothing.
Raise it with your own crew, and stand while he says the name
Pay the carver yourself, so the old man keeps his son's rings (60 d)
Set it upright, take what is owed and catch the tide

Four men, six rollers, a rope and a morning. It stands. The old man says the name three times, to the south, the west and the north, and then stops, as if the east were someone else's business. He pays in his son's rings, eight hundred pennies by weight, and the steward comes down from the hall to say there is a place for the Frisian under the king's hand whenever he lies at Hleidr. At the gate the old man puts a short stick in your hand. It is not a riddle. It says that cattle die and kinsmen die, and one thing does not.

You pay the carver before the old man can reach for his bag. He stands a while with his mouth working. Then it stands, and he says the name. By evening the hall has heard that a Frisian paid for a Dane's stone, and seven hundred pennies of ring silver come down from the king with the steward and a place under the king's hand. The old man gives you one of the three horns that hung over his seat, silver at the lip. "There are three on the stone," he says. "Now you know where one of them went." And a stick, which is not a riddle: cattle die, kinsmen die, and one thing does not.

It stands. You have a tide. The old man weighs out six hundred pennies of rings without a word more than the weight, and the steward names you a guest of the hall, since that was promised. From the fjord you can see the stone for a long time, grey against the green, with a small bent figure in front of it, talking.
The last question

The hall is full and for once it is quiet. The old man has been led to the middle of the floor, between the fires. He turns his white eyes toward your bench, the low one by the door, and asks what he asked Ravn thirty winters ago.
I ask it once. What did the One-eyed say in his son's ear, before the boy was carried to the fire?
I have a ring on the Northman answering. He answered last time. A man does not change what he is because he has been to sea.
Do not help me. Whatever you see me do, whatever you hear me say, do not help me.
Say nothing. It is Ravn's question
Stand up and say it yourself: no man alive knows that
Whisper Ravn a clever answer to give

Ravn stands. He takes a long time. "No man knows that," he says, "and I did not know it then either." The old man lets out a breath he has held for thirty winters. "There. That is the whole of the craft. To know which things you hold and which you do not, and never to fill the gap with your own noise." The king sends rings down the hall and the old man adds his son's: fourteen hundred pennies by weight. A horn from over the high seat. A place for you under the king's hand. The steward's own son to show you the marks of the fjord. Ravn will sail with you while the old man lives. After that, he says, there is a seat he has to go and sit in.

You stand and say it: no man alive knows that. It is right, and the hall beats the boards, and it was not yours to say. The old man turns his face from you to the place beside you. "The Frisian has a head. But I did not ask the Frisian." Ravn says it then, quietly, after you. It is enough. Twelve hundred pennies in rings, a horn, a guest's place. Ravn does not speak to you until the boat is past the narrows. Then he says: "You meant it well," which from him is a hard word.

You whisper him something neat. He does not turn his head. "No man knows that," he tells the hall. Then, louder: "My master here has a guess, if anyone wants it." The hall laughs at the Frisian until the dogs bark. The old man laughs longest. "Thirty winters ago that was you, boy." Six hundred pennies of rings come down the bench for the man who brought him home, and a guest's place, and the skald pays his lost bet with a good grace, to Ravn.
The calfskin book

Nine days of it. The old man speaks with his eyes shut. Beornwine writes with his tongue between his teeth, and Ravn says each line again slowly, so the boy can hear where one word ends. Now there are five gatherings of calfskin, sewn with flax, and the question of where they go.
Read me one back. Any one. No. That is the words. It is not how it goes. Well. A stone does not say how my son laughed, either.

There is no letter for half his sounds. I have used the thorn, and the rune for w, as we do at home, and made up the rest. Any brother who can read English could sound it out. He would not understand a word, but he could sound it.
Master Alcuin wrote to a bishop that a churchman's table wants a reader and not a harper. What has Ingeld to do with Christ, he asked. Master, Ingeld is on the third skin. All of him.
I said it could not be done. It is done badly, which is a different thing, and a better one. I held all of that once and lost most of it. It will not get lost out of there, unless there are mice.
It is your calf, Frisian, and your boy's scratching. Mine was only the breath. So where does it go? Say, and I will tell you if I like it. I will not stop you either way.
Keep the book in your own chest, for the house
Promise it to the school at Eoforwic, which pays for wonders
Leave it at Salhaugar with his daughter's sons, who cannot read it

"A merchant's chest. Between the tally sticks and the scales." He thinks about it. "It has been in worse company. It was in me." He pays for the skins and the nine days in his son's rings, seven hundred pennies by weight, and will not be argued with. The book goes to the bottom of the chest, wrapped in a sealskin. Beornwine reads from it on calm nights, and Ravn tells him where he has it wrong. An heir of yours will open it some day and wonder what house he was born into.

"To the shaven men. Who will keep it in a box and be ashamed of it." He laughs, not kindly. "But they do keep things. I am told they have kept an old king of the south and his songs for longer than there have been Danes." With his rings, and what the masters of the school at Eoforwic give for a thing no library has, it comes to fifteen hundred pennies, and a clerk of the minster who will look after your goods on the Ouse. Beornwine is as happy as you have seen him. Somewhere in that school a man is reading the third skin with his lips moving, and has started to wonder who brought it.

You put it in his hands. He weighs it as he would a child. "My daughter's boys cannot read it. Nor can any man among the Danes." "Somebody will, some day," Beornwine says. "Then let it be here when he comes." It goes into the chest by the old man's bed, under his son's cloak. He gives six hundred pennies of rings and sends to the hall, and the hall names you its guest. On the path Ravn says, "That was the right place," and then, being Ravn, "The roof leaks over that bed."
One word on a stick

A Dane steps down onto the dam at Dorestat, lays a stick of ash on your thwart without a word, and walks back to his ship. There is one word cut on it, deep, in the old way, with the gate and the bar.
Nithing. One word, and he cut it deep. You do not need it turned into Frisian. It is what you call the man who did what we did. I say we. I sat in the boat and held the rope.

The stone is up. A crew from Ripa hauled it for him. Not us. They say he stood by the open mound for a day first, and then had it closed, and asked for nothing to be put back. I sleep ashore from tonight.

I carried his first stick to you and I have carried his last. I will not carry your cloth. Nor will my brother, nor his wife's kin at the Slie. It is a long coast, Frisian. You will find it has got longer.
Burn the stick and wear the ring
Carry the ring to Saint Martin's altar at Traiectum
Send the ring back to Salhaugar with a man's price in silver (300 d)

The stick burns like any other ash. The ring sits on your arm above the elbow, a row of small horns round it, heavy and very fine. Your sons will have it after you and will be told some other story about it. In the Danish ports men look at your boat and then at the sea beside it. Ravn comes aboard at dawn each day, does his work, and goes ashore at dusk.

The priest at Saint Martin's takes the ring in both hands and asks no question a merchant cannot answer. It will hang by the altar with the other gifts, and the bishop's men will know your boat for the church's friend. "Their god will not send him anything for it," Ravn says of the old man. He is right. On the Slie and at Ripa nothing is changed.

The ring goes north in a sealed bag with three hundred pennies' weight of silver, by the same Dane, who looks at the bag a long time before he takes it. At the next moon a stick comes back. Ravn reads it. "It says: put back. That is all. He has not thanked you and he has not cursed you." He turns it over. "The other side is blank. With him that is as good as a blessing." He brings his sea-chest back aboard that night.
At Salhaugar by Hleidr a stone has been set up for Gunnvald, Hroald's son, who had the thul's seat. A Frisian crew hauled it. The old man who kept the hall's words has not named another to the seat.

The dam at Dorestat on a bright afternoon: a weathered Danish skipper in a hide cloak holds out a squared ash stick cut with runes to the merchant in his small boat, while Ravn, broad and dark-bearded, watches from the bow with narrowed eyes.

The muddy river landing at Ripa under a low grey sky: a broad carter in a wool cap leans on an empty cart behind two red oxen, looking sideways at the stick in the merchant's belt; hides and whetstones stacked behind.

Open sea in thin morning fog: a Norse ship with a striped sail passes close under the small boat's lee, her master standing on the stern with one hand on the stay and a stick raised in the other, his mouth open in a shout.

A flat ferry in the middle of the Slie at evening, oars shipped, reed banks far off on both sides: a grizzled ferryman cuts a small heavy bag loose from under his thwart while the merchant sits facing him; still water, long light.

Night at sea under stars, one small lamp: Ravn bent over four rune sticks laid side by side on the thwart, his thumb on the cuts; the young English lookout watching from the bow, the steersman a dark shape at the oar.

The slope below the great timber hall at Hleidr on an autumn morning: a steward with a staff held across the path, and behind him a swineherd counting a sow and her litter out of a wattle pen on his fingers; smoke over the long roof.

Inside the hall at night, seen from the low bench by the door: two long fires, the king a far shape in the smoke with gold on his arm, and close up the young skald holding a great full horn out toward the viewer; faces turned along the benches.

A farm by six grass mounds at midday: an old blind man with white eyes on a bench against the house wall, face turned slightly away, one hand resting on a long grey uncut stone lying by the door; Ravn standing well back at the gate.

A moonless night at the mounds: one mound with raw unknit turf, two wooden spades stuck in the grass, a small jar of ale; three crewmen as dark shapes, Ravn standing apart with empty hands; the farm's roof and one dog's ears against the sky.

Morning at the foot of the mounds: four men with ropes and log rollers tilting a grey stone upright into its hole, two rows of runes, three interlocked horns and a four-armed wheel-cross cut on its face; the blind old man with his hand flat on the carving.

The hall in midwinter, silent and full: the blind old man standing alone between the two fires, face turned to the low bench, where Ravn has just risen to his feet beside the seated merchant; every head on the benches turned to him.

Inside the farmhouse at Salhaugar in spring light from the door: the old man speaking with shut eyes, the young Englishman writing on calfskin across his knees with a goose quill, Ravn beside him marking the words with a finger; sewn gatherings on the bench.

The dam at Dorestat at dusk: a single ash stick lying on the thwart of the small boat with one word of runes cut deep in it; a Dane's back walking away along the planks; Ravn on the dam with his sea-chest on his shoulder; a broad silver arm-ring on the merchant's arm.
Nobody goes to Rouen
A skipper in from the Channel is selling his news for the price of listening. It is about the Seine, which honest ships have left to the Northmen for a lifetime.
Nobody goes up to Rouen. Everybody says so, and so everybody stays away, and so the three boats that do go are paid like bishops.
The heathen men have sat on that river since before my beard came. They do not burn the town now. They live in it. A man called Rollo keeps them, more or less.
An army eats. They have the silver of every church between the sea and Burgundy, and nothing to spend it on but bread and wine.
Blades and horses are another matter. The old king's law is death for that, and it is the one law on that river that still works.
Ask what bread fetches under the wall
Buy him ale and ask how a keel gets up there
Leave Rouen to those three boats
Half as much again as anywhere on the Channel, he says, and paid in good silver with church dust still on it. Wheat, rye, anything that will bake.

Two cups later you have it. Wait in the river mouth for the flood, ride it up, and tie to the bank when it leaves you; the tide reaches the town wall. And wine is cheap at Rouen, because nobody dares fetch it away.
He shrugs and tells it to the next man. The river will still be there.

A Channel strand on a grey afternoon: a weathered skipper on an upturned tub, a cup in his hand, pointing south-west with his thumb over a row of beached boats; two listeners, one already turning away.
The ruined market

Rotomagus stands, in the way a burned house stands. The Roman wall is whole on the river side; behind it the market place is grass. Long ships lie under the wall where the wine boats lay. Two men come down to your boat from two directions.
Ketil. I buy for the camp. You are the first cargo this moon that came of its own will.
I pay in silver by weight, a little over what a Frank would give, because a Frank would not come. Do not ask where the silver was before.
Gozbert, of the archbishop's house. We are still here. People forget that. The archbishop, eleven canons, and the poor, who had nowhere to run to.
Sell to him and you feed the wolf. Sell to us and you feed what the wolf left. We pay less. I will not pretend otherwise.
I am the wine trade of Rouen. All of it. My father had forty casks a week through that gate. I have a cellar and a door that locks.
Sell to the Northmen's steward
Carry your wares up to the archbishop's house
Sell nothing yet. Walk the town with the wine seller

Ketil weighs out hacked silver and half the foot of a chalice against your goods, and adds thirty pennies' weight for the coming. His men carry everything up through the river gate. Nobody on the strand looks at you, which is its own kind of look.
The canon pays twelve pennies over nothing much and has your name written down. The bread goes out at the church door the same evening. Ketil watches you pass and says nothing at all.

Odilard shows you the town in an hour: the two churches with a gallery between them, the empty places where the saints lay before they were carried inland, the old theatre where the Northmen keep horses. Wine here goes at three parts in four of the Paris price, he says, for want of keels to take it to sea.

Rotomagus from the water at low morning light: a long Roman wall of patched grey stone, six long ships drawn up under it, grass and a few goats where a market was; a fair-haired steward with an arm ring and a thin canon in black walking down to one small boat from opposite sides.
The canon's errand
Gozbert finds you on the strand before Prime with a folded sheet sealed in wax. The archbishop wants a letter taken up the river to Count Robert at Paris.
It asks the count for grain for the city's poor before the winter. That is the part I may tell you.

The other part says what the Northmen might take, if a king were to offer it, in place of what they take now. My lord has baptised a few of them. He thinks more would stand still for it if they had ground to stand on.
A clerk on the road is searched by everybody. A boat with casks is only taxed.
The priest has a letter. I would give forty pennies to know what a priest writes to a count about us. I would not need to keep it.
Carry the letter to Paris unopened
Carry it, and let Ketil hear it read first
You carry casks, not letters
You put it in the dry place under the stern board, with the weights. He gives ten pennies for the way and his blessing, in that order.
Ketil has a captive deacon read it to him twice, nods, and has the seal mended with a hot knife so that it nearly fits. Forty pennies. 'He writes well of us,' he says. 'Better than we would.'
He nods like a man who has been refused by better. A boy goes with the letter by the road next morning, on a mule. You hear later that the mule arrived.

Before sunrise on the river strand, mist on the water: the canon holding out a small folded letter with a red wax seal to the merchant in his boat; far behind, on the wall, one Northman on watch looking down at them.
The count's man
On the strand at Parisius a man in a good mail shirt asks every boat where she has come from. When you say Rotomagus he sends his groom away and sits down on your gunwale.
Warin. I serve Count Robert, who holds this river for the king as far down as he can hold it. That is not as far as Rouen.
The letter I will take. The archbishop shall have his grain. My lord does not let a city starve because he cannot reach it.
This seal has been warmed. I will not ask by whom. I will ask you something else instead.
How many keels under the wall? How many men who can stand? Horses? You have eyes and a tally stick. I pay for both.
My lord's brother held this city against them for eleven months when I was a boy. I carried water on the wall. Nobody needs to tell me what they are.
Tell him what you counted
A merchant counts casks, not ships
Double the ships and let him pay for the fright

You give him the count: the ships, the horse lines in the old theatre, the cook fires at dusk. He marks it on a wax board and pays a hundred pennies of Paris, new and sharp. 'Come again,' he says. 'Count again.'

He looks at you a while. 'Then count casks,' he says, and tells you where: the vine growers above the city sell low this year, with nobody to carry their wine to sea. He leaves twenty pennies on the thwart, for the road or for nothing, and goes.
He writes down twice what you saw and pays for it gladly: a hundred and forty pennies. A frightened count buys no battle this year. You wonder, going down the strand, which side you have just helped.
He lets you finish. 'A boatman from Jumièges counted for me at Whitsun,' he says. 'He counted half that.' Twenty pennies, for the road. He does not sit on your gunwale again.

The Paris strand at noon, the island and its wall behind: a broad man in mail and a red cloak sitting sideways on the gunwale of a small boat, a wax tablet on his knee, the merchant standing among his casks counting on his fingers.
Blades and horses
Ketil does not come down to the boat this time. He sends for you, to the bishop's old storehouse, where the camp's silver lies in a heap like turnips.
Bread I have. I want Frankish blades, the kind with a name in the iron, and horses that will carry a man in mail. I pay three times the market.
I know your law. Death for the seller. The old king said it at Pîtres, the same summer he built his bridge. The bridge did not stop us either.
You have iron under those hides now. I can smell the grease.
My cousin sold them four horses in the year of the long siege. The count's men hanged him at the bridge, over the water, where the boats could see. Ketil will not tell you that part.
Promise him the iron and horses you carry
Offer wheat instead, as much as he wants
Nothing the king hangs for

He weighs out two hundred and fifty pennies above whatever the market gives you, now, before the goods have left your hold. There is no writing of it. There is Odilard, who saw, and Odilard has a cousin's widow at Paris.

He is not pleased and not surprised. Six loads of wheat within the half year, at well over the market: he cuts a tally for it and splits it with you. 'A careful man,' he says. It is not praise, and not blame.
'Then you will live long,' Ketil says, 'and thinly.' But he tells you one thing for nothing: the camp is short of salt for the autumn killing, and will pay for it.

Inside a stone storehouse lit by one door: a heap of hacked silver, cups and book mounts on the floor; the steward crouched beside it with a folding balance, holding up one Frankish sword blade to the light; the merchant in the doorway, the wine seller's face at his shoulder.
After Chartres

This year the Northmen of the Seine sat down before Chartres. On the Saturday before the Magdalen's Mass Count Robert and Duke Richard came upon them, and the bishop showed the Lady's shift from the wall, and very many heathen men were killed. What is left has come home to Rotomagus.
We were beaten. There: a thing few of us will say twice. Fewer ships came back than went, and the men in them eat as much as ever.
The country will sell us nothing now it has seen us run. I need bread on trust until the leaves fall. Rollo does not forget who fed him. Nor who did not.
My lord says it is now or not in our lifetime. A beaten man will hear terms. He is sending me up the river to the king's people, and I need a boat that is only taxed.
I know who heard my lord's last letter read. I am asking you all the same. There is nobody else with a boat.
Or a man might go up to Paris and tell the count how few they are, and how hungry. One hard autumn and the river would be clean. I only say what a man might do.
Buy the camp its bread on your own purse
Take the archbishop's clerk up the river
Go up to Paris with what you know

Sixty pennies of rye and barley, bought dear from farms that would not sell to them. Ketil counts every loaf and says a short word in his own tongue to the men who carry it. They look at you differently after.

Gozbert sits in the bows with his hood up through two days of rain and one of sun. At the king's landing he is met by men who were expecting him. He is gone four days and comes back thinner and nearly cheerful.
You say nothing on the strand and cast off on the morning flood. Odilard watches you go. Behind you the cook fires are fewer than at midsummer. You count them, from habit.

The strand under the wall of Rotomagus on a dull late-summer evening: fewer ships than before, two of them scorched; bandaged men sitting against the stones round three small cook fires; the steward, the canon and the wine seller all standing at one small boat.
The ford on the Epte

At the leaf fall the king and the Northmen meet where a road fords the Epte, the king's people on one bank and Rollo's on the other. Your boat is one of those that carry them up to the river's mouth. You wait three days with the keels and hear the rest from those who come back.
It is done. The city and the land about it down to the sea, to hold of the king. Baptism. And he keeps the river against every other fleet. My lord wept. I counted the witnesses.
They wanted him to kiss the king's foot. He would not bend. So one of ours did it for him, standing, and brought the foot up to his mouth. The king went over on his back. Some of them laughed.
That is how it is told already. I was holding horses. Tell it as you like.
Rollo looks at your boat, then at you. He says six words to Ketil, and Ketil makes them Frankish: 'The river is his now. Boats that fed it are his guests.'
He says one thing more, and Ketil does not need to turn it: your name, nearly right.
Ask what a keel pays on his river now
Ask the clerk to write your name in the archbishop's roll
Ask nothing. Mend sail and listen

Ketil asks. The answer is short: what she paid the king, and half of that for half a year for the boats that came when nobody came. He has it cut on a stick, since the clerks have gone home. Thirty pennies for the carrying.

Gozbert writes it on the way down, on his knee, in a hand the river shakes. He reads it to you mark by mark. It is the first time you have seen your own name and known which stroke was which. Thirty pennies for the carrying.
You hear the story of the foot four times before Rotomagus and it is better each time. The men are in good heart, yours among them. Thirty pennies for the carrying.

A small river joining a great one under yellow autumn trees: boats tied in a row at the bank, the merchant mending sail in his; coming down the path, a very big grey-bearded Northman in a Frankish cloak, his steward half a step behind, and a canon clutching a roll.
The bridge at Pîtres
Warin takes you up from the strand to a hall on the island, where a big tired man is eating with his mail still on. Count Robert asks his questions himself.
The king's counsellors say: give the Northman Rouen, which we do not hold, and let him guard it. My lord says: why pay a beaten man? It hangs on how beaten.
The old king's bridge at Pîtres still has its piers. Timber it, man it, and nothing that floats goes down to them or comes up from the sea. An army that cannot eat goes elsewhere. They always have.
You gave me a number once that a boatman from Jumièges halved. So today we will have it slowly, and twice.
There is talk of a keel that sold iron under the wall. I have not asked which. Speak well today and I shall not have to.
So. Ships that will swim. Men who can stand. Days of bread. Take your time. I have fought them since I was sixteen and I can wait another cup.
Tell him all of it: the ships, the bread, the sick
Tell him, and ask that those who go down river are let go
Say they are stronger than he hopes

You tell it. The count stops eating. Before you are back on the strand carpenters have been called for, and a rider has gone to the king to say: grant nothing, wait for the frost. A hundred and fifty pennies. The purse is heavier than it should be.

He hears the first part and frowns at the second. 'Down the river and out to sea, with their women, and nothing burned behind them. Yes. I want them gone, not dead. Dead costs men.' He has it said before witnesses. Eighty pennies.

You hear yourself say it: the walls sound, the ships many, the bread enough. He looks at you, then at Warin, and shrugs like a man who expected little. The king's counsellors will have their way. You go back down the river to see what comes of it.

A timber hall by lamplight: a heavy grey-haired count in mail at a table with bread, a knife and a cup, leaning forward on his elbows; his man standing behind with a wax board; the merchant facing them, cap in hand, the river dark in the open door.
Seven days in white

This year Rollo was baptised at Rotomagus by the archbishop, and Count Robert stood for him at the water and gave him his own name. For seven days he wears the white, and each day he gives land to a church. The town is full, for the first time since your grandfather's day.
Rollo passes in white linen, with a cross on a cord that he keeps touching, as a man touches a new tooth. He is very big and no longer young.

Our Lady's here, Our Lady's at Bayeux, Our Lady's at Evreux, Saint Michael's in the sea, Saint Peter's by our wall, Saint Peter's at Jumièges, Saint Denis's. Seven days, seven gifts. Much of it land he took from them himself. I do not say so this week.

On the eighth day he takes off the white and we get ours. The land is measured with a rope, and every man who followed him has a length of it. I am to have a farm. I do not know what one does with a farm.
Half the camp went into the water behind him. Some went in twice, for the shirt. Good linen is not given away every day.
Forty casks. I have sold forty casks since Sunday, and I have had to hire back my own father's cooper.
Buy white linen for the men who follow him to the font
Stand among the Northmen and learn what they call things
It is a feast. Sell wine
Forty pennies of linen, cut into shirts by the canons' women. The archbishop has it said from the church steps who gave it. Rollo is told too. He looks for you over the heads and nods, once.

A week on the strand among men with nothing to do but drink and wait for the rope. By the end you can ask a price, refuse one, and say what you think of a man's ship without being struck. Their children, you notice, already answer in the speech of Rouen.
You and Odilard sell from one cart, he the wine and you the carrying, to men who have never before paid for wine in this town. A hundred and fifty pennies is your part.

A bright spring day before the two joined churches of Rotomagus: an old, very big man in a long white linen garment with a small cross at his neck, an archbishop beside him; behind them a crowd of Northmen in white shirts, wet-haired; at the edge a wine cart doing good trade.
The plough left in the field

Rollo's law is short: nobody steals. He has ordered ploughs left in the furrow and gear left on the strand. He hangs the thief, and beside the thief whoever knew. This morning a bale of yours is gone from the strand.

You have heard about Longpaon? A wife there hid her own man's plough irons, to teach him to carry them home. The count paid the man five shillings for his loss, tried the whole village by hot iron, found no thief, and then asked the man whom he had told. They hanged the pair of them.
He hung gold arm rings on an oak by a pool, out in the forest. Three winters back. I rode past at Yule. They are still there, and a little green.
I know where the bale is. The net-maker's boy, two boats down. He is twelve. I saw him at first light and thought he was carrying for you. Now you know it as well, which is a pity for both of us.
If you have a thing to say, say it to me before noon. After noon it is a thing you kept.
Bring it before the count's court
Fetch the bale back yourself and say nothing
Let the bale go. Leave the rest on the strand tonight, like everybody

You say it plainly, and the mate says what he saw. The bale is found under the net-maker's floor. The judgment takes as long as a prayer: twice its worth to you, sixty pennies, out of the father's goods. The father hangs, since a boy of twelve does not hide a bale under a floor alone. The boy is given to the canons. You are thanked.

You say it badly, in the wrong order, and the net-maker says the boy carried the bale for you and you forgot. It is found; nobody hangs; you pay ten pennies for the court's morning. Ketil says you should have come before noon.

You and the mate go two boats down at dusk. The boy's mother brings the bale out before you ask, with two baskets of eels on top of it, and cannot speak. Nobody hangs. By the count's law four people on this strand now ought to.

Ketil is sitting on the bale when you get there. He has been told. He takes forty pennies from you as the price of knowing and not saying, and tells you it is the cheapest that price has ever been. The boy he sends to the canons. He does not say what is done with the father.

You know nothing, and you tell the mate he saw a boy carrying for somebody. Next morning everything of yours is where you left it, and the bale is back among it, a little damp. An old riddle about a plough is going from boat to boat along the strand; a canon writes it down for you.

Early morning on the strand at Rotomagus: bales, casks and nets lying unguarded along the whole shore; one gap in the merchant's own neat stack; the mate pointing two boats down, where a boy of twelve looks away; on the hill beyond, small, a plough standing alone in a furrow.
The archbishop's question

A crew newly come from over sea took baptism at Easter for a shirt and a length of the rope. Now there is pig's blood on the stone behind their hall, and they are selling cheap what never came off any farm. The archbishop does not know what the church does with such men. Nor does anybody.

Baptised, and some of them baptised again, and living as heathens all the while. Do I shut the door on them? Scourge them? Wait? I am writing to Hervé at Reims, who has the books and the pope's ear. Somebody must carry it up the river.
New men on his river. It is the one thing Rollo fears. If they sell plunder here, it was taken from somebody who will come looking. He would want to hear of it, and from a friend.
Wax. Good cloth. A cup or two. I do not ask where you got your boat, Frisian.
It was always going to be this. You do not wash the sea out of a man in one Easter.
Tell Ketil what the newcomers are selling
Carry the archbishop's question up the river for Reims
Buy what they sell, cheap, and ask nothing

Ketil goes up to Rollo with it. By evening the new crew's ship is hauled out and her mast unstepped: they will plough, or they will leave on foot. There are forty pennies for you, and Rollo's steward calls you by your name before other men.

You hand the letter to a clerk of Reims on the Paris strand, who has plainly been told to look for you. On the way down you spell out your own copy of the greeting by the stern lantern. The archbishop says the answer, when it comes, will be long.

Forty pennies buys two loads of wax and a bolt of altar cloth with the fringe cut off. The cloth sells the same week for a hundred and thirty; the wax is in your hold. The archbishop hears of it, as archbishops do.

Evening behind a new timber hall outside the wall: a flat stone dark with blood, a pig's head on a stake; in front, a young shipmaster with a new cross on his chest holding out a bolt of rich cloth and a cake of wax; the archbishop watching from the gate, a letter in his hand.
A length of the rope

This year the king's writing names them for the first time: the Northmen of the Seine, Rollo and his companions, to whom land was given for the keeping of the kingdom. At Rotomagus the strand below the wall is being measured out with a rope, and the wine boats lie three deep.
I speak for him. When nobody came, you came. He is measuring the strand today. He says: where does the Frisian want his rope?
Count the keels. English, Flemings, men from the Loire who a year since would have cut us down. They come because nothing is stolen here. It turns out that is all a market is.
Thorstein. I have a ship and no markets. You have markets and a boat a man could carry. Among us that is mended by joining hands.
The blades are not forgotten either. By us, kindly. By the Franks up the river, otherwise. Stay below Pîtres for a few years.
My father's forty casks a week. I passed that at Whitsun. I have stopped saying it aloud, in case God is listening.
Take a plot on the strand and a free keel
Join hands with Thorstein: his ship, your markets
Take his peace and your silver, and no land

The rope is laid from the river gate to a stake, and the stake is yours: room for a storehouse and a slip. Rollo has it said before the whole strand that your keel pays no toll at Rotomagus, in his day or his son's. Nine hundred pennies come with it: your share of the years of bread and carrying, reckoned at last.

You and Thorstein put your silver in one heap before witnesses and take it up again as one purse: fourteen hundred pennies to your side of it, the plot on the strand, the free keel, and a second ship that will sail where you send word. He cannot read a tally. He can count, and he forgets nothing.

A man with land has a lord, and you have had enough of counts. Rollo laughs, which is rare, and gives you what he gives his own shipmasters: his peace, said aloud, so that no man of his on any water lays a hand on your keel. And eleven hundred pennies.

High summer on the strand of Rotomagus, crowded with wine boats three deep: two men stretching a long rope from the river gate to a new stake; old Rollo, huge and grey, pointing with a staff; the merchant beside the stake; new timber houses rising behind the Roman wall.
The saint comes home

This year the monks of Saint Peter's came back to Rotomagus, and Saint Ouen with them, who had been carried inland out of the Northmen's way before most men now living were born. The shrine comes down the river on a barge. Your boat goes ahead of it to sound the channel.
I was a child of the cloister when the old men told us where home was. None of them lived to see it. There is no roof on the dormitory, they say. We have brought the saint and a ladder.
At Longpaon Rollo comes out on foot to meet the barge and puts his own shoulder under the shrine. So the monks say, and will go on saying.

And Reims has answered. Three and twenty chapters out of the fathers, and a letter from the pope. It comes to this: go gently. They are new. Do not break them for being what they were. I could have told myself that, but now it is written.
You carried letters when a clerk could not. The monks need a man on the strand who can sell wine and not be robbed. And I would give your house something to keep.
One letter went up to Paris, years ago, with its seal warmed. I have decided not to know about that. It will cost you a little all the same.
Keep the monks' cellar on the strand and sell their wine
Ask for a cloth that has lain on the shrine
Ask for it in writing: the archbishop's hand, the count's mark

The cellar is the old one under the south wall, dry, with a door on the strand. You hold it of Saint Peter and Saint Ouen for a tenth of what passes through, and you are the saint's man on the river: his name on your tally is worth more than a seal. Eight hundred pennies is the first year's reckoning.

The monks lay a strip of white linen on the shrine through one night's psalms and give it to you in a box of yew. It weighs nothing. Men who would not trust your oath will trust it sworn on that. Six hundred pennies besides, for the letters and the sounding.

The archbishop writes that your house served the peace of Rotomagus when it had none, and that your keel goes free at his city. Rollo, who cannot read it, has it read to him and cuts a cross under it with his own knife. With it come the cloth from the shrine and twelve hundred pennies. It is the only writing your house has that two such men agreed on.

The Seine below a wooded bend at midday: a river barge with a gabled shrine under a cloth and monks singing round it; ahead of it the merchant's small boat, a man in the bows with a sounding pole; on the bank a crowd, and one very big old man walking down to the water alone.
The river shut

The king granted nothing. The bridge at Pîtres was timbered before the frost, and at the first hard cold the Northmen's ships went down the Seine on the ebb, low in the water, and out to sea. At Parisius Count Robert's man is waiting on the strand for you.
They are gone. Some say to the Loire, some over to the English. My lord says: so long as it is somebody else's river.
Rouen? The archbishop has his city back, and his eleven canons, and grass in the market. A wall with nobody behind it. We shall put a count there when we find one who wants it.
They went with their women and burned nothing behind them. That was your asking, and my lord kept it. He says it was cheaper. From him that is thanks.
Some drowned at the bridge, trying it by night. Their friends will learn who counted the cook fires. I would keep clear of long ships for a few years.
And the matter of the iron is closed. My lord closed it himself. You will not hear of it again unless you open it.
Take the count's protection and a free keel at Paris
Ask for the river itself: the count's pilot and the marks down to the sea
Take silver and go back to the sea

Warin has it said at the count's door and written by the count's clerk: your house is under Robert's hand on the Seine and the roads beside it, and your keel pays no toll on the Paris strand. Twelve hundred pennies. The wine above the city is cheap this year, and yours to carry. There is nobody at Rouen to carry it for you.

The count's own river man takes you down from the island to the bridge and through it, and shows you every shoal and loop on the way to the tide. With that go the count's hand over your house, the free keel at Paris, and fifteen hundred pennies. No long ship has a quarrel with you. The men who left know who asked for their lives.

You ask for coin, and he is relieved: coin is easier to give than favour. Eighteen hundred pennies, and his lord's hand over your house, which costs him nothing. On the way down you pass Rotomagus without tying up. The strand is empty as far as the bend.

A cold clear winter morning on the lower Seine: a new timber bridge on old stone piers, armed men along it; beyond, far down the river, the last long ships going out small on the ebb; in front, the wall of Rotomagus with an empty strand and one small boat passing without stopping.
They say there is a market at Rouen again. The Northmen's lord there hangs thieves, takes the king's toll and no more, and the wine comes down the Seine as it did in the old days.
Saint Ouen has gone home to Rouen, on a barge, with his monks. The Northman who holds the city walked out to meet him, they say, and carried the shrine.
The Northmen have left the Seine. Count Robert barred the river at Pîtres and starved them out, and the king gave them nothing. Nobody knows which coast has them now.
The Dane at the dam
Nine long ships lie along the upper bank with their masts down. The man at the toll house has a tally stick in his belt and an arm ring above it, and he is not a Frisian.
Eystein. I take the toll now. Your house's name, your mark, and what is in the boat. I learned your tongue here as a boy, so say it at your own speed.
The king's tenth, as before. It goes into the same chest. The chest goes to a different hall, and from there to the emperor, less the keeping of nine ships.
Last spring those nine ships burned every barn between here and the Waal. This summer they are the count's fleet. The emperor could not beat him, so he hired him. I am told this is statecraft.
My lord is sworn to keep other Danes off this river. He will. He knows how they think, where they water and what they are afraid of. He is what they are afraid of.
Some houses are going round by the Waal so as not to pay a heathen. It is a day longer and the king's man at Noviomagus takes his tenth just the same. But he is baptised, so it feels lighter.
Give him your name and your house's mark, and ask for your father's place at the dam
Ask him plainly what the emperor has granted, and for how long
Tell him nothing, and tell Thiadward you will go round by the Waal next time

Eystein cuts your mark into his stick beside your father's place, which he has from the old toll man's stick. He takes half toll from you for a month. He says his lord wants the old houses to stay, and that this is what wanting costs.

He answers without offence. Dorestat and the counties about it, from the emperor's own hand, on two conditions: the dues paid in honestly, and other Danes kept out. For how long? For as long as both are done. He says it is the same lease any count has, with more rowing.

Eystein writes nothing on his stick and looks at the gap for a moment. Thiadward walks you back to the boat. He says the Waal is a day longer, and that he would go that way himself if his storehouse could be put in a boat.
Hands between hands
The count holds court in the old toll hall. The free men of the bank are called in by name, house by house, and yours is the next.
Your house. Come to the front, stand where the mat is, and do not look at the dogs. He will speak Frankish. He speaks it better than the last count did.

I am Rorik. I hold this place of the emperor and I have sworn to him. Now the free men swear to me, as they did to my brother and me in the old emperor's day. A man who is mine, I answer for. On this river and on the sea.
You are the one who was going round by the Waal. And here you are at my door. A merchant goes where the market is. I have always liked that in merchants.

The oath to the emperor is every free man's. But this is hands between hands. A Christian should think before he puts his hands inside a heathen's, and thinks again before he does it in front of his priest.
Your priest keeps his church because my men stand on the bank. I have not asked him to love me for it. I ask nobody for that. It is not in the grant.
I have this church's relics here in their box. Swear the emperor's peace on them, as your father did, and let the Dane make what he can of it.
Put your hands between his and be his man
Swear the emperor's peace on the priest's relics, as your father did, and put your hands in no man's
Swear nothing: you pay the tenth, and that is all a toll is owed

His hands are dry and hard and he holds yours a breath longer than the words need. Half toll for a year, and a bench at his table at the feasts, his and yours both. Adalger the priest finds something to look at in the roof.

You swear on the box. The count laughs, not unkindly. Then you and he serve the same lord, he says, and of the two of you he is the one with the ships. He has your name kept among the emperor's men. The priest nods to you on the way out.
Nobody is angry. The count says a toll is owed a tenth and he will see that he gets it. Eystein cuts your mark on a second stick, a short one. You do not ask what the short one is for.
Light pennies
The count's steward counts ninety-six pennies onto your hatch for what the hall has had of you. They are new, they carry the emperor's name, and they ring wrong on the board.
Ninety-six. Eight shillings, as agreed. New from the mint this month, with the emperor's name on every one. Count them again if it pleases you. It is the same number each time.
I strike what I am given to strike. I was given the emperor's name and a bar of silver that was not all silver. The name is very good work. I will say that for the name.
You are my lord's man. Between his men a penny is a penny.
You are the emperor's man, I hear. Then you will not refuse the emperor's coin.
My scale is on the bench. It tells the truth to anyone, which is why nobody thanks it.
Take them by tale and say nothing
Ask the moneyer for his scale and be paid by weight
Leave the pennies and take the debt in furs from the fleet's store
