Ninety-six by count. On any scale they are seventy-two, and north of the Eider nobody takes a penny by count. The steward marks that you did not make him say it twice, and has Eystein take half toll from you for two months.

The moneyer weighs them without a word. A quarter short. The steward shrugs, opens a bag of cut silver from the north and drops pieces in the pan until it sits level. He says his lord pays his debts in whatever a man can carry.

The steward puts his hand flat on the pan before the weight goes in. The emperor's name is on them, he says. Do you doubt the emperor? There are a good many men in the hall. You take the ninety-six by count.

He sweeps the pennies back into the bag and sends a boy for a timber of marten: forty skins, winter pelts, tied in the northern way. The fleet's store is full of them. They will be cheap on this bank until it is not.
Two kings' sons go north
The long ships are in the water and being stored. Word came in the winter that the king of the Danes is dead with most of his kin, and the count is of that kin.
The king is dead and so are his nephews, all in one battle. They have made a boy king because he was what was left. My kinsman Godfrid and I are going to look at this boy.
Nine ships, forty men to a ship, and I will not have them stop to rob farms on the way: it is slow, and they are my farms. I need bread that keeps. Who on this bank can find it by the new moon?
He was hired to keep the river. Now the river's keeper is going to be a king somewhere else. If he wins we have no count. If he loses we have an angry one.

The emperor has given all Frisia to his son, the young Lothar. A young king likes to be asked things. Six houses are putting their marks to a word for him: who keeps the river while the count is away? Yours would make seven.
You are my man. If I come back a king, I will need a merchant who knows the way to my hall. If I come back as I am, I will need bread again.
Take his order: thirty sacks of ship's bread on the bank within thirty days
Put your mark with Thiadward's on a word to the young king: who keeps the river while the count is away?
Wish him a fair wind and keep to your own trade
Thirty sacks, at close to twice what bread fetches. The steward does not haggle. A fleet does not haggle in the week before it sails. Bring it within thirty days, to the upper bank.

A clerk of the church writes it on a leaf: seven marks and a cross. Nobody tells the count. Thiadward says that is not the same as the count not knowing, and that he would rather be known for asking the king than for keeping quiet.
The count thanks you for the wind as gravely as if you had it to give. Every oven on the bank is baking for the ships. Bread and ale will be dear at Dorestat until they are gone.
The fleet goes to the Eider
The count is taking his ships north again, this time with the king's leave and a promise of land by the Eider. He leaves the toll man, twelve men and one ship that leaks.

The boy king of the Danes has offered me the land between the sea and the Eider, and my lord King Lothar says I may go and take it. Two kings agreeing is rare. I mean to be there before either thinks again.
I am left with twelve men, one ship and a bailing scoop. If anyone asks, the count is hunting and will be back for supper.
Every skipper between here and Ripa knows by now that the river has no keeper this summer. News like that needs no wind.
My men will be a summer on a bare shore with silver and nothing to spend it on. Bring cloth and wine to Sliesthorp before Saint John's feast and you will not carry any of it home.
My grandfather put the house's silver in the ground in the year of the first fleet and dug it up again in the autumn. I know which post. I am telling you only that it can be done.
Sail north in the fleet's wake with cloth and wine: his men will need both
Stay with the house, and put its silver in the ground behind the storehouse
Take the boat up the river and trade above Noviomagus until he is home

He names the place: the market at the head of the Slie, before Saint John's feast. Cloth and wine will be dear there as long as his men lie by the Eider. He says to come round by the coast and not through the mouths at night.
A pot, under the third post from the water, on a night without a moon. You hear a spade in Thiadward's yard as you tread the earth flat. In the morning you each ask how the other slept.
You tell Eystein you have business up the river. He says he would have business up the river too, if he were not the one who was left. He does not say it as a reproach. He helps you cast off.
Between the sea and the Eider
The count sits on a sea chest at the head of the Slie, selling what a kingdom's edge gives: furs, amber and promises. He greets you in Frisian so that his own men will not follow it.
My merchant. You came by the coast, as I said. Sit. Here I am not a count. Here I am a kinsman with ships, which is a harder trade, and worse paid.
I have the land between the sea and the Eider. It is mostly sea. The boy king was glad to give it to me: it lies between him and the Franks, and so now do I.

The church here was shut after the old king fell. It is open again, and the young king lets us ring a bell. A Dorestat man may hear Mass at the Slie. Tell them that at home. They did not believe it of the last bell either.
You are from the Rhine? I passed forty sail off the islands after midsummer, standing south. Not his. I asked whose, and they asked who wanted to know, so I did not want to know.
Forty. And I left Eystein twelve men. Well. A town can be built again in a year. I have seen it done. I have also seen why it needed doing.
Buy under his peace: a timber of marten and four sacks of amber for 110 d
Ask him for a token his ships will know
Hear the skipper out, buy nothing, and turn for home on the next wind

Forty winter martens and four sacks of amber off the western beaches, for less than half what the Rhine pays. His steward counts in his own tongue, slowly, for your sake. By the last sack you can count to forty in it.

He looks at you a while, then cuts a hand's length from a silver arm ring and scratches three strokes in it with his knife. Hang it at the stem, he says. Any ship of his kin will know it. He does not say what the others will do.
You buy the skipper ale and hear it all twice. Forty sail, standing for the Rhine mouths, a fortnight ago. Whatever they went to do is done. You load water and wait for a wind with north in it.
The other Danes
There are sails below the town that are not the count's. They have been counted three times from the church roof and the number has grown each time.
Not ours. Ours come home in a line and singing. Those are spread across the whole river like a net.
A church can be built again. I have two gospel books, a psalter, the altar silver and three clerks, and none of those can. I need a boat that goes upstream, and I need it before the tide helps them.

The upper dam is narrow and staked. Thirty men could hold it against three boats at a time, if they stayed. I have nineteen who say they will stay. Eystein's twelve make thirty-one. I am one short of comfortable.
The bishop has gone inland with what could be carried in a day. What could not be carried in a day is on this bank, with me. Daventre, he said. Saint Lebuin's, on the IJssel.
You are back from up the river. You have a gift for arriving. Stay this time, or go at once: there is no room on the bank for a man who is thinking about it.

There is a third way and I am ashamed to know it. Their chief sells peace by the house. Five shillings, and a shield goes up on your door post. It works. I have hung those shields myself, in other towns.
Take the priest, his clerks and the church's books up the river to Daventre
Stand at the dam head with Eystein's twelve and the Frisian houses
Row out to their chief and buy your own storehouse free (60 d)

Three clerks, a priest and a chest that takes four men to lift. One clerk reads the psalms aloud the whole way, against fear, and by the IJssel you can follow the short ones. At Daventre the bishop's steward pays the freight: ten shillings, counted twice.

They try the upper dam at dusk, three boats abreast, and the first one opens herself on the stakes. After that they go looking for softer houses, and find them. The dam's houses stand. In the morning they make up a purse for those who stood on it.

The dam is held until dark and lost in the dark. You get the boat off with a cut hand aboard and smoke behind you. Half the bank burns. The men who were on the dam with you do not forget who else was there.

Their chief takes five shillings, bites one penny, laughs at it, and takes them anyway. A shield hangs on your door post while your neighbours' roofs burn. Your storehouse stands. There will be no wine on this bank until new ships come down.
The count comes home
The lower bank is black posts and new planks. The count's ships are back along the upper bank, and the men of the houses stand in the road with their arms folded.
We paid a tenth to a man who was sworn to keep pirates off the river. The pirates came. The man was away getting himself a second country. I ask only what the tenth was for.

It was for the summers in which this bank did not burn. Count them. Before me it burned most years. I went away for one summer with my king's leave, and you have learned what I am worth. I did not plan the lesson. I will not waste it.
This one stood on the dam with me, lord. I say it here, in the road, so that both sides hear it.
This one came north with cloth when I asked. He was where I told him to be. I ask you all how many men that is true of.

The young king is at Noviomagus for the winter. We have a leaf written: let the king send a count of his own people, with horsemen. Somebody with a boat must carry it. None of us wants to be seen going.

I have broken up two ships that were past mending. Oak, seasoned, free to any house that builds on its old plot before Saint Martin's feast. And half toll for a season to those who do. A burned town pays no tenth at all. I can reckon that much.
Speak for him in the road: he came back, and no Frankish count ever did
Carry the houses' complaint to the king's palace at Noviomagus
Say nothing for either, take his ship timber and mend your own dam head

You say it: in all the years of fleets, which Frankish count came back to a burned bank with timber? Nobody answers, and they go home muttering. That evening the steward brings ten shillings in old pennies, the heavy kind. He says his lord noticed which kind.

The houses pay your carriage. At the palace a clerk takes the leaf, reads it twice, and asks whether the Dane has paid in the dues. He has. Then the king, says the clerk, has no other fleet to send. He keeps the leaf. Kings keep everything.

Ship's oak makes good posts. It has already learned about water. You are a fortnight at it, and you say nothing for anyone. Eystein takes half toll from every house that built, until Saint Martin's feast comes round again.
The bishop without a church
The bishop of Traiectum has no Traiectum. He keeps his household in borrowed rooms, and he has asked for any merchant who lies at Dorestat and knows the Dane.
The bishop lodges here by Saint Lebuin's until the king finds him a house. Wipe your feet. The floor is borrowed too.
The bishop is here for three days to see what is left of his church. It is the wall on your right. Yes, that one.
I am Hunger, and I am told the name suits a bishop with no see. You lie at Dorestat. You have seen this Rorik eat, deal and lose his temper. Tell me: is he a man who could be brought to the water?
They say your hands have been between his. I do not ask you to repent of it today. I ask you to use it.
You brought my priest and my books out when the fleet came. I have not forgotten. I am asking you because of it.
I have written to him. With the letter goes a length of white linen, enough for a robe. He will know what it is for. They always do. It is the letter they have read to them twice.
Carry the bishop's letter and the white cloth to the count
Carry nothing, but tell the bishop what the Dane wants: his toll untouched, and a king who cannot unseat him
Say you carry cloth and wine, and that souls are another man's freight

Thirty pennies for the carriage. The clerk reads you the letter twice, in Latin and then in Frisian, so that you can say it if the leaf is lost. It is shorter than you expected. It offers the count a bishop's good word with two kings, and heaven after.

You tell him. The Dane wants his toll left alone and a lord who cannot take the grant back. The bishop listens to the end. Men have come to the water for less, he says, and has the clerk write down what you said, in your own words.

The bishop says that souls are everyone's freight, and that he has noticed merchants prefer the kind that can be weighed. The clerk shows you out. On the stair he says the household has no wax for its altar, and would pay over the price.
The white robe
A tub has been set in the largest church on the bank and filled from the river. The count stands beside it in his shirt, and half his men stand outside with their backs to the door.
He is asked three times if he forsakes the devil and all his works, and three times he says he does. He says it in good Frankish. I have known Franks who put less into it.
You carried the letter and the cloth. So you will stand where I can see you. If the roof falls on me, I want one man there who can tell them it was not my idea.
A merchant. Good. You people understand a bargain, and you can tell the others it was a fair one. Stand where you like.
I wear the cross for the day's business and the hammer for the night's. My lord has decided to wear one of them all day. A count can afford to be simple.

They tell of a man at the old emperor's court who was baptised every Easter for the white robe. One year the linen was poor and he said so. Twenty times washed, he said, and never such a sack. My lord has had the cloth looked at first.
Stand among the witnesses and give wax for the candles (40 d)
Stand at the back with Eystein and ask what a white robe is worth on this river
Stay outside with the men who will not go in, and stand them ale

He goes under three times and comes up blowing like a seal. The first thing he does is look round to see who is there. Your candles burn the whole Mass. Eystein takes half toll from the witnesses for half a year, and calls it a christening gift.

Eystein reckons it up, in Frisian and then in Danish where Frisian lacks the word. A bishop's good word with two kings. An oath that Christians have to keep back. A dry grave. Against that, a wet shirt and some sour faces at home. He calls it cheap.

You stand ale to the men at the door. They say their lord has not changed lords, only taken on one more, and that he was always good at holding of several. Your own crew think better of you for the ale. The priest saw where you stood.
The flood winter
The river is over the lower bank and into the fields behind. A fisherman from the mouths has counted more sails than the count has, and the houses are loading carts for a great estate inland.
We are going to the big estate behind the fields, all the houses, with what the carts will take. It has a ditch and a stone barn, and it is an hour from any river. Ships do not go where carts go.
The fisherman says sixty. Halve what a fisherman says and it is still thirty, and my lord has nine. I can do sums. It is what I am kept for.
Look at the fields. That was a road at Christmas. I could take a ship over it now and not touch. I am not saying where I would take her. I am saying I could.
You have stood with the houses before. If you have something to say against the carts, they will hear you. They may not do it. But they will hear you.
You are the Dane's man. If you tell the houses to get into boats, half of them will ask whose boats, and where the boats are going.
I know whose sails they are. Two of them have eaten at my table. That is worth something, and it is not worth a town. Do not ask me yet which it is worth.
Tell the houses the flood is a road for ships, and take all who will come by boat up the IJssel to Daventre
Go to the count as his man and ask him to put his ships across the river
Take your own boat into the reeds above the town, and watch

You take Thiadward to the edge of the fields and push an oar down: a man's height of water over the cart road. He looks at it a long time. By dusk eleven boats are strung out against a brown river, yours ahead with a lantern. Six houses are on the IJssel before the sails reach the town.

They argue until the light goes. A cart is a thing a man can see the wheels of. You take off two families and a clerk in your own boat, low in the water, and row all night. The carts go inland without you.

He hears you out. Nine ships do not stop sixty, he says; they only choose where to sink. He will talk to them instead. It is cheaper, and some of them owe him. Then he tells you to have your boat above the town by dark, and does not say why.

From the reeds you see the toll chest carried aboard the count's ship, two days before any sail shows. You see the sails come. You see his nine ships lie still at the upper bank while the lower burns. On the second night there is another fire, inland, where the carts went.
On Rorik's advice
The fleet went up the river as far as the island below Neuss and came down again, on the count's advice, they say. Dorestat is ash to the upper bank. Now everyone reckons what he is owed and by whom.

The king came up on one bank and the Saxons on the other, and my lord went between and told the fleet what he would do in their place. They did it. They went home. That is the whole of it, and nobody likes it for being so short.

They found the estate, you know. Over the fields, as you said. The stone barn is full of ash and other men's dead. We should have been in it. Six houses know whose lantern they followed. We have talked, and we have something to put to you.
You took off two families when the rest would not listen. They are alive. I was asked to tell you that the rest of us know it now. Those of the rest who are left.
They went to the estate with the carts. The ships went over the fields after them. Thiadward's house is his widow and a boy now. I buried eleven men I had bought and sold with for twenty years.

You kept your oath in a winter when it was easier not to. I still have my counties, and I mean to have men in them I can name. Nine hundred in old coin, a ship off my own bank, and my mark for her stem. Take it now. I am generous while I am relieved.
You are not my man. So I owe you nothing, and you owe me nothing, and each of us may say what he likes about that winter. I would think for a time before I said it.
Settle the houses you brought out on the IJssel bank, and swear fellowship with them
Take what the count gives the men who kept their oath
Take nothing yet: there are dead to bury, and it is not yet clear whose silver this is

Six houses put a share each into one chest and swear on Saint Lebuin's altar to stand for one another's debts and dead. They mark you the first plot above the landing at Daventre. Thiadward will sail a second boat under your mark. Dorestat's names are on a new bank, and none of them is on a grave.

Nine hundred pennies of the old weight. A Danish-built ship, broad, with a mast that lowers, off his own bank. And three strokes cut in her stem: no ship of his kin will lay you aboard. As you leave the hall the bishop's clerk is at the door, writing names.

You help carry what was found at the estate to the churchyard, and pay for the candles. It takes four days. On the last the bishop's clerk asks where your boat will lie this spring. He writes the answer down.
What the bishop asks
The bishop has a letter from the archbishop of Reims open on the table, and a list of every house that lay at Dorestat in the flood winter. Yours is on it.

From Hincmar, archbishop of Reims, to my lord. If it was by Rorik's counsel that the heathen did what they did, my lord is to lay a fitting penance on him. There is a second letter, to Rorik himself. That one we have not seen. We can guess its temper.

He is baptised. So he is mine to judge, as he never was while he was a heathen. I think nobody explained that to him at the tub. You were at Dorestat that winter. What did you see, and what will you swear to?
You are his sworn man. An oath to a lord does not bind a man to lie to his bishop. I say that as the law has it. I know it is easier to say in this room than on that river.
You have carried for this church before, and you were not paid what it was worth. I remember my debts. It is a habit I have had time to form, lately.
I do not want his counties. The kings may weigh those. I want him at a church door in Lent, where the widows can see him. No lord of that river has stood there yet. One should.
Tell all of it: what you saw, what he said before the sails came, and swear to it
Say only what every man knows: he talked the fleet away, and he talked too late for the dead
Say you saw nothing a man could swear to

You tell it in order and swear on Saint Martin's cloth. The bishop sets the penance. The count stands a Lent at the church door in his shirt, and pays the toll of that winter back to the houses of the dead. He does it. Your share and the bishop's thanks come to eleven hundred pennies. Saint Martin's bank is free to your house, and you are written down as the saint's man.

It is enough for a lesser penance: a fast, and alms to the widows by the bishop's hand. The count pays without a word. The bishop gives your house Saint Martin's bank free of toll, and seven hundred pennies for handling the alms honestly. Eystein, at the next toll, counts your cargo twice.
The bishop looks at you for some time and then at the clerk. The clerk draws a line under your house's name: not through it, and not round it. You are thanked for coming. Nobody sees you to the door.
The Cokingi
The men of the coast have risen against the Dane. They carry eel spears and old swords, they have a name nobody has heard before, and both sides want a boat.

I am Hiddo. I speak for the districts. We paid the Dane a tenth to keep Danes off, and buried our kin anyway. We have told him the lease is up. He is on the wrong side of the water and collecting ships.

I am Hiddo. We put the Dane out three summers ago. Now a king has met him at Noviomagus and made a treaty, and he is to be our count again, by a king we never chose. We are not finished. Neither, it seems, is he.
Your house's mark was on the leaf that went to the king, years back. The king did nothing. We remembered who asked. That is why I come to your boat first.

Two women, a boy, a chest and me. That is all of the count's household on this bank, and the men with eel spears know which house it is in. I need a boat tonight. I never asked a Frisian for anything but the tenth before.
Word from the count, by a fisherman: You are my man still. Bring my household off, and bring the chest. I am coming back with ships, and I will know who carried and who watched.
Word from the count, by a fisherman: You were never my man, and I never burned your house. Stay out of the way of this and you will find the toll no higher when I am back.
Carry the Cokingi's bread and their word along the coast
Take the count's household and his chest off the bank in your boat, as his man
Be nobody's man: sell bread to both, and move your goods to Daventre

Three weeks from terp to terp with bread and one sentence: the day, and the place. By harvest the Dane is off the coast. The districts pay you in cloth and in the toll they did not send him. A pilot of the Vlie takes you out and shows you his marks, the church, the dune and the two withies. He says it is not done, and that his father would have drowned him for it.

Two women, a boy, Eystein and an iron-bound chest, down the river in the dark with muffled oars. The count pays from the chest when he is back with ships, and he is back: thirteen hundred pennies, a ship from his bank, his mark on her stem. On the coast they do not sell to your house for a generation.

A rising eats as much as a fleet and pays sooner. Six hundred pennies in one summer, from both sides, and neither thanks you. A cousin of Thiadward's house takes your goods into his storehouse on the IJssel, where neither side comes, and will keep them there for a share.

This year the emperor Lothar received Rorik the Dane into his fealty and gave him Dorestat and other counties, on his oath to pay in the king's dues and to keep the pirates of the Danes off the river.
This year Rorik, who rules in Dorestat, went with his fleet to the Eider with King Lothar's leave. After midsummer forty sail that were not his were seen standing for the Rhine mouths.
This year in the flood winter the heathen men burned Dorestat and a great estate behind it. The houses of the bank had gone by boat up the IJssel beforehand, and they have taken plots at Daventre.
This year the fleet that burned Dorestat went up the Rhine as far as Neuss and came down again on the advice of Rorik. He keeps his counties, and has rewarded the men who held to him.
This year Rorik the Northman, being baptised, did penance at the word of Hunger, bishop of Traiectum, for the winter in which Dorestat was burned. Merchants who were there bore witness.
This year the men of the coast, who are called by a new name Cokingi, drove Rorik out of Frisia. King Lothar has called out his host, for it is said that Rorik will come again with Danes.
This year there was fighting in Frisia between the people of the land and Rorik the Dane. Houses that were of Dorestat are moving their goods to Daventre on the IJssel.

A grey summer morning at Dorestat's upper dam: a fair Dane in his thirties with a moustache, a Frankish cloak over a northern tunic, a silver arm ring and a tally stick, stands at the toll house door; behind him nine long ships lie along the bank with their masts lowered, and a Frisian merchant in a short cloak watches from a plank road.

Inside a timber hall by firelight, afternoon: a tall fair man of about forty in a Frankish count's cloak and sword belt, gold rings on his arms, sits on a bench holding out his open hands; a Frisian merchant stands before him on a rush mat; to one side a tonsured priest holds a small relic box, and two hounds lie by the hearth.

Midday on a jetty at Dorestat, flat light: a heavy Danish steward tips a row of thin new pennies onto the hatch of a small boat; a Frankish moneyer in a leather apron stands by with a folding balance in his hand, looking at the sky; one penny is on edge, spinning.

A windy spring day on the upper bank: nine long ships afloat, men passing sacks and casks aboard down a line; in front the count, bare-headed, one foot on a gunwale, speaks with two merchants; smoke from many bread ovens blows across the town behind.

Early morning, clear and cold: the count's fleet rowing away down the river in a line, small; in front, on an empty bank, the toll man stands with a bailing scoop in his hand beside one old ship drawn up on rollers, and a Frisian merchant beside him looks the other way, up the river.

A long northern evening at the head of the Slie: the count sits on a sea chest on a shingle strand, bundles of marten skins and sacks of amber at his feet, ships drawn up behind; a Danish skipper leans in to speak; far back, a small wooden church with a bell hung in a frame beside it.

Dusk at Dorestat, the sky red down the river: many sails spread across the water below the town; in front a priest and three clerks carry a heavy chest and books down a jetty to a small boat, while behind them armed Frisians and a dozen Danes crowd onto a narrow staked dam.

A raw autumn day: black burned posts along the lower bank and stacks of pale new planks; the count, in a travelling cloak, stands in a plank road facing a knot of Frisian merchants with folded arms; behind him men are breaking up an old ship for her oak.

A bare borrowed room in winter light from a small window: a lean bishop of about fifty in a plain dark cloak, a wooden staff against the wall, sits at a trestle with a folded letter and a length of white linen on it; a young clerk stands with a wax tablet; a merchant waits by the door with his cap in his hand.

Inside a timber church, candles and daylight from the open door: a big fair man of fifty stands in his shirt beside a large wooden tub of water, a priest with a raised hand before him; a folded white robe lies on a bench; through the door, the backs of armed Danes who will not come in.

A dark winter afternoon, rain: the river spread wide over fields, fence tops and a cart road going down into brown water; on the last dry ground Frisian families load ox carts; in front a merchant pushes an oar down into the flood to show its depth, and a lantern burns in a small boat beside him.

A pale early spring morning on a river bank: in the far distance a burned town, only posts standing; in front the count at a board on trestles with an open chest of pennies, the toll man beside him; to the other side a group of Frisian merchants waits apart, and a clerk stands by a door with a tablet.

A stone-walled room, a single candle though it is day: the bishop, older now and thin, sits with an open letter and a long list before him; the clerk points to one line with a pen; a merchant stands with his hand laid on a small relic box.

Late summer evening on a Frisian shore, long shadows: a crowd of coast men with eel spears and old swords around a grey-bearded spokesman on a terp; below them at the water a small boat, and beside it the ageing toll man with two cloaked women, a boy and an iron-bound chest, waiting to see which way the skipper turns.

The ending 'the count's man': a broad Danish-built ship on a river in clear morning light, three strokes cut in her stem, a Frisian skipper at the steering oar; on the bank behind, the count raises one hand, and further back a clerk writes.

The ending 'the houses brought out': a new plank landing on the IJssel at Daventre in summer, six house frames going up in a row, a church behind; in front Frisian merchants and their wives stand round one chest with their hands on it.

The ending 'the bishop's witness': a church door in Lent, grey light; a big fair man in a plain shirt, bare-headed and bare-footed, stands beside it while widows in dark head-cloths go in past him; the bishop watches from inside; a merchant stands at the edge of the yard.

The ending 'the coast's man': a small boat in the Vlie at low water, evening; a Frisian pilot stands in the bow pointing at a far church, a dune and two withies in line; behind, on a terp, fires burn and no long ship lies anywhere on the water.

The ending 'nobody's man': a storehouse door at Daventre, a man barring it from inside on stacked bales and casks; outside on the river, small in the distance, a long ship and a crowd on a bank face one another, and a loaded boat rows away from both.
The count of the dead
The landing is short of men. At the alehouse a young man with a new arm ring is buying for two kings nobody had heard of a year ago, and the ale-wife is counting on her fingers who has not come home.
Hemming died in his bed in the winter, which no king here has done for a while. Then Sigfred and Anulo fought over the seat. Both are dead. So is everyone who stood near them.
You were not here last year. Hemming died, and Sigfred and Anulo fought over the seat, and both fell. We have had a year to count since. The count has not got smaller.
The Franks will have a number for it by now. They like a number. I have nineteen names, and that is only the men who drank here.
Eleven from this bank of the river. I brew less. Nobody has thanked me for the saving.
Anulo's side held the field, so Anulo's brothers are kings. Harald and Reginfrid. Two, so that there is one to spare. I am Eskil, and I buy for them.
A king who gives no feast is not king for long. I will take what you have. Some silver now, and the rest on a split stick, to be made good at the hall at Hleidr.
You have come to a king-making with an empty boat. That is a Frisian thing to do. Come again with wine, and come soon.
Sell to the new kings: part in silver now, the rest on a split stick
Buy the ale-wife a cup and ask where the beaten men went
Say kings are no Frisian's business, and ask what wine fetches

Eskil weighs out thirty pennies' weight of cut silver and notches a hazel stick for the rest. He splits it down the middle and gives you the half with the bark on. It is good at the hall at Hleidr, he says, for as long as his kings are. He says it as a joke.

She drinks the cup first. The beaten men swore to the new kings, she says, because the other thing to do was to be dead. Some swore and then went east, by Skane and over the water to the Svear. Godfred's sons are there. They were boys when their father was killed. They are not boys now.

Eskil laughs and tells you. Two new kings are feasting every lord who might otherwise remember he fought against them, and wine is a third dearer than it was at midsummer. He seems to think you have said something wise.
A stick in Skane

On the old market ground at the river mouth a man with a bound arm is waiting for a boat east. He has a rune stick he wants carried the other way, to Sliesthorp, and the farmer Hebbi is the only one here who can read it.
I am Styr. I stood with Sigfred, and then I swore to the two brothers with Sigfred's blood still on my shoes. I find the oath sits badly. I am going where Godfred's sons are.
This stick goes to Asulf, who sells people at Sliesthorp and knows every lord in Jutland by what he owes. It asks one thing. He will pay you when he has read it.
Osfrid of Skane swore on the Eider with the great men two summers back. Since then he has been careful to be on nobody's side that anybody can name. He will die old.
My father said: two kings on one bench, and the bench gets no warmer. He said it about his brothers, but it will do.
Carry the stick to the dealer Asulf at Sliesthorp
Have Hebbi read it aloud, and leave it where it lies
Say you carry cloth, not sticks, and ask Hebbi about amber

Styr gives you twenty pennies' weight from a purse that has not much more in it. Hebbi reads the stick to you before it goes in your chest, since a man should know what he carries. It asks who in Jutland will rise when the kings are away from home. It does not say when that will be. Styr says kings are always away from home sooner or later.

Hebbi reads it with his thumb, slowly, and shows you which stave is which. It asks who in Jutland will rise when the kings are away from home. You hand it back. Styr looks at you for a while and then shrugs with his good shoulder. Another boat will take it, he says, or none will, and Godfred's sons will come home either way.

Styr puts the stick back in his shirt. Hebbi is pleased to talk about something else. There was an easterly four nights ago and the shore below the dunes is yellow with amber. Every child in the river mouth has a bag of it, and the price has dropped by a fifth.
Two on the high seat

The hall at Hleidr is feasting two kings on one high seat. Half the benches are filled with men who fought against them a year ago. The steward wants rope for a fleet, and says where the fleet is going.
I have seated men tonight beside the men who killed their brothers. It took me four days. Nobody has thanked me, which means I did it well.

When the barley is in the ground the kings go north to the Vik. The chiefs there keep the landing gifts and send none south. The fleet wants rope. Eight coils of the good kind, before the ships go down the fjord.
You have a split stick of Eskil's. I have the other half. I had hoped you were dead, but I see you are not, so we shall weigh.
Two kings. I have had to make every verse twice, once for each, and of the same length. Reginfrid counts the lines. Harald does not, which is worse.
You have the face of a man who has been in Skane. So has half this bench. Nobody here says so aloud. I would not either.
Take the fleet's order for rope
Lay your half of the split stick on the trestle
Sit low on the bench and listen to the skald

Asgaut names the weight once. Eight coils of rope at well over what the strand pays, to be on the landing before the ships go down the fjord. He does not ask whether you can find it. Across the fire the two kings are sharing one horn, and each is watching how much the other drinks.

The halves fit. Asgaut weighs out a hundred and forty pennies' weight in cut rings and does not round it either way. While he weighs, Thorulf says the old lay of this hall, the one about a king who paid his men in gold. He says it loudly, and in the direction of the high seat.

You sit by the door with the grooms. Thorulf comes down the hall with a riddle about a beast with eight horns and no head, which many follow, and leaves it with you. He looks at the high seat while he says it. From the grooms you learn more than from the benches: the ships go north when the barley is sown, and both kings go with them. Nobody stays behind to keep the hall but the steward.
A boat nobody looks at twice

The chief has walked down from the hall himself. Word has come up the coast that the kings of the Danes are gathering ships. He looks at your boat for some time, as a man looks at a horse he does not mean to praise.
The Danes have two kings this year. They are coming to ask me a question, with a host, so that I shall hear it clearly. I would like to give one answer to both. I am told that is the difficulty.
Your boat is not handsome. Could it carry my daughter and one chest round to the Karmsund, to the woman who keeps the keys on the ness? Nobody counts what is in a boat like that.
The chest is heavier than I am. Father says that if we meet a ship, I am your sister's girl and it is full of whetstones. Some of it is.
You have sat in their hall this winter. Tell me what they want, and say it plainly. I am an old man and courtesy takes me a long time.
Take the girl and the chest round to the Karmsund
Tell him what was said in the hall at Hleidr: they want the landing gifts, not his head
Say four men and a load of cloth are no guard for a chief's daughter

The chest comes down at dusk on a sledge, under hides. Asny sits on it. Asgrim pays forty pennies' weight for the passage and says the rest will be owed, which from him is a large word. He does not wave. He stands on the jetty until the first skerry hides you.

You tell him what the steward said: the landing gifts, sent south each year, and an oath. Nobody at Hleidr spoke of his hall or his head. Asgrim hears it out and asks three more questions to be sure. Then he has four good hones brought down for you. A man can give away gifts, he says. It is the giving of them that he minds.

He nods, as if you had told him the wind. It is a fair answer, he says, and he would have thought less of the boat if you had said yes at once. He will find another way. The hones are stacked on the strand unsold. Nobody wants to buy stone in a summer when iron is coming.
The woman with the keys

The girl and the chest go up the path to the hall on the ness. On the strand a ship's chief is fitting out for the summer, and he would like to know where the kings of the Danes have taken their ships.
Asgrim's chest. I shall weigh it before your eyes and again before his, and it will weigh the same. Tell him Gunnhild said so.
The girl can stay until her father has found his answer. She will learn to brew. Everybody who stays here learns to brew.
A Frisian from the Vik. You will have seen ships. I hear the Danes have two kings and that both have gone the same way. Which way was that?
The sound is narrow and the stream runs like a mill race. There are five stones on the far shore that lean toward it. Stay three days and I will give you every mark in a verse you cannot lose.
Hand over the girl, take what is owed, and know nothing about kings
Tell the ship's chief the Danish host is in the Vik, and every coast south of it unwatched
Stay three days for the skald, and learn the sound from him

Gunnhild weighs the chest, then weighs out sixty pennies' weight for you from her own purse, to be settled with Asgrim later. You tell the ship's chief that you saw fog and a great many gulls. He laughs and says a Frisian sees what he is paid to see. He goes back to his rigging.

You tell him. Both kings and every ship they have are in the Vik until harvest, and there is nobody at home on the coasts to the south. He cuts a piece from his arm ring and does not weigh it. Four ships go down the sound within the week. In autumn, word comes that Northmen have been in Frisia and carried off men and women. You know some of the place names.

Three days. Hallgrim walks you along the sound and gives you each mark in a line of verse: the five leaning stones, the green mound, the skerry that shows at half ebb. He makes you say it back until he stops wincing. Gunnhild weighs the chest and pays what is owed. The girl waves from the brew-house door.
The host in the fjord

The fjord is full of Danish ships drawn up stem by stem. The market is shut and the cattle are gone inland. A host eats, and the kings' man is paying twice the market for anything that can be eaten or can carry.
The Frisian. I buy in the south and you are there, I buy in the north and you are there. Either you follow kings about or kings follow you.
The chiefs here have hidden their cattle and found their manners. We have a great many men and nothing to roast. Bread, ale, a hull to carry fodder. I pay double, in silver, today.
Tomorrow on the heath I swear on the ring to two kings by name. I have asked whether one oath will do for both. It will. I had not hoped for so much thrift from Danes.
They have counted my cattle and my benches. They have found me poorer than they were told. I am obliged to your boat for that.
It is as you said. The gifts and an oath. I have kept my head, and I use it now mostly for nodding.
Sell the host bread, ale and carriage at the kings' price
Go up to the thing heath and stand witness when the chief swears
Tell the kings' man what is said in Skane: Godfred's sons are coming home

For nine days your boat carries fodder and ale between the farms and the ships. Eskil pays as he said, a hundred and eighty pennies' weight, and counts it out where the whole strand can see. The people of the market watch from their doors. Nobody says anything. They do not need to.

On the heath the chiefs of the Vik lay a hand on the ring, one after another, and swear to Harald and to Reginfrid by name. The lawman asks who of the strangers saw it. You say that you did. It costs you a day of trade. Asgrim says nothing to you on the way down, and has ale sent to the boat.

Eskil hears you to the end without smiling, which is new. Then he goes up the strand to the kings' tent and is in it a long time. He comes back with a ring for you, sixty pennies' weight. The kings will take the oaths and go home at once, he says, not after harvest. He does not say they believed it. He says they would rather be laughed at in their own hall than out of it.

Eskil hears you out and laughs. Boys among the Svear, he says, and a few sore losers. The kings have the whole host of the Danes in this fjord, and it has taken them a year to gather it. They will go home after harvest, when the Vik has paid. He advises you to stick to cloth.
The brother given back

Sixteen lords of the Danes have ridden home from swearing peace with the Franks, and they have brought the kings' brother with them. He has Frankish shoes and nobody to give his news to: both kings are in the north.
I am Hemming. My brothers asked the emperor for me two summers running and went north the week I came. I am told it is a great honour to be asked for.
You are a Frisian, so you have been everywhere and will say you saw nothing. I have been so long among the Franks that I know that answer. What is said in the harbours? I ask as a brother.
Sixteen of ours and as many of theirs, beyond the Elbe. They swore, and nobody was sold. A poor summer for my trade. The border is open, though, and that is good for yours.
I hear you have something of mine from Skane. A stick. I do not read sticks in the street. Come behind the pen.
Give Asulf the stick from Skane
Tell Hemming what Skane says, and that his brothers should come home
Sell to the lords' following and say nothing to anyone

Asulf reads the stick with his lips moving. Then he puts it in the fire and weighs out a hundred pennies' weight from his arm ring, and adds two marten skins without being asked. He does not say what answer he will send. He says that he has always bought from whoever won, and that it is useful to know a little early who that will be.

You tell him. Godfred's sons are among the Svear with every man who lost last year, and they are waiting for the kings to be away from home. Hemming goes quite still. Then he asks which is the fastest ship in the harbour and who owns it. By evening it is gone down the Slie with his own man aboard. He gives you forty pennies' weight and two cups of Frankish glass, which are all he has that is his.

The sixteen have followings, and the followings have been three weeks on Saxon bread. You sell what you have for twenty-five pennies' weight above the strand price. The talk at the booths is all of one thing: peace is sworn, and a man may cross the Eider with goods again.

At Sliesthorp they say sixteen lords of the Danes have sworn peace with the emperor's men beyond the Elbe, and that the kings' brother Hemming has been given back. The kings were not there. They are in the Vik with the host.
Leaf fall
The sons of Godfred are home from the Svear with every man who lost last year, and the country has to choose again. Two men are waiting at your boat. They are not waiting together.
Godfred's sons are home. The kings came back from the north with a tired host and found the country had got up before them. There was one fight. It was not a long one.
We are out. I will not dress it. Harald and Reginfrid have two ships and the men who will not leave them. That is still more than Godfred's sons had last year.

We were home before the leaf fell, with the host whole. Godfred's sons landed to find the benches full. They have not had their easy fight. They have not gone away either. It will be settled in spring.
Somebody told the kings. We know it was somebody. I am going back over the water tonight, and I am looking at every boat in this harbour before I go.
A king does not forget who stood by him when he was worth nothing. Kings say so, at least. Give me your hand on it now, and we shall both find out.
The sons of a king who made this market do not ask who a merchant sold to last year. They ask who he sells to now. They will want wine. Their father always did.
You are the man with the stick from Skane. Asulf told us. Come to Sliesthorp when the roads are dry. You will not need to wait at the gate.
Give Eskil your hand: the house stands by Harald, whatever comes of him
Sell to the men who have won, and ask to be shown to Godfred's sons
Tell both that a Frisian has no king here, and go north in spring

You give Eskil your hand. He holds it a moment longer than the custom is. The kings will try again when the roads are dry, he says. If it goes well, come to the hall at Hleidr. If it goes badly, be at Ripa after the spring sowing, with your boat and what you know about the flats. The other man has already walked away.

The envoy buys what you have, sixty pennies' weight above the strand, and pays it from a purse of Svear make. Come to Sliesthorp when the roads are dry, he says, and ask for the youngest. The older ones do not talk to merchants yet. Eskil watches the silver change hands. He does not say anything, and you find you remember it.

You tell them both that your house has a count at Dorestat and finds one lord enough. Each of them thinks it is a poor answer and neither can fault it. In the Vik there is an oath sworn last summer to kings who have other things to think about, and a market that has seen no southern keel since. You will go north when the ice is off the fjords.
A king over the flats

Two ships lie in the river below Ripa with half their oars unmanned. Reginfrid is dead. His brother means to reach the emperor's shore before Godfred's sons reach him, and no Dane aboard knows the channels behind the islands as a Frisian does.
We tried again when the roads were dry. Reginfrid is dead. So is the eldest of Godfred's sons, which is fair. But they had brothers to spare and we did not.
The old emperor is dead as well, since winter. His son is the man to reach now. By sea outside the islands they will have us. Inside, over the flats, we need someone who knows which water is water.
I have been a king for two years and I have been at home for one of them. Take me south, Frisian. I will pay you now, or I will pay you better when I come back. I mean to come back.
You still carry our split stick. The other half is at Hleidr, in a hall we do not hold. The king has two ships and men for one. Think about that before you name your price.
Lead his ships through the channels to the Frisian shore, for a king's thanks
Lead him over and ask nothing now: take his ring as a token for the day he comes home
Lead him over, and take the second ship he cannot man in place of silver

Three tides, lying dry on the sand between them, with your boat ahead and a man sounding with a pole. On the third evening the king of the Danes wades ashore in the emperor's land with forty men. He breaks two gold-washed rings and a silver one for you, eight hundred pennies' weight, and says before all of them that your house is under his hand. It is a small hand this year. He goes inland to find the emperor, and you hear later that he found him.

You lead him over in three tides and take what a careful man would take for the pilotage, no more: four hundred pennies' weight, and six casks of wine he has no use for where he is going. He asks what else. You say he may pay the rest when he is king at home. Harald looks at you for a long time. Then he takes the ring from his own arm, the one with the two beast heads, and puts it in your hand. Show that, he says, to me or to any man of mine, in any year.

You lead him over in three tides. On the Frisian shore Eskil has the second ship stripped of its shields and handed to you where it lies, with its mast, its oars and a hundred and fifty pennies' weight to close the count. She is a sound Danish hull, oak below and built to carry. Harald does not come to see it done. A king minds losing a ship more than a kingdom, Eskil says, because the ship he chose himself.
One on the high seat

There is one king on the high seat at Hleidr and an empty place beside him with a sword laid on it. Godfred's sons are back over the water. The king has sent down the hall for the Frisian who said the right thing in the right summer.
They met when the roads were dry. Reginfrid fell, and Godfred's eldest fell, and after that the sons had no stomach for it. They are among the Svear again. It is a long way to come twice.
I need make each verse only once now. I find I miss the work. Do not tell him.
We were told to come home, and we came home, and I am here. My brother is not. I do not thank you for the half of it. For the other half, ask.
There is a story on the benches that you carried a stick for the other side too. The king has heard it. He has decided it is a story. I should ask for something modest.
Ask a seat in the hall for your house, and take the king's gift
Ask nothing for yourself: ask the king's peace for every Frisian keel at his markets
Ask a plot inside the wall at Sliesthorp, and say the hall is too far from the sea

The steward shows you a place on the bench, not high and not by the door, and says it is yours and your son's whenever the hall is feasting. The king sends down rings to the weight of nine hundred pennies. Thorulf puts a Frisian in a verse for the first time, and rhymes him with a kind of gull. Over the water, Godfred's sons have also learned the name of your house.

The hall goes quiet, because a man who asks nothing for himself is either a fool or dangerous. Harald decides you are neither. It is said before the benches: a Frisian keel lies at the king's markets on the Slie and at Ripa under the king's peace, and pays the king nothing at the gate. He adds six hundred pennies' weight and six marten skins so that nobody can say he was given advice for nothing. The Danes on the benches look at you differently. So, when they hear of it, will Godfred's sons.

The king laughs for the first time since spring. A merchant, he says, to the bone. You are given a plot inside the wall at Sliesthorp, twelve paces of shore with a lane behind it, and seven hundred pennies' weight to build on it. The Wends from Reric are your neighbours on one side. On the other is a man who was for Godfred's sons until last autumn and would rather you did not mention it.
Godfred's sons

Godfred's sons hold the kingdom, one fewer than they were in spring. The youngest of them is at the gate in the wall his father built, learning who trades here. He has been four years among the Svear and counts everything twice.
My father built this wall and brought these merchants here in his ships. He did not ask them. I have been asking people things all morning. It is slower. I am told it lasts longer.
My eldest brother is dead, and so is Reginfrid. Harald has run to the Franks. He will be back with somebody else's army. Men like him always are. Until then there are markets to keep.
I was carried here from Reric in his father's ship, with my scales in my lap. I have done well out of it. I would still not call it an invitation. The young one listens, which the old one did not.
Asulf says the stick from Skane came in your boat. We counted the men who rose for us by what was written back. So I count you with them.
You sold bread to their host in the Vik. So did everyone with bread. I notice it, and I set it down, and that is all I do with it this year.
Ask a plot inside the wall, and sell the new kings what a king-making needs
Remind him who carried the stick, and ask for the Wend Dragomir as your man here
Ask only that your boat pass the gate as it did under his father

Four kings at once need four times the wine, and nobody in the harbour has more of it than you do. By the end of the week you have eight hundred pennies' weight and a plot inside the wall, paced out by Horik himself, who paces it twice. He tells you what the ground rent is before you ask. He is the first lord you have met who knew.

Horik sends for Dragomir and says it before the gate: the Wend keeps this Frisian's goods and sells them in his name, and whoever robs the one robs the king's guest. Dragomir bows to exactly the depth the thing is worth. From the kings' store come eight marten skins and six sacks of amber, and seven hundred pennies' weight for the wine. Among the Danes it is now known that your house was for Godfred's sons before it was safe to be.

It is a small thing to ask, and Horik distrusts it for a moment for that reason. Then he has it said at the gate: this boat passes as it did in Godfred's day and pays the king nothing on what it sells. You make six hundred pennies' weight in the week of the king-making, and keep all of it. Dragomir says you asked for too little. He says it as a compliment.
Two kings for one answer

The market at Skiringssal has had no wine, salt or glass for a year and a half, and the strand is stacked with hones nobody came for. On the heath the chiefs of the Vik are asking what an oath is worth when the men it was sworn to have lost their kingdom.
I swore to two kings in the summer. By winter they had no kingdom. I tell it without smiling. It costs me some effort.
They went home early, and they kept their kingdom, and so I am their man. Somebody gave them good advice. I hope he was paid for it, since I was not.
An oath is sworn to a man, at a place, before witnesses. If the man is gone, the place remains and the witnesses remain. The thing must say which of the three the oath belongs to.
My daughter has been a year on the Karmsund. I am told she brews. I should like to see that, and the chest, in that order.
You fed them when they lay in my fjord. It was good silver, I am sure. Thordis at the alehouse has kept the count of it for you, in case you forgot.
Tell him his daughter and his chest are safe on the Karmsund, and offer to fetch them
Go up to the heath and say before the thing what you saw sworn, and to whom
Leave the heath to the chiefs, and be the first cargo into a hungry market

You fetch them before midsummer. The chest weighs what Gunnhild said it would. Asgrim seats you above his steward and tells the hall how he sent his daughter round the coast in a boat nobody looked at twice. In his telling the plan is his. He gives you ten of the best hones and seven hundred pennies' weight, and says your house lands on his shore without a gift from now on. Then he asks whether you have a son, and how old, and whether the boy would not do well with a few winters in the Vik.

You say it before the thing, in their tongue, slowly: the chiefs laid a hand on the ring and swore to Harald and to Reginfrid, by name, and to no one else and to no kingdom. The lawman asks you twice. Then he says the law: an oath to a man does not pass to the man who drove him out. The Vik keeps its own landing gifts. The chiefs give you nine hundred pennies' weight between them and six good pots of soapstone, and Asgrim says that a Frisian has cost the Danes more with one sentence than he ever did with his cattle.

The first southern keel in a year and a half. Wine goes at half as much again as you have ever had for it, and hones can be had for the carrying. You clear six hundred and fifty pennies' weight in four days. The women of the market settle among themselves that the Frisian should have a booth of his own, so that he comes back. Asgrim lets them think they decided it.
Over the Eider

A host of Saxons and Wends has crossed the Eider with Harald among them and is burning its way north. Godfred's sons have taken two hundred ships to an island and are watching from there. The ferryman has had a busy week.

Seven days' march to the shore, and there they sit. Godfred's sons sit on an island a short row off, with two hundred ships. Neither will cross the water to the other. I have seen cows settle a field with more blood.
Your king is with them. The one you took over the flats. He has come home with somebody else's army, and it is burning his own farms for him.
Your friends are on the island. A king on an island is still a king. Their father would have gone out and fought. Their father is dead.
It will end with hostages. It always does. Somebody's sons will go south to learn to wear shoes, and everyone will call it peace.
Carry bread and ale south to the host, where Harald will know your sail
Carry the country people and their goods over the Slie, at the ferryman's rate
Lie behind the wall and watch what kind of war it is

Harald knows your sail and has his men pay first and ask afterwards: a hundred and fifty pennies' weight for bread and ale, in Saxon silver. He looks older. He asks whether the hall at Hleidr still leans. The host stays three days on the shore, takes forty hostages from the country round about and goes home over the Eider. Harald goes with it.

For six days you carry farm people over the Slie with their kettles, their geese and their grandmothers, at the ferryman's rate and no higher. It comes to forty pennies' weight. Hallbjorn says it is the first time he has seen a Frisian leave silver on a strand. Then the host turns south with forty hostages, and the same people want carrying back.

You lie behind Godfred's wall with the Wends from Reric, who have seen a town burned and are calm about it. The host never comes so far. It wastes the farms to the south, takes forty hostages and goes home. For a month afterwards hides are cheap: the cattle that could not be hidden were killed, by their owners or by the Saxons.

At Sliesthorp they say the emperor's Saxons and the Wends crossed the Eider to put Harald back, and that Godfred's sons lay on an island with two hundred ships and would not fight. The host took forty hostages and went home. Harald went with it.

A grey spring morning on a Danish landing with too few men on it: in the door of an alehouse a woman counts on her fingers, and beside her a young man with a bright new arm ring holds a hazel stick split down the middle; behind them, boats drawn up with nobody working on them.

A sandy river mouth in Skane under a wide sky, cattle grazing on old house plots: a man with his arm bound in a sling holds out a short rune-cut stick, and a heavy-shouldered farmer with a sack of antler on his back bends to read it with his thumb.

The inside of a great timber hall at night, seen from the low benches by the door: a long fire down the middle, and beyond it two kings on one high seat sharing a horn; in front, a tall stooped steward with an iron key at his belt and a slight red-bearded poet in a blue cloak.

Dusk on a new timber jetty in the Vik, skerries beyond: a tall spare chief in a red cloak with two grey hounds looks down into a small Frisian boat; beside him a girl of fifteen sits on an iron-bound chest on a sledge, half covered with hides.

A narrow sound with a fast stream under a bright windy sky, a hall on the ness above and great mounds on the skyline: a woman with keys at her belt weighs a chest on a beam scale on the strand, a girl beside her; behind, a big man rigs a longship and looks over his shoulder.

A summer noon in a fjord crowded with Danish warships drawn up stem by stem, shields along the rails and cooking smoke everywhere: the market booths on the shore stand shuttered, and on the empty strand a kings' man counts out silver in plain sight.

Late afternoon inside the earth wall at Sliesthorp: a man in Frankish shoes and a short Frankish cloak stands alone among dusty horsemen dismounting; at the side a stout dealer with a plaited beard and a hazel switch watches from beside a wattle pen.

An autumn evening on a landing with yellow leaves on the water: a small boat at the jetty, and two men waiting at either end of it with their backs to each other, one with a worn kings' arm ring, one with a sword of Svear make; beyond the roofs, the masts of many newly come ships.

Low tide on the flats of the Wadden Sea at dawn, water and sand the same colour: a small Frisian boat ahead with a man sounding with a pole, and behind it two Danish ships with half their oars shipped; in the stern of the first, a man in a red cloak looks back at the shore.

The great hall at Hleidr by firelight: one king on a high seat made for two, and on the empty half a sword laid crosswise; a Frisian merchant stands before him in the middle of the floor, with every face on the benches turned his way.

A bright morning at the gate in the earth wall at Sliesthorp: a young man of nineteen in a king's red cloak too new for him paces out a plot of shore with long steps; a grey Wendish merchant with a scale case watches, and the harbour beyond is full of ships with shields still on them.

A flat heath above the Vik under a high spring sky: a ring of chiefs standing round a lawman who holds a silver oath ring, a Frisian stranger among them; far below, the market strand piled with unsold whetstones and one small boat at the jetty.

Midsummer on the Slie under a sky smudged with far smoke to the south: an old barefoot ferryman with a white tail of hair poles a flat boat loaded with farm people, geese and kettles; behind them, the earth wall of Sliesthorp with men standing on it.
Whom do you mean to sell to
The toll man does not ask what you carry. He asks whom you mean to sell to. A big man in a red cloak and a mail shirt stands behind him and listens to the answer more closely than the toll man does.
I used to ask what was in the hold. Now I am to ask where it is going. So: whom do you mean to sell to?
They have not gone home. Martinmas is past and their ships are still drawn up on the island. No army has sat a winter in this country before. This one has built huts.
A man who stays the winter must eat the winter. Thanet is good land, but it is not that good. Somebody is going to feed them, and I would like to meet him first.
That is corn in your hold. Corn goes to the strand, in daylight, to people with hearths. I say it once and pleasantly.
From the height here you see every sail that goes into the strait or past it. My watchman sees them too. He cannot tell me what they are.
You are a Frisian. You have seen their ships closer than I have, and lived. Come up at first light and count for me. Count, do not guess.
Go up at first light and count sails for him
Say you sell on the strand, in daylight, where the toll man can see
Ask what an army on an island pays for bread

You stand in the wind beside a shivering watchman and call them as they show: that one a trader, deep and slow; those three not. Forty-one hulls on the island's shore. The ealdorman cuts the number on a stick himself and gives you twenty pennies, and the toll man takes half toll of you for a month.
The toll man cuts his notch. The ealdorman nods, as a man nods at an answer he will check later. Nothing else is asked of you today.

The toll man looks at the ground. The ealdorman looks at you for some time and then says that he would not know, and that he means to. On the strand they tell you without being asked: corn is half as dear again on this water since the huts went up.
The creek and the tide

At dusk a man wades out over the saltings to your boat, up to the thigh, holding a small folding balance above the water. He speaks English like a Dane, slowly and without wasting any. He names a creek and a tide.
I am Ketil. I buy. The others do the other thing. It is cold in this water, so I will be short.
Corn. Ale if you have it. Three times what the strand gives you. I know what the strand gives you. I asked.
Silver by weight, on this balance, and you may bring your own weights and laugh at mine. I cut it where you can see the inside.
You were on the down this morning, counting us. Good. A man who can count is a man I can pay. Men on downs get hungry too.
They say at the toll post that a Frisian asked what we pay. It is not a secret. I am pleased somebody asked.
The creek behind the long bank, east of the crossing. Come in on the top of the night tide, no light. If the ealdorman's man is there instead of me, I was never here.
Take his order: six sacks of wheat to the creek within the month
Hear him out, then give the ealdorman's man the creek and the tide
Say your corn is spoken for, and wish him a dry walk home

He weighs out thirty pennies' worth of cut silver in earnest, an arm ring in four pieces, and wades back the way he came. Six sacks, the creek, within the month. A dog barks somewhere on the Kent shore, and you do not know whose dog.

The reeve's man hears it twice and gives you twenty-five pennies. Three nights later there are spears in the reeds behind the long bank, and nobody comes to the creek. Ketil is not a fool. He will have worked out who knew.

He shrugs with the balance still held up. Going, he lets fall that there are more than forty crews in the huts, that they have salted Thanet's cattle already, and that more ships are looked for in spring. All three are true.
The sisters on the island

At the abbess's ship-house a nun stands over four roped chests and six girls in travelling cloaks too big for them. The minster's own ship lies on her side in the shed, dry and tight, with no one to sail her.
I am Beornwynn, of Saint Mildrith's minster. You know where our minster is. It is on the same island as they are, an hour's walk from their huts.
They have not touched us. They came once, very civil, and counted our cattle. Our abbess says a man does not count what he means to leave.

In our grandmothers' day the sisters of Lyminge were given a house inside Canterbury's wall, for a refuge. The archbishop says there is room in it. So: the books, the altar silver, and the six youngest.
The rest of us stay. Saint Mildrith is not going anywhere, so neither are we. She has seen off worse than Danes. She saw off an abbess once.
We have a ship. The old king freed her of toll here and at Fordwic. Her master went to the ealdorman's levy and her crew with him. A ship is a great comfort in a shed.
People see boats at night on this water. I see them too. I say my prayers and I do not ask whose. Today I am asking only about chests.
Carry the sister, the girls and the chests up the Stour to Fordwic
Give silver for a cart and oxen, and wish her the road
Say the boat is laden, and tell her which tide is safest for the ferry

Four chests amidships, six girls on them, and a nun in the bow who has opinions about your steering. She pays ninety pennies from the abbess's chest before you cast off, so that it is carriage and not charity. The girls ask riddles the whole way up the Stour. You are given one to keep.
Fifteen pennies hires a cart and two oxen at the ferry. They go by the road, which is longer and has no tide in it. She blesses you briefly, like a woman with a cart to load.
You tell her to cross at the last of the flood, when the ferry runs straight and nobody can wade after it. She thanks you for that, and goes to find the ferryman.
An open beach
The Strand is as open as it ever was: no bank, no ditch, booths down to the tide line. Your host wants to know what is on Thanet. The king's reeve wants to know why it should be his trouble.
Nine years ago I stood in that river to my chest with nine people and watched this beach burn. I know what a sail is. Tell me what you saw in the strait.
Huts? They built huts? Then they are not going home to sow. So where do forty crews go in spring, when the island is eaten?
Thanet is in Kent. Kent is the West Saxon's. This is King Beorhtwulf's town. I do not see that a Kentish island is a Mercian reeve's affair.
The ealdorman of Kent sends me a count by a Frisian. Well. How many keels? Say it again, slower.
A ditch across the roads, your host says. A ditch costs a hundred men a month. I have asked the king. The king is thinking about the Welsh.
I keep a spear inside the door now. My grandfather kept a tally stick there. Each of us keeps what he expects to need.
Tell Ceolmund what a wintered fleet does in spring, and help him bury the yard's silver and weights
Give the reeve the ealdorman's count, keel by keel
Sell what you brought and say it is not your beach

You tell him plainly: a fleet that has wintered is rested, hungry and close, and this is the richest open beach it can reach in two tides. That night you lift the hearthstones together. The yard's silver, the lead weights and the bronze balance go under, and his wife's kin are sent over the river before Easter.
Forty-one on the shore, and room cleared for more. The reeve gives you thirty pennies and half toll for two months, and writes nothing down. A count that is written has to be answered.
You sell. Ceolmund says nothing against it; a guest is a guest. A woolman tells you corn is a third dearer than last spring, because none is coming up from Kent, and nobody on the Strand asks why.
Ships wanted
A king's thegn with a new scar and a shipwright with tar to the elbows are going along the shore asking every master the same two things: what he has in his hold, and how well he knows the Wantsum.
You have not heard? Three hundred and fifty ships in the Thames mouth. They broke Canterbury. They broke London, and the Mercian king ran. Then they came over the river into Surrey.
King Aethelwulf met them at Aclea with his son. I was there. It was the greatest slaughter of the heathen army that we have ever heard reported to this present day. And there are still ships.
Wihtgar, from the Dour. I build boats at Dofras. I came here for tar and for hulls, because the king's father has a yard here and nobody left in the town to use it.
Wihtgar. This is my ground. I have built fishing boats on it for twenty years and now I am asked for ships to fight from. I said: the same thing, longer, and God help whoever stands in it.
A man came down from the Strand with nothing but his children. He said a Frisian made him bury his weights before Easter. The yard burned. The weights did not. Was that you?
King Aethelstan means to meet them on the water when they go home laden, in the south mouth by the sand landing. Nobody has done it. We need tar, and a man who knows that bar.
Say you know the south mouth, and will bring the king's ships in through it
Take the wright's order for tar
Tell them what you saw on the strait, and go about your trade

The thegn counts forty pennies into your hand as earnest and tells you to be on the Wantsum about Michaelmas. Wihtgar asks how much water there is on the bar at half ebb. You tell him. He says that is less than he hoped and more than he feared.
Four barrels of tar inside forty days, at four-fifths over the price. Wihtgar spits on his hand and holds it out. He says a ship built in a hurry is mostly tar anyway.

You tell them of the huts, the count, and the creek behind the long bank. The thegn thanks you. The wright tells you, as one tradesman to another, that every yard from here to the Dour wants tar and will pay well over the odds for it.
They fought in their ships

Word runs down the strait that the fleet is coming home out of the Thames, low in the water with Canterbury's goods. In the south mouth, off the sand landing, the king's ships lie with their masts down. Nobody in Kent has done this before, and everybody in Kent has come to watch.
The men are afraid of the water, not the Danes. I told them: a fleet is only men who cannot swim, standing on wood. They said: so are we. Which is true.
My father beat them on land. My brother stood beside him. I have a strait and some green ships, and I mean to be the first of us to beat them where they live.
That is your tar on every seam of them. If they leak, I shall say so to the king, and name you. They will not leak.
Green oak and not enough tar. They will float for a day. I have told the king a day is what he has.
You said you knew this bar. The king's steersmen know rivers. Take the first ship's oar and the rest will follow your stern. I will be standing behind you, so do not turn round quickly.
One thing first. I have a corn sack out of a creek, tied with a knot my reeve calls Frisian. I am busy today. I will be less busy this winter.
They will come on the ebb, heavy, with the sun in their eyes. Where will you be?
Take the steering oar of the first ship and bring them out on the ebb
Stand on the down with the watchman and call the sails as they come
Lie up the Stour until it is over

You take them out over the bar on the last of the ebb with a hand's breadth under the keel, and the laden ships cannot turn. It is short, loud and close. Nine are taken and the rest row for the open sea. The king gives you two hundred and twenty pennies and the ealdorman three bundles of spearheads out of a prize, and says he asked for the second ship and got the fourth.

Your ship touches the bar and hangs there while the others go round you; your shoulder meets the oar loom and loses. They take nine all the same, and the rest row for the open sea. The king gives you a hundred and twenty pennies. The ealdorman says a man who goes aground first has at least gone first.

You call them from the down: sixteen, low, in two lines, the big one third. A boy runs each word down the hill. By evening nine of them are on the sand with English spears in them and the rest are small on the sea. The ealdorman pays you ninety pennies from his own purse and says the watchman can keep his eyes for sheep.

You hear it from up the river as a noise like a fair a long way off. By night the news comes with the tide: nine ships taken, the rest fled. At the hythe they tell you corn is very dear in Canterbury, where the roofs are off and the barns are ash.
A book without its boards

Among hones and combs on a Frisian's cloth lies a book with bare oak boards, the nail holes still bright where a cover was torn off. A priest stands looking at it with his hands behind his back, as a man looks at a horse he cannot afford.
Folcbald, of Dorestat. I buy what the fleet cannot use. They kept the silver off the front. This is the part that was left over. Calfskin, a hundred and sixty leaves, hardly wet.
A hundred and twenty pennies. I gave a Dane a cask of ale for it, so you see I am an honest man: I tell you my profit to your face.
It is a psalter. That is a Canterbury hand, the old good one, not what they write now. Somebody wrote 'pray for Eadhun' at the foot of a leaf. I have been praying for him all morning.

Bishop Aethelwald swore his obedience to the archbishop in writing. He would buy this back for Canterbury today, if the see of Dommoc had a hundred and twenty pennies. It has a cliff and a great many gulls.
Saint Peter's has a wooden cup and a debt to the thatcher. I have offered him forty pennies and a mass every year for ever. He says he has no use for the mass, being a careful man and seldom at sea.
If no churchman buys it by the herring, the leaves go to a man who makes drum skins and book covers. Parchment is parchment. I did not burn Canterbury. I only keep a stall.
Pay his price and take the book for Canterbury
Say bare boards are firewood, and beat him down
Tell the priest whose book it is, and leave it to the Church

A hundred and twenty pennies, counted twice. The priest wraps the book in his own cloak for you and reads you the first psalm from it before he lets go, pointing at each word. You find you know three of them afterwards.
You tell him what oak boards fetch as kindling and what a Frisian's name fetches in Kent this year. He takes seventy pennies and says you drive a hard bargain for a man buying the word of God.
He lets you talk, and then begins to fold the cloth with the book in it. You pay the hundred and twenty. He says next time it will be a hundred and thirty, for the conversation.

You tell the priest it is Canterbury's, and that Canterbury would want to know. He says he will send word south by the next monk who is walking that way. The book stays on the cloth, between the hones and the combs.
Inside the wall

The landing below Canterbury smells of new thatch and old smoke. The archbishop's clerk is at the hythe with a list of what was taken, and the ealdorman is there too, on his way through, in no hurry to leave a merchant he knows.
Wigbeorht, Archbishop Ceolnoth's clerk. This is the list of what they took from Christ Church. It is longer than the list of what we have. I meet every boat, in case.
That is our psalter. That is Eadhun's hand; he taught the man who taught me. Where did you find it? No. First tell me what you want for it. I would rather hear the worst at once.
The six from Thanet are in the refuge and have learned the long psalms. Sister Beornwynn went back to the island by the next ferry. She said she had left bread rising.
We took nine ships. The king had the best, God keep him, we have not seen him since the autumn. I asked for the second and got the fourth. I keep her on the Stour and look at her.
Now. The sack with the knot. I know the creek, I know the tide, and I think I know the boat. I would rather be told than find out. It is cheaper for everyone.
