They are still on the island. Next summer, after the hay, I go over and end it. Huda is bringing the men of Surrey. With his and mine it can be done between two tides.
Hear me, as a friend. Stay off the strait that day. Men who cannot swim will be crossing water in a hurry, and a merchant's boat is the first thing they will climb into.
Lay the psalter on Christ's altar and name no price
Name what you paid and a fair profit on it
Tell the ealdorman about the creek yourself, pay the fine and swear off the camp
Eat the hythe's bread and listen

You carry it up the track and lay it on the altar yourself. The clerk cannot speak for a while. The archbishop sends down a hundred and fifty pennies all the same, because a church that takes gifts from merchants and gives none back gets no more. The writing room gives you a riddle about a thief who ate words, and an afternoon of letters.
You name the price. The clerk counts two hundred and forty pennies out of three different bags, slowly, and writes it on his list in a small hand. He thanks you correctly.

You tell it: the creek, the tide, six sacks. The ealdorman hears it out, names sixty pennies, and has you swear on the hythe's cross to sell the island nothing more. Then he says that a man who tells him to his face may lie where he likes on the day, and he will not ask why.
The bread is new and the ale is thin. You learn that Canterbury will buy oak for a year at nearly half over the price, and that the ealdorman does not make the same request twice.
How wide is that water

There are ditches across the roads of the wic now, a man deep. At Ceolmund's yard a young ealdorman from over the river is buying ale by the cartload and asking Frisians about a strait he has never seen.
We have our ditch. The king found the hundred men the summer after he ran. It is a good ditch. It would have been a better one two years ago.
The house burned over them and they were still there under the hearth, weights, balance and all. I weigh with them every day. You do not pay for a bed in this yard again, nor your sons.
They took the weights, the balance and my wife's brother. I bought new weights. The reeve says they are honest. They feel light to me.
Huda, of Surrey. That fleet walked through my shire on its way to be beaten at Aclea. It took its time. I have barns that are still black.
After the hay I take my men into Kent. Ealhhere and I go over to that island together. He says it can be done between two tides. He is older than I am, so I believe him.
You sail that strait. My men are ploughmen. They have forded the Wey and think they know water. Tell me truly: how wide is it, and what does it do?
Tell him how the Wantsum runs: when the ford bares, and how fast it comes back
Take his order for ale for the march
Wish him luck, and ask Ceolmund what sells

You draw it in spilt ale on the board. Two places only where a man can cross. The ford bares for about as long as a mass and a meal. Then it comes back from both ends at once, quicker than a man walks in mail, and the mud holds his feet while it comes. He has you say it again to his captains. He pays for the ale, twenty pennies, though you drank none of it.
Six casks to this yard inside forty days, at three-fifths over the price. Huda says ploughmen march on ale and fight on the memory of it.
He thanks you for the luck as a man does who has asked for something else. Ceolmund tells you ale is a third dearer in the wic since the levy began to gather, and will be until it marches.
At the ebb
The landing is full of men and no goods. Kent and Surrey are going over to the island when the ford bares. The ferryman has drawn his boat up on the chalk and is watching the water, not the men.
They go at the ebb. The ford gives them the space of a mass and a meal, and then it is a strait again. I have told the ealdorman. He said he would be quick.
I told you to stay off this water today. You are a hard man to keep away from a market. There is nothing to buy.
Well. If you will not go, lie at the ford's end with that boat and keep her afloat. I do not order it. I do not expect to need it. I would like to know it is there.
I have told every man of mine what you drew on that board. When they hear the horn they turn and go back, winning or not. Whether they will do it is another thing.
It is less than I thought. You could throw a spear across. My men have forded worse in a wet spring.
If they are still fighting when it turns, the water will not wait for the better side. Do not be on it in a small boat unless you mean to be.
Lie at the ford's end with the boat through the whole tide, and take off whoever comes
Lie under the minster's shore instead, for the sisters who stayed and the hurt
Go round to the creek on the same tide: whoever wins will want bread
Stay off the strait, as he said

At first they have the better of it; you hear that from the shouting. Then the water turns. The horn sounds and the men of Surrey come back in a body, as they were told, and the Kentishmen behind them, and the tide takes the slow and the Danes who follow. You take men off the mud until the boat has a hand of freeboard. The last is a big man in a red cloak with a broken leg, swearing steadily. Huda is not among them.

At first they have the better of it. Then the water turns, and nobody turns with it. They are still fighting on the far bank when the ford closes behind them, and after that there are men in the water on either hand, in mail, and the mud has their feet. You take off the ones you can reach. Late in the tide you bring the ealdorman over, under his own red cloak. A boy says Huda lies on the other side.

You lie in the minster's creek with the sail down. Before dark the hurt begin to come over the fields, Kent and Surrey together, and the sisters carry them down on hurdles. You cross six times that night. Sister Beornwynn holds the lantern low and counts every head aboard, every time, like loaves.

You go round by the north mouth while every eye in Kent is on the ford. Ketil is at the creek before you, calm as a toll man. Behind him the camp is burning at one end and cheering at the other. He weighs out sixty pennies of cut silver and says the bread will be wanted more tomorrow, whoever is left to eat it.
You lie up the Stour, as he asked. The noise comes over the marsh for half a day and then stops. The news comes after it by the ferry, a man at a time.
Slain and drowned on either hand
The ferry has been carrying back what the water gave up. A grey steward waits at the landing with something wrapped in a red cloak, and asks for the Frisian by name.
At first they were winning. Everybody says that, and it is true. Then it turned. I have fetched over ninety-four so far. I do not sort them. The water did not.
Osferth, steward to Ealdorman Ealhhere, who is dead, and Huda of Surrey with him. The heathen men are still on the island. I say it in that order because that is how it was told to me.
It was your boat that brought him over. The lady knows it. She asked whose, and the ferryman said the Frisian's, and she said: then he is not to wait at any door of ours.
You were not on the strait that day. He asked you not to be. He said the Frisian was the one man in Kent who did what he was told, and laughed. It was the morning of the fight.
There is a corn sack in his hall with a knot in it. He never said whose. I burned it yesterday. I am a steward, not a reeve, and I have enough to bury.
His sister Ealhburh sends you this, which he drank from, and silver. His brother will be ealdorman. He says what Ealhhere promised stands. Which will you have?
Take the gilded cup his sister sends
Ask instead for what he promised: a keel free of toll at Sarre
Say only that you brought him over, and ask nothing
Seven hundred pennies, and the cup: silver, gilded inside, dented at the lip where it hung from a saddle. The steward says it holds more than it looks, like the man. Your house keeps it.

Six hundred pennies, and the new ealdorman's word given at the toll post before witnesses: one keel of yours pays no toll at Sarre while he lives. The toll man cuts a notch of a new shape and shows it you, so that you will know it again.

You say you brought him over and that it is not a thing a man is paid for. The steward goes away and comes back with the lady's answer: eleven hundred pennies, the cup, and the freedom of the toll, and a message that she does not argue with merchants about what things are worth.
The fourth ship
The ealdorman sits on an upturned boat with one leg bound to a spar, drinking from a gilded cup. Drawn up beside him is a long Danish hull, newly tarred, with a shipwright under her counting rivets.
I have said for years that a fleet is only men who cannot swim, standing on wood. I can now add that an army is the same, without the wood. Sit down.
Huda is dead. He turned his men when the horn blew and went back himself for the ones who did not hear it. Surrey came home because of him. Kent came home because of a Frisian with a boat.
Wihtgar. We have met. She is sound: Danish oak, sixteen oars, new rivets where I did not like theirs. I have tarred her twice. She will take six times what your boat takes, and go to windward of it.
That is the fourth of the nine. I asked for the second, you remember. I have looked at her for two years and never once been to sea in her. I am told I am not to go to sea again.
One thing you should know. They are still on the island, and they saw whose sail lay at the ford. They are careful men. They will know it again.
I owe you a leg and whatever goes with it. I am the king's ealdorman in Kent and I have forty hides at Lenham. Ask, and do not be modest. It wastes my time.
Take the fourth ship
Ask ground above the tide here, and a keel free of toll
Say a boat was at a ford, and ask only that his toll men know your sail

He has her run down into the water there and then, and twelve hundred pennies put aboard for her first lading. Wihtgar walks her length once more and hands you a bag of spare rivets. The ealdorman says that in every port of Kent you are now his friend, and that it is a thing with uses.

A plot above the tide at Sarre, paced out by the reeve with the ealdorman watching from his boat; one keel free of the toll here; and fifteen hundred pennies to build on it. He says ground is a sensible thing to ask for by a man who nearly ran out of it.

He looks at you for some time. Then he sends for two thousand pennies anyway, tells the toll man that your keel pays nothing at Sarre, and says before his riders that the Frisian is his friend. He says he will decide what his own leg is worth.
Cut honestly
Ketil does not wade any more. He comes along the shore in daylight with two men and a leather bag. Nobody at the toll post looks up, which is its own kind of looking.
You came on the day itself. I did not think you would. The others say you have a cold heart. I said: no, he has a full hold. It is not the same.
Both their big men are dead. So are a good many of ours; it was not a cheap day. Nobody on your side will write that part down.
We will not sit on this island for ever. There is another, in the mouth of the big river, with sheep on it. Somebody will have to buy for that winter too.
This stick has our notches on it. Show it from your bow and ships of this fleet will look at something else. It does not work on other fleets. I am an honest man.
I have a boat of my own now and no wish to die in a hut. Put your purse beside mine. Or take the bag and go. Either is a fair bargain. The toll man is watching you choose.
Lay your purse beside his and call it one
Take the bag by weight, and no oath
Take what you are owed, and tell him it was the last sack

Two purses on one cloak, and an oath on his arm ring and your cross, each man looking politely away from the other's. Nine hundred pennies is your half. Ketil will sail his own boat where you send it and share what it makes. The toll man has seen all of it, and so by tomorrow has Kent.

Eighteen hundred pennies by weight, in arm rings, cut dirhams and the foot of a chalice you do not look at closely. He cuts where you can see the inside. He gives you the stick as well. At the toll post nothing is said, and nothing will be forgotten.

You take the six hundred you are owed and tell him the creek is shut. He nods, and lets you keep the stick: a bargain is a bargain. It makes no difference at the toll post. Somebody saw the boat three winters ago.
The ship in the shed

The doors of the abbess's ship-house stand open for the first time in three years. The minster's ship has been turned upright and scraped, and the abbess herself has come over the water to see who is to have her.
Six crossings. Seventy-one living, and four who were not by the time we landed. I counted. Somebody had to, and you were steering.
Both ealdormen are dead and the heathen men are still an hour from my gate. I have buried Kentishmen and Surrey men in one row. The saint has not objected.
We stay. We have always stayed. But a house that stays needs someone who goes: to Fordwic, to the wic at London, for salt and wax and news. Our master is under the row I spoke of.
She is free of toll here and at Fordwic by the old king's writing. What she earns is shown to us first. It is a fair rule and I shall enforce it.
I am told merchants like to name their own price, and I like to hear a price before I pray over it. What will you have of Saint Mildrith?
Take the steering oar of the minster's ship, under her freedom of toll
Ask a bay in the ship-house, and a place in the sisters' book of names
Ask the carriage money for a night's work, and no more

She goes down the hard on rollers with six nuns hauling and Sister Beornwynn giving the time. Six hundred pennies for her first lading. You are her master: she pays no toll at Sarre or at Fordwic, and what she carries is shown to the minster first. The abbess says the saint has had worse shipmen.

A bay in the ship-house with your mark on the post, eight hundred pennies, and your name written in the book the sisters read from at the altar. The abbess gives you a folded strip of linen that lay a year on Saint Mildrith's tomb, and tells you to keep it dry and not to sell it.

You ask a night's carriage. The abbess says she knows the price of a night's carriage and this was not that night. A thousand pennies, and one keel of your own free of toll at Sarre: she has the old king's writing, and she can lend a line of it.
This winter the heathen men did not go home. More than forty crews sit in huts on Thanet, and more ships are looked for in spring.

This year three hundred and fifty ships came into the mouth of the Thames. Canterbury and London were stormed and the king of the Mercians put to flight. King Aethelwulf and his son beat the army at Aclea.
This year King Aethelstan and Ealdorman Ealhhere fought in their ships at Sandwich in Kent, taking nine ships and dispersing the rest.
This year Ealhhere with the men of Kent and Huda with the men of Surrey fought the heathen army on Thanet, and at first had the victory. Many men were slain and drowned on either hand.

A grey winter morning at a toll post on a chalk shore: a toll man with a tally stick looking at the viewer, and behind his shoulder a big sandy-bearded man in a red cloak over mail; far across flat water, a low island with thin smoke rising from a row of huts and dark hulls drawn up below them.

Dusk on the saltings, the tide half in, a red band under low cloud: a broad Dane wading thigh-deep toward a small boat, one arm held high with a little folding balance in it; reeds and a long mud bank behind him, no other person in sight.

A cold bright noon at an open boat shed on a chalk hard: a nun of about forty in a dark veil standing over four roped chests, six girls in cloaks too long for them sitting in a row on the chests; behind them in the shed a small clinker ship lying on her side.

A windy spring afternoon on the Strand at London: booths and beached hulls down to the tide line, no wall or ditch anywhere; in front a spare man with a burn scar on his forearm and a spear leaning by his door, talking to a merchant, while a well-dressed reeve stands a little apart looking down the river.

A hot late-summer day on a half-empty shore, grass growing between old house plots: a thegn with a fresh scar across his cheek and a shipwright tarred to the elbows walking along a line of beached boats; behind them a long new hull in frame, ribs bare, and a tar pot smoking.

Early morning, the sun low and behind the viewer, at the sandy south mouth of the strait: English ships with masts lowered and crowded with spearmen pushing out over a bar on the ebb; beyond them a line of laden Danish ships, low in the water, square sails just filling; people watching from a chalk down on the left.

An autumn market on a hurdle bank under a grey sky: a Frisian trader's cloth spread with whetstones and bone combs, and among them a thick book with bare oak boards and bright nail holes; a thin priest stooping over it with his hands behind his back, herring boats beached behind.

A mild day at a river hythe below a walled city with new pale thatch among burnt roofs: a clerk with a long list on a strip of parchment meeting a boat at the water's edge; behind him the big red-cloaked ealdorman sitting his horse at ease, a gilded cup hanging from the saddle.

Evening in a fenced yard at London, a fresh deep ditch cutting the road outside the gate: a young lord in a blue cloak leaning over a board on which a merchant draws a strait in spilt ale; the spare scarred host standing behind with a jug, carts loaded with ale casks at the fence.

A still summer noon at the crossing: hundreds of spearmen wading out over bared mud and shallow water toward a low island with smoke on it, the red-cloaked ealdorman and a young lord in blue at their head; in front a ferryman sitting on his drawn-up boat watching the water's edge, and one small merchant boat afloat at the ford's end.

A grey wet evening at the landing: a ferry boat coming in low with covered shapes in it; on the chalk a grey-haired steward holding a bundle wrapped in a red cloak, the rim of a gilded cup showing; the tide full and flat behind, the island dark.

A bright morning on the hard: the big ealdorman sitting on an upturned boat, one leg splinted to a spar, raising a gilded cup; beside him a long, newly tarred Danish hull on rollers with a shipwright crouched under her; the strait blue and empty behind.

Plain daylight on the shore below the toll post: a broad Dane and two men walking up openly with a leather bag, a notched stick in the Dane's other hand; in the background the toll man at his bench with his head carefully turned away; long ships on the far shore.

A clear morning at the ship-house with its doors wide open: a small clinker ship upright on rollers at the head of the hard, nuns at the ropes, an old abbess with a staff and the cellaress Beornwynn standing by her stem; over the water the island and the minster's two church roofs.
A gilded silver cup, dented at the lip, standing on a merchant's sea chest beside a tally stick with one notch of a strange shape; through the open door behind, the strait at full tide.

A long Danish ship under an English merchant's striped sail standing out of the Wantsum's south mouth past a sand landing; on the down above, a man with a stick and a bound leg, in a red cloak, watching her go.
Two boats lying side by side in a reed creek at dawn, one Frisian, one Danish; two purses on one cloak across the thwarts between them; far off on the Kent shore, a small figure on a horse, watching.

The minster's small ship going up a marsh river under a square sail with a cross sewn on it, a nun in the bow, salt sacks and wax amidships; a toll man on the bank lifting his hand to wave her through.
The abbot's wall
A bank of earth and oak stakes is going up round Saint Philibert's monastery, and the lead is coming off the church roof. The salt is the same price as ever.
Half the stalls in the choir are empty. From early spring to the end of autumn most of the brothers are at Deas on the mainland, and the island keeps a few for the lamps and the salt.
One of the abbey's six river boats lies at the quay loading oak stakes, toll-free and in a hurry. The salt brother from Herio is seeing them counted aboard.
The abbot is building a wall round a house he takes us out of every spring. I have set riddles all my life and I cannot answer that one.
The lead is off the north aisle and lying in a shed at Furca, over the water. A roof is the last thing a house sells and the first thing it hides.
Four loads of oak, squared, before the saint's feast. I pay in salt or in silver. I do not pay for bark.
He wants four loads more, squared, before the saint's feast. He pays in salt or silver. He has told me twice that he does not pay for bark.
And the Bordeaux oil man has not sent his ship this year. He is owed for nine jars, and he has heard what swims in our bay in fine weather.
Take the abbot's order: four loads of squared oak for the wall
Lend your crew to the bank for a day, for bread and the salt brother's talk
Load your salt and ask nothing
The order is cut on a tally: four loads of squared oak, to be landed here. The abbot measures your hold with his rod before he lets you go, out of habit.

Your men carry turf until dusk and eat the abbey's bread. Natalis talks the whole day. He says the wall is so the saint has somewhere to be left from, and gives you a riddle about the wind to take the taste away.
You load salt. Behind you a mallet goes on driving stakes, one every few breaths, until you are out of hearing.
Nine jars owed
Leontius the oil seller, Felix's son, has lamp oil in his store that should have gone north to the salt island. He is not sending his ship.
You have been to the island. Then you have seen my oil burning. Three lamps, day and night, and nine jars of it not paid for.
My steersman saw long ships among the islands at the turn of spring. He is a brave man. He came straight home to tell me so.
My father sold to that house for thirty years and was paid in salt every time. I would like to be the son who was paid, and not the son who put a lamp out.
The jars stand in straw under the city wall, each as high as a child, stopped with clay and scratched with a cross for the saint.
Carry four jars north on his trust, the freight paid now
Buy six jars for yourself at his price
Carry only his letter of demand to the abbot
Four jars go aboard wedged in straw, the abbey's and not yours. Leontius pays the freight in pennies and cuts a tally for the cellarer: thirteen jars owed now, payable in salt.
Six jars, yours, at a price he would not give a stranger. He says to stand them upright, and that he does not ask where oil goes.
The letter is short. Leontius reads it to you so that you know what you carry: nine jars, thirty years, and the name of his father. He pays you six pennies to put it in the abbot's own hand.
The saint's feast
On the feast of Saint Philibert nine ships of the Northmen came to the island, and the island fought them from the ninth hour until evening.
The vigil was kept all night. At the ninth hour a boy on the east head shouts, and there they are: nine sails, low, coming round the point on a flat sea.
They will beach on the ebb and think the sand is theirs. Horse on the hard ground, foot at the gate. Shipman, stand or go, but do it now.
The rakers' children are in the dunes with nothing between them and that beach. Your boat floats. Ours are on the sand.
Trampled sand, the bones of horses, a long new mound above the tide line. The fight is over, and is already told three ways.
One of ours is dead. The brothers say four hundred and eighty-four of theirs. I buried what there was to bury, and I did not reach that number.
The monks say the saint went out by the west gate in white, with a golden sword. I was at the west gate. I saw the count's horses. They were enough.
A flat sea brought nine. The next flat sea can bring ninety, and the ebb will keep the count on the far shore while they dig.
In the basilica three lamps burn at the head of the marble coffin. The oil is Leontius's. The cellarer tells you so twice.
Stand at the west gate with the abbey's men
Take the rakers' children across the lagoon in your boat
Keep off until it is over, then help bury what the tide left

They come up the sand at the ninth hour and are still coming at dusk, fewer each time. The count's horses break them on the hard ground. Afterwards he gives each man who held the gate a handful of pennies, and looks at your face long enough to know it again.
You hold the gate. A spear butt breaks two of your ribs somewhere between the ninth hour and evening, and you see the end of it sitting down. The count sends his own man to bind you.
Three trips over the lagoon with the boat full of children and one old woman who will not let go of her rake. You hear the fight and see none of it. Martinus counts them off the far bank by name.
You dig with the abbey's men above the tide line. There are a good many dead and nothing like the number the brothers give. Nobody who is digging argues with it.
The ebbs
Abbot Hilbod is at the bishop's house in Namnetis, back from King Pippin's assembly with leave to take Saint Philibert off the island.
You sail that bay. Tell me before the abbot does: can a horseman get over to the island when he is needed, or only when the sea allows?
The king's great men said it plainly. Because of the ebbs our men cannot always reach the island. The Northmen can, whenever the sea is calm. So the saint goes where men can reach him.
After Pentecost, on a morning flood, before the summer calms. To Furca by ship, in the coffin, marble and all. Then on men's shoulders to Deas.
I held that sand once, with horses that swam half the way. I will not promise it twice. Show me a road over the water and I will put men on his wall.
The count knows your face from the west gate, and says so to the bishop.
And the people of the island? They are not the abbey's people. Has anyone told them?
I will not be the abbot under whom the founder was dug up and thrown in the sea. I would sooner be the abbot who left.
Offer your ship for the crossing
Say the channel can be marked and a ferry kept at Furca, and offer to prove it
Say nothing in this hall. Go and tell the island

Hilbod asks what your ship carries at the most, and what a marble coffin with a man in it weighs. He answers the second himself. He counts out half a pound of pennies for a frame, rollers and pitch, and names the tide.

The count laughs, then stops. He will come to the far shore before Pentecost with twelve horsemen and watch. The withies, the flat boat and the men to pole it are yours to find. The abbot says only that he has his leave already.
You tell the bishop the ebbs are as the abbot says, which is true. Gunhard watches you go with the look of a man who has had half an answer.
A road over the water

The monastery's channel dries at the ebb and fills on the flood. Between the two there is an hour when a flat boat on a marked line could bring horsemen across. The count has come to the far shore to see it done.
Old Ursus taught me the channel with a pole and a clout on the ear. A withy every forty paces, and the bend marked double. They will stand until the first big tide of spring.
If the count's men can cross, the monks may stay. If the monks stay, somebody buys our salt who also says Mass. I will cut your withies.
Twelve horses and their riders, across and back, on the tide you name. Drown one and I go home.
I have the king's leave. I will watch. I measured that channel myself, shipman, and I did not like the number.
Set the marks and bring the horsemen over on the half tide
Pay Martinus and four rakers to sound every yard first, then try it
It cannot be proved in one spring. Tell Hilbod he was right

Four horses to a crossing, three crossings, and back again before the channel is knee deep. The count rides off the boat last and says nothing until he is on dry sand. Then he says twenty men, changed at each new moon, and has his steward pay you for the ferrying.

The second boatload takes the bend wide. A grey horse goes over the side in the one deep place and is not seen again; its rider is pulled out by the hair. The count goes home. You pay half the horse. Hilbod asks, not unkindly, whether he may have your ship now.
Hilbod nods. He says a man who measures a thing and then says the number is rarer than a miracle, and that he still needs a ship for the tenth day after Pentecost.
What the island is left with
On the salt heaps the rakers ask you what the monks will not tell them: is the saint going, and is the wall to be manned after.
You were at Namnetis. Is he going? Do not tell me to ask the abbot. I have asked the abbot.
We are not going to Deas. Nobody has asked us, and the beds do not walk.
I am to stay for the lamp, they say. One lamp. I learned to count as far as three for this house, and now look.
Three heaps of the year's salt stand under rush thatch above the tide line: one for the abbot, one for the islanders' lord, and one that has always been argued over.
A woman you carried over the lagoon on the feast day puts a loaf in your hand and says nothing.
Tell them all of it, and help carry the third heap to the lagoon side
Tell them, then go up to the abbot with Martinus and ask what he will leave
Say only that the abbot has been to the king, and let them work it out

You tell it: the king's leave, the morning flood, Deas. Nobody shouts. By the next ebb the third heap is under rushes in the dunes on the lagoon side, and four sacks of it are in your hold. The abbot will count two heaps and know why.

Hilbod hears Martinus out standing up. Then he sends for a leaf and has it written: a priest and two brothers to stay, the wall's men paid to Michaelmas, a third of the salt to the rakers. He hands it to you, not to Martinus, and says: you will carry him, then, and they will let you.

Hilbod says the saint is not the island's to keep or to bargain over, and that he had thought better of a shipman than to bring him a raker with a list. Martinus says nothing all the way down the path. The third heap is gone by morning.
Martinus looks at you for a while. He says an abbot does not go to a king to ask leave to stay where he is, and goes back to his rake.
Lead in a shed
Riwal, a Breton master who brings grain to the bay and takes away only salt, has looked through the cracks of the monks' shed at Furca.
There is a church roof lying on the ground at Furca, rolled up like cloth. The keeper drinks. He will sell some of it and not see the rest go.
Not here. Round on the Seine there are abbeys with the rain coming in. Your hull, my buyer, a third to you. Lead has no face.
The monks took it off the saint's house themselves. I only mean to take it a little further.
His ship has a yard, a sail and two anchors, and sits low with rye. His steersman and his bow man watch you from the rail and do not smile.
Take the third share
No. Leave that shed alone
Go to the abbot's man with it

It is done on a dark ebb at Furca, part bought from the keeper and part not. The sheets go under the salt in both hulls. Riwal's bow man crosses himself as each one comes aboard, and Riwal tells him to stop counting.
Riwal shrugs and says there are other hulls. He does not seem to hold it against you. He does not seem to give up the shed either.

The abbey's man at the quay hears you out and goes white. A new keeper is at Furca within the week. Hilbod sends thirty pennies, and an order: when the roof at Deas is ready for it he will want more lead than he has, and he would sooner buy it from you.
The seventh day of June
The founder of the house leaves his island in his marble coffin, by ship for Furca and then by road to Deas.
The tenth morning after Pentecost. The coffin comes down the path from the west gate on its frame, eight brothers under it and the rest singing. The flood is making in the channel.
One tide. Afloat at the top of the flood, out by the channel before it dries, Furca on the north-west wind. If she touches, he sits on a sand bar for the whole bay to look at.
What is your ship called, and your father? I am writing it all down. It is the third hour, unless I am mistaken, and I would be glad if you told me so.
There is a pit in the floor of the basilica and a bare step where the coffin stood. One lamp burns where there were three. He went on the seventh day of June, on a flat sea, and you were not here.
He blessed this salt, they say. Stand where you like, shipman. I know where I am standing.
A priest and two brothers are staying, and the wall's men are paid to Michaelmas. It is written on a leaf, and Martinus has had it read to him twice.
Some lead came back to Furca in sheets. We have cast it in lumps. I do not ask where it had been.
Take the coffin aboard at the top of the flood
Let the abbey's own boat take him. Carry the house's goods and the last of the lead
Stand on the sand with the rakers

She floats with a hand's breadth to spare and goes down the channel like a led horse. The wind is north-west and the sea lies flat. At Furca the brothers lift him out singing, and Hilbod stands a moment with his hand on your stem before he follows.

She touches at the bend and the ebb leaves her. Saint Philibert sits a whole tide on a sand bar in your hold, with the brothers standing round him in the wet, singing the hours. On the night flood she lifts. He is at Furca by first light. Nobody in your crew speaks until then.
Chests, vestments, the cellarer's tallies, a bell and a load of lead in lumps: you set them down dry at Furca and are paid 180 pennies. The monks thank you as they would a carter.
You stand at the tide line among the rakes. Nobody on the sand sings. When the sail is small Martinus says, well, and goes up to the basilica to see how many lamps they have left him.
No wind off Batz
With the monks' lead under the salt, the wind dies off the island of Batz and does not come back. Riwal's ship lies a bowshot off, as still as yours.
A rider. On the water, there, coming up from the south. A white horse, and three spears in his hand. Do not tell me it was a gull.
My bow man has seen it too. He wants to go back. I have told him lead is heavy and visions are light.
At dusk a fishing boat rows out from Batz. They have a lame man ashore who woke this morning walking, and he says a monk in his dream told him why the two ships have no wind.
Put about and take it back to Furca
Out oars. Saints do not ride on water
Vow the saint a tenth of the price and a lamp's oil, and wait

The wind comes before the oars are out, from the north, fair for Furca and for nowhere else. Riwal calls you several things across the water and then, a while later, follows. The sheets go back into the shed by night. No one is ever asked about it.
A day and a night at the oars, and at the second dawn a little air from the west. Nobody saw the rider again. Nobody looked south.

Three days at the oars on a sea like oil, the water cask down to the lees, and the bow man seeing spears in every gull. The wind that comes at last is foul. You make the Seine all the same, with a crew that has stopped looking at you.
You say it aloud, on the lead, with the crew as witnesses: a tenth and a lamp's oil. The air comes within the hour. Riwal says it would have come anyway. He does not say it very loud.
A guest of Saint Philibert
The saint reached Deas on men's shoulders in four days. At Namnetis the abbot settles his accounts before the summer is out.
They say the sick were healed all along the road, at Ampan, at Varenne, at Paulx. And that for this one year women may come in to the tomb at Deas, from feast to feast.
You brought her in on the tide I named. I have thanked God. Now I thank you, by name.
She touched, and he sat a tide on the sand with the brothers singing round him to keep the gulls off. He is at Deas all the same. I count the end.
The goods came dry and the lead came whole. That is a carter's praise, and I mean it as praise.
I shall write that the sea lay flat for him. I shall not name the ship; the book is about the saint. But the house will know.
Is anyone left on the island to say Mass?
You can tell the bishop yes: a priest, two brothers and a paid wall. He shuts his eyes for a moment.
They are calling it faint heart in the city. Let them. The bones are where a count can reach them.
Ask for a guest's place wherever the saint lies
Ask for room in the abbey's six boats on the Loire, toll-free
Ask for the guest's place, and for the island's share to be kept as it was written
Take the carter's fee, and the coffin's frame and rollers

Three pounds of pennies from the abbot's chest, and a thing that is not in any chest: wherever the body rests, a merchant of your line has a bed, a hearing and a place at the guest table. Hilbod says it before the bishop so that it will be remembered.

Two and a half pounds of pennies, and the abbey's man at the quay is told that your goods ride in the saint's boats when there is room. The king's toll does not touch what the saint carries. The toll man will learn your face and dislike it.

Hilbod is silent, then laughs once. Five pounds of pennies, the guest's place for your line, and the leaf about the island's third copied fair with the bishop's mark under it. Martinus is to keep your tally on the island. The abbot says he has been out-measured, and does not seem sorry.

The fee is counted out and is fair. The oak frame and the rollers that took a marble coffin down a beach are no use to the monks now; they are fitted to your ship, and will bring her up any sand you choose.
One lamp
The saint's feast comes round with no saint. The islanders keep it anyway, on the sand, and count what the monks left.
One lamp where there were three. I trim it. Nobody told me to.
What did they say about me at Furca? No. Do not tell me.
The third heap went to a Breton for rye and silver while the abbot was counting stalls at Deas. Your share is in the dune under rushes, like everything of ours.
The abbot took two heaps and left the one nobody could ever agree on. We have agreed. Part of it is yours, for standing where you stood.
The fort stands with eleven men on it. Bread is still baked for the windbound, by a woman now, which is new.
Word from Deas is that the abbot knows who talked. He has not cursed you. He has stopped asking after you.
Leave your tally and your salt with Martinus
Ask for a berth on the lagoon side and a store dug in the dune
Take part of your share in salt, and a raker's welcome

Your share comes to 640 pennies, counted on a raking board. Martinus splits a tally stick and keeps half: from now on your salt waits on this island under his eye, and is sold or held as you tell him.

Six hundred pennies, and a place the monks never knew about: a berth behind the dunes on the lagoon side where a boat cannot be seen from the bay, with a store dug into the sand beside it. The rakers dig it in a day and roof it with a dead man's boat.

Ten sacks of the white salt off the top of the heap, the rest in pennies, and your half of a tally stick. The woman with the rake calls you her son. You have heard what she calls merchants who cheat her, and take it as meant.
Three lamps
The saint's feast, and the marble coffin lies where it has lain since the founder died. The count's men are on the wall, and a flat ferry lies at Furca.
The vigil is kept through the night, as it was the year of the nine ships. At the ninth hour every man on the wall looks at the east head. Nothing comes round it but terns.
I had the king's leave to go and I have not used it. If I am wrong, shipman, we are both in the young brother's book, and not in the chapter either of us would choose.
Twenty men on the wall, changed at each new moon, over your road. They complain of the salt wind. Good. A man who complains is awake.
The big tide took nine withies. I have cut nine more. That is every spring from now on, and somebody must do it or pay for it.
I had begun a book about a journey. Now it is a book about a tomb, which is shorter, unless I am mistaken, and may be better.
Take the locked store inside the wall
Take the ferry at Furca for your house, with its fare
Ask only that your name be said at the tomb

A stone-footed store against the inside of the bank, with a lock and one key, and 900 pennies from the count and the abbot between them. You know the channel now as the islanders know it. The withies are yours to keep standing, every spring.

The flat boat at Furca is your house's, with a fare from every man and beast that crosses and three pounds of pennies for the year past. The count's men cross free; that was the bargain. The withies are yours to keep standing, every spring.

Hilbod looks at you a long time. Your name is said at the tomb that night, after the founder's and before the king's, and will be said each year. He sends two and a half pounds of pennies to the boat anyway, and a guest's place for your line. The withies are yours to keep standing, every spring.
Whose roof it was
At Rotomagus the cellarer of Jumieges is buying lead for a leaking aisle. Jumieges is the first house Saint Philibert founded, two tides down the river.
Good sheet. Old work, with nail holes along one edge. This has been on a roof. Whose?
Our founder went from here to an island in the south and built again. We keep his day at the end of harvest. You will have heard of him, coming from that way.
English lead. Everybody knows the English have hills of it. Tell him, friend.
Two of your men have not spoken to you since the calm. One of them crosses himself each time the cellarer says the founder's name.
You vowed a tenth and a lamp's oil off Batz, and the wind came within the hour.
Say it came from the English, and sell
Sell, and set a tenth and a lamp's oil aside for the saint
Tell the cellarer whose roof it was

The cellarer pays by weight and asks nothing more. Your third is 1,100 pennies. Riwal drinks with you on it and swears partnership, his hull beside yours from now on. Saint Philibert's lead goes up on Saint Philibert's first roof, and only you, a Breton and the saint know.

You sell, and count a tenth into a separate bag before Riwal can speak, with the price of a jar of oil on top: it goes south by the next ship for the lamps. He calls it a waste and swears partnership all the same. Your men talk to you again.

The cellarer sits down on the lead. Then he pays you a finder's price, 650 pennies, has a letter written to Abbot Hilbod, and keeps the sheets until an answer comes. He says a house that owes you its founder's roof can keep your goods under its own at the quay. Riwal has already cast off.
The first book
Abbot Hilduin of Saint-Denis has been sent a book of the wonders of Saint Philibert by a young monk of the west, to be corrected. He has heard that you were there.
A young monk of the west has sent me a book of his saint's wonders to correct. He writes well and counts boldly. You were there, shipman. Sit.
They tell of four hundred and eighty-four heathen dead on a feast day, and one of ours. I am an abbot; I should like it to be true. I am also asked to correct.
There is a chapter here about shipmen and a church's lead, and a rider on the sea with three spears. You have gone a strange colour.
And this I do not follow at all. He had the king's leave to move the body, and he stayed. Whose counsel was that?
Eight monks are singing in the new chapel and can be heard through the wall. A clerk holds the quire open with two fingers and waits.
Tell it as you saw it
Tell it as the monks tell it
Say a shipman counts tides, not miracles

You tell him: the mound above the tide line, the channel, the hour of the flood. He has the clerk read you each sentence in Latin and then in plain speech, and by the end you are following some of the Latin. He changes nothing in the book. He says the boy may count as he likes, so long as somebody once counted properly. Sixty pennies, and an order for skins.

You give him the saint in white and the golden sword. Hilduin listens with his eyes shut and has a hundred pennies sent to your boat. At the door he says he had hoped to meet a witness, and has met a second copy.
Hilduin says that is the most honest answer he has had in a year of asking, and lets you go back to your casks.
On the feast of Saint Philibert nine ships of the Northmen came to the island of Herio. The count of Herbauge and the abbey's men fought them from the ninth hour until evening and beat them off.
This year the monks of Herio took the body of Saint Philibert out of his island for fear of the Northmen, and carried it to Deas on the mainland. The sick were healed along the road.
This year the abbot of Herio had the king's leave to carry Saint Philibert off his island, and did not. The count keeps men on the abbey's wall, and there is a ferry over the channel.

A low sandy island under a wide grey-bright sky, mid-morning: in front, lay workers driving squared oak stakes into a fresh turf bank; a square weathered abbot in a muddy black habit measures the gap with a rod; an old sunburnt monk white to the knee with salt leans on a long rake, grinning; behind, a stone basilica with half its roof stripped to bare rafters.

Under the towered Roman wall of Burdigala by the brown Garonne, hot afternoon light: a stout oil seller in a belted linen tunic stands among tall clay jars bedded in straw, one hand flat on a jar scratched with a cross, the other holding a tally stick; a small ship lies idle at the bank behind him, her yard lowered.

The west gate of a turf-and-timber rampart on Herio, late afternoon, flat calm sea: nine low ships beached on wet sand, raiders running up the shore; Frankish horsemen wheeling on the hard ground; at the gate a line of the abbey's armed men with round shields; small in the dunes to one side, a boat crowded with children pushing off across a lagoon.

A bishop's hall at Namnetis, autumn daylight from a high window: a slight grey bishop in a white alb leaning forward to listen; a square abbot standing with a sealed parchment in one hand and a measuring rod in the other; a Frankish count in a riding cloak with his arms folded; a merchant in sea clothes before them, a rough map of a channel drawn in spilt wine on the table.

A tidal channel between an island and the mainland at half tide, bright windy spring morning: a line of tall withies marching across brown water, doubled at the bend; a flat ferry with four nervous horses and mailed riders poled by islanders; a lean young salter at the bow with a sounding pole ringed in red wool; on the far sand a count on horseback, watching.

The salt heaps of Herio at low sun, evening: three long heaps under rush thatch above the tide line; a ring of islanders with wooden rakes, men and women, bare-legged, facing a merchant; a lean young salter in front with his arms crossed; an old monk sitting apart on an upturned basket, counting on three fingers.

The quay at Namnetis under the Roman wall, dusk, drizzle: a dark wiry Breton master in a hooded cloak talking low with one hand cupped as if weighing something; behind him a beamy sea ship with yard, sail and two anchors, low in the water with grain, a steersman and a bow man staring from the rail.

The beach of Conca on Herio, clear early morning, the flood making: a white marble coffin on a wooden frame carried down the sand on the shoulders of eight monks toward a small ship held in the shallows; an abbot with a measuring rod walking ahead; a young short-sighted monk writing on a wax tablet; islanders standing silent along the tide line with their rakes.

Two ships lying still on a sea like oil off a low rocky island, late afternoon haze, sails hanging slack: on the nearer ship a bow man points south with his whole arm, the crew turned to look; far off on the shining water, small and not quite certain, a rider on a white horse with three spears.

The bishop's house at Namnetis, a summer evening, door open on the Loire: a square abbot counting pennies from a small chest onto a table; a slight bishop beside him with a plain silver cross; a young monk with a wax tablet round his neck writing; in the doorway, leaning against the post, an oak carrying frame and rollers.

Inside the basilica of Herio, dim, evening: an open pit in the floor and a bare stone step; one small lamp burning on an iron stand where three hooks hang; a lean young salter trimming the wick with a knife, a rake propped against the wall; through the open door, islanders eating together on the sand.

The basilica of Herio at night on the saint's feast: a white marble coffin under three burning lamps, monks singing in full stalls; through a window, torchlight on a turf rampart with spearmen looking seaward; an abbot and a Frankish count standing side by side at the back, not singing, watching the door.

The river gate quay at Rotomagus, grey morning, the Seine at high tide: rolled sheets of old lead with nail holes laid out on the stones; a heavy monk cellarer crouched over them with a steelyard, looking up sharply; a Breton master smiling too widely beside him; a merchant between the two, looking at the lead.

A room in the abbey of Saint-Denis, clear north light: a tall elderly abbot seated with an unbound quire of parchment on his knee, one finger on a line; a clerk holding the leaves open; a merchant on a stool opposite, cap in hand; through an inner door, monks singing in a small chapel lit by candles.

A country road through marsh and vines on the mainland, summer noon: a marble coffin on a frame carried on men's shoulders at the head of a long line of monks and country people, the sick laid at the roadside reaching to touch its cloth; far behind, small on the sea, a low island.

The lagoon side of Herio at dawn, mist on the water: a small trading boat lying hidden behind dunes; beside her a store dug into the sand and roofed with an upturned old boat; a salter handing half a split tally stick to a merchant; salt heaps under rushes.

Herio from the sea on a flat calm summer day: a turf-and-timber fort with spearmen along its rampart round a stone church with a whole lead roof; a line of withies crossing the channel to the mainland and a flat ferry half way over with horses; no sail anywhere on the horizon.

The abbey of Jumieges on a bend of the Seine in rain: workmen on a church roof nailing down sheets of old lead; below, a Breton ship and a small trader moored side by side, two masters shaking hands over a bag of silver; at the rail, a crewman crossing himself.
Halfdan, who shared out the Northumbrians' land, was driven out by his own army. He left the Tyne with three ships and was killed in Ireland, at Strangford Lough, fighting other Northmen.
Saint Cuthbert's people are at Crayke, north of York, after seven years on the road. Their abbot says the saint has named a king for the army: a slave boy at Whittingham.

The army at York and the English have one king: Guthred, Harthacnut's son, bought free from a widow. He has given Saint Cuthbert the land between Tyne and Wear, and thirty-seven days' peace to any who flee to the body.
Saint Cuthbert's body is in Ireland, carried over from the Derwent's mouth in a merchant's hull. The north of England has lost its saint, and says who took him.
The army at York has taken a king of its own kind. The boy the abbot of Carlisle dreamed of would not be bought, and Saint Cuthbert's people are still guests at Crayke.
The island empties
On the holy island the church door stands open and a coffin of carved oak is on a cart in the yard. Monks are loading books. Nobody is singing.
We are taking him off the island. Halfdan is on the Tyne with a fleet, and he does not stop at rivers.
Jarrow and Wearmouth had walls and brothers too. I am from Carlisle. I have seen what is left of a place when they have been.
Two hundred and forty-one years since Aidan came here from Hi. I had hoped to be the bishop who did nothing worth writing down.
The cart can cross the sands at the ebb. The coffin I would rather not trust to a cart on wet sand. You have a boat.
He points at the coffin, at your hull, at the far shore, and then holds up one finger: one tide.
Take the coffin and the books over the water on your hull, at the top of the tide
Buy what they cannot carry: the wax and the spare parchment, for forty pennies
Give twenty pennies for the road
The coffin comes aboard on six oars laid crosswise. It weighs less than a cask of wine. Seven young men walk it up the far beach on their shoulders, and not one of them looks back at the island.
Four cakes of wax and two bundles of parchment, at a price that would shame you in a good year. The abbot counts your pennies twice and thanks you once.
The bishop puts your pennies in the coffin, beside the saint. Nothing else they own will be guarded half as well.
The rock shuts
Under the rock of Bamburgh a monk is buying barley with a silver spoon. The gate above him is shut, and the reeve has come down to see who else has landed.
The king's word: no coffin inside this gate. A saint is a fine thing until the Danes hear where he is lodged.
You go where the wind goes. Go to the Tyne, count his ships, and see if they are caulking them or hauling them up. Thirty pennies, now.
We need to know the same thing he does, and cannot pay for it. If the Tyne is shut we go west over the hills, to the abbot's country.
You carried him over the water. Hunred says the boat did not even dip. He says that kind of thing about everything, but still.
You have not heard. The island is empty. Saint Cuthbert is on a cart behind seven of us, and I am the one who can count, so I buy the barley.
Take the reeve's thirty pennies to go and count the ships on the Tyne
Go and look at the Tyne for the bearers instead, and take nothing for it
Sell the monk two loads of barley at a good year's price, and keep the spoon out of it
He pays first. 'I do not expect to see you twice,' he says. 'If I do, I shall know the Tyne is worse than I thought.'
The monk writes nothing down. He says he will name you at the third psalm of every night office, which is when he is most awake.
Fourteen pennies, counted out of a purse that was once a bishop's glove. He keeps the spoon. It has a dead man's name scratched on the handle.
Halfdan's winter
The Tyne is full of long ships drawn up side by side, under a church with no roof. A Dane has spread altar silver on a sail, and beside it stands a boy with a rope on his wrist.
Count them if you like. The English send someone every week. We are staying the winter, so the number will not change.
Two cups, a plate, the cover off a book. I sell by weight. What it was for is your business.
My lady at Whittingham wants a boy for the geese. Twenty pennies. He looks as if he eats.
Harthacnut's son. His father is dead and so are his father's friends, which makes him cheap. Thirty and he is the widow's. More, and he is yours.
Guthred. I can row.
He holds up a cup, then a weight, then closes his fist: silver for silver. For the boy he opens his hand four times.
Buy the altar silver back by weight: ninety pennies
Outbid the widow's man for the boy: forty pennies
Sell the camp two casks of Rhine wine and ask nothing about the silver
Count the ships, eat his fish, and go
Two cups and a plate, bent to fit a sack. On the foot of one cup somebody has scratched a cross and a name. The Dane throws in the sack.
The widow's man shrugs and goes to look at a cheaper boy. Yours climbs aboard without being told, finds the bailer, and starts using it.
They pay in cut silver, one piece of it still shaped like the arm of a cross. The wine is drunk before you have cast off.
Smoked salmon, and no questions about whose man you are. You count the ships twice and get two numbers. They are not caulking. They mean to stay, and they are dry: wine would sell here.
Three ships
At the ship-fort on the black pool a mail coat and a king's saddle are for sale on the strand. A Dane with a new scar is sitting on the saddle.
Albann, we called him. He came into Loch Cuan with three ships to be a king here. Three ships. He got a mound by the water instead.
The merchant who ate my fish on the Tyne. I had a king then. I have his saddle now.
You are from the east side. So was I. Two winters ago I had a king on the Tyne. I have his saddle now.
The English priests say he went mad and stank, and that is why we drove him out. He did stink. That was not why.
At York they are sharing out the land by the rope. A man who is not there gets the bog. I need to be there.
Carry him home to the Humber for his word and nothing else
Hire him for thirty pennies: he knows this sea from the Liffey to the Solway
Buy him a drink and take the news east
He rows without being asked and sleeps on the saddle. Off the Humber he says: 'When you want a thing said in the army's hall, I will say it.' Then he walks north.
He takes your thirty pennies and the steering oar on the same day. He knows where the Solway dries and how the tide sets off Man. He does not explain. He points.
He drinks, and tells it once more for the cup. Before you go he says the fort is short of wine and grain, and has plenty of everything it stole.
Columba's shrine
On the white strand of Hi a shrine of yew and bronze is being lashed into a hide boat. The abbot watches it go as a man watches his own roof carried off.
It goes to Ireland today, with its keepers. The foreigners have left us our lives twice. I will not ask it of them a third time for a box of bronze.
They say Cuthbert of the English is on the road as well. Aidan went from this strand to that island, and some of Aidan is in that coffin. So the coffin is partly ours.
I have written to their bishop. There is a house for them in Ireland with Columba's people, if they can come to it. I have no one going east. You go everywhere.
We have a verse for nights like the last one. The wind is rough, so the sea-kings stay at home. We pray for bad weather here. It is the one prayer that is often granted.
You took him off the island in your own boat? Then you are in the story already. You may as well carry the letter.
Take the abbot's letter for Bishop Eardulf, wherever he is
Take two of the shrine's keepers and their baggage over to the Irish shore
Sell them a cask for the Mass, against an arm-ring by weight
A folded skin, sealed with a thumb in wax. A brother copies you the verse about the wind on a scrap, in Irish letters, and explains it twice.
Two quiet men and a load they will not let you lift. On the Irish shore they give you a psalter the size of your hand. 'It is all we have that a Saxon would call money.'
The arm-ring weighs out at ninety pennies and a little over. The abbot waves the little away.
The waste city
Legacaestir: Roman walls with ash trees growing out of them and six roofs by the landing. A thin monk has been asking every hull on the Dee the same question.
Franco. My grandfather came over for wool, they say, and stayed for a woman. I carry a dead bishop for a living one.
We mean to take him to Ireland. The bishop has told only the old ones. North of here a river called the Derwent meets the sea. We need a keel there before the new moon.
Last week we were nine men with a salted horse's head and one cheese, and somebody stole the cheese. You see how it is with us.
A letter from Hi? Then there is somewhere to go to. I had begun to think Ireland was only a direction.
You are the Frisian with the boat. Hunred still talks about the boat.
Promise your hull at the Derwent's mouth before the moon is new
Give him ship's bread for nine and let them find another keel
Tell him what the Irish shore is like now, and promise nothing
He kneels on the landing, which embarrasses everyone. Then he gets up and gives you the marks for the Derwent's mouth, like a man who has been saying them over for a week.
Two sacks of ship's bread. He carries both himself. You hear afterwards that they found a keel, and what came of it.
You tell him: a ship-fort on the Liffey, and men in it who sell monks. He nods. 'The bishop says the same of the Tyne. We shall go all the same.'
Three waves
Off the Derwent's mouth, with the coffin lashed amidships and the people left crying on the sand. The wind has backed into the west and the first big sea has come aboard.
Wind is backing west and the sky is the wrong colour. We can still run back in on this. In an hour we cannot.
We did not tell them we were going. Listen to them. I can hear them from here, and I am a little deaf.
That is the third sea aboard, and look at the bilge. Red. It will be the ballast clay. I am telling the men it is the ballast clay.
The book! The chest has come adrift. Bishop Eadfrith wrote it with his own hand. Do not let me be the abbot who watched it go.
Hi has a house waiting for us. If God wants us in it, this is a strange way to say so.
Put about and run back for the Derwent
Leave the helm to the steersman, put about, and lash the book-chest yourself
Hold on for Ireland
Give Ketil the helm, who knows this sea, and hold on for Ireland
She comes round with her rail under. Something square and bright goes over the side as she heels, and the abbot cries out. On the beach they wade in to their waists to take your line.

You get two turns of rope round the chest and one round your own leg before the next sea. She comes round. The book is dry, the saint is going back to the beach he left, and the abbot has hold of your arm.
The chest slides, takes the skin off your shin and goes through the rail. You see the gold on its cover once, going down green. She comes round without it.
Two days of it. On the third morning there is a low green shore, and a man herding cattle who crosses himself when he sees what you carry. The bishop does not speak until the coffin is on the sand.
She will not lie to it. A sea breaks the rail and the book-chest goes with it. What is left of the day is spent running back to the river you left, with two men bailing and one praying.
Ketil takes her north of the worst of it, round an island he does not name. On the second evening he points at a line of hills. 'Ireland. I was nearly killed near here.' The coffin goes ashore dry.
The low tide
The bearer Hunred has walked four days down the coast to find a boat. He has had a dream, and he tells it like a man reading out a tally.
You were not there. Three great seas, the water red in the ship, and the gospel book gone over the side. We turned back. The people on the beach took us for ghosts.
The saint came to me in my sleep. I am to go to the shore at Whithorn, at the lowest ebb of the moon, and look.
Also there is a bridle hanging on a tree. I am to show it to a red horse, which will come to me, and it will draw the cart. He was quite exact.
They found who took the cheese. The bishop prayed, and a fox came out of the wood carrying it. I do not say the man became the fox. Others say it.
It is three days north by sea, and three weeks by land round the firth. I am asking for the three days.
Take him north to the Whithorn sands and walk the ebb with him
Give him bread for the road and keep to your trade
Tell him what salt water does to a book, and wish him a dry road

At the bottom of the ebb the sea is three miles off and the sand lies like a floor. The book is on it, shut, with its gold on. Inside, the pages are white. Hunred does not seem surprised. On the way back he finds the bridle.
He thanks you and goes north on foot with the loaf under his arm. Three weeks, he said.
'Yes,' he says. 'The abbot said that also. Until I told him about the horse.' He goes north on foot.
Harthacnut's son
The boy you bought on the Tyne can hand, reef and steer, and eats like two men. The steersman has come aft to ask what he is to be called on the tally: thrall, or crew.
He pulls a man's oar and eats a man's food. The crew want to know if he gets a man's share, or if we are carrying him as your goods.
My father was Harthacnut. He had a hall and forty men. Then he had enemies. I do not need it talked about. I only do not want it forgotten.
A ship is better than a goose yard. I would stay, if I were asked. Nobody has asked.
One more thing. Half the men will not share a bowl with a heathen in Lent. I only report it.
Free him before the crew, with a share like any man's
Free him, and stand godfather to him at the next church: ten pennies for the white cloth
Sell him on: the widow at Whittingham still wants a boy
You say it at the mast with the crew for witnesses, the way it is done. He says nothing. Then he goes forward and takes the worst oar without being told.
A priest with a cold does it in a river. He comes up Guthred still: he would not take another name. He keeps the white cloth in his sea-chest, under the fish hooks.
Sixty pennies from the widow's steward, who remembers being outbid. The boy walks up the road to Whittingham behind a cart of geese. The crew are quiet for two days.
The abbot's dream
York has had no king for six winters and the army's great men drink in separate halls. Abbot Eadred has come in from Crayke to buy lamp oil, and he looks like a man who has stayed awake on purpose.
The saint stood by my bed at Crayke. I am to cross the Tyne to the army and tell them to make a king: Guthred, Harthacnut's son, whom they sold to a widow at Whittingham.
They are to pay her his price, lead him up Oswigesdune at the sixth hour, and put a gold ring on his right arm. I have the dream. I have not got the price.
The book that went over the side is at Crayke. Hunred found it on the sand at Whithorn, where he was told to look. So I have stopped arguing with dreams.
You walked the sand with Hunred. Then you know what I know: when this saint says where a thing is, it is there.
You tied a gospel book to your own leg in a storm. I think you can be told a dream.
A king out of a widow's goose yard, picked by a dead Englishman. It is the best offer we have had in six winters, which tells you about the others.
This one carried me home from Ireland for nothing. If he says the priest is not mad, I will say it louder, in the hall.
Lend the abbot the boy's price, eighty pennies, against the saint's word
Go into the hall and put the dream to the army in their own tongue
Tell him the boy is not at Whittingham. He is on your ship
Hear the dream out and keep your purse shut
Eighty pennies into a sleeve. 'The saint is good for it,' the abbot says. 'He has been dead near two hundred years and has not yet failed to pay.'
They laugh until the ale is finished. Then an old man asks who Harthacnut's enemies were, and whether any of them is still alive, and nobody can name one. That is when they stop laughing.
He looks at you for some time. 'Whittingham,' he says. 'He was quite exact.' Then: 'Do not sail. I shall come to the landing in three days.'
You hear it out. It is a good dream. At the landing they are already saying that the priests at Crayke have found a king somewhere.
The price of a king
The abbot stands on the landing with two of the army's great men behind him. They are all looking at your crewman, who is looking at a rope he has no need to coil.
That is the one. Harthacnut's son. The saint did not say he would be coiling rope, but I know him.
I was told to pay a widow. It seems you are the widow. What is his price?
I am his to sell. I have known that every day since the Tyne.
I am a free man with a share in this ship. I was sold once. Ask me, not him.
He stood godfather to me. If he says go, I go as from a father's house, not from a market.
Give him up for nothing, and go with him to the hill
Name a king's price: four hundred and eighty pennies, weighed
Say he is a free man with a share in this ship, and let him answer for himself
'Nothing,' you say. The abbot writes it down as if it were a sum. Guthred takes his sea-chest, leaves you the fish hooks, and says: 'A king has a long arm. You will find out how long mine is.'
Two pounds of silver, weighed twice on the army's scales. Guthred watches every piece go into the pan. 'Now I know it to the penny,' he says, and goes ashore without his sea-chest.

'No,' he says, in English, so that the abbot will understand it. 'I have been bought. Once was enough.' The great men look at each other. The abbot looks at the sky, as if something had been left out of the dream.
The gold ring
This year the army and the English together took a king: a young Dane bought out of a widow's yard, with a gold ring on his right arm and the saint's coffin beside him on the hill.
The king has given the saint all the land between the Tyne and the Wear. We are building at Cunecacestre, in the old fort. Seven years on a cart, and he chooses a Roman ditch.
And this: whoever flees to the body has peace for thirty-seven days and nights, from any man, Dane or English. Tell that in your ports. Somebody will need it.
There is the man who had me for forty pennies and let me go for none. Stand by me. I want them to see what an honest price looks like.
The merchant. Four hundred and eighty. I had it weighed again after you left, and it was all there. So we are quits. Exactly quits.
They tell me a Frisian was mixed up in this somewhere. I was minding geese, so I did not see. Was it you?
Eighty pennies you lent the saint. He has had me count out his answer.
You took him off the island on six oars. I remember it. I said then that I hoped to do nothing worth writing down.
Take what the king offers the man who gave him up for nothing
Stand among the witnesses as one who lent or spoke, and take the saint's hand for it
Lay the altar silver from the Tyne on the new altar
Ask only the saint's peace for your hull between Tyne and Wear, and the carrying of his first rents

Arm-rings to the weight of fifteen hundred pennies, from the king's own arm and others. A plot on the river at York, the bishop's seal for the Tyne, and a place at the king's table whenever you land. He asks if you still have his fish hooks.
Nine hundred pennies from the king's gift, counted by the abbot. The bishop sets your name in the book among the saint's men and gives you his seal: no toll for your hull between Tyne and Wear.

The cup with the scratched name goes back on an altar. The bishop turns it round and reads the name aloud. It was one of his own priests. Seven hundred pennies, his seal for the Tyne, and a hand's breadth of the cloth that lay on the coffin.
The bishop has land now and no one to carry its wool. Six hundred pennies paid forward, twelve packs of fleeces to find for him, and his seal: no toll for your hull between Tyne and Wear.
Two saints in one house
Cuthbert of the English lies in Ireland now, a day's walk from Columba's shrine, and the bearer who carried him seven years has learned to ask for bread in Irish.
He lies among Columba's people now. Our founder's house sent Aidan to the English, and the English have sent us a bishop back. We consider the account settled.
You carried my letter, and then you carried what answered it. I do not often get to thank the same man twice.
At home the army has shouted for a king of its own kind. Nobody dreamed for them. The land between Tyne and Wear is some Dane's sheep-walk.
And in every port north of the Humber they say a Frisian sold Saint Cuthbert to the Irish. I tell them he was given. They prefer sold.
That Dane of yours, the tall one. The abbot dreamed about a boy like him once, before we sailed. He never did say what it meant.
Take the abbot's protection: his guest on every shore where Columba's word runs
You carried the letter that called them: ask for the abbot's protection, and a strip of the saint's cloth for your house
Ask for no honour: only to be the man who brings the wine for Columba's houses
Take the protection, and swear fellowship here with Harthacnut's son, whom nobody now will come to buy

Eight hundred pennies' weight in arm-rings, the gift of an Irish king who came to see the coffin. And the abbot's word: on any Irish strand you are his guest, with an honour-price like a free man of his own people.
A thousand pennies' weight, the abbot's word, and a strip of the cloth a hand long, sewn into a leather purse. 'Keep it dry,' Hunred says. 'He is used to that now.'
Six hundred pennies' weight on account, and the cellarer's hand on it: twelve casks before next Easter, and whatever you leave in his store will be there when you come back.
You swear it on the strand, hands on the same oar, with the abbot for witness. Guthred has never heard that he was nearly a king. He is pleased enough to be half of a boat.
Not bought twice
The army at York has shouted for another king, and the saint is still a guest at Crayke. A grey Dane has come down to your hull with a bag of arm-rings for the son of a friend he thought was dead.
His father and I shared a bench. We thought the boy was dead. These are his father's rings, and some of mine, for shame.
The army took another man in the end. He is loud. The priests at Crayke say the saint is displeased. The saint may be right.
They wanted to put a gold ring on my arm and stand me on a hill beside a coffin. I have been stood up to be looked at before. Once.
I would rather have half a boat than all of York. Put my silver with yours. Two hulls, one purse. That is how my people do it.
And you are my godfather, so you cannot cheat me. It is a great saving on witnesses.
Swear fellowship: his kin's silver buys a second hull, and he sails it
Take him into the house as a foster-son, with his kin's gift for his keeping
Send him to York with his rings and your good word, and ask a plot on the river from his kin
Hands on the same purse, before the crew. Seven hundred pennies' weight is your half. In spring there is a second hull, with a Dane at her helm who counts everything and steals nothing.
His kinsman pays nine hundred pennies' weight for his keeping, as for a great man's son. From now on there are Danes at York who call your house kin, and mean it.
He goes up the Ouse in a new cloak. Six hundred pennies' weight is his thanks, and by midsummer a plot on the river at York is staked out in your name, beside his kin's.

Lindisfarne at low water on a grey morning. In front, seven young monks lift a carved oak coffin onto oars laid across a small boat; behind them an old bishop holds a book to his chest, and the church door stands open on an empty nave.

The beach under the rock of Bamburgh, midday, a hard wind. A monk holds out a silver spoon to a man with a barley sack; above them a timber gate is shut, and a reeve in a good cloak comes down the path.

The Tyne in winter dusk. Long ships drawn up side by side on the mud under a church with no roof; in front a Dane sits by a sail spread with bent altar cups, and a boy of twelve stands with a rope on his wrist, looking at the viewer.

The ship-fort at Dublin, a wet afternoon. A turf bank and beached ships behind; in front a scarred Dane sits on a fine saddle laid on the shingle, a mail coat folded beside him, a shipmaster standing over him with a cup.

The white strand of Iona in clear morning light. Two monks lash a house-shaped shrine of wood and bronze into a hide boat; an old abbot stands apart with his hands in his sleeves, and a tall stone cross rises behind him.

Chester from the river, evening. Broken Roman walls with ash trees growing from them, a few thatched roofs by a mud landing; a thin monk with a staff stands at the water's edge, speaking up to a man on a boat.

A small open boat in a green breaking sea under a dark western sky. A coffin is lashed amidships, an old bishop kneels with his hand on it, an abbot reaches after a sliding chest, and the water in the bottom of the boat is red.

Wide wet sands at the lowest ebb, early light, the sea a thin line far off. A young monk bends over a closed book lying on the sand, its gold cover bright; a merchant's boat is aground behind him, tilted on her bilge.
On board at anchor, evening. A tall fair youth of sixteen sits on a thwart mending a net and does not look up; the steersman stands aft by the steering oar with a tally stick, waiting for an answer.

The landing at York below old Roman walls, a dull morning. A tired abbot with an oil jar speaks with his hand raised; behind him a broad Dane in a fur cloak laughs with his head back, and a scarred man watches from a doorway.

A river landing, bright noon. An abbot and two Danish lords stand in a row on the planks, all looking at a young crewman in the boat who coils a rope with his eyes down; the merchant stands between them with empty hands.

A bare hilltop at midday. A young Dane holds up his right arm with a gold ring on it; beside him stands a carved coffin on a cart, a bishop with his hand on the lid, and below them two crowds, Danes with shields and English with staves, standing together.

An Irish monastery yard, soft rain. Small stone huts and a high cross; in front a carved English coffin rests on trestles under a thatched shelter, an Irish abbot and a young English monk on either side of it, a herd of cattle passing behind.

A quay at sunset. A tall young Dane in sea clothes and the merchant stand with their hands laid on one leather purse; a grey-haired Dane pours arm-rings out of a bag onto a cloak at their feet, and two boats lie side by side behind them.
Seven named
A man was knifed in the press at yesterday's wool sale and nobody saw the hand. His brother has named the seven who stood nearest. Your steersman is the fifth.
Seven named, and no more than seven: that is the law. Each swears with eleven of his own rank. Then the lots go on the altar, because eleven friends prove a man is liked, not that he is clean.
Two twigs, wrapped in clean wool. One is cut with a cross. If the cross is lifted, all seven go home. If the bare one, each man cuts his own mark, and we draw until one twig is left.
The law says a priest draws, or a boy without guilt. I would rather the boy. A boy has no opinion of anyone yet.
I sold a fleece and scratched my ear. That is all I did in that crowd. I have eight who will swear. I need eleven.
A shipmaster's oath is good here if he is a free Frisian. Nobody will ask where his boat was built.

You go east of the Lauwers? Then carry a word to Saxmund at the Ems mouth. Say: the three lands should agree what a man is worth before a stranger asks. Say it as I said it. It is not a thing to write.
Swear with him, and find the other helpers
Pay the brother to drop the fifth name
Let the law run and get the wool aboard

You swear on the relics with ten others, and two of them you talked into it yourself. The boy lifts a twig out of the wool, and it is the one with the cross. Seven men go home. Wlemar tells the dead man's brother he must now think again, and that this is what law is for.

The boy lifts the bare twig. Seven men cut seven marks, and it takes three days and a good deal of your ale before the last twig left on the altar is a cattle dealer's from Aalsum. Your steersman's came out fourth. The dealer pays. He does not deny it for long.

The brother takes thirty pennies and finds he is no longer sure about the fifth man. Six swear, and the lot is drawn for six. Wlemar says it is allowed. He says it the way a man says a fish is fresh enough.

You load fleeces while your steersman goes round the houses asking men to swear for him. He has his eleven by dark, and the lot clears him. He does not speak of it again. He does not sing at the oar for a week either.
Beyond the Lauwers
Saxmund, who says the law for the land between the Lauwers and the Weser, is mending a net outside his sister's house. He hears Wlemar's word through to the end before he puts the needle down.
