Before a stranger asks. He means the king's clerks. Wlemar smells weather a year off. It is his one fault.
What is a man worth? Here, a noble is a hundred and six shillings and two pennies, which sounds more than over the water. We count two pennies to the shilling. Do not envy us.

Ask him what a dead man's land is worth. My husband went to the Weser in the year the churches burned and did not come back. For that, King Charles took from all who rose the right to leave land to their sons. Mine plough their father's field for the count's man.
It was done by law. That is the worst that can be said of a law.
Bernlef says the old judgements go best to a tune. A man forgets a number. He does not forget where the verse turns.
If you want to be useful and not only sorry: four black quernstones from the Rhine. Ours are worn as thin as plates.
Take Saxmund west to Winaldum in your boat
Take the widow's order for quernstones
You have said the word; go on with your trade

Saxmund comes aboard with a net, a cheese and no farewell worth the name. He sits in the bow and watches how your men handle the flats, and says once that the channel was further north in his father's day. He means it kindly.

The widow cuts the order on a stick and splits it, half for her and half for you: four stones, before the winter after this one, and she will pay over the price. Saxmund says he will go west by his cousin's boat when the hay is in.
You have said it as it was said to you. Saxmund nods and takes up the net again. He will go west when the hay is in, he says, and not before. Wlemar can wait. He is good at it.
Three numbers for one man
On the terp at Winaldum two wise men sit with a heap of beans between them, pricing a dead noble in three lands. They want a man who handles the king's new pennies every day.

Here a noble is eighty shillings, at three pennies the shilling. Beyond the Lauwers a hundred and six and two pennies, at two. West of the Vlie a hundred, at two and a half. Three numbers for one man.
It may be one number said three ways. Or it may be that you are cheap.
And all of it was judged in the old light pennies. The king's new ones are heavier, since the hungry year. You take them over the gunwale every day. Reckon it.
He reckons the tide well enough. I have seen him do it.
The west has not come. The old man at Medemelacha says his legs are finished with boats. Somebody must fetch what he knows before he takes it under the turf.
Reckon the three scales in the king's new pennies
Reckon it so the middle land comes out dearest
Say a carrier is no reckoner

Eighty threes are two hundred and forty. A hundred and six twos and two more are two hundred and fourteen. A hundred at two and a half are two hundred and fifty. You say so, and that the new penny is heavier by about a third, so nobody's dead are as dear as they sound. Saxmund counts the beans again and finds no fault. Wlemar pays you with a riddle about counting, which is what he has.
You lose the count at the half pennies. Wlemar finishes it on his fingers while you are still moving beans, and is kind about it, which is worse.

You let the middle land's shilling stand a little fat. A Westergo farmer who has been listening sends twenty pennies down to your boat that evening. Saxmund counts the beans himself afterwards and says nothing to you at all.
Wlemar nods. A man who knows what he is not, he says, is half a wise man. They go back to the beans.
The old man of the west

The man who says the law west of the Vlie sits by his fire at Medemelacha with a rug over his knees. He will not go in a boat again, but he will say it all three times, slowly, for whoever is to carry it.
A noble a hundred, a free man fifty, a half-free man twenty-five. Four, two, one. And men to swear with you by the same count. A child could keep it.
A wound we pay by its length. The others pay by what it did. Tell them that in the west a thumb's breadth is a thumb's breadth.
My daughter's son has all of it. He has sat at my knee nine winters.
I can say it backwards. I would like to see something that is not a cow.
If anyone asks you why it is so, say: because it was judged so. He will want a better reason. There is none better.
Learn it by heart, three times through
Take the grandson as a hand; he has it all
Cut the numbers on a tally stick

Three times through, and a fourth in the boat with the steersman hearing you. You have it: the numbers, the lengths, and which oath goes with which. The old man says you would have made a poor wise man and a good witness, and that the second is rarer.

The numbers stay. The lengths of wounds and their prices run together somewhere past the Vlie, and by Winaldum you have a hand's breadth costing what a hand costs. Wlemar hears you out and says the west will have to be content with its numbers.

The old man takes sixteen pennies for the boy's first summer and tells him to say the law every night before he sleeps, so that it does not wash out. The boy is aboard before the silver is counted. He rows badly and remembers everything.
A hundred, fifty, twenty-five: three rows of notches on a hazel stick. The old man looks at it for a while. That is what it costs, he says. It is not why. But a stick does not forget, and you might.
The emperor's question

Two of the emperor's messengers are at Dorestat, a count and a churchman, strangers to the district as the new order has it. The churchman's clerk is asking along the dam heads who knows the Frisians' law, and the toll man has pointed at you.

After harvest the emperor will have every people's law read before him at Aachen, mended where it needs it, and written. The Saxons' I have. The Franks' fills a chest. The Frisians' is not on any skin in the realm.
I am told it lives in two or three old men on mounds in the sea. I am told you know which mounds.
After this the judges judge by what is written, and take no gifts. That is the whole of it. You may tell your old men so.
The emperor pays carriage. Ten shillings of twelve, on the tally, to the man who brings them to the palace at Noviomagus. I pay for wise men delivered dry.
Undertake to bring the wise men to the palace
Tell the clerk what was said on the terp
Say you carry wool

The clerk counts a hundred and twenty pennies onto the toll man's table and splits a tally: your half, the emperor's half. The toll man watches silver go past him untaxed and breathes through his nose.

You tell him the three scales and what a shilling is in each. He writes fast and pays forty pennies for it. A week later a rider reaches Winaldum who already knows what a noble costs beyond the Lauwers, and Wlemar is not a man who wonders long how.

You say you carry wool. The clerk writes that down too. By midsummer a rider has found Winaldum without you, and Wlemar sends word that if he must go in a boat, he will go in one whose master he has seen swear.
Two wise men and one boat
The summons has come to Winaldum. Wlemar and Saxmund stand on the beach with a bundle each, and have been disagreeing since first light about what they will say when a Frank holds a pen over it.
We say all of it, as it was judged. A law is not what we would like to have judged.

All of it. Then say this to a bishop's clerk. Who breaks into a shrine and takes the holy things is led to the sand the tide covers. His ears are slit, he is gelded, and he is given to the gods he robbed. That is judged, beyond the Lauwers. I did not make it.
It is judged. Nobody has asked for it in my lifetime. The gods are owed a good deal they do not get.
And why should the emperor have our law in his chest while he keeps our sons off their fathers' land? Let him give that back. Then I will remember things for him.
The rider knew our numbers before he got down from his horse. Somebody reckons aloud.
You have heard both. You stand between Frisians and Franks every day and still have both ears. What would you say?
Say all of it, as it was judged
Say what a Christian king can put his name to
Ask for the land first
Wlemar says that makes two against one and gets into the boat as if the matter were closed. Saxmund gets in after him and says it is closed at Winaldum. It is a long way to Noviomagus.
Saxmund asks whether you sell short measure too. Wlemar says a merchant thinks of the buyer; it is his trade, not his fault. Both of them come aboard. Neither of them sits near you.

Saxmund looks at you for a while, as a man looks at a plank he had taken for rotten. Wlemar says a king gives nothing to a man who asks before he is asked, and then, more quietly, that it would need to be in writing, from somebody a palace believes.
Saint Martin's opinion
The way south goes up the Vecht under Saint Martin's. The bishop's deacon is waiting on the bank; news of two wise men in one boat has outrun you.

The bishop asks that some things be said first. That a man in feud has peace in church and on the way to it. And that work on the Lord's day is four shillings, twelve beyond the Lauwers, where they need it more.
And that one judgement be left where it lies. A book with the emperor's name on it cannot hand a man to devils on a beach.
I have a letter for the palace clerk that says so. It will get a Frisian through a door faster than his blood-price would.

If it is the widows of the Ems mouth your easterner is brooding on: that right was taken by law, for broken faith. What a law took, an emperor may give back. But it must be asked in writing, and Saint Martin's poor are many this year.
Take the bishop's letter to the palace clerk
Give alms for Saint Martin's poor, and ask him to write for the widow's sons
Say the wise men speak for themselves

The deacon reads the letter aloud to you once, pointing at the words, so that you know what you carry. You know four of the words by the end. Saxmund asks what it says. You tell him. He says the bishop has spared him the trouble of deciding what he thinks of bishops.

Twenty pennies go into the alms box. The deacon writes a second letter, shorter than the first: that the mother is baptised, that the sons were children in the year of the rising, and that the bishop of Saint Martin's asks mercy for them and those like them. He reads it to you, pointing. Saxmund hears it and looks at the river.

The deacon says the bishop will be sorry to hear it, in the voice of a man who will enjoy telling him. Wlemar says from the boat that he has peace in church by his own judgement and does not need a letter for it.
The palace above the Waal

Noviomagus is full of law. Saxons with the faces of hostages, Franks of the IJssel with a chest of their own, and clerks walking fast. The Frisians are to be heard after the Saxons, and the Saxons have a great deal to say.
Twelve days, if the Saxons are brief. They are not a brief people when it is about cattle.
I have waited sixty years for someone to ask. Twelve days will not hurt me. It may hurt your trade.
There is a doorkeeper here who can count to thirty. I watched him do it for a Saxon.
Two wise men, and dry. Your tally is good. I did not think to see it again.
Wait your turn behind the Saxons
Send in the bishop's letter
Find the doorkeeper who can count to thirty

Twelve days under the palace hill. Wlemar sits on the bank and tells the Saxons' law-men where their law and his agree, which is more often than either side likes. Your boat earns nothing. You learn what a Saxon noble costs, and it is a great deal.

The letter goes in by a boy and a clerk comes out by himself. Five days, he says, and the Frisians will be heard in the small room, where it is warmer. A bishop's seal is a kind of weather; doors open before it.
The doorkeeper counts to thirty without moving his lips. Three days, he says. Wlemar asks what you paid, and when you tell him he says that among Frisians it would have been a matter for the lots.
What is written

A bare room, a trestle, a clerk with a pen and a boy with a horn of ink. The wise men speak Frisian; the clerk has Frankish and Latin. You stand between, and what goes on the skin goes through your mouth.
Begin with what a man is worth. Everybody does.
Between the Vlie and the Lauwers: a noble, eighty shillings. Tell him. And tell him it is three pennies to the shilling, or he will think us rich.
Three scales? The emperor would like one. One is tidier.
And the west, as the old man gave it: four, two, one, and a wound by its length. Say it for him. You have it better than I do.
And the west: a hundred, fifty, twenty-five. The rest of the west stayed by a fire at Medemelacha. Tell him the numbers.
Now the sand. Say it to him as I say it. I want to watch his pen.
My hand is cold, the ink is thin, and now there are gods in it.
Or say nothing more yet. He has asked us for a great deal. Nobody in this room has asked him for anything.
Put it into Frankish as they say it, all of it
Help the clerk make one clean law of it
Lay the letter for the widow's sons on the trestle before a word is said
Tell them it has kept in their heads this long

You put it across as it comes: three scales, the lots on the altar, the kettle, the Lord's day, the harper's hand, the river that may not be blocked, and the sand the tide covers. The clerk writes all of it. At the head of two leaves he writes whose judgements they are: Wlemar's, and Saxmund's. Then he sands the last leaf and says it will want tidying, later.

You and the clerk make one law of it. One scale, in the emperor's pennies. The church's peace first. The lots stay, since they lie on an altar. The sand goes: you simply do not put it into Frankish. Saxmund understands more Frankish than he has let on. He does not speak to you again on that side of the Lauwers.

You lay the bishop's letter on the trestle before the first word. The clerk reads it twice and takes it out of the room. He is gone until the lamps are lit. When he comes back he says the emperor will hear the Frisians' law, and after it the matter of the sons of those who rose. Saxmund sits down. It is the first time you have seen him do it. Then the wise men say their law, all of it, and the clerk writes.

You turn to the wise men and say it in Frisian: it has kept in your heads this long. Wlemar looks at the pen, and at Saxmund, and says he is outvoted by a merchant. He gets up. The clerk asks what was said. You tell him the Frisians find they have forgotten their law, and will send word if it comes back to them.
As it was said
Winaldum, after the assembly. Wlemar is back on his mound. The clerk's leaves went to Aachen in a chest with the Saxons' law and the rest, and were read out before the emperor, the old gods and all.
They read it out. The emperor asked whether the sand was still used. The clerk said he would ask. Nobody has asked.
It was to be mended and written fair. I think they have a great many laws to mend, and one clerk with cold hands. It will lie as it is. I have seen worse things happen to a law.
The three lands gave a penny a hearth for the man who carried it. It comes to more than I thought. There are more hearths than I knew.
And this, which is not silver. In any court from the Zwin to the Weser, when you swear, your oath is taken as a man's of that land. You will not go looking for helpers at dusk again.
He wrote our names over it. Mine and Saxmund's. I had not thought to be written. I find I do not mind as much as I should.
Take the hearth pennies and the oath-right
Take less silver, and his sister's son to keep your goods here
Ask for a house plot by the landing as well

Eight hundred pennies in three bags, one from each land, and the eastern bag the lightest and the most carefully tied. Wlemar says your name at the next court day, and what it is now worth. The law lies in a chest at Aachen as it was said, and nobody mends it.

Six hundred pennies, and a young man of Wlemar's kin who can count and has been told what happens to a man who counts wrong for a friend of the three lands. Your goods will lie dry on the terp. The law lies in a chest at Aachen as it was said, and nobody mends it.

Wlemar walks you to the foot of the terp and paces out a strip between the landing and the sheep track. Nobody carried it truer, he says, the west and all. Nine hundred pennies, a kinsman to keep your goods, and ground of your own among the Frisians of the middle land. The law lies in a chest at Aachen as it was said.
The emperor's law of the Frisians
Dorestat, after the assembly. The clerk is back from Aachen with a fair copy under his arm and a sealed skin for you. The toll man is reading the seal upside down and not liking it.
It was read before the emperor from the first word to the last, and he did not stop it once. He stopped the Saxons' four times.
One scale. The church's peace at the head. No gods anywhere. It is to be read out at every court from the Zwin to the Weser, and the judges are to judge by it.
This is yours. The emperor's own word that your boat pays no toll at Dorestat, in his time and his son's.
I knew a man who had one of those. He was an abbot.
I am told the old men beyond the Lauwers do not thank you. Old men do not thank pens. Their grandsons will not know there was ever another way.
Take the charter and the emperor's silver
Take the charter; send the silver to the widow at the Ems mouth
Ask to be reckoned among the emperor's own merchants

Nine hundred pennies and a skin with the emperor's seal. The toll man waves you past with two fingers. East of the Lauwers a law is read out at the courts that no one there remembers judging, and at the Ems mouth they know which boat carried it to the pen.

You keep two hundred pennies and the charter, and send the rest east with a man you trust, for the widow and for those like her. Word comes back in spring: Saxmund has said at a court day that the merchant is a fool about laws and not about people. From him it is a good deal.

The clerk says the numbers in the fair copy were right the first time, which he has not seen before, and writes your name on a second skin: a merchant under the palace's own protection, answerable to the emperor's court and no other. Eleven hundred pennies. East of the Lauwers they know which boat carried the law to the pen.
The sons of ninety-three

The Ems mouth, after the assembly. The count's man has ridden off the widow's farm with his tally sticks, and there is smoke from more roofs than there was. Saxmund is waiting at the landing, which he has not done before.

It was given at Aachen, after the law was read. The sons of those who rose have their fathers' land again, Frisians and Saxons both. The emperor said it was mercy. The clerk wrote it as law, which is better. Mercy dies with the man.
My eldest ploughed the long field yesterday. It is the same field. He ploughed it as if it were another.
And our law is written, sand and all. I said every word. I find a man remembers better when he has been paid first.
Every house that has its land again has sent something down for you. Some sent silver. Most sent what they had: cloth, hides. Do not weigh it in front of them.
There is ground by the landing that is nobody's. It is yours. Ask for something else as well. I am not often in this temper.
Take the ground by the landing and what the houses sent
Ask for the younger son to keep your goods here
Ask for the elder son as a sworn partner, with a boat of his own

A strip of ground above the tide mark, five hundred pennies in small silver, eight bolts of good grey cloth and ten hides. You do not weigh any of it in front of them. East of the Lauwers, fathers leave land to sons again, twelve years before anyone had a right to hope for it.

The younger son is seventeen and has never been further than Leer. He will keep your goods on your own ground by the landing and send word by any boat going west. His mother tells him, in front of you, what she will do if he counts short. East of the Lauwers, fathers leave land to sons again.

Saxmund is silent a while, and then says the boy has a field now and may not want a boat. The boy says he wants both. They swear it at the landing, his hand and yours on the same oar: one purse, two boats, and the truth told between them. East of the Lauwers, fathers leave land to sons again.
Kept in the head
Doccinga, after the assembly. The two wise men are in Boniface's church, by the altar where the twigs lay. The emperor's chest went to Aachen with a gap in it the size of the Frisians.
The emperor was told the Frisians are a forgetful people. They say he laughed. With an emperor that is not always good.
So it is still ours. A count who wants to know the law here must ask a Frisian, and wait for the answer.
And when I die it is a little smaller, unless I have said it to somebody. That is the price. I had hoped a skin would pay it for me.
We have put our hands on this altar for you. In the three lands you have peace in your boat, at the landing and on the way to both, as a man has in his own house. Who breaks it pays ninefold.
The clerk will remember your face. Sell elsewhere than Noviomagus for a year or two.
Take the peace of the three lands and the hearth pennies
Ask as well for a man who knows the Lauwers mouth
Ask to be taught the law itself, all three lands

Seven hundred pennies, a penny a hearth from three lands, and a peace that every Frisian court will hold to. The law goes home in two grey heads. Nothing of it is on any skin in the realm, and the palace knows whose boat that was.

Six hundred pennies and the peace, and a fisherman of Saxmund's kin who takes you out on the ebb and shows you the Lauwers mouth: where the channel runs this year, and the three ways to tell when it has moved. Nothing of the law is on any skin in the realm, and the palace knows whose boat that was.

It takes most of a winter by Wlemar's fire: the middle land from him, the east from Saxmund, the west from your own mouth while both of them mend it. At the end Wlemar says you are to say it to your heir, whole, before you are too old to be corrected. Nine hundred pennies and the peace besides. The law is in three heads now, and one of them sails.
What the son gave back
The Ems mouth, a long time after. A man of thirty is setting boundary stakes along a ditch as if each one were a nail in something. He knows your boat before he knows you.

The old emperor died at Aachen in the winter. His son has given back what the father took: the right of the fathers' land, to Saxons and Frisians both. Some say he is generous. The count's man says he is a fool.
My mother did not see it. She ground her corn on your kind of stone until the stone was a plate, and said every day that a king's anger does not last as long as a ditch.
My uncle Saxmund says it should not have needed a king's death. He says most things should not have needed what they needed.
They read us the emperor's law every court day. There was nothing in it about us. It took a new king to find the room.
He says also that your house asked for this before anyone was listening. We do not forget that here. We do not forget anything here; it is all we own.
It was your father's boat, then. You have his way of looking at a landing.
Be remembered as the house that asked first
Ask what a farm with an heir needs
Wish him a dry harvest and go

He sends a boy running. By evening there are two hundred pennies on your thwart from houses you have never traded with, an order for iron, and a cousin of his who will keep your goods at the landing and count them twice. Twelve years is not long, east of the Lauwers.

Iron, he says. Spades, a plough share, nails. A man does not mend what may be taken from his sons, and nothing here has been mended for twenty years. Every farm from here to the Weser will say the same this spring.
He thanks you and drives in another stake. There are a great many still to do.

The Frisians' law has been written for the emperor, as two old men of the terps said it: three lands, three prices for a man, and an old judgement about the tide sand that the clerk wrote down with the rest.
The emperor has given the Frisians one written law, read out at every court from the Zwin to the Weser. The judges are to judge by the writing and take no gifts.
At Aachen the emperor has given back to the Frisians and Saxons who rose the right to leave land to their sons. Beyond the Lauwers the count's men are riding off the farms.
The emperor asked for the Frisians' law and was told they had forgotten it. The Saxons' law fills a book. The Frisians' is where it was, in the heads of old men on mounds.

Inside a small timber church at Doccinga, grey morning light from the door: a boy of eight reaches for two twigs wrapped in white wool on a plain altar, a priest and a grey-bearded lawman watching, seven men in wool cloaks standing in a row behind, one of them a boatman with tarred hands.

A sod-walled farmhouse on a low terp at the Ems mouth, flat grey tide flats behind, late afternoon: a lean man of forty-five sits mending a net and does not look up, a widow in a dark head-cloth stands in the doorway with a worn quernstone at her feet, the merchant before them with his cap in his hand.

The top of the terp at Winaldum on a windy bright day, sheep and the sea behind: two men sit on a turf bench with three heaps of beans on a cloak between them, the older counting on his fingers, the younger with folded arms, the merchant kneeling with a handful of silver pennies.

Inside a low house at Medemelacha by firelight: a very old man with a rug over his knees holds up four, then two, then one finger, a boy of seventeen crouched at his knee mouthing the words, the merchant on a stool with a hazel stick and a knife, a cow's head showing over the byre wall.

A dam head at Dorestat on a spring morning, boats and casks along the bank: a young tonsured clerk with wax tablets faces the merchant, a Frankish count in a red cloak stands behind with a hand on his sword belt, and the toll man at his table points at the merchant with his tally stick.

The beach below the terp at Winaldum at first light, the small boat drawn up with her mast stepped: two lawmen with a bundle each stand arguing, the older calm with his hand raised, the younger pointing out at the wet sand the tide has left, the crew waiting at the oars.

The bank of the Vecht at Traiectum under a stone church and the old fort wall, a still overcast noon: a deacon in a white alb holds out a folded, sealed letter over the gunwale, two Frisian lawmen sitting in the boat with their backs half turned, the merchant standing between.

The river bank below the palace hill at Noviomagus, timber halls and a stone chapel above, afternoon sun: groups of Saxons and Franks wait with chests and bundles, clerks hurry between them, and two Frisian lawmen sit on the merchant's upturned boat watching a doorkeeper count coins.

A bare whitewashed room in the palace, one small window, lamp not yet lit: a clerk at a trestle with a pen raised over a skin, a boy holding an ink horn, two Frisian lawmen standing opposite, and the merchant between the two sides with one hand toward each.

The terp at Winaldum in late autumn, low sun and long shadows: the old lawman paces out a strip of ground between the landing and a sheep track, three tied bags of silver on the turf bench behind him, the merchant's boat on the beach below.

The toll table at Dorestat on a cold clear morning: the clerk, back from Aachen in a travelling cloak, hands the merchant a skin with a hanging wax seal, a bound book under his other arm, the toll man leaning over to read the seal upside down with his mouth turned down.

The landing at the Ems mouth in autumn, smoke rising from a dozen low roofs on the terp behind: the lean lawman stands waiting at the water's edge, the widow beside him with two grown sons, and on the sand a heap of folded grey cloth, hides and a small bag, a rider going away small across the marsh.

Inside the timber church at Doccinga, evening, one candle: the two lawmen stand with their right hands flat on the altar and look at the merchant, the old one tired, the younger almost smiling; the altar is bare where a book might lie.

A field edge at the Ems mouth in spring twelve years on, wide sky and wet ditches: a man of thirty in a patched tunic drives a boundary stake with a wooden maul, a line of fresh stakes behind him, a worn-out quernstone set as a step at the house door, the merchant's boat in the creek.
The people on the bank

Some hundreds of people sit on the river bank with spearmen walking round them: Saxons, with their children, their old people and what they could carry. Nobody is tied. There is nowhere to run to. An officer of the host walks along the boats, asking for hulls.
Shipman. I have four hundred heads to put over the river and one ferry with a split plank. Two pennies a head, counted in and counted out.

They are the emperor's Saxons, from Wihmodia and from over the Elbe. They go into Francia, a few here and a few there, where there is nobody to rise with. Thirty years of war, and this is how it ends: on foot.
The emperor sits by the Elbe this summer with the whole host. The land beyond it is to be empty before Michaelmas, and the Wends are to have it. Ask me again who won.
These are the last. The ones who sat out the winter in the woods and came in when the snow did the count's work for him.

Frisian. You go down the river and along the coast. My sister Aldburg and her man did not come in to be counted. They said the Ems, and then the Danes. If you see them, say Ricburg lives, and went west.
Take the officer's hire and carry a boatload over
Buy bread and have it carried down the line
Say your hold is full, and stand and look

Twelve of them at a time, two crossings. They sit where they are put and hold the children by the wrist. A woman in the second load says a name to you, Aldburg, and a river, the Ems. The officer counts them out on the far bank and pays in new pennies, twenty-four.

The baker's boy carries the baskets down the line and the spearmen let him. Nobody thanks you. One woman breaks her loaf in three, looks at you over it, and says a name, Aldburg, and a river, the Ems.

The officer shrugs and goes on to the next boat. You stand and look for as long as it takes to see that it is a whole country sitting there. A woman by the water calls something to you in Saxon about her sister and the Ems.

A wide river bank in flat afternoon light: some hundreds of Saxons sitting on the grass with bundles, children and old people, a loose ring of Frankish spearmen round them; in front an officer in a red cloak speaks up to a Frisian standing in a small open boat; behind, one ferry barge loading and the far bank low and green.
Five in the sheep house

Tetta brings you to the sheep house after dark, with no light. Behind the hurdles, among the ewes, sit a man, his wife, his old mother, a boy of twelve and a small girl. They are Saxons, with marsh mud dried on them to the hip. The man stands up when you come in. The others do not move at all.
They came over the flats two nights ago at low water, carrying the old woman. I have had stranger lodgers, but none so quiet. His name is Meginward. He has silver on his arm and no boat.
You have been up the Rhine. Then you have seen where the rest of them are going, and I need not tell you why these five would sooner sit with my sheep.
We are from Wihmodia, between the Weser and the Elbe. When the count's riders came to count us onto the road we were in the reeds. Eleven nights from there to here. We ate what the tide left.
My brother Meginfrid went to the Danes six summers ago, after the fight on the Sventana. He has a boat and a hearth there. Set us on the Danes' strand and he will pay you what I cannot.
You have seen the people on the road. Was there a woman called Ricburg, with a mark on her cheek like a thumb? No. Do not tell me now. Tell me when we are at sea.

Know what you are doing before you do it. The count keeps a boat of twelve oars at the river mouth, and they look under sails. A man who carries Saxons out is a man who has broken the emperor's order.
Take them aboard on the night tide, for Ripa
Pay Tetta for their keep and say you will think on it
Tell them you carry cloth, not people

Meginward lays his arm on the hurdle and cuts a finger's length from his arm ring with his own knife: eighteen pennies' weight. They come down to the creek in the dark holding each other's clothes. The old woman is lifted in last and sits on the cloth like a bale. Five people is most of what the boat will carry.

Tetta takes the ten pennies and says that for that they can have milk as well. Meginward says nothing. He has heard men say they will think on it before. They stay behind the hurdles, and you have a few days.

Meginward nods, as at a price he expected. The woman pulls the girl's hood down over her face. Tetta walks you back to the creek and says only that the tide is at the fourth hour, in case cloth should change its mind.

Inside a low turf-walled sheep house at night, lit only by moonlight through the door: a tall fair Saxon stands among the ewes, a silver ring on his upper arm; behind wattle hurdles his wife, an old woman, a boy and a small girl sit close together, mud to the hip; a stout Frisian woman in the doorway and the merchant beside her, seen from behind.
The count's man counts heads

At the toll post a Frank with six spearmen reads the emperor's order to every shipman on the creek. He reads it badly, from memory, with a clerk's tablet held up for show. Then he asks each man alone what he has seen. His name is Gundhart, and he does not like the coast.
Every Saxon of Wihmodia and of the land over the Elbe, man, woman and child, goes into Francia by the emperor's word. Not most of them. All. I have a number to bring to the road, and I am short.

A man who finds me one has his share by the head, paid at the count's court when the count sits. It is honest silver. Nobody is harmed by it. They are fed on the road, which is more than they were in the reeds.
A man who carries one out of the realm has carried off what is the emperor's. He answers for it with his goods, and the boat is goods.
You I have heard of. You lent your hull on the Rhine when it was asked for. Good. Then you know these people are not hard to count once they are sitting down.
So, shipman. This is a small mound in a great deal of mud. A stranger here is seen by somebody. What have you seen?
Tell him: five, in the sheep house on the mound
You carry cloth. You have seen sheep
Give him something for his trouble on this wet coast

He sends four spearmen up the mound and stays to make his mark on the clerk's tablet, five strokes and your name. There is no noise from the sheep house. They walk down between the spears, the old woman carried. Tetta stands in her door and looks at you until you look somewhere else. Your share is to be had at the count's court, a season on.
He looks at your cloth, lifts a corner, and lets it fall. Sheep, he says, there are plenty of. He goes on up the coast with his six men and says he will be back with the spring tide.

He looks at you longer than at your cloth. Sheep, he says. He has the clerk write your name and the look of your boat, the patch on the sail and all. Then he goes on up the coast, and says he will be back with the spring tide.

Thirty pennies go into his glove without either of you looking at them. He says a man could count this coast for a year and still be short, and that he will begin at the far end of it. Your toll on this creek is lighter for a month.

A timber toll post on a muddy creek bank under low grey cloud: a Frank in a wet red cloak faces the merchant, one gloved hand held out flat; a clerk behind him holds up a wax tablet; six spearmen stand about, bored; on the green mound behind, small and far off, a sheep house with its door shut.
The guard boat

A boat of twelve oars pulls out from under the bank and a man in her bow holds a spear up crosswise: stop. The five are lying on the bottom boards under the spare sail. The small girl has her mother's hand over her mouth. The ebb is running, and to seaward the flats are beginning to show brown.
Frisian boat! Lower your yard and lie to. The count's watch. What is under the sail?
We look in every hull that leaves this river until the counting is done. If you carry cloth, you lose a little of the tide. If you carry Saxons, you lose more than that.
A boat with a patch on her sail, shaped like a boot. I was told to look out for one.
Heave to and let them look, with the cloth piled on the sail
Run over the flats on the ebb: she draws more than you
Put about for Emuthon before she is near, and set them ashore again

A spearman steps aboard and walks on the cloth. He lifts two bolts, finds a third under them, and is tired of cloth. Under his feet nobody breathes. The captain waves you on. When the guard boat is small astern the old woman says one word in Saxon, and the boy laughs and is hit for it.

The spearman steps on the sail and the sail has a foot in it. They are lifted out one by one into the guard boat, the old woman last. The captain fines you forty pennies on the spot and has your name. Meginward looks back once. He does not look angry. That is worse. They will go into the column on the Rhine road, where a priest might still ask for them.

You put the helm up and go where the water is the colour of ale. The keel touches twice and comes free. The guard boat follows as far as the first bank and stops there with her oars in the air. Somebody aboard her will know your sail again.

You put the helm up and go where the water is the colour of ale, and then where it is the colour of mud. She sits down on a bank with the ebb leaving her. The guard boat waits in the channel for the tide to do her work, then sends men across the sand on foot. They take the five, and a mate's tooth for his manners. They will go into the column on the Rhine road, where a priest might still ask for them.

You go about while there is still half a mile between you, like a man who has forgotten something. The guard boat watches you all the way in and does not follow. The five go back up the mound by the sheep path. Tetta says nothing, loudly.

A broad river mouth on a falling tide, early morning, grey and windy: a Frankish guard boat of twelve oars pulling across the bow of a small open Frisian boat, a man in her bow holding a spear crosswise over his head; in the small boat four crewmen and a heap of cloth and sail, a child's hand just showing under the sail's edge; brown sand flats drying to seaward.
The night after

The count's man has gone up the coast and will be back with the next spring tide. Tetta has thought about it over her spinning, and says the sheep house will not hide five people twice. Meginward sits on an upturned trough with his knife and his arm ring on his knee, waiting to hear what he is worth.
Nine days to the spring tide. Then he comes back and counts my sheep, and he can count that far. They go before then, or they stop being Saxons.
And he has your sail written down. I would sew a new patch on it. A different shape.

There is the priest. Liudger. He is one of ours, a Frisian, and the emperor has set him over the western Saxons as well. He is up the river at Daventre or on the Ruhr this season. If any man can ask for five Saxons in daylight, he can.
North to my brother, if you will. If not that, anywhere they do not count. I can herd, plough, thatch and keep quiet. My wife weaves. The boy can learn anything that does not need reading.
You said cloth, not people. I did not hold it against you. A man has one boat. I ask again because I have nobody else to ask.
Whichever way you take them by water, mind the guard boat. Twelve oars, at the mouth, and up the river another like it. They look under sails.
Take them north to the Danes, tonight
Take them up the river to the priest Liudger
Make Frisians of them: the outer terp, Tetta's name, and your silver for their keep

Meginward cuts eighteen pennies' weight from his arm ring and holds it out on the flat of the knife. They come down to the creek in the dark holding each other's clothes. Tetta gives the girl a cheese to hold, so that she has something to do with her hands.

It is the long way and the one that can be spoken of afterwards. They go aboard before light. Meginward asks if the priest is the kind who asks what a man ate in Lent. Tetta says he is the kind who asks, and then feeds you.

Tetta had a brother who went out to the island of Bant and died there with his name still good. These are now his people, come home. Meginward gets a Frisian cloak, a crook and forty of somebody else's sheep on the outer terp. He is told to talk as little as he likes. That, he says, he can do.

A Frisian house on the terp at night, a peat fire and one tallow light: a stout woman spinning on a bench, speaking; the Saxon father on an upturned trough with a knife and a silver arm ring on his knee; in the shadow behind him his family asleep in a heap of fleeces; the merchant by the door with his cloak still on.
Whose guests are these

The five stand on the strand among the booths, in everybody's way. An old Dane with a staff comes down and looks them over like a cargo nobody has claimed. He asks, through a boy who has some Frisian, who answers for them here.
A man with no host here is a thing found on the beach. Anyone may pick up what he finds. I would be sorry to see it. I have seen it.

Meginfrid the Saxon? He is a real man, and he has a hearth here. But he is at Sliesthorp with his boat, like every man who has one. The king is there with the fleet and all the horsemen, looking at the emperor over a river.
Meginfrid the Saxon? He is a real man, and he has a hearth here. He is away east with his boat after furs. A month, if the wind likes him.
Until he comes, somebody of standing says before me: these are mine, I answer for what they do and for what is done to them. That is all the law there is to it. It is enough.
I have half an arm ring and five mouths. I am not much of a guest.
Answer for them yourself until the brother comes
Pay a householder to take them under his roof
You were paid to the strand. Here is the strand

You say it before him, in Frisian, and the boy says it after you in Danish with more words than you used. The old man strikes the sand once with his staff. They are yours until the brother comes. The booth-holders stop looking at the girl. The talk on the strand is all of the king's fleet lying at the Slie.

A comb maker with a wide house takes twenty-four pennies' weight and the five of them, and says the old woman can have the place by the fire because his own mother is dead and it is empty. The lawman is content. The talk on the strand is all of the king's fleet lying at the Slie.

You push off. They stand where the boat was, the water filling the mark of her keel. The old man with the staff watches you go and then, since somebody must, says a short thing in Danish and takes them up the bank himself. The talk on the strand, behind you, is all of the king's fleet lying at the Slie.

A Danish market strand at midday under a high pale sky: plank booths and beached boats; the five Saxons standing close together on the sand with one bundle; an old Dane with a long staff and a silver-ringed cloak pin faces the merchant, a boy between them turning his head from one to the other; booth-holders watching.
What the Frisian saw

Meginfrid has come: a Saxon in a Dane's cloak, older and broader than his brother, with a purse for you. With him is a man with gold on his arm who speaks for the king. The king wants to hear, from somebody with no side in it, what the Franks are doing with the Saxons.
You carried five of my blood past the count's boat in a hull I would not put a pig in. I do not have words for that in any of my three tongues. I have this.
They tell me you left them on the sand with nobody to speak for them. I will pay what my brother promised. Take it. A debt is a debt.

The emperor's men have come over the border about people like these. They say: give back what ran to you. The king lies at Sliesthorp with the ships and has not gone to their meeting. Before he answers he would know what he is asked to give back, and to what.
The summer the emperor emptied the land, his men asked the king to give back what ran to him. The king remembers being asked. He would know what became of the ones who did not run.
You trade on the Franks' rivers. You have eyes. Say what you saw. Nobody will hear who said it.

There is one thing more, and it is not the king's business. My brother says our father's brother's people did not come in to be counted either. Forty of them, in the reeds by the Jade, when he left. Forty is not a thing I can ask of a man with one small boat.
Tell it as you saw it, on the Rhine and on the Ems
You are a guest here and the emperor's man at home: you saw the weather
Offer to go back for the forty in the reeds

You tell it flat: the bank, the counting, the children held by the wrist, the land given to the Wends. The king's man listens without moving his face and at the end unties a bundle of forty marten skins and lays it by your knee. It is said afterwards that the king gave nobody back. Meginfrid's purse holds sixty pennies' weight of cut silver.

The king's man says that a merchant who sees only weather will live to be old, and gets up. Meginfrid waits until he has gone and then laughs, once. His purse holds eighty pennies' weight of cut silver, and he counts it into your hand piece by piece, like a man paying a wergild.

Meginfrid looks at you for some time. Then he puts eighty pennies' weight in your hand as earnest and tells you what his brother told him: a reed island at the edge of the Jade, two tides east of the Ems, where the gulls nest. Ask at Emuthon for a pilot who knows the gullies. The king's man says that the king likes a man who finishes what he starts.

Inside a Danish booth by the water in the evening, a small fire and the door open on masts: a broad Saxon in a Danish cloak holds out a purse to the merchant; beside him sits a still, well-dressed Dane with gold arm rings and a bundle of dark marten skins at his feet; outside, in the dusk, the younger brother's family sits round a pot.
Forty in the reeds

Folcger the pilot has been out to look, in an eel boat, as a man after eels. They are there: forty people on a reed island at the edge of the Jade, two tides east of here, eating mussels and gulls' eggs. They have a fire they light only in fog. Your boat holds five.
I counted forty-one. One is very new. They thought I was the count's man and were going to drown me. Then I said your Saxon's name, and his father's, and they gave me an egg.
Forty-one people, five to a boat like yours. You can do that sum. Eight runs and a bit, two tides each way. That is four nights if nothing goes wrong, and on four nights something goes wrong.
The guard boat rows the coast every third night and does not say which. One run she will not see. Eight runs she will. I tell you this now so that you cannot say afterwards that nobody did.
And they know your sail. I would not show it east of the mound at all.

Or: my cousins have three eel boats, deep ones, and no love for a Frank who counts their catch. One night, one tide, all forty to a ship's side off the islands, and your Saxon's Danes take them from there. Ninety pennies between us. For that we were never born.
Hire Folcger and three eel boats: one night, one tide
Do it with your own boat: eight runs, four nights
Forty is a levy, not a cargo. Send them word of the road and no more

A night with no moon and a little rain, which Folcger says he ordered. Four boats go in on the flood with muffled oars and come out on the ebb low in the water and silent, even the new one. Off the outer island a Danish hull is lying with no light, Meginfrid in her bow. By morning there are four eel boats on the creek, full of eels.

Four nights. Eight times in over the flats and eight times out, five and six at a time, to a Danish hull lying off the outer island. On the last run the guard boat passes so near that you hear a man in her complain of his supper. The crew do not speak of it afterwards, except to each other, often.

Three nights go well. On the fourth the guard boat is lying in the gully with her oars shipped, waiting. You get clear over a bank she cannot cross, with one man hurt by a thrown spear and nobody aboard but your own. Twenty-two came out. Nineteen are still in the reeds, and now the count knows where the reeds are.

Folcger carries the word out with his eel traps: the Ems, the sheep house, the name of the Danes' strand, and that nobody is coming. He says they heard it without complaint. He says that people who complain do not last long enough in a reed bed to hear news.

The creek at Emuthon at dusk, low water: a lean weathered Frisian pilot squats on the mud beside an eel boat, drawing channels in the mud with a stick for the merchant; three more eel boats drawn up behind; far to the east over the flats a line of reeds under a darkening sky.
The priest asks for them

Liudger hears it through without a word, walking, leading his horse. Then he says that the emperor's order tells where Saxons may not live. It does not tell whose land they must live on. He has land on the Ruhr, at Werden, and not enough hands on it.
Five, in your boat, at this bank. Then bring them up to the church before somebody counts them for me. Nobody is taken from Lebuin's door. Not even by a count's man in a hurry.
Taken from your boat and put in the column. Then they are on the Rhine road, and I know which clerk at Colonia holds the lists. A name can be found on a list. It is what lists are for.

They are to be settled among Christians, far from their woods, where they can do no harm and learn some good. Werden is among Christians. It is four days' walk from their woods, which I grant is not far. I will not measure it if the count does not.
I am a priest with a wide parish and a king's letter, no more. The count need not listen to me. But he was baptised by a man I taught, and he knows it.
They have made me a bishop since Lent, at Mimigernaford, over the western Saxons. I did not ask for it. It turns out to be useful. A count answers a bishop's letter.

It will cost something. The count's man is paid by the head, and he will want his heads' worth from somebody. The Church can pay, slowly, after letters. Or a man can lay the silver down today and have God for a debtor, who is slow as well, but sure.
Lay down the count's price for five heads yourself
Carry his letter to the count and let the Church pay
Swear for them before him: they will work Werden's land, and you answer if they run

A hundred and twenty pennies, counted onto the church step. Liudger does not thank you. He writes your name in the book where the dead and the givers are prayed for, which he says will last longer. Then he has a leaf of the vow copied for you, the one every Saxon has had to say. Know, he says, what was asked of them before you judge how they answered.

He writes it standing, on his saddle, in a hand like a hedge, and seals it with a ring that is too big for him. It goes to the count by your boat. He asks, since you are going that way, for four cakes of wax for the altar, at a fair price and a little over. An answer will take until the next feast but one.

You swear it with your hand on the book: they will work the land at Werden and keep the peace, and if they run you answer for them with your goods. Liudger has a leaf of the vow copied for you, the one every Saxon has had to say, and reads you the Latin at the head of it twice over until some of it stays.

A river bank path below a timber church on a bright cold day: a tall spare tonsured man of sixty in a travel-stained cloak, a book satchel on his shoulder, leads a horse and listens with his head bent to the merchant walking beside him; behind them the small boat at the bank and Saxon converts and Frankish soldiers going up to the same church door.
The list

Gundhart is back on the creek, older and wetter, with a clerk and a list: the people of Wihmodia who were never counted onto the road. Somebody has told him of a shepherd on the outer terp whose Frisian is odd. Meginward's boy, Folcward, is fourteen now and as tall as you. He has been waiting for your sail since Easter.

Two winters the clerks have been at it. Every household of the district, from the old tithe rolls, and against each one a stroke if it reached the road. There are households with no stroke. One of them is a man, a wife, a mother, a boy, a girl.
And you I have written down already, shipman, from the first time. The boat with the patch. You see a great many sheep.
You were open-handed once before on this creek. I have not forgotten it. I say so only so that we understand each other.

He is my brother's man from Bant, and he talks like that because everybody on Bant talks like that. It comes of living on a sandbank with seals. I will swear it. I will bring six of my neighbours to swear it with me. That is our law, and it was our law before there were counts.
I can row and I can splice, and I can say every Frisian word there is for mud. Father says I may go if you will have me. He says a boy who is at sea cannot be counted.
And the women have something for you. Three bolts, two winters' weaving, on my loom. Do not say no to it. They have been looking for a way to stop owing you.
Swear beside Tetta that they are her dead brother's people
Say nothing, and move them to the island of Bant before he walks out there
Pay him to find the list complete

Eight people swear on the tide sand with the water coming in, which shortens the pleading. Gundhart knows what a Frisian oath is worth in a Frisian court. He has the clerk make a stroke: gone to Bant, dead. The boy comes aboard with a bundle and a new knife, and the three bolts go in under the thwart.

Eight people swear, and Gundhart asks the shepherd to say the Our Father in Frisian. He says it in something. The oath stands, because eight is eight, but Gundhart fines you thirty pennies for wasting a court and writes a long line beside your name. That night the family goes out to Bant in an eel boat. The boy comes with you instead, with the three bolts.

A night's work with the tide. By the time Gundhart has walked out to the outer terp in the morning there are forty sheep on it and a deaf old Frisian who has herded them, he says, since the flood. Bant is a low island with a chapel and nothing else, and nobody rows there to count. The boy comes aboard with the three bolts.

Forty pennies. Gundhart has the clerk make a stroke against a household of five and says the marsh takes a great many people and returns very few. He does not say goodbye. The boy comes aboard with a bundle, and the three bolts go in under the thwart.

The tide sand below the terp at Emuthon, a windy morning with the water coming in: a greying Frank in a red cloak and a clerk with a long parchment roll face a stout Frisian woman with six neighbours ranked behind her; to one side a tall fair boy of fourteen with a bundle stands by the merchant's beached boat; sheep on the far mound.
Saxons under a Danish roof

There is a new long house behind the booths with smoke coming through the thatch, and Saxon is spoken in it. The girl, Gerburg, is carrying water and scolding a goose in Danish. The brothers have set a bench for you by the fire. They have something to say about what is owed.
The king gave nobody back. He said a guest is a guest. He also said that Saxons who can ride are worth feeding, which is nearer his reason. We do not mind his reason.
Five of us, under a roof, uncounted. The old woman has a place by the fire. When they ask me in this country who my people are, I say your name after my father's. That is how it is done here.

Forty-six of us now, with the new one. A whole kin, with its old men and its quarrels. We have held a meeting, as our fathers did by the Weser and as the king's law forbade us. The meeting talked of you for most of a day.
Twenty-two came out. Nineteen went onto the road with the rest. It is not what you meant. It is twenty-two more than there were. We do not count it the way the count would.
They know your sail on the Frisian coast now, the count's people. That is a cost, and it came of our business. We have reckoned it in.

Here you are a guest for as long as any of us has a door: I have said it before the lawman, and it holds for your son. For the rest, there is silver. Or there is more than silver, if you want a thing that lasts.
Lay your hand to Meginfrid's: one purse, two boats
Take what they have weighed out, and their word
Leave them their silver: ask for a booth place on the bank beside theirs

It is done the Danes' way, hands laid together over a ring before the whole kin. One purse: what his boat earns in the east and yours in the west is shared at the year's end. The kin lay down their first share at once, nine hundred pennies' weight and four bundles of marten, gathered among forty-six people who came out of a reed bed with nothing. Meginfrid's boat is yours to send as your own.

Five hundred and twenty pennies' weight of cut silver, weighed twice on a folding scale, and a bundle of marten on top because the old woman said so. Meginfrid says a Saxon pays his debts so that he can afford his grudges. You have guest right here under his roof, and so will whoever comes after you.

Meginfrid walks you down the bank and paces out a booth's breadth next to his own, and the lawman drives a peg at each corner. The brothers will not let you go with nothing in the hold: five bundles of marten, the best of a winter's trading. A neighbour, Meginward says, is a thing his family had run out of.

Inside a new timber long house in the evening, firelight: two fair brothers, one in a Danish cloak, face the merchant across the hearth, a folding scale and cut silver on a bench between them; an old woman wrapped by the fire, a small girl with a water pail and a goose at the door; many faces along the walls if the forty came, few if they did not.
Counted onto the road

Gundhart has come from the count's court with a clerk and a bag. The five were counted onto the road with the last column before the frost. He has your share, and the count's good word if you want that more. He is in a good humour. His number came out right.
Five strokes, and your name against them. The clerks at Colonia were pleased. A household entire is neater on a list than odd heads.
They go west, a long way, to some abbey's land on the Seine, I think. Among Christians and vineyards. In ten years the children will speak like Neustrians and thank the emperor. So I am told.
That is twice you have been of use in this business, on the Rhine and here. The count remembers a name he hears twice.
The share is in the bag. Or the count will put his mark to something for you in place of part of it. A man who is known to be the count's man lands easier on this coast.

One thing, and I say it as a friend. The man looked at your boat a long time from the road. They are a people who remember, the Saxons. It is most of what they have left. I would hire no Saxon oars for a while.
Take the bag, and the name of count's shipman
Take less silver and a toll-free landing on this creek, in writing
Take the least, and ask that the five be set down on one piece of land together

Nine hundred pennies, new ones, with the emperor's name round the cross. Gundhart says before the toll man and the clerk that you are the count's shipman and are to be dealt with as one. Tetta sells you bread that evening at the stranger's price. The crew are quiet at the oars, and somebody has cut a small mark in the stem post that nobody will own to.

Six hundred pennies, and a strip of parchment with the count's mark: no toll on what you sell on this creek, for your life and your heir's. The toll man reads it with his lips moving. Tetta sells you bread that evening at the stranger's price. Somebody has cut a small mark in the stem post that nobody will own to.

Gundhart is surprised, and then not. He has the clerk write it: the household entire, to one holding, not to be parted. It costs you a third of the bag and he thinks you a fool, kindly. Six hundred pennies. It is said later that on abbey land by Rotomagus there is a row of huts, and in one of them five Saxons who speak to nobody. One of the men asks every ship for the Weser.

The toll post on the creek on a clear frosty morning: the Frank in the red cloak, pleased, sets a heavy leather bag on the toll bench before the merchant while a clerk unrolls a parchment; in a house door up the mound a Frisian woman stands with folded arms; on the small boat's stem post, close in the foreground, a fresh knife-cut mark.
Werden's people

The count has answered: five Saxons more or less on the bishop's land are the bishop's business. Meginward stands at the landing in a clean tunic with a tally stick in his belt, counting casks for the abbey. Liudger has the look of a man who has won a small case and means to enjoy it for a week.

The count writes that he has no objection, in eleven lines, nine of them about his own piety. They are on Werden's land, in a house that had no roof at Easter and has one now. The old woman has found fault with the well. I take that for a good sign.
You laid down the price when the Church was still looking for its purse. I told you God was a slow debtor and a sure one. He has been quicker than I said. I am almost put out.
You swore for them, and they have not run. They have not so much as walked fast. You may have your oath back, with interest.

It is not the Weser. The ground is hard and it stays where you leave it. But I have ploughed it, and my mother will be buried in it under a cross with her own name. The bishop asked what I could do besides plough. I said I could count without a clerk.
When they lifted us out of your boat I thought, there, that is the end of that Frisian. Then the priest came down the column with your name in his mouth. I had the wrong end.

Now, what is owed. The abbey pays its debts in what it has: wax, honey, and its good word, which opens doors on this river. And Meginward keeps our landing here. He could keep a merchant's goods beside ours, if the merchant were one we knew.
Take back your silver with the Church's thanks, the bishop's hand over your house, and Meginward at the landing
Ask for the bishop's hand over your house
Ask for Meginward at the landing, to keep your goods with the abbey's

Liudger gives you everything he offered, and says a man who pays first should not be made to choose after. Four hundred and twenty pennies from the abbey's chest, ten cakes of wax, six crocks of Saxon honey. A letter under his seal says your house is under his hand, and the toll men of this river are to go gently with you for a year. Meginward takes your mark onto his tally stick, next to the abbey's.

A letter under the bishop's seal: this house and its boats are under his hand, and who wrongs them wrongs him. A count's man will read that twice before he lifts your cloth. With it go two hundred and sixty pennies and nine cakes of wax. Meginward carries them down to the boat himself and will not let the crew help.

Meginward takes your mark onto his tally stick, next to the abbey's. What you leave at this landing he will keep dry, count right, and sell when the price is good and not before. Ten cakes of wax, six crocks of honey and a hundred pennies go into the hold. He says he owes you five lives, and means to pay by the cask.

A river landing on a mild bright day, casks and wax cakes stacked on the bank: the Saxon father in a clean undyed tunic with a tally stick in his belt; the tall old bishop beside him, smiling a little, a sealed letter in his hand held out to the merchant; behind, the abbey's barge and a road going up a wooded valley.
The empty land

Six winters a Frisian shepherd, Meginward has heard what every shipman on the creek is saying. The Wends could not hold the north. The emperor's counts are building a fort on the far side of the Elbe. And on the Weser marsh, where the war is over at last, nobody is counting heads any more.

They gave our land to the Wends, and the Danes took it from the Wends, and now the Franks have taken it back and found nobody in it to pay a tithe. An empty land is no use to a count. He will not ask a man with a plough where he has been.

And this summer the Danes came here, two hundred ships, and took their silver from the Frisians by weight. Tetta paid with the rest. I stood on her mound with a crook and watched a king's fleet rob the people who hid me from an emperor. I am tired of other men's mounds.
They have sworn a peace on the Eider, twelve men from each side, I hear, with their hands on their swords. When great men swear peace, small men can go and look at their fields.

I will tell you a thing I have told nobody. Under my hearth stone there is a pot. My father's rings and mine, and the bride silver. I buried it the night before the riders came. The house is burned. A hearth stone does not burn.

And I say he is a fool. There is nothing there but nettles and that pot. Here he has forty sheep and a name. The girl is asked for by a man with his own boat. Fetch the pot by all means. Then come back and be Frisians. You are good at it by now.
We have lived on Bant, too, on a sandbank with a chapel. I have seen what the sea means to do with that island. I would sooner trust the Weser.
Carry them home, and buy them seed corn, an axe, a plough iron and a cow
Carry them home across the Jade on a quiet tide
Tell him what Tetta says: there is nothing there but his silver. Fetch it, and stay

Two tides east, then up a gully Meginward names turn by turn with his eyes shut. The house is a black square in the nettles. The hearth stone has not moved. He lifts the pot out, takes one ring for the girl's wedding, and pushes the rest across to you, eleven hundred pennies' weight. Then he takes off the arm ring he cut for your first passage, the cut still bright, and puts it on your arm. The cow goes ashore last, complaining. By harvest there is smoke on the Weser marsh, and by the next there are three smokes.

Two tides east, then up a gully Meginward names turn by turn with his eyes shut, so that you learn them too. The house is a black square in the nettles. The hearth stone has not moved. He counts out seven hundred pennies' weight from the pot and keeps the rest to begin again with. They stand on their own ground and watch you down the gully. The old woman is already pulling nettles.

He goes with you across the Jade and digs, and stands a while in the nettles with the pot under his arm. Then he comes back to the boat. He gives you three hundred and sixty pennies' weight of it. The women add six bolts of cloth. In the spring he buys the house next to Tetta's and takes your goods under his roof as his own. His grandchildren will say they were always Frisians. Nobody will write down that they were not.

A wide green marsh under a huge summer sky, a tidal gully with the small boat nosed into the bank: in the foreground the Saxon father, greyer now, kneels in nettles beside a blackened hearth stone tipped on its edge, lifting out a clay pot; his wife, old mother, tall son and grown daughter stand round him; a cow being led down a plank from the boat.

The Saxons of Wihmodia and from over the Elbe are being walked into Francia, whole households, and set down far apart. The land beyond the Elbe is given to the Wends. Grain and bread are dear along the Rhine road while the columns pass.

The king of the Danes has lain at Sliesthorp with his ships and all his horsemen, on the border of the Saxons. The emperor's men asked him to give back those who fled to him. Nobody has seen any given back.
A coin with no face

On the dam a Svea trader is paying for wine. He does not count his silver, he weighs it, on a small scale that folds into a bronze case. Among the cut pieces lies a thin broad coin with writing on both sides and no king's head. The moneyer has come down from the upper town to look at it.
Three casks. I said three and I have counted three. Now the silver. Watch the beam, not my hand.
It weighs a penny and two thirds. The silver is better than mine. There is no head on it, no cross, no name I can read. Who strikes a coin and does not sign it?
The king's law says his penny is taken at its face in every market. This has no face. So it is only silver, and silver I may buy.
You carry a scale. Good. Then we need not talk about whose head is on anything.
You have no scale. Then you take my word for the weight, or his. I would not take either.
Buy the coin for its weight and half again, and give it to the moneyer to study
Sell him a cask of wine on his own scale
Ask him where such silver comes from

The Svea repeats your offer slowly, weighs the coin once more, and takes it. The moneyer carries the thing up the hill in both hands. That night there is a lamp in the mint long after the anvil is quiet.

You watch the beam and not his hand. It comes level, and stays level when he takes his fingers away. He pays in cut silver and one thin coin with writing, and you find you have sold a cask for more than the dam has paid all summer.
The beam comes level, you think. He did not cheat you: you cannot yet read a scale, and he is not a man to point out an error in his own favour. It is still more than the dam pays.

From the east, he says. Past Birka, past the sea, up a river, and then other men bring it up other rivers. He has never seen the men who strike it. Come to Birka in the summer market, he says: wine is dear there, and he will show you a bowlful.
Counted twice

At Birka nobody asks whose head is on your silver. Holmfast's booth has furs to the roof, a scale on a peg, and a bowl of coins cut in halves and quarters like cheese. The man in the next booth offers to lend you his own scale. He steadies the beam with his thumb.
The Frisian from the Rhine. I said to my son a Frisian would come this summer or the next. He said the next. He owes me a marten.
You bought the coin with the writing and gave it away to a man who makes coins. I have counted that twice. It comes out better than it sounds.
Here a coin is silver or it is not. You cut it to make the weight. You nick the edge to see what is under the skin. A king's name does not make lead any lighter.
Eight ounces to the mark. My weights are lead with a bronze coat, and every one has been on Holmfast's scale. He sent two back.
Buy a scale and a bag of weights, and have Holmfast teach you the nick
Trade on the neighbour's scale and watch his thumb
Sit a day by his booth and watch the weighing

Two pans, a beam that folds, a case that shuts with a hook. Holmfast makes you weigh the same quarter-coin nine times, until you get the same answer nine times. Then he shows you the nick: a knife's point on the edge, and bright metal or dull. By evening the next booth has stopped offering to help you.
You watch the thumb. When it comes near the beam you stop talking and look at it, and it goes away again. Holmfast, at his own booth, counts something on his fingers and almost smiles.
You watched the thumb. You did not watch the weights, which were his too. Holmfast says nothing. He has seen it done to better men, and he lets a lesson finish before he speaks of it.

You sit on a bale all day. He weighs, cuts, nicks, and marks each sale on a stick in short straight strokes that you begin to tell apart. Nobody is cheated at his booth. Two men are cheated at the next one.
What the east wants

Holmfast is baling skins for the winter. He goes east when the ice lets go of the bay and comes home with the silver before the night frosts. He has been thinking about what a man from the Rhine could put in his ship.

Five days east over the sea. A short river, a wide lake, another river. A place called Aldeigja. There the skins come out of the woods and the silver comes up from the south. I buy one with the other.

They want three things I cannot make. Blades from your smiths, without hilts: they hilt them their own way. Glass beads, green ones first. Wine. For a good blade they give what I give for forty marten.
Your king forbids mail coats to leave his land. A Frisian told me. He has said nothing yet about a bare blade. Kings think of things late.
Your king now forbids arms to leave his land at all, and takes the ship of the man who tries. A Frisian told me. A forbidden blade weighs the same. It is your neck; I only say what it would fetch.
Come next summer when the birch is in leaf. We sail east four ships together. Bring what you bring. I will count it.
Promise him four blades from the Rhine smiths
Promise beads and wine, which no toll man will take your boat for
Promise nothing; say you will come and see
Four blades, he says back to you. Four. He lays a timber of squirrel on your arm as earnest and does not ask how you will get them past your own toll man. That is your side of the sea.

Beads and wine, he says back to you. He thinks about it for the time it takes to tie a bale. Then he lays a timber of squirrel on your arm as earnest. A man who keeps his boat, he says, comes back a second year.
You will come and see, he says back to you. He nods and goes on baling. He has counted nothing, so there is nothing for him to count twice.
Low in the water

A Gotland boat lies low in the water with her steering oar gone and a lee shore half a mile under her. Her men bail and do not wave. There is a chest amidships with a hide lashed over it, and nobody aboard her looks at it.
We have lost an oar. I would not call it more than that. If you have one to spare, I will remember where I got it.
That is ballast. We find it steadies her.
Lay alongside, give her your spare oar and tow her off the shore
Name a price for the tow before you throw the line
Stand by to windward until the wind eases, and do no more

The line holds. You drag her head round a boat's length at a time until she has water under her and your oar on her quarter. Her skipper is Botmund, of Paviken on Gotland. He hands over a fistful of thin silver with writing on it and does not count it, which from a Gotlander is a speech.

The line parts and takes the skin off a man's hand on your own boat. An hour later the wind backs and she claws off by herself, with your oar. Her skipper, Botmund of Paviken, calls over the water that he saw who tried.

He looks at the shore, then at you, and names a weight of silver before you can. He pays it out of the chest that is ballast, in thin coins with writing. He does not give his name, and he does not ask yours. He will know the boat.

You lie to windward of her through the afternoon, which costs you the afternoon. Towards evening the wind eases and she rows off the shore with a plank lashed for a steering oar. A man in her stern lifts one hand, once.
In company
Four ships lie loaded off Birka's jetties, Holmfast's among them. They sail east together or not at all. He looks at your boat, which is the smallest thing in the bay, and then at what is in it.
The birch is in leaf and here is the Frisian. My son said you would not come. He owes me a second marten.
Four blades, you said. I have told a man in the east four. I do not like to tell a man a number twice.
Beads and wine, you said. I have told nobody, because beads break and wine is drunk on the way. Show me.
After the short river there is a lake with no far shore. It is shallow and it stands up in a north wind. We cross it in the night calm or we wait. Men who do not wait are found in the reeds.
On the south shore of the gulf there are men in small boats who count ships. Four they let pass. One they follow. Keep where I can see your sail.
Show him the blades under the ballast
Show him beads and wine
Come as you are and offer to keep his tally

He draws one a hand's breadth out of its greased wool, flexes it against the thwart and lets it spring back. Four, he says. Then he tells his steersman to give you the place astern of him, which is the safe one.

He holds a string of green beads up to the light and counts a cask by knocking on it. It will do, he says. The men of the woods take beads before silver; he does not know why and has stopped asking. You sail third of five.

He looks into your empty boat for some time. Then he hands you his tally stick and a knife. If you cut one notch wrong, he says, he will know by Aldeigja. You sail last of five, and learn to count in his tongue on the way.
The landing at Aldeigja

The river is brown and fast, and the sea ships go no further: above the town it breaks over rock. Log houses, a smithy, skins stacked like firewood, wax in cakes. Men from the woods stand apart with their bundles and speak a tongue nobody on your boat knows. In the biggest house a man named Vigmund weighs out thin silver with writing on it.
This is a Frisian from the Rhine. I have weighed with him two summers. His weights agree with mine.
From the Rhine. That is further than I can think. Sit. Nobody here is anybody's king; you deal with me because my house has the most roof.

It comes up from the south, from men who come from other men. Some pieces have marks scratched on them by every hand they passed. I have one with four kinds of scratching. I cannot read any of it. It weighs true.
Holmfast says you have blades. Lay them on the bench. I pay for those before I pay for anything.
No blades. A pity. The men down the rivers ask me for blades first and everything else second. Show me what you have.
Sell him the four blades
Sell him ten strings of beads
Sell him three casks of Rhine wine
Sell nothing; keep Holmfast's tally through the selling and take a hand's share

He bends each blade over his knee and listens to it. Then he weighs out silver until your scale pan will hold no more, and starts again, and throws a timber of marten on top as if it were a rag. You have never been paid like this for anything. He asks the smith's name. You find you would rather not say.

He does not want the beads himself. He walks them over to the men from the woods, who do, and comes back with two bundles of beaver he did not have before. Then he pays you in silver for the trouble of having stood between.

He has the first cask opened on the landing and drinks standing. Wine has come this far before, he says, but sour. He pays in thin silver and a cake of wax, and has the other two casks carried into his own house and not the storehouse.

You cut Holmfast's notches for three days while skins go one way and silver the other. Not one notch is wrong. He pays you a hand's share and two timbers of squirrel, and you have seen every price on the river without paying for one of them.
What the silver buys

Vigmund walks you behind his house to show you what goes south. A pen of split logs, roofed at one end. Some twenty people sit in it, roped by the neck in fours: Slavs from up the river, two women who speak something like Danish, and a boy with a tally stick who looks up when he hears your crew talk.
You think the silver comes for skins. Some does. A boatload of skins brings a bag. A boatload of these brings a chest. The men in the south have no end of silver and never enough hands.
Are you from the Rhine? I am Folkbern. I was ship's boy on a boat out of Wijnaldum. They took us off the Danish coast two summers back. The others were sold south. I can count, so he kept me.
That one talks like you. He keeps my tally and has not cut a wrong notch yet. I would rather keep him. A mark and two ounces, weighed, and I will have to learn to count again.
