Or this. Your coast is full of people and your boat has room. Bring me six next summer, sound and young. I pay what Holmfast has never seen, and I pay it to you and not to him.
Weigh out a mark and two ounces and take the boy home
Give him your hand on six, sound and young, by next summer
Say your boat carries things that do not need feeding

You weigh it out on your own scale and he checks it on his. He cuts the rope himself, with some regret, and takes back the tally stick. The boy walks to your boat without looking round at the pen. He does not speak until the town is out of sight, and then he asks what day of the Church's year it is.

He takes your hand and holds it a moment longer than a bargain needs, looking at you to see what kind of man it is. Then he weighs out an earnest in cut silver. Behind him the boy with the tally stick has gone back to looking at the ground.
He shrugs. Skins do not eat, he agrees, and they do not fetch much either. He walks you back round to the front of the house. Nobody in the pen had looked up for long.
Under the floor
Paviken smells of tar and hot iron. A shipwright named Botmund is laying a new floor of planks in his storehouse, over ground that was dug not long ago. He sees you look, and goes on laying planks.
The Frisian with the spare oar. I said I would remember where I got it. It is on that wall. Sit down.
A Frisian. They say you have been to Aldeigja in the Svea's wake. A long way to follow another man's stern.
A floor keeps the damp out. Every house on this island has a good floor. We do not talk about floors.

The Svea shows a man the way east and takes a skin in ten from him for ever after. I take a fee once and forget your name. I know the short river and the lake as well as he does. He will not thank you.
Take his pilotage on the strength of the oar you lent him
Pay him his fee, once, and go east next summer without the Svea
Say you went east with Holmfast and will go east with Holmfast

He nods and lays another plank. Next summer, he says, when the ice is out of the gulf: come here first and not to Birka, and tell nobody at Birka. He does not shake hands on it. On Gotland a thing said once has been said.

He looks at you over the plank for a while. That is an answer too, he says, and not a bad one to hear from a man you might sail with. Then, because you asked for nothing, he tells you what the island is short of this year. It is cloth.
Twenty and thirty-four

You tip a bag of the east's silver onto the moneyer's bench in the upper town: whole coins, halves, quarters, all writing and no face. He weighs twenty of the whole ones against the king's pennies, and then does it again.
You brought me one of these before. I have it still. I have looked at it more nights than I would tell my wife. Now you bring a bag.
Twenty of these weigh what thirty-four of the king's pennies weigh. And the silver is better than mine. I do not like that. I should like to know who does it, and how.

A pilgrim back from Rome showed me the like. It is the Saracens' writing. They put no face on their coin; their law forbids images, he said. What the words say he did not know. Nothing about our Lord, I should think.
By the king's law I take only his penny at its face. This has no face, so it is bullion, and bullion I may buy for the pot. What comes out will have his name on it and be none the worse.
Is there more where this was? I do not mean a bag.
Sell him the bag for the pot, less his cut, and promise him more
Keep it whole: north of the Eider it buys more than his pennies do
Give him one whole coin to keep and ask only what he makes of it

It goes into the pot that afternoon and comes out as the king's pennies, more of them than you had reckoned, because the silver was better than he is used to. He takes his cut and for once does not round it up. Bring more, he says. He will speak to the count's steward about a man who brings silver into the realm and not out of it.

You sweep it back into the bag. He watches every piece go. North of the Eider nobody melts good silver to put a name on it, and a man who can reckon the king's penny, the cut piece and the writing coin against each other is cheated by none of the three.

He turns it over and over. Every one the same breadth, he says, and the letters as fine on the last as on the first. Whoever does this has more silver than the king and more moneyers than Francia. He puts it away where the first one is, and says your word on foreign silver is good at this bench.
Three kinds of silver
The purse is open on a thwart: the king's pennies, cut silver from Birka, and the thin coins with writing. Two of your men were asked what the boat is worth, and they have two answers.
That is a penny. It has the king's name on it and the count's man must take it. The rest is scrap. I would not give you a herring for what a heathen scratched on a bit of plate.
I've tried your penny with a knife. It's a good penny. It's mostly silver. The writing ones are all silver, and I know which I'd rather be owed.
And who wrote on it? Nobody you can find and bring before a court. A coin should have someone to hang.
Kings die. All of them, I hear. Silver I've never seen do it.
Put it all on the scale: silver is what it weighs
Change it all at the next mint and know what you have
Let them argue; it passes the watch
You weigh the whole purse on the thwart, piece by piece, with the boat lifting under the scale. It comes to more than either of them said. The Dane looks pleased and the Frisian looks at the horizon.
At the next mint, you say, it all goes in the pot and comes out with a name on it. The Frisian is content. The Dane says a moneyer's cut is the only toll a man pays twice and thanks the taker for.
They are still at it when the watch changes. By then it is about whether a king or a scale has ever been wrong, and the whole boat has taken a side. Nobody has been this cheerful since the last port.
One purse
Holmfast has set out two stools and a scale at his booth, and ale, which he does not often buy. A silver arm ring lies on the bench between the stools.
Three summers. You came when you said you would come. Your weights agree with mine. I have counted you twice.
The blades cut. Vigmund asked me the smith's name. I did not have it to give, which saved me refusing.

You paid a mark and two ounces for a boy and then gave him away. I have counted that three times and it is a loss each time. Still. A man who pays for a thing and does what he said with it: I can sail with that.
A Gotlander offered you my road for a fee. I hear things. You said no. He told it himself, as a thing against you.

So. One purse for the east goods. I sail east, you sail west. Skins and wax to the Rhine, wine and beads and what else you dare to me. We halve it here each summer when the birch is in leaf. Say it back to me.
Swear it his way, with your hand on the ring
Swear it your own way and let him swear his
No oath: a price each summer, and a man of yours kept at his booth

You lay your hand on the ring and say it back to him, word for word, and he says it to you. Then he weighs out your half of this summer's purse, which he had ready. It is a great deal. Your crew, who are baptised men, say nothing about the ring until Birka is astern, and then a good deal.

You swear by your own God with your hand on your own breast, and he swears on his ring. He turns that over: two oaths, two witnesses in two heavens. Harder to break than one, he decides. Then he weighs out your half of this summer's purse, which he had ready.

No oath, he says back to you. A price each summer and your man on a stool at his booth, watching. He thinks it a thin way to do a fat trade, and says so, once. Then he weighs out this summer's price to the grain.
Six, sound and young
Vigmund has the six brought up from your boat and looks at their teeth and their hands. The Frisian boy stands behind him with the tally stick, a year taller, and cuts six notches without looking up.
Six. You gave your hand on six and here are six. I had a marten on it with Holmfast that you would not.
I said I would pay what the Svea has never seen. Bring your scale. We will be some time.
Six. Four men and two women. One of the women speaks my tongue. I have cut it as six.
And there is a ship on my bank that a man left me for a debt. She is too deep for the river and I do not go to sea. You will need a bigger hull for this trade. Take her as part.
Take the silver and the ship
Take less silver, the ship, and the Frisian boy
Turn back at his door: say the bargain is off

It takes until dark to weigh. The six are walked round behind the house. You do not go with them. You sail in a ship twice the length of the boat you came in, with more silver than the count's steward sees in a year, and the story is at Dorestat before you are. A priest there will know your name now, and not for alms.

Vigmund laughs: a dealer in people with a soft place, he says, and it is the first time anyone has called you that to your face. He cuts the boy's rope. The boy comes aboard the new ship and sits as far forward as he can get. He is going home. He also cut the six notches, and you both know it.

He does not shout. He tells you what a hand is worth on this river once it has been given and taken back, and it is not much. The six are still in your boat, and they are still yours to answer for. Holmfast's road is open to you yet. This man's door is not.
A mark and two ounces

A man on the landing knows the boy's face before the boy knows his. It is his mother's brother. By evening there are kin enough to fill the boat, and cloth and a little silver laid out on a cloak in front of you.
I come up to the dams every year with the terp's cloth. Two years I have asked every boat from the north for a boy named Folkbern. I had stopped asking this summer. God forgive me that.
His mother saw the sail from the terp and said it was nobody's she knew. Then she saw who was in the bow. You will have to forgive the noise. Nobody here has had anyone back before.
We know what a boy costs in those places. We are not rich. This is the terp's cloth for the year and what silver six houses have. Take it. We will not have it said that a stranger paid for our blood.

I can count their way. I can talk to the Svear, and some to the men who bring the skins. Nobody on this coast can. Send me back when the ice goes, as your man, with a house to answer to. I would sooner go back there free than stay here owing.
Take what his kin lay down
Take back the mark and two ounces, and not a penny over
Take nothing; ask only that the boy sail with you when he is ready

You take it, and it is fair, and they are easier for having paid. The cloth is good. In the spring the boy goes east in a Svea ship with your mark on a stick, to sit at Aldeigja and count for your house. He is nobody's thrall and nobody's son there. He is your man.

You weigh a mark and two ounces out of their silver on your own scale, in front of all of them, and push the rest back across the cloak. The uncle says that is how a debt between honest men ends. In the spring the boy goes east with your mark on a stick, to count for your house at Aldeigja.

You push the cloak back. There is a long quiet. Then his mother takes your hand and puts the boy's in it, before witnesses, and that is a fostering on this coast, and he is of your house. In the morning the cloth is in your boat all the same, and the silver under it, and nobody will say who put it there. He sails with you. In the spring he goes east.
Ground on the Volkhov

Botmund has brought you up the short river and over the lake in a night calm, and you lie at Aldeigja a week before any ship from Birka. Vigmund comes down to the landing himself. He counts your crew, then looks behind you for a sail that is not there.
You come without the Svea. Then his tenth stays in your purse or in mine. Let us weigh which.

There is ground between my house and the smithy. Put a house on it and a man in the house, and I deal with you before any ship from Birka is in the river. Nobody from the Rhine has ever wintered here. I should like to see if it can be done.
I said I would forget your name. I say one thing more and then I do. Build above the line the spring ice leaves on the bank. The river does not care whose house it is.
They tell me you have a man at home who melts my silver and puts your king's name on it. Good. Silver that turns into something else comes back wanting more silver.
Holmfast will know by the next moon. He counts everything twice. He will count this more often.
Take the ground, and carry the silver straight to the pot on the Rhine
Take the ground, and keep the silver working in the north
Take the ground, and send Holmfast a third with your word on it

Four posts go into the bank above the ice line, and a man of yours stays to roof them. You carry home a chest, not a bag, and the moneyer at Dorestat works three nights on it. The pennies that leave his bench that week have the king's name on them and the east's silver in them, and nobody who spends one will ever know. Botmund has told you the lake and the river once, and you have them. At Birka a Svea trader has stopped saying your name.

Four posts go into the bank above the ice line, and a man of yours stays to roof them. The silver you keep whole and working, at Paviken, at Birka's far jetty, at Sliesthorp: it buys more there than any pot would give you for it. At Holmfast's booth they have stopped saying your name.

Four posts go into the bank above the ice line. A third of the purse goes to Birka by Botmund's hand with a stick cut in your own notches: the tenth was his, here is more than the tenth, the road is wide enough. Word comes back before the ice. It is one notch, which in his tally means counted, and nothing else. It is not friendship. It is not a feud either.
The moneyer in the upper town has been buying foreign silver for the pot: thin broad coins with writing and no king's head. He says it is better than his own and will not say who brought it.
A house of Dorestat has sworn one purse with a Svea of Birka. Marten and wax from beyond the eastern sea will come up the Rhine each summer, and the wine goes back the same way.

A boat of Dorestat went east with people under her deck and came home a ship. The priests of the upper town have the name of her master. So has the count's steward, who has read the king's law on selling Christians aloud at the toll.
A ship's boy of Westergo, taken by sea-robbers two summers ago and sold beyond the eastern sea, has come home alive. A merchant of Dorestat weighed out his price to a heathen and brought him back.
A house of Dorestat has put up a storehouse on a river beyond the eastern sea, where no Frisian has wintered before. The mint in the upper town has not been so busy since the king made the new penny.
A Frisian has taken ground at Aldeigja and brought his own ship in a week before the Birka fleet, with a Gotlander at the steering oar. Nobody at Birka is pleased, and one man there least of all.

Dorestat, a timber dam at midday in summer: a spare, pale-eyed Svea in a fur-trimmed cap holds a small folding scale over a wine cask; a stooped moneyer in a leather apron bends close to one thin broad coin in the pan. Boats and the river behind.

Birka, a booth on the jetty in clear northern morning light: furs stacked to the roof, a bowl of coins cut in halves and quarters, the Svea showing a knife-nick on a coin's edge; in the next booth a man with his thumb on a scale beam.

Birka at dusk, late summer: the Svea kneeling on a bale of skins to rope it, talking over his shoulder; behind him his ship drawn up on the shore for the winter, and a bare sword blade drawn with a finger in the dust of the floor.

The open Baltic, grey afternoon, a hard wind: a Gotland boat low in the water with no steering oar, men bailing, a hide-covered chest amidships; a low dark shore with breakers close under her; your small boat coming down from windward.

Birka's bay early on a bright day in first summer, the birches in new leaf: four loaded ships at anchor and one very small Frisian boat alongside the nearest; the Svea leaning over his gunwale to look down into her.

Aldeigja on the brown Volkhov under a low white sky: log houses on a bank, skins stacked like firewood, wax cakes, trappers in hide coats standing apart; in a doorway a heavy man weighs thin silver on a scale; white water on rock upstream.

Behind a log house in flat evening light: a pen of split logs, people sitting roped by the neck in fours, faces turned down; one boy of thirteen with cropped hair and a tally stick looking straight out at the viewer; the dealer's back, pointing.

Paviken on Gotland, inside a storehouse with the door open to a bright beach and a half-built hull: a shipwright on his knees laying floor planks over freshly dug earth, not looking up; an oar hung on the wall behind him.

The mint in Dorestat's upper town by lamplight: a heap of whole and cut coins covered in writing on a bench, the moneyer holding a balance with twenty of them against a pile of pennies; a priest peering at one coin held to the lamp; anvil and dies behind.

Aboard the boat at sea in a fair wind, late afternoon: an open purse on a thwart with three little heaps of silver; a Dane testing a penny's edge with his knife, a Frisian hand jabbing a finger at him, the rest of the crew grinning.

Birka, the booth at midsummer evening, long light: two stools, a jug of ale, a scale, and a plain silver arm ring on the bench between the Svea and the Frisian merchant, who faces him; a divided heap of silver ready at the Svea's elbow.

Aldeigja's landing in hard noon light: six roped people standing in a row on the bank, the dealer looking at one man's teeth; behind him the Frisian boy cutting notches in a stick, eyes down; a long sea-going ship lying empty against the bank.

A Frisian landing under a wide evening sky, a terp on the skyline: a boy held hard by a woman and a big farmer, kin crowding round; in front of the merchant a cloak spread on the ground with folded cloth and a small heap of silver on it.

The bank of the Volkhov early on a still morning, mist on the water: four new posts of a house standing in bare ground between a big log house and a smithy; the dealer pacing out the plot, a Gotlander pointing at the ice line on the bank, one small Frisian boat alone at the landing.
The withy parts

Full dark and a full storm. The twisted withy that holds the steering oar to her side has parted, and she lies across the sea with two men hanging on the loom. Three of your crew are shouting, and only one of them is shouting about the oar.
The worst first. The withy has gone and she will not answer. There is a shore under our lee. I cannot see it. I can hear it.
Now what can be done. A rope on the oar and two men to it. And somebody with a free hand asks for help. Mine are busy.
Saint Cuthbert! He turned the wind for the brothers on the rafts when he was a boy, with the whole shore laughing at them. A candle as tall as yourself, and carry it to him. Say it!
The one who has the weather tonight is Thor. I know his hand when I am under it. Promise him the best thing in the hold, and mean it. He has no use for wax.
And the best thing in the hold. Say that to the saint too. Saints can count.
Saint Martin holds one promise of yours already. Ask somebody who is not still waiting to be paid.
Vow Saint Cuthbert a candle your own height, carried to his island, and the best thing in the hold
Vow Thor the best thing in the hold
Promise nobody anything: get a rope on the oar

You shout it down the wind, all three parts, because the lookout shouts each one back at you until you do. The rope goes on the oar at the fourth try. Some time before light the noise under the lee is behind you, and nobody can say when that happened.

You say it once, loudly, to nobody you can see. The hand nods as a man nods at a fair price. The rope goes on the oar at the fourth try. Some time before light the noise under the lee is behind you. The lookout does not speak to you until noon.

You say nothing and go aft over the thwarts. The rope goes on the oar at the second try, and with three of you on the loom she comes round. Behind you the lookout and the hand are both still talking to the sky. You hear a little of what they promise it.

You say nothing and go aft. The loom comes across as the rope takes it and breaks two fingers of the man beside you. She comes round all the same. Behind you the lookout and the hand are both still talking to the sky, and what they are promising is yours.
What was said
The sea has gone down and the oar hangs on a new withy. Nobody has spoken of the night. Now the lookout does, because he cannot leave a thing alone, and the others stop what they are doing to listen.
I heard it and so did he. A candle of your own height. Carried to the island by you, not sent. And the best thing in the hold on the day you land. Three things. I counted them on the bailer.
The worst first. His island is the far end of England, and a candle that long eats two cakes of wax. Now the rest: wax is cheap where the Wends sell it, and nobody said which month.
You said the best thing in the hold. I heard it over all that wind. Not a good thing. The best. He took his time letting us go, you will remember. I would not give him a reason to think again.
He has no house with a door. It is given where an ox is killed for him and men are watching. That is north. I know a man who will tell you the rest. He has it better than I do.

You said nothing, so I said it for you. A candle your height to Saint Cuthbert, carried by you, and the best of the hold. A boat's vow is the master's debt. That is in no book. It is true all the same.
I said a thing too. I will not hide behind him. Mine was shorter. The best of the hold, to the thunderer. You may choose which of us lied to the sky.
Custom gives a vow a year and a day. I will keep a cord by the mast and put a knot in it each morning, so nobody need ask.
A man can say the wind made the words. I have sailed with two who did. One of them is still alive.
Stand by it: the candle, the journey and the best of the hold
Stand by it: the best thing in the hold, given in the north
Say you promised a gift, and a gift can be small
Say the wind made the words
You say all three parts again in daylight, which is harder. The lookout lets his breath go. The steersman cuts a length of cord, ties the first knot in it and hangs it by the mast.

You say it again in daylight: the best thing in the hold, in the north, before the year is out. The hand says, good. The steersman ties the first knot in a cord and hangs it by the mast without looking at either of you.

You say that a promise made with a mouth full of sea water may be read generously. Nobody argues. The steersman hangs his cord by the mast all the same, and the men go back to work a little too quickly.

You say the wind made the words and the wind may have them. The lookout goes forward and sits with his back to you. The steersman says only that the priest at Doccinga is a patient man, if it should ever come to that.
Heel to crown

The boat lies quiet. The lookout has borrowed a trough, a pot and somebody's fire, and stands you against the mast with a tarred line in his hand. He dipped the great candle for Easter when he was a boy, and has been waiting to be good at something aboard.
Heel to crown. Stand straight. No, as you stand when nobody is owed anything. There. You are a finger shorter than you think you are.
Two cakes of clean wax, a wick of twisted flax, and a week hanging before it will bear carrying. At home the cellarer weighed the wax out to us and weighed the stump back in.
The same line. I kept it. You have not grown, and the saint has not forgotten how tall you were.
There is a way with one cake: mutton fat at the heart and wax over it. It looks the same. It does not smell the same, and it weeps in the sun. I only tell you there is a way.
All that sea for what bees leave behind! Well. My people throw good swords into a lake, so I'll say nothing.
An old abbot of ours made a riddle on it. The wax says: now I keep words, now I drive back the dark. Tablets and candles. I can say you the Latin while it sets.
Give him two cakes of clean wax from the hold
One cake, and mutton fat at the heart
Send ashore for wax at whatever is asked: a hundred and ten pennies
Not yet. Wax first, where it is cheap

He dips for two days, forty times down the trough and back, and will let nobody help. The candle hangs from the yard like a pale oar, your height to a finger. He says the old abbot's riddle over it in Latin, twice, the second time more slowly.

He does it and does it well, and does not speak while he works. The candle hangs from the yard, your height to a finger, and looks like any other. On the second warm day there is a bead of grease at its foot. He wipes it off before the others see.

The wax costs what wax costs when a man must have it. He dips for two days and will let nobody help. The candle hangs from the yard like a pale oar, your height to a finger, and he says an old abbot's riddle over it in Latin.

He coils the tarred line and puts it inside his shirt with his tablet. He says he will ask again. He does not say it as a threat, but the steersman ties the day's knot in the cord while you are both looking.
A hand's length

The candle lies along the thwarts in a wrapping of old sailcloth, and it has been seen. A woman in a good cloak gone thin at the hem has come down to the boat. She has stood there since the tide turned and does not mean to go.
My son has had a fever in his chest since the moon turned. The priest says a light before the altar, night and day. There is no wax in this place. The reeve had the last of it for the king's chapel.
A hundred and fifty pennies for that one. It is what I have. You can make another candle. I cannot make another son.
It is the saint's. It has been his since the night it was said. You would be selling what is not yours.
Then a piece. A hand's length off the foot. He will not miss a hand's length. Does he measure?
He has no need to. We did.
Cut her a hand's length from the foot, for nothing
Sell her the candle for a hundred and fifty pennies, and dip another
Keep it whole, and give her twelve pennies to send down the coast for wax
It is not yours to cut or to sell

You cut it with the ship's knife, a hand's length from the foot, and trim the wick out for her. She takes it in both hands like a living thing and goes without a word of thanks, which is the right way to go. The candle is now the height of a man who stoops a little.

She counts the pennies onto the thwart, some of them old and thin. Two of her people carry the candle up the strand between them. The lookout watches it go, takes the tarred line out of his shirt and says: two more cakes, then.

She looks at twelve pennies as at twelve days she may not have. Then she takes them, and asks which way the wax boats come. The steersman tells her, and tells her the name of an honest man there. The candle stays whole.

You tell her it is promised and that you may not cut a promise. She says she knows what a vow is; she made one herself this morning. She stands a while longer and then goes back up the strand. Nobody aboard speaks until she is out of sight.
Which of them
A slack afternoon with the sail asleep. The mate, who speaks perhaps ten times in a voyage, has been looking at you since noon the way a man looks at a knot he means to undo.
Which of them did you mean?
At home the priest stood us in the river and we said the words after him. That night my father went out to the tree as he always had. The barley came up.
Pay both. A candle to the one and a thing from the hold to the other. Then whichever of them it was has had his due.
And whichever it was not has watched you pay the other. I would sooner owe one lord than insult two.
I can say the whole of what they made us say. It is short. They wanted it remembered.
One debt, one creditor
Pay both: a candle to the saint and a thing from the hold to the thunderer
Ask him to say the words they made him say
You say a man who pays two lords for one night has two lords. The mate thinks about it for as long as it takes to coil a rope, and says that is also true. He does not speak again that day.

You say: both, then. The mate nods. The steersman crosses himself and looks at the water, and the hand, who has heard all of it, says the thunderer does not mind company; it is the other one who is jealous. The cord by the mast now counts for two.

He says them flat, in his own tongue, the way a man gives the marks of a channel: I forsake the devil, and all the devil's works and words, Thunaer and Woden and Saxnot. Then he says them again more slowly so that you have them. He does not say whether he meant them.
The pilgrims' sand
The island lies a mile off across wet sand that shines like a shield. The house's boatman stands at the edge of it with a pole taller than he is. He looks at the candle, and then at your shoes.
She is out for three hours yet. After that she comes round both ends at once and makes no noise about it.
Them that come to him walk it. Shoes off; the sand keeps shoes. At my heels, and off the grey patches. Or lie in the Ouse like a trader and carry it up from the boats. He gets his light either way.
Do not look for doors on the church. The heathen had them off for the hinges.
That is a hand short of you.
I know the way and the brothers know me. I could carry it over. But it was said: carried by you. I only say what was said.
Take off your shoes and carry it over the sand at his heels
Bring her round into the Ouse and carry it up from the landing
Let the lookout carry it over; see to the boat

The sand is colder than the sea. He walks ahead and does not look back, prodding with the pole, and you follow with the candle on your shoulder like an oar. Half way over he says, without turning, that most of them talk. On the far side a brother is waiting who has seen you coming for an hour.

You take her round with the flood and lie in the Ouse among the house's boats. The candle goes up the path from the landing on your shoulder. It is a shorter walk and a dry one, and the brother at the gate takes it from you as he would take a sack.

The lookout takes his shoes off before you have finished speaking. You watch him go over at the boatman's heels, small and then smaller, the candle a pale stroke on his shoulder. When you come round by the harbour it is already standing in the church, and the boatman does not greet you.
The tallest light in the church

The candle stands by the carved oak coffin at the right of the altar and is lit at the evening office. It is the tallest light in the church. When the brothers have gone out the bishop stays where he is, and asks what else was said in the storm.
It will burn to the Advent fast if the sacrist trims it. We have had few lamps since the heathen men came. He has had gold from kings, and I think he liked it less.
It will burn a season if the sacrist trims it. He has had gold from kings in his time, and I think he liked it less.
There is mutton fat at the heart of it. I have a nose. He has had worse from better men and taken it. But do not tell me it was all the wax you could find.
It is a hand short of you, and your lookout has told me who has the hand. Then it is whole. He would have cut it himself.
The boy carried it over the sand and you came round by the harbour. That is not how it was said. I only note it. I am not the one you promised.
Now the rest. The best thing in the hold. Men say that in storms and bring me a cheese.
If you ask me what is best in any hold, it is wine. Without wine there is no Mass, and we have said ours over the dregs since Lammas. But I did not make your vow.
There is the silk. I say nothing. I only know what is in the hold.
Lay the bolt of silk on the coffin: the best, as it was said and by the road it was said
Give two casks of Rhenish for the altar
Lay a hundred pennies on the altar in place of goods
The candle was the vow. Ask his blessing and go

You lay the bolt on the lid. The bishop looks at it a long time and says the saint was wrapped by poor men and will be wrapped again by rich ones, and this will serve. In the morning there are two books by your sea chest, in bare boards with the metal torn off, and silver from the saint's own rents; a strip of old linen, folded small, that came off the body when it was raised; an order for wine and wax at twice the price; and your house's name, he says, is in the book that is read at the altar.

Two casks go up from the landing on the brothers' shoulders, and the cellarer taps one before it is through the gate. The bishop says the saint drank water and his priests cannot. In the morning there is a book by your sea chest, in bare boards with the metal torn off, a little silver from the saint's rents, a strip of old linen that came off the body when it was raised, and an order for six casks more at twice the price.

A hundred pennies on a bare altar make a small heap. The bishop does not count them. He says silver is what a man gives when he would rather not choose, and that the house needs it and thanks you. In the morning there is a book by your sea chest, a strip of old linen that came off the body when it was raised, and an order for wine at twice the price.

He blesses you, the boat and the candle, in that order. He says that a man is the judge of his own words until he meets a better one. At the door a brother gives you what every pilgrim is given, a pinch of earth from the place where the washing water was poured, and the cellarer an order for wine and wax, because the house must buy from somebody.
No house with a door
The hand has brought an old shipmaster down to the boat: a man with a rope-burned palm and a stick, who looks into your hold before he looks at you, and takes his time over both.
Here he is. He's been in more bad water than both of us and come out of it drier, and I never learned how. Go on, tell him what you said that night.
The thunderer keeps no house where you can leave a bundle. A thing is given where an ox is killed and men are sitting down to it, so that it is seen. Otherwise you have only dropped something.
At winter's start, when the beasts come off the hill. The hall above the market at Skiringssal does it, and the lord at Ogvaldsnes on the sound. Either. He is not particular about halls.
The Franks say we kill a man for a fair wind. A wind is not worth a man. An ox, a good blade, and he has been known to settle for drink.
Now. Best. Not dearest; any fool with a tally stick knows dearest. The best thing in a hold is the one your eye went to when the water came in. Which was it?
Say it was the sword, and let him put his mark on the scabbard
Say it was the wine
Say you will know it when you stand in the hall

He draws the sword a hand's breadth, breathes on it, and watches the breath go off the iron. Then he cuts three strokes in the scabbard with his own knife. Now it is spoken for, he says; sell it and you have sold another's goods. He tells the hand the marks of the way north, and you find you follow half of it.

He laughs once, like a block running. An honest man, he says: most say the sword and bring the wine. Take him two casks and let the lord's horn be filled first. They are dry up there before the feast and will pay well for whatever you do not give away.

He says that is a merchant's answer, and that the thunderer has heard merchants before. But he tells you the halls and the season all the same, and the hand walks him back up the strand with a hand under his elbow.
Winter's start

The beasts are down from the hill, an ox has been killed in the yard and the hall is full of the steam of it. The lord of the place has heard why a Frisian is at his door, and has had a bench cleared near the fire.
Sit. A man who crosses the sea to pay what he said in a storm can eat at my board. I know men who would not cross the yard.

It is done so. You say before these what you promised, and when. Then the drink goes round, his horn first. A blade goes into the tarn behind the hall, where he will find it and nobody else will. Silver the same. Drink, we drink.
The old man sent word which thing you named. I had it from a skipper before you were past the skerries. So did the thunderer, I expect.

Men sat at this board at midsummer who had been west over the sea, to an island with a church and nobody on it who could fight. They go again when the days lengthen. A river mouth this time, with two churches. I tell you because you are eating my ox.
Say it loud, mind, louder than you think. He's not deaf, but the hall is.
Say the vow before the hall, and give the marked sword to the tarn
Say the vow, and broach two casks of Rhenish for the hall, his horn first
Say the vow, and throw a hundred pennies' weight of silver into the tarn
Eat his ox, and say the thing is not aboard this voyage

You say it, and the hall is quiet for as long as it takes. Then you walk out behind the lord with half the benches after you and throw a Frankish sword into black water. It goes in point first and makes less noise than a fish. In the morning there are furs on your bench, marten and one bundle of sable, and four tusks; the lord says his door knows you now, and his own pilot will take you up inside the islands as far as you care to go.

You say it, the casks are broached, and the first horn is carried to the high seat and poured out on the hearthstones before any man drinks. After that it is a feast like another, and a long one. In the morning there are four bundles of marten and four tusks on your bench, and the lord says his door knows you now.

You say it, and walk out behind the lord, and throw a purse's weight of cut silver into black water in the dusk. The hand watches where it goes in, from habit. In the morning there are furs and tusks on your bench. The lord says silver is what a man gives who would rather not choose, but his door knows you now.

You eat, and when the horn comes round you say the thing you promised is not aboard this voyage. The lord says the thunderer has a long memory and he himself a middling one, and has your horn filled all the same. The hand does not sit with you. On the way down to the boat he says only: there is a priest in your steersman's marsh. Go and ask him, since you will not ask mine.
The cord is full
A year and a day have gone by since the night the withy parted. The men have counted; they keep a cord by the mast with a knot for every day, and today there is no cord left to knot.
The worst first. The year is out and the thing is not paid. The men look at the sky before they look at you.
Now what can be done. Swear it again before them with a nearer day, and go. Or ask a priest what a vow costs when it is not kept. The one at Doccinga will not shout.
With mine there is no priest to ask. I wish there were. There is only the next bad night.
You have sworn it twice already. I have no more cord.
Or say the wind made the words. I told you I had known two.
Swear it again before the crew: before this sailing season is out
Ask what an unkept vow costs: lay a course for Doccinga
The wind made the words. Cut the cord down

You say it again with your hand on the mast, and name the season. The steersman finds another length of cord, shorter than the first, and ties one knot in it. He holds it up so you can see how much is left.

You say you will hear what it costs before you decide whether to pay. The steersman says that is how his father bought cattle, and gives the course for the Lauwers mouth without being asked. The cord stays where it is.

You cut the cord down yourself and drop it over the side. It floats, which nobody expected, and follows the boat for a while. The steersman says the church on the mound at Doccinga is open to any man, even now. Nobody else says anything.
Another coin
The wooden church on its mound in the salt marsh, where the old bishop was killed. The priest is mending a sheep hurdle by the door. He hears the whole of it without putting the hurdle down.

A vow to a saint is a debt, and saints collect. I have buried men who found that out. But the books let a debt be paid in another coin when the first is out of reach: days on bread and water, or their worth to the poor, or a work.
You promised a devil the best of your hold. That promise does not bind. The making of it does, and the books have a price for that too. I did not write them.
You promised nothing. You let your men's promise stand in your hearing and then put it down. That is a smaller thing than breaking a vow, and a meaner one. The books have it.
You have been here before, and went away. The hurdle is the same hurdle. So is what I said.

Here is a work. On storm nights the boats cannot find this creek. We pulled two men out of the reeds last winter and did not pull out a third. A horn lantern on the mound from Martinmas to Easter, oil, and a boy to mind it: a hundred and fifty pennies sees three winters.
Or keep the fast. Forty days on bread, water and salt, and you bring the wax and the wine for the old bishop's day up this creek for no freight. The marsh will see you do it.
I was baptised in this house. I would like to be able to come back to it.
Pay for the light on the mound: a hundred and fifty pennies
Keep the forty days on bread, water and salt, and carry for the church for nothing
Pay for the light, and keep the fast as well
A vow to the wind is wind. Thank him and go

He counts the pennies on the church step and puts them in his shirt, and then at last puts the hurdle down. By evening the post is cut. The weavers of the mound send eight bolts down to the boat without a word about price: their men use that creek. The priest gives you the church's order for wine and wax, and says the lantern will be lit on Saint Martin's night whether you are here to see it or not.

Forty days is a long time to watch other men eat. You keep it, and carry the church's wax and wine up the creek on the day, and the marsh sees. The widow of the long mound, who feeds strangers before she asks their names, says she will keep whatever you leave with her and sell it when the price is right. Six bolts of cloth come down to the boat. The priest says the debt is paid, and that he would not make a habit of it.

You pay for the lantern and keep the fast as well, and carry for the church on the day with your belt drawn in. The marsh does not know what to make of a merchant who pays twice. It sends twelve bolts down to the boat, and the farmers of the long mound put two hundred pennies of their own toward the oil and give them to you to buy it with. The widow there will keep your goods. The priest says the saint is paid, and that he rather thinks the saint is surprised.
You thank him. He says you are welcome, and that the door has no lock, and picks up the next withy for the hurdle. The steersman stays in the church a while after you have gone down to the boat.
A new knot

The guest-master has a new knot in his cord of ships and has not ladled anything. A fisher of the house came in over the bar at first light: long ships lying under the island off the Coquet, a day's sail to the north. The abbot has come down to the mud himself.
Six, he says, or seven. He did not stay to count twice. Lying to, not fishing. Nobody lies to off the Coquet for pleasure.
We were written to last year. You live by the sea, the letter says, from which this plague first came. I have had it read to the brothers until they can say it. It does not say what to do.
You said you would come back and tell me if there were sails. You are here, and there are sails. I take that as it is meant.
They tell me you are a man who was heard in a storm. I do not ask you to be heard again. I ask what a man does who has a boat and a day.
The book chests. Father, the master's own books are in those chests. Plate can go in the ground. Books cannot go in the ground.
Up the river is all shoals above the island on the ebb. Go on this tide or not at all, and keep the south bank until the old wall.
Take the book chests up the river on this tide, and tell him to send for the reeve's men
Tell him: plate in the ground, boys inland, and the reeve's spears in the reeds by the bar
Kneel with the brothers, and sail on the tide

Nine chests come down to the mud on the brothers' backs and your cargo goes up the bank to make room. You take the flood up past the island with the lookout calling the south bank, and by dark the chests are under a thegn's roof inland with two brothers sitting on them. When you come down on the ebb there are spearmen in the reeds by the bar, and the abbot is having the altar plate buried under the calf pen.

Nine chests come down to the mud and you take the flood up past the island. Above it she touches, hangs, and lies over far enough for the river to come in across one chest before the men can shove her off; somebody's shoulder goes with the shoving. The chests reach a thegn's roof inland all the same, one of them dripping. When you come down on the ebb there are spearmen in the reeds by the bar.

You tell him what a man tells his own household: bury what will not spoil, send the boys and the old inland with the books on a cart, and have the reeve's men at the bar by night, in the reeds, not on the sand. He thanks you first, as he does, and then for once does not say no. A rider goes up the river bank before you have cast off.

You kneel with them in the stone church through one office, and it is a good one. Then the tide serves. The abbot blesses the boat from the bank. The lookout watches the two churches until the river bends, and after that he watches the sea to the north.
A roof on both

Broken ships lie on the south sand at the river mouth, ribs up, with gulls on them. The two stone churches stand on their rise as they stood, and there is a roof on both. The abbot walks you to the door and counts on his fingers what is still inside.

They came at first light, eleven days after you. They found the church swept, the chests gone and the reeve's men in the reeds by the bar. Their chief was killed on the mud. Then the wind got up from the north-east and did the rest.
Two days it blew. Them that came ashore alive did not get far.
The brothers say the saint sent the weather. I say it fell on both of us, and we were the ones standing on a hill. But somebody carried word, and that was not weather.
Every chest came back up the bank with its lock on. The master's own hand is in three of those books.
One chest took the river. Forty leaves have been drying on the refectory rafters like fish. They will read. I have looked at each of them myself.
The king has been told who it was. He is not a grateful man by nature, so I asked for you while he was still surprised.
The king who was told of it is dead, by his own men. His writing was made while he lived and the reeve at Eoforwic has seen the seal. I would use it soon.
Take what the house gives: two books, the reeve's silver and the cellarer's key
Take the house's gift, and the king's writing for the strand at Eoforwic
Ask only that the boat be named in the house's prayers on the master's day

Two books in plain boards, copied in this house: the abbot says they are what it has that travels. A bag from the king's reeve, who was glad of a fight he could win. And the cellarer, who likes merchants and counts it a fault, shows you the dry end of his store and says a bale left there will be there when you come back. The lookout says an English riddle over the wrecks on the way out, about who it is that stirs the sea from under.

Three books in plain boards, a bag from the reeve, the dry end of the cellarer's store, and a strip of sheepskin with a king's mark on it: this man's keel pays nothing on the strand at Eoforwic. The abbot says that a house which keeps the books of the dead should know what to do for the living, and that he is sorry it has taken a heathen fleet to teach him. The lookout says a riddle over the wrecks on the way out, about who stirs the sea from under.

The abbot thanks you first, and then says no: the boat will be named on the master's day for as long as the house stands, and you will take the books as well, because he has already had them carried down. The cellarer shows you the dry end of his store. The lookout stands in the door of the school a while, and comes back to the boat of his own will, saying a riddle about who stirs the sea.
The same sea
Hard weather again, and the same sea coming over the same quarter. This time nobody on the thwarts shouts a name at you. They bail. Now and then one of them looks aft, and then goes on bailing.
The worst first. It is as bad as the other night. Now the rest: the oar is sound, and nobody aboard owes anything.
His light is still burning, or the stump of it. The sacrist said to the Advent fast. I counted the weeks.
He has a thing in his tarn that he did not have before. So he is paid, and he knows it. But I would not ask him twice in one life.
There is a light on the mound at home tonight, if the boy is awake. Somebody is finding the creek by it.
The brothers had a riddle on a leaf about who it is that stirs all this up from under. I will say it when I have a hand free.
Say nothing. Steer
Say thanks aloud for the last time, and promise nothing
Vow again

You steer. It blows itself out before morning, as they do. When there is light enough the lookout says his riddle, and the steersman takes the old cord with its year of knots down from the mast, coils it and puts it in your sea chest. He says a house should keep one thing that cost it something.

You say thanks aloud, to whom it concerns, and add that nothing more is offered. The hand laughs. It blows itself out before morning. The lookout says his riddle, and the steersman takes the old cord of knots down from the mast and puts it in your sea chest, where your heir will one day find it and wonder.

You begin to say it, and the steersman says over the wind, without turning his head: once is a debt, twice is a habit. You finish it anyway. It blows itself out before morning. The lookout says his riddle, and somebody cuts a new length of cord.
A Frisian skipper has brought a candle his own height to Saint Cuthbert's island for a vow made at sea. It burns by the coffin, the tallest light in the church.
A Frisian gave a Frankish sword to the water behind a lord's hall in the north, at winter's start, for a vow made in a storm. The lord has made him a guest of the house.
There is a lantern on the church mound at Doccinga on storm nights now, from Martinmas to Easter. A skipper who owed a saint paid for it.
This year the heathen men came to the monastery at the mouth of the Don and found it swept and watched. Their chief was killed there, and a storm broke their ships on the bar.

A small open boat lying across a breaking sea at night under torn cloud: the steering oar swinging loose at her quarter, the steersman and one man hanging on its loom, a thin boy standing at the mast with his mouth open to the wind, a dark-bearded Northman bailing and looking up.

The same boat in a flat grey morning, sail drying: the boy counting three on his fingers with a wooden bailer in his other hand, the Northman whetting a knife, the steersman tying a first knot in a cord by the mast.

A boat on a strand at evening, a fire and a long wooden trough of melted wax beside her: the skipper standing against the mast while the boy holds a tarred line from his heel to his crown; a pale candle as long as an oar hanging from the lowered yard.

An English shingle strand at low tide, dull afternoon: a woman in a good worn cloak standing at the boat's side, a small leather purse held out; along the thwarts a man-long candle in old sailcloth, the boy's hand flat on it.

The boat becalmed, sail hanging, low sun: a big fair Saxon with a long knife across his belly sitting on a thwart with his elbows on his knees, looking steadily aft at the skipper; the steersman behind, looking at the water.

A mile of wet shining sand at the ebb with a low island beyond it: a short weathered boatman in a sealskin jerkin walking ahead with a tall pole, a barefoot man behind him carrying a pale candle on his shoulder like an oar, their prints filling with water.

Inside a plain timber church at dusk, the doorway open with no doors in it: a carved oak coffin raised by the altar, one great candle burning beside it taller than the gaunt white-haired bishop who stands with his hand on the lid; the skipper facing him.

A jetty at a northern market on a clear cold day: an old shipmaster leaning on a stick and looking down into the open hold of a small Frisian boat, the dark-bearded Northman at his elbow, the skipper standing among his casks.

A long timber hall at night in autumn, a fire down the middle and a cauldron steaming: a lord in a blue tunic rising with a horn in his hand, benches of men turned to look at a Frisian skipper who stands holding a sword in its scabbard across both palms.

The mast of the boat close up, calm weather: a cord hanging from it knotted along its whole length to the very end, the steersman holding the last hand's breadth between finger and thumb, the crew looking at the sky.

A small wooden church on a green mound in a flat salt marsh under a wide sky: a sturdy priest with mud to the knee weaving a sheep hurdle by the door, listening, and the skipper with his hood in his hands; behind, a creek winding out to grey sea.

A tidal mudflat below two small stone churches on a rise, early light: a lean abbot with an ash staff, a round monk holding up a knotted cord, and a line of brothers carrying iron-bound chests down toward a beached boat.

A river mouth after a storm, torn sky clearing: the ribs of broken clinker ships in pale sand with gulls on them, a barelegged fisherman among them, and behind on the rise two stone churches whole, with smoke from a kitchen roof.

The boat in a gale at dusk, well reefed and holding her course: every man bailing or hauling with his head down, the skipper at the steering oar, and by the mast an old cord thick with knots swinging in the wind.
The great candle burned down to a stump in a pool of its own wax beside the oak coffin, a folded strip of old linen and a book in bare boards lying on a sea chest in the foreground.
A black tarn behind a hall at first light with one ring spreading on the water, and on the bank a pile of marten skins and four walrus tusks.
A horn lantern burning on a post on the church mound at night in driving rain, and far out on the dark water the small sail of a boat turning toward it.
A book chest standing open in a stone-walled room with coloured glass in the window, the books upright inside it, and through the door the wrecks on the sand.
The smiths' street

On the smiths' street at Colonia a count's man counts sword blades into a cart, one by one, and makes his mark on a stick for each. When the cart has gone the smith, Reginbald, lifts a hide in the corner of his forge. Under it are four blades the count's man did not count.
For the count's own men, at the count's price. The king's word is that no mail coat leaves the realm. A smith who wants to keep his forge reads swords into it as well.
For the count's own men, at the count's price. No arms go over the border now, mail or blade. The merchant who is found with them loses everything he carries, down to the boat's bailer.
A Frisian. You people look at a blade the way other men look at a cask. You do not ask if it is good. You ask how many the boat will hold.
The count pays at Martinmas, in promises, and less than he said. A Dane pays in weighed silver before the thing is in his hand. These four were never on the stick. Forty-five pennies the blade.
Look under the tang. A hammer in a ring, in twisted wire. That is mine. I put it on all of them. A man should be able to find his work again.

There is a man up the river who has begun to put his whole name in the iron, with a cross before it and a cross behind. Buyers ask for the name now and do not look at the blade. I have a hammer and a ring. It will have to do.
Buy the four blades (180 d) and stow them under the ballast
Buy one, openly, for your own belt (50 d)
Say your boat carries wine and stones, and drink his ale

Reginbald wraps the four in greased hide and ties them with bast. He names a man on the Slie who deals in people and carries a hazel switch. After dark the bundle goes under the ballast stones, and the stones go back as they lay.

A free man may wear a sword, and no toll man can say otherwise. Reginbald fits it with a plain hilt while you wait and tells you a riddle about it that he had from an English buyer. The other three go back under the hide.

His ale is thin and his talk is good. The Danes, he says, pay half again for Rhenish tools, and nobody searches a boat for axes and adzes. You part friends. Somebody at the end of the street watches you go.
Ballast out
The toll man is not alone on the dam at Dorestat. A man of the count's stands beside him with two spearmen, and a boy has been sent for baskets. They mean to have your ballast out, stone by stone.
This is not my doing. I take a tenth of what a man sells. I do not lift his floor.
A Frisian was seen on the smiths' street at Colonia ten days ago, after the count's cart had gone. Your boat came down from Colonia. Stand on the dam, shipman.
The king's word names mail coats. The count has decided it means anything with an edge. I would not argue the difference with a spear at my back.
Since Thionville it is everything aboard, not only the arms. Half to the palace. The other half between the officer and the man who finds. Look how keen he is.
You wear nothing I can take from you. Then you will not mind the stones being moved.
Leave the blades under the stones and let them look
Thirty pennies in the toll man's hand before the spearmen reach the boat
Say the blades were bought for the count's own men, and sell them to him at his price
Lift the boards yourself and show them everything

They take out the top course of stones and the casks, find bilge water and a dead eel, and tire of it. The count's man looks at you a little longer than he needs to. The bundle lies a hand's breadth under where they stopped.

The boy's basket catches on a knot of bast. The count's man unrolls the hide on the dam where every shipman can see, and counts four. The blades are the king's now, the court will hear of the rest, and your boat's name is on a stick in the count's hall.
The toll man remembers that the flood is making and the dam is needed for a wine ship. The count's man is told the boat was searched at Noviomagus. He is not sure he believes it. He goes.

You say it before a stone is lifted: four blades, bought for the count's following, to save his cart a second journey. The count's man pays what the count pays, which is less than you gave. He almost thanks you.
You have the boards up before the baskets come. Stones, casks, bilge. The count's man looks, nods, and loses interest in you. The toll man takes it as a kindness that you made his day short.
What lies under the stones
The men know what lies under the ballast. Nobody told them. The steersman wants it said aloud before the boat is out of Frankish water, and he has waited until the others can hear.
Four blades under the stones. I have counted the ways this ends. In most of them I am standing next to you.
And it is not the blades alone any more. They take the boat's whole lading, and then they ask who steered her.
The Franks made that law because they fear the edge. A man who fears a thing pays to be rid of it or pays to have it. Either way somebody is paid.
The king calls the Danes his enemies. He called us that, on the Weser. I would carry.
Promise each man a share of what the blades bring
Have the bundle over the side tonight and say no more of it
Tell the steersman his work is the tide, and yours the cargo

A share is a different thing from a wage, and the men sit differently on the thwarts after it. The steersman says a share of a hanging is still a hanging, and steers. The Northman, who is pleased, gives you a riddle about two dead things that boil a wound-leek.

In the dark of the middle watch the bundle goes over the lee side with a ballast stone tied to it. It makes less noise than a hundred and eighty pennies should. The steersman says nothing, which from him is thanks.
He hears you out, looks at the sky, and puts the helm over a little for the ebb. He does not speak of it again. He does not speak of much else either, that day or the next.
The man with the hazel switch

A stout Dane in a good grey cloak has watched your boat since she touched the strand. He carries a hazel switch and a folding scale. Behind his booth is a pen with people in it. He asks, through nobody, in slow plain words, what else came from the river.
You are from the river. Men from the river bring wine and say they have nothing else. Then they show me what else.
Four. With the hammer in the ring. I know the hand. It is a small lot for so long a road.
Nothing. Then you are honest or you are slow. I have work for either.
Four ounces of silver the blade, on my scale and then on yours. Or three people from the pen for the four: Wends, sound, taken this spring. I do not say a price twice.
The king has burned Reric and brought its merchants here to the Slie. There are more buyers than blades now. That is good for a man with blades.
Sell the four blades for weighed silver
Take three people from his pen for the blades
Sell him no blades, and hear what else he wants

He weighs it twice: cut arm rings, a bent brooch, half a foreign coin with writing like worm tracks. Sixteen ounces. He bends each blade over his knee and watches it come back straight. Then he tells you his name, Asulf, which he had not done before.

A man, a woman and a boy of twelve, tied wrist to wrist with hide rope. Asulf says he keeps kin together when it costs him nothing. They are heathen Wends, which the king's law lets a merchant carry, and they eat like crewmen. What you do with them is your affair.

He is not offended. He wants Rhenish tools, six bundles before the winter, and will pay half again over the price. As you go he says the name Asulf, and that a man who changes his mind knows where the booth is.
A cask with no wine in it
A wine cask stands in Reginbald's forge with its head off. There is straw in it, and tallow, and room for eight blades. His journeyman, Hrodwin, is at the grinding stone and listens with his back.
You came back, and with your boat. So the four went where they were going. Good. Now look at this.
You came back. I heard how it went with the four. Do not tell me. Look at this instead.

Eight, hilted, in straw and tallow, and the head pitched on like any other. It is how the big houses send them. There is one at Dorestat who has done it for ten years and has never had a cask opened. Fifty pennies the blade.
Hear this before you say yes. They keep a boat at the river mouth now, with a captain who likes to hear ballast move. He opens casks. Go out on a dark ebb, or do not go out with this.
Every man with twelve farms must own a mail coat now, by the emperor's word, or lose the farms. So the lords take every ring of mail I can make, at their price. I have not been paid since Easter.
The abbey's steward has old mail and nine swords in a chest and may no longer sell them to any stranger. He cannot say so, and he cannot stop saying so.
When you are there, ask something for me. Ask what a smith is worth among them. Not his work. The man.
Buy the cask of eight (400 d)
Carry his lawful iron instead: six bundles of tools (90 d)
Buy nothing, and promise the boy to ask his question in the north
The head is pitched on and the cask is rolled to the strand between two that do hold wine. It rolls like the others. Only its sound is wrong, if a man thinks to knock on it.

Axes, adzes, shears and spoon bits, six bundles tied with bast. Reginbald sells them the way a man sells his second-best ale. Nobody on the river will look twice at them, and the Dane asked for them by name.
Reginbald puts the head back on the empty cask and says the offer will keep until someone else takes it. Hrodwin walks with you to the strand and says nothing more, having said it once.
The watch boat

A long boat with a painted shield at her stem stands out from the river mouth under twelve oars. A man in her bows calls on you to lie to. To seaward the shoals are breaking white, with a channel through them that a small boat might know.
The count's watch. Drop your sail and lie to.
The king's coast watch. Drop your sail and lie to. We are here for Northmen, and for what goes to them.
I know this boat. They cut her on a stick at Dorestat. Today we look at all of her.
Ballast, bilge, and every cask sounded with a mallet. If it rings like wine, you sail on with my blessing.
Lie to with an empty conscience and let them look
Lie to, with the cask standing among the wine
Put her over the shoals where a long boat cannot follow
Roll the cask over the lee side while their sail hides you, then lie to
They sound the casks, lift two stones, and find a merchant's lading. The captain says it is a dull thing to search an honest boat and wishes you a fair wind. He means both.

The mallet goes down the tier. Your steersman has the fourth cask wedged tight between two full ones, with a wet sail thrown over it, and the mallet finds it dull enough. The long boat backs her oars and lets you go.

The fourth cask does not ring like wine. They stave the head in on your own thwart. Eight hilts in straw. The captain takes the blades, sixty pennies for his trouble, and the look of your boat, which he will know again.
She goes over the tail of the bank with a hand's breadth under her and the long boat's oars stop at the white water. They shout something. It is your boat's description, and they have it right.

She touches. Not hard, but long enough for twelve oars. They take what they find, and eighty pennies for the chase, and the captain tells you the day you are to stand before the count. A boat that runs is a boat they remember.

The cask goes in on the side away from them and sinks like the iron it is. When they come aboard there is a gap in the tier the width of one cask. The captain looks at the gap, and at you, and can make nothing of either.
The net and the fish

Asulf has a guest at his booth: a tall man with gold on his arm who does not say whose man he is and does not need to. He wants blades. When that is settled he wants something more, and Asulf leaves the two of you to it.
This one buys for a lord with many ships. He will take every blade you can bring, this summer and the next. I take a tenth for the introduction. I say so now.
This one still carries nothing. A careful man. Careful men live long enough to hear offers.
My lord has forty men who will follow him and nine swords among them. The rest carry axes and hope. You see the trouble.
The king counts his ships against the emperor's, and he is content. Then he counts swords, and he is not.

Blades are fish. We buy them one at a time and they are eaten. I would sooner have the net. Bring the man who makes them, and he shall have a house by the water, iron, charcoal, and nobody over his hearth but one lord.
You asked what a smith is worth here. You have heard it. It is more than a count gives him, and he would have to live among us to spend it.
Sell the eight blades from the cask
Sell six bundles of Rhenish tools, and no blades
Sell nothing; hear the offer out and drink with them

The tall man draws each blade, looks along it, and bends it until the point nears the hilt. All eight come back straight. He pays five ounces the blade without a word about the price. The swords go up the strand in the arms of eight men who did not have one that morning.

Asulf buys the tools himself, for the shipwrights, and pays well. The tall man watches a bundle of adzes change hands as if it were a slight. Then he makes his offer for the smith anyway. He has decided you know the street.

You drink their ale, which is better than a Frank's, and listen. By the end of the evening you have a good deal of their speech, the price they would give for Rhenish wine, and an offer for a man who is not yours to sell.
The mark below the hilt

Men stand round a small boat on the landing with their hoods off. A dead man lies in her on his own nets: Folcbod, who set eel traps in the outer channels. The sword that killed him was left in him, and his wife has drawn it out and holds it across her two hands.

This year a fleet of two hundred ships came from the land of the Northmen to Frisia. The islands off the coast were wasted, the Frisians were beaten in three fights, and a hundred pounds of silver were paid them as tribute.
Three ships lay in the outer channel for water, the men say, and wanted a sail. They were gone on the next tide. Nobody will write it down.
He would not let go of the sail. They left this in him. It is worth more than the sail and the boat. They must have been in haste.
A hand's breadth below the hilt, in twisted wire, is a hammer in a ring.
You have held this blade, or its brother. It went north under your ballast or in your cask, and you were paid for it in silver weighed twice.
You did not sell this blade. You have stood in the forge it came from, you know who carries for that forge and how, and you have told nobody.
You are a merchant. You know marks. Whose is it?
Is it ours now?
Tell her whose mark it is, and all you know of how it came here
Tell her, and lay a hundred pennies on the thwart toward the man's price
Say only that it is Frankish and good, and buy it from her (60 d)

You tell her: a smith at Colonia, a road down the river, a booth on the Slie, and where you stood on that road. She hears it to the end. Then she says that she asked whose mark it was and has had more answer than she wanted, and turns back to the boat.

You tell her, and count a hundred pennies onto the thwart beside the dead man's hand. It is not his price. The men who owe that are at sea. She does not thank you and she does not push it away. The boy counts it after you, moving his lips.

You say it is Frankish work and good, and that she should not keep it in the house. She sells it to you for sixty pennies and is glad to see it go. It lies in your boat under a sailcloth. The men step round it.
What lies between

The king's men are at Dorestat, asking who carries blades north. They sit in the count's hall with a clerk and a bundle of tally sticks. They know a street in Colonia and a booth on the Slie, and this morning a spearman came down to the dam and asked for you by your boat.
They have come as the king's men come now, two together, a count and an abbot, both strangers to this river, so that nobody here has fed them or is their cousin.
A letter has come from the palace, and the count has a stranger at his elbow who reads it to him and watches how he listens.
We have a forge at one end and a dealer in people at the other. We lack what lies between. You sail between.
We have a forge at one end and a dealer in people at the other. And between them, cut on a stick, we have your boat.
Half to the palace. Of the other half, a part to the officer and a part to the man who finds. The emperor has thought about what makes men find.
The king rewards a service. He also remembers the lack of one. I would not want to be remembered so.
Whatever you say in there, say it once and the same way. They ask everything twice.
Give them the road: the forge, the cask, the booth on the Slie
Tell them nothing, go up the river by night and take the smith north
Tell them what you did and what you saw, and take the blade to Saint Martin's
Say you carry wine, and go on carrying blades

You give it all: the hide in the corner, the cask with straw in it, the wine shipper in the lower town who fills the casks for others, the hazel switch. The clerk cuts it on three sticks. The count says to be at the court in forty nights, and to bring a bag.

You tell them you carry wine and are sent away to think. That night you are on the river, rowing against it. Reginbald hears you out with his hands black to the elbow. He takes his hammers, his tongs, his wire, and a bag of his own charcoal, which makes you laugh, and him not.

You tell them what you carried, if you carried, and what you saw, and that you are done with it. You name no names they do not have. The count looks at the abbot, and the abbot says a man who lays a thing down should lay it somewhere. He names Saint Martin's at Traiectum.
Wine, you say, and stones, and cloth. They ask it twice and get it twice the same. You are let go. On the dam the toll man does not look at you, which is the kindest thing he can do.

Wine, you say. The second time you say wine and stones. The clerk cuts something on a stick. You pay sixty pennies for wasting a court's morning, and your boat goes on the list of those to be looked at twice.
The river's man

Asulf has ale on the board and the lord's man beside him. They have counted, between them, what your boat has brought north, and what she could bring in ten summers. They mean to keep you, and they have thought about how.
There was a road from the river with many feet on it. Now there are fewer. The Franks have been pulling men off it. You are still here. So you are the road.
There is a plot by the water, six paces of strand and back to the wall, with my lord's peace on it. No man may draw iron there. Even ours.
They tell me a blade of yours was left in a Frisian. Blades are left in people. It is what they are for. You bought it back, I hear. That was tidy.
They tell me you told a widow whose blade killed her man. That was honest, and it was not wise. Her kin can count. Do not sleep ashore in Frisia.
The king forbade it again, and his son after him, and his grandson on pain of death. The blades went north all the same.
Take the plot by the water and the lord's peace on it
Take silver and a guest's seat, and no house the Franks can name

Four posts are driven and a rope is run between them, and that is a house plot on the Slie. Asulf weighs out the silver that was owing and lays three marten skins on it for luck. On the Rhine they will hear that a Frisian has a house among the Danes. On the Frisian coast a family knows whose cargo it was.

You take the silver, more of it, and a seat at the lord's board whenever your boat is on his strand. No posts are driven. A man with no house here can still say, at Dorestat, that he sells wine. On the Frisian coast a family knows better.
The finder's share

At the count's court at Dorestat a clerk reads out what was taken: a cask of blades opened on the dam, a forge at Colonia sealed with the count's seal, a wine shipper of the lower town in irons. Then he reads your name, and every shipman on the river turns to see whose it is.
Item, twenty-three swords and four mail coats. Item, one boat. Item, wine to the number of thirty casks. Item, the said shipper's house and dam.
Half to the palace. Of the rest, the officer's part and the finder's part. It is the law, and it is weighed here before the court so that nobody can say it was not paid.
No law yet says what the finder is owed. So it is the king's grace, and I am to be generous with it. I have been told how generous.
The smith is too good to waste. He goes to the palace forges with his tools. He will make blades for the rest of his life and never sell one. Unless somebody here speaks for him.
There is a bigger house on this river that we did not touch. We had no cask of his. Men like that are never found with the cask.
This year the road by which swords went from Colonia to the Danes was closed. The next year there was another.
Take the finder's share, weighed out before the court
Take a third of it, and ask that the smith keep his forge and his hands

Sixteen hundred pennies, weighed, and a strip of parchment with the king's name on it: your goods pass the toll at Dorestat free, and your house is under his protection. Reginbald goes up the river in a cart with his tools. Nobody on the dam drinks with you that night. On the Slie a man with a hazel switch will hear how it was done.

You take a third and say the smith only sold what the count would not pay for. The abbot likes the answer. Reginbald keeps his forge, with a count's man counting every blade out of it, and the parchment with the king's name is yours all the same. On the Slie a man with a hazel switch will hear how it was done.
A forge on the Slie

There is a new house by the water at Sliesthorp, with a turf roof and a smoke that is not a cooking smoke. Reginbald is at the anvil in a borrowed apron. The lord's man sits on a chopping block and watches him work, as he has every day since the boat came in.
He came north in your boat between two casks, with a sail over him at Dorestat and at the river mouth. He was sick the whole way and complained only of the damp in his charcoal.
Their iron is bog iron and comes in lumps like bread. Their charcoal is birch. I said it could not be done. It can be done. It takes twice as long, and I have nothing else to do.
Hrodwin has the forge at Colonia and my mark with it. He will tell the count's men I fell in the river. He has wanted to say that for years.
I said a house, iron, charcoal and one lord. He has asked for a second bellows and a boy who does not talk. He shall have them. Men have been given land for less than what he is making.
This is the first. Look under the tang. The same hammer, the same ring. A man should be able to find his work again, wherever he has had to do it.

No book in Francia tells of this. In the north they said afterwards that the good blades began on the Slie in those years, and that the first smith there was a foreigner who never learned to like the ale.
Take a third of the forge's work to sell, and keep your goods in his house
Take the first blade and the lord's purse, and no part in what follows

You shake hands on a third. His house will hold your goods between voyages, and nobody steals from the lord's smith. The lord's man weighs out eight hundred pennies' worth for the bringing of him. Blades are cheaper on the Slie from this year. On the Rhine your name is on a stick beside his.

He gives you the first blade himself, hilted in the northern way, because the hilt was all they would let anyone else make. The lord's man weighs out the purse. You have sold a man his freedom and a king his swords, and it is hard to say which of them paid more. On the Rhine your name is on a stick.
Iron for the saint

The blade lies on a linen cloth before the altar of Saint Martin at Traiectum, with the hammer in its ring turned upward. The dead man's widow, Liafburg, has come up the river with her son to see what is done with it. The priest has not yet touched it.
Iron given to the saint is the saint's. The smith here will draw it out into a strap for the west door. Men will go in past it for as long as the door stands, and none of them will know.

A man who has laid one trade down wants another. The saint has wine to carry down to Dorestat, and his men pay no toll on the banks there. The steward will pay your freight before you sail. He does that for nobody.
You paid toward him when you owed nothing by law. I have not forgotten it. I have not forgiven the rest of it yet. One thing at a time.
I came to see it done. I did not come to make it easy for you.
My father's boat is too big for me and my mother has sold the traps. Do you need a boy who can scull?
