This year a merchant of Dorestat gave a sword to Saint Martin, and it was made into a hinge.
Take the boy aboard as your fosterling, and carry the saint's wine
Leave the boy with his mother, pay his keep to the church, and carry the saint's wine

Liafburg puts the boy's hand in yours before the altar and says his name and his father's name, so that the saint has heard it. Eilger comes aboard with a bundle and an eel spear. The steward counts out the freight. Your house is Saint Martin's man now, and the toll men on the banks know the saint's mark on a cask.

The boy stays with his mother, and a hundred and twenty pennies go into the church's chest for his bread until he is grown. He looks at your boat as you go down to her. The steward counts out the freight. Your house is Saint Martin's man now, and the toll men on the banks know the saint's mark on a cask.

This year, at the count's court at Dorestat, a wine shipper of the lower town was found to have sent swords to the Danes in casks. His goods were taken, half for the palace. A forge at Colonia was sealed. The Danes are paying half again for any blade they can get.
This year a Frankish smith set up his forge at Sliesthorp, under a lord of the Danes, and made swords there with his own mark. A blade is cheaper on the Slie than it has been in any man's memory.

Inside a dark forge on the smiths' street at Colonia, late afternoon: a broad grey-bearded smith in a leather apron lifts a hide from four bare sword blades in a corner; through the open door behind him a count's cart rolls away up a street of low workshops under the old Roman wall.

The dam at Dorestat on a grey morning: a Frank in a red cloak points into a small open boat while a boy carries ballast stones up in a basket and two spearmen wait; the toll man stands aside with his tally stick, looking at the river.

The small boat under sail at dusk on brown water, four men aboard: the steersman at the side rudder speaking without turning his head, an old Northman smiling at the bilge, a big Saxon with folded arms; the ballast stones at their feet.

A beach market in the north, a clear cold noon: a stout Dane with a plaited beard and a hazel switch holds up a small folding scale; behind his booth a wattle pen with people sitting in it, and boats drawn up on the sand.

The forge at Colonia by firelight: a wine cask with its head off, straw spilling from it and eight sword hilts showing; the smith with one hand on the rim, and behind him a young man at a grinding wheel, his back turned, his head tilted to listen.

A river mouth in a fresh breeze under a broken sky: a long twelve-oared boat with a painted shield at her stem bears down on the small merchant boat; white water on the shoals to seaward, low dunes behind.

Evening at a booth on the Slie: a tall Dane with gold arm rings bends a sword blade into a bow across his knee by lamplight, watching the merchant and not the blade; the stout dealer stands back in the doorway; ships' prows dark against the water.

A Frisian landing at low water under a flat white sky: a small boat on the mud with a dead man laid on his nets; a woman in a dark cloak holds a sword level across both hands toward the viewer, a boy of ten at her side; men with their hoods off stand around.

The count's hall at Dorestat, daylight from the door: a Frankish count and an abbot sit side by side on a bench with a clerk and a bundle of tally sticks before them; the merchant stands alone on the rushes; a spearman at the door post.

The strand at Sliesthorp on a bright windy day: four posts and a rope mark a plot of sand by the water; the stout dealer weighs cut silver on his scale and lays three marten skins beside it; longships lie along the shore behind.

The count's court at Dorestat held in the open by the dam: a scale with a heap of silver pennies on a board, a clerk reading from a strip of parchment, a man in irons at one side, and a ring of shipmen all looking at the merchant.

A turf-roofed forge by the water at Sliesthorp in the blue light of a northern evening: the Frankish smith at the anvil holds up a new blade to look along it, sparks at his feet; a tall Dane sits on a chopping block watching; the fjord and the boats beyond.

Inside the small stone church of Saint Martin at Traiectum, morning light from one window: a sword on a white cloth before the altar, a priest with his hands not yet on it, and a woman in a dark cloak with a boy who is looking back at the merchant.
The empty frame

By the door of the wooden church stands a frame of new oak, two posts and a beam, with nothing hanging in it. Under it a priest is beating a plank with a mallet. A few Frisians and Saxons come up from the jetties at the sound. The Danes mending nets do not look round.
Folcward. I am the priest here. This is how I call them: a board and a mallet, like a man mending a boat. On a still day it carries as far as the second jetty.

After the old king fell, the count of this port nailed that door shut and I went south with the cup under my cloak. Then the young king put the count out and sent to the bishop for me. So I am back, and the nails are still in the post if you care to count them.

The king has given leave for a bell. A bell, here. The heathen hold it a thing not to be spoken of, and he allowed it anyway. I built the frame the same week, before anyone could change his mind. I have the leave and the frame. I have not got a bell.

Hebbe, of Dorestat. We have made up a purse among those of us who summer here: Frisians, some Saxons, two Danes who would rather not be named. Seven hundred pennies' weight for the man who hangs a bell in that frame, and a hundred and twenty now toward the metal.
Nobody north of the Rhine pours one. There are founders at Colonia, on the smiths' row. It need not be big. It must be heard on the water.
The bishop is at Bremen and has no ship. You have a boat and you go up the Rhine. Will you fetch it?
Take the errand, and the purse toward the metal
Take the errand; let them keep their silver till it hangs
Ask first what the Danes say of it
It is not your church. Go about your trade
Hebbe weighs out a hundred and twenty pennies' worth in cut silver and old coin, and has two men watch him do it. The priest goes back to his plank. You are now a man who owes a town a bell.

Hebbe puts the purse away slowly, as if it might be a trick. The priest laughs for the first time. 'Then bring me wine for the altar as well, and I will pay for that like an honest man: four casks, and more than the market gives.'
The priest stops smiling. 'Ask Asgaut. He sits in the alehouse by the brook most evenings and he will tell you without being asked twice. He is the old count's kinsman. Hear him, and then come back.'
The priest nods and picks up his mallet. The plank sounds flat and wooden behind you all the way down to the boat.
What they fear

The alehouse by the brook is low and full of smoke. On the best bench sits a grey man with a ship-owner's hands, whom the others make room for. By the door a bronze caster has spread a cloth, with a heap of broken green metal on it and a pair of tongs.

Asgaut. You are the one they asked. Listen, then. This land has keepers that were here before us. They do not like iron dragged over stone, or shouting at the wrong time. A thing made only to make noise, hung up and beaten every day? They will go. The herring go with them, and then the corn.
Hovi shut that house and he was right, and the boy king put him out for it. Hovi is my mother's brother's son. I am still here. Think about why.
They rang one at Birka before the thing, I hear, and the Svear let it stay. The Svear also eat seal. I am not a Svea.

I will say it once so that nobody can call it a trap. Bring that thing here and I will not lay a hand on you. I will buy what is in your boat, at a good price, and it will go into the inner water where it is deepest. That is my offer and my warning, both.

Tosti. I make brooches. This lot came down from the king's hall: taken on the Elbe, the summer the ships burnt the Saxons' town. Look at the curve on that piece. Thick as my thumb. It was all one thing once, and somebody hit it hard. Ninety, by weight, and you carry it.
You have my Elbe bronze. I hope it makes something better than brooches. No, I do not. Brooches are what feed me.
Ask him, in his own tongue, what a ship does in fog on the Slie
Buy the broken bronze on the caster's cloth: ninety pennies' weight
You have heard enough. Thank him for the warning

He is quiet for a while. 'It blows a horn, and the man at the narrows blows one back, if he is awake and sober. Three winters ago he was neither. My brother's boat went onto the bar with eight men.' He drinks. 'A horn does not carry. Why do you ask me that?' You say you only wondered.

Tosti weighs the silver, not the bronze. It fills two sacks. One piece is the rim, a hand long, and when your man knocks it against the gunwale it gives one short clear note and stops. Everyone on the jetty looks up.
He lifts his cup a finger's breadth, which among these people is a good deal. 'You were told,' he says. 'That is all I wanted.'
The founder

On the smiths' row under the wall a broad man with burn scars to the elbow is scraping the seam of a cauldron. He hears the errand out without stopping. Then he puts the scraper down and holds his hands apart, knee high.

Reginbert. For a wooden church among the Danes? So high, then, and round in the shoulder like a beehive. What a boy of ten weighs. Two men lift it, one man rings it, and it is heard over a mile of water. Bigger would pull their church down.

Four parts of copper to one of tin, and no monk's tale will change it. Bring me six bars of copper and one of tin. My own old bronze makes up the tin, and the fire eats a tenth whatever I do. Tin is Cornish and comes by Hamwic. Copper comes from wherever something old has been broken.

First a core of loam. Then the bell itself in wax, laid on the core as thick as the bronze will be, every line of it. Then loam over that. Bake it, the wax runs out, and there is a bell made of nothing, waiting. Forty days before I dare pour into it.

Let me see that. Hm. This has rung before. See the rim, and where the clapper wore it bright? And burnt, after. Whose was it? Never mind. Bronze does not remember. It will ring again and not know the difference.

And tell your Danes nothing about what a bell wards off. The year of the great storm the whole town ran into Saint Peter's and rang every bell there, and the lightning came in regardless and killed three at the altars. A bell calls people. That is all it does.

They tell of a founder in the old emperor's day who asked for a hundred pounds of silver to put in the pot in place of tin. He kept the silver and used the tin. The bell would not sound. He climbed up to pull the rope himself and the clapper came down on his head. So I ask for tin.

Four hundred and twenty pennies for metal and work together. Or bring the bars yourself and pay me a hundred and fifty for the work, on the day. If you are going for tin anyway, bring me three bars more. I will pay well over the market, and complain of it.
Pay him for metal and work together: 420 d
Bring him the bars yourself and pay only his work
Give him the broken bronze from the north and 150 d for the work
Stay the day and watch him pour a cauldron first
He counts the pennies into a pot and puts the pot under his bed. 'Forty days. Come at the dark of the moon after that if you want to see it run. I pour at night.'

He shrugs. 'Your back, your boat. I start the core tomorrow either way. Six of copper, one of tin, and three of tin for me. If you come with five I will pour you a smaller bell and you can explain it to the priest.'
He turns each piece over before it goes in the basket, and sets the rim aside on the sill. 'That one goes in last,' he says, and does not say why.

He lets you hold the skimming ladle, once. In the afternoon, waiting for the pot to cool, he gives you a riddle he had from an English monk, about a thing dug out of the ground and tormented by fire. And he tells you about the founder who asked the emperor for silver.
Six bars and one
The founder has the core built: a mound of baked loam the shape of a beehive, standing on a board in his yard under a hide. He looks past you at what your men are carrying up from the strand.
There is your bell's inside. The outside is whatever you have brought me.
Six. And one of tin. Good bars, too. Put them by the furnace, not in the wet.
I can count, and that is not six bars of copper and one of tin. I can sell you mine. It will cost more than it would have, because I kept it back for you and turned a cauldron away.
The work is a hundred and fifty, as I said. I do not pour on promises.
Hand over six bars of copper and one of tin, and 150 d for the work
Pay for his metal after all: 440 d with the work
Give him the broken bronze from the north instead, and 150 d for the work
Tell him the bars are coming
He rings each bar on the anvil and listens with his head on one side, like a man buying a pot. All seven pass. 'Now it is only the waiting,' he says.
He has the bars out from under a bench before you have finished counting. They were never far away.
He turns each green piece over before it goes in the basket, and sets the rim aside on the sill. 'This has rung before,' he says. 'That piece goes in last.'
'So is the Last Day,' he says, and pulls the hide back over the core.
The pour

The mould is buried to its lip in a pit in the founder's yard, with the earth trodden hard round it. The furnace has been alight since noon. He means to let the metal run after dark, when he can see its colour, and the neighbours have wet their thatch.
When the fire over the pot goes green and then white at the edge, it is ready. By day I cannot see that. So we wait for dark, and nobody speaks to me after sunset.
Your old rim went in last. It took longer to melt than the rest. I do not make anything of that.
I have two boys for the bellows. Four pairs of arms would be better. If the blast drops while it runs, the metal goes in cold.
Cold metal meets itself in the mould and does not join. You get a line in the bronze no wider than a hair, and a bell that says 'clank'. It has happened to better men than me.
Put your crew on the bellows and stand the night with him
Leave it to his two boys and sleep aboard
Offer sixty pennies for the pot, to sweeten the voice

Your men blow until their arms shake. When he knocks out the plug the bronze goes down the channel like something alive, bright as a low sun, and the pit groans once and is still. He stands over it a long time. Then he says, 'That went in hot,' and goes to bed.
You wake to a red sky over the wall and hear nothing more. In the morning the founder is asleep against his own furnace and the pit is steaming gently. One of the boys shows you his hands and grins.

In the morning the founder is sitting on the edge of the pit and does not get up. 'The younger one fell asleep on the bellows. A dozen breaths, no more. It filled. What it sounds like, we will know in twelve days.'

He closes your hand over the pennies. 'Silver does nothing for a bell but make it dear. Take that to the poor at Saint Peter's door, come back, and blow.' You do both. The metal runs white, and the poor of Colonia eat on a Danish church's account.
The voice

The bell stands on two billets in the yard, brown and rough as bark, its casting lugs sawn off and the saw marks still bright. The founder has a mallet of applewood in his hand. He has waited for you before using it.
Listen. ... There. It goes on after you have stopped hearing it. Put your hand on it. That is a bell. I have made eleven, and three were as good as that.

Listen. ... You hear it. It starts well and then it shuts its mouth. There is a cold line in the shoulder. It will call people to church, and they will know it is that church's bell and no other. Or I break it and pour again, and you pay for my wood and my time.
Whatever church that old bronze came out of, it has gone back into one. I thought you should hear someone say it.
Straw under it, straw round it, and lash it low, on the keel. Do not let it roll. And do not let anyone hit it with iron. Wood, or its own clapper. The clapper is in that sack.

It is going among the heathen? Then let it not go bare. Bring it to Saint Peter's. We will wash it, and sign it, and say what is said over a thing given to God. No, we do not baptise it. The old emperor forbade that. We bless it. There is a difference.
Load it as it is. Its own priest can bless it
Have it washed and blessed at Saint Peter's first: twelve pennies at the altar
Pay him to break it up and pour again: 120 d and twenty days

Two of your men carry it down through the river gate on a pole, and the boat settles a plank's breadth when it goes in. Covered with straw and a hide it looks like a cheese. The founder watches from the wall until you are round the bend.

It stands on the floor of the minster while the priest goes round it with water and a branch of hyssop. Your crew stand straighter than they have all year. On the strand afterwards a Dane selling furs asks what the singing was for, and somebody tells him.
He breaks it himself with a sledge, in four blows, and does not let the boys do it. 'Twenty days,' he says. 'And this time everybody stays awake.'
A bell going north
The toll man has the straw off before you can speak. By the time he has decided what he is looking at, a priest and half the upper bank are standing on the jetty staring down into your boat.

Bronze, by weight, is a tenth. A church's own goods pay nothing. This is a church's goods that have no church yet. I will have to think. My lord Rorik is a Dane and so am I, and neither of us thought to see one of these carried north on purpose.
Hildulf, of the upper church. We had a bell. It went down the river in a longship, the year they burnt us, and I suppose it is a hundred brooches now. Since then we send a boy round with a horn.

Hildulf, of the upper church. We had a bell. It went down the river in a longship. Then they came again while Rorik was away, and nobody knew until they were at the lower jetties. A boy with a horn is no use against that.

Six hundred and fifty pennies, and ground of the church's own on the bank. For that one, there, today. The Danes have been without a bell since the world was made. They can wait another year for the next.
You carry their pledge? Then send it back to them. I would not have it said that Dorestat's bell was bought with a northern church's silver.
It is promised north. Cover it and sail on
Sling it from the yard and let Dorestat hear it once
Let it hang here. Hear what the upper church will give
The priest lays his hand on it before the straw goes back. 'Then ring it loud up there,' he says. The toll man decides it is a church's goods after all and waves you through.

You hoist it on the halyard and your steersman gives it the clapper, six strokes. Work stops along the whole bank. An old woman crosses herself and throws a penny into the boat, then others do. 'For the church among the Danes,' they say, as if it were a long way off.

It goes up the bank on four shoulders with the priest walking backwards in front of it. 'Fourteen days for the carpenters,' he says. 'Come and hear it.' On the jetty a Frisian bound for Sliesthorp has seen all of it.
A horn in the fog

The fog has come down so thick that the stem is gone from the steering oar. The lead finds four fathoms, then two. Somewhere to leeward a horn is blowing, short and often, and it is closer to the bank than you are.
Two fathoms and sand. The bank is that way. I think. With this weight on the keel she will sit hard if she touches.
That horn is blown by a man who does not know where he is. He is going in. If he could hear us he would know where the deep water lies.
Do not uncover it. Not out here. There are things in a fog that are only looking for where the noise is.
And that one has been sung over. Everyone on the strand at Colonia knew it. What is in the fog will know it too.
Unwrap the bell and strike it, so they hear where the deep water is
Keep it wrapped and feel your way off with the lead
Anchor where you are and wait for it to lift

The note goes out flat over the water and does not die. The horn stops. Then it comes again, nearer, and a boat's shape grows out of the white: Danes, six of them, grey in the face. Their steersman throws a bundle of marten skins into your boat without a word, and looks hard at the thing that called him.

You strike it a dozen times. The horn goes on a while, further off, and then is not there. Nobody comes. Your Dane sits with his back to the bell until the fog lifts, holding something under his shirt.
Two fathoms. Three. Three. Five. The steersman lets out his breath. The horn is behind you now, and fainter, and then you cannot say whether you hear it or not.

She touches, lifts, and sits. With the bell on her keel there is no heaving her off until the flood, and it is a long cold night on the edge of the bank with the sea talking under the planks. Nobody is hurt much. Nobody sleeps.

You lie to the stone anchor and listen. The horn blows until about the middle of the night. In the morning the fog is gone, the bank is a long bowshot off, and there is nothing on it and nothing on the water.
The strand

The grey ship-owner is on the jetty before your line is fast, with six men who are not carrying anything. Up the slope the priest has seen your sail and is running, his skirts in his hand. He will be too late to speak first.
I know what is under that hide. A man came from Dorestat four days ahead of you. So. You were told, in the alehouse, in front of witnesses.
They say it was washed and sung over in the great church at Colonia, like a child given a name. That does not make it better.

And my sister's son came in off the sea nine days ago, saying a Frisian's kettle called him off a bank in the fog. He is a truthful boy and a poor liar. I have been thinking about that for nine days and I do not like it.

My offer stands. Name a price for what is in the boat. Or carry it up the hill and we will see what the thing says, and what the gods say. I will not touch you either way. Others here may not be so careful of the king's peace.
The king has given leave! The count Burghard is coming to say so before the whole port. Bring it up to the church. Twenty days, no more. Do not listen to that man. He is counting on you being tired.
And if you will not wait, then for the love of God do not sell it to him. The king has given ground at Ripa too. There is a priest there under a sail with no bell and no door to hang one by.
Carry it up to the church and wait for the king's man
Tell him what this one did in the fog, and what it could do on the Slie
Keep it aboard and take it round to Ripa, where the king has given ground
Ask him what the boat's cargo is worth to him
Your men carry it up between two lines of people who do not move aside quickly. The priest locks it in the church and sleeps in front of the door. Asgaut watches from the jetty and then goes home.

You say it in his own tongue, plainly: a horn does not carry, and this does. He hears you to the end. 'Say that at the thing,' he says. 'I will be there. I do not promise what I will say after you.' And he lets it go up the hill.

The priest sits down on a mooring post as if his legs had gone. Asgaut nods once. 'Ripa is the king's affair and the western sea's,' he says. 'What they frighten off there will not be mine.' His men cast off your line for you.
'Good,' says Asgaut. 'Then we are two merchants.' He sends a man for his scales. The priest has reached the jetty, and has heard, and says nothing at all.
The lot

The thing meets on the open ground inside the bank. The king's man stands on the stone. The bell sits on a hurdle before him where everyone can see it, and an old man squats beside it cutting marks into three slips from a fruit tree.

Burghard. I speak for King Horik. The house of the Christians stands open. Their priest stays. They may hang this and sound it. That is the king's word, and I was kinsman to the old king and am kinsman to this one, so do not tell me what either of them meant.

It is also the custom of this port to ask before a new thing is done in it. The king does not forbid the asking. If the slips fall against, the thing may hang and keep silent for a year, and be asked about again.
I say what I have said. It is a noise made for a foreign god in a place that has keepers of its own. If the herring fail, who pays? Not the Frisian. He will be at home.

I have something to say that I did not expect to say. The Frisian asked me what a ship does in fog on the Slie. I told him: it blows a horn, and sometimes it is heard. Let him tell you the rest himself.
Strike it for them. ... You hear? Even their own smith could not make it speak cleanly. It is ill made, and it knows it.
I am not allowed to speak here. I am allowed to stand here. I am praying, and I would be glad if you did not let it show.
Stand back and let the lot fall as it will
Offer it to the port first: rung in fog for any ship, before it is rung for Mass
A gift to the old man who cuts the slips: eighty pennies' weight

The old man throws the slips on a white cloth, looks up at the sky, and takes one without looking down. He holds it up. A murmur goes round the bank. 'They allow it,' says Burghard, before anyone can ask the old man what he saw. 'Hang it. Ring it at their next feast.'

The old man holds up the slip and shakes his head. Asgaut does not smile, which is courteous of him. 'Then it hangs silent a year,' says Burghard, 'or it goes elsewhere. The king's leave stands. I did not ride here to quarrel with a stick.'

You say it to the whole thing: hung by the water, rung in fog, for any keel, whoever owns it. Then Asgaut stands. 'My brother went onto the bar with eight men because a horn does not carry. Let it be tried.' Nobody calls for the slips. The old man puts them in his sleeve, offended.

The old man's hand closes on the silver without his eyes moving. The slip he draws is the right one. Burghard looks at you a moment longer than he need. Asgaut looks at the old man. It will be talked about.

The old man takes the silver, and draws the slip against. Perhaps the gods are not for sale. Perhaps Asgaut paid first. Either way the whole bank saw your hand go to his, and you are eighty pennies lighter.
The first ringing

The bell hangs in the oak frame by the church door. The Christians of the port stand close round it. Further off, on the jetties and along the bank, stands everyone else, at a distance they have chosen with care.
It is the feast. The rope is walrus hide. A Dane gave it and would not say his name. You carried it from the pit to this post, so the first pull is yours. Hard, and let it swing back by itself.

A year it has hung there with its mouth empty, and I have beaten my plank under it every morning. The herring came. The corn stood. Nobody's cow died that was not going to. The clapper is back in. The first pull is yours.

The slip fell against. I may hang it and not sound it. I have waited two years for a bell and I can wait a third with it over my head. Or you can take it down and carry it to Ripa, and I will bless you for that too, more slowly.
They say its voice is short. It is. It sounds like a man clearing his throat before he says something true. I would not change it now.
The founder sent word of what went into the pot. I knew the church on the Elbe. I was a boy in its school when the ships came. I will not tell the Danes. I will tell the bishop.

I have a boy at the narrows who will run here when the fog comes down. Ring it then, before you ring it for your god, so that the first time it is heard it is heard for a reason anyone can understand. After that, ring it when you like.
The old man has a new knife with a silver ferrule. Everyone has seen it. Ring your bell, Frisian. But do not ask anyone here to cut lots for you again.
Seven hundred pennies' weight, as pledged, less nothing. I have had it buried under my hearth so long I had begun to think of it as mine.
Ring it for Mass, and take what was pledged
Wait for the first fog, and ring it from the jetty for the boats before it is rung for Mass
Hang it without its clapper and let a year go by
Take it down again and carry it to Ripa

You pull. The note goes out over the roofs and the jetties and the still water, and on the far shore a dog begins to bark. The Christians are weeping, or laughing. Along the bank some of the Danes have turned their backs and some have not. Nothing else happens. The herring boats go out as usual.

The fog comes on the fourth morning. You ring from the jetty, slow strokes, for the length of a tide. Three boats come up the Slie on the sound, one after another, and the last is Asgaut's own. He ties up, looks at the bell, and has two timbers of marten carried to your boat. On Sunday it rings for Mass and nobody turns his back.

The priest ties the clapper in a cloth and hangs it on a nail inside the church. The bell hangs in its frame and says nothing through herring time, harvest, midwinter and the thaw. People stop looking at it. That may be the point.

It comes down in an afternoon. The priest helps lash it into the boat himself. 'Tell him at Ripa to ring it toward the east now and then,' he says. The frame by the door is empty again, and somebody has hung the plank back in it.
The king's ground at Ripa

South of the river, across from the market plots, a square of ground has been pegged out and four corner posts stand in it. A young priest is living under a sail stretched between two of them. He has seen what is in your boat and is trying not to hope.
This is the church at Ripa. I grant you it needs walls. The king gave the ground, and leave for a priest to live on it, and here I live. I say Mass on a sea chest. In wet weather, under it.

It was for Sliesthorp? And they would not have it rung? Then they have sent it to the right door by the wrong road. I would hang it on that corner post tonight, and build the church up round it afterwards.
The king's leave at Sliesthorp was for a bell. Nobody told me the leave stopped at the heath. Hang it. If the market complains I will say the wind was from the east and I heard nothing.

Ripa looks west. Half the men on these plots have been in Frisia or among the English and have heard a bell and come home alive. And a ship coming in over the flats in thick weather could use something to steer for. There is a plot free by the river, the third from the ford.
You carry the Sliesthorp men's silver? Then that is theirs, whatever becomes of the bell. Send it back, or I will be ringing a debt every morning.
Hang it on the corner post, and take what Ripa's Christians and the king's man will give
Give it, ask no silver, and send the Sliesthorp men their purse back
Not here. Sail on

It hangs from the corner post under a hat of thatch. The first stroke goes out over the marsh and puts up every goose between the river and the sea. The Christians of the market weigh out five hundred pennies' worth and six sacks of amber, the king's man walks you to the plot by the river, and an old pilot offers to show you where the channel really runs.

The priest cannot speak, so he rings it. Every goose on the marsh goes up. By evening there are ten sacks of amber on your jetty that nobody will admit to leaving, the king's man has walked you to a plot by the river, and an old pilot is drawing the channel in the mud with a stick. The purse goes east with a comb-maker who can be trusted.
He helps you push off, which is more than you deserve. From midstream you can still see him under his sail, looking at the corner post.
The inner water
The ship-owner sends a man for his scales and sits down on your gunwale to wait. The bronze caster has come along the jetty behind him and is looking at the bell the way a butcher looks at a calf.
Nine hundred pennies' weight, in hack silver and rings. That is twice its metal and more than the Christians have got. I am not buying bronze. I am buying quiet.
You will row it out yourself, tonight, past the last stakes where the inner water is black. You brought it, you put it down. Then nobody can say I laid hands on what the king allowed.
And after tonight you are my guest whenever you tie up here. My ships know your sail. My friends' ships will know it. That is worth more than the silver, on this coast, and you know it.

Or sell it to me. Six hundred and twenty and a share of the work. That is forty pair of brooches hanging there. I do not care about keepers and gods. I care that it is the best bronze I have seen in this town, and he wants to give it to the eels.
The Christians' purse you keep or give back as you please. I would give it back. A man should only be hated for one thing at a time.
Take his silver and row it out to the deep place yourself
Not the water. Let the caster have it, for brooches
Hear the price, and say no after all. It goes to the church

It goes over the side mouth up, fills, and is gone with less noise than a man makes spitting. You sit in the dark over the place for a while. On shore the priest has not gone to bed. In the morning the frame by the church door is empty, as before, and Asgaut's men greet you by name. Perhaps somebody will find it one day.

Tosti breaks it with a stone maul behind his workshop, and it rings at every blow. Within the month half the women of the port have new brooches, and wear the Christians' bell to the old gods' feasts without knowing. He gives you eight pair to sell, and the first pair out of the mould to keep.

Asgaut gets up off your gunwale without hurry. 'Then you wanted to know what you were worth,' he says. 'Now you know. Carry it up.' The priest, who has not moved or breathed, takes one end of the pole himself.
The upper church
The bell hangs under the eaves of the upper church, on a beam two carpenters have let into the gable. A boy sits on the roof beside it watching the river both ways, as he has been told to.

Hear it. ... The whole bank, down to the last jetty, and they say as far as the ferry. We rang it first for Mass and then for the dead of the burning, by name, as many as we knew. It took the afternoon.

There is a boy up there from first light to dark. Three strokes and three again means sails on the river that nobody knows. It will not stop them. It will give a man time to get his children and his scales into a boat.

My lord Rorik says a town that hears them coming is a town still worth holding. He did not say thank you. He said your boat need not stop at my post, if you would rather have that than the priest's ground.
You still have the northern church's silver in your chest. I said it before. Send it back, and then come and be thanked.
Take the church's silver, and the strip of bank it offers below its yard
Take less silver, and Rorik's man's word that your boat passes the toll free
First send the Sliesthorp men their purse back, with twenty pennies for the wait

Six hundred and fifty pennies, counted on the altar step, and a strip of bank below the churchyard with room for a house and a jetty. From your own ground you can see the bell. Up at Sliesthorp a priest is still beating a plank.
Six hundred pennies, and the toll man's hand on it before witnesses: your boat passes his post free while Rorik holds the town. Up at Sliesthorp a priest is still beating a plank.
A Frisian bound for the Slie takes it, a hundred and forty pennies sewn in a cloth, with two men to watch him receive it. Whatever they call you up there now, it will not be thief.
A Frisian boat lay at Dorestat with a new bronze bell under straw, bound for the church among the Danes at Sliesthorp. It was rung once from the yard and the whole bank heard it.
At Sliesthorp the Christians have a bell in their church, by the young king's leave, and it has been rung. Men of Dorestat and of Hamburg who trade there say they go more easily for it.
At Sliesthorp there is a bell by the water that is rung in fog for any ship, Dane or Christian, and rung for Mass besides. The ship-owners of the port asked for the first and put up with the second.
The bell that was made for Sliesthorp hangs at Ripa instead, on the ground the king gave for a church there, before the church has walls. At Sliesthorp the priest still calls to Mass with a board.

The Christians of Sliesthorp had a bell brought from Colonia, and it never hung. Some say it lies in the inner water and some that the women are wearing it. The king's leave stands, and the frame is empty.
The upper church at Dorestat has a bell again, and a boy on the roof beside it who rings three and three when strange sails are on the river.

Sliesthorp on a grey still morning: a small plank church with a new oak frame beside its door, two posts and a beam with nothing hanging in it; under the frame a spare tonsured priest beats a hanging plank with a mallet; a few merchants in short Frisian cloaks walk up from the jetties, and Danes mending nets in front keep their backs turned.

Inside a low smoky alehouse at dusk: a grey, heavy Danish ship-owner with silver arm rings sits alone on the best bench, one finger raised; by the open door a young caster squats behind a cloth heaped with broken green bronze, one piece plainly the curved rim of a bell.

The smiths' row under the Roman wall of Cologne at midday: a broad man with burn-scarred forearms and a leather apron holds his hands apart at knee height to show a bell's size; a half-scraped bronze cauldron and a cold furnace behind him, a Frisian merchant in front.

A founder's yard in dry afternoon light: a beehive-shaped mound of baked clay on a board, a hide pulled half off it; the founder rings a bar of copper on an anvil with his head on one side, while two boatmen set down more bars and one bright bar of tin.

Night in the founder's yard: white metal runs down a clay channel into a mould buried in a pit; four men heave at two pairs of bellows, lit from below; the founder stands over the pit with a long iron rod, his face turned from the glare; wet thatch steams on the roofs behind.

Morning in the yard: a rough brown beehive bell, knee high, stands on two billets with fresh saw marks on its crown; the founder has just struck it with a wooden mallet and holds the mallet still in the air; the merchant has his flat hand on the bronze; a young priest waits at the gate.

The long jetties of Dorestat under a white sky: a small boat lies alongside with straw thrown back from a bronze bell on her bottom boards; a Danish toll man in a Frankish cloak crouches over it; above, on the jetty, an old priest and a crowd of townspeople lean out to look down.

A small open boat in dense white fog, her stem already lost in it: a man in the bow swings a sounding lead; amidships another pulls the hide off a bell lashed low on the keel, while a Dane sits with his back to it gripping an amulet under his shirt; the faint grey shape of a second boat to one side.

The jetty at Sliesthorp in flat evening light: the grey ship-owner stands with six empty-handed men looking down into a boat where a hide covers something round; on the slope behind, small and far off, a priest runs down from the church holding up his skirts.

Open ground inside an earth bank at noon, ringed with people: a richly cloaked Danish count stands on a flat stone; before him the bell sits on a wattle hurdle; an old man squats by a white cloth holding up one of three marked slips of wood; the ship-owner stands on one side, the priest with clasped hands on the other.

The church door at Sliesthorp on a bright feast-day morning: the bell hangs in its oak frame and the merchant hauls on a rope of pale hide, the bell at the top of its swing; Christians crowd close, some weeping; along the bank beyond, Danes stand at a distance, some with their backs turned and some watching.

Ripa at low water under a wide sky: on a pegged-out square of bare ground by the river four corner posts stand, a sail stretched between two as a tent; the bell hangs from a third under a small hat of thatch, a young priest pulling its rope; geese rise in a cloud from the marsh behind.

Night on black still water past the last harbour stakes: a small boat, two men tipping a bell over the gunwale mouth up, the water just closing over its rim; far behind on the shore one small light burns by a church with an empty frame at its door.

The upper church at Dorestat in late afternoon: a bell hangs from a beam let into the gable under the eaves; a boy sits astride the thatched ridge beside it, shading his eyes down the river; below, an old priest looks up, and beyond the roofs the long jetties and a wide brown river.
The closed fist

On the bank an Englishman asks a Tiel merchant for the price of twelve sacks of wool. The Tiel man holds up a closed fist and swears he owes nothing. Six men of Tiel step up and swear with him. Nobody seems surprised but the Englishman.
Twelve sacks, shorn at midsummer, weighed on his own beam. He said: after the herring. The herring has come and gone and so, it seems, has my wool.
I swear by God and Saint Walburg that I owe this man nothing. There. It is sworn, and these six swear I swear true. That is how a thing is ended where I come from.
You. You were lying next to him when they went aboard. You have eyes. Did I dream twelve sacks?
Do not look for a court. We took our last complaint to the emperor himself, and what came of it lies in the ditches at Flardinga. Since then we settle things at home.
I know this one. He put pennies in our purse once, when it was for the complaint. Let him say what he likes. He paid for the right.
Say what you saw: twelve sacks went over his gunwale
Ask the Tiel man what a seat on that bench costs
Say nothing, and watch how it is done

You say it: twelve. One voice against seven. The oath stands, because there is nobody on this bank to make it fall. The Englishman grips your arm and tells you what he can give: wine is a third dearer in London than it was at Lammas.

The Tiel man laughs and opens his fist. It is empty. More than this, he says, and less than you fear. Come down to Tiel in three weeks, early, and ask for Sibrand. The Englishman spits and goes to his boat.
You watch. Seven oaths, one closed hand, and a debt is gone like frost off a thwart. A boy tells you they are Tiel men and it is always so. Come and see them at home, he says. They start early.

At Tiel a man who owes swears that he does not, and his fellows swear with him, and there the matter ends. A stranger will not win a case against one of them. They say the emperor wrote that they might. Nobody has seen the writing.
The morning cask

Sibrand takes you down the Waal to Tiel. The sun is not yet over the dyke. The bench by the stone toll house is already full, and the cask already open, and somebody is already shouting the end of a story.
We asked the emperor for help against the count. He sent three bishops' men and a duke into a marsh. Now we ask each other. It is cheaper, and nobody drowns.
The rule of the bench: the man who tells the foulest story loudest drinks free till noon. A priest once won. We do not say which priest.
There was a monk here last month for Saint Walburg's wonders. He looked at my cask the way you look at a leak. He wrote something down. I charged him double.
A seat. Two of us to swear you are what you say. A pound of pennies in the chest, counted on the cloak. And one year in which no brother has cause against you. That is all. It is not little.
You spoke against Wigbold on the bank. Good. Now I know you can count, and that you say the number aloud. We will see which side of the bench that is useful on.
This is the one who saw seven men swear and asked what it cost to be the eighth. I like him. He will go far or be hanged, and either way not at my cost.
Tell the one about what stands up in a bed and makes a wife weep
Pay for the next cask
Drink what is poured and listen

You tell it slowly: it stands tall in a bed, it is hairy below, a churl's daughter grips it, and her eye is wet. The bench roars before you say onion. An Englishman at the end scratches it on bark for you, as his own people have it in a book.
You say onion too soon. There is a silence, then Wigbold laughs at you and not at the story, which on this bench is worth nearly as much. Your cup is filled all the same.

Thirty pennies on the board and the ale-wife knocks the bung from a new cask. Nobody thanks you. Three men move up to make room, which is the thanks. Sibrand says their man in London should know your face before Easter.

You drink and listen until noon. You learn who owes whom, who is lying up for the winter, and that the bench keeps a man in London who is short of something. Sibrand says: go and see him. A seat starts with an errand.
The emperor's men
Below the bridge a Tiel man has a store of his own and a tally of what the bench owes the king's reeve before Easter. He is counting gloves, and coming out one pair short every time.
Here we are the emperor's men, and the law of this town says the emperor's men who come in their own ships have as good a law as a Londoner. I have heard it read. I had it read twice.

For that, at Christmas and again at Easter: two grey cloths and a brown one, ten pounds of pepper, five pairs of gloves, two kegs of vinegar. The gloves are for the reeve's men. They have very many hands.
Cloth I have. Vinegar makes itself. Pepper I have not. The Cologne boats are late and the reeve does not take a promise in place of a pound.
What did the count take from you at the mouth? No, do not tell me. Every keel from home tells me, and each time it is a little more, and each time I am told it is the last.
The king here is a Dane now. The reeve is the same reeve. The toll is the same toll. I have stopped asking who is king. I ask who is reeve.
Take the order: ten pounds of pepper for the reeve's due
Lend him 100 d against eight bolts of English cloth
Hear how the emperor's men stand in London, and promise nothing

He cuts a stick for ten pounds of pepper at six tenths over the price, to be here before the reeve asks twice. And he says, not looking up from the gloves: when Sibrand asks who will swear for you, he may say my name.

A hundred pennies cross the board. Eight bolts of good English cloth come back as a pledge he does not expect to redeem. He says he will swear for you at Tiel. A man who lends to the bench at need is already half on it.

He talks while he counts. Pepper will be dear here until the Rhine boats come. He gives you a leaf an English schoolmaster wrote, a merchant answering for his trade. It is the only kind word about us, he says, that I ever saw written down.
The count's man at the mouth
At the river mouth, under the count's fort, his man came aboard as he comes aboard every keel. This time he knew your name, and your cargo, and on which bench you had been drinking.
The count takes a toll here. The emperor said he might not, and sent an army to say it louder. You sailed in over that army. So: the toll.
I was on the dyke that day. They came ashore among the ditches in mail. Somebody shouted that the duke had fallen. After that we hardly had to do anything.

My lord is no robber. He sells cheese and wants English cloth, like anyone. Carry his cheese, pass here free, and tell me now and then what the Tiel bench means to do next. They are always meaning something.
You have paid here before without a face on you. I marked it. A man who pays without a sermon is a man the count can talk to.
Take the count's tally: his cheese to London, no toll at the mouth, and a word now and then
Tell him you carry cargo, not words, and pay as every keel pays
Refuse, and tell Sibrand that the count is buying ears

He counts out a hundred and twenty pennies and has twenty wheels of cheese swung into your hold. The tally he gives you is short and has three notches. Show it at the mouth, he says. Do not show it at Tiel.
He shrugs and takes the toll, no more than from anyone. Cargo, then, he says. It is a pity. Cargo pays once. He goes over the side to the next keel.

You pay, and at Tiel you tell Sibrand. He is not angry. He is pleased, the way a man is pleased to find the hole in his net. So the count wants to know what we mean to do, he says. Then we mean something.
A monk with a wax tablet

A monk waits by your boat with a tablet and a stylus. He has heard that you drink at Tiel. He asks his questions like a man who has already written the answers and wants only to be sure of the spelling.
I am Alpert. I am writing down what has happened in these parts in my own time, for a bishop on the Rhine who likes to know. Most of it is counts killing each other. Tiel is a rest from that.
Is it true that if a man can close his hand over a thing, he may swear with the other hand that he never had it? I was told so. I should like to hear it from someone sober.
They say the emperor gave them a charter to judge as they please. I have asked to see it. Each of them says another one keeps it. I have run out of Tiel men to ask.
I do not hate them. I wrote down their saint's wonders, and there are many. Saint Walburg is very patient at Tiel. She has to be.
Tell him all of it: the fist, the oath, the morning cask
Tell him the other half too: the chest buries a drowned brother and feeds his widow
Say a guest does not carry the bench out through the door

You tell him. His stylus does not stop. When you are done he reads it back in Latin and then in plain speech: hard men, used to no discipline, judging not by law but by their will. He has left your name out. He thinks that is a kindness.

You tell him the fist, and then the rest: the chest that buries a drowned man and keeps his widow in bread. He writes the first part quickly and the second part slowly. That will not fit my chapter, he says. But I will remember it.

He closes the tablet without anger. A guest's answer, he says, and a good one. But the ale-wife talks, and the Englishmen talk, and the page will be filled. He blesses your boat, which costs him nothing.
Seven hands
On the bank at Tiel a Cologne man says Wigbold had fifteen casks of him at Martinmas and has paid for six. You were there when they were rolled ashore. There were fifteen. Sibrand is looking at you.
Fifteen casks of the white, from above Andernach. My mark is burnt in every head. Nine of them I have not seen a penny for, and I have come down the river three times to say so.
Six I had and six I paid. If there were more casks on the bank that day they were another man's, or the river's. I will swear it now and save us all the afternoon.
Wigbold will swear, and six with him. I have five. You have drunk our ale since harvest. A man who wants a seat can show it today with one hand.
Seven hands. I know how it goes here. I ask only this: let one of the seven be a man who can count to fifteen.
You counted wool sacks aloud once, for an Englishman. I have not forgotten. Today I should like you to have forgotten how.
You told us the count was buying ears. That was a brother's act before you were a brother. I say so in front of them all. Now do the other thing a brother does.
Lay your hand with theirs and swear he owes nothing
Keep your hand down, and say the chest should pay him and take it back from Wigbold
Say you stood too far off to count, and keep your hand in your belt

Seven hands, and one of them yours. The Cologne man looks at you a long moment and goes to his boat without a word. That evening Wigbold counts a hundred and fifty pennies into your cap. It is the price of about four casks.

You say it plainly: pay him from the chest, and let Wigbold owe his brothers, who know where he sleeps. There is a long quiet. Then Sibrand laughs. We judge by our own will, he says. Today our will is to pay. Wigbold does not laugh.

You say it plainly, and nobody hears it. A sixth hand is found. The oath is sworn without you. The Cologne man nods to you as he leaves. Sibrand says nothing at all, and pours your cup a finger short.

You say you could not see for the sun. Sibrand finds another hand; there is always a hand. The oath is sworn. Nobody on the bank believes you about the sun, and both sides think a little less of you for it.
What Cologne remembers
Wezelo's cellar is under the old wall, cool and full. He knows your boat before she touches the strand, and he comes down to the water himself, wiping his hands.
The seventh hand. I have a good memory for hands. Buy what you like here; my silver does not know you. But nobody in this street will let a cask go to you on trust. I have seen to it.
I was paid. Nine casks, from their own chest, by their own will, because a man with a small boat said so. I told it in every cellar on this strand. Nobody believed me until I showed the pennies.
You kept your hand down. It did me no good and I do not forget it. A man who will not swear false is rare enough down there to be worth a cup. Sit.
We need them and they know it. Every cask for England goes past their toll house. So we sell to them, and we count twice, and once a year one of us is robbed with seven oaths.
There is one court a Tiel man cannot swear his way out of with his friends. Their church is the bishop of Traiectum's. A false oath is the bishop's business. I have had my claim written out.
Take his order: twelve casks down the river on your own name
Pay him for the nine casks out of your own chest, and say why
Offer to carry his claim to the bishop's court at Traiectum
Buy your wine like any stranger and say nothing of Tiel

He gives you eighty pennies of earnest and an order for twelve casks at half over the price, on your name and no other. I will sell to Tiel through you, he says. Then at least I know which hand to watch.

You count Wigbold's hundred and fifty onto his board and say what they were paid for. He does not touch them for a while. Then he sweeps them up, and has two casks rolled to your boat. You swore false and paid true, he says. I have known bishops do worse.
He gives you a folded sheet, sealed with a wine merchant's ring, and twenty pennies for the carrying. Give it to the bishop's clerk, he says, not to a Tiel man, and not to the river.
You buy and he sells. He says only that the potters' boats came down from Pingsdorf yesterday, all at once, and the grey ware is going for four fifths of its price until they are gone.
The common chest
The boats are drawn up at Tiel for the winter and the chest is carried out. Three men have its three keys. The year's gain is counted on a cloak, and Sibrand asks the bench what it should buy.
Every brother puts in. In spring it goes out again on the keels, to England, to Cologne. In winter it comes home fatter. What a man put in he takes out, and his part of the fat. The rest we drink.
A newcomer's pound goes on the cloak today, where all can see it counted. If you have not got it, sit down anyway. The cask does not ask.
I say what I say every year. Martinmas, Christmas, Easter, Pentecost: four feasts, and we get drunk at each one properly, as if it were laid on us. It is why God sent the gain.
The monks ask for our charter. The bishop will ask next. We have always said the emperor gave us one. My father said it. I have never held it in my hand, and I keep the chest.
This one put his hand with mine against the Cologne man. I ask no more of a brother. Let him count his pound and I will pour for him myself.
This one made the chest pay a stranger. It cost us nine casks, and the Cologne boats came down a week early this autumn. I have reckoned it. We are ahead.
There is a monk at Traiectum who knows what our cask looks like at sunrise. Somebody told him. I do not ask who. I say only that the bench has long ears, as well as a loud mouth.
Put in your pound, and let it be drunk as it always was
Put in your pound, and say: buy the writing you say you have
Put in your pound, and say: offer the count a fixed sum each Martinmas and be done
Keep your pound this winter and drink as a guest

Two hundred and forty pennies, counted on the cloak, twelve at a time. The lid comes down on them. Then the cask is opened, and nobody at Tiel does any work that could be called work until the third day.

You say it: the emperor is alive, the chancery sells calfskin, buy the thing you swear by. Wigbold shouts that it is a waste of good ale. Sibrand lets him finish. Then he says: after Easter, when the emperor is on the hill. And you will come, since it was your tongue.

You say it, and the bench laughs you down. Buy what we have had since the old emperor? Your pound stays on the cloak all the same. Sibrand does not laugh. He looks at the chest for a while, and then at the door of the church.

A sum to Dirk? There is a growl along the bench. Three years ago they would have thrown you in the Waal. Now nobody stands up. Sibrand says: the bench does not send to the count. If a man knew the count's steward, the bench would not ask where he had been.

You keep your pound, and you drink, and nobody counts your cups. A guest is a guest. Sibrand says the cloak will be spread again whenever you are ready, and that a bishop's clerk has been asking for the names of those who trade here.
What is to be written
The emperor is on the hill at Noviomagus. In the clerks' room a chaplain rules a sheet of calfskin and asks Sibrand what, exactly, the emperor is to have granted. Sibrand looks at you.
A charter says a thing, and afterwards it says that thing for ever. So. What do the merchants of Tiel want the emperor to have always meant?
All of it. That we judge whoever trades on our bank. That a brother's oath ends a debt. Write that, and no monk will ever ask me another question.
The bishop of Traiectum is in the hall today. If I write that an oath ends a debt, he will ask to read it before the seal. He reads quickly. I should not count on that sentence.

The merchants of Magdeburg have a writing from the emperor's father's time: free of toll everywhere, save four places. Yours is one of the four. Emperors remember Tiel. Ask for what an emperor can sign without frowning.
You follow the Latin. Then stand here by my elbow and follow it. Most men who buy a charter find out what it says from the next man who sues them.
Ask for what is true: Tiel men judge trade among themselves, and answer strangers before the king's man
Ask for all the bench claims: its own judgement over anyone who trades at Tiel, and the oath that clears a debt
Ask for what is true, and read the draft yourself before the seal goes on
Tell Sibrand the price is too high, and carry the chest home

The chaplain writes: that the merchants of Tiel may settle among themselves what belongs to their trade; that a stranger's claim goes before the king's man; that they are in the emperor's peace. The bishop reads it and hands it back. On the third day it comes down the hill with a seal.

The gifts go up the hill. Word comes down: the emperor rides for Saxony tomorrow and the matter can wait for his return. Forty pennies of wax and courtesy are gone. Sibrand says: so we go on saying we have one. It has served.

The bishop is called away to a quarrel about a chalice, and the sheet goes under the seal unread. It says everything Sibrand wanted. He carries it down the hill inside his shirt. He does not sing until the boat is past the ferry.

The bishop reads it. He reads the sentence about oaths twice, aloud. The sheet is scraped clean before the ink is dry, and eighty pennies of gifts are not given back. Now the bishop knows what you would have liked to have, Sibrand says. That is a new kind of poor.

You read over his elbow. Twice you put a finger on a word and he changes it without a quarrel: 'among themselves', not 'at their will'. The bishop reads it and finds nothing to scrape. The seal goes on. The chaplain says you have cost him a week of later lawsuits.

The Latin is right; you have seen to that. But the emperor rides tomorrow, and a right sheet without a seal is calfskin. Forty pennies of gifts are gone. Keep the draft, the chaplain says. Kings come back. Sometimes.

You tell Sibrand what the chaplain's friends expect before a seal is so much as warmed. He counts it on his fingers and runs out of fingers. The chest goes home full. It was your tongue, he says. At least it was not our silver.
The bishop's question
The bishop's clerk fetches you from the Stathe. In the hall the bishop has a monk's book open before him and a row of river merchants on the bench, none of them from Tiel.
I stood beside the Tiel men before the emperor. I went down the river with the army for their sake, and came back from Flardinga in a boat, quickly. Nobody may say I am their enemy.
A monk of my diocese writes that at Tiel a false oath is held as nothing. Their church is mine. If souls are being sworn away on my ground I must know it, and not from a book.
You trade there. You are not one of them. So I ask you, before these men: when a stranger claims a debt at Tiel, what happens?
A man from Tiel was at the gate this morning asking who had been called. He left a message for you. It was one word. I think you know the word.
They asked the emperor for a writing this spring and did not get it. I was in the hall. A thing that must be asked for is a thing one did not have.
Brother Alpert says you were plain with him once. I ask you to be as plain with me. It is the same truth; it only stands in a bigger room.
Speak for the bench: they pay the king's toll, bury their dead, and no law forbids a man to drink with his friends
Hand in the Cologne man's claim, and ask only that he be paid
Tell the bishop what you have seen sworn
Say you are a stranger at Tiel and saw nothing worth a bishop's time

You speak for them and you speak well. The king's toll is paid at Tiel to the penny. Their dead are buried from their own chest. The bishop hears you out. That is a defence of their purse, he says, not of their oaths. But it is a defence. He closes the book for today.

You speak for them. The bishop asks whether you have ever seen a debt sworn away there, yes or no. You are slow to answer, and the hall hears how slow. He thanks you coldly. At Tiel they will hear only that you stood up.

You lay Wezelo's sheet before him and ask one thing: nine casks, paid. The bishop reads it and sends a clerk to Tiel that day. The chest pays within the week. Sibrand grumbles for a month, and tells the story as his own idea within a year.

You tell him: the closed fist, the seven hands, the casks. The clerk writes. The bishop says he will send for the priest of Saint Walburg's, and for the men by name. You have just named them. He tells you to come back when the corn is in.

You say you are a small man with a small boat and see little. The bishop looks at you as a man looks at a shut door. Then he calls the next merchant. Outside, the Tiel man at the gate nods once and walks away.
The bishop of Traiectum has asked the merchants of the river how debts are sworn away at Tiel. A monk has written it in a book. The Tiel men say they have the emperor's leave, and drink as before.
The cup goes round
It is a feast day at Tiel and the bench is set out under the toll house wall. A place has been left on it, next to Wigbold. The chest stands open and the big cup is full.
A year, and no brother has cause against you. Two will swear for you; I am one. There is the cloak, there is the cup. After today your oath is seven oaths, anywhere a Tiel keel lies.
Drink it to the bottom. If you leave any, you pay for the cask. If you spill any, you pay for two. Those are the only laws we have that are written down.
You stood up for us in the bishop's hall, where it cost something. The bench heard it by nightfall. I have heard it told four ways since. In all of them you are taller.
You made us pay a stranger what we owed him. I was angry until the Cologne boats came early. A chest needs one key in the hand of a man who can count. Dodo is dead since Lent. Here is his key.
And you told us about the count's ears before you owed us anything. I have not forgotten. I forget very little. It is why they give me the chest.
The new king has made the bishop our count. So the man who asks about our oaths now also holds our court. We shall drink to his health, loudly, and go on as before, quietly.
Take the cup, and the third key of the chest that Sibrand holds out
Take the cup and your share of the year
Count your pound onto the cloak now, and take the cup
Stay a guest of the bench: carry for them, swear for nobody

You drink it to the bottom. Sibrand hangs the key round your neck on a thong and counts out your part: fourteen hundred pennies. The store below London bridge is yours to use as a brother's. Somewhere a monk is writing that the Tiel men judge by their own will. Today their will was you.

You drink it to the bottom. Your pound has come home with company: eight hundred pennies on the cloak. Wigbold swears for you, which makes the bench laugh, and Sibrand after him. From today a debt claimed against you at Tiel meets seven hands.

Your pound goes on the cloak, twelve at a time, and the year's fat is laid beside it: eight hundred and forty in all. Then the cup. From today your oath is seven oaths. Wigbold says you paid late and must tell the first story. You know which one.

You leave the place on the bench empty, and nobody is offended; a guest who knows he is a guest is welcome for ever. Sibrand gives you six casks and the carrying of the bench's wool from London, at double. Wigbold takes you out at low water and shows you where the Waal hides its sand.
The writing is read

The whole bank of Tiel stands before Saint Walburg's door. The priest holds a sheet with the emperor's seal hanging from it and turns the Latin into plain speech, a line at a time. Nobody has brought a cup. That is how you know it is a great day.

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Henry, by God's mercy emperor of the Romans. Let all our faithful men know, those now living and those to come. That is how they all begin. Now it is about you.

That the merchants of Tiel may settle among themselves what belongs to their trade. That a stranger's claim against them be heard before the king's man. That they stand in our peace. It is short. Short ones last.

That the merchants of Tiel judge all who trade upon their bank, and that the oath of one, upheld by his fellows, ends a claim. It says so. I have read it three times. God forgive whoever let that sentence through.
My father swore we had it. His father swore it. I have sworn it to a bishop's clerk and felt my ears go red. Now a child can come and look at the seal. It hangs in the church. I had a nail put in.
Send word to that monk at Traiectum. Tell him to come and read it. Tell him the ale-wife will charge him the ordinary price.
Take the seat, and have your house named in the writing among those who asked for it
Take the seat and your share
Take silver for your part, keep the toll freedom, and stay your own man

The priest reads the last line again, slowly: at the asking of Sibrand and of your house, by name. Fifteen hundred pennies from the chest, a seat on the bench, and no toll for your keels at the king's house on the Waal. A sheet of calfskin outlives everyone on this bank. Your name is on it.

You take the place next to Wigbold, and a thousand pennies as your part. The cup comes out after all, once the priest has gone in. From today the Tiel men judge by a writing, and it was your tongue that made them buy it.

Sibrand counts twelve hundred pennies and does not press you. The toll man on the Waal is shown the sheet and told your boat goes under it. You sail before the cask is opened. A man can do a town a great service, Sibrand says, and still not want to live in it.
A page without your name
In the bishop's hall a clerk has a strip of parchment ready and the bishop's ring lies on the table. On the Stathe, a Tiel man you know turns his back as you pass.
The priest of Saint Walburg's has been told what he must ask a Tiel man before he gives him the Body of the Lord. Three have done penance. One paid a Cologne man for nine casks. It is a beginning.
The king has given this church the count's rights over that land. Their court is my court now. They will find that I judge by the law, and that I have read it.
My chapter is finished and has gone to Worms. You are in it, in a way. I wrote 'it is said'. That is you. It is the safest place in a book.
You told the truth where it was dear to tell. Saint Martin does not leave such a man to the mercy of a bench. Say what you want of this church.
Ask the bishop's writing: your keels free of his toll at Traiectum, as Saint Martin's man
Ask ground on the Stathe and a man of the bishop's to keep your store
Ask him to take the false oath from the Tiel men and leave them their cup and their chest

The clerk writes, the ring comes down on the wax. Seven hundred pennies, your keels free at the bishop's toll, and the saint's name over your house. At Tiel they have a name for you too. No man of that bench will swear for you again, or drink where you drink.

Six hundred pennies, a strip of ground on the Stathe with its end in the water, and a bishop's man with a key to keep what you leave there. It is a good plot. The Tiel boats lie two berths down, and their men look through you as through a net.

The bishop is silent, then nearly smiles. The oath is mine, he says. The cup was never my quarrel. He gives you six hundred pennies and his protection. Sibrand hears what you asked. He sends no thanks. But the next Tiel keel you meet dips her yard.
The fort in the marsh
On your way in, at the river mouth, the steward did not come aboard. He waved you into the creek under the round fort, and the count himself came down the mound to look at your boat.
They call it a robber's fort, up the river. I drained this marsh. My men dug every ditch in it. The emperor's army learned the ditches in one afternoon. I have known them all my life.
A toll that an emperor cannot lift is a lawful toll. The Tiel men will say so themselves within ten years. Until then I like to know what they say in the meantime.
His words have been worth more than his cheese money, my lord. We knew of the complaint to the bishop before the bishop did.
I hear somebody at Tiel stood up and said: pay Dirk a sum and be done. I hear the bench did not throw him in the river. That is news. Who was it?
Bring him the bench's offer: a fixed sum each Martinmas, and no Tiel keel searched
Be the count's shipman: his goods in your hold, his men showing you the sands
Ask for silver: a share of this year's toll, counted now

He walks the dyke with you for an hour. Then he names a sum, and it is one the chest can bear. Fifteen hundred pennies to you from both ends of the bargain, his men to show you the Merwede, and at Tiel a place on the bench: the man who ended the toll war drinks free.

He hears it and shakes his head. A sum is fixed; a river grows. He will keep his toll and his searching. But he pays you seven hundred pennies for having tried it, and has his men show you the sands. At Tiel they will know only where you were seen.

Nine hundred pennies, his sign cut on your stem, and two days with his boatmen learning where the Merwede shifts its bed. No toll man from here to the sea will stop you. At Tiel your name is said with another word in front of it, and the word is dog.

The steward counts twelve hundred pennies out of the toll chest, some of them, no doubt, once your own. The boatmen show you the channel because the count tells them to. He does not offer his sign for your stem, and you do not ask.

A river bank in late summer, low evening sun: a Tiel merchant in a good blue cloak holds up a closed fist; six men behind him each raise a hand; an Englishman in a short hooded cape points at wool sacks in a boat; a small Frisian boat alongside.

First light over a river dyke, mist on the water: a long bench under a small stone toll house, full of merchants with wooden cups; an ale-wife with her hand on an open cask; one man standing, arms spread, mid-story; boats drawn up on a timbered bank.

A storehouse door below a timber bridge on the Thames, grey noon: a Frisian in a fur-trimmed cap lays out pairs of gloves on a barrel head beside folded grey and brown cloth and two small kegs; a tally stick in his teeth.

A wide tidal river under a low round fort on a mound, wind and broken cloud: a steward with a rod and a leather purse stands in a small boat's stern, speaking low to the skipper; armed men watch from a jetty; cheeses stacked on the bank.

The Vecht side at Traiectum, a still afternoon: a lean monk of fifty in a black habit sits on a mooring post with a wax tablet on his knee and a stylus raised; the skipper coils a rope and does not look at him; the fort wall behind.

The bank at Tiel, a bright cold day: six men each with a right hand raised; an old merchant gestures to an empty space among them; a Cologne wine seller stands alone by fifteen casks drawn in the mud with a stick; the skipper between.

The strand under Cologne's Roman wall, morning: a broad wine seller in a wine-stained apron stands at a cellar door with arms folded; rows of casks with a burnt mark on each head in the dark behind him; river boats nosed to the gravel.

Inside a timber hall at Tiel, winter firelight: an iron-bound chest with three locks stands open on a table; silver pennies counted in rows on a spread cloak; three men each holding a key; a cask being rolled in at the door, snow outside.

A clerks' room in the palace at Nijmegen, spring light from a narrow window: a chaplain with a ruling stick over a blank sheet of calfskin, quill ready; an old merchant leaning on the table; the skipper at his elbow; a seal press and red wax.

The bishop's hall at Traiectum, a dull day: a bishop of fifty in a plain cope with a book open on a lectern, one finger on the page; a row of uneasy merchants on a wall bench; the skipper standing alone on the floor before him.

The bench under the toll house at Tiel on a feast day, banners of green boughs, clear noon: an old merchant holds out a great two-handled wooden cup to the skipper; an empty place on the bench; the open chest; everyone watching.

Before a small timber church at Tiel, bright morning: a priest holds up a sheet of parchment with a wax seal hanging from it; the whole bank crowded close, caps off; an old merchant with his hand over his mouth; no cup in sight.

The bishop's hall at Traiectum, evening, two candles: a clerk pressing a ring into wax on a strip of parchment; the bishop seated; a monk with a finished book under his arm in the doorway; through the door, a merchant on the quay turning his back.

A creek under a round turf fort in a flat green marsh, wide sky, afternoon: a count of forty in a red cloak, no mail, stands on a dyke looking down into a small boat; straight ditches run to the horizon; a steward with a toll chest.
A great wooden cup, empty, upside down on a bench, with a ring of ale drying on the wood.
An empty place on a crowded bench, and beyond it a small boat loading wool sacks.
A sheet of parchment with an emperor's seal, hung on a nail on a church wall.
An open book on a lectern, a line of small script, and a merchant's shadow across the page.
A boat's stem post with a count's sign newly cut in it, a flat marsh and a round fort behind.
Teeth on the jetty
A ship from the far north lies at the jetty, a month's sail behind her. Her master has laid out long yellow teeth and coils of dark rope, and nobody here can tell him what they fetch in the south.
You are from the south. Good. I have come a month along the land, and every man here tells me the price in his own harbour, which I know already.
The southerner again. I have not sold them. Nobody here has told me anything new since you went by.
Teeth of the horse-whale. He is not a big whale, seven ells at the most. But the bone in his teeth is noble, and his hide makes the best ship's rope there is.
I am Ohthere. I live northmost of all Northmen. I say so because I went and looked. North of me there is waste, and Finnas who hunt and fish.
I am told the Christians carve their god out of tooth. I have not seen it. Have you?
Ask what he wants of a southerner
Tell him plainly what tooth fetches in the south
Wish him a good market and go by
He looks at you for some time, as a man looks at a sky. Then he picks up a coil of rope and walks to the boat shed, and plainly you are to follow.
You tell him what you have seen: a bishop's staff, a book cover, and that the great tooth from the south comes seldom now and costs gold. He has you say it twice. He does not write, so he listens.
He nods. He has a month's sail home in front of him and is in no hurry about one afternoon. The teeth are still on the jetty when you go back to the ship.
What the Finnas pay
In the boat shed he shows you the year's tribute laid out by kind, and tells you what each man of the Finnas owes him. Then he says what he wants.
Each pays by his birth. The best-born pays fifteen marten skins, five reindeer, one bear skin, ten measures of feathers, a coat of bear skin or otter, and two ship's ropes.
Each rope sixty ells. One of whale's hide, one of seal's. Cut round and round the beast in one strip. Pull on it. Harder.
I have six hundred deer, tame, and six more that draw the wild ones in. Also twenty cattle, twenty sheep and twenty pigs. In the south that is a poor man. I know it.
You told me a price before I asked you to buy. That is not how it is done in harbours. I noticed it.
I want one man who has stood in a southern market with one of these in his hand. Take a pair. Show them where teeth are carved. Then tell me what you saw. Not what you were told.
I come down the coast again after midsummer. The king's farm on the Karmsund is on my way. Look for me there.
Take a pair on his trust
Pay him for the pair, and owe nothing
Take the rope and carry only the question
He puts the pair in your hands and a coil of rope on top. No witness, no tally stick. He says the rope is not trade, it is manners, and the teeth are his until he hears what they fetched.
He weighs your silver twice on his own scale and once on yours. The pair is yours now, and he adds a coil of rope, which he says is not trade but manners.
He shrugs and gives you a coil of rope anyway, so that the south may at least pull on something. The question goes with you. The teeth stay in the shed.
The comb-maker's saw
A comb-maker at Sliesthorp works antler from first light to dark. He takes the tooth in both hands and turns it to the light before he says anything.
Horse-whale. I get one in three years, and never a pair. Who sent you?
Look at the broken end. Outside it is white and close, like the best bone. Inside it is clouded, like curds. A carver keeps his figures in the white. So the thick teeth are the dear ones.
The Christians' priests ask for it. They want it white and broad, for the boards of their books. The great tooth from the south does not come any more, they say. I am only told this.
For this pair I give silver to the weight of a hundred and ten pennies, cut and weighed here. A priest's carver on the Rhine would give more, and take until Yule to do it.
The pair is Ohthere's until he has heard what it fetched. He did not say you could not sell it. He said he wanted to know.
Sell him the pair for weighed silver
Pay him to cut a gaming king from the tip
Thank him and keep the pair whole
