He cuts hack silver into the pan until the beam is level, and then puts in one more sliver, for the pair. He carries the teeth to the back of the shed himself and does not let the boy touch them.
He saws a thumb's length off the tip and by evening it is a small king with his hands on his knees and a beard like a spade. The tooth is shorter. The king goes in your purse.
He gives the tooth back slowly. He says that if you change your mind he is here every day but the day they bury him.
A tooth on the reeve's table
Since the king took London the trade is moving inside the old walls. The reeve who sees to the landing has a clerk beside him, and the clerk has seen ivory before. Neither has seen this.
It is not elephant. I have handled elephant, on a bishop's staff. What beast is it, and who kills it?
The king asks every stranger about his own country. Franks, Frisians, Bretons, heathen men too. He would sooner hear a hunter than a flatterer, and he gets more flatterers.
Our carvers cut whale's bone, because there is nothing better to be had. A book board in this would be asked for by every minster in the kingdom, and by two I can think of across the sea.
A heathen from north of everything, you say. Heathen men have come up this river before. They did not come to sell.
This small king is cut from it? Leave him with me until evening. There is a man I want to see him.
A rope of hide that held when the bast parted. The king has ships at sea every summer. Say that part again, slowly.
Ask the king's peace for the Northman to come himself
Ask to be the man who brings the teeth
Ask only what the king's goldsmith would pay

The reeve does not say yes. He has the clerk write that a Frisian asked the king's peace for a Northman of the far north with teeth to sell, and the day. In this town a thing written down is half granted.
The reeve says the king does not much care who brings a thing so long as it comes. He orders four pairs against next year at a good price, and asks no more about the man who hunts them.
The goldsmith is sent for. He names a price, then looks at the tooth again and names a better one. By evening the Strand has heard there is a new kind of ivory, and nobody has any.
The halyard parts
A squall comes down out of a clear sky. The bast halyard strands at the masthead and the yard hangs by what is left of it. The coil of hide rope lies under the thwart.
The steersman looks at the masthead and then at the coil. He says nothing. He is a man with opinions about new rope.
Hide rope wants grease, the Northman said, or it goes slack when it has been wet a long time. It need not be a long time.
Reeve the hide rope and hoist on it
Knot the bast and keep the hide rope to sell
Lower the yard and ride it out

The yard goes up on the dark rope and stays up. The squall leans on it for an hour and goes away. The steersman greases the rope that evening without being asked, which is the nearest he comes to praise.
The knot holds. The sail sets a hand lower than it should for the rest of the passage, and the coil stays dry under the thwart, worth what it was worth.
The knot draws through the block and the yard comes down across the thwarts. A man has a split scalp and nobody has much to say to you. The coil is still under the thwart, quite unharmed.
You get the yard down before it falls and lie to the sea with the sail bundled. It blows itself out by dark. Half a day lost, and the halyard to splice in the morning.
Held at the sound
Ohthere's ship lies under the king's farm with her sail carried ashore. The king's steward says the tribute of the Finnas is the king's to share out, not a Halogalander's to sell.
King Harald has the land now, from the Vik northward. What the Finnas pay, they pay to the man the king names. I have not heard him name this one.
My father took that tribute, and his father. I did not hear that any king came north to help them carry it.
Four ounces of silver for the sound, and he has his sail back. Or he waits for the king, who is at another farm. The king may come before the snow.
You came. Good. Tell me what the tooth fetched. After that, tell me whether you know how a man talks to a steward.
A hundred and ten pennies' weight at Sliesthorp, for one pair. Then a steward's four ounces is not much. I will remember who told me.
You have been in the south with one of those teeth. I would like to know what it is the king lets sail past his own door.
Lay down the four ounces for him
Speak for him before the men of the sound
Tell the steward what the teeth are worth
Wait with him until the steward tires

The steward weighs the silver and has the sail carried down. Ohthere does not thank you. He puts two pairs of teeth in your boat while you are looking the other way, and says the Heaths are five days from Skiringssal and he will be there.

You say that a due is owed on what passes the sound, and a tribute is not a cargo until it is sold. The farmers like it. They pay the steward too. He gives the sail back with a face like a shut door. Ohthere says he will be at the Heaths.

You speak well and in the wrong tongue, and the farmers laugh in the wrong places. The steward halves the due to be rid of the noise, and you pay it. Ohthere says a bad speech for a man is still a speech for him. He will be at the Heaths.

You tell the steward what a comb-maker gives and what a king's goldsmith would. He counts on his fingers and stops. Ohthere's cargo is carried up to the king's shed. Ohthere watches you from his own deck and says nothing at all.

Nine days. Ohthere mends a strap, then every strap. On the tenth day the steward wants the beach for another ship and has the sail carried down unpaid. Ohthere says he will be at the Heaths, and that you wait well for a southerner.
A sail from the islands

Two days out, with Denmark to port, a long ship comes out from behind an island under oars. She has seen two laden hulls and no shields. Ohthere's ship is a bowshot ahead of you, and she is the slower.
Twenty oars or more. They are not hurrying yet.
Ohthere's steersman holds a spear up flat, points it at you and then at the water beside him. It is a question.
Two traders and only one of me. Heave to, and we shall see which of you is the open-handed one.
Close up beside Ohthere and show iron
Run inside the islands where she cannot follow
Heave to and pay them

Two hulls side by side, a spear at every thwart, and Ohthere's men hunt whales for their living. The long ship rows a wide ring round you, twice, and goes back behind her island. Nobody was open-handed.

They come on anyway, and for the time it takes to say a prayer it is oars and axes over the rail. Then they find the hide rope will not cut and the whale hunters will not give way, and they leave with a purse and a bloody nose. You have your own to bind up.
You put the helm over for the gap between two islands where the water goes pale. Ohthere follows your wake without a question. The long ship draws too much, and knows it, and stops.

The gap is narrower than it looked and the wind dies under the land. They come up with you on oars, cheerful, and take what is nearest to hand. Ohthere, who followed you in, loses a bundle of skins and does not mention it.
You heave to and count silver into a shield held out on an oar. The man with the shield bites one piece, nods, and wishes you a fair wind. Ohthere's ship waits a bowshot off until it is done.
At the Heaths

Five days from Skiringssal, and the jetties of the market at the head of the fjord. Ohthere has never been further south than this. A skipper who knows the eastern sea is drinking with him, and a Frisian from the Rhine has already asked the price of the whole cargo.
Five days. Three with Denmark on the left hand and open sea on the right. Two with the islands on the left. I say it so that you can say it after me.
And on the second day a long ship, which went home. You came up beside me when you could have gone on. I counted that too.
I am Wulfstan. I ran from here to Truso in seven days and nights, and the ship was under sail the whole way. Wendland on the right hand as far as the mouth of the Vistula.
The king of the West Saxons will sit a whole evening for a thing like that. I have seen him do it. He asks which hand the land was on, and he knows if you guess.
The Frisian's silver is on the scale now. The English king's is across a sea I do not know. One of those is nearer. I have not decided that nearer is better.
Lay your goods with mine and we share what comes back. Or pilot me for a tenth. Or take the teeth up the Rhine yourself, and I go home. Choose. I have deer to see to.
Lay three hundred pennies in with his goods and sail for England
Pilot him to England for a tenth
Buy the teeth outright for the Rhine
Carry the teeth up the Rhine on shares

Your silver goes into his chest and his hand into yours, in front of Wulfstan, who says he has witnessed worse bargains sober. From here you sail ahead and Ohthere follows. By the fifth evening you understand half of what his men shout at each other.

A tenth, then, and no silver of yours at risk. You sail ahead and he follows, a bowshot astern, the whole way down the Frisian shore. By the fifth evening you understand half of what his men shout at each other.

He weighs your silver and has the teeth carried across to you in two chests, tied with his own rope and his own knot. He sails north the next morning. He says the English king will have to find out about the north some other way.

Two chests come across to your hold, tied with his own knot, and half of what they fetch is to lie for him with the Frisian here by next summer. He sails north in the morning. He does not look like a man who expects to be cheated, which is a hard thing to cheat.
A heathen at the hythe

Ohthere's ship lies off the hythe inside the walls. The reeve will let the teeth land. The priest beside him says a heathen who has not so much as been signed with the cross does not sit down at a Christian king's table.
Let him take the first signing. It is not baptism. It is a cross on the forehead and a few words, and after it he may eat with Christian men. Merchants do it in every northern harbour.
I have been told about this signing. I am told it does no harm. I have not been told that it does my deer any good.
Or a man the town knows swears for him: that he comes in peace, and that any harm he does is paid out of the swearer's purse.
You asked the king's peace for him a year ago. I had it written down. That counts for something, even with a priest.
Or you go in with the teeth and my words. You have heard them often enough. I can mend a strap here as well as anywhere.
Swear for him yourself
Ask him to take the signing
Go in alone with his teeth and his words

You swear it on the reeve's relics: his peace, your purse. The priest says an oath for a heathen is still an oath, and that he will be watching the heathen. Ohthere is to come ashore in three days, when the king sits.
He stands still for it like a horse being shod. Afterwards he asks whether it wears off in salt water. The priest, who has done this before, says only if he wants it to. The king sits in three days.
The teeth go ashore in two chests. Ohthere sits down on his own thwart with a strap across his knee and does not watch you go. The king sits in three days.
He said to his lord
The king sits with a clerk at his elbow and the teeth on the board in front of him. He does not ask the price. He asks how far north the land goes, and whether any man lives beyond the waste.
I wished to know that myself. So I sailed north three days with the waste on the right hand and the open sea on the left. Then I was as far as the whale hunters go. Then three days more.
The Beormas told me many things about their land and the lands about it. I do not know what is true in them, because I did not see it.
Sixty in two days, with five other men. Say the number again for my clerk. He has stopped writing.
Sixty. With five others. I was there.
And the hide rope held when this man's bast parted? Then I want rope before I want teeth.
This small king was cut from one of these teeth, they tell me. I wondered what kind of man brings in the beast he is made of. A quiet one, it seems.
He says 'I do not know' more often than any man I have ever written down. The king likes him for it.
And you brought him. What does a man want, who carries another man's story across the sea?
Ask for your share of the fellowship's goods
Ask for your pilot's tenth
Ask for the king's peace on Ohthere's ships and your own

The king buys every tooth and all the rope, at the goldsmith's second price. Half is yours by the hand-clasp at the Heaths. The reeve is told your ship pays no toll at the hythe, and Ohthere says that if you lay goods with him again he will not count them twice.

The king buys every tooth and all the rope, and Ohthere counts your tenth out on the board himself, to the penny, with the king watching. The reeve is told your ship pays no toll at the hythe. The clerk is still writing when you leave.

The king says that is the first thing anyone has asked him all week that costs him nothing and is worth having. It is granted, for both houses, in his day. Ohthere pays your pilotage in teeth, the thick ones, and a little silver he says is for the oath.
Whose story
You stand before the king with the teeth and a year of another man's words in your head. The clerk has his pen ready. The king asks how far north the land goes, and then he asks who saw it.
You tell it well. Three days, and three days, and the land bending east. Were you in the ship?
Which hand was the land on when it turned south? A man who was there does not stop to think.
Ohthere is sitting on his own thwart off the hythe, a bowshot from this hall, mending a strap.
A year ago you asked the reeve to make you the man who brings the teeth. He is standing by the door, and he remembers it.
Say that Ohthere saw it, and you only carry it
Say that you were in the ship
Ask leave to bring the Northman in on your own oath

You say whose eyes it was. The king nods, and the clerk writes 'Ohthere said' at the head of the leaf, and you tell it as he told it, days and hands. The king buys the teeth, pays your carrying, and frees your ship of toll at the hythe.

You have heard it so often that the hands come right. The king pays like a king and names you his man for the teeth. On the way out you hear him tell the clerk to leave it out of the book: the man knew the price of everything he had seen. Off the hythe a ship from the north is hoisting her sail.

You stop to think. The clerk puts down his pen. The king, quite mildly, has the reeve go down to the hythe and bring up whoever is sitting there. You are paid for the carrying, and you stand by the door while Ohthere tells it, and nobody looks at you.
The king says he would rather have the hunter than the tale of the hunter, and gives you two days. You go down to the hythe to tell a man who is mending a strap that he is wanted after all.
Tooth for the altar

Cologne was burned by Northmen not many years back and is building again. The archbishop's carver works in a shed against the cathedral wall. He is planing the old figures off a tablet older than the city's walls remember, because he has nothing new to cut.
This was a consul's writing tablet once, in the Romans' time. I take a heathen off it and put a saint on. Every year the tablets get thinner, and so do the saints.
And this is from a whale that walks? I do not care if it is from a cow. It cuts like the true thing. The white is thin. I can work in thin. I have had practice.
Northmen's goods, in this city. The archbishop will ask whether it was hunted or stolen. Hunted is acceptable.
You meant it for the English king, and he is dead. Kings die. Altars need covering every year.
Bring me ten pairs a year, and I keep a man in this city to hold them for you. Or sell me these and be gone. Or give the best pair to Saint Peter, and see what the archbishop gives back.
Agree to bring ten pairs a year
Sell your own teeth at the carver's price
Give the best pair to Saint Peter's altar

The clerk writes it and the carver makes his mark under it with the point of a graver. Your share is counted out in good pennies. A man of the archbishop's household will keep your chests in the city from now on, and the carver puts the consul's tablet back on the shelf with some respect.

They were your teeth and the carver knows it, so he pays what a thing is worth when nobody else has one. The archbishop's man will keep your chests here, and the Frisian at the Heaths sends word that the plot beside his is yours if you mean to do this again.

The best pair goes on the altar on a white cloth. The archbishop's answer comes next morning: a fair price for the rest, and a writing that says the bearer is Saint Peter's man and to be let alone on the river. The carver is already drawing on the tooth with a nail.
The king's share

A year on, the steward at the king's farm has a shed full of teeth and rope that came down the coast in the king's name. Ohthere's ship did not come with it. The steward has not forgotten who told him what it was worth.
The king was pleased. He said a tribute nobody counts is a tribute somebody else is spending.
The Halogalander still has his deer. He has the king's leave to keep them. He does not have leave to sell the Finnas' rope.
The king wants a man who knows the southern markets. He gives silver and his friendship to such a man. Or one of his own ships, sound, eighteen winters old. Which?
Or if your conscience is sore, say so. I will show you the sound and its rocks, and you may sail it without paying me, and we say no more about the Halogalander's share.
On the ridge above the farm the old ship mounds stand in the grass. The men in them took their due from this sound as well.
Carry the king's teeth south each year
Take the ship
Ask that Ohthere keep the selling of his own share

The steward counts out the king's thanks and gives you a tally for eight pairs against next summer. You are the king's guest on this coast now, and may say so. North of here there is a man with six hundred deer who also knows your name.

She lies on the rollers below the farm: clinker, pine above and oak below, a patch at the turn of the bilge and nothing else to say against her. The steward adds a purse so that you can rig her. It is hide rope in the shed, as it happens, and it is the king's.

The steward looks at you as at a man who has sold a horse and wants to pay for its hay. Then he shrugs. Ohthere may sell his own share at his own risk, and the king's goes by the king's men. He pays you the king's thanks all the same, and takes you through the sound at slack water, rock by rock.
The king's book

A priest who copies books for the king has a quire open on his desk: the history of the world by Orosius, put into English. Where the old Roman had little to say about the north, something has been added, or has not.
'Ohthere said to his lord, King Alfred, that he lived northmost of all Northmen.' It goes on for three leaves. Teeth, rope, deer, what the Finnas owe, the days to the Heaths.
No. It does not say who brought him. It does not name his ship either. The book is about the world, not about who held the door.
Here Wulfstan tells of the Este and his seven days to Truso. Of the far north the book says what the Romans said: that it is waste, and cold, and that is all.
A merchant told the king a tale of the north once, with teeth to show for it. The king had it left out. He said the man knew the price of everything he had seen.
They say the carvers at Cologne have a new white tooth to cut. Nobody here has seen it. It would be a fine thing for the boards of a book like this.
The king of the Northmen sells teeth now, I am told, through his stewards. Stewards do not tell stories. It is a pity. The king would have liked to hear one.
Pay for a copy of the seafarer's leaves
Ask for the passage on a leaf, with your name at the foot
Thank him and go down to the ship

He copies Wulfstan's voyage for you in a clear hand, the lands to starboard and the lands to port, and blots it with sand. He says seamen are easy to copy. They never use a long word where a wind will do.

He will not put a mark in the king's book. But he writes the opening of the passage on a clean leaf, and at the foot, small, that a merchant of your house brought the Northman over the sea. He says the foot of a leaf is where the truth usually ends up.
He turns the leaf back and bends to his ruling. Down at the hythe the tide is making, and nobody there has read a book or needs to.
A Frisian has shown the reeve at London a tooth as long as a man's forearm, from a small whale the heathen men hunt north of all dwellings. The goldsmiths are asking where more can be had.
At the king's farm on the Karmsund the steward held a ship of Halogaland with the Finnas' tribute aboard, and asked whose it was to sell.
This year a Northman from the far north sat with King Alfred and told him how the land lies and who lives there. The king had it written down, and bought his teeth.
A Frisian merchant has brought the king whale's teeth from the north and is to bring more each year. He says he has sailed further north than any man.
The archbishop's carver at Cologne has a new white tooth from the north to work, and a Frisian house brings it up the Rhine.
The tribute of the Finnas comes down the coast in King Harald's name now, and his steward on the Karmsund sells the teeth.

A timber jetty at Skiringssal on a grey late-summer afternoon: a tall weather-dark Northman of fifty in a marten cloak stands over a row of long yellow tusks and coils of dark hide rope laid on the planks, his pine-built ship behind him, the wooded shore of the Vik beyond.

Inside a boat shed, light falling through the open seaward end: the tribute laid out by kind on the sand, marten skins, a bear skin, sacks of down, reindeer hides, coils of rope; Ohthere holds one end of a hide rope and the merchant pulls on the other.

A comb-maker's open-fronted shed at Sliesthorp in low morning light, antler offcuts ankle-deep on the floor: a Danish craftsman holds a walrus tusk up to the light with both hands to show its broken end, a small folding scale on the bench beside his saw.

A table under a lean-to against London's old Roman wall, an overcast day: one long tusk lies on the board between an English reeve with a staff and a tonsured clerk bending close to it, the Thames and beached boats seen through a gap in the wall.

A small open boat heeled under a sudden squall in bright hard light: the yard hanging askew from a stranded halyard at the masthead, the crew looking up, and one man's hand on a dark coil of hide rope under the thwart.

The beach below the king's farm on the Karmsund at midsummer evening: a northern ship drawn up with a bare mast, two men carrying her rolled sail up the slope, a steward with an arm ring barring the way to Ohthere, and two grassed ship mounds on the ridge behind.

Open water among low Danish islands at dawn, a light breeze: a long ship under twenty oars coming out from behind an island toward two laden trading hulls, a man in the nearer hull holding a spear up flat as a signal.

The jetties at the head of the Schlei on a clear evening: Ohthere and an English skipper with a string of rough amber sit on chests with ale horns, two roped chests of tusks between them, a Frisian in a short cloak waiting a few paces off with a scale in his hand.

The hythe inside London's river wall on a windy morning: Ohthere's ship lying off on a line, he himself seated on a thwart; on the shingle a priest with a small cross raised, a reeve, and the merchant between them with one hand lifted to swear.

A timber hall by firelight: a slight, intent king in his forties leaning forward over a board where tusks and a coil of rope lie, Ohthere standing before him counting on his fingers, a clerk at the king's elbow with his pen stopped above the leaf, the merchant at the edge of the light.

The same hall by day, shutters open on the river: the merchant alone before the king with two chests of tusks, the clerk looking up with his pen ready, the reeve by the door; through the door, small and far off, a ship at the hythe with one man sitting in her.

A carver's shed built against the wall of Cologne cathedral, scaffolding and new timber above, noon light: an old Frankish carver with a plane in one hand and a worn Roman ivory tablet in the other stares at a walrus tusk on his bench, a clerk behind him with a wax tablet.

A storehouse door standing open at the king's farm on the Karmsund, a bright cold day a year later: tusks stacked like firewood and rope hanging in coils inside, the steward counting silver onto a barrel head, an old clinker ship on rollers below and the two mounds on the ridge.

A copying desk by a small window in winter light: an English priest with ink-stained fingers holds a quire open and points to a line with his pen, the merchant, older now, reading over his shoulder, a ruled blank leaf and a pot of sand at the desk's edge.
A second keel

Radbern has gone up the Seine to the fair of Saint-Denis every October for twenty years, with a ship and a boat. This summer the boat is firewood. He stands on the dam and looks at yours for a long time before he speaks.
Twenty Octobers I have drunk the saint's health in the saint's own wine. I would like to make it twenty-one.
My ship carries the wine. But the river above Rotomagus is all bends and shoals, and a ship wants a small boat ahead of her that can turn. Yours can turn.
And the kings have made it up. A merchant is to have his old protection again on both sides of the water. The English will be on the Seine this year with wool, so cloth must be there first.
Cloth up, wine down. Carry my best bolts going and my best casks coming, and take a share. We leave after Michaelmas and we are home by Martinmas, if God and the bungs hold.
I cut the tally, not him. He has never brought home the same number he took out. He says casks leak.
Join hands: sail as his second keel for a share
Sail in his company, but for your own purse
Not this year. Ask him what cloth fetches at the fair

Aldburg splits a hazel stick down its length and gives you the half with your notches. Four bolts of his best cloth go under your thwarts. You are to be at Rotomagus for the flood tides after Michaelmas, and at the saint's strand for his Mass.
He shrugs. A man may sail beside another man. He pays you twenty pennies to carry two bolts and tells you the day: the saint's strand, for Saint Denis's Mass, nine days into October.

He tells you anyway, since it costs him nothing: the monks and the vine-dressers pay a fifth over the Dorestat price for good Frisian cloth while the fair lasts, because every man there has wine and none of them has a cloak. He will ask you again next summer.
The tide and the toll

Under the south wall of Rotomagus the boats for the fair lie in a row, waiting for the flood to carry them up. Frisians, men of Hamwic, a boat of monks. The king's toll man works along the row with a tally and a boy.
Cloth going up, wine coming down. Every autumn the same, and every autumn somebody tells me his bolts are a gift for his sister. The king takes his part of what goes up to be sold.
That boat pays nothing. Saint Germain's men, with the king's writing. If you had a saint you could try it. You have a sister.
Leofstan, of Hamwic. Wool, mostly. We were shut out of here for six years while two kings argued about a wedding. I mean to make up all six this month.
Half this row will be pilgrims when he reaches them. A staff, a bundle, a sad face. The king has written that true pilgrims go free and false ones pay. He did not write how to tell.
From here to the saint the river goes five days to cover two. Sit a tide with me and I will tell you where it lies to you.
Show the cloth and pay the king's toll
Put the bolts under a pilgrim's bundle and say you are bound for the saint
Lie over a tide and have the river man tell you the loops
Six pennies. He notches his tally and yours, and says that a man who shows his cloth going up will find the toll lighter coming down.
He looks at the bundle, at your face, and at the long row still ahead of him. He blesses your journey without warmth and moves on. The Englishman, two boats down, has been a pilgrim since noon.
The boy lifts the bundle with one finger. Underneath is a great deal of cloth for a penitent. The toll man takes twice the toll, twelve pennies, and says the saint will be told.

You lose the flood and gain the river. He names every loop, the island where the stream splits, the bank that was not there last year, and the abbey you will see on your left hand a day before you see the city. By the time he has finished, the toll man has gone up the row and not come back.
Saint Denis's Mass

The strand below the abbey is boats from the willows to the island. Bells, smoke, carts of casks coming down from the vineyards. The abbey's man takes the toll at the water. Behind him a man in the count's colours is counting heads.
There. The saint's church, the saint's strand, the saint's toll man. For a month everything here is the saint's, down to the mud. It saves argument.
They say the church has a hundred windows and one. A man of ours began to count them once. He stopped when he thought of the price of the glass.
From the saint's Mass until the market ends, every toll in this country is Saint Denis's: boats, landing, carts, pack beasts, wheels, bridges, gates. You pay me, and you pay once.
And four pennies a head to the count, for every free man who comes to trade. It was paid in his grandfather's day. Four men: sixteen pennies.
A slave pays five. He must first swear that he is a slave. I have never understood why more men do not think of it, and then I remember the penny.
My father paid that. Then the merchants stopped coming, the monks went to King Pippin, and the king struck it down. Before I was born. This one is hoping we are all too young to know.
Pay the sixteen pennies for your four heads
Say aloud, before the abbey's man, that King Pippin struck this tax down
Pay nobody yet. Walk up to the abbey gate and ask whose toll it is
Sixteen pennies. The count's man is pleasant about it. The abbey's toll man watches the silver go into the wrong purse and writes nothing down, which with him is a way of remembering.

You say it loudly enough for the next six boats. The abbey's man says that he has seen the writing, with the old king's mark, and that it is kept in a chest not two hundred paces from here. The count's man remembers business in the city. The abbey halves your toll for the month.
You say it, but you say the wrong king. The count's man corrects you kindly, takes eight pennies as a friend, and goes on down the strand. The abbey's man was talking to a carter and heard nothing.

It costs you the first day of the fair. The porter sends for the cellarer, the cellarer listens with his head on one side, and says the toll is the saint's and nobody else's, and that he will be glad to know which of the count's men thinks otherwise. He asks your name, and your boat's.
The cellarer's wine

The cloth is sold, and your part of it is in your purse. In the abbey's long storehouse Brother Waldric, the cellarer, walks you between three rows of casks. Radbern has bought for his ship already. The casks for your boat he leaves to you.
This row is the wine of this year, pressed at Saint Remigius's Mass. Cheap. That row is last year's, and has stopped arguing with itself. Dear. The third row is the lord abbot's and is not for sale.
Listen. The new wine is still working. Put your ear there. Leave its bung loose until Martinmas or it will open the cask for you, between two staves, at night.
And any wine: keep the cask full and keep it still. An empty hand's breadth under the bung is where vinegar begins. More wine is spoiled by rowing than by years.
You are the one who spoke about the saint's toll. The lord abbot heard. There are two casks of his own that want carrying north, to be paid for when they are sold. He does not offer that to pilgrims.
Three of the cheap or two of the dear. I have lost money both ways. Choose, and then you cannot blame me.
A book-bishop of the English made a riddle on this very thing. Take it with you. If you cannot answer it by the time you are home, ask the cask.
The wine of this year: cheap, three casks, still working
Last year's wine: dear, two casks, settled
The abbot's own casks, under the abbey's mark, on trust
Three casks of the year's wine go down to the strand on a cart. They tick and whisper in the boat like something asleep. The bungs are loose, and stay loose until you decide otherwise.
Two casks of last year's wine, quiet as stones. The cellarer drives the bungs himself and says they may stay driven.

Two casks with the abbey's mark burned into the head. Old wine, settled, better than anything on the strand. Brother Waldric writes your name on a strip of parchment and puts it where he will find it again.
The partner's casks

Twelve days into the fair Radbern does not come down to the strand. He is in the hospice at the abbey gate, on straw, with a fever. His steersman has the ship. His tally and his best casks are in your boat.
It comes with the fair every year. Too many men, one well. Some are up in a week. Some we carry across the yard.
The stick. Take the stick. Aldburg has the other half. The casks under your thwarts are the best I bought. Put them on her floor. Not on the dam. On her floor.
We joined hands. I do not have to say the rest.
You sail for your own purse. I knew that when I put my casks in your boat. I am asking all the same.

A word, away from the door. Sick men's wine is hard to carry and easy to quarrel over. I will give two hundred and forty pennies for his casks today, on this strand. His daughter gets silver, which does not leak.
If you mean to wait for him, know what you are waiting into. After Martinmas the wind goes round to the north-east and the river smokes in the mornings.
Take his tally and his casks, and sail for Dorestat while the weather holds
Stay by him until the fever turns, and sail late
Sell his casks to the Englishman here for ready silver

You put the stick inside your shirt. He nods, and turns his face to the wall to save his strength. The brother says they will do what is done. You sail on the morning stream with the weather still soft.

Nine nights. You fetch water, since the brothers have forty others, and one of them teaches you the words they say over the cup, to pass the time. On the tenth morning Radbern asks what day it is and whether the bungs are loose. You sail after Martinmas, late, into a north-east wind.

Two hundred and forty pennies, counted twice on a cask head. The Englishman's men roll the casks along the strand. The tally stick is still inside your shirt, and the silver is his daughter's until you stand in her house and say otherwise.
The cooper under the wall
At Rotomagus a cooper works along the boats under the wall with a mallet in one hand and a jug in the other. He raps each of your casks with his knuckle and listens, like a man at a door.
Hear that? That one says yes. This one says maybe. A cask should sound like a full man, not a hungry one. You have lost a hand's breadth since the saint.
And this is this year's. Still talking. Whatever you do at sea, do not hammer that bung home because it frightens you. It is meant to frighten you.
Settled wine. Good. Fill it, drive the bung, and then leave it alone. It has finished with the world. Let it be.
Twelve pennies, I fill and hoop the lot. Or thirty for the winter and I come with you. I have made casks for the sea all my life and never seen where they go.
Have him fill the casks to the bung and drive the hoops
Hire him for the winter: he wants to see the sea
Keep your pennies. Ask him what the English boats said of the price
He fills each cask from his jug until it wets the bung, and drives the willow hoops down a finger with the mallet. Rapped again, they all say yes.

Ursio comes aboard with his mallet, his jug and a bag of hoops, fills every cask before he will sit down, and is sick over the side before the city is out of sight. He goes on rapping the casks between times.

He does not hold it against you. The Hamwic boats came in on yesterday's flood, he says, and their men were saying that over the sea wine pays a fifth more than it did, and will until Christmas, since the lords there have six dry years to wash out.
Frost on the bung

In the night the wind goes north-east and hard. By morning there is ice on the sheets and a white rim on the gunwale. The casks work against their chocks with every sea, and one of them weeps at the bung.
She is weeping. There. I can stop it with the mallet, or we can slow down and coddle them. Or we run and trust the chocks.
It is the new wine. The monk said loose until Martinmas. He was standing on a stone floor when he said it.
It is the settled wine. The monk said a driven bung would do it no harm. Shaking would.
We are a fortnight behind every other boat. I say that as a fact, not a complaint.
Shorten sail, bed the casks in the cloaks and ease the bungs
Carry all sail and get in before the frost does
Drive every bung home with the mallet and hold your course
A slow, cold day. The men give up their cloaks to the casks and say what they think of wine. The weeping stops. Nothing moves under the thwarts but the boat.
She carries it. The chocks hold, the coast goes by, and you are inside before the frost has made up its mind. The men are pleased with themselves and say so.

A sea comes over the quarter and a chock goes. For half a watch the casks roll a hand's breadth each way before they are wedged again. One man has a crushed foot. Whatever had settled in the wine is all through it now.
The mallet stops the weeping at once. The casks are tight as drums and silent. Whether that silence is good news depends on what is inside them.
The first cup

The first cask is broached on the quay with half the landing looking on. The wine runs clear and dark and smells of the stone cellar it came from. A lord's steward holds the cup. A priest stands behind him and looks at it.
That is wine. I had forgotten. For six weeks I have been pouring my lord something a Rhine man swore was wine, and my lord has been very patient with me.
He keeps Christmas with forty at his table. Name me a price before somebody from the other bank does.
It is Lent, and wine is all the comfort a fasting house is allowed. Name me a price.
We have said Mass since All Saints with wine I would not offer to a creditor. I do not ask a gift. I only mention it, in your hearing, twice.
Sell the fleet's casks on the quay today
Sell half, and take the steward's order for more at his price
Give one cask to the church for the Mass, and sell the rest

By evening the fleet's casks are gone and wine is a little cheaper on this quay than it was at dawn. Your part is a hundred and eighty pennies. The casks under your own thwarts are still yours to sell.
Half goes on the quay, a hundred and ten pennies to you. For the rest the steward cuts a tally: three casks of Seine wine within a hundred and twenty days, at half as much again as the quay pays.

One cask is rolled up to the church door, and the priest walks beside it the whole way with his hand on the staves. The rest sells the better for it: a hundred and fifty pennies to you. Your name is said at the altar on Sunday, with the saint's.
The first cup
The first cask is broached on the quay with half the landing looking on. The steward tastes. He holds it in his mouth for a moment, looking at you, and then looks about for somewhere to spit.
I have a crock of herrings at home that would thank you for this. My lord would not.
Look at the staves. Started, here and here. Somebody drove a bung on working wine. It let the air in to get its own back.
And thick as a ditch. This has been rolled about like a drunk at a wedding and never filled after.
I will take it. Not as wine. Fish do not mind. Forty-five pennies for the lot, and you tell nobody I paid so much.
Call it vinegar and sell it to the salter as vinegar
Mend it with honey and pepper and sell it up the coast as spiced wine
Pour a cup for anyone who asks, and say whose hand was on the bung
Forty-five pennies. The salter's boys roll it away. It is honest vinegar, sold as vinegar, and there is nothing more to be said for it.

Ten pennies of honey and a pinch of pepper, by an old Roman rule. Three landings up the coast, where nobody saw the steward's face, it sells as spiced wine for a hundred and forty. It is even quite good, warm.
Honey and pepper, by an old Roman rule. The first buyer is the steward's cousin. You get twenty pennies from a man who wants it for his horses, and the steward gets the story.

You pour for whoever asks and say plainly what was done to it and who did it. People pay a little out of kindness, thirty pennies in all, and for the cask wood. The steward says he will buy from you next year, to see whether a man learns.
The two halves of the tally
Radbern's house, on the second dam. Aldburg clears the table, lays her half of the hazel stick on it with the notches up, and waits for yours.
The steersman came in two days ago. My father died at Martinmas. They put him in the monks' ground, in a plaster box that others have lain in before him. He would have asked what they charged.
I am told you fetched my water for nine nights. I do not remember it. Aldburg says that is no reason not to believe it.
They say on the dams that the wine kept. So there is something to reckon.
They say on the dams that the wine turned. Then we reckon what there is. A tally is for bad years too. Mostly for bad years.
The steersman says our best casks went along the strand to an Englishman, with my father on the straw. I would like to hear what they fetched. From you.
Your half.
Lay your half beside hers, and every cask and penny with it
Count the Englishman's two hundred and forty pennies onto her table
Give her a short reckoning: casks leak, and the dead keep no tally

The two halves close like a mouth. She counts the notches with her thumbnail, twice, and then counts out your part: a hundred and twenty pennies. She says it is the first year the stick has come home the same length as it went.

You count it out in twelves. She watches every one. When the last is down she pushes a hundred back across the table for your part, and says an Englishman's silver is as good as wine, and keeps better.
You tell her that casks leak. She says her father always said so. She does not ask to see your half of the stick. When you have gone she sits a long while with hers, counting notches.
The next October

Saint Denis's Mass again: the same bells, the same strand, the same mud. This year three people want your boat. Radbern's ship lies by the willows, the cellarer is coming down the path from the gate, and the Englishman is already waving.
I came up with the ship myself. The house needs a small boat that can turn, and a master who brings a stick home whole. I know of one.
I counted the notches. I say nothing more on the saint's day. There is room on this strand for both of us, a good way apart.

The lord abbot has casks for a city over the sea, and a letter for the king's reeve there. He says the saint was once promised a landing place on that strand, and that promises to saints do not die with kings. He wants a boat that can turn, and a master who can be quiet.
I heard about last year's cargo. Everyone spoils one. The lord abbot says a man who has spoiled one is safer than a man who has not yet.

Or do it my way. Your silver and mine in one purse, no old man's stick, no monk's letter. I have found a cellar at Rotomagus with a door on the strand. Buy here, lay it down there, and sell it when we like and not when the weather likes.
Sail with Radbern's house again
Take the abbot's casks and his letter over the sea to Lundenwic
Buy for yourself this year, with the Englishman's silver beside yours
Aldburg splits a new stick. The buying takes a fortnight. She says there will be something to say when the fair closes, and that you should be on the strand to hear it.

Two casks with the abbey's mark, and a letter sewn in oiled linen that you are to give into the reeve's own hand on the Strand at Lundenwic, before Lent if the sea allows. The cellarer blesses the boat. He has not done that before.
You buy beside Leofstan, cask for cask, and argue over every one. Aldburg watches from the willows and does not come over. He will wait for you at Rotomagus on the way down, he says, with the key.
Hands on the strand
The fair is closing. The stalls are coming down, the strand is half empty, and the casks are stowed in the ship and in your boat. Radbern's house offers you its hand before the other shipmen.
Twenty-two Octobers. I am too old for a twenty-third at the steering oar. Aldburg has the head for it and you have the boat. I will sit in the stern and tell you both what you are doing wrong.
My father lies up there by the church wall. I would like him to hear this, so I will say it loudly.

One reckoning for the ship and the boat. Each bears the other's fire and wreck. No oath: the king does not like merchants swearing to one another, and a hand given before witnesses has always been enough on the dams.
You spoiled a cargo and came and said so. I have known men who never spoiled one and whom I would not trust with a bucket.

The cellarer tells me the Frisians and the English wish to ask me something together. That has not happened before in my time. I am a Lombard: I know what it is to be a stranger at another man's fair. Ask.
Join hands: one reckoning, two boats, no oath
Join hands, and go with the English to ask the abbot for a strand of your own
Take your share in silver and stay your own man

Hands are joined on the strand before nine shipmen and the abbey's toll man, who was passing. Your part of two Octobers comes to nine hundred pennies. From now on the ship and the boat keep one tally, and you know the river from the sea to the saint as well as any Frisian living.

Hands are joined; then Frisians and English go up to the gate together, which the porter has never seen. The abbot hears them out. He has it written: the strand from the willows to the island is for the men from over the sea while the fair lasts, a plot above it for their casks, and the toll taken by the keel, once, and not by the cask. Fifteen hundred pennies is your part of the two years. It is the first time the merchants of this fair have had anything of the saint's in writing.

You thank her and take silver: eleven hundred pennies for two Octobers. She says the offer does not spoil, unlike some things. The boats go down the river together, as Frisian boats have every autumn since anyone's grandfather, and part at the sea.
The saint's landing place

On the Strand at Lundenwic the king's reeve has the abbot's letter read to him twice by a clerk of Saint Paul's. He holds a cup of the abbot's wine while he listens, and by the second reading it is empty.

The abbot greets the reeve. He says that the late king, of good memory, promised Saint Denis a landing place in this port, and that he trusts the promise is remembered here as it is there. He sends wine. He names the bearer as a man to be believed.
The late king promised a great many things to a great many saints, and told me about none of them. I witness every sale on this strand. I witnessed no such gift.
It is very good wine. I say so freely. It does not make the letter truer. It makes me more willing to wish that it were.

I can do this much. There is an empty plot above the tide line. If a man I know stands surety for the dues, before witnesses, I can let it to the saint, and the king can make it a gift or not when he hears. I know you. I do not know the abbot.

The abbot's last lines are for the bearer. If there is a landing place, he is to keep it. If there is none, he may ask the abbot's writing for himself at the fair, or take a carrier's wage. The abbot says he is to choose with his head.
Stand surety yourself: the plot for the saint, and you its keeper
Leave the plot to the kings. Ask the abbot's writing for yourself at the fair
Sell the wine, carry the silver back, and take a carrier's wage

Sixty pennies go on ale for the witnesses and a gift the reeve does not look at. Posts are driven above the tide line. From this winter Saint Denis has a landing place at Lundenwic, and it is true because you made it so; you keep it, sell the abbey's wine from it, and take your part, thirteen hundred pennies in the first season. You owe the saint a cask a year for ever, and the abbot can count.

You tell the reeve that plots are for kings to give. He is relieved, and buys the wine. At the next fair the abbot has it written that you trade as Saint Denis's own merchant and pay no toll there. Nine hundred pennies is your part of the wine. The landing place stays a thing the abbey says it was promised.

The wine sells on the Strand in an afternoon. You carry the silver back across the sea, short by nothing, and the cellarer counts out a carrier's wage, six hundred pennies, and shows you a dry corner of the storehouse that is yours to use. He says the lord abbot had hoped for more, and expected this.
A cellar under the wall

At Rotomagus the Englishman unlocks a vaulted cellar under the south wall: old stone, dry, cold, with a door on the strand. Three berths down lies Radbern's ship, and her steersman is watching you both go in.

Roman, the man says, or older. It has kept something cold for five hundred years. It may as well be ours. Wine laid here in November can go over the sea at Candlemas, when the others have none left to sell.
Your boat this side, mine on the Hamwic side, the cellar between. Half and half. I do not swear. I pay.
She counted the notches. She told me to say nothing to you, so I am saying that she told me.
So you go alone. She said you would, sooner or later. She said to wish you a dry cellar, and she meant most of it.
The house has a ship and no master. A woman cannot take her up this river every autumn on a hired steersman's word. If somebody offered silver for the hull, she would have to listen.
Take the cellar with the Englishman, half and half
Buy the dead man's ship from his daughter, at a price she cannot refuse
Take the cellar, and send Aldburg a third of the first winter unasked

The key is cut in two patterns. The first winter's wine, sold at Candlemas over the sea, brings you eight hundred pennies. Radbern's ship still comes up the river in October. Her people do not berth near you, and nobody on the strand asks why.

Four hundred pennies for a sea ship worth several times that. The steersman carries the offer home and carries back her mark. The ship is yours, with the cellar to fill her from. Radbern's house sells its place on the dam before spring. On the strand at the next fair the Frisians make room for you, and no more than room.

You take the cellar, and at Candlemas you send a third of your winter down the coast to the second dam, with no message. Six hundred pennies remain to you. In October her steersman lays the ship alongside your boat on the saint's strand, as if it had always been so.
Radbern's house on the second dam at Dorestat sails with a second keel now, on one tally.
At the fair of Saint-Denis the abbot has given the men from over the sea a strand of their own in writing, and takes his toll there by the keel.
Saint Denis of the Franks has a landing place on the Strand at Lundenwic. A Frisian keeps it and sells the abbey's wine there.
Radbern's daughter has sold her father's ship, and the house's place on the second dam is for sale.

A timber dam head at Dorestat on a late summer evening: a grey-bearded Frisian shipman in a long cloak looks down into a small open boat; behind him a young woman holds a split hazel stick; a broken boat lies hauled out on the bank.

A row of small ships under the grey Roman wall of Rotomagus at slack water in autumn mist: a toll man with a tally and a boy works along them; in one boat a man sits very still with a pilgrim's staff and a large bundle.

The crowded river strand below the long church of Saint-Denis on a bright October morning: boats drawn up side by side, carts of casks, stalls, smoke; in front a tonsured toll man and a Frank in a short cloak each hold out a hand to the same merchant.
Inside a long stone storehouse lit from one door: three rows of casks; a stout monk with keys at his belt bends with his ear to a cask and one finger raised; two merchants wait behind him.

A low hospice room at the abbey gate by rushlight: an old Frisian on straw presses half a hazel stick into a younger man's hand; in the doorway, against the grey day, an Englishman stands with a purse.

Under the wall of Rotomagus on a cold clear day: a wiry cooper kneels in a small boat with his ear near a cask and his knuckle raised to rap it, a mallet and a jug beside him, willow hoops over his shoulder.

A small open boat running under a reefed sail in a steep grey winter sea at dawn: ice on the ropes, three casks lashed amidships, a man crouched over one with a mallet, looking up at the steersman for the word.
A winter quay with a small crowd: a cask on its side with a spigot, dark wine running into a cup; a well-dressed steward drinks with his eyes shut; a priest behind him leans in to look.
The same winter quay and crowd: the steward holds the cup at arm's length with his mouth twisted; a cask with two sprung staves; at the edge a man in a salt-stained apron counts on his fingers.

A Frisian house by the hearth in winter: a bare table, half a notched hazel stick lying on it; a young woman sits with her hands folded, looking up at the merchant in the doorway who holds the other half.

The strand of Saint-Denis again in October sun: the merchant stands by his small boat; from the left a Frisian woman by a ship, from the path a monk with keys, from the right an Englishman with his arm raised, all three looking at him.

The emptying strand at the close of the fair under a low November sky, stalls coming down: a man and a woman clasp hands over a cask head before a half-ring of shipmen; the abbey church stands behind.

The open beach at Lundenwic on a winter afternoon, ships drawn up on the shingle: an English reeve with a silver cup, a young clerk reading from a strip of parchment, the merchant waiting, two casks with a burned mark at their feet.

A low arched door in the foot of the Roman wall of Rotomagus, open on a dark vaulted cellar: an Englishman holds up a key to the merchant; down the strand behind them a steersman on a larger ship watches with folded arms.
A man on a hatch board
Two fishermen are carrying a man up the bank on a hatch board. He is alive, blue to the lips, and he will not let go of the board.
We took him off the north point at first light. He had walked the sand all night with that board under his arm. He says he is a steersman. He was steering something.

Hunfrith. I had the steering oar of the abbess's ship, of Thanet. Lead and cloth for this river, and six for Rome who paid their passage. Ealdred was master. He is on the banks now with the lead on top of him.

We had the emperor's fire behind us and lost it in the murk, as you do. Then a fire ahead, low. Ealdred said it was the monks on the saint's hill, burning furze for us. The river is north of the saint's hill. So he put her north of the fire.
It was not the hill. It was two leagues south of the hill, on the bare sand. North of that fire there is no river. There are the banks.
He should say that more quietly on this bank.
Have him carried to the guest hall at Saint Josse, and hear all of it
Give him your second cloak and eight pennies, and hear all of it
Ask the fishermen first what they make of it
A wreck is a wreck. Go about your trade

The brothers put him by the fire with a bowl of pulses and he tells it twice, the same both times, which is how you know a true account from a good one. Nine in the crew and six pilgrims. He saw three men wade ashore to the south, toward the fire. He went north, away from it, and cannot say why.

He puts the cloak on over the wet and counts the pennies without meaning to, like any steersman. Then he tells it: nine in the crew, six for Rome, a fire on the wrong sand. Three men went ashore to the south. He says he will not forget the cloak, and seamen say that less often than landsmen do.
Gundbert looks at the river for a while. He says the alehouse is a better place for that question than the bank, and that he will be there after the tide.
They carry him on up the bank. By evening the long street knows that English cloth will be cheap this month, and nobody says why.
The custom of the strand
Gundbert the fisherman has the end of the bench nearest the door. He talks into his cup, so that it could be said afterwards he was talking to the ale.
What the sea lays on the sand is the lord's. That is not a law anyone made. It is like the tide. A third to the people who find it and carry it up, two parts to the hall.
Men too, if nobody on that shore speaks for them. A stranger on a strand has no kin and no lord. He has his keep to pay, and the keep is counted by the one who feeds him.
The Englishman's ship is the third on those banks since the saint's fire first had a brother. Before that, one in ten years.

It began after the wet summer, when the corn rotted standing and the cattle died. That winter the south sand ate lead and cloth and Rhine wine, and nobody there buried a child. I do not say more than that.

A Breton pedlar walked the south sand at night last year asking who kept the fire. He was found in the next river with his pack still on him. Nothing was taken. That is how you are meant to know it was not thieves.
Fill his cup and ask how the banks lie south of the river
Ask who holds the south strand
You have heard enough. Thank him

He draws it in spilt ale. Three banks like the fingers of a hand laid on the table, and between the second and third a gut with two fathoms in it at half tide. 'A boat your size can lie in there all night and be thought a seal. Nothing bigger can. Do not tell me why you asked.'

'Odalric. The emperor's vassal, for his service, from the river to the next river. He is at the palace half the year and knows nothing. His steward Adalwin is on the sand before the gulls are and knows everything. Ask the one what the other knows and you will have two answers and both sworn.'
He nods to the cup. On your way out the woman of the house says, to nobody, that Gundbert has a brother on the south sand and has not spoken to him in two winters.
The evening ebb
You can drop down the river on the evening ebb and lie off the south sand for a night. Hunfrith asks to come. He says he would like to see it from a ship that is not sinking.

North, there. A hand above the water, steady, a little red. That is the emperor's fire at Bononia. It does not move and it does not flicker much. A man can trust it for exactly as long as he can see it.
Now the murk comes off the land and it is gone. This is the hour. A master counts in his head and looks for the next thing he knows.

And there. Low, on the sand, where there is no hill and no house. It burns bright and then dull, the way a fire does when it is fed with something wet. I thought so that night and said nothing, because he was the master.
The old man's gut should open under us about here. If he drew it right.
Anchor well off and watch it till dawn
Creep in with the lead and fix which dune it burns on
Lie in the gut between the banks, close enough to count the men
It is a fire on a beach. Stay in the river

It burns till the tide turns and then somebody lets it die. No ship comes. At first light there is a smear of smoke on the dunes and, north of it, the ribs of the abbess's ship standing out of the sand with carts round her like flies. You have seen the fire. You could not swear to the dune.

Three fathoms, two, two, and the fire comes clear: an iron pan on legs, set on the seaward face of the third dune south of a wreck-post, and a man beside it with a shovel. You have it lined up with a notch in the dunes behind. You could find it again blind, and you could say where it is on oath.

Two fathoms, then the keel is on sand with the ebb still running. You spend the night aground on the outer bank with the fire looking at you, and float off at dawn, wet and bruised and seen. You have seen the fire. So has the fire seen you.

Gundbert drew it right. You lie in two fathoms with a bank on either hand and the fire a long bowshot off: an iron pan on legs on the third dune south of a wreck-post, one old man with a shovel, and a child asleep under a hide. Nobody else. Whoever profits by it is in his bed.
Hunfrith says nothing. He goes back to Saint Josse and sits where he can see the river mouth.
The south sand

At low water the abbess's ship lies on her side a bowshot from the dunes with her planks sprung. Women and children carry bolts of wet cloth up the sand. A man with a bundle of tally sticks stands by an ox cart and cuts a notch for every load.
Adalwin. I keep this strand for Odalric, who holds it of the emperor. You are a trader, by the boat. Good. Then you know what a thing is worth wet.
Everything you see is my lord's by the right of the strand, less the third that goes to those who carry it. I count the two parts. They count the third, and I count it after them.
Three of her men are at the hall, warm and fed, which is more than the sea offered them. Their keep is running. The rest we buried above the tide mark, with a priest. Ask anyone.
It is good cloth. It was good cloth last time. My children have English cloaks now and I pray for whoever wove them.

Fire? The salt pans. People boil brine on this sand when the weather is thick, because thick weather is no use for anything else. If a shipmaster cannot tell a salt pan from Saint Josse, that is a matter between him and his steersman.
Walk round the wreck and look at what is hers
Buy from the steward's cart: six bolts of cloth and two pigs of lead for 60 pennies
Carry a bolt up the sand for the woman, and ask her who keeps the fire

The lead is still in her, forty pigs under the sand, and every pig has a small cross cut in its upper face with a chisel: the minster's. So has the one on the steward's cart. He sees you look and turns it over with his foot. You have seen it both ways up.

Less than half their worth, weighed and paid before witnesses, which on this sand means before the people who carried it. Adalwin cuts a notch for you too. 'Now you have bought of my lord in the open, by day. Remember that you did.' The lead has a small cross cut in it. You are a man who owns that now.

She lets you carry it. 'Old Ragenulf boils salt on the third dune. He boiled it there before any ship came to it. The first one was God's doing, or the master's. After that the steward told him which nights the salt needed boiling.' She takes the bolt back. 'He does not sleep. Ask him yourself, he would thank you for it.'
The lord of the strand
Odalric's hall stands behind the dunes among wind-bent thorn, with a new roof. He has you in at once, and sends for ale, and for the three Englishmen from the byre so that you can see they are whole.
You have come about my guests. Look at them. Fed, dry, a blanket each. I found them naked on my sand and I have had them three weeks. I am told I have a kind heart. It is expensive.
Fifty pennies a head covers their keep and the burying of the others. I do not sell Christians. I am owed for bread. There is a difference, and the emperor's judges know it as well as I do.
I can keep them till Martinmas. After that I cannot feed idle men through a winter, and a dealer comes by on the Amiens road who finds work for such people a long way from the sea.
Eadhelm, of the minster's ship. That is Sigehere, and the boy is Wiga. We ask for nothing but that somebody tells the lady abbess we are above ground.
I light no fires. I am at the palace from Easter to harvest. My people boil salt. If you want to know what my people do at night, you have more leisure than I have.
Pay their keep now: 150 pennies for the three
Give your word to carry the news to their abbess and come back before Martinmas
Ask him by what right, and about the fire on his sand

He has the silver weighed and says it is a pleasure to deal with a man who does not argue about bread. The three walk out of the yard behind you in borrowed shoes. At the first dune the boy starts to run and Eadhelm catches him by the hood. 'Walk. We are guests leaving.'

Odalric says a merchant's word is as good as silver until Martinmas and not a day longer. Eadhelm tells you where to find the lady: at the ship-house at Serrae, or wherever her ships are being counted. The boy asks if you could bring his mother's answer too.

'By the right my father's lord had and his before him. The sea is God's and what it puts down is the land's.' He is not angry. He has given the answer before. About the fire he says what the steward said, in nearly the same words, which tells you who taught whom.
The abbess's ship
In the ship-house at Serrae there are rollers on the floor and no ship on them. The abbess stands where the stem would be. A nun with a wax tablet stands half a pace behind her.
The lady asks: how many living, and their names. Then the lead. Then how you come to know.

My house has had ships free of the king's toll since King Aethelbald's day. The charter says: if she is broken, or worn out with great age, or lost by wreck. Whoever wrote it had seen all three. It does not say: or steered on to a sand by a fire.

When King Offa was alive, King Charles wrote to him that our merchants should have his protection in his kingdom, and that if they were wronged they might go to him or to his judges. Both kings are dead. The letter is not. I have had it copied twice.
The archbishop would be glad to hear I had lost a ship and done nothing. He keeps a list of such things.
The lady has been told that our cloth was sold from a cart on that sand. She does not ask who bought it. She notices who offers to say.
Take her silver for the men's keep, and her sealed complaint for the emperor's judges
Take the sealed complaint and leave her silver in her chest till the men stand here
Say what you bought on the sand, and lay it at her feet

The nun counts out a hundred and eighty pennies, fifty a head and thirty for your wind. The abbess seals a leaf: her complaint, the charter's words and King Charles's. 'The emperor's judges sit at the wic after the feast. Forty days; the toll clerk will know the day. You are my mouth there. Try to be a short one.'

The nun stops counting. The abbess looks at you for the first time. 'Then the minster will owe you. I dislike that less than I expected.' She seals the leaf, and has the nun write an order for four casks of Rhine wine for the altar, at a price a Frisian would be ashamed to ask.

Six bolts and two pigs of lead on the ship-house floor. The nun turns a pig over and finds the cross. The abbess says: 'You bought it in the open, by day, of a man who had it by custom. No court would touch you. And you brought it across the sea to me.' She has your sixty pennies added to the hundred and eighty, and the pig with the cross goes in with the sealed leaf, as a witness that cannot be frightened.
The byre
The three Englishmen are mucking out Odalric's byre. They have been given work, so that it can be said they were given work. The boy has a cough.
The merchant, and before Martinmas. I told my steward you would come. He had a penny on it that you would not.
A hundred and fifty, as we said. I have not added the weeks since, though bread did not stop being eaten.
Master. Whatever you do in there, know this first: the carts were on the sand before we struck. I saw the oxen by the fire's light. Nobody yokes oxen at midnight to boil salt.

I hear a sealed leaf has come over the sea. I have stood before judges with twelve good men at my side who will swear what I swear. How many will swear for you on this shore? Count them on the way home.
Pay the hundred and fifty
Offer a hundred, and argue the rest
Pay nothing yet. Tell him that free men in a byre are a thing judges ask about
Weighed, counted, and a cup of ale on it. The three walk out behind you. Eadhelm does not look back at the byre. Sigehere does, and spits, and Eadhelm tells him to save it for the sea.

You say that three weeks' bread for three men is not fifty pennies a head on any coast you have traded, and that the boy has been worked. Odalric laughs and takes a hundred. 'I am told Frisians count the holes in a net and pay for the string.' The men walk out with you.

He hears you out, takes the hundred, and has the steward cut a tally for seventy more, twenty of it for the insult. 'Your half of the stick. Mine stays here. I shall know where you are when I want it.' The men walk out with you. You owe a lord seventy pennies on a split stick.

Odalric says that is a brave thing to say in a man's own yard and that he will remember the day. Eadhelm, behind him, nods to you once: go on. The boy coughs. Nobody goes with the dealer before Martinmas; that much was promised before witnesses.
What they saw

At Saint Josse the four Englishmen sit along the south wall of the guest hall in the sun, the three from the byre and Hunfrith. They have been comparing what each of them saw, the way a crew does after a bad night.
The carts were on the sand before we struck. Oxen yoked, by the fire. That is not finding. That is waiting.
And the fire was fed with pitch. I smelt it over the water and took it for our own seams. Furze does not smell like that, and brine does not need it.
Ealdred was a careful master. I want that said somewhere it will be heard. He steered for a thing he knew, and somebody had made him a second one.
It is written: cursed be he who makes the blind man lose his way. A master in the murk is a blind man. I have said so to people of that shore in confession, and I may not tell you what they answered.
The boy has a riddle for you, for the bread. It is the one about the thing that fights the wind and the wave and holds fast when it is let alone. Every boy has it. Let him think he is the first.
Take the three home to Serrae in your own boat
Send the three home by the next Kentish keel, and take Hunfrith at your steering oar
Ask all four to wait here and swear to it before the emperor's judges

They come aboard with nothing to stow. Eadhelm takes a rope without being asked and Sigehere finds the bailer. By the time the chalk is in sight you have a good deal more English than you sailed with, most of it about weather. Hunfrith stays: he says he will wait at Saint Josse till the fire is out, one way or another.

Hunfrith says he has no ship, no master, and a lady who will ask him why he is alive. A Frisian boat is small, but it floats. He knows the Kentish sands from the Wantsum to the Dour and now, he says, one more sand than he wanted. The other three sail on a Fordwic keel two days later with a letter from the guest-master.

Eadhelm asks whether a foreign seaman's oath is worth anything in a Frankish court. The guest-master says it is worth what the men who stand beside him are worth, and that he will find out how many of the wic are willing to stand. They will wait. The boy wants to know if he must swear too. 'You must tell the truth,' says Eadhelm. 'It is the same thing, done slower.'
The salt-boiler

After dark a girl of nine or ten finds you on the bank and says her grandfather is behind the boat sheds and will not come nearer the houses. He is an old man with burnt forearms and salt in the cracks of his hands.
Ragenulf. I boil salt on the third dune. I have boiled it there since before your beard. You know what else I do or you would not have come round the sheds.

The first ship was nobody's doing. I was boiling late. She came in on my pan like a moth. In the morning there was wine on the sand, and it was the winter the children were eating bark. I thanked God for it. I did.
Then the steward came and said: on thick nights your salt wants boiling on the seaward face, old man, and it wants pitch. He did not say why. He has never said why. He sends pitch.
The brother at Saint Josse will not loose me while it burns. I have not had the Body of the Lord in two Easters. I am old. I count Easters now.
The steward has sent pitch again. Rhine ships are looked for at the wic, Frisians, deep with wine. The next thick night I am to boil. I am telling you because you carried the Englishman up the bank.
Tell him to do as he is told. You will be out there in the gut, between his fire and the ships
Give him thirty pennies for the winter's bread, and ask him to leave the pan cold
Tell him to boil his salt, and say you will be on the sand in the morning with silver
Not tonight. Tell the girl you will think on it
He nods. 'Then if they hang me they hang me for boiling salt, which is my trade.' The girl will come to the bank at dusk on the night. You are to be at sea before the murk.

He holds the silver as if it were hot. 'A cold pan on a thick night. Adalwin will know by midnight.' He will do it. He says you had better be out there all the same, because the steward has hands of his own and knows where the pitch is kept. And he says that if the judges ever ask, he will tell them who sent it.

He looks at you a long while. 'So. I took you for the other kind.' He goes. Four nights later the murk comes down, and in the morning a Frisian ship is on the second bank with her back broken. You buy three casks off Adalwin's cart for the price of one. Your crew stow them without talking. Nobody mentions how many Frisians came ashore.
The old man is gone from behind the sheds when you look again. The girl says he walks back along the sand in the dark and knows every step of it.
The second ship

The murk came down at dusk, as the girl said it would. You are off the south sand with the tower's fire gone. A fire is burning on the dunes. To seaward, a big hull under a reefed sail is standing in for it, deep in the water.
Frisian by her sail. Deep. That is wine, and a master who has done this run before and thinks he knows where he is.
The old man's pan, on the third dune, burning dirty. He has done as he was told.
The third dune is black. The old man kept his word. That fire is north of it, on the beach itself, and it is burning clean pitch. The steward has lit his own.
She has the length of a psalm before she is on the outer bank. If we show a light she may take us for a third lie. If we do not, she is the fourth ship.
Hold your place in the gut, burn a pitch torch at the masthead and wave her off to seaward
Run down across her bows with a torch and hail her
Anchor in deep water and stand by to take her men off
Let her strike, and be first on the sand in the morning

A light where no light should be, lower than the fire and moving: a careful master does not understand it, and what he does not understand he stands away from. She comes round with her sail slatting, a ship's length from the bank, and you lead her out by the gut's mouth with the torch. At dawn a Frisian the size of a door leans over her rail. 'Liudbrand, of Dorestat. I had that fire for Saint Josse. I had it for Saint Josse.' He sends over two casks and a purse, and says the rest he will say at the wic, before people.

She sees the torch late and puts her helm the wrong way. She takes the outer bank beam on and the mast goes. You work the gut in the dark and take nine men off her quarter two at a time before the tide leaves her, with your own boat pounding. At dawn the carts are on the sand, and nine Frisians are standing in your boat watching them.

You cross her bows close enough to see the lead-line in a man's hand and shout the one word every tongue on this sea has for it: sand. She comes round. At dawn her master leans over the rail, a Frisian the size of a door. 'Liudbrand, of Dorestat. I had that fire for Saint Josse.' Two casks and a purse come over, and the rest, he says, at the wic, before people.

You cross her bows and shout, and she holds on: a small boat with a torch, off a strange shore, at night. Then she strikes. You lose skin and an oar getting alongside, and take nine men off her before the tide leaves her. At dawn the carts are on the sand, and nine Frisians are standing in your boat watching them.

She strikes the outer bank a little after midnight. You hear it. At first light you are alongside before the carts are, and nine men come down a rope into your boat. Her master is the last. He looks at the fire, then at the sand, then at you. 'Liudbrand, of Dorestat. You were lying here. You knew.' You tell him what you knew. He is quiet for some time. 'Then we will talk at the wic.'

She strikes a little after midnight. In the morning you are on the sand before Adalwin's carts, and he laughs out loud when he sees whose boat it is. Four casks for the price of one, 'for a man who rises early'. Your steersman stows them and does not look at you for two days. How many of the Frisians came ashore you do not ask.
The emperor's judges

The emperor's two judges, an abbot and a count, sit on a bench before Saint Peter's with the men of the wic standing round. Odalric is there in his good cloak with twelve neighbours behind him. The toll clerk has the abbess's leaf open and is waiting to be told to read.

The complaint of Cwenthryth, abbess, by her seal. A ship of her minster lost on the strand south of this river. Three of her men held for payment. Her goods carried off. And the words of the lord King Charles to King Offa: that their merchants have our protection, and if wronged may come to us or to our judges.

I took what the sea put on my land, as my lord's father did. I fed three naked men and asked the price of bread. The fire is a salt pan. I will swear it, and here are twelve who will swear I am a man to be believed.

Twelve. And for the abbess, a Frisian with a leaf. The emperor sent us to do right by churches, widows, orphans and strangers, and he did not say it would be easy. Merchant: who stands with you, and what have you seen with your own eyes?
If it comes to it we can put the neighbours on oath ourselves and ask them what burns on that sand. They will say salt. Neighbours do, until somebody they fear less than their lord stands up first.
Call them: the Frisian master whose ship you turned, the English seamen, and the proof of the fire
Lay the abbess's leaf and your own oath before them, and let them weigh it
Not at this sitting. You have not the oaths yet

Liudbrand swears first, in Frisian, with his whole crew behind him, and it takes some time because there are nine of them and the judge lets every man speak. Then the Englishmen: the oxen yoked at midnight, the smell of pitch. Then what you saw. The count asks Odalric's twelve whether any of them will swear that carts wait on that sand by chance. Nobody does. The judgement: the men were never owed for; the worth of the lead and the cloth to the abbess, and a third of it to the one who brought the suit, 'since thirds are the custom of that strand'. No fire on that shore by night from this day but one, on the saint's hill, kept by the brothers at Odalric's cost, under the emperor's ban of sixty shillings. And the stranger who brought it is under the emperor's own protection, 'since he will need it'. Odalric bows to the judges and does not look at you at all.
