You say what you saw and swear to it alone. The abbot asks Odalric whether he will swear that he never took silver for a Christian man. Odalric considers the abbot, and the emperor behind the abbot, and says he would rather make the lady a gift. The men go free without payment; the worth of the lead is paid, and the judges give you a share of it and the emperor's word over your head for bringing a stranger's wrong to them. Nothing is said about the fire. Nothing was proved about it.

You swear alone. Odalric swears with twelve. The count says, not unkindly, that one oath does not outweigh thirteen, and that a salt pan is a salt pan until somebody shows him otherwise. The suit falls. You pay the clerk thirty pennies for the bench. Odalric says, passing, that his table is still open to a man who knows the price of things. The abbess, the skippers and the sand are all still where they were.
The clerk folds the leaf. The judges go on to a quarrel about a mill. They will sit here again in two months, he says, or their successors will; the emperor's justice comes round like the herring.
The ship in her place

The three seamen are home: the boy's mother has him by the ear on the strand and will not let go. In the ship-house the rollers are still empty. The abbess has the old charter out of its box, which the nun says she has not done since the archbishop last asked to see it.
Three men out of nine, and six pilgrims who will see Rome from a better place than this. I have had Masses said. Now the living.
The king's word is that when a ship of mine is lost by wreck, another may stand in her place, free of his toll as she was. It does not say I must build her. It says: another.
The lady knows the ransom came out of your own chest. That is counted first, and separately.
The lady hears that the lord of that sand holds half a stick with your name on it. She says a debt to such a man is paid quickly or not at all, and she would choose quickly.
And the fire burns still. Yes. I am an abbess, not the emperor. I get my men home and I count what is left. That is what there is.
Let your own keel be the ship in her place, free of toll on this strand
Ask for the mastering of the ship she will build, and the right to one like her
Ask nothing. They were seamen on a sand
Not yet. There is still the fire

She has it said on the strand before the toll man and two witnesses: the Frisian's boat is the minster's ship from this day, in the place of the one lost by wreck, and passes free as she did. The toll man repeats it in the voice of a man learning a psalm he dislikes. The nun counts out six hundred and fifty pennies in three bags. On the far shore the fire burns on thick nights, as it did, and masters who know of it stand further off, and those who do not, do not.

'You want oak, then, not parchment.' She is having a coaster laid down on the strand before winter, ten ells longer than your boat, and the wright is to build a second on the same moulds for whoever the minster names. She names you. Six hundred pennies besides. Hunfrith's cousin is cutting the keel scarf already and says it will be a better ship than the last, 'which is not what one says to an abbess'.

The nun writes nothing for a moment, which in her is astonishment. The abbess says that Mercians do not leave a debt lying where the archbishop might find it. Your boat is named the ship in the lost one's place whether you like it or not. Twenty bolts of the minster's cloth come down to the strand on a sledge, and three hundred pennies 'for the wind'. The boy's mother brings a cheese and will not be refused either.
The abbess puts the charter back in its box herself. 'Then come when it is out, or when you are tired. Either is an answer.'
Help in shipwreck
The alehouse is full of shipmasters, Frisian at one end and English at the other, and for once they are sitting at one table. Liudbrand has a small oak box in front of him with nothing in it yet.

This man burned a torch in a gut I would not take a duck through, and I have a ship and forty casks because of it. I have told that at every table from here to the Rhine and I will tell it at Dorestat till they pay me to stop.
I have no ship. I have nine men, and I have them because this one was lying off that sand when he need not have been. A ship can be built. I have told that at every table from here to the Rhine.

The old king's law says we may not swear together. Good. I do not like oaths, they are for people who cannot remember what they said. It also says we may agree to help each other in shipwreck. So: we agree. Nobody swear anything.

Two pennies a keel each time she clears this river. From the box: half a lost hull made good, bread for the men who get ashore, and a boat with a horn at the bar on thick nights, so that nobody steers by fires at all.
And the strand stays the lord's. We do not touch his custom. We only mean to stop feeding it.
Put two hundred pennies in the box, and your name first on the stick
Put your name on the stick and no silver: you have paid in already
A box does not put a fire out. Not yet

Your silver is the first sound the box makes. Then Liudbrand's, then the Kentishmen's, then a Saxon nobody knew was in the room. Nobody swears; everybody drinks, which the law does not forbid. The woman of the house keeps the box and, since she now answers for it, keeps a corner of her store for your goods as well. Each master cuts his marks for the bar on one long stick, and you are given the copy. And the Frisians of Dorestat, who have had Liudbrand's story at every table for a fortnight, send down nine hundred pennies by his hand: 'for the nine', he says, 'or the forty casks. They did not say which.'

Liudbrand says that is fair and the Kentishman says it is Frisian, and both are right. Your notch is cut first all the same. Each master cuts his marks for the bar on one long stick and you are given the copy. Six hundred pennies come down from Dorestat by Liudbrand's hand, from men who have heard his story once too often to send nothing.
Liudbrand shrugs and says the box will be empty a while longer, then, since nobody wants to be the first fool. He will be at the wic till his hull is tight.
The lord's table

Odalric has sent a horse for you. At his table there is roast heron, and wine that came by sea and paid no toll. Adalwin the steward stands behind his lord's bench with his tally sticks, like a man waiting to be asked a sum.
You bought on my sand and did not run to a priest about it. So I can speak plainly, which I enjoy and seldom get to do.
My strand gives me cloth, lead, wine, wax. I am a soldier. I sell it like a soldier, to the first man with a cart, for a third of its worth. You know what things fetch and where.
Three ships in three winters. Sold as my lord sells, four thousand pennies. Sold properly, by a man with a boat and friends at Dorestat, nearer nine.
A third of what you sell for me, and my hand over you from this river to the next. No toll man on my shore will know your name and every one of my men will.
One thing, said once. A man who eats at this table and afterwards goes to the judges is a man my people will not show the gut to on a thick night. I say it now so that it need never be said again.
Take the third, and his hand over you
Sell this year's for him, once, and take silver and no stick
Thank him for the heron, and say you sell only what was bought

Adalwin splits a stick and you take your half. Nine hundred pennies on account, ten bolts of English cloth to begin with, and a man of Odalric's to show you the gut and the wreck-post and which dune not to look at. The three Englishmen, if they are still in the byre, are sent home at the lord's cost: 'a gift to my partner's conscience'. You are a rich man on this coast and a safe one. On thick nights you will know, wherever you are, what is burning.

Odalric says a careful man is a kind of honest man and he will take what he can get. You sell the winter's cloth and lead for him at the wic and up the Rhine for nearly three times what the carts brought, and keep six hundred and fifty. His hand is over you on that shore for it. Adalwin keeps your name on a stick anyway. He says he keeps everybody's.

He is not offended. He says most men find their price at the second asking and he will not ask a second time. The horse takes you back. What you bought on the sand is still yours, and still has a cross cut in it.

The emperor's judges sat at the wic on the Canche and gave judgement for the abbess of Thanet against the lord of the south strand. No fire is to burn on that shore by night but one, on the hill of Saint Josse, kept by the brothers. A Frisian brought the suit.

The lord of the strand south of the Canche has let three English seamen go without payment and made the abbess of Thanet a gift for her lead. Nobody says the judges made him. The judges were sitting at the wic that week.

Three men of the abbess of Thanet's lost ship are home, bought back off a Frankish sand at fifty pennies a head. Masters bound for the Canche are told: the fire you want is the high one. Do not turn in on a low one.

The shipmasters at the wic on the Canche, Frisian and English, have agreed to help each other in shipwreck: two pennies a keel into a box, half a lost hull made good, and a boat with a horn at the bar on thick nights. Nobody swore to it. The law allows that.
Early morning on the river bank at Quentovic, grey and windy: two fishermen carrying a soaked man on a hatch board, his arm locked round it; behind them the long street and a row of beached boats.
Inside a long alehouse by firelight: an old fisherman at the bench end by the door drawing three lines in spilt ale with one finger, a merchant leaning in, other drinkers carefully looking elsewhere.

Night at sea off a low dune coast under thick cloud: a small boat at anchor in the foreground with two men at the rail, a single low fire on the black shore burning unevenly, and far to the north nothing where a steady light ought to be.

A wide grey strand at low water in morning light: a ship on her side with sprung planks, women and children carrying wet bolts of cloth toward the dunes, an ox cart with grey pigs of lead, and a lean man cutting notches in a stick.

A timber hall behind sea dunes with a new thatch: a well-dressed Frankish lord on a bench with an ale cup, three thin English seamen in borrowed tunics standing in a row by the door, a merchant facing them.

Inside a long oak shed open to a chalk strand: empty rollers on the floor, a tall pale abbess in a dark veil with a staff standing where a ship's stem would be, a small nun with a wax tablet behind her, a merchant with a wet cloak before them.
A cattle byre in low autumn light: three thin men with dung forks, one a coughing boy, a Frankish lord in a good cloak at the door with his thumbs in his belt, a merchant holding a purse.

The sunny south wall of a small guest hall inside a fence, dunes and a hill behind: four weathered English seamen on a bench, one a boy, a tonsured monk standing with a pot, a merchant crouched before them listening.
Night behind boat sheds on a river bank, one rushlight: a bent old man with scarred forearms and a girl of ten holding his sleeve, a merchant facing them, the black river behind.

Black night at sea off a dune shore: a small boat with a flaring pitch torch at her masthead in the foreground, a big deep-laden ship under a reefed square sail looming out of the murk, a dirty orange fire low on the land behind.

Open ground before a small stone church on a bright cold day: an abbot and a count on a bench, a clerk with an open leaf, a Frankish lord with twelve men behind him on one side; on the other a merchant, a huge Frisian shipmaster, four English seamen and a grey pig of lead on the ground.

A chalk strand under a high pale sky: a woman holding a thin boy by the ear, two seamen kneeling to an abbess at the doors of a ship-house with a cross over them, a nun reading from a small charter, a little Frisian boat afloat behind.

A crowded alehouse by firelight: Frisian and English shipmasters shoulder to shoulder at one long table, a huge Frisian with a small empty oak box before him, a long tally stick being notched, a woman with a jug watching from the cask.

A lord's table by torchlight in a timber hall: a roast heron, a silver cup, a well-dressed Frankish lord leaning forward with open hands, a lean steward behind him holding a split tally stick out toward a merchant.
The long-haired star
Nobody on the landing is working. There is a star with hair in the evening sky, and a skipper in from London who says he can tell you what it is for.

It stands over the roofs after sunset, a star with a tail like a torch in the wind. It was first seen on the eve of the Greater Litany. Men have stopped pointing at it and started counting the nights.
It shone seven nights from the eve of the Greater Litany and then went. It is weeks gone now and nobody talks of anything else. Every man who saw it has since learned what it meant.
The books call it a comet, the long-haired star. They say it comes for the death of a king. They do not say which king, and this year there is a choice.

King Edward died on the eve of Twelfth Day and was buried in his new church the next morning. Earl Harold was hallowed king the same day, before the candles were out. Quick work, even for the English.
The duke of the Normans says the kingdom was promised to him, and that Harold swore to it on relics. He is not arguing the matter. He is building ships. Rope is very dear at Rouen.
And there is the king of the Norwegians, who has fought everyone from here to the Greeks' city and has an old bargain between dead kings to stand on. He has not said anything. He seldom does first.
Keep clear of the Kentish havens for a month. The king's brother Tostig wintered with the count in Flanders, and he is coming home with ships. He is short of crews, and he is not asking.
Buy the skipper his ale and get all three stories straight, with the names
Give at the church door, as everyone else is doing this week
Stars are the clerk's business. See to the mooring and the cargo

Two pennies of ale buy you three claims to one crown, a warning about the Kentish shore, and a price: rope, sailcloth and pitch will sell at Rouen all summer for half as much again. The star is thrown in free.
Six pennies in the bowl. The crew see it and are easier for it. The beggar at the door says God will remember you, and looks up at the star as if to make sure it heard.
You see to the mooring. The star stays where it is without your help. In all the years of the house nothing in the sky has yet paid a toll or carried a cargo.
Some willingly, some unwillingly
The king's brother has come home from Flanders with a fleet and without the king's leave. His men are going from ship to ship along the haven, and they are not asking for the toll.
Sandwich haven and the channel behind Thanet are full of his sails, Flemish hulls among them. He took money and food on Wight and has burned his way east along the coast since. Now he wants shipmen.
The skipper who talked under the star said this would happen, and when. You paid two pennies for the warning and came here anyway.
Earl Tostig pays a man who comes willingly. A man who has to be fetched comes all the same, and pays his own way. You have a sound ship and a full crew. Which kind are you?
We go north to the Humber, sixty ships. The earl has friends in Lindsey. He says so himself.
I have eleven men and a horn. I blew the horn. There is a creek behind the salt pans where a boat your size could lie four days and see nothing.
The king is in London and ought to hear how many they are and which way they went. I cannot leave. You can. Count them as they pass the point.
Go north with the earl for his pay: sixty ships to the Humber
Slip the mooring on the night ebb and be gone before they reach your berth
Give his man silver to find your ship too small to be worth pressing
Lie quiet with the reeve till the earl sails, then take the count of his ships to the king's men in London

Three weeks. The earl's friends in Lindsey meet him with two earls and an army, and he is driven back to his ships. The shipmen leave him by night, and so do you, with sixty of his pennies and every sandbank of the Humber mouth by heart. He goes on to Scotland with twelve small ships.
No lights, a rag round the oar looms, and the ebb does the rest. By first light the haven is a line of masts astern, and none of them is following.

A guard boat is lying across the channel, and not by chance. You go north with the earl after all, unpaid, and thirty pennies lighter for the trouble you gave. You learn the Humber sands. When the other shipmen leave him, you leave too.
He weighs the purse in his hand and then looks at your ship for some time. He decides she is very small. He is right that it is cheaper than the Humber.

Four days up a creek with the mast down. On the fifth he sails north and you count sixty past the point. At London the king's men have heard it already from three riders. They write your count down anyway, since it is the only one that agrees with itself.
Bread for the ships
The king lies off Wight with more ships and men than any king here has gathered, and every one of them eats. His steward is on the hythe buying corn from anybody who has it.
A ship-force and a land-force greater than any king gathered in this land before. That is how the monks will write it. I write it as loaves, and it comes to a great many.
You are the one who counted Tostig's ships and got the same number twice. The king was told. Sit down.
Thirty loads of wheat landed on this hythe within sixty days. I pay four tenths over the market, in the king's pennies, which are good ones.
You are the Emperor's men. You come in your own ships and the law here holds you as good as a Londoner. King Æthelred's men wrote that down. Nobody has yet written that you will not sell us bread.
I am from Rouen. I sell wine, as my father did, at this same wharf. I also know how to count loaves. Do not look at me like that. Everybody on this river is counting something this summer.
You have counted too: keels on the Seine, yard by yard. The steward does not know that yet. The wine man from Rouen may suspect it.
Take the king's order: thirty loads of wheat landed here, at his price and a good one
Sell him what you counted on the Seine: the duke's keels, by yard and by week
A king's order is paid when the king wins. Decline, civilly
He cuts a tally and you take your half. Thirty loads by sixty days, four tenths over. The wine man from Rouen watches the stick change hands and goes on rinsing a measure.

He hears it through twice and has a clerk put it on wax: how many keels, how far planked, and how many weeks until they can swim. A hundred and twenty pennies. He says the king will want to hear it from the man who saw it.
He nods. He has heard it from better men than you this week, and expects worse before harvest. He goes on to the next ship.
Every hull that floats
Both banks below the bridge are shipyards this year. A clerk with wax tablets comes down your gangplank before the mooring is made fast, and looks at the ship before he looks at you.
I serve the duke's steward. The duke takes every hull that floats, and he pays for it. I am told to say both parts, in that order.
Rope first. Then pitch, sailcloth and iron for rivets. Twenty coils of rope landed here inside sixty days, and I pay six tenths over what the market asks. The market has stopped arguing with me.
These ships were trees at Easter, with the leaves on. Green oak, and split, not sawn. They will swim one summer and cross one sea. Nobody has asked me for more than that.
A hired ship lies with the fleet from the first week of September until the wind serves. It does not leave before the wind does. I say this now so that nobody need say it to you later with a spear.
There is half of a tally stick in your chest for the English king's bread. The clerk has not asked what else you carry, and it would be a poor moment to tell him.
Take his order for rope: twenty coils, landed here, at six tenths over the market
Put the ship at the duke's hire for the crossing: silver now, the rest on the far shore
Sell him nothing. Walk the yards, drink with the wrights and count keels
He writes you down between a man from Caen and a man from Bruges. Twenty coils, sixty days, six tenths over. Rope is rope, he says. It does not know whose anchor it holds.
Two hundred pennies, counted out on your own hatch. She is to be with the fleet in the first week of September, with stalls built for six horses. The rest is to be paid, he says, on the other shore.

The wrights drink like men paid by the keel. By dark you know every yard from the bridge to the bend, how many hulls stand in each and how far planked. They can swim by Lammas. Nobody saw you count, or nobody who was sober.
A sergeant finds you pacing out a slipway. He walks you back to your ship, very politely, and charges twenty pennies for the walk. You have half a count, and half a count is a guess.
Half the levy of the land

Ships have been going north up the sound for nine days, to a gathering in the Solund isles. The king's man on the landing wants two things of a foreign skipper: food, and what he knows of the English rivers.
They go by in tens and twenties, shields inboard and sails patched, farm boats rowing after them with the last sack of meal. Nobody on the landing cheers. They are counting who is aboard.

The king has called out half the levy of the whole land. That is one man in two who can pull an oar, and the ship to put him in. The English earl has promised him friends over there. We will see how many.
We know the sea road. Shetland, Orkney, then down the coast. What we lack is a man who knows the river to York: where the sand lies in the Humber, and how far up the Ouse a long ship floats.
You were in the Humber this spring with the English earl. It is a small sea and men talk. Then you have seen the sands, and you can tell me whether he has any friends there.
If he pays you in the king's pennies, bite one. They are one part silver and two parts kettle. A man who served the king nine years threw his pay on the floor in front of him. Ask for it by weight.
My husband and my eldest are both gone north. Every farm on this sound has sent a man. The king has been at war for thirty years and it has not killed him yet. I say that to myself each night.
Sail with them as a pilot for the Humber and the Ouse, for silver by weight
Sell him ship's bread and stockfish, and argue for weighed silver, not counted pennies
Wish him a fair wind, and keep your keel out of it

A hundred and fifty pennies' weight of hack silver and broken rings, weighed on your own scales. You are to lead the fleet in past the Spurn sands when it comes, in September. You will be at York when the ships are.
He argues for an hour and then sends for the scales. Seventy pennies' weight in cut silver. The farm wife, passing with a pail, does not look at either of you.
He pays in the king's pennies, very new and very many. The farm wife was right. Melted down they are worth twenty-five. You have heard the king has a hard hand. It seems he also has a thin one.
He shrugs and goes back to his tally. With the men gone, the farms will sell their cloth cheap for bread until spring. The farm wife says so herself, and what she will take for it.
The food is gone
The steward has no corn to buy and no silver left to buy it with. The ships have lain off Wight since May. On Our Lady's birthday the men will be let go home, unless somebody feeds them on trust.
The men's food is eaten and no man can keep them there longer. They have reaped nothing at home all summer. The duke has not come. They say he never will, and that their barley is rotting.
Three weeks' bread would hold them past Michaelmas. After Michaelmas nobody crosses that water with horses. I cannot pay you until the king's rents come in. I can only tell you that he pays.
You filled the first order to the day, which is more than my own reeves did. So I ask you before I ask the others.
There is corn on the Rhine. The harvest was good and the barns at Tiel are full. Six hundred pennies down would load our keels, if a house we know goes first. We follow a house we know.
A king's debt is a good debt while there is a king. I have seen four kings of the English in this town. Think about the wind as well. Corn that comes a week late is only corn.
You know what the steward only fears: how many keels the duke has, and that they could swim by Lammas. He has not sailed because the wind has not let him. That is the only reason.
Stake 600 d, and tell him to the keel what the duke has and when it can sail: let the king open the minster barns on that
Stake 600 d of the house's silver on Rhine corn, and every keel of the Emperor's men that will follow you
Put in 150 d with the others, for the ships that are coming home, and promise nothing
No. Men who cannot be fed go home, and that is not a merchant's to mend

You put the silver down and then the count beside it. The steward rides that night. Within the week the bishops' barns in Kent are opened by the king's writ, and eleven keels of the Emperor's men come up the Thames with Rhine wheat. The ships stay off Wight. Whoever writes this year down will have to write it differently.

Nine days. Eleven keels come over from the Rhine mouth with a fair wind, and the corn goes down the river to Wight in the king's own boats. On Our Lady's birthday the men are fed, and they stay. The elder says he has never seen the like, and that he would not do it twice.

The wind sits in the west for eleven days. When the corn comes the ships are already coming up the river, those that are coming, for some were lost on the way. The steward buys it for the city at what the city will pay. You have 380 of your 600 back, and his thanks.

It feeds the crews as they come up the river. On Our Lady's birthday the men were let go home, and the king rode up from the coast. You are paid at Michaelmas with forty pennies over. By then it does not matter to anybody.
On Our Lady's birthday the men were let go home, and the ships were sent up to London. Many were lost before they came there. The steward does not hold it against you. He has no time to.
Waiting for a south wind
The duke's fleet lies in the mouth of the Somme under the abbey of Saint Valery, and the wind has blown from the north for two weeks. A sergeant sends you round to join it, loaded or empty.

The Canche is full of the duke's stragglers. The fleet itself lies a tide to the south, in the Somme. You are sent round, and by evening you are anchored among more ships than you have seen in your life.

The Seine yards are empty and the wrights are drunk. The fleet went up the coast to the Somme a fortnight ago. You are sent after it, and two days later you anchor among more ships than you have seen in your life.
You are on the list: hired at Rouen, two hundred paid. Six horses, and their grooms, who will be sick. Do not let the grooms near the steering oar.

A ship that lies in the duke's water, waiting on the duke's wind, is the duke's ship. He pays for it. Two hundred and fifty to carry six horses over. I would take it. The other way of asking is worse.

We lost ships coming up from the Dives, and the men in them. They buried them at night so the army would not count. The guard boats row the bar from dusk to dawn now. That is for us, not for the English.

The duke has asked for our saint to be carried out of the church and set down on a cloth in the open, where the whole army can kneel. He watches the weathercock on our roof more than he watches the altar. He pays for what his men eat, I will say that.
Nobody here knows that the English ships were not sent home. You know it. You paid for the bread.
Take the horses aboard and cross with the fleet when the wind comes round
Slip out on the night ebb with the count of his ships, and run for the English shore
Sell the camp what it will eat, at the duke's fair price, and be gone before the wind changes

Two days before Michaelmas the weathercock turns. You sail at dusk behind a lantern on the duke's masthead, with six horses stamping on the bottom boards. At the third hour of the day the keel takes the shingle at Pevensey. No English ship is there, and no English spear.

You go out with the ebb, between two guard boats that are shouting at each other. At Dover the reeve pays eighty pennies for the count and sends a rider north with it. The king, he says, is at York, fighting somebody else.

A guard boat lays a grapnel on your quarter before you reach the bar. Sixty pennies for the duke's trouble, and six of his horses in your hold for nothing. You cross with the fleet after all, behind the lantern, with a sergeant sitting on your sea chest.
Sixty pennies, paid at once, by a clerk who writes down everything the army eats. On your way out you count the masts. You lose the count somewhere past six hundred.
The Sunday before the bridge

York has given hostages to the king of the Norwegians and has not been burned. His ships lie ten miles down the Ouse. On the staith a carter is telling anyone who will listen what he saw on the Tadcaster road.

On Saint Matthew's eve the two earls met the Norwegians outside the city, at the ford, and were beaten. Men say you could cross the ditch there on the dead. York has agreed to feed the victor and to march south with him.
You brought them in yourself, past the Spurn sands and up the Ouse as far as a long ship floats. They have been pleased with you ever since. It is not altogether a comfortable thing.

I came by the lanes. The road is shut. King Harold is at Tadcaster with an army I could not see the end of. They stop every man going north, so that nobody runs ahead of them. Nobody here believes me. Do you?
Tomorrow we go to the bridge on the Derwent, to be given the hostages of the whole shire. Two men in three go, and one stays with the ships. It is hot. Nobody wears mail to count hostages.
The English king is in the south, watching the sea for the Bastard. Everybody knows that. He cannot be in two places. Kings cannot. I have served one for twenty years, and he has tried.
You are a foreigner, and you have been among them. I will not say whose man I am. Where do their ships lie, how many stay with them, and where do the rest go tomorrow?
Go down the river to the ships tonight and tell the king's men what the carter saw
Tell the thegn where the ships lie, and that the Northmen go to the bridge tomorrow without their mail
Say nothing to anyone. Shift the berth upriver and keep the hatch shut

They laugh until you name the carter's village and the colour of the banners he saw. Then an old man with a scarred mouth goes to wake the king. By dawn the whole host is going to the bridge, and it is going in its mail. Whatever is written of tomorrow, it will not be that they were taken unawares.

They give you ale and laugh. A Frisian frightened by a carter, they say. On Monday they went to the bridge in their shirts, and King Harold came on them unawares. You told them. You are one of very few men alive who know it.

He listens without moving and gives you sixty pennies from his own purse. On Monday King Harold went through York without stopping and came on them beyond the bridge, unawares. It would have gone so without you, most likely. You will never know.

You lie two bends up the river with the hatch shut. On Monday the army goes through the city, and by evening the news comes back. You sold nothing and you told nobody anything. Both kings would call that wise.
After the battle
The king is dead on a hill above Hastings, and two of his brothers with him. The duke's army has come along the coast taking the harbours one by one, and half of it is now too sick to stand.

Dover gave itself up before it was asked, and was burned anyway, by squires after plunder. The duke has paid for the houses. He has not paid for anything else. The smell from his camp is of sickness, not of fire.
Dover gave itself up and was burned anyway. Sandwich has sent its keys. Here on the Wantsum the ferrymen take pennies from both sides and keep their boats on the Thanet bank at night.

It is the water here, and too much fresh meat. Half the army cannot ride. The duke leaves his sick behind and goes on. I need them carried home, and I need flour, since our bread at least does not kill us.
You carried horses over. I have it written. The duke remembers who carried horses. He is busy just now, and has not yet remembered what he owes for them. Come to London at midwinter.
My husband went with the king and has not come back. They are giving the land to men with other names. I have a boy and a girl, and a cousin at Ganda. I have this brooch. I do not have a fare.
You carried word to the king's men this year, and it was written down. It lies in a chest in London now, with everything else King Harold knew.
Carry the duke's sick over to Normandy, and take his order for flour on the way back
Take the widow and her children over to Flanders, and ask no fare
Buy what the fire and the foragers left: eight bolts of wool cloth for 60 d
Fill the water casks and go. There is no market here this month

A hundred and twenty pennies for a hold full of grey-faced men, who are quiet the whole way over. The order is for twenty loads of flour inside forty days, at six tenths over. The sergeant says again that you should come to London at midwinter.

She sits on the thwart with a child under each arm and does not look back at the land. At Ganda her cousin is on the quay. She has left the brooch on the thwart. The boy asks your steersman what every rope is called.
Eight bolts for sixty pennies, with the smoke still in them. The man who sells them is not the man who wove them. Several people watch you carry them aboard. One of them is the widow.
You water from a spring above the town, well away from the camp, and leave on the ebb. There are places a merchant does no good by staying. This is one of them, this month.
Twenty-four ships
The king of the Norwegians is dead at the bridge, and Earl Tostig with him. What is left of three hundred crews is at the ships, sworn to peace and waiting to be told how many hulls it may take home.

King Harold came on them unawares beyond the bridge, and the fight lasted far into the day. The king's son Olaf and the earl of Orkney have sworn to keep peace with this land for ever. Then King Harold went south in haste.
You brought them up this river. You know which ships these were when they were full. Some of the men at the oars now are boys who were left to mind the kettles.
We came with three hundred ships. The English king has counted us and says twenty-four will carry what is left. He counts well. I have gone over it twice myself and cannot make it more.
There are more hurt men than there are benches to lay them on. I am from the Karmsund. So are nine others who cannot row. We have nothing to pay you with. They took even the rings.
The king had the news at table: the duke has landed in the south, at Pevensey, on Michaelmas eve. He was on the road the same day. I am left here to count ships and see them gone.

There is mail for sale behind the tanners' sheds, and swords, cheap. I have not seen it. Mind that the toll man at your next harbour has not seen it either. They look hard at mail in a merchant's hold.
Take as many of the hurt as the ship will hold home to the Karmsund, for nothing
Buy the dead men's mail and swords from the men who stripped them: 120 d the lot
Leave it. Run south with the news while it is still worth a cup of wine

Ten men on the bottom boards, and a late crossing of the North Sea with the wind rising. One dies off the Naze and is put over the side with a prayer in two tongues. The rest will see the sound. They say very little. One of them asks the name of your house, and says it over twice.
Two mail shirts and four swords for a hundred and twenty pennies, a fifth of what they are worth. One shirt has a hole in it the width of a spear. Somebody on the Karmsund paid a farm for that shirt.

A Humber skipper pays thirty pennies to hear all of it first, with the names. News is the one cargo that takes up no room and spoils fastest. By the time you reach the Thames, the other news will have met it coming north.
The ships that stayed
The king's ships were still at sea at Michaelmas, on your corn. The duke's fleet came over in the dark on a south wind and found them in the way.

This year, two days before Michaelmas, the duke of the Normans put to sea by night with a great fleet. The king's ships met it before the land. Many were sunk, and many were driven ashore. The duke got back to the Somme with what he had left, and the winter shut the sea behind him.
He had a lantern at his masthead, so that his own ships could follow him in the dark. So could we. I never saw a kinder thing done at sea.
Some of them came ashore at Romney with their horses, thinking the rest were behind them. The men of Romney did not wait to ask. I ate your bread all through September, master. It was good bread.

The king himself was not there. He was at York, where he killed the king of the Norwegians at a bridge. He came south in eight days ready to fight a second battle, and found that there was nobody to fight.

The king himself was not there. He was thrown back from a bridge near York by Norwegians who were waiting for him in their mail. He holds the south and the sea. He does not hold York. You had some part in that as well.
Six hundred pennies, on trust, in the one week when nobody would lend the king a loaf. He has not forgotten it. He told me to pay it back three times over, and then to ask what else you want.

There is an old rule an archbishop wrote down in King Æthelred's day. If a merchant throve so that he crossed the wide sea three times at his own cost, he was from then on worthy of a thegn's right. You have crossed it rather more often than that.
Ask what the old law gives a merchant who has crossed the wide sea three times at his own cost: a thegn's right
Ask for ground instead: a hythe of the house's own on the Thames
You brought the count of the duke's keels as well as the corn. Ask for the thegn's right and the king's writ on the toll together

Eighteen hundred pennies, and your name is read out as a thegn's before the king's reeves. A thegn's oath counts for six common men's. A thegn also owes the king a ship and its crew when the fleet is called out. The steward mentions this last, and smiles.

Two thousand pennies, and forty feet of the Thames bank below the bridge, with the right to land there and sell from your own ship. You are no man's lord and no man's thegn. You are a house with a hythe in London. Your first forefather had a boat for four men and a debt.

Twenty-six hundred pennies. A thegn's right, with a thegn's ship to find when the king calls. And a writ with the king's seal hanging from it: this house goes free of toll at London, it and its heirs. The steward says the king laughed, and then had it sealed.
Midwinter at Westminster
On midwinter's day the archbishop of York hallows the duke king in King Edward's new church. From the river you hear a great shout inside it, twice, in two tongues. Then there is smoke.

They asked the English in English and the French in French whether they would have him for king, and both shouted yes. The guard outside took the shouting for treachery and set fire to the houses by the church. He was crowned while they burned. He swore to rule as well as the best kings before him.

He is king as far as the Humber. Beyond it a king of the Norwegians is keeping Yule at York. There are two crowns in this land tonight, and a foreign skipper had a hand in that. Nobody in this church knows his name.
I have you on the list of ships. The king pays what the duke owed. He has also laid a tax on the whole land, to pay it with. You need not mention that on the hythe.

Or the king can give what costs him less than silver. A word over his seal. Or ground, of which there is suddenly a good deal with no man on it. Or a hull: we have more transports than we shall ever load again.

The Emperor's men give two grey cloths and a brown one, ten pounds of pepper, five pairs of gloves and two casks of vinegar, at Christmas and again at Easter. King Æthelred's men wrote it down. A new king, and the same toll.
I know what you carried over, and for whom. So does every man on this hythe. We will go on trading with you. A man has to eat. Do not ask us to drink with you as well.
The cloth you bought in the burned town sold well in the end. Wool does not hold smoke for ever. People hold it rather longer.
Ask for the king's word that your house keeps the law it had in King Edward's day, and goes free of the toll
Ask for a hythe whose owner did not come home from Hastings
Ask for nothing a clerk can write. Take the freight you are owed, and one of the transports he no longer needs

Twelve hundred pennies, and a strip of parchment no longer than your hand: this house is worthy of all the law it was worthy of in King Edward's day, and goes free of toll at London, and every child of it shall be his father's heir. It is in English. The king cannot read it either.

Nine hundred pennies, and forty feet of the Thames bank with another man's mooring posts still in it. His widow lives across the lane. She does not curse you. She looks at the posts each morning, as she always has.

Seven hundred pennies, and a transport of green oak with horse stalls still in her. Pull out the stalls and she will carry twice what your old ship did, for as long as her planks hold. You owe the new king nothing. On the hythe that is noticed.
Yule at York

The king of the Norwegians keeps the feast in York, with Earl Tostig on his left hand. His men went to the bridge in their mail, all of them, because a foreign skipper came down the river on a Sunday night.

This year King Harold came upon the Norwegians beyond the bridge and found them ready. The fight lasted the whole day and neither side held the field. In the night King Harold went back to Tadcaster, for word had come to him that the duke had landed in the south.

He fought the duke nineteen days later, with the men he had left, and was killed. So the duke is hallowed king at Westminster this midwinter, and Harald Sigurd's son sits in York. Neither has yet sent the other a greeting.
I have half a verse for it. 'The ring-giver slept light by the river; a Frisian's tongue was his watch-horn.' The second half wants an English king in it. I have not decided which one.
The king pays you by weight, in rings and cut silver. Not in his pennies. He said that himself, and laughed. It is the only time I have heard him joke about the pennies.
He offers a seat among his guests and his peace on your ships in every harbour he holds. Or ground here on the staith. He does not offer both. He says a man with both would be an earl.

We have had Northmen for kings here before. My grandfather's grandfather buried one. They go to Mass in the end, and their sons speak like us. Mind the king in the south, though. He will hear whose guest you are.
Take a seat among the king's guests, and his peace on your ships in every harbour he holds
Ask for ground on the staith by the Ouse bridge, and no seat at anybody's table
You brought his ships up the river as well as the word. Ask for the seat, the ground and the ring from his arm

Fifteen hundred pennies' weight of silver on your own scales, and a seat on the lower bench at the Yule ale. From the Humber to the Lofoten no king's man of his will lay a hand on your cargo. South of the Humber the other king's men have been told your name.

Thirteen hundred pennies' weight, and thirty feet of the staith below the Ouse bridge, paced out by the king's man in the frost. Frisians had houses in this city three hundred years ago, and left them in one night. It has taken the house a while to come back.

The king looks at you for some time. Then he pulls a gold ring off his own arm and says a pilot who can also hear is worth an earl who can do neither. Twenty-four hundred by weight, the seat, the ground, and the Humber is yours to pilot for good. Earl Tostig does not laugh.
The year written down
Midwinter. Three fleets put to sea this year and two kings are dead. The ship is laid up, the men are paid, and what is left is the reckoning.

On midwinter's day the duke is hallowed king at Westminster. From your mooring you hear a shout across the fields, and then you see smoke: his guard has set fire to the houses by the church. On the hythe the toll is what it was at Michaelmas.

Twenty-four ships came home up the sound, of three hundred that went. On the landing they read out no list. The women counted the ships, then the men in them, and then went home, some one way and some another.

The news comes in by the last ships of the year, in pieces and out of order. A king dead at a bridge. A king dead on a hill. A duke hallowed king at Westminster on midwinter's day. The priest writes it on one line.
I have a loom, six ells of cloth and a share in a boat that nobody is left to row. I do not want pennies. I want meal, and a fair measure. They say you give one.

Nine men are alive on the Karmsund who would not be, if your ship had gone south with the news. It was not good trade. Their king's son knows the name of your house, since one of them said it to him twice.
The Kentish widow is with her cousin at Ganda. Her boy has sent word by a wool skipper. He knows the name of every rope now. He asks whether the house has room for one more.
The mail shirt with the hole in it is still in the hold. Nobody has offered for it. The crew step round it.

You fed no king and carried no king's horses, and you still have a ship. Most years that would be nothing to boast of. This year it is. We keep a seat for a house like that. We also drink a good deal. I say so in fairness.
The monks will give this year a page, and it will be all kings. If you want it written the way your house saw it, with what corn cost and who paid, you will have to pay a priest. I am a priest.

It began with a boat for four men and a debt of two pounds to a count, thirteen days after the heathen men came to Lindisfarne. No king has outlasted the house since. Several have tried to borrow from it.
Have the priest write the year down for the house, plainly, with the prices
Take the seat the elder offers among the sworn merchants, and drink the year out with them
Send word to Olaf, Harald's son: the house that carried his father's men home asks his peace for its ships
The Kentish widow's boy has asked to learn the sea. Take him into the house

Seven hundred pennies clear at the reckoning. The priest writes on one skin: 'This year a star with hair was seen, and three fleets put to sea, and wheat stood at such a price at London.' He leaves the kings to the monks. It is rolled up and put in the chest with the scales, for whoever comes next.

Eight hundred pennies clear, and a seat on the bench. They judge their own quarrels, lend to each other without witnesses, and drink at fixed feasts as if it were a duty. A monk once wrote that they were hard men who feared nothing. They have had it read to them, and are pleased with it.

Nine hundred pennies clear. In spring a man comes down the sound with the young king's word: the house's ships go in his peace wherever he is king, and the sound's own pilots will take them through for nothing. They will call him Olaf the Quiet. He builds a market town, and he never once sends a fleet to England.

Seven hundred pennies clear, and a boy of eleven with a Kentish father's name who is sick for two days and then never again. He has kin at Ganda and kin under the new king's hand in Kent. In ten years the house will be glad of both.

This year King Edward died on the eve of Twelfth Day, and Earl Harold was hallowed king. The duke of the Normans is building ships, and the king of the Norwegians is saying nothing. A star with hair was seen for seven nights.
This year the king's ships were not sent home on Our Lady's birthday, for corn came to them from over the sea. They lie off Wight still.
The duke's fleet lies in the Somme under Saint Valery, more than six hundred sail, waiting on a south wind. The duke pays for what it eats.

This year Harald, king of the Norwegians, and Earl Tostig were killed beyond the bridge on the Derwent, and of three hundred ships twenty-four went home. The duke of the Normans landed at Pevensey on Michaelmas eve.
This year the duke of the Normans put to sea by night, and the king's ships met him. He went back to the Somme with what he had left. Harold is king of the English.
This year King Harold was killed near Hastings, and on midwinter's day William, duke of the Normans, was hallowed king at Westminster by Archbishop Ealdred.
This year Harald, king of the Norwegians, kept Yule at York, and William was hallowed king at Westminster. There are two kings in England.
A landing at dusk in a clear April: every head turned up to a comet with a long tail over thatched roofs; a clerk pointing, a weathered skipper with an ale cup, one deckhand still coiling rope.
A Kentish haven on a bright windy morning, crowded with striped sails: an armed housecarl with one foot on a merchant ship's gunwale, an old reeve with a horn standing useless on the shingle behind.
A London hythe at noon in summer: a tired steward splitting a tally stick over sacks of corn; behind him a Rouen wine merchant rinsing a measure and watching; the timber bridge beyond.
The Seine at Rouen on a hot afternoon: both banks lined with half-planked hulls and men with axes, felled oaks in the mud; a clerk with wax tablets stepping onto the merchant's gangplank.
The Karmsund under a grey summer sky: a line of long ships going north with shields inboard; on the landing a king's man with a tally, and a farm wife with a pail watching one ship.
A London storehouse at evening in late summer, the corn bins empty and swept: the steward with open hands, an old merchant in a grey Frisian cloak counting on his fingers, one candle.
The Somme mouth in rain and a north wind: hundreds of masts at anchor; on the shore monks carrying a reliquary out to a cloth on the grass, an army kneeling, a weathercock on the abbey roof.
The staith at York on a hot Sunday evening: a dusty carter talking with both hands, a Norwegian steersman laughing over an ale bowl, a hooded man listening from a doorway; the minster behind.

Dover in a wet October, burned roofs under the cliff and the old Roman lighthouse above: a widow with two children and a small bundle on the shingle, a Norman sergeant with a list, sick men lying under cloaks.
The Ouse below York on a cold clear morning: a long row of empty long ships on the bank, a few being loaded with wounded men; a survivor on a crutch, an English reeve counting hulls on his fingers.
The Channel at first light after a night fight: English ships under oars among wreckage and swimming horses; one distant ship with a lantern still lit at its masthead, heading away south.

Westminster from the Thames on a midwinter afternoon: the new stone church against a red sky, houses burning beside it, mounted guards in the smoke; a merchant ship moored in the foreground, her crew watching.

A hall in York at Yule by firelight: a very tall grey king on the high seat with an English earl at his left, a skald standing; a foreign skipper on the lower bench with scales and cut silver before him.
A merchant's room at midwinter by one lamp: a ship's sail folded on the rafters, a chest open with a pair of scales in it, a priest writing on a single skin while the master of the house dictates.
A London reeve reading out a merchant's name as a thegn's before the king's men; the merchant in a plain cloak among sacks of corn; ships at anchor on the Thames behind.
A hand holding a strip of parchment the length of a palm, a wax seal hanging from it; behind it, out of focus, mooring posts on the Thames bank and a woman looking at them.
A heavy gold arm ring lying in the pan of a small pair of merchant's scales, the other pan empty; firelight, and the shadow of a very tall man across the table.
The landing on the Karmsund in winter dusk: twenty-four long ships drawn up where three hundred sailed, women standing in a line on the shore; one small merchant ship unloading sacks of meal.
At York the king changes with the season: Olaf of Dublin, Eric son of Harald, or the English king. A safe-conduct there is good only while the king who gave it sits in the hall.
Dublin pays well for wine and for York jet, and sells hides, wool cloaks and captives. The road over the hills from York is its king's road.
Eric son of Harald was driven from York and killed on Stainmore with his son and his brother. King Eadred has the kingdom and Oswulf of Bamburgh is earl. There are no more kings at York.
Eric son of Harald was not killed when York drove him out. He went down the Ouse by night in a merchant's hull, and holds the islands north of the Scots with a fleet.
Olaf of Dublin, called Cuaran, holds York a third time: his ships came up the Humber before the English king's reeves. Eric son of Harald died on Stainmore.
Whose penny
At the landing below the bridge a moneyer's man turns your pennies over on a board. They carry the wrong king. A townsman watches and waits to be asked.
Good silver and the wrong face. I can weigh these or I can strike them. I cannot take them as they are.
At Tanshelf we swore to King Eadred, so it was his penny. Now Eric, Harald's son, is in the hall and I am cutting his name. Ask me again at Martinmas.
Ripon burned this year for the sake of one king, and we paid another to go home. The die on my bench is English again. I keep the old ones oiled.
Olaf is back from Dublin, so it is the knot and the banner. I have struck for him before. My hand knows the way.
A stranger here sells through a townsman or sells to the wind. I have a roof, a yard, and a name the bench knows. My cut is one penny in twelve.
Whose word did you come up the river on? Never mind. A king's word here lasts as long as the king. I have known cheeses that lasted longer.
Have forty pennies struck anew; the moneyer keeps six
Take the townsman's roof and trade through him
Ask who is king, and who was, and say nothing else
Forty pennies go into the pot and thirty-four come back, bright, with this season's king on them. The toll man takes them without biting one.
His name is Ulfketil: a Danish father, an English mother, and a yard behind the landing. Your goods go under his roof and his name goes on your sales.
He tells it on his fingers: Olaf, Olaf, Ragnall, Edmund, Eadred, Eric. He has fingers left, and nobody on the landing thinks he will not need them.
Three doors
Your host walks you through the town before the market opens. He stops three times: at the king's hall, at the minster gate, and at the Dublin ships.
Three doors in this town. Knock at one and the other two hear it. Knock at none and you pay full toll and sleep on your cargo.
The hall. Whoever sits in it wants wine and is short of it. The steward is the one man in there who is never changed.
I have poured for five kings in this hall. A gift laid on the table is remembered by the table, whoever sits at it.
Saint Peter's. The archbishop swore to the English king at Tanshelf and unswore before the hay was in. He is still archbishop. Think about that.
You are the one with the round hull. Sit. In Dublin they give a cow's price for what you sell here at a calf's. I say it for nothing.
Lay a gift of thirty pennies on the hall's table
Drink with the Dublin shipmaster on the landing
Stand witness for your host at the moneyers' bench, and be seen doing it
The steward counts the gift twice and names what the hall will pay for six casks of Rhine wine: half as much again as the market. He sends you off with a riddle the king's men ask over their cups.
Gilli's mother was Irish and the ship was his father's. By the bottom of the jug you know what wine fetches on the Liffey, and he knows your name.
You stand at the bench while his silver is weighed and say aloud what you saw. Four townsmen nod. It is a small thing and they will remember it.
The price of a king
The town owes King Eadred silver for having taken another king. A clerk with a tally goes from hull to hull along the landing, and he has reached yours.
You saw the smoke over Ripon. That was Wilfrid's church. Eadred said he would come back and burn the rest, so the council gave up Eric and promised silver.
This is still Ripon's silver. The year Eadred burned Wilfrid's church we gave up Eric and promised to pay for the wrong. Kings forget oaths. They do not forget a sum.
Every hearth pays, and a hull that has lain here a week is a hearth. I did not make the rule. Fifty pennies is a townsman's share.
The first chest must go down to the king's men on the Humber, and the archbishop's own boat leaks. A hull that carried it would be written down differently.
There is a watch at the bend below the Foss mouth: two men and a boat. They sleep sometimes. I am only telling you where the bend is.
Pay a townsman's share, fifty pennies, though you are no townsman
Drop down the Ouse on the night ebb before he comes back
Offer your hull instead: carry the clerk and the first chest down to the king's men on the Humber
The clerk cuts your notch among the townsmen's, not the strangers'. Ulfketil says nothing about it and pays for the ale.
The ebb takes you past the bend without a sound. In the morning there is a notch against your name on the tally and no silver beside it.
The watch at the bend is awake. You are brought back up on the flood and pay the share, and a fine on top, with the whole landing looking on.
Three days down the Ouse and back, with a clerk who is sick over the side and a chest nobody may sit on. The king's man at the Humber writes down the hull that brought it.
The king with the sandal
Olaf of Dublin sits in the hall again and the Dublin ships lie three deep at the landing. Their shipmaster has more lading than hulls.
Olaf is back. They call him Cuaran, the sandal. Do not ask me why: I have heard four reasons. He was baptised in the south once, and some of it stayed on him.
I have combs and jet for Dublin and no hull to put them in. Carry them round. My partner pays on the plank path, in silver by weight.
And that is Rhine wine under your cover. The hall has drunk nothing but ale since Easter. Name three casks and I will name a price.
Carry for the Dublin men if you like. But this is the second time Olaf has sat in that hall, and I saw how he left it the first time. Quickly.
Take his lading on trust for Dublin: six bundles of combs and two of jet
Sell him three casks of Rhine wine for the hall, at the hall's price
Carry nothing of his, and ask what Dublin buys
Six bundles of antler combs and two of cut jet go under your cover on Gilli's word alone. He tells you the marks for the Liffey mouth, twice over.
Three casks go up to the hall on a sledge. Gilli pays in new pennies with the banner on them, and more of them than the market would have.
Wine, he says, and jet, and salt; and what comes back is hides, cloaks and people. He says the last word the way another man says herring.
The other end of the road
Dublin: wattle houses in fenced plots, a new bank of earth, and pens by the water. A man on the plank path knows whose hull you are before you have made fast.
You see the new bank. The Irish burned us out, not ten winters ago. We learned to dig.
Gilli's bundles? Then you are the round hull from York. Land them on the planks and I will fetch the scales.
It is hides and cloaks this year, and whatever the ships bring back. Come again after a good summer if you want to see the pens full.
The pens are full. Three thousand head came down from Kells, and their cattle with them. I have never seen people so cheap. It will not last: they die, or they are ransomed.
I kept the guest-house at Kells. I can bake, brew and say the psalms. Tell that to whoever buys, so that it is not the quern.
Land Gilli's combs and jet, every bundle
Buy two of the Kells people at the pens, cheap
Buy two and put them ashore at the church up the river
Walk the bank, count the hulls, and eat at his hearth
Every bundle is counted onto the planks. He weighs out silver in cut rings and throws in four hides, because a carrier who arrives is rarer than one who sets out.
Two of the Kells people are led aboard, a man and a boy. They do not look at you. The partner calls it a good price, and it is.
You pay the pen's price and row the two of them up to the church by the ford. The priest writes your name in a book and asks nothing about your friends.
Fenced plots along one street, a hundred hearths, and more hulls on the strand than you count at York. You eat at his fire, and after that the plot knows your face.
Eric, Harald's son
The pennies have a sword on them now. Olaf has gone back over the hills, Eric sits in the hall, and the archbishop has been taken south to the English king's prison.
Count it with me. Olaf out. Eric in. And the archbishop, who had a hand in making both, in the English king's prison. Only the moneyer is where he was.
Your Dublin friend went over the hills with Olaf. He left word that the plot on the Liffey is where it was.
I am Thorgils. I keep the king's ships, and I am taking the names of the hulls on this river. I do not write them. I remember them.
The king's peace costs forty pennies and a handshake. Without it you are a hull I have not met. I meet a great many of those at sea.
They took the archbishop south in fetters. We have a letter for him and no road. A merchant's hull goes where a priest's feet may not.
Give Eric's shipmaster your hand and forty pennies for the king's peace on the river
Take the minster's letter south, for whoever can reach the archbishop
Trade through your host and be nobody's man
Thorgils takes your hand and the silver in the same grip. The toll man is told. So is everyone else: by evening the landing knows whose peace you bought.
The letter is small, sealed twice, and sewn into a strip of calfskin. The priest gives fifteen pennies for the road and does not say who else knows of it.
You sell through Ulfketil and berth below the bridge with the fish boats. Nobody at the hall learns your name. That was the purpose.
What did you see
At London a quiet man in a good cloak has asked the port-reeve which hulls come from the Humber. He sits down on your cargo without being asked.
You come from the Humber. I do not ask what you sold. How many ships lie below the bridge at York, and whose? Who strikes the penny?
The king cannot keep meat down. He sucks the juice and leaves the rest, and still rides. A man like that does not wait long for anything.
You carry something from Saint Peter's. I can see it in how you sit. The archbishop is alive and is fed. More than that I may not say.
They tell me you gave Eric's man your hand. Hands are given. I would sooner know what the other hand is doing.
Give him the minster's letter, sealed, and ask that it reach the archbishop
Tell him what you saw: the hulls, the hall, the mint
Tell him the price of wine at York, and nothing a child could not see
He breaks neither seal and pays forty pennies for the road. His clerk shows you, on the outside, the three Latin words that say whose it is, and how to read them.
You tell him: so many hulls, so many of them long, the sword on the penny, the moneyer's name. He pays in old southern pennies, heavy ones, and forgets to thank you.
You talk of wine until he stands up. At the gangplank he says the north is dry of it this year, as if he owed you something for your time.
The rock
Below the rock of Bamburgh the high-reeve himself comes down to the beach to look at a York hull. He asks about the wine first, and then about the king.
My fathers held this rock before there were kings at York of any tongue. We will hold it after. What is in the casks?
A king who leaves York for the western sea rides by Stainmore. There is no other road for horses. Olaf's people have used it like a street.
I pay for one thing: the week the hall empties, and whether he rides or sails. A hundred pennies now. More after, from a grateful man.
You have Eric's peace on your hull. Good. Then nobody at York will wonder why you sit so near his hall.
Take his silver and agree to send word when the hall empties
Sell him what you carry and promise nothing
Hear him out, refuse the silver, and remember every word
A hundred pennies, counted by his own steward. He names a fisherman at the Tees mouth who will carry three words north faster than a horse.
He buys at a good price and does not raise the other matter again. He does not need to. You know now what is wanted, and by whom.
You push the purse back across the cask head. He looks at you a while, and then at your hull, as a man looks at a field he may buy later.
Whose men are we
Evening on the Ouse. The men have counted three kinds of penny in their pay, and the steersman has been sent aft to ask what it means.
Raven, banner, sword, and two with the English king's name. That was one week's pay. The men ask which of them will buy bread next year.
I am not asking for them. I am asking for me. When the shouting starts on this river, which bank do we row for?
They saw you give the Norwegian your hand. Half of them think that makes us safe. The other half can count kings.
And there was the purse at Bamburgh. I did not see it. I heard it when we pushed off, and so did the lookout.
Tell them all of it: whose silver you took and whose you did not
Count out twenty pennies of good weight and say the rest is your worry
Say a merchant has no king, and send him forward
You tell it in order and leave nothing out. Nobody speaks. Then the oldest hand laughs, and the steersman says the worst is known now and can be steered round.
Twenty pennies, all English, all heavy. The men bite them from habit. The question is not asked again that month.
He goes forward. The talk under the awning stops when you pass, and starts again behind you.
The hall empties
The lawmen have met without the king. By evening everyone on the landing knows it: Eric is to go, and he means to ride west over the moor with his son and his brother.
The lawmen sat this morning, the four of them, and nobody sent to the hall. That is how a king hears it here: by not being asked.
The king rides west by the moor with his son and his brother, and takes Dublin's road in spite of Dublin. The ships go round to meet him.
I need the river clear for three nights, and every round hull out of my way. Yours I would sooner have beside me than behind me.
You know something Thorgils does not: at Bamburgh a man has paid to learn the day and the road.
Keep your boat on her ropes. They will count heads this week. Be one of the heads, not one of the hulls.
Tell Thorgils the moor road is sold, and offer your hull down the Ouse by night
Send Oswulf his word: by the moor, with few men
Send to the Dublin men over the hills: the hall is empty, come before the English king's reeves
Keep the boat moored and stand with your host when the lawmen count heads

No sail, the oars wrapped, the ebb under you. A big man sits on your cargo with a boy beside him and says nothing from the bridge to the Humber. His ships are waiting at the river mouth. On Stainmore, men wait for nobody.

The townsmen have boats chained across the bend. You are turned back and fined on the landing, and the steersman has a cut scalp for his trouble. In the morning the hall is empty: he has taken the moor road.
Three words go to the fisherman at the Tees mouth. You sell that week as in any other, and you do not go near the western gate.
A rider goes over the hills with Gilli's token and a tally of what you have seen: the hall empty, the English reeves not yet come. Whatever comes of it, the English king will hear who sent.
You stand in Ulfketil's yard among his neighbours when the lawmen's man comes round, and you are counted with them. The boat does not move for a week.
No more kings
Eric is dead on Stainmore with his son and his brother. An English reeve sits in the hall, an earl from Bamburgh is over the land, and the moneyer is cutting a new die.
This year the Northumbrians expelled Eric; and King Edred took to the government of the Northumbrians.
On Stainmore, in the empty part. A man called Maccus, Olaf's son, did the killing. The earl at Bamburgh did the knowing. The son and the brother lie with him.
Thorgils was not on the moor. He was at the Humber with the ships, cursing a chain of boats. He asked for you before he sailed, and not in anger.
The archbishop is out of prison and has a bishop's seat again: at Dorchester, far to the south. They freed the man and kept the archbishop.
There are no kings here now. There is the king. His peace is given by hand, and whoever breaks it pays more than you will see in your life.
Earl Oswulf sends a purse and his seal for a hull he names. He says you will know what for. I have not asked.
Take what the earl sends for the word you sent: silver, and his seal on the river toll
Ask the reeve for the king's peace, given by hand, on your hull and your sales
Ask nobody for anything: buy what a fallen hall sells cheap, and keep what the river has taught you

Sixteen hundred pennies, and the earl's seal on your freedom from the river toll. Ulfketil pays what he owes you that week, in full, and does not ask you in. In the Norse harbours it will be known who sold the moor road.

The reeve takes your hand before witnesses. Your hull and your sales are in the king's peace at York, free of his toll. Eight hundred pennies of old debts are paid you by men who were waiting to see who won.

The hall's goods go cheap on the landing: silk, swords, a king's bedding. You buy and sell before the price finds its feet. After these years you know every bank and shoal between the bridge and the sea.
The town keeps its own
Eric is dead on the moor and an English reeve sits in the hall. In your host's yard the men who counted heads that week are counting something else, and they have kept a place for you.
This year also Archbishop Wulfstan received a bishopric again at Dorchester.
We counted every man who stood in this yard that week and moved no hull for any king. It was not many. It was enough to be asked what the town wants.
I have cut dies for Olaf, for Eric and for Eadred, some of them twice. This one I may be let finish. A town with one penny can sell to anybody.
The plot beside mine has no heir: its man rode west with Eric. The fence line is older than my father, and the neighbours would sooner have you than a reeve's cousin.
The minster knows who carried its letter when nobody else would. The archbishop is at Dorchester now, but his clerks are here, and clerks write things down.
Take the long plot beside his, and a seat among the men who witness sales
Take your share in silver, the seat, and his son to keep your goods here while you sail
Take the plot, and ask that the minster name you as the man who carried its letter

The fence is walked and the bounds are said aloud. Fifteen hundred pennies come to you as your share of what the yard sold while others ran. You have ground at York, a seat at the bench, and an order for ten casks.

Ulfketil's son can count, keeps his mouth shut, and is tired of his father's yard. Your goods lie under his key from now on. Eighteen hundred pennies, and a seat at the bench whenever you are in the town.
The plot is yours, and in the minster's book you are named as its man on the river. A clerk reads you the entry and makes you read it back until you can. Twelve hundred pennies besides.
A king without a town
A warship with a striped sail lies off the landing, and the man who steps ashore is one you last saw in the dark on the Ouse. He has been asking for your hull in every harbour.
Round hull. I have asked for you in six harbours. The king says a debt left unpaid goes bad like fish.
He is in the islands north of the Scots, with forty ships and no town. He says it suits him better. Towns have lawmen.
York took the English king the week we left. There is an earl now, and a penny with no sword on it.
The man at Bamburgh had riders on the moor for nine days, waiting for us. He knows whose hull we went down the river in. Stay off his beach.
Take the king's gift: a sea-going trader from his fleet, and silver to fit her
Take the arm-ring off his own arm, and the rest by weight
Ask for less silver and one thing more: that his ships let your hulls pass, and your heirs'
She lies astern of the warship: deep, broad, built to cross open sea. Taken or bought, he does not say. Nine hundred pennies to fit her out. Thorgils puts the steering oar in your hand himself.

The ring is twisted gold, as thick as a thumb, still warm from another man's arm. The rest is cut silver weighed on your own scales: eighteen hundred pennies' worth. Your grandchildren will be told where it came from.

Thorgils cuts a mark in your stem-post with his knife. Any ship of Eric's, or of his sons', that sees it will let you pass. Seven hundred pennies besides: he says the king thought you would ask for more.
One kindred, two towns
The Dublin ships came up the Humber nine days before the English king's reeves. Olaf sits in the hall at York a third time, and Gilli has been looking for you with a tally in his belt.
Nine days. We were up the Humber nine days before the English reeves, because a rider came over the hills with my token. Lawmen like a king who is there.
Eric? Dead on Stainmore. He met a son of Olaf on our road. I was not there and neither was the king, and that is what we both say.
A third time, the same Olaf. The moneyer did not even cut a new die. I do not say it will last. I say the hides are coming over the hills again.
The English king knows your hull now. He is sick and he has a long memory. Do your trading in the south under another man's name.
Swear fellowship with Gilli: one purse, his boat on the western sea and yours on the eastern
Ask the king for ground at York and freedom from his toll there
Take your share by weight, and a man on the plot at Dublin to keep your goods
You swear it on his ring and your scales: one purse, the losses halved, his boat west of the hills and yours east. Nine hundred pennies are your share of this year already.
Olaf gives ground at York the way he took the town: quickly. A plot by the river, and his word to the toll man. Seven hundred pennies besides. The word lasts as long as he does.
Thirteen hundred pennies' weight in cut silver, and from now on the man on the plank path keeps a locked chest for you by the Liffey.

The river landing at York below a timber bridge, grey morning: a moneyer in a leather apron turns silver pennies on a board; the merchant stands by his round-hulled boat; a townsman in a Danish cloak leans on a post, watching.
A York street of wattle houses at first light, the host pointing three ways: a long timber hall with carved door-posts, the stone minster behind old Roman wall, and lean Dublin ships at the landing.
The landing under a low autumn sky, a smear of smoke far to the north-west: a tonsured clerk with a tally stick and an iron-bound chest stands at the merchant's gangplank; townsmen queue with purses.

Dublin ships three deep at the York landing on a bright windy day, a banner with a three-cornered knot over the hall behind; a lean shipmaster with red-brown hair counts bundles of antler combs on the planks.

Dublin from the strand, a wet evening: fenced plots of low wattle houses, a raw earthen bank, a plank path; in front a wattle pen with people sitting in it, a woman looking straight out; ships drawn up on the mud.

The York landing in hard noon light: a broad Norwegian in a mail shirt, hands empty, looks along the row of moored hulls; behind him a longship with shields on the rail; a priest waits in a doorway with a small sewn packet.

A quay inside London's old Roman river wall, evening: a quiet man in a fine dark cloak with a silver pin sits on a wine cask in the merchant's boat; the merchant stands; a reeve looks away on the quay.

The beach under the rock of Bamburgh, the timber hall and palisade high above, cold clear morning: a tall lord in a red cloak with a gold-hilted sword looks into the beached boat; a steward holds a purse.

The boat moored on the Ouse at dusk, the awning half rigged, York's roofs and hall dark behind: the steersman stands aft with an open hand full of mixed pennies; the crew watch from forward, faces in shadow.

The king's hall at York in a summer dusk, doors open and nobody at them, saddled horses in the yard; on the landing in front, the Norwegian shipmaster and the host stand either side of the merchant, one pointing down river, one at the mooring ropes.

A bare moor road under heavy cloud with a stone cross stump and riderless horses, seen as if remembered; in front, at York, a moneyer cuts a new die at his bench while an English reeve holds out his open hand.

A long fenced plot at York running down to the river, late summer sun: townsmen walk its bounds with hazel rods, the host and the moneyer in front, the merchant between them; an empty hall roof beyond the fences.

A northern harbour in clear cold light: a warship with a red-and-white striped sail lies off; on the landing the Norwegian shipmaster holds out a twisted gold arm-ring; behind him a deep broad trading ship rides at a rope.

Lean ships crowding the Ouse below York bridge at sunrise, the knot banner over the hall again; on the landing the Dublin shipmaster grips the merchant's forearm over a pair of scales; pack-horses with hides come in at the western gate.
The reckoning
The cargo is sold. The mate speaks for the men: they want what the tally says they are owed.
Evening at a mooring: the mate stands in the boat holding out a notched tally stick; three men sit on the thwarts behind him, not looking at the merchant; a small iron-bound chest on the stern board.
Thirty pennies are cut on the tally stick by the mast, a penny a man for every four days.
The cargo is sold and the silver is in the chest, where the men can hear it. They ask for their share now, before the alehouse asks for it.
They know about the Wōkerer. They say he has a full plate, and they have an oar each.
Count it out on the thwart (30 d)
Half now, the rest at the next landing (15 d)
Open a cask of the cargo's ale tonight; silver at the next sale
Ask them to wait
Thirty pennies go round in fours and fives. The mate cuts the tally stick across and throws the old half over the side. Nobody says thank you. It was owed.
Fifteen pennies. The mate splits the tally down its length and gives you one half, with the notches still owed. He keeps the other.
The cask is empty by the time the fires ashore go out. In the morning the tally stick has the same notches on it, and everyone aboard can count.
The mate nods and goes forward. You do not hear what he says to them. You hear what they do not say back.
The promise
You promised the men their pay at the next landing. This is the next landing.
A quay in the morning: the mate holds up his half of a split tally stick beside the merchant's half; the notches match.
You said the next landing. This is a landing.
I can see the chest as well as you can. Tell me what I am to tell them.
Pay what was promised (20 d)
Cut a bolt of the cargo's cloth among them: worth more than they are owed
Tell them there is nothing yet
